item.title: Lex. Boots buyout proves old age can be an asset on the UK high street
item.description: A pivot to beauty products has helped. Its next opportunity may lie in offering more services, such as in-store health checks
item.content:encoded:
A pivot to beauty products has helped. Its next opportunity may lie in offering more services, such as in-store health checks

By all rights, Boots should no longer exist. The UK retailer is 177 years old, and has spent decades fighting to keep its footing on a high street that has seen waves of new challengers and technological threats, killing off countless other retailers. Yet this week the UK chain was bought by Canada’s Weston family for a respectable $8.9bn, suggesting it has a reasonable future ahead of it.

It’s worth pondering how Boots has managed to survive, and why it might even thrive. One thing that sets it apart from other retailers is its pharmacy licence, and its ability to get customers who come in for prescriptions to buy other things too.

True, this cross-selling has taken various forms: in the 1980s, Boots stretched into other kinds of retail, buying the parent of bike and car parts maker Halfords. At one point it was selling everything from video cameras to toasters. Supermarkets eventually muscled in on that business, but Boots was saved by a pivot to beauty products. By the mid nineties, non-prescription sales were roughly 85 per cent of revenue, according to archived annual reports.

Boots is now more reliant on its health division than it was. And beauty and wellness are a growing trend: LVMH-owned Sephora, for instance, has increased revenue at an annual rate of 14 per cent over the past five years. Boots has managed about half that pace. Its next opportunity may lie in offering more services, as well as products, such as in-store makeovers and health checks.

For retailers, old age actually appears to confer some advantages — such as a general sense of affection from customers. It’s rare to find companies as venerable as Boots: fewer than 1 per cent of the active businesses registered with Companies House are over a century old, but a disproportionate share of them are in consumer businesses like retail, leisure and hospitality. Other centenarians include Twinings Tea and fashion brands Barbour and Burberry.

This is analogous to the so-called Lindy effect, named after a New York delicatessen, which theorises that the longer something has existed, the longer it might survive. But there are examples to the contrary too. Department store Debenhams survived the Napoleonic Wars but was doomed by private equity ownership that stripped away its assets and left the retailer saddled with onerous lease liabilities. It closed its final UK stores in 2021.

That points to the third reason for optimism: the Westons, who say they want to improve Boots “for generations to come”, can take a long-term view on the business without the pressures of private investors or public markets. Having come this far, perhaps Boots will see in its third century too.

gaia.freydefont@ft.com

item.title: Big Tech sets out its pitches on AI agents
item.author: Richard Waters
item.description: Race to develop new services has moved into high gear with a series of launches
item.content:encoded:
Race to develop new services has moved into high gear with a series of launches

Richard Waters

In the years before the iPhone, there was general agreement in the tech world that mobile access to the internet would be the next big thing. But it took many false starts, from Windows Mobile to Nokia’s Symbian operating system, before Apple showed the way, in the process resetting the direction for much of the tech industry.

Something similar seems to be happening now with the development of AI agents. Many tech leaders believe software that can take actions on your behalf, removing the drudgery of routine work and personal tasks, represents a huge opportunity. Exactly what form this will take, however, is less clear. The rewards for finding the right formula are likely to be huge: personal agents could become a new entry point to the digital world and turn their makers into the next gatekeepers.

So far these include Muse from Meta and dots from OpenAI, while Microsoft has revamped its Copilot assistant to act more autonomously, Apple added agentic features to its Siri assistant in its latest iOSG and Google launched a new work assistant in Gemini. Several start-ups are also angling for attention, most notably Instinct, which launched an invitation-only test over the summer.

The contrast between Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s dots shows how far apart the agent visions are. Both feature cute, personalisable mascots and come from companies with a large number of consumer users, but their intentions could hardly be more different.

Meta pitched its agent as a tool for handling day-to-day tasks of all kinds. By contrast, OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman brushed such things off as almost beneath his company’s interest, dwelling instead on the kind of complex work tasks you would normally give to a “high-agency engineer or chief of staff”. Other companies’ agents generally fall somewhere in between. 

To some extent, the positioning appears to be as much a reflection of the business models of the companies concerned as a sign of where agentic AI is likely to have its most immediate impact.

For Muse, that means extending Meta’s advertising business into taking a cut from transactions its agent instigates, making itself more central to ecommerce. It may be a difficult evolution. At the moment, about two-thirds of travel, commerce and reservation sites on the internet block Muse in some way according to analysts at Jefferies, putting pressure on Meta to forge more direct links with individual sites. As these links harden into commercial deals and traffic is steered inside a new ecommerce ecosystem, the buying habits of billions of people could be at stake.

OpenAI, by contrast, hopes to monetise the more intensive use of its work agents through high-priced subscriptions, with dots at first available only to customers on ChatGPT subscription plans of at least $100 a month.

Regardless of positioning, all face the same challenge of persuading billions of people to learn entirely new digital habits. Central to that will be instilling trust. As Microsoft showed two years ago, when an AI feature designed to remember everything a user did on their PC provoked a privacy outcry, powerful new capabilities need to be handled with care.

Central to the question of product design is the extent to which companies need to display the capabilities of their new agents, rather than just leaving people to find their own way. Muse takes the hand-holding approach, peppering users with suggestions of things to do, while OpenAI maintains more of a blank canvas. Microsoft’s latest Copilot offers a choice between three different tabs, including a new Autopilot mode for agents that can take on longer work tasks.

Behind the issue of design lies a deeper question: will people want a single, infinitely malleable personal agent to handle everything they do, or will they turn to more specialised agents, many of them embedded in different applications? For now, many companies are hedging their bets. Walmart has its own shopping agent, called Sparky, but has also allied itself with Meta to make it easier for Muse users to browse its site. Amazon, by contrast, blocks agents from Anthropic, OpenAI and Meta, at least for now.

A world of specialists, or one agent to rule them all? The latter would confer huge power on the companies involved, particularly if it led to the sort of market concentration already seen in search, social networking and ecommerce. But any company aspiring to achieve that will first have to find the right formula to cause billions of people to transform their digital behaviour. 

richard.waters@ft.com

item.title: Repeated US Treasury interventions risk an erosion of credibility
item.author: Mohamed El-Erian
item.description: A key policy tool to stabilise stress in markets could turn into a source of moral hazard and deeper volatility
item.content:encoded:
A key policy tool to stabilise stress in markets could turn into a source of moral hazard and deeper volatility

Mohamed El-Erian

The writer is the Rene M Kern professor of practice at Wharton School, chief economic adviser at Allianz and chair of Gramercy Funds Management

For much of the past year, both the real economy and financial markets have operated under the expanding shadow of US economic statecraft.

This has ranged from more aggressive industrial policy to tariff escalation and export restrictions as well as expanding moral suasion. As a result, resource allocation and price discovery in markets have increasingly drifted from commercial and economic logic, influenced more by geopolitics, national security and domestic political expediency.

One of the most striking features of this geoeconomic era is the US Treasury department’s growing willingness to intervene directly in financial market pricing. One such intervention, aimed at stabilising the Argentine peso, achieved its objective. A second, intended to suppress long-term Treasury yields and damp bond market volatility, has stumbled. The jury is out on a third initiative to bolster the Japanese yen.

Taken together, these three examples provide critical lessons on when unconventional direct market intervention can succeed — and importantly when the credibility of this tool can be eroded.

In Argentina, a depreciating peso fuelled domestic inflation and undermined support for President Javier Milei ahead of key elections. The US Treasury stepped in by providing a dollar swap line — an agreement to exchange currencies — to a strong ally of President Donald Trump.

Framed by Treasury secretary Scott Bessent as an effort to contain regional systemic risk, markets saw the move more as a political lifeline. The intervention succeeded. The peso stabilised and inflation dynamics moderated. The success was aided by the fact that the Argentine foreign exchange market is small and Milei’s policy stance is generally supportive of the currency.

A subsequent attempt by the US Treasury to manage domestic sovereign yields has proved far less effective. Reacting to a sharp rise in yields, Bessent announced that the Treasury would step up its buyback programme for long-dated bonds and consider other measures, if needed. The rationale was to smooth out “disorderly” moves during illiquid summer conditions. Many market participants, however, viewed it as an attempt to suppress mortgage rates ahead of the US midterm elections. Over the weeks that followed, yields across the curve continued to surge, rising about 0.5 percentage points.

The US Treasury market is immense, globally integrated, and driven by powerful structural dynamics that cannot easily be overcome. They include rising government bond issuance to fund a fiscal deficit of 6 per cent of GDP, the refinancing of maturing debt at much higher rates, and heavy corporate borrowing to fund tech-related investments. This is occurring as demand from some historically reliable buyers is diminishing.

The experience in the currency markets with the Japanese yen falls between these two extremes. The intervention was framed as mitigating global financial instability and protecting US trade from an excessively cheap currency. Yet markets quickly recognised another motive: the need to minimise the risk of higher US yields from Japan’s sales of Treasuries as it sought to raise dollars to defend the yen. While the yen initially appreciated, it has slipped back since. Unsurprisingly, the tactical intervention has struggled to overcome fundamental issues in Tokyo’s monetary, fiscal and structural policy mix.

When asked in an Axios interview about the interventions, Bessent declared: “The house doesn’t win every hand. The house plays percentages.” This referenced his earlier claim — “I am the house now” — evoking the casino saying that the house always comes out ahead. Viewing sovereign market interventions through the lens of a casino operator risks misdiagnosing the factors at play. The power of policymaker interventions in pricing depends largely on market size and the state of the underlying fundamentals.

Market intervention is meant to be a “circuit breaker” to interrupt non-fundamental, self-reinforcing market dynamics or severe liquidity stress. When deployed sparingly during genuine dislocations, it carries immense signal value and potency. But when used repeatedly to try to counter underlying market fundamentals, achieve short-term political objectives, or manage prices in deep, liquid global asset classes, its effectiveness can diminish. Using it as a routine policy lever rather than an emergency safety valve risks turning a market stabiliser into a source of moral hazard and deeper volatility.

item.title: The UK cannot afford to waste its DeepMind dividend
item.author: John Thornhill
item.description: A shortage of domestic capital and the lure of the US threaten the benefits of Britain’s biggest AI research success
item.content:encoded:
A shortage of domestic capital and the lure of the US threaten the benefits of Britain’s biggest AI research success

John Thornhill

Bizarrely, one of the most energising things happening in Britain right now was barely mentioned during party conference season. Nor is it much discussed by institutional investors. Despite the ambient indifference of Westminster and the City, Britain has built the world’s third-strongest innovation economy over the past 15 years. And now a new generation of entrepreneurs is busily launching scores of ambitious AI-enabled start-ups. 

The latest ranking, published last week by Sifted, the FT-backed media group that I co-founded, shows that 32 per cent of the 250 fastest-growing, early-stage start-ups across Europe are from the UK. They follow previous cohorts of venture capital-backed British companies that are growing robustly. Silicon Valley is not the only place to play the VC game. On some measures, the pooled returns of British VC firms, investing between 2020 and 2024, outstrip those generated over the same period by their US peers, according to the British Business Bank.

Given how fast technology is evolving, the next 12 to 18 months may be critical for determining whether these British start-ups flourish or fade. The hope is that some can seize the moment, diffuse the benefits of AI across different industries, revitalise the British economy and emerge as global players. Fast-growing London AI start-ups, such as Wayve, ElevenLabs, Synthesia, CuspAI and PhysicsX, are already promising to transform industries as varied as autonomous driving, audio and video generation, material science and engineering.

But the risk is that another wave of the country’s most ambitious entrepreneurs will decamp to the US. Faced with rising taxes and energy costs at home, they may prefer to join the west coast’s AI-driven gold rush.

Much of the credit for turning London into a global AI hotspot goes to Sir Demis Hassabis, the Nobel Prize-winning co-founder of Google DeepMind. Founded in 2010, DeepMind rapidly became the leading AI research company, attracting talent from around the world. 

Massive injections of capital, computing power and data, following the company’s acquisition by Google in 2014, enabled DeepMind to pioneer some of the machine learning techniques powering the latest AI surge. But Google is increasingly shifting its AI focus back to California, triggering a series of departures from DeepMind in London. 

What happens to these alumni may be one of the most important strategic issues facing the country. Zeki, which tracks AI researchers, has found that DeepMind remains a big talent magnet in Europe. But more researchers have left to join rivals Anthropic and OpenAI than the other way around.

Hassabis, who remains chair of Google DeepMind, is also chief executive of its London-based spinout Isomorphic Labs, which has raised $600mn to accelerate drug discovery. Several other former DeepMind researchers have launched labs. 

Most notably, David Silver has founded Ineffable Intelligence, which has raised a record $1bn seed round to explore ways of reaching “superintelligence”. DeepMind’s former principal scientist Tim Rocktäschel has co-founded Recursive Superintelligence, raising more than $500mn. DeepMind alumni are also behind three other ventures: Emulate, Revolution Labs and Metis Reasoning. 

“I think this is a great moment for London. There is a lot of very interesting . . . activity across a wide spectrum of ideas,” says one former DeepMind researcher working on a new start-up. “The DeepMind dividend is incredible.”

Some of these start-up founders complain that non-compete clauses make it harder for them to hire from big US tech companies. But the government is working “extremely rapidly” on a solution, Kanishka Narayan, Britain’s AI minister, said last week. He has also promised the government will place more contracts with UK start-ups.

The lack of domestic growth capital is another industry bugbear. Behind the scenes, successive governments have helped improve financial support systems, says Saul Klein, chair of the investment group Phoenix Court. The British Business Bank has been expanded, local pension funds are being consolidated and 17 fund managers have pledged to increase domestic private-market investment.

But, to date, domestic capital is only trickling in. It mystifies Klein why US, Canadian, Japanese and Singaporean investors are more enthusiastic backers of Britain’s young companies than the country’s own institutional funds. An obvious investment opportunity lies under their own noses. It would be tragic for Britain if they fail to act.

john.thornhill@ft.com

item.title: Cyber war won’t be the same in the age of AI
item.author: Ahana Datta Fasel
item.description: The old Russian maskirovka doctrine doesn’t apply when non-human agents create uncertainty for both attackers and defenders
item.content:encoded:
The old Russian maskirovka doctrine doesn’t apply when non-human agents create uncertainty for both attackers and defenders

Ahana Datta Fasel

The writer is the author of Full Stack Spies: Cyber Espionage in the Age of US–China Competition

Last month, the Australian government revealed that AI agents had breached its healthcare systems. A fortnight earlier, Anthropic reported that Russian cyber actors were using AI to perform reconnaissance, hacking and data theft more cheaply and efficiently. These and dozens of other cyber attacks are not yet fully autonomous, but they are beginning to show the cost of delegating control to machines.

For human defenders, autonomous cyber attacks are a perfect storm, clouding an attacker’s intent and complicating the task of holding a human “hand on the keyboard” accountable. But using AI also creates uncertainty for the attacker. The AI will adapt its behaviour based on what it encounters — networks, defences and opportunities — deciding for itself how to pursue a human-provided objective. This behaviour may not always be predictable, and soon may not always be controllable.

Moscow has a tradition of exploiting uncertainty. In 1918, Russian military thinkers incorporated surveillance evasion lessons from the first world war into the broader concept of maskirovka. Deception creates uncertainty in an adversary’s mind about intent and capabilities, delaying, confusing and constraining its response. A century later, this strategy often appears in Russia-linked cyber operations.

Historically, deception was an adversarial act: one side deliberately created uncertainty for the other. But autonomous systems introduce uncertainty in both directions — and not necessarily intentionally. A defender must account for the future behaviour of an autonomous system; an attacker has to weigh the risks of losing control over how a defender might interpret its behaviour.

Maskirovka sought to weaponise uncertainty to exploit a basic logic of deterrence: an adversary is less likely to act when it believes the cost of doing so, including the risk of retaliation, will outweigh the gains. That is no longer a clean calculation. Today, uncertainty can change the willingness to act on both sides. For the attacker, the loss of control has become part of the calculation. A misinterpretation can make escalation harder to contain.

What sort of state (or AI lab) might wish to take that risk? An actor seeking a tightly controlled outcome may not want to offload consequential decisions. But one that values adaptive and persistent access to networks may be willing to accept uncertainty, despite the risk of unintended consequences. Likewise, one with its back to the wall may seek to create room to manoeuvre.

Criminal and state-backed actors are now showing a willingness to trade control for capability, whether for espionage or ransomware. The more autonomy is delegated to AI systems, the harder it may become for defenders to distinguish a machine’s unintended action from escalation and for attackers to control the consequences. Deterrence today must target this trade-off.

Imagine a scenario like the recent cyber attacks on the French defence industry or Polish power grid, but where the operator sets an objective instead of dictating every step. In one network, the AI steals credentials and collects information. In another, it finds a connected system and probes it to help preserve access. A defender watching the second operation cannot see the original instruction, only hostile actors moving deeper into its network. The defender must decide: is this espionage, preparation for sabotage or something else? What is the appropriate response?

The value of deception lies not in hiding the truth indefinitely, but in doing so long enough to compress a defender’s decision-making window. Introducing autonomous systems into the mix changes the old bargain. The deceiver can no longer be certain that the ambiguity it creates will remain on the other side. In a crisis, that could leave both sides scrambling to respond to an action whose meaning neither can discern.

item.title: On the LLMternet, nobody cares you’re a plant
item.author: Louis Ashworth
item.description: Are reccs set to get wrecked?
item.content:encoded:
Are reccs set to get wrecked?

Louis Ashworth

Jerry is an insurance comparison company based in Palo Alto, California. The company, which has “truth seeking” as its first brand value, is currently hiring for a copywriter. Here’s the job description:

Redditors can smell a corporate ad from a mile away and will downvote low-effort marketing into oblivion. But when someone breaks down how car insurance premiums are actually calculated, or writes a step-by-step guide on negotiating a used car purchase, r/personalfinance and r/whatcarshouldibuy pay attention.

We need a Reddit Copywriter who lives and breathes textual storytelling. You won’t be writing marketing copy—you’ll be writing high-value, educational, human text posts that turn complex financial and automotive topics into top-voted Reddit threads. You know how to capture sub-culture tone, write hooky titles, and turn technical jargon into clear, engageable prose.

The list of qualities the ideal applicant will “own” include a “[m]astery of Reddit voice” and the ability to:

Write comprehensive, search-optimized Reddit copy designed to index well on Google search and serve as cited reference material for AI models.

We wrote earlier this year about the challenges facing Reddit — at its best, a decent platform for esoteric discussion — as the remorseless logic of capitalism enshittifies its content, corrupts its communities and feasts on the goo inside.

As home to an immense corpus of ranked written language, Reddit is a popular resource for LLMs. As a question-and-answer-friendly space, it’s a popular resource for people seeking product recommendations. And as both of those things, it’s a great place for astroturf marketing, the kind of thing being described in that Jerry job ad.

As we wrote back in April:

The proliferation of generated search summaries means that for users who — quite reasonably — just want to know what’s a good, inexpensive [kettle/time of year to visit Canada/haircare routine] in this crazy world can now get that information from Reddit without even the small step of actually going on Reddit.

We should note that this isn’t new. Marketers have probably been manipulating Reddit since Reddit first became Reddit, and shilling has probably been around since crowds became crowds.

But LLM dynamics mean it’s probably going to get a lot worse. Here’s the précis of a UBS note published on Monday:

Generative AI is emerging as a new gateway for product discovery, potentially influencing where consumers shop before they visit a retailer’s website, open an app, or enter a store. We conducted [a] study to assess which retailers AI platforms recommend across common shopping occasions and what those recommendations reveal about competitive positioning, brand authority, and digital discoverability.

Author Michael Lasser has run the numbers across the major LLMs for recommendations in New York, New Jersey and Minnesota. The winners are . . . incumbents:

[…] AI models consistently gravitate toward scale, value, convenience, and brand familiarity.

Across the grocery, general merchandise, warehouse club, sporting goods, and household essentials categories, the largest and most established retailers captured a disproportionate share of recommendations. Based on the citation tracker, Walmart had the highest number of both “Top Choice” mentions and “Total Mentions,” with Costco ranking second. This is a meaningful finding because it suggests the models are not simply generating random responses but are converging around a relatively small group of retailers that have established strong consumer awareness and clear value propositions.

Walmart, Lasser found, appears to be the “default answer” for most questions about everyday consumption you can throw at an LLM — meaning America’s biggest retailer is poised to benefit if handing off your shopping decisions to an agent does end up becoming common practice. Costco and Aldi also scored highly on value.

Notably, these are all well-established brick-and-mortar retailers:

Predominantly online retailers surfaced far less frequently than many investors might expect. Despite the rapid growth of e-commerce and the increasing influence of digital shopping, the AI models overwhelmingly favored retailers with large physical footprints, established store networks, and broad consumer awareness. Amazon appeared less dominant than anticipated, and many online-only or predominantly online retailers were largely absent from the top recommendations. This suggests that AI systems currently place significant weight on retailers that combine price, convenience, assortment, and physical accessibility.

A common feature of AI search winners was “[f]requent third-party references validating their strengths”. As Lasser notes:

The implication is that recommendation share could become a new indicator of competitive advantage. Retailers that are consistently surfaced by AI may receive incremental consideration from consumers, while retailers that fail to appear could face a subtle but meaningful headwind over time.

Finally, one of the most notable aspects of the analysis is that the models generally reinforced existing industry leadership rather than producing random or unpredictable outcomes . . . 

This suggests that generative AI is currently acting more as an amplifier of existing competitive advantages than as a disruptor of them . . . 

The companies that succeed may not necessarily be those with the largest digital businesses, but rather those that become the default answer when consumers ask AI where they should shop.

All of which is a roundabout way of saying that manipulating neutral-seeming information sources is going to become even more important to advertisers. And right now Reddit is the neutral-seeming information source. If you think the well is already poisoned, you ain’t seen nothing yet.

Further reading:
— Reddit may need to sell its soul for scale

item.title: Badenoch’s punchy plan to reunite the right
item.author: Robert Shrimsley
item.description: It was just a speech, but the Tory leader’s rejection of Reform reveals a new and determined strategy
item.content:encoded:
It was just a speech, but the Tory leader’s rejection of Reform reveals a new and determined strategy

Robert Shrimsley

Tough on Reform. Tough on the causes of Reform. After two years of self-doubt, of fighting for survival, of the drumbeat of demands for a deal with Nigel Farage to “unite the right”, Kemi Badenoch’s Conservative Party has come up with its own strategy to do so. Take Reform on and clobber it. 

Just articulating the idea immediately points to the scale of the challenge. For all its issues and scandals, Reform still leads the Conservatives in most polls. It is winning council seats across the country while the Tory activist base is being hollowed out. Farage’s party may be in what he admits is a trough but it is not about to disappear. 

But what Badenoch’s conference speech, policy announcements and other recent attacks on her rightwing challenger show is that after a year of timorous efforts to out-Farage Farage, she has taken both the strategic decision to turn her fire on Reform and the emotional step of believing it can work. 

It will take a lot more than one speech to a conference few were watching. But recent months have seen Badenoch growing in confidence in her attacks on Reform. In her visible contempt for its leaders she shows there can be no accommodation with their rule-breaking instincts and toxic grievance culture. This instinct also offers Tory strategists a possible path towards their central challenge of winning back lost voters on both left and right. 

For while Badenoch has gained confidence and popularity, the Tories have not. This gap was glaringly obvious at the conference. Badenoch was like a human lightbulb. But the energy she brought to a room faded as soon as she left.

The muted conference had an unreal air of optimism. “Economic reality is coming for Andy Burnham,” said one shadow minister. “Reform is busted,” said a financial backer. Tax and the economy would pull back the self-interested Lib Dem voters, said a strategist. 

Maybe so, but as Badenoch says about Burnham, “hope is not a strategy”. Even if Reform support fell back to the level at the last election, that 14 per cent is more than enough to split the vote on the right and give the election to Labour. Burnham is a visibly superior political operator to Starmer. And Labour will use fear of Reform to depress the Tory vote, talking up the prospects of a deal that could put Farage into office. 

After this week, Badenoch’s strategy is clear. First, on the causes of Reform. She draws a distinction between the scandal-hit, financially questionable leadership and its voters. By siding with those who want far stricter immigration controls, repatriation of criminals and unauthorised migrants, more vigorous policing and a huge expansion of prison places, Badenoch’s Tories have an offer for those drawn to Reform. 

Next, the economy. Burnham’s drift left has opened a political space. Badenoch pledges a growth agenda built around lower taxes, spending cuts and deregulation. There are still gaps, not least excluding the possibility of closer ties with the EU. Her commitment to savings is undermined by opposing Burnham’s plan to reshape the triple lock for pensioners. But the broad bet is that as voters tire of a sluggish economy and higher taxes they will grant the Tories another look. Meanwhile, her headline policies like scrapping inheritance tax on family homes show her aiming squarely at more affluent voters. 

Were this the entire platform, it would fall short. Values and identities still matter too much. But by attacking Farage’s party in terms that rule out any alliance this week, she placed the Tories among the anti-Reform camp. Her gutsy, sincere and correct denunciation of those who question the Englishness of non-whites — her mixed-race children included — sent lost moderates the reassuring signal they need. This means she must now do better at policing the tone of Reform-adjacent frontbenchers. 

Finally, if those reclaimed liberal-minded Tories help her get ahead of Reform, she can win back the transactional voters who switched to Farage as Labour’s main electoral opponent. Crucially, Badenoch has seen the road back lies first in reclaiming the centre right.

Well that’s the theory. There are a lot of ifs in there. There may be a “Keminaissance” at Westminster but the party remains deeply distrusted. It is not clear voters are ready to listen. It would be an achievement just to secure clear primacy on the right. Even if Reform support plummets, Farage is a fierce fighter and has a hard core of support which may now be entrenched. Lost Remainers may demand more than not being Farage — Badenoch’s own uncompromising instincts may push them away. Meanwhile, she is relying on the economy to defeat Burnham.

But the Tories can only challenge Labour if they first see off Reform: Badenoch’s speech shows she accepts that reality. She is now secure enough to follow through. Farage’s failure to broaden his appeal, retreating to his hardline base, has gifted the opportunity. If the right cannot be united by alliance and Reform’s leader has hit the limits of his appeal, the only way left to rebuild the bloc is under the Tories. The odds are against her and such tactics have failed elsewhere but under our electoral system she can fall back on one other argument — that Reform cannot win.

So far this is just a speech and a plan. But for the first time since its defeat in 2024, her party has found two things it lacked: a plausible strategy and the backbone to fight Farage. As she might say, it’s the right direction.

robert.shrimsley@ft.com

item.title: Irate farmers should not limit the EU’s geopolitical ambitions
item.author: Alan Beattie
item.description: Resistance to Ukraine’s agricultural exports is undermining the bloc’s influence
item.content:encoded:
Resistance to Ukraine’s agricultural exports is undermining the bloc’s influence

Alan Beattie

If the EU wants to get geopolitical, Ukraine is its chance to prove it. A European country invaded by its belligerent neighbour is desperate to anchor itself in the EU sphere of influence. The shortage of grain consequent to the Russian invasion is driving up global food prices. The EU could expand its reach, show that bloc membership means security as well as prosperity and help head off the threat of widespread hunger in developing countries. But standing in its way is the most consistent block on EU reform down the decades: its recalcitrant farmers.

For months after the US started attacking Iran in February, the widely feared increase in global food prices largely failed to arrive. But they have risen sharply since July, as they did after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Russian and Ukrainian attacks on each other’s Black Sea shipping have reduced world food supply: the two account for about a quarter of global wheat exports.

Ukrainian grain is stuck inside the country and on railways to the Black Sea ports. Alternative road and rail routes go through Poland and Romania, but those governments are refusing to expedite Ukraine’s exports, citing their own farmers’ interests. They claim supply routes are at full capacity, but it seems unlikely they are acting in good faith. 

In 2023, Poland, Hungary and Slovakia essentially went rogue and declared that they would simply ignore EU rules and block food imports from Ukraine, claiming they would leak into local markets and undercut their farmers. Poland went so far as to threaten to cut off military help to Ukraine.

There is something of an irony here. The EU has traditionally exercised soft power through trade and diplomacy much better than hard power through defence and security. In the early 2010s, it sought to bring Ukraine into its orbit with a trade agreement offering generous market access — but without the military assistance that might have deterred Vladimir Putin from annexing Crimea.

By contrast, EU member states and the Commission have substantially taken on the burden of financing the Ukrainian military after the US withdrew, but have found it politically hard to offer access to the EU market. Their difficulties have clear implications for Ukraine’s accession to the EU, which started just after the 2022 Russian invasion and which its government says is critical to the country’s security. 

The Commission now suggests restricting some access for Ukraine to the EU’s food markets and farm subsidies even after accession and potentially indefinitely. It’s only a proposal at this stage, but an extraordinary signal nonetheless. The EU promises it will help Ukrainian exporters regain access to their traditional third-country markets, but it is not taking the chance to display that political will right now. Raising the stakes, Ukraine says it cannot join the EU if such restrictions are in place.

Agriculture is one of the EU’s most important areas of intervention: about a third of its permanent budget is agriculture, and it retains high World Trade Organization tariffs and other trade barriers for some sensitive products. Creating a halfway house for Ukraine doesn’t suggest confidence in accession as one of the bloc’s most reliable means of extending influence. Absorbing a country like Ukraine may take a lot of adjustment by EU farmers — and almost certainly more public spending to aid the process — but if the EU can’t take unprecedented action when a bordering country is threatened with obliteration then it’s not a geopolitical power. 

The Ukrainians argue that keeping the country’s exports going both now and after it joins will help the EU build the geoeconomic clout it wants. “It is important for the EU that Ukraine keeps exporting to third markets — the country feeds more than 400mn people globally and is a key contributor to global food security,” Oleksandra Avramenko, head of the EU accession committee for Ukraine’s agribusiness association, told me.

“Keeping Ukrainian products competitive on these markets will also help the EU maintain its soft power against producers like Russia, which wants to use food as a weapon,” she said. Avramenko also notes that there are certain long-term import needs, such as Italy buying durum wheat to make pasta, that Ukraine might be able to help supply. It’s a plausible pitch, but it’s not making any headway in the EU at the moment.

It was always going to be hard to absorb Ukraine into the EU. A relatively impoverished and corrupt country with a population bigger than all but five EU countries and super-competitive agricultural exports inevitably sets multiple alarm bells ringing across existing member states. But on trade and the single market, the official attitude is reactive rather than proactive. Geopolitical power begins at home, and the EU has so far failed to come up with a convincing strategy to project it beyond its existing borders.

item.title: France’s far right goes woke. Or is it neoliberal?
item.author: Martin Sandbu
item.description: Marine Le Pen gives a cognitive dissonance-inducing economic speech
item.content:encoded:
Marine Le Pen gives a cognitive dissonance-inducing economic speech

Martin Sandbu

Who had on their bingo card that Marine Le Pen, leader of France’s far-right populist party and the frontrunner for next year’s presidential elections, would call for new pan-European taxes? Or commit to reaching net zero before 2050 (“an ethical and economic imperative”)? Or that her party would claim financial markets lower the borrowing costs of the French state whenever she appears in “the Anglo-Saxon press”? Me neither. So here are some reflections on the weirdly through-the-looking-glass economic speech Le Pen made on Tuesday.

The Rassemblement National (National Rally), Le Pen’s party, has manoeuvred towards claiming the mantle of fiscal responsibility for some time — at least since before the latest accusations of youthful antisemitism by Jordan Bardella, the party’s number two. So, presumably, the move was not motivated just by a desire to change the conversation. Instead, it fits with Le Pen’s long agenda of “de-demonising” the party founded by her father, who was never shy about his rightwing extremism.

Still, anyone who has followed populist politics over the past decade or four could suffer a real hit of cognitive dissonance listening to her speech (video recording here). A central part of the proposal is a referendum on a “golden rule” that would make it impossible for the legislature to pass a budget with a deficit that exceeded the level compatible with shrinking the public debt-to-GDP ratio. That level would be calculated by independent experts.

As presented by Le Pen in an op-ed last week, the rule would demand fiscal consolidation by 0.5 per cent of GDP each year until the ratio came down to 60 per cent. Those parameters could well have been designed to match closely what a group of elite economists set out as necessary earlier this year. (More on this from Ben Hall.)

This is very much not what we are used to calling a populist economic policy offering. Of course, it’s wrapped in the predictable railing against elites who have betrayed the people by governing the country badly. And the goal of fiscal consolidation is presented, in good populist fashion, as recovering lost national sovereignty (fair enough, if you think of sovereignty as freedom of action). But the content of the plan looks, let’s admit it, serious. The numbers add up.

That is not saying it’s credible, in the sense that it is going to happen. Le Pen and her sidekick also presented their “counter-budget” and longer-term plans for actually meeting the golden rule (and then some, she claimed). Here the old populism briefly reared its ugly head: savings will be made by spending less on immigrants! But the RN says much more can be found from reorganising the state administration. That is standard centre-right fare, and not exactly wrong: the French state certainly has bloat that good policy would reduce. But, of course, promises to find “efficiencies” in the state administration of prosperous countries often fail, either by not finding much to cut, or by actually ruining the state’s ability to do the things it has to do.

But the point here is that the plan is non-credible in the ways all politicians are non-credible. In electoral contests, they overpromise; in the dilemmas of governing, they underdeliver. Unlike what we should often fear from the far right, these are not the sort of flaws that undermine the republic or overturn liberal democracy. If France’s populist right has turned into just an ordinary flawed political force, playing within the rules, we should sit up and notice, especially given what some other movements from that end of the political spectrum are up to elsewhere in Europe, let alone across the Atlantic.

The surprises don’t end there. There is a mix of ideas here, some legitimate, some silly, some unrealistic. But they are not, in many cases, what we expect from this wing of the European populists. For example, Le Pen wants a rebate on France’s contributions to the EU budget. Good luck, you have the right to try of course. More interesting is the endorsement of a harmonised pan-EU tobacco tax to be paid straight to the EU. With Eurosceptics like these, who needs euro-enthusiasts?

On domestic policy, there is the usual red meat (a flat tax on incomes, lower taxes on fuel and energy) but also the complete opposite (subsidies for clean cars). There is also the good idea of cutting taxes on production — ie business taxes that just add to costs rather than being assessed on profits. (On this particular issue, Le Pen beats the European Commission for economic competence — Brussels is doubling down on its idea of a lump-sum tax on big corporations).

I was particularly interested in two policy proposals involving the European Central Bank. Le Pen’s opposite number on the populist left, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has infamously said the ECB should cancel the French bonds it holds from its asset purchases. Le Pen professes the orthodoxy that honouring the public debt is a moral duty. But she calls for the ECB to intervene to bring down state borrowing costs.

There are two ways of reading this. One is as a standard populist and irresponsible call for something — monetary deficit financing — that would end in tears, and in any case be illegal under the EU treaties. Another is that Le Pen is signalling that she would not see it as a subjection of French sovereignty to the globalist overlords if the ECB were to implement its “transmission protection instrument” even though this would come with strict conditions on national fiscal policy. Her choice of words, I think, suggests a positioning to be able to play by the European rules (the italics are mine):

It is indispensable to enter a discussion with the ECB so it can intervene to lighten the burden of yields. From the moment France takes back control, the ECB must intervene so Eurozone countries achieve financial room for manoeuvre to invest in our sovereignty, defence and technological catch-up.

And immediately after these words, she goes positively woke:

The ECB must also fully accomplish its mandate to help states finance the energy transition and respect the Paris agreements. We are accumulating an ecological debt that is much more perilous than any financial debt, because it puts in danger our survival in dignified living conditions. Climate warming itself has inflationary consequences. Helping to finance hundreds of billions in necessary investments for decarbonisation is an ethical and economic imperative. By granting financing at low rates to every serious structural project, without fraud or conflict of interest, that allows realising carbon neutrality, the ECB will be within its mandate.

To top it off, she says she wants to reach net zero before 2050.

This policy — to use a dual-rate system to boost green transition investments — is heterodox, to be sure, and has so far been associated with the progressive left. It is also a good idea (as I have explained before), and has been mentioned as a possibility by several ECB board members.

The bigger point, however, is that by embracing activist policy for a green industrial transformation, Le Pen sounds greener than the 2019 vintage of European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen.

How to make sense of this?

One possibility is that ahead of next year’s presidential election, Le Pen judges that she has cemented her support among the third or so of French voters who have committed to her, are protest voters or who were previously disengaged — so the challenge is not to lose the next 25 per cent who would take her over the top. A bold commitment to fiscal rectitude is a pitch to the conventional centre-right — and leaves its native candidates on the back foot. Either they match her rule (and look like copycats while granting her leadership on the issue) or they don’t (and leave her as the sole fiscal responsibility candidate).

Another (compatible) possibility is that she now realises she is sufficiently likely to win this thing and that it’s time to turn her mind to how she will govern. The dog will have caught the car — and then what will it do? If so, this is about building a mandate for policies that may be necessary in order not to be the plaything of events.

Of course, it could be that this is all pretence, and that if the RN wins, the de-demonisation and pitch for responsibility will evaporate and the old nasty party will show its true nature. There are many in France who fear this. So I accept that it is wishful thinking to expect that we just may be seeing the civilising force of liberal democracy, through which the prospect of real power can domesticate (or alternatively destroy) fringe, protest and anti-system parties, as we have seen in the Nordics, Italy and elsewhere. It may even demonstrate the force structurante of the EU — that maligned, over-democratic bureaucracy with too many veto players, but which in the end is a sovereignty enhancer for each of its member states.

As I said, wishful thinking, but wishful thinking could turn out to be true. If it is, we should recognise the achievement of European democracy, and grudging congratulations will be in order all round.

Other readables

● In my latest FT column, I write that France’s sabotage of EU sanctions policy last month undermines its call for strategic autonomy.

● Philip Augar is right to say lenders protest too much about possible taxation or lower interest on their central bank reserves.

● While European leaders panic about Chinese exports, one German car company is happy to invest at home. Perhaps what some call “China shock 2.0” is just a Schumpeterian structural transformation after all?

● Too much eschatology!

item.title: Kemi Badenoch’s speech drew a moral dividing line between Tories and Reform
item.author: Stephen Bush
item.description: Opposition leader’s remarks will help distance her party from unpopular views on Englishness and court professional voters
item.content:encoded:
Opposition leader’s remarks will help distance her party from unpopular views on Englishness and court professional voters

Stephen Bush

Good morning. Kemi Badenoch made a major announcement on reforming inheritance tax in order to exempt family homes in her speech yesterday. But the most significant thing she did, in my view, was for the first time draw an explicit dividing line between the Conservatives and Reform UK. Some thoughts on that below.

Clear red line

The most important section in Badenoch’s speech directly addressed those in her own party calling to “unite the right” by reaching some kind of merger or alliance with Reform:

To those who say unite the right, we are not uniting with that.

People deserve better than that and we are going to give them better than that.

Character, conduct and standards matter.

I don’t want to live in a country run by people who threaten journalists, call veterans “traitors” and debate whether my mixed-race children are English.

I don’t want to explain to my son when we’re watching our brilliant England team play football that some people don’t think our black players are English.

I remember back in the day when Ian Wright and John Barnes were playing, nobody was questioning whether they were English.

We certainly didn’t have sitting MPs questioning whether they were English.

We must not let these people take us backwards.

That is not the country we are.

Reform MPs are openly questioning people’s identity.

They are not like us; we are not like them.

“They are not like us; we are not like them” is a sentiment that some senior Conservatives who are no longer on the frontline, such as John Major in his excellent speech earlier this year, have made publicly. Moreover, it is easy to hear this sentiment expressed privately, that the differences between the Conservatives and Reform are not differences of opinion of the normal kind that separate Labour, the Liberal Democrats and the Conservatives.

Rishi Sunak took on the growing debate about this in his Sunday Times column:

 We cannot have a situation where people who live here, who feel British, who embrace our culture and embody our values, who strive to be the best members of society they can be, are marked down because you won’t find their name in the Domesday Book.

Tactically, strategically and morally it is the right thing for Badenoch to have done.

Tactically, the Conservatives need to have an argument against Reform and parties yet further to their right that resonates. That senior members of Reform are now regularly suggesting that Sunak, Meera Syal, Bukayo Saka or Lenny Henry cannot really be English is something most people do not agree with and frankly makes them sound mad. It is simply good politics to point out that the Conservative Party does not believe mad, unpopular things and that Reform does.

Strategically, while an awful lot about the next general election is hard to predict, I think it is safe to say that one attack line that will get a lot of play against the Tory party, from both the Lib Dems and Labour, is that a vote for the Conservatives risks letting Reform into power by the back door. “Don’t go to bed with Badenoch because you’ll wake up with Nigel Farage” could be really destructive to the Tories’ prospects.

It has not been helpful to the Conservatives that for much of the past two years, Tory frontbenchers have sounded as if they regard Reform as a lost sibling, that these extreme and corrosive positions about national belonging are ones they might themselves give house room to, and that their biggest underlying philosophical objection to Reform might be a difference of opinion on benefits spending. It was not good politics for Badenoch to stay silent when others on the right — including a man whose podcast she appeared on — argued that Sunak could not be English because he was a “brown Hindu”.

Remaining silent would have made it harder for the Conservatives to attract the professional voters they are courting with their plans to expand free childcare or cut inheritance tax. No viable Tory party can go into an election without a serious financial offer to workers at the top of the income distribution. But these offers are much less likely to win votes if people fear the party selling them is indifferent or actively hostile to them and their interests.

Most importantly, it was the right moral position to have drawn a clear red line on these topics. It was not a speech without risks because, having drawn a line, Badenoch will now have to police it. But it gives her party something it badly needed: a differentiator between it and Reform that is clear, popular and right.

Now try this

I’ve just finished Dark Reading Matter, the last in Jasper Fforde’s Thursday Next series, a genre-bending collection about a detective agency inside fiction. This final instalment really is terrific: it leans heavily on both the fourth wall and the readers’ goodwill to carry off twists and turns, with some great jokes along the way. A really well put-together ending: new readers should give his first book, The Eyre Affair, a go as a starting point.

Top stories today

  • Budget blow | The Iran war has blown a near-£12bn hole in Britain’s public finances, according to FT estimates, piling pressure on John Healey.
  • ‘Europe’s Silicon Valley’ | Andy Burnham’s government is promising to push on with linking up Oxford and Cambridge, as the prime minister seeks to reassure investors.
  • ‘Shared prosperity’ | Burnham will today hold talks in Berlin with Friedrich Merz, as he seeks to rebuild ties with the EU.

item.title: Tips and Linkers
item.author: Hakyung Kim
item.description: Not as safe as they seem
item.content:encoded:
Not as safe as they seem

Hakyung Kim

Good morning. The price of five-year credit default swaps on SpaceX debt jumped to 194 basis points yesterday after our colleagues reported the AI-slash-rocket maker is trying to raise another $40bn in debt to buy Nvidia’s chips. The costs for other Big Tech companies’ CDSs have risen to near-record highs in the past few weeks. Investors prudently taking out a little insurance, or speculators sensing blood in the water? Email us: unhedged@ft.com.

Tips

The yields on Treasury inflation-protected securities look attractive right now. Five, 10 and 30-year Tips yields are 2.6, 2.9 and 3.4 per cent, respectively, the highest since the financial crisis. If held to maturity, those are compelling yields, especially if you think inflation is set to rise further.

Larry Kotlikoff, of Boston University and the Economics Matters Substack, argues there’s a strong case for Tips right now:

To me, Tips dominate nominal Treasuries. They have the same default risk . . . and, given survey data, the same expected real return. But Tips come with seemingly free insurance against a massive risk — another major bout of inflation . . . A strategy of buying and holding, through maturity, a portfolio of Tips — building a Tips ladder — appears the safest way to secure one’s retirement.

If that seems a bit too good to be true, it is. Tips compensate investors for realised inflation, as measured by the consumer price index. But vanilla nominal Treasury rates change with moves in expected (that is, break-even) inflation, along with moves in underlying real rates. So for Tips to outperform vanilla Treasuries, it’s not enough for inflation to rise. If nominal rates rise even more than inflation, because of higher inflation expectations or higher real rates, Tips underperform regular Treasuries.

Ed Al-Hussainy, Unhedged’s fixed-income svengali, is firmly against Tips:

The quip is ‘Tips are for losers’ and it’s very hard to find evidence to challenge that. Often investors come to the Tips market thinking it will protect them from inflation — that’s the intuitive power of Tips. What can often happen [is that] you can get punished even more in the Tips market than the nominal Treasury market because it’s so small and the investor base for that market is so thin relative to nominal Treasuries.

But can’t these risks be avoided by holding to maturity? Well, Al-Hussainy of Columbia Threadneedle notes, “everyone thinks they’re going to hold Treasuries until maturity, whether it’s Tips or nominals”. Nobody plans to need liquidity all of a sudden, but sometimes they do. Tips are just about 7 per cent of the total Treasury market; the figure is an astounding 25 per cent in the UK (see next item). But the lack of liquidity in the Tips market compared to Treasuries creates wide bid-ask spreads when volatility goes haywire, making them look more like corporate bonds than a safe-haven government security, notes Brij Khurana of Wellington Management.

If you’re confident inflation is set to run hot for years and are certain you can hold until maturity, Tips might be a good bet. Otherwise, just buy plain old Treasuries.

(Kim)

Linkers

Inflation-linked gilts — “linkers”, in the parlance — have marginally outperformed their plain-vanilla siblings this year. This isn’t surprising. We’re experiencing an inflationary shock, which is precisely what linkers are meant to protect against. What is perhaps surprising is that they’ve done so poorly: the return in 2026 has been negative and only 1.5 percentage points better than conventional gilts.

With CPI inflation tracking at 3.1 per cent and expected to rise above 4 per cent early next year, why aren’t linkers doing better? Both linkers’ principal and their coupon payments adjust regularly to reflect realised inflation. But (just as with Tips, see above) the attractiveness of buying linkers at any given moment hinges on the break-even expected inflation rate, implied by the difference between linker’s yield and a same-maturity conventional gilt. For example, the 10-year gilt yield is now just less than 5.5 per cent, while the real yield on the linker is 1.9 per cent. The difference of 3.6 per cent is the embedded expectation for inflation. If the inflation over the life of the bonds comes in lower than this, the linker underperforms the gilt, and vice versa.

As Jonathan Hill at Barclays told us, the market is pricing in a sizeable inflation risk premium in the UK. “This complicates the attractiveness of gilt linkers,” he said.

But there is some nuance to this story, which is that short-duration linkers have generally performed better than longer ones. According to Hill, this is in part because the short end has accrued the positive returns from recent inflation and is not as exposed to the higher term premium — that is, higher real interest rates — at the long end of the curve. Inflation-indexed bonds hedge inflation, but their price (like that of Tips) remains sensitive to changes in real rates (as the world discovered, in Technicolor, in the 2022 Liability-Driven Investment crisis). In the UK, where about a quarter of the debt is indexed to inflation (the highest level in the G7), and the stock of linkers is also unusually long-dated, the performance of the broad linker index therefore reflects a hefty dose of duration risk.

Another issue is that the UK is still dealing with the transition from one inflation index to another. The official policy target is measured by the consumer price index. But linkers are still indexed to the retail price index, which ceased to be an official national statistic in 2013 because of flaws in the methodology. RPI inflation has tended to run at between 0.7 and 1 percentage points above CPI inflation. From 2030 the calculation of RPI will be aligned with CPIH (Consumer Price Index including housing costs of owner-occupiers), and any linkers maturing after that date will reflect the new methodology. So, the investor in long-dated linkers needs to account not only for inflation expectations but also for which measure of inflation they’ll ultimately be compensated against. That wedge is already reflected in the price, but it does make deciding whether to invest in linkers quite a bit trickier.

Linkers are providing inflation protection, but they’re already expensive; they do not protect investors against higher real interest rates. For them to be a good investment, inflation would need to get a lot worse than what’s already in the price, and real rates have to stabilise. Maybe just buy the gilts.

(MacFadden)

One good read

Trouble with ‘The House’
