item.title: Crowding out pits sovereigns against AI
item.author: Ryan Avent
item.description: A battle for capital between rate-insensitive borrowers could end badly
item.content:encoded:
A battle for capital between rate-insensitive borrowers could end badly

Ryan Avent

Ryan Avent is a journalist, author of In Good Faith, and writes a newsletter called The Bellows.

Have you thought about borrowing money lately? If the answer is ‘no, obviously not, have you seen what’s happening with interest rates?’, then congratulations: you’re a victim of “crowding out”.

The hot economic craze is popping up everywhere, from the commercial real estate, to residential mortgages, and, as MainFT notes, it’s spreading to cuspier corporate borrowers too.

What’s going on and how likely is it to lead to trouble?

Basically, crowding out is a competition for scarce real resources which plays out in credit markets. It is a gross simplification but a useful one to say that savers and borrowers are swapping around claims on the productive potential of the economy today for claims on the productive potential of the economy some time in the future.

And there’s real economic activity at stake, which is why a sudden spike in desired saving relative to desired borrowing often sees unemployment soar and the economy fall into a recession.

Suppose, though, that we were to see a pronounced and sustained rise in desired borrowing, as actors in one part of the economy tried ever harder to obtain claims on the productive potential of the economy today. Prying these claims away from others means outbidding them with ever-greater offers of jam tomorrow.

In some cases, these offers might induce people who were thinking about using their claims to obtain goods and services today to save instead, because the market reward for patience has increased.

In other cases, people and businesses may find that the price they need to pay to obtain their desired claims on the economy’s present purchasing power has become exorbitant.

Or in jam terms, some regulars at the café are excited about their daily jam portion, but could be persuaded to go without jam today for a triple portion tomorrow. One or two others enter with plans to offer a patron or two precisely this bargain, because an eccentric inventor down the street has agreed to swap an improved jam-making device for a few portions of jam today. But there’s also another customer in the café today, who promises to come back tomorrow with the OpenJam whizzmatronic bottomless jam-spouting fountain if everyone hands over all of their daily jam portions today. When everyone obliges, the schemers with the more modest jam-making plans are out of luck.

Hopefully that’s clear.

This latter effect is crowding out. Low interest rates imply that people will swap their claims on today’s productive potential for a song. In such cases, a debt-financed investment plan need not yield very much to pencil out. As rates rise, however, the expected return on an investment plan needed to justify the borrowing costs also goes up. Decent investments get squeezed out, then good investments, and then maybe really excellent investments that stand to deliver big economic benefits. So it goes.

We are experiencing this today, and you’ll never guess which part of the economy is responsible for the pronounced and sustained rise in desired borrowing.

The AI complex can go to markets and pay what it takes to get the capital they need, because they expect — and investors believe — that money poured into AI capex will deliver enormous returns in the future. Firms in other parts of the economy can’t promise those same returns, and so they are relinquishing their investment capacity to all things AI. In a new Substack post, Paul Krugman charts the phenomenon (with a typo in the header, which should say 2023 rather than 2003:

Krugman argues that this could be a problem for the economy. Sure, AI execs believe that future returns will be massive, but they could be wrong. And if AI doesn’t deliver on its promise then we face a double blow to growth: because AI didn’t expand our productive capacity as hoped, and because other investments which might have didn’t take place.

It is interesting to note, however, that crowding out like this didn’t take place during the tech investment boom of the 1990s. Another chart tells the tale:

What’s the deal here? Krugman writes:

Most of the answer is that during the 90s boom America attracted very large inflows of investment from abroad, which essentially financed the tech boom even as other investment rose.

That’s certainly true, but a quick look at US current account data suggests that there’s still quite a lot of foreign money flowing America-ward. There is another big difference, though, if you can guess it. Yes! Governments are borrowing a truckload more than they were three decades ago.

To the extent that “crowding out” entered the popular imagination, it did so in the late 1980s and early 1990s, when economists warned that government borrowing was pushing up interest rates and choking off private investment. Bond-market ructions in the early 1990s prompted fiscal consolidation efforts in the US and elsewhere, however, and from 1998 to 2001 the US government actually ran a surplus.

(Krugman knows all this, by the way, I’m not trying to pwn him. He made his big splash as a political commentator pointing out that the tax cuts promised by George W Bush in his campaign for president would in effect hand the surplus to well-off households. He made his big splash as an economist long before that, doing groundbreaking work that ultimately won him a Nobel Prize. But none of you children remember.)

Anyway, gross government debt across advanced economies rose from 67 per cent of GDP in 2001 to 108 per cent today. So one could say that AI borrowing is crowding out other private investment, but one could also, and perhaps more reasonably, say that government borrowing is stymieing what might otherwise be a very broad-based, AI-driven, private sector investment boom.

If this turns out to be the better way to think about it, we’ll know soon enough. Firms in non-AI sectors may abandon efforts to claim more of the economy’s productive potential in the face of rising interest rates, but governments almost certainly won’t. For governments to give way, budget deficits need to fall. Accomplishing this means disappointing people who are expecting to receive claims from the government. It also means people have to give up more of their own claims to the government through higher taxes. In this fractious age, governments that do such things tend to be tossed out in favour of crazier governments which are even less able to do the needful.

Unfortunately, this likely means that we are on one of two paths. Either the AI complex ultimately smashes itself against the irresistible borrowing needs of the public sector and is forced to retrench, with potentially unpleasant consequences for growth, or rising interest rates cause one or another sovereign to slip into a market-destabilising crisis first.

Vote for which outcome you favour in the comments.

item.title: Norway lays down a line for EU on AI glasses
item.author: Richard Milne
item.description: Proposed ban will be test case for broad restrictions on the eyewear after fierce backlash over their use
item.content:encoded:
Proposed ban will be test case for broad restrictions on the eyewear after fierce backlash over their use

Richard Milne

“Pervert glasses” that enable privacy intrusion or one of the most important retail products in decades? Few recent consumer technologies have sparked such a fierce backlash as the AI-enabled eyewear now being offered by the likes of Meta.

Now Norway is set to provide a test case for broad restrictions on their use. Up until this week, any bans around the world have been largely piecemeal. Courts in the UK and US, Norwegian oil company Equinor and schools in Oslo are among those to prohibit their use in recent months.

But on Monday, Norway’s centre-left government became the first in the world to propose a ban — albeit temporary — on the use of AI glasses in certain public places. Many of the details remain to be worked out, including exactly where the ban would apply — the idea would be to enact it in the most sensitive areas such as schools and changing rooms. But bringing a proposal to Norway’s parliament is “a high priority” for digitalisation minister Torgeir Micaelsen.

For many policymakers in Europe, there is a distinct sense of righting wrongs and avoiding a laissez-faire approach that they now regret for other technologies.

“We must avoid making the same mistake we made 15 years ago with social media, taking no political action,” Micaelsen says.

AI glasses have been pushed particularly hard by Meta, but others such as Huawei offer them and Apple and Google could follow. Tech companies argue they could be a better gateway to AI than smartphones.

But these companies also like the idea of training the glasses on real-life interactions involving audio and video — something that causes great disquiet. Barely a day passes without a headline on the potential misuse of smart glasses, from men approaching women on the street without telling them they are filming to this week’s revelations by one Danish MP that he recorded members of parliament at work.

Worries abound about how the glasses could be used to spy on women and children, particularly in settings such as changing rooms, and how privacy safeguards — such as a flashing light that shows when they are recording — could be overridden.

A survey by France’s data protection office, Commission Nationale de l’Informatique et des Libertés, this year found the vast majority of people — 67 per cent of respondents — thought smart glasses posed a risk to people’s privacy.

Norway is not alone in taking action. The European Data Protection Board, an independent body representing privacy regulators across Europe, has commissioned a report on the social acceptability of smart glasses to guide lawmakers. Australia’s government has asked for advice on whether to ban them from its offices and service centres after a number of the country’s local councils prohibited them from swimming pools, offices and more. And Dutch retailer Hans Anders this month became one of the first in the world to stop the sale of Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses over privacy concerns.

Norway, for now though, has gone the furthest, and says it will bring out a proposal for a temporary ban soon as well as setting up an expert group to lay the groundwork for permanent regulation. The locations for a ban could include beaches, museums, shopping centres, kindergartens, playgrounds, healthcare facilities, changing rooms for fitness centres, and even universities, the government has indicated.

Micaelsen concedes “regulating this type of technology is complex and raises a number of questions”. But the EDPB report may guide the development of a common EU approach to regulating smart glasses in much the same way that early, fragmented national positions on cookies and ad tech eventually converged into harmonised guidance, according to law firm Gerrish.

The French regulator CNIL has already called for enhanced vigilance on smart glasses. “The rise of smart glasses could give rise to a significant risk of widespread surveillance and its trivialisation . . . The relatively moderate cost of these devices could lead to a saturation of the social space by sensors,” it said.

Any restrictions will probably be met by strong protests from tech companies given their commercial importance. Analysts at Counterpoint Research forecast more than $1tn will be spent on wearable devices between now and 2032. But the concerns among campaigners about what social media has done to a generation of children show the risks for governments in Europe and beyond of allowing tech companies free rein.

richard.milne@ft.com

item.title: The race for Britain’s car market is wide open — for now
item.author: Soumaya Keynes
item.description: All manner of trade barriers loom
item.content:encoded:
All manner of trade barriers loom

Soumaya Keynes

Picture some cars racing to win a trophy: the British market. The stakes are high. Ranked by value, Britain is the third largest vehicle importer in the world. The contest is relatively open. Unlike the French who favour Renaults or the Germans who value Volkswagens, Britons are unpatriotic car buyers. And increasingly, the competition is dangerous. Given the backdrop of geoeconomic tension, the participants will be lucky to avoid a crash.

For years, the EU was the undisputed champion of the UK market, at least when judged by where its cars were made. (Most of the US, Japanese or South Korean brand cars sold in the UK come from factories on the continent.) But since the pandemic and Brexit, the bloc’s dominance has waned. Whereas in the 2010s it contributed some 90 per cent of UK vehicle imports by value, over the past year its share has been below 70 per cent.

The EU is in no mood to lose this race. The UK has become the top destination for its vehicle exports since President Donald Trump’s tariffs crushed US sales. Germany is particularly keen to win, having seen its share of exports to the UK fall by more than the EU average since the pandemic. Its sector has been struggling with a years-long downturn, stoking fears of deindustrialisation and diminished economic strength.

The main challenger is, of course, China. After years of cut-throat competition and muscular industrial policy, its carmakers can produce vehicles with tech that makes YouTube reviewers swoon, and batteries for 35 per cent less than Europe. These competitors are also hungry for business given their massive capacity and terrible home demand. Over the first half of this year, car sales in China dropped by 20 per cent year on year. Over that same period, its vehicle exports to the UK grew by over 80 per cent.

It’s worth noting that others have it worse than the EU. The value of vehicle imports into the UK from the bloc has grown over the past year, so China has only limited some of the EU’s post-pandemic recovery. Over the same period, imports into Britain from Japan, South Africa, Turkey and North America all fell, though from a lower base.

But this won’t make anyone in the EU feel better. Coming at the same time as the transition away from internal combustion engine vehicles, this is a race for the future. Splitting the contest by vehicle type, China’s export surge has most momentum in the category of hybrid vehicles — which is where EU exports have plateaued.

The bloc has had enough, and wants Britain to intervene. They have asked for tariffs to offset the advantage Chinese producers have had from domestic industrial policy over the years. But even without any “unfairness”, there is an argument for pushing back against Chinese dominance of car production, given its habit of weaponising supply. (Chinese makers already dominate parts of the battery supply chain.)

The British government is mulling tariffs, but is in a tricky spot. It’s possible the public could be persuaded. While on a fellowship at the University of Oxford, senior civil servant Jenny Bates told me about her research based on a focus group suggesting voters might accept higher costs if it made the country more secure. But it’s also possible that the public really likes cheap cars kitted out with massive flat screens.

The plight of Britain’s sputtering car industry doesn’t simplify the choice. Production has shrunk from 1.7mn vehicles in 2016 to just 0.7mn in 2025. But since most of this output is exported, the UK industry seems less interested in protection from Chinese competition than in lobbying for lower energy costs and less ambitious green targets, and in attracting Chinese investment.

The EU is pointing to a different race as an incentive for the UK to take action. The bloc’s Industrial Accelerator Act is a policy in development, aimed partly at strengthening the European auto industry. If the UK stays open to Chinese cars, it risks being shut out. Given that the EU is the UK’s biggest export destination, that would hurt.

Forced into a stark choice between the EU and China, geography, history and ideology all push the UK towards its neighbour. But next time there are demands for tariffs, I would recommend asking a question. What happens if China retaliates by shutting off its market, or worse, its supply chains? The EU is invested in this race. But if there’s a crash, will it help to clean up?

soumaya.keynes@ft.com, @SoumayaKeynes

The Economics Show with Soumaya Keynes is a podcast from the FT bringing listeners a deeper understanding of the most complex global economic issues in easy-to-digest weekly episodes. Listen to new episodes every Friday on Apple, Spotify, Pocket Casts or wherever you get your podcasts

item.title: Lex. Japan’s small-cap cull is an opportunity for AI funds
item.description: Finding needles amid haystacks is a task for AI
item.content:encoded:
Finding needles amid haystacks is a task for AI

Stock market reforms don’t come much more brutal. Japan’s Topix, followed by about $1tn of funds, has ditched almost 700 companies because they’re too small. The cull is designed to make the survivors a simpler and more attractive investment proposition. It is an opportunity, too, for AI-enabled funds to prove their worth among the ejected minnows. 

As elsewhere, Japan’s stock market wealth is concentrated in its biggest companies. But its indices are sprawling things. The Topix, preferred by money managers to the better-known Nikkei 225, currently contains more than 1,600 companies ranging from mighty $272bn Mitsubishi UFJ Financial to $22mn Prored Partners, a management consultancy.

The Topix’s myriad small fry are fiddly and expensive to trade — and have virtually no effect on index performance anyway. The scale of the issue is writ large in exchange operator JPX’s overhaul: the 683 companies it has named for potential eviction only account for 3 per cent of the index’s total market capitalisation, and that’s after an earlier cull of roughly 500 even smaller companies in 2025.

Smaller companies the world over have been rendered less accessible to investors who tend to put their money in passive index trackers, rather than pay for active managers more likely to seek an edge in niche segments. MSCI’s Japan index, for example, covers 85 per cent of what it deems Tokyo’s investable market with just 167 companies. 

Sifting through small caps is a lot of work: BlackRock counts more than 6,000 of them, while MSCI’s All-World small-cap index has more than 5,600 companies from 47 countries and its smallest constituent is valued at just $6.2mn. But help is at hand: finding needles amid haystacks is a task for AI and its ability to crunch thousands of company reports and utterances.

The number of potential opportunities may be on the rise. The AI frenzy isn’t just boosting suppliers of chips and electricity. Bottlenecks are appearing in unexpected locations and Japanese manufacturers’ deep involvement in so many supply chains may result in unexpected windfalls. Meanwhile, AI tools — with their potential to cut costs and increase productivity — may over time reduce the inefficiencies of being a minnow compared to a whale.

Early adopters of this idea are looking smart. In February, Rotterdam-based Robeco launched a global small-cap exchange traded fund combining AI with quantitative models to pick stocks. So far, its offering is up 13 per cent, against 9 per cent and 3 per cent respectively for MSCI’s All-World and global small-cap gauges. BlackRock, too, has been touting its use of large language models and other technology to identify “non-obvious” links and themes between small-caps across the world.

Index huggers will doubtless still prefer the newly streamlined Topix. But for a new generation of tech-enabled investors, there should be plenty of interesting material among the offcuts.

jennifer.hughes@ft.com

item.title: Real men don’t do climate change
item.author: Pilita Clark
item.description: Research on the gender differences in how people think about global warming suggests campaigns and communications may need a rethink
item.content:encoded:
Research on the gender differences in how people think about global warming suggests campaigns and communications may need a rethink

Pilita Clark

If you are a man who cares about climate change, are you a bit of a dweeb? Put another way, if a man says global warming is rubbish, does he seem more manly?

In my 15 years of writing about climate change, these are not questions I have considered before. But I have begun to do so since coming across research that suggests a lot of men brush off the climate problem for fear of seeming too feminine.

The analysis by Michael Haselhuhn, an associate professor of management at University of California, Riverside, helps to answer one of the more baffling climate questions: why do studies and polls across the world consistently show that men care less about global warming than women? 

Some studies suggest that men feel they have more to lose from policies to fight climate change. Others conclude it is because women are socialised to care more about things like the environment. But researchers who focus on socialisation tend to look at it from the perspective of the women being socialised. 

Haselhuhn thought the same patterns of conditioning might be having a separate but overlooked effect on men. So he did a series of linked studies that suggest this is indeed what is happening.

Using data from the US, and a long-running survey of more than 40,000 people across Europe, he showed that men who say they want to save the planet are perceived to be more warm and caring. In keeping with this finding, he also showed that men who are strongly concerned about maintaining their sense of manhood express less concern about the climate problem and say they feel less responsibility for managing it.

This does not, of course, mean that all male climate sceptics are worried about their manhood. Other views also matter. A study of more than 9,000 scientists in 115 countries published this week shows that those who believe technology will largely solve the climate problem are 23 per cent less likely to go on a climate march, sign a petition or take similar civic actions, compared with scientists who lack such faith. The techno-optimists are also 18 per cent less likely to make big lifestyle changes to cut carbon. In other words, many personal views matter, even for experts.

But Haselhuhn’s work does raise a question about the best way to sell the need for climate action, especially to men. He is now trying to determine which messages might land best, with mixed results. At first he thought it might be effective to suggest that real men take care of their family and are good parents, but that “just didn’t move the needle at all”, he told me. 

More success came when highlighting the financial benefits of climate action. For example, when men are choosing between a regular showerhead and an energy-efficient one, about 80 per cent of them will choose the greener one if it is described as a way to save money. But if told that the same showerhead uses less water and is more environmentally friendly, that support falls by 10 percentage points. Taking out the word “environment” seems to help, says Haselhuhn. 

All of this gels with the ideas of climate scientists such as Katharine Hayhoe, a Texas Tech University professor who has worked extensively on effective ways to talk about climate change. This includes advice on dealing with the inevitable uncle who tells you at every family gathering that the climate has always been changing and today’s record temperatures are just part of a natural cycle.

It doesn’t help to spout scientific facts to show why he is wrong, Hayhoe told a recent FT conference. That’s because the real issue here is not science denial but solution aversion, or concern that climate policies will clash with a person’s identity, ideology or ideas about a better world.

Because it’s unpleasant to say openly that you don’t want to fix a serious problem, people use so-called motivated reasoning to find grounds for why climate change cannot be real or serious. In other words, they process information in ways that align with what they already believe or want, rather than with objective evidence.

Happily, Hayhoe says, the same uncle’s views can reverse completely if he buys solar panels that save him money or does something else that improves his own circumstances as well as the climate.

There is a message here for those of us who rightly worry about warming temperatures. Scientific facts really matter, as does the health of the environment. But there will be times when the best thing you can do for the planet is not talk about it at all.

pilita.clark@ft.com

item.title: What is the real price of oil?
item.author: Amrita Sen
item.description: Crude futures are no longer a reliable guide to the inflationary impact of fuel prices
item.content:encoded:
Crude futures are no longer a reliable guide to the inflationary impact of fuel prices

Amrita Sen

The writer is director of market intelligence and co-founder at Energy Aspects

This year has shown more clearly than ever that there is no single price of oil. The futures contracts quoted everywhere as “the price” certainly can’t be considered that. Physical crude prices have always diverged somewhat from futures but the gap has never been this large.

According to Argus Media Group data, the Brent futures price is now only about 60-70 per cent of the landed crude cost in Asia compared with about 90 per cent usually. And it represents only 50 per cent of the diesel price, versus the usual 80-90 per cent of the price.

Between 2007 and 2019, the standard deviation of the spread between the spot price for Brent and futures was about $1 a barrel. This year, it has risen to nearly $8 a barrel and even exceeded $20 in September, highlighting how ineffective futures are at capturing the true state of physical balances.

And that is even before the cost of shipping, which has increased by anywhere between five and 10 times compared with levels before the Iran war. Prices for Atlantic basin crude landing in Asia are five times higher than prewar levels, primarily driven by higher freight costs.

The value of a barrel of crude oil increasingly depends on where it is, when it is available and how easily it can reach the refinery that needs it. Flows through the Strait of Hormuz have recovered from their lows of about 2mn barrels a day in April to about 11mn. Total Middle Eastern flows (including on pipeline bypasses) are now about 2.5mn barrels a day below their prewar levels. But vessel availability is constrained and barrels are taking longer, more complicated routes to reach buyers. A barrel crossing Hormuz is not necessarily a barrel readily available to the marginal refiner.

Not only are futures increasingly unreliable as a proxy for genuine supply and demand, they are also no longer useful as a hedge either and further disconnected from the fuel prices that drive inflation.

There are several reasons for this. First and foremost, the constant jawboning by the US administration to get prices down has left fewer participants in the crude market, according to our data. The view that the US will do whatever it takes to lower prices before elections has dominated sentiment. So despite global crude stocks falling about 650mn barrels since the conflict began, according to Kayrros inventory data, traders are scared to hold long positions — largely because the volume of bearish headlines coming from the administration, leaving prices at the mercy of algorithm-driven trading.

Secondly, the increase in flows through Hormuz is entirely driven by ship-to-ship transfers of crude, a costly process that has pushed shipping costs to record highs with the “very large crude carrier” market in uncharted territory since early September.

The bottom line is that the infrastructure needed to move crude and products has become constrained and expensive. Higher Hormuz flows reduce the risk of outright shortages but cannot restore the buffers or flexibility that previously kept the marginal barrel cheap. And given the reliance on ship-to-ship transfers, the more oil flows via this route, the higher the floor is for shipping rates, which feeds through to the prices we pay at the pump. 

Finally, the shortage of global refining capacity outside of China, the constant attacks by Ukraine on Russian refineries and the shutdown of regional export-oriented refineries in the Middle East have meant products such as gasoline, jet and diesel are at record-high prices.

This is why products have been trading at double the price of crude during the past few months, something that has never happened before. Ultimately, diesel and gasoline drive inflation, not crude oil. Crude has always been used as a proxy because it moved in tandem with products and was the biggest driver of product prices. That relationship has now broken down. In fact, since May, 10-year US Treasury yields have correlated more closely with diesel prices than crude prices, for the first time ever.

That is why the US government has now turned its attention to calming diesel prices. Yet, in all the government’s efforts to keep crude futures prices lower in the belief it would keep the bond and equity markets in check, the real price of oil has run away. It is not that those who believed oil would be $200 due to this conflict were wrong — it was just the choice of financial instrument that was incorrect.

Robert Campbell contributed to this article

item.title: Japan was never normal — and it’s not going to be now
item.author: Leo Lewis
item.description: The LDP needs to rethink decades of small-business policy for an era of far bigger problems
item.content:encoded:
The LDP needs to rethink decades of small-business policy for an era of far bigger problems

Leo Lewis

To lose one century-old, Sendai-area producer of leaf-shaped sasakamaboko fishcakes may be considered a misfortune. To lose two looks like carelessness. Lose three in quick succession, as Japan has done in the past 12 months, and people start talking about a “new normal”.

But should they? If ever there were a moment for Japan, for those that engage with it and those that invest in it, to embrace the certainty of a new abnormal, that time is surely now.

Clearly, times are cruel in the northeastern Japanese fishcake game. Surging costs, from pollock paste and plastic packaging to logistics and labour, are straining business models to breaking point. Changing diets have less space for fishy fare; tourists prefer local beef tongue. Behind all of these pressures, one can see the vast hydraulics of geoeconomics, climate change and demographics.

These fishcake makers have previously survived military dictatorship, world war defeat, oil crises, tsunamis, generational handover and deflation. So as well as being saddened by the abrupt, back-to-back shutterings of Takeda no Sasakamaboko (est. 1935), Bajo Kamabokoten (est. 1912) and Kaneko Hashinuma Shoten (est. 1927), there is huge temptation to conclude this is part of an unusually forceful shift away from life as Japan knows it. Key political figures actively reinforce that view. On Tuesday, Ryosei Akazawa, Japan’s minister for economy, trade and industry, used a press conference to upend decades of his own party’s thinking on the role of small and medium-sized enterprises. 

Akazawa is someone who knows a bit about epochal disruption of norms. His current role puts him prominently on the front line of America’s redefinition of friendship and of China’s redefinition of hostility. When Japan needed someone to negotiate its way through Donald Trump’s arbitrarily calculated “reciprocal” tariffs, and to pledge $550bn of infrastructure investment to an economy nearly 10 times its size, Akazawa was the one trusted to put on a Maga hat and give a double thumbs-up to the new world order. 

And for almost a year, he has also had to field the concerns of the business lobby as diplomacy between Beijing and Tokyo has entered a deep freeze and Japanese companies have pulled out of China — Japan’s biggest trading partner — at a record rate.

In his presentation earlier this week, Akazawa did not mention the three fishcake makers, but his thesis was that Japan should expect and embrace a spate of company closures. Crucially, he argued, it has resisted this for far too long.

For decades, the government has seen its enormous SME sector as the bastion against mass unemployment. Those businesses, no matter how economically illogical at the individual level, were collectively legitimised by a broader national goal. They were given what Akazawa called a “warm and comfortable atmosphere” of subsidy and incentives in hard times. But however flabby and irrelevant they became, it remained core LDP policy that, wherever possible, no SME should go bankrupt.

With the working population now in permanent decline, that policy is clearly brimming with moral hazard. “Most SMEs have no ambition to grow,” he said, adding that “this is not exactly a capitalist mindset.” His argument? The LDP needs a new policy and Japan needs a new mindset.

Thinking in terms of “new normals” is the wrong way to form such a policy — however alluring that sounds. Japan, however desperately it would like to  imagine itself as having evolved through a series of established normals, is perhaps more usefully defined by its rolling embrace of abnormality. An economy in which tens of thousands of companies are over 100 years old gives the impression of permanence; in fact it represents abnormality stacked on abnormality.

The Bank of Japan, in its long build-up to sustained monetary tightening, has talked a lot about the necessity of “normalisation”. Akazawa’s comments suggest that the country’s entire approach to capitalism needs a similar overhaul. Others lament Japan’s focus on its pacifism or immigration rules. Too often, these debates underplay just how resistant it is to having normality defined for it — either domestically or by the outside world. 

At the most recent census, 11 per cent of Japanese were under 15 and 17 per cent were over 75. Others may well follow Japan down this road, but no modern country has yet arrived at these extremes — and no country will experience the transformations of environment, geopolitics and technology from a similar starting point. There is no lingering “normal” to be had for Japan, new or otherwise.

leo.lewis@ft.com

item.title: The Big Read. Why people don’t want to have children any more
item.author: Camilla Cavendish
item.description: Social contagion can help explain falling birth rates — and offers a way out of the demographic trap
item.content:encoded:
Social contagion can help explain falling birth rates — and offers a way out of the demographic trap

Camilla Cavendish

When Susannah McIntyre, 37, hauls her three young sons through her Cambridgeshire village, pedestrians mutter, she says. Cafés seem relieved to see them depart. When she was growing up, it was families with five children that seemed big. But at the local primary school, only two other families have three kids. Now she says she feels like an “outlier”, one who is looked down on with suspicion by people “who regard parenting as a self-indulgent lifestyle choice”.

Across the world, parenthood is on the wane. In Europe, the only child is becoming the norm, with half of families with dependent children having only one. In the UK, the figure is 45 per cent, with just 14 per cent of families having three or more. This is repeated in unexpected places. The United Arab Emirates and Tamil Nadu in India now have lower birth rates than Germany. Mexico’s rate has fallen behind the US, where one-child families now outnumber families with two.

Birth rates in more than two-thirds of the world’s countries have fallen below the “replacement rate” of 2.1 children per woman needed to maintain a stable population. The world population will soon start to decline, for the first time since the Black Death of the 14th century, with one estimate putting “peak human” as soon as 2064.

There are many factors behind the baby bust. Young people are less likely to be in a relationship than previous generations were at the same age. It is harder for young couples to get on the housing ladder and to feel economically stable enough to contemplate adding a baby to the mix. And some worry whether it would be right to bring a child into a febrile world.

But after five years of research, I have come to believe that there is something else at play too: a form of social contagion. In a world that appears to treat parents with hostility, where the advantages of raising children are obscured, remaining childless is easier if the same decision is made by everyone around you. As a phenomenon, it can become self-perpetuating.

This extra factor — network effects — can explain the remarkable similarities between falling birth rates across very different places and cultures. It also offers humans a way to reverse the decline by making having children attractive again.

Falling birth rates are often presented as a simple matter of choice. But in research of 10 low-fertility countries by Ester Lazzari and Eva Beaujouan, up to half of men and women end their reproductive years wishing they had more children. While passing peak human will ease the burden on natural resources, the drop in global population is projected to be rapid, ushering in legions of elderly who will strain welfare states and economies. In China, where a one-child policy introduced in 1980 distorted family planning for 35 years, there is now the “4-2-1 problem”, with an only child supporting two parents and four grandparents.

There are other, subtle effects. As children become less visible, our tolerance for their noisy capriciousness dwindles. In Japan, crowdsourced Dorozoku maps show people how to avoid streets where “children play with balls”. In a smart Paris suburb, judges last year ordered a junior school to close its playground after neighbours complained about noise. At a clinic in Boston, Massachusetts, in 2022, I met Wanda Baker, who had been asked to stand outside because her sick baby and his two siblings were upsetting other patients. “I feel second class,” she said.

“Families are society’s most basic unit and humanity’s most indispensable institution,” says Nicholas Eberstadt, demographer and Henry Wendt chair at the American Enterprise Institute. “But as families and their branches thin out, they will become ever less able to bear weight.” Policymakers, he adds, are “not ready for the age of depopulation which will recast societies, economies and power politics”.

A low fertility trap

Humans copy each other, a primal drive that goes all the way back to our early need to protect ourselves in tribes. Social norms developed as a way to outsource some of our decision-making. Co-operation with the group became instinctive. 

Even in the modern world, the need to conform is powerful. In an early experiment demonstrating the power of social contagion from the 1950s, the psychologist Solomon Asch asked participants to do a simple task, matching lines on a card, where the correct answer was obvious. Unaware that other participants were actors instructed by Asch, more than a third of participants went along with the group’s choice, despite this being obviously wrong.

The impact of network effects on birth rates was well documented by a study in Brazil. The gradual introduction of broadcast signal into different regions in the 1980s was accompanied by a cliff-like fall in birth rates. People with signal had become gripped by telenovelas – soap operas – showing urban female protagonists with few or no kids. In 1960, the average Brazilian woman had just over six children. Forty years later it was just over two: a drop almost as rapid as China’s. The impact was strongest on the female viewers who were closest in age to the female characters, with whom they identified most strongly.

More recent studies have corroborated such findings. Research from Sweden in 2010 showed that women working in offices were more likely to have a baby if a colleague of similar seniority did so, with no effect from co-workers at other levels. A separate study of 6,500 German companies similarly found that female employees’ transition rates to first pregnancy roughly doubled after a colleague had a baby, with the effect lasting about two years.

The German social scientists Daniel Lois and Oliver Arránz Becker have found that couples’ interest in having a child strengthens if friends become parents. They suggest three possible factors: couples with children demystify parenthood for the network, create a social pressure on others to join them, and create a feeling that not joining might disrupt social ties.

“Peer group behaviour signals what people like me are expected to do, and at what point in the life course,” says Anna Rotkirch, research professor at Finland’s Population Research Institute. “We have evolved to be very conscious of reproductive cues in our environment,” she says, adding that she feels these have become increasingly negative.

The acceleration of the birth rate fall since the advent of the smartphone may have less to do with time spent on screens distracting from romance and more to do with negative images of childbirth and positive ones about being single. “Fear of pregnancy and the discourse about motherhood as sacrifice have become more common in the past 15 years,” says Rotkirch, with “many childless women mentioning fear of what happens to your body in childbirth as a reason for not having had a child”. 

Several studies have found that seeing and holding real babies makes women keener to have their own baby — although they may be self-selecting.

Social media increases the extent to which young adults interact with peers or role models they do not know and are not related to. “I have talked to young mothers who are surprised that posting on Instagram about having a baby is creating fewer ‘likes’ than posting about a fancy holiday trip,” says Rotkirch. “Young adults are increasingly taking their reproductive cues from people or platforms with no real interest or stakes in their family formation goals.”

The situation today in England and Wales is that women born in 1979 are having smaller families than their baby boomer parents and greatest generation grandparents, while their Gen Z daughters are projected to have even smaller families still.

A big reason that people end up with fewer children than they wanted is that we are leaving it later to start a family. European first-time mothers are 31, and fathers 34, compared with 1975 when the average ages were 26 for mothers and 30 for fathers. This in itself makes it harder to have multiple children.

But the overarching pattern fulfils the “low fertility trap” hypothesis proposed by the economists Vegard Skirbekk, Wolfgang Lutz and Maria Rita Testa in 2006. They contended that once fertility declines below replacement level, the subsequent shrinking of each generation may entrench childlessness as a norm which becomes harder to reverse. The downward spiral lessens social pressure to have a family.

It is true that no country that has fallen well below two children per woman has yet rebounded to anything like that level. South Korea has ticked up a little, from 0.75 in 2024 to 0.8 in 2025, but it’s not yet clear whether that is a temporary phenomenon, a result of women having one child a little younger.

As time goes on, a rebound could become less and less possible. In China, the writer Helen Gao has suggested that “none of China’s only children can imagine what raising multiple children could look like”. If you grew up without siblings, and your friends did too, why would you want something different? Add in the absurd demands of modern intensive parenting, and all the other things you can do with your time in the modern world, and it’s no surprise that so many couples now declare themselves “one and done”.

Eberstadt, of the American Enterprise Institute, thinks that mimetic theory, the cultural influences on human behaviour, is playing an overlooked role in the baby bust. “The increasing rarity of large families could make it harder for humans to choose to return to having them — owing to what scholars call loss of social learning — and prolong low levels of fertility,” he says.

Baby bonus

Hopes of filling the demographic gap are often pinned on immigration. But newcomers to a country are also influenced by social norms. In a Norwegian survey, majorities of first-generation immigrants from Vietnam, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Turkey said that it was very important to have children in order to have a happy marriage. By the second generation, fewer than half expressed this view. Somali-heritage women have an average of seven children in Somalia, but two in Norway.

One study has even found that Polish women moving to England and Wales ended up having more children than their peers back home, mirroring the household average of their new country, even though it often costs more to raise a child in London than in Warsaw.

Groups that retain stronger ties to their countries of origin, and which have strong religious faith, are less immediately influenced. But the data suggests they still eventually produce smaller families. The fertility rate among Pakistani women in the UK dropped by 38 per cent between 2001 and 2021, according to the Migration Observatory.

If immigration provides no solution, perhaps network effects themselves can be used. Making children seem desirable, possible and visible is a feature of two companies that are bucking the birth-rate trend in low-fertility countries.

In Taiwan, chipmaker TSMC’s employees make up around 0.3 per cent of the population but were parents to 1.8 per cent of Taiwanese babies in 2023. Hsinchu County, where the company is based, has more children per 100 working-age adults than any other region. It has created an environment in which children are highly visible, with wraparound childcare on site and a pre-school on each of its campuses.

Similarly LOTTE, the South Korean retail empire, has an internal birth rate which is more than double the national one, at 2.05 babies born per woman compared to 0.8. The company, which employs around 60,000 people, has strong parental leave policies. For example, it is compulsory for fathers to take at least one month of paternity leave on full pay. In recognition of its efforts, the company has been commended by South Korea’s Population Strategy Committee.

The pattern can be transposed. In Nagi, a Japanese mountain town, population decline became an existential issue in 2002, when the dwindling number of residents created pressure to merge with other prefectures. The mayor instead worked hard to offer financial incentives including baby bonuses, generous daycare and free healthcare for children. Residents take a whole-community approach, with pensioners stepping in to help out, and children are seen as a positive. The result is that while half of Japanese families have only one child, in Nagi, 47 per cent of households have three or more. 

An earlier version of the chart on ideal and actual family size was mislabelled. The keys for “Actual family size” and “Unfulfilled fertility” were transposed. 

Camilla Cavendish is the author of ‘Generation Maybe: Why We’re Having Fewer Children, and What It Means For Us All’ published by Penguin

Data visualisation by Keith Fray

item.title: Letter: Sanctions policy sometimes must be compromised to save lives
item.description: From Frank Vogl, Adjunct Professor, Georgetown University; Co-founder, Transparency International, Washington, DC, US
item.content:encoded:
From Frank Vogl, Adjunct Professor, Georgetown University; Co-founder, Transparency International, Washington, DC, US

Martin Sandbu, in his column on EU members using their veto powers to lift sanctions on targeted oligarchs, is sharp in his criticism of France for the actions it took to free a French citizen from jail in Azerbaijan (“EU countries shoot themselves in the foot when they veto sanctions”, Opinion, October 5).

However there is not the slightest recognition in his article of the vital humanitarian concerns that we all should have for innocent hostages jailed by authoritarian regimes, such as those in Russia, Azerbaijan and Iran.

We need to be concerned about every individual who is taken as a pawn in international strategies, often tortured, often facing death, as, for example, Emad Shargi recounts about his more than five years in Evin prison, Tehran. This Iranian-American businessman was on a business trip when he was arrested, subsequently interrogated, tortured and confined to solitary by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and held for ransom, which the Biden administration negotiated to secure his freedom along with four others.

Then, in a complicated exchange that involved a Russian murderer in a German jail, American journalist Evan Gershkovich was freed from a Russian prison — he describes his terrible ordeal in his new book This Cursed Beautiful Land.

The stories these victims tell of the nightmare situations in which they found themselves ought to convince Sandbu, and others who share his view, that there are times when broad sanctions policies need to be compromised in order to save lives.

The actions taken by western governments to rescue hostages is vital to provide us all with a sense of safety, and give hope for all those who today are political prisoners.

Frank Vogl
Adjunct Professor, Georgetown University; Co-founder, Transparency International, Washington, DC, US

item.title: Letter: Recalling the British input to the EU’s single market
item.description: From Catherine Stihler, Former MEP for Scotland (Scottish Labour), Carmel-by-the-Sea, CA, US
item.content:encoded:
From Catherine Stihler, Former MEP for Scotland (Scottish Labour), Carmel-by-the-Sea, CA, US

Your Big Read “Is Britain welcome to return?” (October 3) leaves out an important piece of history: for more than two decades, the UK was one of the European single market’s leading architects and defenders.

In the European parliament, the internal market and consumer protection committee was chaired by British MEPs, both Labour and Conservative, for most of the years after it was created in 2004. Michel Barnier, the EU’s chief Brexit negotiator, knows this well. As internal market commissioner, he worked closely with those British chairs to deepen the very market he now says cannot be taken “à la carte”.

As a former MEP, I saw this commitment at first hand. British members were often the strongest voices for open markets, consumer protection and fair competition.

Barnier is right that the single market’s integrity matters. But Britain is not asking to join a club it never understood. It helped write the rules. After a decade of failing to find a relationship that works, both sides should be open to closer economic ties, whether through the European Economic Area and European Free Trade Association route or a tailored arrangement built on that shared history.

Catherine Stihler
Former MEP for Scotland (Scottish Labour), Carmel-by-the-Sea, CA, US

item.title: Letter: Merz’s reforms could help blunt the appeal of the AfD
item.description: From Tjaco van den Hout, Riga, Latvia
item.content:encoded:
From Tjaco van den Hout, Riga, Latvia

Janan Ganesh (“Leadership is not the problem in the west”, Opinion, September 24) suggests that resistance to Friedrich Merz’s reforms reflects voters’ unwillingness to surrender comforts acquired over generations of the welfare state. Yet, as Harvey Clark Greisman recently noted (Letters, September 23), some East Germans remember reunification as their loss of economic security. Apprehension about further change cannot simply be dismissed as excessive expectations.

In a course on geoeconomics I taught at the Riga Graduate School of Law, I used Sheri Berman and Hans Kundnani’s 2021 essay “The Cost of Convergence” to examine the risks of Germany’s over-reliance on exports to drive economic growth. The essay argued that this reliance left Germany vulnerable to external shocks, and proposed higher wages, stronger household consumption and investment in the digital and green transitions.

Merz’s infrastructure and climate programme addresses part of that agenda. Whether his wider reforms bring tangible benefits to communities at risk of being left behind matters for Germany’s resilience and could reduce one source of insecurity on which the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) draws. The question is not whether reform hurts, but whether it leaves Germany and its people more secure.

Tjaco van den Hout
Riga, Latvia

item.title: Letter: The benefits of HS2: a sceptical northerner’s take
item.description: From Peter Hardwick, Manchester, UK
item.content:encoded:
From Peter Hardwick, Manchester, UK

Jennifer Williams’ Inside Politics piece “Burnham’s Blind Spot” (FT.com, September 11) alludes to the benefits of HS2, Britain’s high-speed rail project. Really? Cui bono as we say “oop” north.

What is the point of a train its promoters say will get you from Birmingham to London in under 50 minutes, when most families with two kids will not be able to afford the fares, unless they can plan in advance or take trains at times nobody wants to travel at? Up north, the taxes of Mancunians like me will pay for HS2 but we will not get to use it.

Peter Hardwick
Manchester, UK
