item.title: The FT View. Badenoch’s UK Conservatives are a work in progress
item.author: The editorial board
item.description: Burnham’s leftward shift opens space in the centre. The Tories should occupy it
item.content:encoded:
Burnham’s leftward shift opens space in the centre. The Tories should occupy it

The editorial board

Kemi Badenoch has come quite a distance in 12 months. A beleaguered figure at last year’s Conservative Party conference, she is today master of her party; her personal ratings have improved markedly. Her party has come less far. It is still hollowed out, languishing in third place in the polls and under huge pressure from Nigel Farage’s populist Reform UK on the right. It remains far from being a credible party of government. It is, though, beginning to shape up as a credible party of opposition.

That is significant in itself. New Prime Minister Andy Burnham is shifting his government alarmingly towards the big-state, high-spending Labour of old, seeming to repudiate not just Thatcherism but the Blairite blend of social democracy and free markets. After the Starmer government heaped taxes on business, his successor seems less committed to freeing animal spirits than to expanding public control.

This not only opens up a space in the political centre that Badenoch’s Conservatives ought to be seeking to occupy. It also makes it all the more important for a centre-right opposition party to be holding Burnham’s Labour firmly to account.

The Tories are showing some progress on both. Most welcome is the re-embrace of business, in rhetoric and policy. Despite business scepticism given the Conservatives’ economic record in the 14 years to 2024, the party is earning a hearing for its emerging offer: lower taxes on work, wealth and business, with fewer regulatory constraints and stronger incentives to work and invest.

Halving employer national insurance contributions for 21- to 24-year-olds, cutting business rates for 250,000 high street businesses, simplifying Britain’s bloated tax system and abolishing a childcare support cliff edge for higher earners are encouragingly pro-business or pro-work policies. Badenoch’s pledge to scrap inheritance tax on family homes, with an additional £1mn tax-free allowance, is a stark contrast to Labour’s post-2024 extension of taxation on wealth.

Less favourable is the Conservative leader’s insistence, for now, that she would keep the unsustainable triple lock on pensions, which Burnham said he would loosen in 2030 to help fund a national care service. It betrays a tendency to play politics rather than to make savings wherever they can sensibly be found.

Among the party’s big weaknesses are its neuralgia over the EU. Burnham’s pragmatic pitch to improve the UK’s post-Brexit relationship with the bloc — messy and time-consuming as that may be — is one area in which many in business may favour Labour. The Conservative proposal to rip up any UK-EU deal made by Labour to liberalise trade in agrifood has raised concerns that the food industry could face ever-shifting regulatory regimes.

The Conservatives have also spent too long trying to ape Reform’s hardline stance on immigration, hoping to win back voters lost in 2024 — but risking alienating centrist waverers. Here, however, there were signs on Wednesday of a shift. Badenoch repudiated any idea of “uniting the right”, insisting Reform “are not like us, we are not like them”. In a sometimes emotional speech that decried “people” debating whether Badenoch’s mixed-race children were English, she appealed to Reform-leaning Tories to come home to her party.

A final issue is the shrunken parliamentary party’s shortage of talent beyond Badenoch herself; new shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith’s speech failed to enthuse despite sounding some of the right notes. The leader herself is beginning to show a little more political subtlety and depth. Her rebuilding of the broader party remains a work in progress, though it is showing moves in the right direction.

item.title: The important judgments for Healey in the coming Budget
item.author: Chris Giles
item.description: No fancy equations or AI models will illuminate the right path for the chancellor
item.content:encoded:
No fancy equations or AI models will illuminate the right path for the chancellor

Chris Giles

At a time of geopolitical tension and bond market volatility, the UK’s economic and public finance outlook is shrouded in uncertainty. No system of fancy equations will enable the Office for Budget Responsibility to produce perfect forecasts for the Budget. And no agentic John Maynard Keynes will reliably tell John Healey what he should do. Everything instead rests on sound judgments from both the fiscal watchdog and the chancellor.

By far the most consequential decision the OBR needs to make is to set the potential level of GDP at the end of its five-year forecasting horizon. This is an informed judgment, complicated this year by movements in its underlying drivers. The Office for National Statistics has revised productivity growth up and hours worked down. It has also revised the path of net migration down and is now advising everyone to focus on tax records rather than surveys to discern employment trends. These are weaker.

The OBR would be well advised therefore to judge that the potential growth of the UK economy is just a bit worse than in March, with hours and productivity growth cancelling each other out, while the scope for more employment growth is more than offset by lower migration. Together, these broad assumptions would generate a little less tax revenue than previously expected.

On top of that, the inflation profile will be higher due to the prolonged energy shock the UK has suffered in 2026. This will raise the costs of pension and welfare payments in future and is unlikely to generate a corresponding amount of additional tax revenue. The final piece of bad news is that higher interest rates will raise forecasts of government debt-servicing costs by roughly 0.3 per cent of GDP by the end of the decade.

You might notice that I have been able to talk about the economy and the public finances without any mention of fiscal headroom in billions of pounds. The final OBR judgment should be to ditch this unhelpful invention, follow the letter of the law and start reporting on the sustainability of the public finances as economists rather than officials seeking to get themselves noticed.

Putting this all together, the news Healey will receive from the OBR is likely to be unwelcome but not disastrous. The forecast path of deficit reduction will be slower and debt-servicing costs higher, but the UK will still be set to balance its current budget and stabilise its debt-to-GDP ratio by the end of the decade.

The chancellor’s core judgment will be to decide how to respond; the prime minister and his cabinet colleagues are fizzing with ideas but have few plans ready for implementation. It would be reasonable in these circumstances for Healey to deliver a steady-as-she-goes Budget so long as he meets the following conditions.

Any fiscal loosening in the early years of the forecast to meet Andy Burnham’s pledge to give people a bit of breathing space needs either to be credibly temporary or to be matched with spending cuts or tax rises in later years. That means there must not be a sustained discretionary fiscal loosening. It is OK for deficit reduction to be slower because the world has become more difficult, so long as the UK government does not aggravate the trends.

The deficit must also stay on a downward path. This will mean that any cost-of-living breathing space is followed by some tougher fiscal years towards the end of the parliament. Healey would be wise to put his political capital behind that necessity.

Finally, the chancellor should outline his longer-term strategy for tax and public spending. The aim will be to provide some reassurance to financial markets so that speculation can be held in check. Details are not necessary. These are difficult times in public finance. There is nothing more important than demonstrating the UK is facing them with sound judgments on both the forecasts and policy.

chris.giles@ft.com

item.title: Lex. Sleepy European telcos turn to data centre craze
item.description: With data centres, companies in the sector may finally be on to happier hunting grounds
item.content:encoded:
With data centres, companies in the sector may finally be on to happier hunting grounds

European telecoms groups have scant access to exciting investment trends. They operate in mature, competitive markets, grow their top lines by a couple of percentage points a year and struggle to lift returns above their cost of capital. But, in one aspect of their business at least, they now resemble much racier US neoclouds such as CoreWeave: Europe’s push for tech sovereignty is turning them into data centre builders.

In the UK, BT is partnering with US chipmaker Nvidia and Nscale to build up to 14 megawatts of AI data centre infrastructure across three existing BT sites. France’s Orange, together with private equity firm Morrison, is developing data centres with a €3bn investment that will increase its current capacity 10-fold, while Iliad too has earmarked €3bn for data centre infrastructure.

The sector doesn’t have a great record when it comes to jumping on to tech bandwagons. Just think of the giant debt piles accumulated in the 2000s by companies overpaying for 3G mobile licences and vainglorious mergers. But with data centres, they may finally be on to happier hunting grounds.

For one thing, they don’t have much competition. Europe is keen to reduce its reliance on US hyperscalers: domestic builders don’t run the risk of having to hand over data to the US administration, as could be the case with Google and Amazon operating on European soil. Deutsche Telekom has leaned into these fears, touting its services “made for Germany, made in Germany”. And, with the European hyperscaler conspicuously absent from the ecosystem the telecoms groups, which already run critical infrastructure and are tightly regulated, have an unimpeded shot at the prize.

Returns, too, come without taking on too much risk. In this cycle of telco investment, the big operators are teaming up with providers of tech and finance rather than just overextending their balance sheets and throwing around cash.

Europe’s sovereign cloud market will be worth $70bn next year, forecasts Polaris Market Research. That is small by hyperscaler standards — Anthropic alone will spend that much on AI infrastructure in a year and a bit, according to Reuters — but helpful for the sector’s pedestrian growth.

Chances are that these numbers will continue to grow. Canada’s decision last month to build its own sovereign broadband backbone to connect the country from coast to coast, rather than continue to route data through the US, highlights erstwhile allies’ anxiety. A fracturing world could pay dividends for tech-adjacent domestic companies.

louise.lucas@ft.com

item.title: We need a US debt conversation — will the Republicans have one?
item.author: Brendan Boyle
item.description: Borrowing heavily to finance tax cuts for the wealthy leaves us less prepared for emergencies when they come
item.content:encoded:
Borrowing heavily to finance tax cuts for the wealthy leaves us less prepared for emergencies when they come

Brendan Boyle

The writer represents Pennsylvania’s second congressional district and is the ranking member of the House Budget Committee

When the US national debt crossed $40tn in August, I knew exactly what Republicans would say: America spends too much money. 

Spending does matter and, as the top Democrat on the House Budget Committee, I am very conscious of how taxpayer dollars are spent and where this can be done better. However, my Republican colleagues who say that we got to $40tn because of spending alone are ignoring half the story. 

Over the past 25 years, major tax cuts, primarily benefiting the wealthy and large corporations, have reduced federal revenues by trillions of dollars. 

One analysis using data from the Congressional Budget Office (CBO) and Joint Committee on Taxation found that President George W Bush’s tax cuts, their extensions and Donald Trump’s 2017 tax law added roughly $10tn to the debt through 2023. Any honest account should acknowledge that Democrats also voted to make the Bush tax cuts permanent. 

But over the past 10 years, President Trump and Republicans have gone even further. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, passed in 2017, added nearly $2tn to the debt, according to the CBO. At the time Republicans promised that faster economic growth would make up for the lost revenue. It did not come close. 

Then last year, Trump and Republicans passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. That legislation, according to the CBO, will add a staggering $4.7tn to the deficit over the next decade, making it one of the most expensive pieces of legislation in US history. 

Tax cuts are not the sole reason for the debt. The government borrowed heavily to pay for wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. During the Great Recession and the Covid-19 pandemic, we spent a tremendous amount to keep the economy afloat and prevent economic devastation.

Those situations also show why America’s fiscal health matters. In times of emergency, the nation needs the capacity to borrow. Piling up structural debt during normal times, such as by borrowing heavily to finance tax cuts for the wealthy, leaves us less prepared for emergencies when they come. 

Another factor that has added to the debt, but is often left out of the story, is taxes that are owed but never collected. 

The Internal Revenue Service estimates that nearly $700bn in federal taxes owed for 2022 were not paid on time, and roughly $600bn of this will never be collected. Not all of that is fraud, but the scale of not complying with the tax code is enormous. 

Nevertheless, Republicans repeatedly cut IRS enforcement funding. That has had a serious impact. A report from the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration published in August showed that IRS audits brought in 35 per cent less in revenue in fiscal year 2025 than in the previous year. That sharp decrease has come after Trump, supported by Republicans, cut the number of IRS staff dedicated to audits by roughly 30 per cent. 

The negative impact of our deteriorating fiscal health can no longer be ignored, as it has been by many on both sides of the aisle. The national debt is now so large that annual net interest costs are projected to be higher than $2tn. Every dollar that goes towards servicing the debt is money we cannot use on healthcare, infrastructure or education. 

So, what do we do about it without asking working families to make sacrifices?  

First, large tax giveaways, especially to the wealthy, should not be permanent. They should face periodic non-partisan reviews on their impact and whether economic growth has covered the cost of the tax break. In addition, Congress should be forced to vote to renew them on an annual or biennial basis. Congress, rightfully so, carefully examines spending line by line. The same should be done for tax cuts.

Second, my Republican colleagues must get serious about tax enforcement. If they are truly serious about “waste, fraud and abuse” and tackling the deficit, they should join Democrats to give the IRS the resources to audit wealthy tax cheats and large corporations. 

The debt is $40tn and rising — quickly. Republicans have proved to be hypocrites on the issue. But that does not make the debt problem any less real.  

If they want a serious debate about how we got here and how we fix it, I am ready to have one. We need an honest discussion, followed by a credible plan, before it’s too late.

item.title: Kemi Badenoch’s European nightmare
item.author: Janan Ganesh
item.description: The biggest threat to this potential prime minister is that she defends an unpopular hard Brexit
item.content:encoded:
The biggest threat to this potential prime minister is that she defends an unpopular hard Brexit

Janan Ganesh

A while ago, this column advised readers to bet on the Conservatives winning the most seats at Britain’s next general election. The odds at the time were 13/2. Now? 3/1, and shortening. Don’t mention it.

Their leader Kemi Badenoch might soon be overpriced — more on which in a minute — but underpricing her was the real offence. It should have been obvious that people would tire of big government under Labour. Voters want tax cuts even at the expense of public services, and have done for a year. This is politics at its most thermostatic: the ruling idea sets off a counter-reaction. (Notice that “austerity” has not been cited as the national ill for a while.) The Tories’ poll rating is still in the sewer but it might just lag their better, underlying numbers on economic trust.

So, what’s all this about overcorrection? Well, one issue has undone talented Conservatives before: Europe. There is reason to think it shall again.

Scarcely one voter in three believes it was right to leave the EU. That figure has not moved for four years. A plurality favours much closer co-operation with the bloc, even if that entails accepting its rules. Total re-entry would be provocative. But imagine that Andy Burnham offers a fudge, such as single market membership. A fragmented left would at once consolidate behind Labour. The right would have to defend an unpopular status quo, citing — what? — Britain’s freedom to set lighter AI rules than Brussels, just as voters come to fear AI. If indeed Burnham did clinch a half-in deal with the EU, the Tories seem set to promise to reverse it in office. Could anything be sillier?

Foreign affairs never decided an election, Tories will argue. But the UK-EU relationship is different. It is inseparable from economic management, which is the paramount issue for voters. Some of the business leaders now despairing of Labour would endorse the single market.

Also, in two anglophone democracies of late, Canada and Australia, conservatives have lost winnable elections due to their association with the American right. That is, a foreign entity. A man of Burnham’s demagogic gifts can frame Badenoch’s anti-EU line as American servility. She is not Maga, no, but she is not not Maga. She made her name in US-flavoured culture debates. She got into a mess over the Iran war, reflexively backing America until that became untenable, at which point she backed off with a clumsiness that was hard to watch. If she defends pure Brexit, for the sake of US trade and perhaps AI frontier-model access, Labour should rejoice.

Britain has settled into a routine that should trouble Badenoch. Labour proposes some accommodation with the EU, the right alleges betrayal and . . . almost no one cares. Last week, Burnham outdid all the post-2016 prime ministers in calling Brexit a mistake that should at least be softened. His poll lead held. The Tories are right that voters don’t think much about the issue, but that means Burnham can do a lot without risk. Forget the next parliament. The time to torture the Tories is now. He could trade single-market access for rule-acceptance, sector by sector, Swiss-style, and dare them to oppose it. Their political prize for doing so would be, what exactly? A better third or fourth position in long-lost Red Wall seats?

And this is just the politics. The larger problem with the status quo is that it is bad in practice. Badenoch’s most appealing trait is a sort of engineer’s innocence. She seems to care about getting to (what she sees as) the right answer on a given subject. Most politicians let electoral calculation, tribal feeling or ideological priors muddle the cold act of problem-solving.

In private moments, the engineer in her must ask what the hardest of all possible Brexits has achieved. Essentially no European democracy chooses to be as cut off from the EU as Britain. Even Turkey is in the customs union. Switzerland, where independence is the national ethos, is three decades into a rolling negotiation with Brussels, in which it mostly gives ground. Norway, with mineral wealth galore, is in the Schengen visa-free zone. Most of the western Balkan states have candidate status.

You have to think of the EU in terms of general relativity: as a mass that bends space-time around it, forcing smaller entities into its orbit. Britain won’t resist the gravitation indefinitely, because it can’t. This is why the subject of Europe never goes away here. A place in the middle-to-outer orbit is destined to materialise. The question is whether Badenoch confronts it now, at a time of personal strength, or under duress later, when the untenability of hard Brexit becomes plain.

As the election approaches, she will have a voter in mind: an upper-middle earner who feels fleeced under a Labour government but recoils from Nigel Farage. That person might vote for a Conservative platform that offers no particular thaw with the EU. But not one that proposes to reverse an ongoing thaw. It would reek too much of dogma, of wilful disruptiveness.

If Badenoch is shrewd, she will let Burnham do the hard work of easing Brexit, then accept it as a fait accompli at the election, and win on the tax burden instead. If not? If she defends the status quo, or what would then be the status quo ante? Sell the bet at 2/1.

janan.ganesh@ft.com

item.title: Corporate climate risk picture is still murky
item.author: Simon Mundy
item.description: Setbacks have hit drive for expanded reporting by businesses
item.content:encoded:
Setbacks have hit drive for expanded reporting by businesses

Simon Mundy

Welcome back.

This month marks the centenary of Ernest Hemingway’s The Sun Also Rises, in which a character explains how he went bankrupt with the immortal phrase: “Gradually, then suddenly.”

Will the market response to climate change follow the same dynamic? And can better corporate reporting help avoid that danger?

Tackling the corporate climate data deficit

In late September 2016, Mark Carney took to a Berlin stage to warn of the risk of “a climate Minsky moment”.

The then Bank of England governor was alluding to the work of economist Hyman Minsky, who described how long periods of calm in the financial markets could set the stage for roiling panic. The gradual but severe progress of global warming — and the dramatic changes needed to tackle it — threatened to produce just such an outcome, Carney warned.

A crucial part of the solution, he added, would be more comprehensive and standardised disclosures by companies of the risks they faced around climate change and the energy transition. That, he said, would “help smooth price adjustments as opinions change, rather than concentrating them at a single climate Minsky moment”.

A decade on, progress on that agenda has been decidedly mixed — with some notable recent setbacks. Last week, UK authorities announced that listed companies would be allowed to take a “comply or explain” approach to new climate reporting rules that they had previously said would be mandatory. That came a few months after a similar announcement from Brazil.

In May, the US Securities and Exchange Commission formally proposed the scrapping of “overly burdensome and costly” climate disclosure rules introduced under the Biden administration.

Even the EU, long seen as the trailblazer for this area of regulation, this year dramatically reduced the scope of its sustainability reporting rules. These will now apply only to businesses with more than 1,000 employees and over €450mn in annual revenue — a change that’s reduced by roughly 85 per cent the number of companies required to report.

Yet global momentum in this area remains strong, insists Emmanuel Faber, head of the International Sustainability Standards Board. The ISSB was set up under the IFRS Foundation in November 2021 to create a single set of standards that companies around the world could use to report on environmental and social risks and opportunities.

Governments in 48 jurisdictions have now committed to use or align with the ISSB framework — a figure that is likely to rise to 50 by the end of this year, Faber says, with “frankly, incredible traction in Asia”. Notably, China has said it will introduce a mandatory reporting regime aligned with the ISSB standards, though many of the details remain unclear. South Korea in July expanded the scope of its sustainability reporting rules, citing this year’s turmoil in fossil fuel markets as a major factor.

And while the EU has decided to stick with its own sustainability reporting standards, it’s been collaborating with the ISSB to minimise friction between the two systems, Faber notes.

But whatever their regulators are up to, companies are facing growing pressure from investors for climate-related information beyond what the law requires them to share, says Tamara Tisminetzky, director of research at Sustainable Fitch. “Investors are not only asking for this kind of transparency, but they’re getting used to having it,” she says.

Investor appetite for this kind of data is set to keep rising as climate-related risks get harder to ignore. See, for example, this summer’s extreme heatwaves in Europe, which cost $128bn in lost output according to insurer Allianz, with companies from steelmaker Thyssenkrupp to chocolatier Lindt reporting business disruption and sales hits. Meanwhile, the continent’s big carmakers are providing a prime case study of “transition risk” as they struggle to cope with the rise of Chinese electric cars: shares in Volkswagen and Stellantis are down 62 and 74 per cent, respectively, in the past five years.

All this will create opportunities for companies that can help investors to make sense of the climate risks that companies are disclosing — and those they’re not. A flurry of deals this year highlights the growing interest in these businesses from some well-known financial sector names.

In June, the major European private equity firm Permira announced the buyout of the new for-profit business of CDP, which runs the biggest system of its kind collecting environmental information from thousands of global companies. In the same month, MSCI announced the $120mn takeover of climate-risk analytics firm First Street. Earlier in the year a joint venture between BlackRock and Temasek led a $100mn funding round into German sustainability software provider Osapiens, valuing it at more than $1bn. And last month proxy advisory firm Glass Lewis merged with sustainability analytics firm Clarity AI to build a bigger presence in the space.

There’s no question that, overall, the depth and breadth of climate-related corporate data has improved significantly since Carney’s 2016 speech. Technology advances, including in AI and satellite monitoring, promise to boost it further.

But the fundamental problem of incomplete, fragmented information that Carney identified remains — as does the risk of a climate Minsky moment. And even if a comprehensive, globally uniform reporting system were to be achieved, it would be no substitute for more ambitious policies to tackle the economic and financial risks of climate change, such as expanded carbon pricing.

Disclosure regulation can play an important role in pushing corporate leaders “to think about important issues systematically”, says Ben Caldecott, director of the sustainable finance programme at Oxford university. “But let’s put it in perspective . . . it won’t produce the big, major changes required.”

Smart reads

  • African governments have launched a new credit rating provider, to challenge the global agencies that they believe have given unfairly harsh ratings for African issuers.
  • The EU is moving to weaken its rules on pesticides, after successful lobbying from chemical and agricultural companies.
  • California will soon vote on whether to introduce a wealth tax on its 246 billionaires. The result could change the US, writes Edward Luce.

item.title: Lex. AI agents could cost banks $500bn — by winning savers better rates
item.description: But banks will gain from AI as well as lose
item.content:encoded:
But banks will gain from AI as well as lose

It is a fact of banking that the less you care, the more your bank earns. Lenders make a handsome profit by taking money customers leave idle in their bank accounts and investing it at higher rates. Agentic AI, the buzz-phrase of the moment, will upset this cosy arrangement. And while it would take more than that to knock banks off their perch, they have quite a lot to lose.

The theory is that AI assistants like Meta’s Muse could help customers put trillions of dollars of “lazy money” to better use. That could just mean flagging when a saver could get a better deal on their surplus balance. Or more ambitiously, automatically sweeping the excess into a money-market fund offering more than the nearly nil paid on instant-access deposits today.

This would be a big change. Banks make about two-thirds of their income on the spread between what they pay and what they lend. JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo hold $1.6tn of non-interest bearing deposits — 16 per cent of their liabilities. Paying a 3 per cent rate on those would cost them $47bn a year, almost half of their collective annual earnings.

Will bank profit really evaporate to that extent? Not likely. Shrill talk of “agentic bank runs” reckons without the manifold frictions that stop customer funds from flying hither and thither. The simplest barrier is trust: will households hand control over their finances to companies known for moving fast and breaking things? Who takes the rap if the agent sends funds to the wrong place?

But AI will no doubt make customers less inert — and there’s a way to estimate what that will cost their banks. Whenever a lender buys another in the US, it must quantify the financial benefit from acquiring sticky, cheap deposits, as opposed to raising funds in the market. This is called a “core deposit intangible”, and is typically equivalent to 2 or 3 per cent of the relevant account balances, according to analysis by Mercer Capital.

Run that back-of-the-envelope ratio across all US banks, with their $20tn of deposits of which roughly 80 per cent are “core”, and it comes out at about $500bn. That, in other words, is the chunk of equity value banks would lose if all of those deposits received market-like returns. It’s about one-tenth of the total value of listed US banks, based on S&P Capital IQ data.

True, banks will gain from AI as well as lose. Cutting costs, pricing lending more effectively and avoiding costly human error — no more Citigroup-style bungled $900mn wire transfers — should all generate gains. Bank of America chief Brian Moynihan said last month that his institution spent $400mn on AI improvements and saw $800mn of benefits. As agents gain traction, the fruits of efficiency drives will increasingly flow to depositors as well as shareholders.

For now, there are bigger things to fret about. More than half of bank investors think Federal Reserve rate hikes are the biggest risk to valuations, lender Truist found in an investor survey at the end of September. Very few cited the threat from bots. And as JPMorgan chief Jamie Dimon regularly warns, the banking system hasn’t weathered a proper credit downturn for well over a decade, and one is long overdue. The real agents of chaos are already with us.

john.foley@ft.com

item.title: Five things Kemi Badenoch must do to win
item.author: Stephen Bush
item.description: While Tory leader’s popularity is clear, she must still neutralise areas of weakness and move closer to the Labour government
item.content:encoded:
While Tory leader’s popularity is clear, she must still neutralise areas of weakness and move closer to the Labour government

Stephen Bush

Good morning from Birmingham. Ahead of Kemi Badenoch’s speech to Conservative Party conference, here are some thoughts on the broad things opposition leaders need to do to be successful.

Lessons in Kemistry

What should an opposition party do to improve its standing? The usual checklist is as follows:

  • Get a popular leader, or at least one who is less unpopular than their rivals.
  • Move towards the party that defeated you. There is usually a reason why voters picked it, which should give you a clue about what direction you need to move in.
  • Neutralise your areas of weakness. In our country, for the Tories that typically requires that they minimise fears that they will knacker public services; for Labour that generally requires it to minimise fears that it will spend like a drunk in a casino.
  • Convince voters that you are competent and that you’ve changed.
  • Form a viable programme for government.

Tony Blair and David Cameron are examples of opposition leaders who made the transition to government by pulling off all five.

Keir Starmer managed four but failed the fifth point on forming a viable programme for government, which is why his premiership got into trouble so quickly.

And Margaret Thatcher has an outsized grasp on the imagination of most UK political parties because she is the only opposition leader since the war to have managed to pull off all of the steps other than the second on moving towards the party that defeated you.

Whether it is a Labour or Conservative opposition, parties do not like having to move towards their opponent. So the usual failure mode of an opposition leader is to construct all sorts of narratives about why they are a Thatcher-like figure and why this is a 1979 moment where they win not by moving to the centre but by shifting away from it.

The paradox of the Conservatives under Badenoch is that they are succeeding on the first point on leader popularity. But they are consciously not moving towards the party that beat them in 2024; they are not, per the polls, neutralising their areas of weakness; and most voters do not think the party has changed.

(They are also very far from having a viable programme for government. But the election is three years away, so I don’t think that tells us all that much at this stage.)

A big part of why Badenoch is popular is that her House of Commons appearances have performed well on social media, most importantly on Facebook. Under Starmer, people responded positively to her confidence in attacking a government they came to intensely dislike.

This is a great asset — there is a reason why I put it first on the checklist! — not least because it gives Badenoch the political latitude to go about achieving the other four points. The big question for her in her speech today, and more broadly, is whether she is willing or able to do so.

Now try this

I had a lovely dinner last night at Blacklock, a small chain that has spread from London to Manchester and, crucially for our purposes, to Birmingham. Food, service and company were all exemplary.

Top stories today

  • Paint the town red | The Green Party is braced for loss at tomorrow’s Holborn and St Pancras by-election, with bookmakers giving Zack Polanski a less than 12 per cent chance of beating the Labour candidate, Sagal Abdi-Wali.


  • ‘The Putin Tax’ | The economic impact of Russian hostile activity against Britain totals at least £2bn to £2.5bn annually, according to a new report by Labour MP Graeme Downie, the vice-chair of the all-party parliamentary group on rearmament.
  • Upset the apple cart | UK producers have expressed concern at the “huge uncertainty” created by Conservative Party proposals to rip up any deal with the EU to remove post-Brexit trade barriers on the food and agriculture sectors.
