item.title: Neat tricks to help French bonds
item.author: Daire MacFadden
item.description: And why they won’t work
item.content:encoded:
And why they won’t work

Daire MacFadden

Good morning. Everything is terrible and stocks are at record highs. OK, “terrible” might be an exaggeration, but corporate America is starting to suffer from the rise in borrowing costs, and for good measure, here’s the CEO of the world’s largest independent oil trader warning of $200-a-barrel oil. And yet the S&P 500 has never had it so good. As we’ve discussed already this week, in this newsletter and in its sister podcast, the answer to this apparent madness of course lies in AI. Tell us why this is fine, actually: unhedged@ft.com.

Uh OAT

French government borrowing costs have shot up more than 1.5 percentage points since the start of the Iran war and more than 0.5 percentage points in just the past month. We’re not quite in debt crisis territory, but we’re not far off: the all-important OAT-Bund spread — the difference between French and German 10-year borrowing costs — peaked at 1.6 percentage points last week before falling back to just shy of 1.3 percentage points yesterday. 

The start of the budget process last week may have halted the sell-off but it hasn’t done much to dispel the sense of dread that’s threatening to hang over the French economy from now until the presidential elections next spring. For yesterday’s Big Read, a team of our intrepid news colleagues summed up what’s at stake:

Tensions are rising as the confrontation over the budget deepens and the country prepares for an April presidential election that could end in a face-off between the far right and hard left.

The fear among investors is that the country could be tipped into a full-blown debt crisis that could not only rock France’s economy but also shake the Eurozone.

On Monday, the euro fell to a 17-month low against the dollar as worries intensified about the impact of the French debt sell-off on the single-currency area.

Obviously, the best possible outcome would be for France to pass the budget and get serious about fiscal consolidation, but we’re not counting on it; the country hasn’t run a balanced budget since 1974. Unhedged would never wish for a full-blown debt crisis, but absent a structural fix to the toxic mix of low growth and high debt, we can almost understand the arguments of those that do. Until then, we’re stuck in something of a stalemate.

But if there’s one thing a looming crisis is good for, it’s the increasingly outlandish ideas about how to fix the mess at little or no cost (aka “one neat trick to rid you of this troublesome bond market”). Here, in no particular order, are a few of the proposals in the air.

The European Central Bank should intervene in the French bond market. This is the idea that the central bank should use its balance sheet to mop up OATs, bring down yields and restore calm. Market discussion has focused on the transmission protection instrument, an as-yet untested tool introduced in 2022 to “counter unwarranted, disorderly market dynamics that pose a serious threat to the transmission of monetary policy across the euro area”. Never rule out some kind of fudge to justify wheeling the TPI out, but right now the ECB has little mandate to use it. OATs are being repriced but the market is functioning fine. It would work, but it’s probably not going to happen, at least not without a big outbreak of infectious market instability. Activating the TPI for what is largely a political jam of France’s own making would be extremely controversial and almost certainly trigger political and legal backlash across the wider Eurozone.

The ECB should stop shrinking its balance sheet. Since 2023, the ECB has been letting the bonds it purchased under quantitative easing to roll off at maturity rather than reinvesting the proceeds in new bonds. Its balance sheet reduction programme has been among the slowest of the lot, but there’s no question that the retreat of central banks from government bond markets has put upward pressure on rates. Continuing to reduce the balance sheet during a global sell-off is unhelpful. It should probably stop. Here’s former ECB policymaker Lorenzo Bini Smaghi making the case:

[R]eturning to normal has been presented by the central bank as an “obligation”, motivated apparently more by nostalgia for the world that existed before the financial crisis than by rigorous analysis. In fact, there is nothing inherently “normal” about the size of a central bank’s balance sheet, especially when underlying economic and market conditions change in fundamental ways over time.

This may be the least contentious proposal. But it’s not without its issues. What it would mean in practice is that the ECB would restart bond purchases, replacing maturing bonds with new ones, to keep the balance sheet at its current level. Some will call this QE in all but name. Let them. There’s a difference between expanding the balance sheet to stimulate the economy and choosing not to shrink it during market volatility.

France should cancel the debt it owes to itself. OK, we feel like we might lose brain cells even trying to explain this one. But this is the idea from the far-left party La France Insoumise to convert €488bn of the OATs that the Eurosystem bought during QE into perpetual, zero-coupon debt. In other words, the bonds would stay on the central bank’s balance sheet, but France would never pay interest on them and never have to repay the principal. The problem is the central bank would still need to pay out interest on the reserves it created to purchase the debt and the bond market might take fright at a government so willing to meddle with its debt obligations.

Of the three, only the QT pause has any chance of happening, and it would barely move the needle.

One good read

FIMA protectionism

item.title: Who’d be betting against Webuild, the builder that built Italy?
item.author: Bryce Elder
item.description: Treni, porti, politica, ma nessun ponte
item.content:encoded:
Treni, porti, politica, ma nessun ponte

Bryce Elder

Let’s not entertain stereotypes. Italian construction companies should be approached no differently from any other companies. The sometimes-fraught environment in which they have operated in the past should absolutely not lead an observer to jump to any conclusions.

The Italian construction company we’re writing about today is Webuild. It’s a civil engineering contractor that employs more than 85,000 people and has operations that span five continents. The company can trace its own history back to 1906, though its current form owes more to Salini Costruttori’s acquisition of sector peer Impregilo in 2014. The stock is listed on Borsa Italiana, where it has a €2bn market valuation.

We’re writing about Webuild because Italian daily Il Fatto Quotidiano published a story last month saying the company “wants €22bn in extra costs” tied to Italian railway projects.

Citing a letter sent by Webuild CEO Pietro Salini to the government in late July, Il Fatto reported that Webuild had variation claims amounting to €22bn across 18 construction sites for contracts with the state railway company’s infrastructure arm, PNRR, that had an original value of around €30bn.

Webuild has since filed a complaint with Consob, the Italian market regulator, that accuses Il Fatto of market manipulation. The company said:

The article contains statements that are manifestly false and entirely unfounded, distributed in a manner liable to have a significant and distortive impact on the Group’s share price, which immediately recorded a decline following its publication. The Company will assess every action necessary to protect its reputation and the orderly trading of its shares on the stock market before the competent authorities.

[ . . . ] The Company has not made any “request for extra costs”: it has sent formal, confidential communications to the relevant institutions concerning contractual obligations that have already accrued — including receivables for works completed and certified, recovery of costs already incurred, and contractual advances provided for by law.

The €22 billion referred to in the article, misleadingly characterised as requests made to the Government, instead represent the total amount recorded in the works accounting registers in accordance with the procedures provided for under public contracts. A substantial portion of these amounts has already been submitted to the Technical Advisory Boards, independent bodies provided for by law and also composed of members appointed by the contracting authority, which are responsible in providing an opinion on the relevant matters. Presenting this figure as a request for public funds addressed to the Government constitutes a distorted and unfounded representation of the contractual and institutional reality of the matter.

Webuild confirmed to us that the letter cited by Il Fatto is genuine. “The Company did not circulate and does not comment on the contents of confidential correspondence beyond what it has already stated publicly,” said a Webuild spokesperson.

Il Fatto is an independent, small-circulation paper that tilts anti-establishment. Its journalists responded by updating its story with more from the letter, which has the subject line: “scaduto, riserve iscritte e recupero anticipazioni. Situazione di grave squilibrio economico finanziario e richiesta di decisioni e di una road map entro la prima settimana di agosto 2026”.

Any translation of legal terminology introduces misalignment risks. Our best attempt with the above text is: “Overdue payments, recorded reserves, and recovery of advances. Situation of severe economic and financial imbalance, and request for decisions and a roadmap by the first week of August 2026”. All the English translations in this post are approximate.

As reported by Il Fatto, Salini wrote in the letter that “the contracts currently under execution are burdened by recorded reserves of approximately €22bn, of which €13bn refer to costs already fully incurred” and that “no decision has been made on this dispute through ordinary contractual channels”.

In Italian law, reserves (“riserve”) are formal claims registered by a public procurement contractor against the state. A contractor has to keep following the site director’s orders, and can’t unilaterally walk off site before the job’s complete, but can claim all potential excess costs by immediately booking a claim in the official accounts.

The goal is transparency. The client learns of potential overruns as soon as they arise, meaning it can top up funding, rework the project, or find an amicable settlement. Contractors must set an upper bound on their overrun compensation claims that cannot be exceeded.

Before any large public project begins, the authority and its contractors appoint a Technical Advisory Committee of representatives and independent experts (“il Collegio Consultivo Tecnico”) that signs off design changes and acts as an informal arbitrator. As work continues, the CCT weeds the reserves book for any claim that has been exaggerated, is unsupported, or was the fault of the contractors themselves.

The state gets its project delivered without intractable decision bottlenecks and stings in the tail. Contractors can avoid pending legal claims that would starve them of working capital. The system mostly seems to work. Very few government contractor disputes end up in court, and only a handful go to formal arbitration.

All that background is because Webuild’s complaint requires some interpretation.

Salini’s letter to the government identifies €6bn–€7bn of “additional costs”. This, Salini says, is 29 per cent of the total value claimed — 29 per cent being the CCTs’ historical reserve recognition rate. It’s a net compensation estimate, in effect, whereas the headline Webuild has objected to was citing the €22bn gross maximum.

The letter also refers to costs “in the order of €10bn” that comprise “additional resources — in terms of both budget allocation and cash flow — required to complete the projects”. The amount is said to cover “price revisions and the actual volume of work needed for completion, neither of which is accounted for in the current financial plans”.

Salini says in the letter that the CCT had been acting too slowly to clear the backlog of disputes. Construction at its current pace “is no longer sustainable in the absence of decisions”, Salini is said to add. He is reported to propose amending CCT regulations to allow the termination of its mandate, “in the event of unbalanced decisions or timelines incompatible with the project’s needs”.

The letter also flags an “immediate cash requirement” of €2.1bn, which could be funded “by rescheduling works not currently underway”. As things stand, Salini says, “the more work we do, the more our financial position deteriorates”.

Webuild said in its Consob complaint:

It should also be clarified that the short-term cash requirement referred to in the news, amounting to approximately €2.1 billion, is directly and exclusively related to the continuation of construction sites currently under execution on behalf of public contracting authorities. It is not related to any stand-alone cash requirements of the Group as a whole, which, on the contrary, confirms its 2026 guidance.

Much of the above may look like typical brinkmanship between a builder and a public authority, while talk of a deteriorating financial position could be dismissed as scaremongering. With €110mn of reported net cash on the balance sheet at the 2026 half-year, and a target for net cash to exceed €300mn by the year-end, Webuild’s short-term liquidity shouldn’t be a worry.

The political angle is much harder to read.

In its half-year results, Webuild reported €5.9bn of contract liabilities (meaning the value of billed work that’s not yet done). Advances for the Italian railway contracts and a new breakwater for the port of Genoa during the period helped offset the loss of Neom’s scrapped Trojena Dam project in Saudi Arabia.

This deepened Webuild’s near-term reliance on its home territory, which accounts for about 34 per cent of group revenue but is 70 per cent of contract liabilities:

Webuild has been a relative winner from Italy’s post-pandemic National Resilience and Recovery Plan, which was heavily reworked after Giorgia Meloni’s centre-right government came to power in 2022. The recovery fund’s single largest recipient is RFI, Italy’s rail network owner, which has thrown money at contractors including Webuild to speed up project delivery and meet an August 2026 completion milestone set by the EU.

Webuild told us:

All PNRR milestones regarding railway projects have been achieved to date. On payments: following the allocation of resources from Italian Ministry of Economy and Finance and Ministry of Infrastructure, and Transport, Employer RFI has started partially settling overdue invoices. We have received partial payments in respect of outstanding amounts. Discussions with Government and with Employer are in progress.

The contract liabilities line of the balance sheet statement is exactly where an analyst would expect to see evidence of pre-payments for high-value, quick-delivery work. All else equal, liabilities would normalise once these exceptional jobs are delivered, while any project cost overruns would be assumed to eat more quickly into the downpayments. And of course, since the cash was collected when the liability was created, revenue recognition for work done won’t generate new cash.

Managing group liquidity through the tumult is no easy task. Any disputes with government officials over expenses incurred would add an unwelcome uncertainty.

As we said earlier, €110mn of net cash should give plenty of flex, even for a company that’s involved in the consortium financing of complex long-term infrastructure projects.

Financial assets are, to state the obvious, on the asset side of the balance sheet. Their recognition and measurement under IFRS 9 are subject to review by an independent auditor. Nevertheless, understanding how easily these assets could be used to pay off debt requires some judgment. It might not be simple for a company to draw on its financial assets at short notice if they are held in escrow or restricted by contractual agreements, particularly when third parties are involved.

Webuild reported at the 2026 half-year that it had €806mn of current financial assets (meaning that they’re expected to be converted into cash within 12 months), nearly 93 per cent of which was in the form of loans and receivables to third parties. Non-current financial assets (meaning they fall due beyond 12 months) were €245mn, mostly in the form of loans and receivables to unconsolidated group companies and other related parties. The sums are not insignificant.

On the liabilities side of the balance sheet, Webuild’s gross debt was €3.3bn at the half-year:

Metrics would look better if Webuild were ever allowed to break ground on the Strait of Messina bridge to link Sicily with the Italian mainland. The country’s audit court last year denied approval of a €10.6bn contract awarded to a Webuild-led Eurolink consortium to build the bridge on the basis that it would breach EU rules on public procurement and the environment.

Critics of the Messina bridge plan say it concentrates political power and enriches private interests for benefits to the region that are unproven at best. The contract award process was also atypical. As the FT reported last October:

The original tender took place in 2006, when Milan-listed builder Impregilo won with a €3.8bn bid. After the project was scrapped Impregilo, acquired by WeBuild in 2014, filed a lawsuit against Rome seeking €700mn in damages — a case WeBuild has now agreed to drop in exchange for Meloni’s government “reactivating” the contract. [University of Messina constitutional law professor Antonio] Saitta questions the legality of the arrangement. “This resurrection of the old project with the old contractors is not possible under the constitution or European law,” said the lawyer.

In June, the Rome Public Prosecutor’s Office said it had launched an investigation into allegations of corruption in connection with the project.

Webuild told FTAV that it “has no ongoing investigation before the Rome’s Public Prosecutor’s Office” and cannot comment in relation to third parties. “The Company maintains rigorous compliance and control systems [ . . . ] and fully co-operates with the Authorities whenever requested,” it added.

None of the above should be news to Webuild investors. Fitch rates the company’s debt on a long-term B+, meaning highly speculative, while S&P is one notch below investment grade at BB+.

Having hit a 10-year high last August, the shares are down by more than 50 per cent:

And short interest — a volatile measure due to the stock’s less than 25 per cent free float — has moved a bit higher than the market average:

In an upgrade note published in November 2025, S&P welcomed Webuild’s “strong order backlog, disciplined contract management, and leading positions in key markets in low-risk geographies”, while also flagging a reliance on relatively few big projects, and that advance payments on its balance sheet were “well above the peers in relative terms”. Operating cash flow improvement was uncertain, with management’s ability to deliver unproven, S&P said.

Investors in construction companies are jittery by default about cash. Carillion’s collapse in 2018 gave everyone a lesson in how premature revenue recognition can flatter reported figures, and how aggressive use of supply-chain finance can hide leverage by turning bank borrowing into operating cash flow.

Webuild operates in the same sector that Carillion once did, but shouldn’t be assumed to share any other characteristics. What we can say is that the same sorts of funds who bet against Carillion have taken an interest in Webuild.

It’s a very different proposition. Salini comes from a Roman construction dynasty whose fortunes were built over generations. The company his grandfather founded built Rome’s Stadio dei Cipressi. His father expanded the business into Africa on the back of state-backed development and aid programmes.

Salini, on taking charge in 1994, consolidated power first with the takeover of Impregilo then with the rescue of troubled peer Astaldi, helped by an investment from state-owned Cassa Depositi e Prestiti, which remains a key shareholder. Webuild is deeply entwined with the Italian establishment.

An Italian parliamentary report last month cited figures showing that more than €27bn of Webuild’s €46.6bn backlog at the end of June related to Italian public contracts, the majority in rail. It describes Webuild as having acquired a position of “substantial monopoly” in large public works following the state-backed consolidation of the construction industry. Webuild says it wins tenders like any other company and strongly disputes the characterisation that it has a domestic monopoly.

Rome’s own budget constraints add another layer of complication. Meloni’s government has been cutting spending to ensure that Italy’s fiscal deficit stays below an EU threshold. And while Italy’s railways upgrade spending comes largely from the EU, a public procurement contractor with a large state shareholder can’t be seen to take a significantly different line to government during a cost-of-living crisis.

It all makes Webuild a difficult stock on which to take a view. The story is as much about politics as what’s reported on the balance sheet. As we said at the top, stereotypes can be unhelpful.

Further reading:
— Why Sicilians hate Meloni’s bridge (FT)

item.title: Tribology makes the economic world go round
item.author: Anjana Ahuja
item.description: The science of friction and wear plays a central role in making industry run more smoothly
item.content:encoded:
The science of friction and wear plays a central role in making industry run more smoothly

Anjana Ahuja

The writer is a science commentator

In the early 1960s, just after Labour leader Harold Wilson rose to power on his promise of harnessing the “white heat of technology”, the British engineer-turned-steelworks boss and entrepreneur Peter Jost sensed his moment.

Jost, with a background in lubricants and a well-oiled contacts book stretching across industry, academia and politics, persuaded the government to commission a report into the kind of machinery failures afflicting steelworks all over Europe. The 1966 Jost report championed lubrication, unsurprisingly, but also laid the groundwork for a new discipline called tribology, the science and technology of how surfaces move against each other, creating friction and wear. Jost even consulted the editor of the Oxford English Dictionary before settling on the name, based on the Greek word tribo, meaning “to rub”.

Writ large, tribology is the discipline that literally keeps parts of the economy moving — and, like so much research that focuses on prevention, remains largely invisible. And yet, 60 years on, one of the report’s key messages remains relevant: that the unseen business of optimising surface interactions, such as tyre against asphalt, at an industrial scale can save vast amounts of energy and raise GDP.

“The irony is that tribology affects almost everything we use, yet most people have never heard the word,” says Daniele Dini, professor of tribology at Imperial College London, accurately describing my own experience of discovering the term last week in a Physics World essay. Without tribology, Dini adds, “machines would wear out rapidly, vehicles would consume much more fuel, manufacturing processes would be less efficient, and many medical devices would simply not function reliably”. 

Substances like toothpaste, shaving cream and cosmetics are all triumphs of tribology, as is the action of swiping a phone. Our lives are filled with carefully calibrated surface contacts to ensure a suitable balance of grip, feel, resistance, texture and motion. Robert Wood, professor of surface engineering and tribology at the University of Southampton, describes toothpaste as “a carefully engineered tribological slurry”, designed to remove debris from teeth without stripping enamel or damaging gums.

More widely, Wood characterises tribology as “one of the enabling technologies that silently underpins industrial productivity” in sectors including wind and nuclear power generation, automotive, rail, aerospace, biomedical implants — including joint replacements — and food processing. It can comprise the study of ball bearings, lubricants, coatings and additives in an industrial factory; while oral tribology looks at the friction between food particles and tongue, palate and teeth, to ensure that ice cream tastes creamy.

Energy use is a vital consideration. Not all a car’s fuel, for example, is spent on going from A to B. Some is expended on overcoming the friction between tyre and road surface, some to counter aerodynamic losses, and some to make up for friction losses within the engine and transmission.

“Despite its huge economic impact, tribology remains less visible than fields such as AI, robotics, semiconductors or biotechnology,” Wood says. That could be because it cuts across existing disciplines, including materials science, chemistry and computing.

Tribology is a central concern in the path to net zero (Wood chairs a committee advising government on the relevant issues). Wind turbine gearboxes regularly fail before the end of their design life, sometimes because lubricant films on their moving parts are prone to shearing with changes in wind speed and direction. Scientists are also exploring the “triboelectric effect”, in which the rubbing of surfaces is used to generate electricity.

Future tribological goals include predicting and preventing wear, rather than measuring it after it happens, and the development of sustainable lubricants. Advances like graphene and materials that are smooth at the atomic scale are also raising hopes of “superlubricity”, where friction between moving parts drops to near zero. If scaled up, that would revolutionise energy efficiency.

It is all a long way from Jost and, before him, Leonardo da Vinci, who, according to forensic engineering professor and tribologist Sarah Hainsworth from Durham University, scribbled notes about friction in his 1493 Codex Forster. It is even further from the ancient Egyptians, who applied oil and fats to the sled runners used to move the stone blocks for building the pyramids.

Throughout history, it seems, the course of tribology can always run that little bit smoother.

item.title: Lex. If supermarket M&A is back, Sainsbury’s is in a sweet spot
item.description: Consolidation makes sense because there are too many stores chasing a market where demand is not growing
item.content:encoded:
Consolidation makes sense because there are too many stores chasing a market where demand is not growing

There is one big takeaway from recent merger discussions between Sainsbury’s and its rival Morrisons: UK supermarkets no longer believe mergers are completely unthinkable. If they are right, and the competition watchdog has softened its hawkish stance on consolidation among the country’s grocers, it ought to be good for Sainsbury’s itself — and bad for market leader Tesco.

Why supermarkets would like to merge is no mystery. There are too many of them, chasing a market where demand is not growing. Discount chains Aldi and Lidl have taken about 10 percentage points of market share over the past decade, taking sales from private-equity-owned Morrisons and Asda, and profitability from everyone. Tesco generates an operating margin of only 4 per cent. Sainsbury’s manages about 3 per cent. Bigger supermarkets are better at fighting price wars.

Until recently, tie-ups weren’t on the cards: the Competition and Markets Authority blocked a proposed union of Sainsbury’s and Asda in 2019. Since then, however, it has changed its definition of discount retailers to include them on the same terms as supermarkets. Factoring them in fully would change the calculus on national market share and competition within specific regions, two of the most important considerations.

In any future consolidation, Sainsbury’s is best placed to play kingmaker. With 15 per cent of the market, it could combine with either Morrisons or Asda and still be smaller than Tesco in national market share terms. Its skew to the south of England also means it could buy either Morrisons or Asda, both of which have larger footprints in the north, without having to dispose of too many stores.

Having broken off talks with Morrisons already, Sainsbury’s risks seeing its struggling rival combine with Asda instead. The two would have roughly 20 per cent of the national market, overtaking Sainsbury’s as the number two. But both businesses have large positions in the north of England, meaning they would probably have to dispose of a big chunk of their store base. Sainsbury’s would be an obvious potential buyer, and — as a larger operator — would likely be able to outbid smaller groups such as Waitrose and Marks and Spencer.

Besides, it would be rash to conclude that Sainsbury’s and Morrisons can’t still find terms that appeal to both sides. The sticking point may well be price: CD&R bought Morrisons for £9.8bn, equivalent to 9 times ebitda; Sainsbury’s trades at nearer 5. But there is much to be gained if that obstacle can be surmounted. In 2018, the retailer estimated that buying Asda would enable it to lower prices on essentials by 10 per cent. Achieving that would roughly halve the gap with the discount chains.

What, then, becomes of the market leader? While Tesco might be able to pick up assets here and there, with a near 28 per cent market share and widespread local presence it is too big to take part in any meaningful consolidation. It has had a good run of late: since 2020, it has grown its market share by 1.3 percentage points. There’s no potential combination that would be bigger than Tesco, at least — but an outbreak of M&A would give it a run for its money.

gaia.freydefont@ft.com

item.title: Lex. Bank mergers arrive in Europe with a whimper rather than a bang
item.description: More banking consolidation requires things that don’t yet exist, such as harmonised regulation and acquiescent local politicians
item.content:encoded:
More banking consolidation requires things that don’t yet exist, such as harmonised regulation and acquiescent local politicians

Europe has a Nimby problem when it comes to banks. Politicians, regulators and executives agree the continent needs cross-border consolidation, just as long as it’s not their banks being consolidated. An agreement between France’s BPCE and Spain’s Sabadell offers an imperfect way to tiptoe around the issue.

BPCE has bought a “friendly” 7 per cent stake in Sabadell, worth around €1.2bn at Monday’s closing price. It will take a seat on Sabadell’s board and the two groups will consider ways to work together. That could mean, for example, BPCE-owned Natixis providing investment banking services to Sabadell’s business customers. BPCE says it won’t lift its holding above 9.9 per cent.

BPCE will be hoping the capital buys it some of the upside of an acquisition — in the form of indirect exposure to the fast-growing Spanish economy — without the political wrangling. European cross-border deals tend not to include many cost savings, owing to the continent’s patchwork of different regulations, so it isn’t missing out on much there. 

If BPCE did eventually decide it wanted full control, spending a few years getting to know Sabadell’s board and local politicians could smooth the way. In the meantime, it is busy with the integration of Novo Banco, which it bought for €6.4bn last year. Taking a stake in Sabadell makes it harder for other bidders to swoop in while it is distracted. Sabadell, meanwhile, can focus on its standalone strategy without worrying about another hostile bid, after it spent 18 months fending off local rival BBVA. 

UniCredit’s Andrea Orcel has had success with a more aggressive version of this strategy. The Italian bank earned healthy returns from investments in Germany’s Commerzbank and Greece’s Alpha Bank even before it launched a bid to take control of Commerz earlier this year. And, once it became clear that UniCredit was likely to win, previously recalcitrant German politicians became more willing to negotiate.

There are downsides, however. Minority investments tie up capital that could be used elsewhere, and give financial exposure without much control — Sabadell and BPCE are on the same page for now, but a crisis or simply a change of strategy could leave the French bank lumbered with a stake to offload at a loss. And if the mooted strategic partnership were truly attractive, it should be possible without BPCE taking a stake. Any investment, then, needs to be attractive on its own terms — banks shouldn’t buy in solely as a means to an end.

Step back, and there’s a bigger issue. Europe needs larger banks to support investments in defence, energy and infrastructure. That is why former central banker Mario Draghi and others have been pushing for banking consolidation. But that requires things that don’t yet exist, such as harmonised regulation and acquiescent local politicians.

Those projects are needed now, not in 10 years. So while slow-motion takeovers might be the best available way for bank investors to edge towards a more efficient industry, for Europe more broadly they are very much a consolation prize.

nicholas.megaw@ft.com

item.title: How much longer can the world absorb the Iran shock?
item.author: Martin Wolf
item.description: The disruption to oil supply, oil prices and the world economy has been surprisingly manageable so far
item.content:encoded:
The disruption to oil supply, oil prices and the world economy has been surprisingly manageable so far

Martin Wolf

The war that was intended to deliver a swift overthrow of the Iranian regime is now in its eighth month, with no end in sight. So, what might happen next? My preliminary conclusion is that one should never underestimate human stupidity or human ingenuity. So far it is a rough draw between the two. How long will this last? That is the question.

In a devastating analysis, John Mearsheimer of the University of Chicago describes the war on Iran as “The Mother of All Strategic Blunders”.

Among other things, he notes, the US went into the war on the false claim that Iran was on the verge of acquiring a nuclear weapon; it thought air power alone would produce regime change, which has never worked; it had no contingency plan for dealing with Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz. It has also failed to achieve any of its four principal objectives — regime change, ending Iran’s nuclear enrichment capability, ending its long-range missile capability and ending its support for Hamas, Hizbollah and the Houthis. The closure of the strait has done significant damage to the international economy and may do much more; and the US alliance structure (in the Gulf and elsewhere) has been damaged. All this, moreover, is only about half of the full charge sheet.

The stupidity is indeed impressive. Even now we cannot guess how it ends. Yet there is a counter-argument. The war may indeed be a strategic blunder. But the economic damage has been surprisingly modest. As Johannes Urpelainen of the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies noted in August, “Many experts initially thought that this supply disruption would send oil prices to USD 200 per barrel, causing massive inflation and a global recession. Instead, oil prices peaked at USD 126 per barrel in April 2026.” Today, the real price of crude oil is still near its long-run average since 1972. (See charts.)

How can this be, given that Fatih Birol, head of the International Energy Agency, said in March this was “the greatest global energy security threat in history”? The ingenuity is the answer.

Urpelainen notes that: “First, the energy transition has reduced the global economy’s dependence on oil. Second, supply chains have proven resilient and adaptive. Third, producers outside the Middle East have acted fast to produce more oil and natural gas. Finally, drawdowns of global oil inventories have filled the remaining gap.” Flexibility is notably true of the Gulf. As former diplomat Mohammed Elsoukkary writes: “by the end of September preliminary estimates placed regional crude exports at approximately 16.3 million barrels per day, compared with 19.5 million in February, including roughly 9.7 million moving through Hormuz.”

This is an impressive achievement. Yet do not forget that we consume products, not crude oil. There has been substantial damage to refineries in the Gulf. Moreover, refineries are set up to process specific crude oils, so shortages of products have emerged. One notable example is diesel. This even led President Donald Trump to consider a plan (now abandoned) to halt the US exports. But other products have also had bigger price rises than crude, notably natural gas and sulphur.

Nevertheless, the disruption to oil supply, oil prices and the world economy more broadly has, in truth, been quite surprisingly manageable. In terms of the overall economy, this is, as Nouriel Roubini notes in Project Syndicate, in large part due to the massive investment boom triggered by AI. But, for the future health of the world economy, it is not the level of investment, but its rate of growth, that matters, as does the ultimate economic contribution of AI itself. Surely at some point investment will slow. As to the economic contribution of AI (or indeed its doomsday properties), who knows with confidence?

There exist other sources of fragility. One, which I discussed last week, is the manageability of global debt at a time of rising interest rates. France, the UK and US are in the crosshairs. There is a particular risk for countries whose public debt is overwhelmingly short-term since, as a result, they enjoy little insurance against the impact of higher inflation on interest rates.

One of the biggest questions, then, is whether the stand-off between stupidity and ingenuity will continue. If it does, the energy shock at least should remain contained. But that cannot be taken for granted: the present situation, not least the drawdown in stocks, cannot continue forever. China’s noteworthy suppression of domestic demand might not last either. If these come to a halt, crude prices might jump to more disruptive levels.

A still bigger question is where the war itself will go. Might Trump greet the passing of the midterm elections as a chance to release his bellicosity? Then a lame duck, he might think it would be the right time to sort out those pesky Iranians. If so, how far might Iran be able (and willing) to go in damaging the oil infrastructure of its neighbours? What is remarkable, after all, is how much Gulf oil is still flowing. Might that again be disrupted?

Alternatively, could (or would) a post-midterm Congress halt such efforts? Or might Trump get bored with the whole thing and let hostilities peter out into an ill-tempered (and probably informal) ceasefire?

An advantage of arbitrary despots is that they can so easily get bored. I cannot imagine that Trump finds the war with Iran much fun any longer. Even he must also find it really difficult to believe that it has been a great triumph. After all, as Mearsheimer says, he has achieved none of his objectives. Iran is battered, but its ghastly regime and influence in the Gulf look rather secure. Trump will surely be tempted to declare victory and move on. The American people would be delighted. So, might it all end “not with a bang but a whimper”?

martin.wolf@ft.com

Follow Martin Wolf with myFT and on Twitter

item.title: The tide of bank branch closures is starting to reverse
item.author: Patrick Jenkins
item.description: The business virtues of having a network are being rediscovered in the US and UK
item.content:encoded:
The business virtues of having a network are being rediscovered in the US and UK

Patrick Jenkins

Banks have spent the last few decades frantically closing branches, cutting real estate overheads and trying to keep up with fast-growing digital fintechs. Now, though, some have come up with a radical new strategy: to open branches.

UK banks have been among the most extreme in the world in slashing their high-street presence. Across the country, there are now barely 4,000 bank and building society branches, down 80 per cent in 40 years.

Barclays, which has been the most aggressive in closing branches of late (shrinking its estate from nearly 1,000 in 2019 to 206), is now keen to highlight a reversal of strategy: over the past fortnight it has opened two branches — one in Bishop’s Stortford, north of London, and one in Poole on the south coast — declaring itself “the first large bank that’s opened a branch in about a decade”. (The stripped-back stores, to be joined by Beverley in Yorkshire next month, have a handful of cubicles and a couple of ATMs but no counters, and appear chosen to attract retail customers and small and medium-sized enterprises in three reasonably affluent locations.)

Yet this is no aberration. In the US, the trend has been under way for some time. In 2024, JPMorgan Chase said it would open 500 branches. Last year Bank of America announced 150 new “financial centers”. PNC is adding 300 branches.

In Europe, a general trend of declining branch numbers has continued — down 42 per cent over the past decade, according to consultancy Kearney. Aside from the UK, the most acute reductions have been in the Netherlands and Spain, while France experienced the smallest decline — at barely half the average EU rate.

In the UK, though, some smaller operators with throwback business models have been expanding. Sweden’s Handelsbanken has steadily built out a British network of 120 outlets, each run by a highly autonomous branch manager. Metrobank, despite financial and regulatory stresses, has continued to expand its footprint and now has about 80 outlets, reminiscent of the large, slick “stores” that its US co-founder Vernon Hill pioneered with his US Commerce Bank chain.

Some institutions have tried to make their branches more appealing in original ways. Although Santander has continued to trim its UK network (and is expected to close more outlets once it integrates its TSB acquisition), it has also begun adding “work cafés” to a number of its city-centre branches — an attempt to tap into the trend for co-working spaces.

Others have made a virtue of retaining large branch networks. Nationwide, Britain’s biggest building society, has nearly 700 branches and has pledged not to close any until at least 2030. The mutually owned group, which makes a point of empowering branch managers, reckons this has helped it top the table of current account switching (with more than double the net switching tally of the next most popular, Lloyds). It is also playing on its community-friendly image by adding new facilities: defibrillators and bleed-control kits are being fitted outside all its branches by the end of this year. 

But much of the pro-branch thinking is about the core business that can be done in these spaces. As banks seek to deepen their relationships with customers, many are realising that branches — if they are transformed from the old model of tellers doing low-value cash transactions — can be a great route to broaden the business they do with each customer.

New UK rules giving banks greater scope to provide advice on investments and other topics should open up an opportunity to sell the kinds of products that customers might be wary of committing to in an online-only environment. 

That is certainly a key focus of US branches, where many bank customers also have brokerage accounts and may feel more comfortable opening them or discussing investments in a branch.

But there is also something less concrete going on. Particularly striking is data suggesting that US banks sell more products to their customers in areas where they have a high-street branch: PNC, for example, reckons it is six times more effective at marketing to purely digital customers if they live near a branch. Who’d have thought it? There’s brand value in having a shop with a massive sign over the door — even if it does make for a rather expensive form of advertising.

patrick.jenkins@ft.com

item.title: The Big Read. The taxman comes for China’s offshore riches
item.author: Edward White and Leo Lewis and Owen Walker and Sun Yu
item.description: The crackdown has rattled the country’s wealthiest people and the businesses in Hong Kong, Singapore and Tokyo that manage their money
item.content:encoded:
The crackdown has rattled the country’s wealthiest people and the businesses in Hong Kong, Singapore and Tokyo that manage their money

Edward White and Leo Lewis and Owen Walker and Sun Yu

“To get rich,” according to a saying often attributed to Deng Xiaoping, “is glorious.”  The great Chinese reformer’s slogan became synonymous with his campaign to open the country up to the outside world and its capitalist forces.

And over decades of astronomical growth, many in China did get rich. Today, the country boasts the world’s second-biggest economy, with more than 1,000 billionaires and 5mn millionaires.

Now the pendulum is swinging back again. Strongman Xi Jinping wants those who benefited the most from China’s economic ascent to increase their contributions back to the state, embarking on what could be the most ambitious global tax hunt in history.

From October 22, authorities will begin collecting a 20 per cent tax on dividends and interest earned from offshore trusts, explicitly targeting wealthy Chinese who shelter their assets overseas.

Analysts at Barclays view the measures as “potentially the first steps” in a broader campaign to “[expand] scrutiny to areas such as exporter earnings held offshore, overseas investment income, overseas employment income and, over the longer term, estate or inheritance taxation”.

The sudden move announced this summer came as a shock to many of China’s wealthiest people, arriving at a pivotal moment when the country faces a generational handover of wealth. Many Chinese entrepreneurs who built fortunes during the early decades of reform are nearing retirement, raising pressing questions about how their assets will be passed on, who will take control of the family empires — and who will pay the taxes.

The shockwaves have been felt in financial, legal and property industries across Asia. Hong Kong, Singapore and Tokyo are in flux as their status as havens for money channelled offshore from China faces an existential test. Others, including New York bankers, spy an opportunity to shield Chinese customers from their country’s taxman.

If successful, the campaign has the potential to help Beijing fill a deepening fiscal hole in central government coffers. Revenue collected by local authorities from land sales has plateaued or fallen, and the central government has been siphoning more funds to provinces in recent years to cover basic services such as education and health and to pay civil servants. The situation is “becoming untenable on [its] current trajectory”, says Victor Shih, professor of Chinese political economy at the University of California, San Diego. Technocrats “have to find another source of revenue”.

It could also bring China’s tax system in line with the US and Europe. “For China, wealth became international much faster than the tax system did,” says Lizzi Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis. “Now the tax system is just closing that gap.”

But the campaign also serves Xi’s long-term desire to redistribute wealth in China, tackle inequality and create a more egalitarian society. Redistribution and taxation are a means of achieving “common prosperity”, he wrote in the fourth of his five-volume collection of speeches and essays, which is “an essential requirement of socialism with Chinese characteristics”.

It marks a further step along his journey of redrawing the social contract between the business elite who helped propel China’s rise and the ruling Communist Party.

“The shift in focus is away from the ‘to get rich is glorious’ mantra of Deng Xiaoping,” says Willy Wo-Lap Lam, a China expert and fellow at the Jamestown Foundation, a US think-tank. “Xi frowns on wealth accumulated by the filthy rich.”

The brass tacks of Chinese tax

The news came via a typically bland notice issued by the national tax office.

On July 24, Beijing announced it would begin taxing income generated by offshore trusts. Not only would this be retroactive, but it would also be levied at numerous points, from when the trust is established, as the underlying assets appreciate, and including when income is realised and distributed to beneficiaries.

A further one-off 20 per cent tax would apply when trust assets are inherited or when a Chinese individual ceases to be a mainland tax resident, including by acquiring foreign citizenship.

The statement said the rules would apply to gains on offshore assets from 2023 to 2025. Individuals and their advisers were allowed a 90-day grace period — until October 22 — to get their affairs in order. After that, the payments would be collected annually.

A few days later, in early August, the FT revealed that tax officials are, in fact, probing beyond the 2023-2025 period, beyond trusts, and well beyond China’s borders.

According to multiple officials, bankers and advisers, Chinese banks and other financial institutions have been instructed to review overseas investments by wealthy Chinese people to check if income has been declared to authorities. In some cases the authorities’ scrutiny of overseas capital gains and investments went as far back as 2000.

China’s business establishment was caught off guard, as well as the vast industry helping to manage their money inside and outside the country.

One Chinese tech investor, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, says he and friends of similar high net worth were shocked by the precision with which the tax reforms target key offshore holdings and historic income, and the tight deadline set to pay.

“They have the system, they know your investments overseas . . . they can actually break open those trusts,” he says. “I think they’ve been thinking about this for a long time.”

Harry Yu, a senior partner at Hong Kong-based Fung Yu Trust Services, who advises China-connected families on cross-border wealth structuring and succession, says that although Beijing’s “direction was foreseeable”, the detailed trust rules arrived sooner than he expected.

“After the announcement, my [messaging app] filled up with worried questions. I spent that weekend responding to messages,” he adds. “Families are having to address past transactions, present cash needs and future succession arrangements together.”

Over recent weeks government officials have been co-ordinating efforts to put pressure on certain entrepreneurs, nudging them to meet the 90-day deadline.

In one example, an executive at a Beijing-based internet company was contacted by the local branch of the powerful National Development and Reform Commission as well as other local government officials over tax payments since the new taxing rule took effect, according to a person familiar with the executive’s tax issues.

The Chinese tech investor says that the implementation of the tax seems to be “discretionary”, with a spectrum of severity across different provincial tax authorities.

With Beijing’s deadline looming, Yu is urgently working with clients to reconstruct their historical offshore records to establish a reliable factual basis before they move towards an official Chinese tax assessment and discussions with the relevant local tax authorities.

In many cases, this is no easy task.

“Sometimes it is closer to archaeology than planning: you have to put the pieces back together before deciding what to do next,” Yu says. “The information isn’t always sitting in one complete trust file. Some records may be missing or incomplete. Others exist, but are scattered across institutions and weren’t organised to answer the questions now being asked.”

The global fallout

The repercussions have rattled Hong Kong and Singapore, where Chinese offshore wealth is highly concentrated.

Cross-border wealth booked in Hong Kong reached $2.9tn last year, with the financial centre overtaking Switzerland as the world’s largest offshore wealth centre, according to Boston Consulting Group.

But as Beijing’s authority over Hong Kong has tightened, the city has struggled to maintain its identity as a financial hub independent of China. Singapore, meanwhile, has become a magnet for wealthy Chinese nationals, who set up family offices in the low-tax jurisdiction to manage their fortunes while buying luxury properties and high-end cars.

Financial and legal advisers in the city-state say their Chinese clients flew into a panic upon hearing the news. “There was a sense of disbelief,” recalls Sim Bock Eng, head of private wealth at Wong Partnership, a Singapore law firm. “Many had set up trusts when they relocated to Singapore and thought that would protect them from paying tax in China.”

Among the highest-profile Chinese expats in Singapore are Zhang Yong and Shu Ping, the married co-founders of Chinese hotpot restaurant chain Haidilao. Forbes estimates that their combined fortune is more than $7bn. The pair have taken up Singaporean citizenship, set up a family office and spent tens of millions of dollars on properties in the city-state in recent years.

In September, Shu abruptly sold more than $350mn of stock in the Hong Kong-listed company, sending its shares down 12 per cent. While the company did not disclose the reasons for the sale, equity analysts speculated that Shu was trying to generate cash to pay her tax bill.

The prospect of other Chinese émigrés living in Singapore having to undergo a fire sale of assets — such as company shares and properties — in order to pay Chinese taxes has caused anxiety. Singapore’s 55 billionaires include several Chinese-born entrepreneurs with extensive business ties to their homeland.

These include Li Xiting, the co-founder of China’s largest medical equipment manufacturer, Mindray, who is worth $10.6bn, according to Forbes; Jason Jiang, founder of Shanghai-based Focus Media, who has a net worth of $3.9bn; and Ji Qi, executive chair of Chinese hotel operator H World, who has a $3.4bn fortune.

One option for wealthy individuals such as these would be to borrow money from banks, using collateral such as company shares and property, to pay their tax bills.

“Most clients prefer to look at financing options because that gives them a quick remedy without having to make longer-term moves,” says Kevin Teng, chief executive of wealth manager Wrise. “There will be more of these than outright sales of trophy assets.”

He said assets such as property in Singapore would be among the last to be sold because they provided the most security.

Mike Tan, global head of wealth planning and family advisory at Standard Chartered, says there were plenty of lower-profile examples than Shu of company executives selling shares apparently to raise funds, but this tactic was fraught with problems. “This can cause drops in the share price, which damages the rest of your holdings,” he says.

He adds that in one situation, the value of shares in a Chinese businessman’s company is now a fraction of what they were worth when he set up his trust. As a result, his 20 per cent tax bill could be larger than the value of shares he owns.

“He tried to explain this to the tax officer, but understands that the new tax rules still apply and he would have to take advice and decide what he wishes to do,” Tan says.

The fallout has also been felt in Japan. Even though it is not among the largest repositories for offshore assets, it has for many years been quietly attracting a huge flow of Chinese, many of them wealthy and with businesses still in China.

Until recently, Chinese people could set up businesses in Japan cheaply and without huge technical barriers, and those businesses could then sponsor visas that allowed them and their families to live in Japan. Some managed to circumvent capital controls to move large amounts of money into Japan via underground banks, which are managed by a combination of mostly Chinese and some Japanese operatives, according to Japanese bankers and wealthy executives.

These people have been extremely aggressive buyers of higher-end property, either in central Tokyo, Osaka or other major cities, or in some of the favourite ski resorts, notably Niseko in the northern island of Hokkaido. In some parts of the market, say multiple brokers, the Chinese money has been a major factor in inflating property prices. Some have also been diversifying their assets in Japan, buying small unlisted businesses in areas that interest them, sake brewing among them.

Now, all the expatriate Chinese are urgently seeking out advice on how to keep on the right side of the tax man in China, while also not raising too many questions about how they got so much money out — and how much the businesses they are supposedly running in Japan are worth.

“Until about a year ago, all the conversations we had at dinner among [Chinese] friends in Tokyo were about where to buy good properties, how many more family members could be brought over from China, where the best schools were, that kind of thing. Now, a lot of the conversation is about tax, tax, tax,” says a Chinese businesswoman who runs a tech investment firm in Tokyo.

“How hard is it going to hit? Is it still viable to stay in Japan? . . . There are some answers but I’d say there are still more questions at this point.”

The search for safety

For those hoping to shield their assets from the Chinese authorities, there are options available.

Some Singaporean advisers report clients who are weighing moving their assets to Taiwan or the US — two countries that are not formally signed up to the OECD’s Common Reporting Standard (CRS) framework, which facilitates the automatic exchange of financial account information between jurisdictions.

Morgan Stanley’s private wealth business in New York, for example, has seen a sharp increase in enquiries, account openings and asset transfers from Chinese clients in Hong Kong and Singapore, according to two bankers with knowledge of the matter.

The team has received transfers from the two Asian financial centres very frequently in recent weeks, they say, reflecting growing demand among wealthy Chinese for broader investment access, lower fees, favourable US tax treatment and greater protection from Chinese government scrutiny. “This is a trend that all financial firms are seeing,” they add.

Many of the Morgan Stanley clients moving assets to New York already hold money or securities in Hong Kong or Singapore. Moving capital out of mainland China remains the most difficult step and is not something Morgan Stanley can facilitate, the people say.

Once the assets are offshore, however, transferring them to the US is straightforward. Cash sent from Hong Kong or Singapore can generally reach a Morgan Stanley US account on the same day or within one business day.

Clients can transfer US dollars, Hong Kong dollars and offshore renminbi. Eligible stocks, bonds and mutual funds can also be moved directly from a Hong Kong institution without first being sold. Morgan Stanley declined to comment.

In the US, non-resident foreigners are generally not required to pay capital gains tax on investments there. The bankers say that many Chinese clients using the New York platform also do not report or pay Chinese tax on their US investment gains.

The opportunity to avoid paying capital gains tax in the US and in China is a major reason for moving assets from Hong Kong and Singapore to New York. And the absence of US participation in CRS reduces the likelihood that the accounts will be disclosed automatically to Chinese authorities through that system.

The perceived security of the US financial system appears to be a further attraction. Political agreements between Washington and Beijing, or executive proposals targeting particular countries or groups, are not seen automatically to translate into action by banks, regulators and courts.

This institutional fragmentation is regarded as an additional layer of protection. Chinese clients tend to view assets held with a large private US financial institution as better insulated from abrupt government intervention.

A more extreme move would be for wealthy Chinese nationals to apply for passports in countries such as Turkey and New Zealand — which can be processed relatively quickly for wealthy individuals — and renounce their Chinese citizenship.

But that tactic would only work to shelter assets already outside China. And giving up citizenship is also not a feasible option for many executives whose businesses fall under the watch of Beijing’s regulators.

“Clients who are already in the C-level position of A-share listed firms have no choice: they cannot have overseas status,” says one China-based wealth manager who serves a group of founders.

And for people who want to take their companies public, personal tax clearance is also, in practice, a condition for listing in the mainland market, according to several IPO bankers familiar with current listing standards.

Some warn that there is little China’s elite can do to escape Beijing’s long reach, as authorities tighten controls on overseas travel for its citizens, including expanding the use of exit bans. “The government feels like it has access and a right to pursue people back to ‘the motherland’,” says Minxin Pei, an expert in Chinese governance at Claremont McKenna College in California. “This is this mindset, you can never be un-Chinese.”

Beijing’s rigid tax authority is clearly a high priority to Xi, who views the campaign as part of a broader “egalitarian push”, says Jamestown’s Lam. He notes that it builds on earlier episodes during his 14-year rule when Beijing has cracked down on private tech giants, property developers and high earners as it seeks to align business with socialist values.

Faced with this level of determination, many of China’s high-net-worth class are bowing to the inevitable. A senior executive with a Chinese tech group says he considered closing his offshore trust immediately but decided against it because that would trigger the 20 per cent closure tax. Emigrating from China was not immediately possible because he still has family in the mainland.

“Financial advisers told me to learn more about obtaining foreign citizenship or setting up a ‘foundation’, which can be done in Europe without paying tax. I am still thinking about it [for the future]. But for now, I’ll just pay.”

Yet one of the wealthy Chinese investors who spoke to the FT for this story noted that China’s leaders, who are urgently trying to address a worsening employment crisis, must balance not pushing the business leaders too far, given that the private sector is responsible for about 80 per cent of the nation’s jobs.

“Running a business means taking on a lot of risk already. You become like, ‘this is too much’,” he says, adding: “It is a pendulum swing: right now, the direction is this. It could swing back.”

This article has been amended to reflect that the Chinese businessman whose company fell in value is not a Standard Chartered client.

item.title: Letter: Bringing US inflation to heel needs more aggressive tightening
item.description: From Mariano Torras, Professor of Economics, Adelphi University, Garden City, NY, US
item.content:encoded:
From Mariano Torras, Professor of Economics, Adelphi University, Garden City, NY, US

I strongly agree with Sheila Bair’s support for the Federal Reserve’s quarter-point increase announced on September 16, and with her claim that conventional wisdom misunderstands how changes in rates affect Main Street (“For once, the Fed has put Main Street before Wall Street”, Opinion, September 28).

I nevertheless believe she understates what is required.

If a quarter-point rise is correct because households suffer from the price of things rather than the price of credit, then we should be honest that said increase will not meaningfully relieve the former. Bringing inflation genuinely to heel implies far more aggressive tightening — the kind that carries a Volcker-sized bill. That bill is real: severely diminished output and unemployment borne disproportionately by those with the least cushion. There is no way to dismantle a four-decade debt pyramid gently. Yet having spent 40 years deferring the cost, we no longer have the luxury of choosing whether to pay it.

Bair is correct that the financial system is the mechanism of transmission, and therefore that those at the top of it capture the gains from cheap money. Yet there is an irony here that she leaves unexplored. A higher-rate regime is, arguably, a gift to the rentier. The holder of existing claims earns more on them without producing anything new.

It is the entrepreneur — the one actually attempting to create value, who must borrow against an uncertain future — who suffers most. This is the strange inversion in which easy money flatters the owner and punishes the builder, while dear money does the reverse. We should not pretend that the inversion is costless.

What recommends it, at least, is that we have run out of alternatives. Opportunities for productive wealth creation have withered as finance has detached itself from economics, and what remains is largely financialised return — asset appreciation transferred from the credulous to the endowed. In that setting, higher rates do at least one useful thing: they make debt expensive enough to stop growing and so begin the slow work of dismantling the pyramid.

Note that it is not a vindication of high rates as a policy ideal — far from it. It is merely the modest consolation available to us now.

Mariano Torras
Professor of Economics, Adelphi University, Garden City, NY, US

item.title: Letter: A warning not to push EU merger law too far
item.description: From Tomás Espuny Carreño, Barcelona, Spain
item.content:encoded:
From Tomás Espuny Carreño, Barcelona, Spain

I enjoyed reading Barbara Moens’s opinion piece “Dealmakers keen to test Brussels’ policy on regional champions” (Opinion, October 2). It shows again how much depends on which way the political wind is blowing in Brussels. No wonder companies and their advisers argue for lighter or tougher enforcement depending on whose deal is on the table.

Competition law is not economic policy. It rests on legal principles that have to be applied the same way whoever the parties are and wherever the buyer comes from. That neutrality is what gives businesses certainty and it is also what keeps the system legitimate. Once it becomes negotiable, both are lost.

The article quoted a European Commission official saying “we need one deal that shows we are serious about the shift” to creating regional champions. That worries me. A decision taken to send a political message is a poor foundation for the coherent body of precedent that dealmakers are rightly asking for, and it may not hold up in the Luxembourg-based Court of Justice of the European Union.

The new guidelines give more weight to scale, innovation and resilience, but they are still guidance. The legal test is the same as before.

This is not new. Back in July, your pages were already asking the same question in “Europe’s wind turbine makers examine merger prospects to create champions” (Report, July 29). Two months later, the debate is no longer whether one sector should get special treatment but which deal will get it first.

Competition law is where it should be. Pushing it too far in either direction is likely to backfire, and the first deals to try will find that out.

Tomás Espuny Carreño
Barcelona, Spain
