item.title: Letter: An American investor ‘ill-versed’ in Shakespeare
item.description: From Vipin Bharathan, New York, NY, US
item.content:encoded:
From Vipin Bharathan, New York, NY, US

In his opinion piece “Don’t own bonds and be cautious with equities” (Markets Insight, October 1), Bill Gross says “William Shakespeare wrote ‘neither a borrower nor a lender be’”. He uses this to assert that one of history’s greatest authors is “obviously ill-versed in economics”.

The philanthropist, private investor and co-founder of Pimco may not be the first person to attribute a character’s utterances in a play to the play’s author. In this speech from Hamlet, Shakespeare was establishing Polonius’ hypocrisy with a series of bits of advice offered to his son Laertes. Soon, “a convocation of politic worms were e’en at him”. Polonius’ speech drives the tragedy forward to its culmination in the confrontation between Hamlet and Laertes. Many phrases from this series of homilies have been misquoted and attributed, erroneously, to Shakespeare.

Vipin Bharathan
New York, NY, US

item.title: Letter: SkyNet satellites must be under sovereign control
item.description: From Professor Keith Hayward, London SW20, UK
item.content:encoded:
From Professor Keith Hayward, London SW20, UK

The possibility that the next generation of SkyNet satellites could be dependent on US technology (“SkyNet battle tests UK pledge to ‘buy British’”, Report, FT.com, October 3) would be a retrograde step of considerable magnitude. As the sixth generation since the UK pioneered development of a dedicated military communications satellite system in the mid 1960s, SkyNet has successfully progressed from total dependence on US technology to almost full autonomy. Moreover, unlike several key procurements, SkyNet has been delivered on time, on cost, and completely fulfilling operational requirements. Even after a problematic launch of a SkyNet 2, which left it out of its proper orbit, it still did enough to serve the UK military and other users.

In time, SkyNet vehicles were sold to Nato allies and the underlying technology served as a basis for an impressive UK civil satellite capability.

I have great respect for Lockheed Martin’s longstanding commitment to the UK defence industrial base, but SkyNet represents a core capability that must remain under sovereign control. The alternative might bring economic gain, but the loss of such a fundamental asset would undermine future opportunities in the space industry, one of the growth areas over the next decade.

Professor Keith Hayward
London SW20, UK

item.title: Letter: Why this MP is backing the Lockheed Martin bid
item.description: From Luke Akehurst, MP (Labour, North Durham), House of Commons, London SW1, UK
item.content:encoded:
From Luke Akehurst, MP (Labour, North Durham), House of Commons, London SW1, UK

I was disappointed at your characterisation of the competition between Airbus and Lockheed Martin for the contract to supply the UK with its next-generation military communications satellite (“SkyNet satellite battle tests UK pledge to ‘buy British’”, Report, FT.com, October 3).

In fact, the rival Lockheed Martin bid would be manufactured in County Durham, helping to reindustrialise an area with a proud manufacturing and mining heritage and existing strengths in advanced manufacturing. It would create a new manufacturing facility with 400 new skilled jobs and many more in the supply chain. Lockheed Martin has already invested millions and created hundreds of jobs in the North East Space Skills and Technology Centre at Northumbria University in Newcastle. The US company is offering a highly capable sovereign satellite solution for the UK that will be a catalyst for the growth of the space and defence sectors in the North East.

Luke Akehurst
MP (Labour, North Durham), House of Commons, London SW1, UK

item.title: Letter: The globalisation of AI borrowing is a problem
item.description: From Edoardo Porrato, Turin, Italy
item.content:encoded:
From Edoardo Porrato, Turin, Italy

Your September 28 Big Read on the transformation of debt markets by AI hyperscalers raises a less obvious problem for the investors absorbing all this issuance: diversification may be becoming harder to measure.

A portfolio can own an Alphabet bond in sterling, Amazon debt in Canadian dollars, a Meta issue in euros and Microsoft paper in dollars. By conventional measures it appears diversified across issuers, currencies and markets.

Economically, however, these securities may increasingly depend on the same underlying proposition: that enormous investment in computing capacity, data centres and their supporting infrastructure will generate sufficient future cash flows.

The distinction matters as AI financing spreads beyond the hyperscalers themselves to chipmakers, data centre operators, utilities and other suppliers. An investor can reduce exposure to any individual borrower while inadvertently increasing exposure to the same investment cycle.

Diversification is most useful when different assets fail for different reasons. The globalisation of AI borrowing may make portfolios look more diversified precisely as one common risk factor becomes more important.

The challenge for credit investors is therefore not merely to count issuers. It is to identify how many genuinely independent economic bets they own.

Edoardo Porrato
Turin, Italy

item.title: Letter: Recursive self-improvement — a phrase of the year?
item.description: From Toby Zanin, Toronto, ON, Canada
item.content:encoded:
From Toby Zanin, Toronto, ON, Canada

Martin Wolf’s sober and thoughtful assessment of the societal and related safety risks associated with the ascent of AI left this reader with two contrasting and contradictory takeaways (“With AI, ‘I told you so’ will be too late”, Opinion, September 16).

The good news is that we seem to have found an early and almost certain winner for any dictionary word or phrase of the year award, with the ominous entry “recursive self-improvement” edging into the realm of our collective self-consciousness.

The consequential bad news, however, is that given the implications and the potential dire ramifications of that phrase, we may not be in need of any such word or contest in the very near future.

Toby Zanin
Toronto, ON, Canada

item.title: Letter: What London’s empty bike racks really tell us
item.description: From Stef Lehmann, Head of Government Relations, Lime UK & Ireland, Lime Technology Limited, c/o WeWork, London EC4, UK
item.content:encoded:
From Stef Lehmann, Head of Government Relations, Lime UK & Ireland, Lime Technology Limited, c/o WeWork, London EC4, UK

There is a fundamental piece of the puzzle missing from your article on underused bike racks in office buildings (“New offices in London are full of empty bike racks, complain developers”, Report, October 5). Demand for cycling has gone only one way — up, to record levels across London.

Just because people may not cycle using their own bikes doesn’t mean London isn’t desperately short of spaces to park shared e-bikes. Lime trips into the Square Mile rose by nearly 50 per cent last year, and parking space always lags behind demand.

Gyms and spas have their place, but there isn’t exactly a shortage of them across London.

If private cycle parking isn’t being used as much as expected, investment in it should pivot to also include dockless e-bike parking.

Lime has already committed millions to improve London’s e-bike parking. But building it on public land takes time. As our submission to the London mayor argues, if developers were able to count shared e-bike parking on private land against their existing requirement, it could have a major impact towards a common good.

People are still choosing to commute more actively — it just looks different. So let’s not throw the baby out with the bathwater.

Stef Lehmann
Head of Government Relations, Lime UK & Ireland, Lime Technology Limited, c/o WeWork, London EC4, UK

item.title: The FT View. Pedro Sánchez’s big electoral gamble
item.author: The editorial board
item.description: Opinion polls suggest it may be the last for the Spanish prime minister
item.content:encoded:
Opinion polls suggest it may be the last for the Spanish prime minister

The editorial board

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has made a career out of high-stakes gambles. His latest is to call snap elections for November 29, seeking to use a housing crisis that has prompted mass protests as an opportunity to face down his rightwing opponents. Opinion polls suggest it could be his last.

Sánchez’s Socialist party (PSOE) on 26 per cent is well behind the opposition People’s Party on 32 per cent and its probable coalition partner, the rightwing populist Vox, on 18 per cent. PSOE’s far-left allies Podemos and Sumar, both in single figures, are divided and rudderless, weakened by Sánchez talking the language of the populist left.

This is a fight not just for the direction of Spain but also for the future of the left in Europe. Spain had become a “global reference point for peace, feminism and prosperity”, Sánchez boasted on Monday. He is a lonely progressive standard-bearer in the EU: pro-immigration and tech regulation, sceptical on rearmament, and staunchly anti-Trump. His defeat could usher in another centre-right/nationalist-populist coalition — which could spell trouble for the EU.

Sánchez has never had a parliamentary majority since becoming prime minister in 2018. His latest administration has turned into a zombie government, largely unable to pass major legislation, buffeted by events and mired in corruption scandals. The prime minister frequently warns of the dangers to democracy from an authoritarian right, but has increasingly resorted to rule by decree. It is good for Spain to have an earlier-than-scheduled chance at a parliamentary reset and at least the possibility of a more stable government.

His conservative opponents have long questioned Sánchez’s mandate to govern. He has led a series of minority governments since 2018 when the PSOE united the opposition, including nationalist parties, against the PP premier Mariano Rajoy in a no-confidence motion. After snap elections in 2023, the second-placed Socialists formed a weak minority government with the support of the Catalan pro-independence parties in return for an amnesty for people convicted of offences during the illegal Catalan secession attempt.

The amnesty has been the government’s main legislative achievement. It helped achieve détente in Catalonia, defusing tensions. But it was deeply contentious in Spain and, to Sánchez’s critics, looked like a self-serving partisan arrangement.

The prime minister’s latest sharp manoeuvre is to try to harness the outpouring of anger over Spain’s housing crisis and the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her Madrid flat. He is presenting himself as a progressive champion of tenants’ rights against a conservative opposition — which last week voted down two emergency bills on housing from Sánchez’s government — that he says is protecting the interests of an exploitative elite.

Sánchez has a record of outfoxing flat-footed opponents, but his latest gambit seems a stretch even for him, given that the housing shortage has worsened during his eight years in power, aggravated by mass immigration. His populist answer, aimed at curbing soaring rents and preventing evictions, does little to address the root causes.

The Spanish premier has a decent record on the economy. But the twin motors of EU pandemic funds and unbridled immigration are ending or reaching the limit of public acceptance. Government drift and allegations of graft involving members of the prime minister’s inner circle have left their mark.

In a polarised and highly charged political system, Sánchez’s critics have often vehemently questioned his legitimacy. But Sánchez himself is not afraid of polarising the debate by playing up the dangers of the far right, when it turns attention from his own performance. This time it may well not be enough.

item.title: Lex. Silicon Valley’s acqui-hire ruse may have passed its prime
item.description: Nvidia’s raid on a rival’s top talent has raised hackles among employees not invited to the party
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia’s raid on a rival’s top talent has raised hackles among employees not invited to the party

Imagine not being invited to the office party — one where attendees are gifted with swag bags containing millions of dollars. That’s the position two employees of chipmaker Groq found themselves in when mega-sized rival Nvidia hired most of their colleagues. Selective guest lists may work for elite soirées, but they’re not so well suited to corporate M&A.

Nvidia paid $20bn to get what it wanted from Groq. But rather than doing so through a traditional acquisition or asset purchase, it set aside a $3bn bonus pool with which to lure Groq’s top talent, and paid $17bn to the company to license Groq’s intellectual property. The disgruntled engineers, as shareholders, got their cut of that $17bn, but that was less than they would have got if Nvidia had bought the company for $20bn. They have therefore sued Groq’s board.

Their chagrin, as shareholders at least, is understandable. So-called “acqui-hires” are one way of buying the guts of a business without triggering antitrust processes that apply to conventional mergers. In practice, they can leave shareholders feeling as though they have lost prized human “assets” without being compensated adequately.

It doesn’t help that the Groq board seems to have given Nvidia what appears to be a bargain. When the Groq shell was finally liquidated, the chipmaking giant offered a “squeeze-out” payment for cash and sundry assets of just a few hundred million dollars, only to then revalue its purchases at $3.5bn.

Imagine Nvidia had gone the more direct route, and bought Groq outright. The engineers might have received a more generous offer for their shares. But such a deal would have taken a long time to close, and might well have been blocked outright by competition watchdogs. Of course, in that scenario they might have at least kept their jobs.

The big question is whether acqui-hires will come to be treated as mergers from a competition standpoint. The Biden administration reviewed thousands of similar arrangements, taking the view that substance mattered more than form. The Trump administration has expressed concerns too, though no formal challenge has yet arrived.

The objections of irked former employees add a new challenge for such deals. If they win, future acqui-hires will probably become more expensive, and thus less attractive. Either way, lawsuits give regulators another reason to wise up to the acqui-hire strategy. Kudos to tech titans for finding innovative ways to hack the system, but in future they may be forced to take a more direct approach.

sujeet.indap@ft.com

item.title: The Big Read. France: between the bond market and the barricades
item.author: Leila Abboud and Sarah White and Ian Smith and Olaf Storbeck
item.description: The country is being hit by a pre-election debt sell-off. Many fear it could shake the Eurozone
item.content:encoded:
The country is being hit by a pre-election debt sell-off. Many fear it could shake the Eurozone

Leila Abboud and Sarah White and Ian Smith and Olaf Storbeck

As hundreds of thousands of people poured on to the streets of France to protest against planned budget cuts last week, the bond market made clear its own deep discontent with the country’s public finances.

Teachers, nurses and civil servants marched against what they denounce as unbearable austerity in a demonstration of the public anger that could sink the government’s plans to rein in its deficit. In parallel, the brutal sell-off in the country’s bonds took borrowing costs close to 5 per cent, their highest in almost a quarter of a century.

“Schools with no money, a country with no future,” read one sign held aloft by a protester in Paris. Angry students have adopted more radical tactics by shutting down high schools across France, clashing with police and setting destructive fires, leading to 5,000 arrests.

France is caught between the protesters on the street calling for more funds from the government and “bond vigilantes” in the markets who punish perceived fiscal irresponsibility by betting against the country’s debt.

Not only does it now cost France more to borrow than it does Italy and Greece; a rising number of big French companies enjoy lower market interest rates than does the French state. Of all the G7 nations, it has suffered most from the debt sell-off triggered by the Iran war.

“We are already in a slow-burning, deep and structural crisis,” says Pierre Moscovici, finance minister during the tail-end of the Eurozone crisis in 2012. “France is probably too big to fail, but it is not too big for the markets to punish.”

Tensions are rising as the confrontation over the budget deepens and the country prepares for an April presidential election that could end in a face-off between the far right and hard left.

The fear among investors is that the country could be tipped into a full-blown debt crisis that could not only rock France’s economy but also shake the Eurozone.

On Monday, the euro fell to a 17-month low against the dollar as worries intensified about the impact of the French debt sell-off on the single-currency area.

Emmanuel Moulin, the governor of the Bank of France, says the market ructions are “serious and worrying” although he maintains that the country can get back on track.

“Whoever is elected president will face a situation in which interest rates are high, the cost of servicing the debt is high, the deficit has to be brought back below 3 per cent, and the debt has to be cut,” Moulin tells the FT.

“If we don’t act, there is indeed a risk of being gradually strangled by rising interest rates. We have to remain in control of our own destiny.”

At present, France’s debt has reached €3.5tn, at nearly 120 per cent of GDP, far above the Eurozone average. Servicing costs have climbed fast to become the state’s single biggest expenditure ahead of education or defence.

In just a month the additional interest rate that France pays to borrow over ultra-safe German debt — a key barometer of investor concern — has surged by almost two-thirds to around 1.4 percentage points on 10-year debt at the start of the week, heading towards the heights charted during the Eurozone debt crisis.

The sell-off in French debt continued even after the government set out a belt-tightening 2027 budget plan last week.

In the worst-case scenario, some think the European Central Bank could be forced to come to the rescue. That could come at the cost of demanding structural reforms, such as slashing pension spending, which the French public has long rejected.

“France has been sleepwalking down the path that leads towards a financial crisis,” says Mike Riddell, a fund manager at Fidelity International. “It feels like broader markets are starting to notice.”

The budget showdown

In Paris, ministers and former officials play down the idea that France could fall prey to a full-blown debt crisis. They cite the country’s solid economic and institutional foundations — high domestic savings, reliable tax collection and a stable banking sector.

As the global bond market sells off, France is not alone in facing rising long-term yields, which move inversely to prices, nor have the country’s fundamentals worsened overnight, they say. Bond auctions continue to be oversubscribed.

“France is not Greece during the Eurozone crisis,” says Moulin, the Bank of France chief. “If it can pass a budget this year to reduce spending and narrow the deficit as the government has proposed, then markets will be reassured by this concrete step of fiscal consolidation.”

Speculating about the ECB swooping in to help France is beside the point, he adds: “The safety net lies closer to home. It lies in the capacity of the French and their elected representatives to recognise the need to repair public finances.”

But debt has risen by more than a trillion euros during the nine-year presidency of Emmanuel Macron, whose business-friendly reforms quickly gave way to big spending to blunt the impact of successive crises.

Since Macron called snap parliamentary elections in 2024, the gridlock of a hung parliament has turned budget debates into trench warfare, claiming the heads of two prime ministers and leaving the deficit stuck above 5 per cent of GDP for three years.

The rapidly widening spread over German Bunds has added a new urgency.

“This is where you can really see the protection that the euro represents for France,” says Moscovici. “If we still had a system of national money, then the spreads of interest rates would be even higher.”

Some investors suggest the pain inflicted by increasing borrowing costs — and the risk of still worse travails — could force French fiscal policy back on track, much as former British prime minister Liz Truss ditched unfunded tax cuts when confronted with a gilts crisis in 2022.

Indeed, last week Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu proposed a €43bn package of spending cuts and tax rises for next year’s budget, including unpopular curbs on pension increases and partial freezes on civil servant salaries.

Lecornu had been urged on by Macron to make ambitious cuts to project determination and calm the markets. The risk is that the bigger and more unpopular the proposed cuts, the more vulnerable Lecornu’s minority administration is to being toppled by parliament — particularly with the opposition preparing for next year’s presidential contest.

While the French government has constitutional tools to ram through a budget, passing it by decree would be unprecedented and would inflame the opposition.

Another convulsion on debt markets will be all but certain if the government collapses during the budget debates that could last to year-end.

In any case, investors are sceptical that the budget can deliver spending cuts to reach Lecornu’s goal of bringing the fiscal deficit down to 5 per cent in 2027. This year, instead of holding steady as hoped, the deficit is projected to rise to 5.4 per cent because of the economic slowdown and higher borrowing costs. France once promised to rein in the deficit back within the EU limits of 3 per cent of GDP by 2029; at present such targets are firmly out of reach.

Next year’s presidential race provides still more uncertainty.

Marine Le Pen, the far-right politician leading the polls, sought on Tuesday to reassure the markets and voters by promising €140bn in budget cuts over five years.

Amid the bond rout, she has called for a national debt limit of 60 per cent of GDP — half of current levels — to drag the country back “from the brink of a financial, economic and moral crisis”.

But she is also campaigning on lowering the retirement age for some and slashing VAT on energy and food essentials — which could add tens of billions to the debt.

One big question is whether, if elected, she would follow in the path of Italy’s prime minister Giorgia Meloni, who managed to quell the market anxiety that accompanied her rise to power in 2022.

“Unless you think they are so extreme they are willing to blow the whole thing up, I think some kind of natural caution prevails,” one big bond investor says of Le Pen and other populists.

Meanwhile, more mainstream centrist and rightwing candidates who urge fiscal rectitude are flailing in the polls.

Surveys show far-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon within striking distance of a hypothetical run-off with Le Pen, although they also indicate he would be roundly defeated in a second-round vote. The former Trotskyist recently proclaimed that French bonds held by the central bank could be thrown “into the fire”, or cancelled with no consequence. Debt investors were spooked that such a radical idea was even in the public debate.

And yet the fiscal plight of the Eurozone’s second-largest economy is worsening. France has not balanced its budget since 1974; even when interest payments are excluded, it has run a deficit every year since 2002.

Increasing taxes to deal with the rising cost of debt servicing could also be perilous. At 44 per cent of GDP, the tax burden is already among the world’s highest; the average in the OECD club of rich countries is 34 per cent.

Almost a quarter of public spending is gobbled up by pensions. French retirees leave the workforce earlier and receive relatively generous benefits by OECD standards. Attempts to push back the retirement age trigger angry protests.

Eric Lombard, who served as finance minister last year, says there is no way to fix public finances without increasing the retirement age and reducing unemployment. “The fundamental problem in France is we don’t work enough,” he says. But if more people are in employment and benefits curtailed, he adds, with “a bit of luck in five years we can turn things around”.

Some consider this wishful thinking.

“France has a great history of trying to be less profligate and failing to achieve that,” says Andrew Jackson, head of investments at Vontobel Asset Management.

But he also cautions that there is a risk that spending cuts could hit the country’s already “anaemic” growth, worsening the debt squeeze still further.

A vicious spiral

Nowhere has France’s declining economic status been more apparent than in the bond market.

Paris was long deemed a “semi-core” Eurozone borrower for its safe status, trading at a modest spread to German Bunds. Debt trouble spots such as Italy and Greece, by contrast, were badged as the Eurozone “periphery” for their greater debt risks and higher spreads.

France’s political gridlock and worsening debt have made things very different. A series of ratings downgrades has helped push up the country’s borrowing costs, which passed Greece’s in late 2024 and Italy’s last year. Investors now label France the “new periphery”.

Despite the government’s tax-raising powers, its borrowing costs now exceed those of big French multinationals such as LVMH, the luxury group, and Sanofi, the pharmaceutical company. According to Goldman Sachs, more than a quarter of investment-grade French companies had a lower yield on their bonds than comparable government debt as of the end of September.

All big western economies have endured rises in borrowing costs since the end of the pandemic. Benchmark interest rates have returned to more normal levels after Covid-era lows. Central banks scrapped their vast asset-buying programmes just as bond issuance from sovereign and corporate borrowers hit record levels, while Japanese investors have also pulled back from French bonds and other Eurozone debt.

The phenomenon has gained pace since the outbreak of the Iran war, as central banks have raised interest rates to combat oil price-fuelled inflation.

But France has been hit hardest among big bond markets, as investors demand a much bigger premium to compensate for the growing risk to its public finances.

Downgrading French government debt last month, the rating agency Scope said rising yields would hurt the country through “further constraining fiscal flexibility and increasing the scale of the adjustment required to stabilise public debt”. A further test will come in a review by Moody’s late this month.

Market interest rates take time to feed through into countries’ debt servicing costs, but France’s are already painfully high. The government expects interest payments to total €79bn this year and €91bn, or 2.9 per cent of GDP, in 2027.

Even those figures are based on a yield below the current market rate; they assume an average of 4.3 per cent on the yield for 10-year government debt from 2027 onwards. Since they were calculated, it has climbed to 4.8 per cent. Analysts at Morgan Stanley said that yields running above the assumption were a “significant upside risk on interest payments for the coming years”.

Some observers worry that France is entering into a self-fulfilling spiral: the cost of debt servicing rises, increasing the country’s deficit, and then investors respond by pushing bond yields and debt costs even higher.

The European dimension

The widening spreads between French bonds and those of the country’s European neighbours have set off market speculation about the ECB stepping in.

French government officials and some opposition figures privately signal that such outside intervention may be the only way to force deep spending cuts.

Alain Minc, an influential adviser to French corporations who has informal ties to the government, argues that the crisis could snowball even before the presidential election.

“The question that investors will be asking themselves is if the ECB is prepared to support France with no strings attached until the presidential election,” he says. “The mere fact that people are asking will make the crisis worse.”

Bond investors are also debating whether a certain level of French spreads above German Bunds would force the ECB to step in to calm the markets that determine Eurozone economic conditions.

Most think the central bank would be especially likely to act if there is serious contagion from France to other European debt markets.

“The move is no longer just about France,” wrote TD Securities strategist Pooja Kumra in a note last week, as European bonds sold off, together with other areas of the debt market. “Broader financial tightening may require a more forceful response from the ECB to help stabilise markets.”

A much bigger sell-off may be needed for the ECB to act, but investors are aware that political conditions in France could amplify the risk.

Asset management giant Vanguard warned last week that “grandstanding” from political parties ahead of April’s presidential election could threaten the fiscal adjustment outlined in Lecornu’s budget proposals. Spreads could then widen across the Eurozone.

In such a scenario, the ECB’s capacity to buy huge quantities of bonds could provide the ultimate backstop on the basis that the central bank would not allow a big European economy to tip into a full-blown debt crisis.

ECB president Christine Lagarde, a former French finance minister, has in the past been reluctant to react when differences emerge between countries’ borrowing costs.

Months after taking office as ECB president, she told journalists in March 2020 that it was not the central bank’s job to “close spreads”, triggering short-term market unrest that only eased after she almost immediately backtracked.

Two years later, the central bank announced it had designed an emergency bond-buying tool to fight “unwarranted” and “disorderly” swings in bond prices that are a “serious threat to the transmission of monetary policy”.

Details of this so-called Transmission Protection Instrument are opaque, and it has never been used so far. Analysts think that the hurdles are high; in the summer of 2022, the ECB declined to intervene when the Italian spread with Germany shot up to 2.5 points, more than a percentage point above the French spread’s current level.

The ECB said it would only use the instrument to buy the bonds of countries that pursue “sound and sustainable fiscal and macroeconomic policies”, an argument that might be difficult to make for France. “Widening spreads without clear fiscal consolidation efforts will not trigger TPI,” says Carsten Brzeski at ING.

Morgan Stanley’s chief Europe economist Jens Eisenschmidt, a former ECB official, says he suspects the bank’s governing council “would prefer not to touch TPI”, highlighting the political sensitivity of emergency bond buying. He also cites “scant evidence so far” that the rise in borrowing costs is pushing the central bank’s monetary policy off course. “But surely, the ECB will be closely monitoring that situation.”

Some insiders think it is just a matter of time before the ECB switches into crisis mode. There could soon be change at the top. Lagarde’s mandate officially ends in October 2027 but she recently said that she might be “leaving a few months before the end of my term”.

One former European central banker adds that the institution’s next leadership will have to walk a fine line between preventing a crisis and escalating it: “There is a high probability that the next president of the ECB at some point during their tenure will have to buy French government bonds.”

item.title: We should call time on the ‘end times’
item.author: Nicolas Guilhot
item.description: Narratives of looming apocalypse are a sign that something has gone seriously wrong with our politics
item.content:encoded:
Narratives of looming apocalypse are a sign that something has gone seriously wrong with our politics

Nicolas Guilhot

The writer is professor of intellectual history at the European University Institute and author of ‘Conspiracy: The History of a Political Obsession’

From the climate meltdown to the possibility of a runaway AI triggering a paper-clip apocalypse, catastrophic scenarios aren’t in short supply these days. Whether it is in order to prep for impending doom or to denounce the toxic ideology of new corporate overlords, everyone seems to have settled on “end times” as the expression that best captures the zeitgeist. 

Much of this has to do with the idea, widespread among tech elites, that only the unfettered development of AI will see the elect through the coming catastrophe. The eschatological subtext is occasionally made explicit. In a recent interview, US vice-president JD Vance mused that his political work might be paving the way for the consummation of human history. The conversation also touched upon the uninvited guest who crashes the party at the eleventh hour: Vance confessed he would not be surprised “if the Antichrist was walking among us”. 

Peter Thiel too has expatiated on this intriguing figure, warning that he might be masquerading as a do-gooder bent on regulating AI or fighting climate change. The spat that followed the publication of Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical about AI was a throwback to medieval times, when pope and emperor hurled accusations about being the Antichrist at each other.

Secular thinkers as well have shored up the notion that we are living through the end times, from Peter Turchin’s prognosis of societal collapse to Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor’s recent warnings about the form of elite “survivalism” they call “end times fascism”. Whether the end is nigh or not, everyone thinks we have run out of rope.

What is striking about all these discussions is how bleak they are. Even those who claim the authority of scripture for their politics or their corporate pitch do not have much of a future to offer.

Yet, from Christian expectancy to secular ideologies that envision “the collapse of capitalist society and the dawn of classless society as a mighty apocalypse”, as the philosopher Jacob Taubes once put it, visions of the end have not always been a source of terror. For centuries, they gave hope to the downtrodden and reconfigured crises as opportunities for renewal and redress. The “end” was not only the end-as-catastrophe; it was also the end-as-telos, which gives a sense of purpose and meaning to the present.

This is no longer the case. Today’s political culture has lost the capacity to discern a redemptive future beyond a horizon of crisis. We have, literally, nothing to look forward to. 

This condition isn’t new. It is the one Francis Fukuyama diagnosed more than 30 years ago as the “end of history”. It has become fashionable to dismiss his idea, yet Fukuyama was very clear that he wasn’t talking about world events but about the exhaustion of the liberal imagination: the end of history arrives when we can no longer imagine “a world that is essentially different from the present one, and at the same time better”. 

Everything indicates that living at the end of history may not be sustainable — especially if it did not turn out to be the blissful dispensation that was promised. In the absence of desirable alternatives to the current state of things, the world ceases to be the space in which we experience our creative powers and, therefore, our freedom. It becomes opaque and alien, as if invisible forces were thwarting our agency.

A century ago, psychiatrists identified the “apocalyptic experience” as a typical symptom of schizophrenia. The narratives that best comport with this experience are also apocalyptic in the etymological sense of the term: the revelation of what is hidden. The end times are when the dark forces acting in history will be revealed, the dots connected, the enemies unmasked. 

Today, politics swaps the pursuit of a future good for the defeat of an enemy; conspiracy theories spread and become the only possible vision of history.

This is certainly cause for concern. Yet it is also an indication that the catastrophe is not written in stone — or in algorithms. It is the result of faulty politics that, like Dorian Gray, have embraced the fantasy of eternal youth promised by the end of history, while their decay was increasingly visible. The fact that some things age badly does not mean history ends with them but that it’s time to let go of them and contemplate new departures.

item.title: Why are bond yields so high?
item.author: Chris Giles
item.description: An attempt to shed some light on the big question of 2026
item.content:encoded:
An attempt to shed some light on the big question of 2026

Chris Giles

The enduring financial market story of 2026 is the rise in long-term government borrowing costs. The median rise in 10-year sovereign yields in G7 countries has been one percentage point, causing a nasty shock for finance ministers.

The big question is why yields have risen so much. Is it because investors want more compensation for perceived fiscal unsustainability? Does it reflect expectations of much faster growth? Is there a global war for investment funds and limited lenders? Has the Iran war raised the prospect of continued high inflation? Is it that central banks signalled the need for persistently higher short-term interest rates and markets are parroting this back? Have monetary policymakers lost inflation-fighting credibility? Or are bond markets now dominated by flighty hedge funds that can make huge returns if they get a negative narrative to stick?

Everyone has their own answers. Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh said there were three broad reasons at a press conference in September: US economic strength, competition for capital and difficult geopolitics.

The more important thing he said, however, was that explanations for changes in bond yields “tend to be overdetermined”. In other words, there are many competing but unprovable theories. And he is right.

For example, you might argue that expectations of short-term interest rates have changed. But these measures are horribly volatile and often wrong, as the chart below shows.

Or perhaps investors need more compensation for holding long-term debt (a rising term premium). But again, term premiums cannot be measured with any precision. The New York and San Francisco Feds both estimate the term premium on a daily basis using different methods to wildly different results. The New York Fed tends to report that the US 10-year term premium has decreased this year, while the San Francisco Fed says it has increased, as the chart below shows.

Warsh is right to talk only in broad terms about what bond markets are telling us. So what can we confidently say?

Central banks have broadly maintained inflation-fighting credibility

The difference between the yield on nominal and inflation-linked bonds provides an estimate of market inflation expectations. Ignoring the fact that inflation-linked bond markets are thin in some countries, break-even inflation expectations derived from this decomposition give an encouraging result for central banks: their inflation-fighting credibility remains intact.

The red line in the chart below shows longer-term market inflation expectations for the five-year period from five years ahead (that is, from 2031 to 2036). These have broadly been stable and close to target in most countries. The UK stands out here mainly because of a difference between the inflation measure used to uprate gilts and the inflation measure the Bank of England targets.

Rich-world five-year five-year forward market inflation expectations have been volatile this year thanks to the war in Iran. But higher UK rates suggest the BoE should probably be concerned that it appears to have less credibility than other central banks.

To keep inflation controlled, central banks are expected to set higher interest rates

There is no doubt that short-term interest rate expectations have risen across advanced economies. At the start of the year, the Fed was expected to cut rates to almost 3 per cent and now is expected to raise them to 4.75 per cent. That is a huge shift. There have been similar shifts in other countries’ expected policy rates, too. This is clearly an important underlying factor explaining the rise in bond yields.

Nasty geopolitics and higher oil prices are part of the story

The single clearest cause of the rise in bond yields, as the chart below shows, was President Donald Trump’s decision to initiate war with Iran, before which yields were generally falling. They moderated as tensions subsided in June and have risen since, along with the intensity of the conflict.

These movements suggest investors expect central banks to set higher interest rates to keep inflation under control in a world of fraught geopolitics and higher volatile energy prices.

Are markets parroting back signals sent by central banks?

This is a possibility. Recent research by Paul Beaudry, Paolo Cavallino and Tim Willems found a link between movements in long-term yields since 2020, US non-farm payroll data releases and central banker speeches. There is no doubt that central banks became more hawkish this year, but it is quite a leap to say higher yields are caused by loose talk from officials alone. Moreover, the Fed and European Central Bank have recently attempted to talk down interest rate expectations without huge success.

Are high yields an expression of economic strength?

Warsh thinks so, even though signs of immediate economic strength are much clearer in the US than elsewhere. In reality, signs of US strength are exaggerated occasionally by very strong quarterly figures, which are then annualised per convention. For example, the Atlanta Fed’s GDPNow model estimates 3.7 per cent real annualised growth in the third quarter, despite real growth rates in the first and second quarters being nothing to write home about.

Since we are looking at nominal yields, it is perhaps more informative to examine the performance of the nominal US economy. For sure, software and IT investment grew about 20 per cent in the year to the second quarter of 2026, and overall private non-financial investment grew almost 10 per cent. But GDP growth was just a little more than the average since 2011. And anyone who remembers 2022, when the US Inflation Reduction Act led to excitement about green growth that did not materialise, should be wary of predicting a massive increase in US growth rates.

That said, I have added the chart below not to say Warsh is wrong, but to show that if economic strength is the cause of higher yields, it must be an expectation of strength. And expectations are not always correct.

A war for capital

Higher yields could simply reflect a massive increase in demand for investible funds that is not met by increased supply. The chart below, which I have borrowed from Toby Nangle’s excellent piece, shows that debt issued by AI hyperscalers accounts for 13.8 per cent of US Treasury issuance, up from only 1.3 per cent in 2024. In other words, there has been a big increase in demand for debt from the AI sector.

A very important qualification, however, is that overall US corporate debt has not increased as a proportion of US Treasury debt, as the chart below shows. It is therefore hard to argue that AI or US corporate investment is the cause of higher global bond yields.

That said, there could still be a general change in the balance between overall debt issuance and debt demand among investors. To the extent that the war for capital is a valid explanation of higher long-term yields, it is more a story of excess debt overall than one to be pinned on the tech bros. Recent Fed research suggests that a $100bn increase in US Treasury supply raises five-year yields by 0.03 percentage points.

What about fiscal incontinence?

No one I have spoken to thinks government debt markets in advanced economies are currently disorderly or signalling impending default. But countries that have very high levels of debt, difficult politics or no coherent plans to reduce their deficits have seen a bigger rise in bond yields than elsewhere, with France, Italy, the US and Japan performing worst. So some explanation behind the yields story must be investors wanting more compensation for fiscal risks.

Could it all be financial market fashion?

As you can see, the real causes of rising yields are rather hard to pin down with any precision. This problem is exacerbated by a huge increase in hedge fund activity in government bond markets, with these potentially flightier investors replacing stickier pension funds, insurance companies and foreign governments. As the FT reported last week, some hedge funds have made a lot of money by betting against government bonds and ensuring the negative narrative sticks. This may well be an example of government bond markets failing to be as efficient at pricing as we might like, especially if hedge funds are using momentum strategies to position themselves.

So what?

Remember that we cannot know for sure what is causing bond yields to rise. The one thing we know quite clearly is that central banks still have broad inflation-fighting credibility. On top of this, there is strong evidence that nasty geopolitics are playing a role, and that financial markets are reflecting central bankers’ increased hawkishness which, in turn, is justified by the fundamentals. Moreover, there are signs that high government debt issuance is applying upward pressure to yields and that markets prefer lending to countries doing something about their deficits. There is weaker evidence that high yields are caused by current economic strength, borrowing by AI companies or the risk of sovereign default.

Of course, none of these explanations are mutually exclusive.

What I’ve been reading and watching

  • Fed officials have been damping speculation about a back-to-back US interest rate rise later this month.
  • Philip Lane, ECB chief economist, reminded people yesterday that energy prices were not the sole determinant of Eurozone interest rates. Other forces warranted more caution, he said.
  • Sanae Takaichi, Japan’s prime minister, has felt the need to reassure markets that her government will not engage in rapid public spending growth, which is the opposite story she told in July.
  • The US jobs market is still fine.

One last chart

The G7 agreed on Friday to release 100mn barrels of crude oil and diesel over the next four months, including a “substantial” release of diesel reserves within the first 20 days. Diesel prices dropped on the news but were rising again yesterday. Wholesale diesel prices remain about twice as high as what they were before the Iran war, as the chart below shows.

The price drop seen at the end of last week will not substantially relieve pressure on US Republicans as the midterm elections approach.

Central Banks is edited by Harvey Nriapia

item.title: California’s oligarch tax would change America
item.author: Edward Luce
item.description: The goal of its framers is political rather than budgetary
item.content:encoded:
The goal of its framers is political rather than budgetary

Edward Luce

What happens in California rarely stays in California. Should the state’s voters pass a wealth tax on its 246 billionaires next month, some of them might flee to Texas or Florida. Yet the idea (known as “Prop 40”) — a 5 per cent windfall tax on wealth above $1bn — might also spread. America’s future will be deeply affected by either result. At stake is whether the US super-rich’s largely unimpeded ascent in the last generation will continue uninterrupted. The tax’s goal is thus political, not budgetary.

In fiscal terms, Prop 40 is badly designed. One-off taxes are a headache for accountants. By earmarking its roughly $100bn in revenues mostly for healthcare, it limits California’s leeway. Anyone wanting genuine reform would propose a minimum tax on those above a certain net worth (say $100mn). That would permanently shift the burden and give California’s legislators control of how to spend it. On both counts it fails.

Prop 40’s political framing is nevertheless smart. America’s anti-tax reaction began in California in 1978 with the victory of Prop 13, which put a strict lid on property taxes. That backlash spread to the nation via the presidential victory two years later of California’s Ronald Reagan. Prop 40’s goal is to trigger a corresponding backlash against untaxed exorbitant wealth. The aim is thus to shift the so-called Overton Window that dictates what is politically possible. In that respect, a yes or a no could be just as momentous for America’s future as the widely forecast Democratic midterm win on the same day. That is how California’s most vocal billionaires see it.  

Chief among these is Sergey Brin, co-founder of Google, who compares Prop 40’s intent to the Soviet system that his parents fled in the 1970s. Supported by Peter Thiel, America’s most influential libertarian, Brin has spent more than $100mn of his own money to defeat it. Billionaires have also devised another measure, Prop 42, that would ban any new taxes on personal assets other than real estate. Since this would be a state constitutional ban, its approval would seal off any kind of wealth tax.

Plebiscitary democracy being what it is, Prop 40 and Prop 42 could both pass, which would trigger rampant confusion. Any such train wreck would be down to two factors. The first is the opposition to Prop 40 of Gavin Newsom, California’s Democratic governor, who leads many prediction markets for his party’s 2028 nomination. Newsom says that the tax would only make sense if it were federal. He has a point. But this stance also serves his campaign needs. Chris Larsen, the billionaire co-founder of the blockchain company Ripple, and an opponent of Prop 40, has promised to boost Newsom “any way we can”.

The second cause of defeat would be a disinformation campaign, which says the tax is really an “everyone tax”. In a recent ad, a Trojan hog filled with scowling bureaucrats is unleashed on a middle-class Californian neighbourhood. They assault old people and children in a scramble to seize assets such as bicycles, televisions and surfboards. Their message is pure demagoguery. Prop 40’s tax threshold could be lowered only with a two-thirds majority of California’s assembly and within the legal spirit of the measure. Conflating billionaires with ordinary Americans is a bold sleight of hand. But the campaign has depressed support for Prop 40, which is now too close to call.

Brin is no fool. Though America’s top income and capital gains tax were both close to double the rates in the 1970s of what they are today (at just under 40 per cent and 20 per cent, respectively), his Soviet analogy strikes a nerve with other wealthy Americans. Their fear is that Prop 40 is the thin end of the wedge. Brin also claims that the money would be squandered by a failed bureaucracy. That point has some merit. To anyone who thinks California’s state is efficient, I have a high-speed Los Angeles-San Francisco rail link to sell you.

Yet Brin, Thiel and others would be more convincing if they were championing any idea of government reform. Their true goal appears to be to disable it. The line from the US Supreme Court justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr that “taxes are the price we pay for civilisation” is as true today as when he made it a century ago. A rational billionaire would see the merits of buying social peace. An enlightened one would acknowledge his debts to federal science, public education and chance.

Alas, there are few such super-rich to be found. Should Brin get his way on November 3, it could turn out to be a Pyrrhic victory.

edward.luce@ft.com

item.title: A plausible theory for reviving the Conservatives
item.author: Stephen Bush
item.description: Tories could attract swing voters on economic grounds who might otherwise, on constitutional and cultural grounds, agree with Labour
item.content:encoded:
Tories could attract swing voters on economic grounds who might otherwise, on constitutional and cultural grounds, agree with Labour

Stephen Bush

Good morning from Birmingham. The mood at Conservative Party conference is pretty elated. Some thoughts on why in today’s note.

Buoyant mood

There is a plausible theory underpinning the Conservatives’ buoyant mood. The government is pursuing classic Labour Party economic policies, which have left the centre ground completely vacant. Reform is mired in scandal and is otherwise too polarising to win. The Liberal Democrats aren’t really interested in challenging the Tories on the centre right. Current global economic conditions are bad for incumbent governments. Therefore, the theory goes, Britain will at the next election turn its grateful eyes back to the Conservatives.

This is, in theory, really plausible. Kemi Badenoch’s big eve-of-conference policy announcement about giving everyone who earns more than £100,000 free childcare tackles a real problem in our system, as the current “cliff edge” incentivises people to reduce their hours. Moreover, the offer is laser-targeted at the voters the Conservatives badly need to win back from the Lib Dems.

That said, the policy may not have the desired effect because almost everything else the Conservatives under Badenoch do and say is laser-targeted at telling Lib Dem voters that her party doesn’t share their values. Hers is still a Tory party committed to Brexit, and opposed to the European Convention on Human Rights and net zero. Some argue that the Conservatives simply aren’t going to win over many forty-somethings with these positions, no matter how much free childcare you give them.

But it is equally plausible that swing voters will choose a Conservative Party they are economically aligned with over a Labour Party they have more in common with on constitutional and cultural grounds. As I say, the Tory party has a fantastic theory that might well come off.

The problem is, in the here and now, it hasn’t yet. The Conservatives are polling at 20 per cent and their electoral record in local elections is still pretty dire.

Now try this

This week, I mostly listened to From the Edge by Richard Bundy and Anna Phoebe while writing my column.

Top stories today

  • Put the brakes on | Richard Parker, the Labour mayor of the West Midlands, has urged John Healey to water down Britain’s electric car production targets to prevent damage to carmakers and their suppliers across the region.
  • ‘Master storyteller’ | Jeffrey Archer, former Conservative politician and colourful bestselling author, died yesterday at the age of 86, the day before the publication of what he said would be his last book.
  • ‘Cautious optimism’ | Can Kemi Badenoch return the Tories to power? FT reporters crunch the numbers.
