item.title: How AI could scupper the dollar
item.author: Katie Martin
item.description: Things are fine until they’re not
item.content:encoded:
Things are fine until they’re not

Katie Martin

Good morning. I just spent a very pleasant weekend in Rennes, France — beautiful buildings, amazing food markets, good vibes, rebellious students. Nobody seemed overly troubled by soaring French bond yields, but investors disagree, with wide spreads to German bonds and the euro on Monday sinking to a 17-month low. The Eurozone rates market has been vicious for a lot of hedgies this year, and the Eurozone debt crisis veterans among us are breathing rapidly into paper bags. Meanwhile in Japan, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi asked bond investors to trust her over fiscal plans. Record-breaking highs in the Japanese 30-year yield suggest this is not going super well. Would you rather hold 30-year France or 30-year Japan? unhedged@ft.com

Rock me, Amodei

The upward turn in the dollar last month took quite a few people by surprise, as we pointed out in this newsletter the other day. At 102-ish, the DXY dollar index is now perching at its highest level since the spring of last year.

A large chunk of this ascent is attributable to the rise and rise in Treasury yields. Some of it is about the decline in dollar hedging. But, related to that, some of it also seems to be about AI, which I will refrain from calling SI here even though that would be a nice way to annoy Rob. 

The logic here, as laid out last month by another Rob — Rob Subbaraman at Nomura — is elegantly simple. In short, the AI trade, writ large, has been so enormous, and sucked in such huge investment flows from all around the world, that suddenly, the planet is very, very long dollars. The US is the AI trade, and the AI trade is the US capital markets, to a very large degree.

Subbaraman looked at the US’s NIIP — its net international investment position — up to the end of 2025 (so this does not capture this year).

He wrote, in a note alongside colleague Yiru Chen:

US NIIP liabilities (ie, the rest of the world’s holdings of dollar assets) have ballooned because of net capital inflows and extraordinary capital gains from the AI-driven US equity boom . ..

Strikingly, the ratio of US NIIP liabilities to the sum of all rest-of-world net creditor nations’ NIIP assets has surged to 80 per cent — a vivid measure of the concentration of the world’s savings that have been funnelled into dollar investments. 

More striking still, in 2010, US NIIP liabilities matched the NIIP asset holdings of the world’s top net creditor nation, Japan. 

By 2025, it took the top 10 net creditor nations combined to match the US NIIP liabilities.

For the visually minded/data nerdy among you, that looks like this:

And this:

Now of course, that is all fine until it’s not. But wise readers of this newsletter are all capable of dashing off a list of half a dozen things that could go wrong with the AI trade, from vanishing moats to issues with monetisation to deadly robots and, even more terrifying, lawyers.

If something did go wrong, what would investors do? If they had any sense, they would sell AI-related assets. For non-US investors, that obviously means selling a lot of dollars. 

Geoff Yu at BNY makes a similar point, albeit without direct reference to the AI trade, in a report about dollar hedging. From that, this chart shows cross-border US equity and fixed-income holdings net of dollar holdings up to the end of September.

So, again, as we discussed in the last newsletter on this topic, dollar hedging levels have collapsed, very much against the run of expectations. Investors are happily taking on the assets and the currency risk (Yolo!). That means either a reversal in hedging ratios or a big knock to US markets (aka the AI trade) would demand a decent whack of dollar selling by non-US investors.

Normally, the dollar loves a good crisis, even a homegrown one. This type of potential wobble? Not so sure.

This is all theoretical for now, and none of it might crystallise. If it did, we might be talking only about a stumble, and then a recovery. Nonetheless, this all illustrates the power of the world of one trade. Everything is computer. 

If you’re keeping score, the things that are borked if AI encounters a serious problem now include:

  • The entire global stock market
  • Private markets
  • The dollar

But on the plus side, it might pull down Treasury yields and maybe stop the robots from killing us? Swings and roundabouts.

One good read

Potus vs Scotus

item.title: The not very secret life of A7’s front companies
item.author: Chris Cook
item.description: The Tolkien shops and ring cycles at the centre of Russia’s money laundering network
item.content:encoded:
The Tolkien shops and ring cycles at the centre of Russia’s money laundering network

Chris Cook

The US Treasury last week decided to hit A7, the Kremlin-backed payment service money laundering network, with a wave of new sanctions. This includes designation as a Transnational Criminal Organisation — a status that gives them a few new tools to go after it.

The designation press release set out something that FT readers already knew:

The A7 Network exploits the international financial system by leveraging Sub-Agents, falsified trade documents, falsified import-export records, and misleading goods descriptions to make sanctioned or illicit payments appear to be ordinary commercial activity.

The Treasury also published a proposed set of new regulations from FinCen, plus an alert which set out some useful advice on how to spot A7 front companies.

As it happens, we had revealed the week before how $6.9bn was laundered through conventional correspondent banking. The US government’s analysis is, broadly, the same as ours. But there’s something in here that gives me pause.

We’ll get to it — but first, it is worth explaining the whole universe of A7 subagents / front companies.

To start at the beginning, at the start of 2025: at the core of the system, early on, a small number of fronts in the UAE were performing some critical functions for the network, whose purpose was to enable Russian importers to pay their suppliers abroad after Moscow’s banks were cut off from the world banking system.

First, these central accounts took hard currency from Russian exporters. Second, they used that float to make payments abroad on behalf of A7 customers. And finally, they would distribute this cash to other A7-linked entities, which needed reimbursement or topping-up.

But this place in the system — doing the FX work — puts them one hop from Russian exporters and traders, lots of whom are sanctioned. And they are directed by A7, which is also sanctioned. So they are intrinsically exposed.

We know from the leak A7 had rules for operating these big central treasuries: nothing attention-grabbing. No payments to Belarus, Russia or the US. Staff are cautioned against payments to Citi, JPMorgan Chase, HSBC and ICBC — banks whose AML seems to be on to them.

They were also compartmentalised so that if one of the exporters’ fronts got busted, they wouldn’t all get busted. One internal chat message notes:

Assign each dirham supplier [the Russian exporters] to one paying company; mixing dirham suppliers under one ultimate owner is forbidden.

These things were often huge, but were fundamentally just puppet entities that were discarded at will.

For example, here is a message that was sent out to A7 staff on their internal messenger about Favnir, one of their biggest UAE front entities, and which was handling millions of dollars every day in early 2025:

From 10 March Favnir stops working. Gimli will be used for crypto and receiving dirhams. Solara for buying dirhams. Xentra for client payments.

These are the names of other front companies — Gimli, Solara and Xentra. The staff who make payments on behalf of customers were told:

Effective March 10, 2025, Favnir is suspending operations; payments from the UAE will be processed through the new company XENTRA L.L.C-FZ

It might fair to suspect that, if you were an AML officer who was on to Favnir, you might spot Xentra. That switch was not subtle. The two companies had 225 beneficiaries in common. Both held accounts at First Abu Dhabi and Dubai Islamic Bank.

The Swift messages for Favnir give its name and address as:

FAVNIR L L C FZ MEYDAN 6TH GRANDSTAND FLOOR MEYDAN 118256 DUBAI AE

Xentra, meanwhile is:

XENTRA L L C FZ MEYDAN GRANDSTAND 6TH FLOOR MEYDAN ROAD NAD 340671 DUBAI AE

You see similar artlessness through the leak. Ring enthusiasts might have already spotted a pattern: Gimli LLC-FZ appears to be named after a dwarf from Tolkien, while Favnir LLC-FZ seems to take its name from a Norse character popularised by Wagner.

There’s more Tolkien: you also get a Galadriel Trading FZCO and Boromir Trading FZCO. The successors of Favnir include Sigizmund FZCO and Zigfrid LLC-FZ, which might be how a Russian transliterated Siegmund and Siegfried, other characters from Wagner.

The FinCen notice also points out that a lot of the puppet entities have a “blank or minimally active website” operating on a fixed IP range. Again, it’s even less subtle than that.

The leak shows there were 71 email domains hosted on A7 infrastructure. Of these, 54 of these are held through the same registrar. And the records for the web registrations show A7 prepared these names in batches, with as many as nine being processed at once.

I don’t wish to labour the point, but there were other clues that these big entities in the UAE were not quite what they seemed, and had been created to serve A7.

For example, someone might have pondered these supposed Emirati companies seemed to have time off on Russia Day and Victory Day, and why their Christmas-New Year break followed a Russian calendar.

A7 also had a distinctive payment ledger-numbering system, which sometimes even showed up in the description fields of their Swift messages.

So it starts with a big, fairly unsubtle collection of fronts, which it is setting up and shutting down. By the end of the period covered by the leak, however, something else is starting to happen.

First, the sheer number of entities was starting to rise. There were probably about 200 such entities in operation during the period of the leak, which ran to August 2025. And, based on the leak, we could see and identify about half of those in operation and match them to specific flows.

The problem for FinCen’s rules is that, as A7 matured, the crude puppets were being joined by other companies with more convincing back stories. Some were older entities which A7 seemed to have taken some measure of control over. So the patterns of payment change.

But there was something else going on: according to A7’s payment ledger, two related entities in the UAE called “Celestial Bazaar” and “Zenith Global Mercantile”, for example, took in $445mn of internal payments.

In the central ledger, these things are treated much like the other paying bodies: they were assigned a code inside the A7 system as a “payer”. But, an internal A7 note written in late May 2025 notes:

These are “rented” treasuries. DBO in the UAE. No invoice replacement. Payment restrictions due to licenses. Amount limit of no more than $1 million USD per payment.

The implication of that word “rented” in the document seems to be that they may be controlled by a third party who is just doing some local payment processing for them. And these things are not empty companies. They have fully working websites and real businesses.

Here is a sample of some other bodies described in the leaks as “rented”.

The “rented” treasuries
Company nameA7’s assigned payer codeOutgoing payments logged
Celestial Bazaar Trading FZCOPAE003$61mn
Zenith Global Mercantile FZCOPAE005$72mn
Green Day Motors and Traders FZCOPAE006
Manfaa Global LLC FZCOPAE012$12mn
El Nasr Export & Import Co (Gosoor)PEG001$1.3mn
Imex InternationalPEG003$196,000
Ewings International Trade Co., LimitedPHK003$3mn

(We’ve written to each of these companies at their publicised addresses, but had no replies other than some email bounces.)

We should be clear, too: they may also not know they are working for a transnational criminal organisation. And this brings me back to the FinCen release.

Here’s a line in there that jumps out. The proposed new rules would state:

transactions involving any company operating outside of the United States that is controlled by the A7 Network . . . are a class of transactions of primary money laundering concern in connection with Russian illicit finance

The interesting word there, to me, is controlled. Later on, it also says:

Although on paper, these companies are typically represented to be owned or managed by non-Russian third-country nationals, they are ultimately controlled by with [sic] the A7 Network.

It’s that word controlled that I suspect might need a tweak. Increasingly, I suspect, we will find these payments flowing through a broader range of payment agents, for whom the payments are only part of their work. In this sort of situation, I am not sure the proposed regulation covers them.

But there is, in any case, a second problem here: these new types of payers are much harder to spot. The payments are buried inside a real business.

Maybe the designation and rule changes will help, precisely because A7 is making this move.

Zach Tvarozna, a former US government banking analyst who wrote a report on A7, said: “Making A7 a TCO is a huge step. It puts the network in the same category as a drug cartel, and alongside the FinCen rule it gives the US a much wider set of tools.”

Tvarozna (who has an excellent Substack on transnational financial shenanigans) added: “You need a lot of those powers, especially if the entity gets cleverer and starts infiltrating legitimate businesses who may not realise what they’re actually getting themselves involved with. These are the types of networks that sanctions alone can’t stop.”

All quite daunting.

But there is a real upside for people fighting money laundering: it will be much pricier to move cash this way. Trying to get the millions-of-dollars-a-day flows that moved through Favnir or Gimli through real companies is going to be very hard without the cost base shooting up.

The test of financial and trade sanctions effectiveness is not whether they stop Russia doing something. Things always get through. You measure effectiveness in the price they can be forced to pay for doing it.

Further reading:
— Kremlin-backed forgery scheme moved $6.9bn through global banks (FT)
— Rosneft billions fed Kremlin-backed money laundering network (FT)
— UK businessman given senior role at group linked to Kremlin money-laundering operation (FT)

item.title: Lex. BT’s swoop on TalkTalk has regulators over a barrel
item.description: UK watchdog typically takes a robust view of reduced competition in telecoms market but is taking a back seat this time
item.content:encoded:
UK watchdog typically takes a robust view of reduced competition in telecoms market but is taking a back seat this time

Half a century after losing its monopoly on UK telecoms, BT Group still holds sway. Its swoop on TalkTalk, a debt-laden broadband rival that’s currently in administration, shows the way.

While the financials of the deal are modest by the standards of the UK behemoth — a cash cost of £400mn in exchange for picking up £1.2bn of revenue — the key issue here is that the government is exercising powers to consider “the wider public interest” once the Competition and Markets Authority has reported on competition concerns. 

Upon completion, BT’s share of the retail customer base will rise from 31 per cent to 36 per cent. Depending on the measure used, it will have 65 to 90 per cent of the wholesale market. Yet under the so-called public intervention notice, the Competition and Markets Authority will not examine the transaction through its usual lengthy consultation process. Instead, it will have a fortnight to come up with findings.

One justification for this is the notion that if TalkTalk simply disappears, it will rip away essential services, ranging from health authorities to traffic lights that depend on TalkTalk for connectivity. BT, as a major provider of UK infrastructure, is definitely a safe pair of hands in this respect.

But, unusually, the UK telecoms company appears on multiple sides of this deal. TalkTalk, like many broadband suppliers, relies on physical infrastructure run by BT Openreach — a fully owned but legally separate part of BT — for which it pays up to £80mn a month.

For its part, BT may argue that there wasn’t anyone else who could have acquired TalkTalk. This is an accelerated end to a slow-drip saga. TalkTalk has long struggled, prevailing upon its put-upon lenders and investors to keep infusing cash. Several proposed deals have ended up going nowhere; other smaller ones — such as selling blocks of customers — barely moved the needle.

BT’s position in the ecosystem, coupled with the importance of the work it does, means that it is hard to imagine a different outcome for TalkTalk. But that has pushed the CMA into a difficult position. The watchdog typically takes a robust view of reduced competition in the telecoms market. For example, it looks minded to block a proposed deal by the owners of Virgin Media O2 to acquire a rival

That it is taking a back seat this time round, at the behest of government, may relieve TalkTalk’s long-suffering backers. It raises the question of why, if TalkTalk really is so essential, watchdogs did not get involved earlier to make sure it remained financially viable — or make sure there were potential buyers other than BT if push came to shove. As things stand, the potential for less choice and higher prices will do few favours to other stakeholders.

louise.lucas@ft.com

item.title: The politics of losing sleep
item.author: Sarah O’Connor
item.description: There is still a class divide when it comes to work that tramples over your body clock
item.content:encoded:
There is still a class divide when it comes to work that tramples over your body clock

Sarah O’Connor

In the 1920s, a pair of sociologists set out to study “the interwoven trends that are the life of a small American city” at a time of rapid change. In their subsequent book about Muncie, Indiana (which they anonymised as “Middletown”), they wrote that the community was divided by time as well as class. At 6am, the lights were going on in working-class households because their jobs generally began between 6.15 and 7.30am (when they weren’t on night shifts), while the “business class” households remained slumbering until later.

These different working rhythms became political in 1925 when a deadlock emerged over whether the city should adopt “daylight saving time”, which would mean longer light on summer evenings. The working-class early risers argued they would lose sleep, while the businessmen urged the change “because of golf” and the need to deal with businesses on the East Coast.

The competing demands for leisure and business on the one hand, and of our body clocks on the other, have not gone away over the ensuing century. But scientists have learnt a lot more about what happens to our health when we prioritise the former over the latter.

In short: nothing good. Many researchers now agree that daylight saving time can interfere with our circadian rhythms. But there are much more dangerous ways to meddle with our biological clocks, the worst of which is to work at night.

It is a myth that night-shift workers can become nocturnal over time. According to the book Life Time by professor of circadian neuroscience Russell Foster, studies suggest that 97 per cent of night shift workers remain synchronised to daytime, which means they have to sleep when their bodies are primed to be awake, and vice versa. There are consequences for blood pressure and the immune system. The correlations with cancer are so clear that night work has been classed as “probably carcinogenic to humans” by the World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer.

Even if you don’t work overnight, evidence suggests that just working against your “chronotype” can be bad for your health. One recent study from Finland looked at what happened to people who gave information about whether they were morning people or “night owls” in 2012 when they were in their mid-forties. Over the following 12 years, those with evening chronotypes were more likely to end up on disability pensions, even after adjusting for socio-economic factors. One possibility, according to the researchers, is that “traditional working times interfere significantly with the sleeping preferences of late chronotypes, leading to social jet lag”.

But while the prevalence of night work has declined gradually in the US since Middletown was written, there is still a class divide when it comes to work that tramples over your body clock. According to research published this year, most US night workers have no more than a high-school education.

More broadly, the pandemic-induced shift towards remote work has been a bigger boon for white-collar workers (who already had more flexibility over their hours) than anyone else.

In Europe, for example, managers have the highest levels of autonomy according to 2024’s vast European Working Conditions Survey, with 40 per cent able to adapt their working hours within certain limits, and 19 per cent having full control over their schedules. In contrast, workers at the bottom end of the pay scale continue to have little control: nearly 80 per cent have schedules set entirely by their employers.

It is possible that advances in automation will eventually do away with the need for humans to work against their body clocks. Already, some logistics companies are beginning to experiment with “lights-out night shifts” in which robots work overnight alone, setting aside those orders that require human assistance until the morning shift arrives. Self-driving trucks, meanwhile, could cover long highway stretches overnight, saving the “final mile deliveries” for human drivers to do in daytime.

Such a transition would be economically challenging for workers — not least since night-shift work usually pays a premium — but could have huge benefits for human health. It would require careful navigation by policymakers with an eye on science, inequality and the future.

Yet US President Donald Trump sounds much more like a voice from the past. His latest intervention into the “politics of time” is to push for daylight saving time to be made permanent, arguing that it would be good for people who would “like to play golf a little bit without having to run home after 14 holes”.

sarah.oconnor@ft.com

item.title: Andy Burnham’s Manchester City problem
item.author: Stephen Bush
item.description: The prime minister’s economic vision looks dangerously like a game of two halves
item.content:encoded:
The prime minister’s economic vision looks dangerously like a game of two halves

Stephen Bush

The fact that Manchester City have been found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges brought against them by the Premier League over breaches of its financial rules divides people. It divides me. On one hand, as an Arsenal fan, I think that City are cheats, and that the only solution is for the club to be hit with huge fines, stripped of their trophies and banished to the lowest reaches of the football pyramid. Among fans of City’s rivals, this makes me a relative moderate in that I don’t want the club’s ground to be paved over and salted.

However, what I don’t want is for the UAE to stop investing in office and retail space in Manchester, London and the UK’s other great cities; for British wealth managers to lose out on Emirati clients to the Swiss or the Americans; and for England’s elite private schools, whether at home or their overseas franchises, to have fewer children from Abu Dhabi in them. So perhaps the paving over of the Etihad Stadium should be put on hold.

Andy Burnham, the prime minister, faces a similar dilemma. In his first gaffe since entering Number 10, when asked what he made of the charges, he responded by extolling the Abu Dhabi United Group, which owns City, for its investment in and around Manchester.

Now, I’m sympathetic to the notion that City’s punishment, whatever form it ends up taking, should be accompanied by warm words about the UAE. But I do have two nagging objections. The first is that Burnham’s words about City’s owners were warmer than anything he has said since becoming prime minister about, say, Qatari investment in Canary Wharf in east London. They were warmer, too, about money coming from Abu Dhabi than about anything that might flow from American banks or Chinese international students.

The second, and more important, objection is that Burnham’s defence of City’s owners came not 24 hours after a speech in which he railed against 40 years of economic choices that, he claims, have made Britain poorer and angrier than it should be. You can’t coherently maintain that it would be a crying shame for east Manchester to lose out on the UAE’s investment and at the same time insist that the economic policy choices made since the 1980s have been a complete disaster.

What could be more in keeping with the past 40 years of economic policy than the previous Labour government standing by when Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan bought Manchester City in 2008, and then watching approvingly as his investments in land and property, as well as the football club, reshaped the city? It’s incoherent to rail against such choices at a national level, as Burnham does when he promises to break with decades of “neoliberalism”, but to embrace and celebrate their impact on Manchester, where he was mayor for nine years.

What we are seeing here is “Manchesterism”, as a narrative about Burnham’s mayoralty designed to make the Labour Party feel good about itself, colliding with the reality of actually existing Manchesterism. In the latter, Manchester was reborn by ruthlessly marketing itself to global investment capital. Either Burnham’s premiership is defined by applying the real and useful lessons of actually existing Manchesterism to the country as a whole, or it simply allows the Labour Party to lurch towards its usual destination of electoral defeat via its preferred route of its own navel.

Which is it going to be? The signs are mixed. Burnham’s conference speech last week featured calls to scrap the triple lock and a willingness to risk votes for a closer relationship with the EU. So it isn’t entirely fair to suggest his schedule was “Tuesday — tell the Labour Party what it wants to hear; Wednesday — reflect on the things that actually help the British economy”. But it isn’t wholly unfair either.

The optimistic case for Burnham is that he might be the prime minister who gets Labour to accept that the desire for better public services and a happier society has to be preceded by a determination to deliver growth and compete on the world stage, including for the money and custom of people we don’t necessarily like.

But I can see the merits of the pessimistic case, too, which is that his vagueness about the trade-offs the country will have to make in its bid for growth reflect a large hole where a proper economic policy prospectus should be. While Burnham’s government has a surer touch than Keir Starmer’s on social care, the triple lock and public services, the Man City affair shows that it is still panicky, inconsistent and uncertain when it comes to the economy.

stephen.bush@ft.com

item.title: Lex. Why accountancy firm listings don’t add up
item.description: Private equity’s role in consolidating the sector is raising the stakes, making partnerships less sustainable
item.content:encoded:
Private equity’s role in consolidating the sector is raising the stakes, making partnerships less sustainable

Accountants should be whizzes at working out how best to structure and fund their firms. Instead, it turns out there’s a great deal of trial and error.

Take RSM, the fifth biggest of its breed by revenue in the US and seventh globally, now mulling a flotation. It has been here before. The US business spent a decade on the stock market as part of H & R Block. Meanwhile, RSM Tenon, a precursor of the UK sister firm, was publicly traded in London until it met with insolvency and a quiver of fines.

If that doesn’t deter RSM from going public again, there are other things that should at least give it pause — including the tyrannies of regular earnings updates, market gyrations and fickle owners.

Consider the example of CBIZ, an accountancy firm of three decades’ standing. Its shares have been in a tailspin for much of the past two years, pummelled by earnings disappointments. Grant Thornton in the US, backed by private equity firm New Mountain Capital, swooped earlier this year with a takeover offer. Even that was no higher than the share price just six months previously.

In the broader professional services universe, Accenture and Capgemini have been buffeted by on-off fears of AI detonating a so-called SaaSpocalypse — a reckoning for anyone selling software as a service. Mishcon de Reya, a favoured law firm of the glitterati, abandoned its listing plans twice, initially after partners revolted; smaller DWF languished before private equity rose to the rescue.

Accountancies, and businesses like them, make investors squeamish for good reason. Their main assets are people, and people are liable to leave if they get a better offer. They may be especially inclined to be so if the spoils divvied out among partners must henceforth be shared with outside investors.

Where accountants have an advantage over lawyers, say, is that their earnings are somewhat more predictable. Companies may rein in dealmaking, and thus the fees they generate for their legal advisers, but they still need to be audited. However, that advantage wanes with smaller clients such as start-ups that may fold or be sold. Other clients may use technology, be it AI or simpler apps, to do more of the work themselves.

For companies that want to grow briskly, private equity ownership stacks up better. Look, for example, at the managers who branched out of Big Four firms to launch their own boutiques. Indeed Grant Thornton in the UK, majority owned by private equity group Cinven since 2024, is even pulling ahead in the talent wars by offering graduate trainees higher salaries than they’d receive at the Big Four. 

The irony is that it is partly private equity’s role in consolidating the sector that is raising the stakes for other firms: they need to invest more to keep up with their bigger brethren. Shifts towards employing AI and away from the billable hours model mean partnerships are increasingly less sustainable, but there are better alternatives than heading to market.

louise.lucas@ft.com

item.title: Britain has turned digital ID into a growth industry
item.author: John Gapper
item.description: Start-ups such as Yoti and Luciditi are meeting demand for age and identity verification as the government retreats
item.content:encoded:
Start-ups such as Yoti and Luciditi are meeting demand for age and identity verification as the government retreats

John Gapper

Along with many FT readers, I have reached an age at which no one who sees me questions whether I am legally entitled to buy alcohol. So it feels like a waste of everyone’s time that an alert flashes when I reach a self-service till at a supermarket with a bottle of wine in my basket and an assistant must walk over to approve the purchase.

This shopping ritual, which absorbs a collective 5.8mn hours of customers’ time in the UK each year according to one Home Office calculation, could soon be eliminated. Adults who download a government-approved digital age verification app to their phones will instead be able to swipe a QR code to authorise themselves.

Digital age verification through apps offered by start-ups such as Yoti and Luciditi became legal last month. Young people who must prove they are allowed to buy alcohol in pubs and clubs will be able to do so without displaying their full identities. These face-verified apps show only a photo, a QR code and confirmation of being over 18 (or 25) to protect privacy.

One small step for age verification is a giant leap for digital ID. One of Andy Burnham’s first moves as prime minister was to drop a £1.8bn plan to create an official UK digital identity scheme, which would have been mandatory for those having to prove their right to work. Nearly 3mn people signed a petition protesting that it would infringe civil liberties.

Demand for digital ID is growing, even if the state cannot satisfy it. Proof of identity is needed for many things, including opening a bank account or visiting many City of London offices. It should be easier to do so digitally, rather than having to carry or scan a driving licence or passport. A new British growth industry is filling this gap.

About 275 companies with total annual revenues of £2bn now offer UK digital identity services, from employment and right-to-work checks to age verification for video gaming, gambling or buying tobacco. “Regulation is driving demand,” says Robin Tombs, Yoti co-founder and chief executive. The government now plans to impose a social media ban for under-16s from next year.

Britain has not wholly abandoned the development of official digital ID. The government is building a platform for people to sign on to its services online with verified identities. It is also developing a wallet that will let people hold digital versions of their official documents: this now accepts military veteran cards and driving licences are coming next.

But the UK also made a smart decision six years ago to build a trust framework for private companies that provide digital verification services. Instead of monopolising the market, it let companies build applications that complied with its security and privacy standards. This started under Boris Johnson and continues under Burnham.

That approach was far-sighted. It enabled the development of digital ID and verification services to continue despite reversals in government policies on identity cards, which reach back decades. It also encouraged innovation, such as the choice given by Yoti (and the Post Office’s EasyID app that uses its software) of how much information a user shares.

These start-ups must convince people that they can keep secure personal data such as the encrypted passport scans used to register users. They undergo security audits to remain on the UK’s approved register but face the wider backlash against tech companies. Yoti was fined €950,000 by Spain’s data protection agency this year over its use of facial recognition for authentication and is appealing.

Digital ID also needs to reach a societal tipping point, where so many people use the apps that they are widely adopted by businesses. That is still some way off, although the Yoti app has been downloaded 8.9mn times in the UK. Yoti took more than a decade to gain traction after it was founded in 2014; its revenue rose by 58 per cent to £32mn in the year to March.

Private enterprise has already helped Britain to gain a strong position in an emerging technology: more than 60 per cent of the sales of UK-based digital ID companies are international, a government study found. Phil Young, co-founder and chief technology officer of Luciditi, compares the advance of digital ID with touch payments.

“People will stop carrying physical ID one day. It is going to happen,” Young says. Burnham has retreated but the demand has not.

john.gapper@ft.com

item.title: Letter: The lessons of Jimmy Carter’s energy transition policies
item.description: From Teju Akande, Climate Change Manager, Border to Coast Pensions Partnership, Leeds, UK
item.content:encoded:
From Teju Akande, Climate Change Manager, Border to Coast Pensions Partnership, Leeds, UK

Moritz Kraemer (“The bill for stabilising the climate is rising”, Opinion, September 16) is right that higher interest rates, rising debt-servicing costs, strained public finances and more cautious capital markets make it harder to finance the investments needed both to reduce emissions and to adapt to the effects of climate change.

They also expose the limits of relying on aspirational commitments alone.

However, history suggests that investment in energy transition is not driven solely by abundant capital and low interest rates. A notable historical exception is the major US push into alternative energy in the late 1970s under President Jimmy Carter, largely in response to the oil shocks and concerns over energy security.

Tax incentives, federal research funding and deployment programmes were introduced despite high inflation and sharply rising interest rates. Although the economics were challenging, policymakers took the view that energy diversification was sufficiently important to justify intervention and long-term investment.

Today’s environment may have more in common with the 1970s, marked by supply shocks, geopolitical uncertainty and elevated financing costs, than with the era of ultra-low interest rates that followed the global financial crisis.

If so, the lesson is that success will depend less on cheap capital and more on policy clarity, strategic commitment and international co-operation.

Teju Akande
Climate Change Manager, Border to Coast Pensions Partnership, Leeds, UK

item.title: Letter: A happy ending to your Secret Service altercation
item.description: From Professor Siddartha Khastgir, Head of Safe Autonomy, WMG, University of Warwick, Coventry, UK
item.content:encoded:
From Professor Siddartha Khastgir, Head of Safe Autonomy, WMG, University of Warwick, Coventry, UK

Reading Joe Miller’s Outlook piece “What to do when your Waymo holds up a Secret Service motorcade” made me chuckle (September 24). Not only because it was written with great sarcastic humour, but also for unearthing one of the best-kept secrets of every driverless car service — namely the remote support functionality that every robotaxi service will need.

With various autonomous vehicle announcements worldwide, and London becoming a global battleground for various robotaxi companies, much of the talk around the safety of the technology is about its ability to handle weird and diverse situations.

But remote support is the conveniently ignored or forgotten aspect of a “good” and “non-nuisance creating” robotaxi service.

The support interaction with the occupant, the emergency responders and how they all handled a deadlock situation was on full view in Miller’s example, albeit not in a great light.

No robotaxi or driverless car service can be safely deployed in practice without some level of remote support set-up. The good news is that regulators have identified this as a gap in existing regulations and standards. It is being addressed but will take time. And while we wait, people need to know, there will always be this unspoken support backup present for every autonomous vehicle journey.

Professor Siddartha Khastgir
Head of Safe Autonomy, WMG, University of Warwick, Coventry, UK

item.title: Letter: Draghi’s argument risks skirting AI’s big questions
item.description: From Alberto Alemanno, Jean Monnet Professor of EU Law, HEC Paris, France
item.content:encoded:
From Alberto Alemanno, Jean Monnet Professor of EU Law, HEC Paris, France

Mario Draghi presents faster AI adoption as the route to restoring European growth and competitiveness (“Europe’s difficult choices on AI”, Opinion, FT Weekend, September 12). But his argument risks skirting the more consequential questions: who gains, who loses, whose power is strengthened, and whether AI adoption automatically advances broad-based prosperity at all.

Yet faster uptake of AI is not an economic strategy if the benefits concentrate while its costs fall on workers and communities. Labour displacement and the concentration of economic and political power must be addressed well before AI’s productivity gains accumulate. Those factors should help decide which AI Europe builds, deploys and rewards.

Europe was right to regulate AI before its consequences were fully known. It should not now let competitiveness turn speed into an end, rather than a means to shared prosperity and stronger democratic power.

Alberto Alemanno
Jean Monnet Professor of EU Law, HEC Paris, France

item.title: Letter: Bond market gives verdict on the data centre build-out
item.description: From Subir Grewal, Washington Square Capital Management, New York, NY, US
item.content:encoded:
From Subir Grewal, Washington Square Capital Management, New York, NY, US

Your report “Anthropic IPO filing reveals costs and outlines ‘existential risks to humanity’” (September 30) suggests an alternative explanation for the recent sharp rise in interest rates.

No, bond investors hadn’t decided AI was going to end the world and that they would rather spend it all now. Rather, institutional investors, looking at Anthropic’s S-1, the mandatory registration statement submitted to the Securities and Exchange Commission, probably surmised that AI would not help the US grow out of its deficit. At least not soon enough to make a difference to 10-year Treasuries.

The AI labs will require vast amounts of capital to meet their commitments to the hyperscalers, which is showing up in the marks on hyperscalers’ bonds issued to fund the data centre build-out.

In our youth, we scoffed at old hands who told us that trying to make sense of stocks was a mug’s game. Rates, they said, were the thing that mattered. Another generation of young investors may well have to learn the same lesson.

Subir Grewal
Washington Square Capital Management, New York, NY, US

item.title: When a label costs you $4bn in market cap
item.author: Ramsay Hodgson
item.description: Liquidia feels the pressure
item.content:encoded:
Liquidia feels the pressure

Ramsay Hodgson

Baseball might be America’s pastime, but sodium is its true love.

While too much of the former can result in an obsession with Sabermetrics, or a sore elbow, a side effect of excessive salt consumption is high blood pressure. An estimated more than 100mn Americans are afflicted.

One North Carolina-based drug company, Liquidia, has gone gangbusters over the past year in an effort to address a specific form of this condition: pulmonary hypertension.

The company sells the drug treprostinil under the brand name Yutrepia. This is an inhaled dry powder used to treat two types of pulmonary hypertension: pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and pulmonary hypertension associated with interstitial lung disease (PH-ILD).

Liquidia’s revenues surged following Yutrepia’s launch in June 2025 (a month after it got FDA approval): up from $12mn in the first six months of 2025 on an $80mn loss, to $304mn in the same period this year on a $127mn profit.

Shares duly did their thing:

All this success appears to have set blood boiling at United Therapeutics, Liquidia’s larger rival.

United’s brand is Tyvaso, a nebulised version of which was first approved in 2009 for PAH and for PH-ILD in 2021. It launched Tyvaso DPI, a dry-powder model, in 2022.

United’s patent covering the treatment of PH-ILD via inhaled treprostinil is number 11,826,327 and runs to February 2042.

In July 2023, Liquidia sought approval from the FDA to use Yutrepia for PH-ILD on top of PAH and notified United of a challenge to its patents.

United sued. In federal court in Delaware in September of that year, United accused Liquidia of infringement of a different patent, number 10,716,793. This, however, had previously been deemed “unpatentable” by the US Patent and Trademark Office in 2022, a ruling later upheld on appeal in December 2023.

In the meantime, United received patent 11,826,327 on November 28 2023. Two days later, it included it in an amended complaint and in January 2024 withdrew patent ’793.

The trial was held over four days in June 2025, by which point the focus had narrowed to six claims.

Last Wednesday, Judge Richard G Andrews issued his opinion, all 55 pages of which are here for your delectation.

At the heart of United’s claim was that Liquidia had encroached on its territory by issuing an FDA-approved label on Yutrepia — one that told doctors to use the drug to treat PH-ILD with inhaled treprostinil at specific doses, which United said was covered by patent ’327.

Liquidia had conceded that Yutrepia infringed two of the claims — 1 and 14 — under the patent but sought to claim that they were nonetheless invalid. Judge Andrews disagreed, and Liquidia was ruled to have infringed the patent. The other four claims were in effect deemed to be incidental to claim 1.

The patent infringement means Liquidia, at worst, could be forced to pay damages and temporarily take Yutrepia off the market altogether while it gets a new label without PH-ILD approved by the FDA.

Shares duly did their thing:

That’s one expensive labelling “issue”. Circa $2bn of market value apiece for an extra “L” and “D”.

Investors to have had almost two-thirds of their gains wiped out include Tom Steyer’s Farallon Capital — he of I am a billionaire and I believe I shouldn’t exist “fame”.

On the flip side, United’s shareholders seem pretty chuffed.

The two sides need to agree a remedy on the labelling by Wednesday at the latest. If they can’t reach a deal, the Court will step back in.

Liquidia plans to quickly “skinny” its label by removing PH-ILD and keeping the drug on the market to treat PAH. It has suggested it may appeal against the ruling. The company declined to comment further.

United — which is a public benefit corporation — wants the FDA to withdraw the entire approval for Yutrepia for both PH-ILD and PAH while it approves new labelling without PH-ILD, de facto removing Liquidia’s product from the US market until the new label is ready. They also plan to seek damages for past infringement, likely through royalties on historic sales. Investors in Liquidia expect litigation about the latter to be drawn out.

An investor in Liquidia told FTAV that if United goes ahead with this request, “thousands of patients — including patients for the non-infringing treatment of PAH — will be denied a life-saving treatment while the FDA considers the matter”.

United’s COO Michael Benkowitz said in a press release last Wednesday:

Our immediate priority is ensuring that no patient goes without the therapy they need, and we are ready to support a seamless transition to Tyvaso or Tyvaso DPI should PH-ILD be removed from the Yutrepia label.

Meanwhile Liquidia has warned “it is not possible at this time to reasonably estimate the range of potential outcomes or financial exposure”.

United told FTAV its “highest priority” remained the care and continuity of therapy for all patients with PAH and PH-ILD.

The company added that it had “established programs to help ensure that eligible patients can quickly and seamlessly transition” to its products “without interruption or increased cost”.

Some investors clearly aren’t waiting around based on the stock unwind, while others have made up their mind on how they think things will go later this week:

Not everyone is worried though.

the $LQDA buying opportunity is significant. stock will double as it becomes clear that the court ruling is not existential. drug is approved for PAH. never been a drug pulled over a patent. compulsory royalty of 10% would double stock instantly. courts will not harm patients.

— Martin Shkreli (@MartinShkreli) October 1, 2026

item.title: The FT View. Brazil’s Bolsonaro comeback exposes Lula’s weakness
item.author: The editorial board
item.description: Incumbent’s fading appeal has opened the door to a family revival in Brazil
item.content:encoded:
Incumbent’s fading appeal has opened the door to a family revival in Brazil

The editorial board

When former president Jair Bolsonaro was given a 27-year jail sentence last year for plotting a coup, Brazil received plaudits for its willingness to defend democracy and insulate itself from the more dangerous aspects of far-right populism. Unlike the US failure to bring Donald Trump to trial over efforts to overturn America’s 2020 presidential election, Brazil took decisive action against Bolsonaro and his allies for attempting to overturn the result of the 2022 Brazilian election.

Yet just as Trump defied the odds to become US president for a second term, so the Bolsonaro family has a strong chance of making its own remarkable comeback. Flávio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of the far-right former leader, beat the incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva 47-45 in the first round of voting in this year’s presidential election. He goes into a run-off on October 25 as favourite.

A victory for the younger Bolsonaro would cap a remarkable run for Trump-friendly candidates in Latin America. The right has already won all seven presidential elections held in the region since Trump returned to the White House, in many cases with Maga-style campaigns. Mexico would be the only major economy in the region still governed by the left.

If elected, Flávio Bolsonaro risks sparking a new institutional crisis if he pushes ahead with his pledge to free his father from jail without the decisive support of Congress. He would also face the issue of what to do about his brother Eduardo, a former member of Congress who is living in the US and was convicted by Brazil’s Supreme Court of trying to interfere in the case against their father.

How have the Bolsonaros managed to bounce back to the verge of power? The answer lies less in the achievements of Flávio Bolsonaro, who has been a mediocre candidate, and more in the failure of Lula. A late recovery by Lula cannot be ruled out, especially if new corruption allegations emerge against his opponent, but his weaknesses as a candidate have been exposed in this campaign.

Like voters across the region, Brazilians have consistently listed organised crime as a top concern. Over many years at the forefront of Brazilian politics, Lula has struggled to convince voters he has an effective answer to the rise of drug gangs; many on the left have given the impression that they do not see it as a priority.

On the economy, many headline indicators have been strong, including record-low unemployment. But lax fiscal policy has contributed to very high interest rates, which are punishing the 82 per cent of Brazilian families who have personal debts. Having been elected in 2022 with the help of some centrist parties, Lula has all too often retreated to the comfort zone of his leftwing Workers’ Party, which has left him more politically isolated this time.

Lula’s biggest problem is that he has become part of the furniture in Brasília. This is his seventh run for the presidency — the first was in 1989 — and he is asking for a fourth term overall. Presenting himself as a defender of democracy has only enhanced that impression.

The result is he is blamed for the failures of others. One of the biggest stories of the election has been revelations about the links between several members of the Supreme Court and the former owner of a bank that collapsed. These included a key judge in Jair Bolsonaro’s conviction.

Lula was not directly linked to the scandal — unlike Flávio Bolsonaro, who solicited financing from the banker for a proposed film about his father — but widespread revulsion at the perception of elite corruption has damaged him badly. Brazil acted to contain Jair Bolsonaro, but amid the heavy polarisation, with outrage constantly cultivated on social media and ingrained suspicion of elites, Lula has been unable to vanquish Bolsonarismo.

item.title: Lex. Schneider’s bet on a new world clashes with finance’s old rules
item.description: It is harder to be good at many things than one — and branching out into software leaves the stock exposed to AI threats
item.content:encoded:
It is harder to be good at many things than one — and branching out into software leaves the stock exposed to AI threats

Schneider Electric’s $23.7bn purchase of software company PTC is tantamount to a bold call that the rules of manufacturing are undergoing dramatic change. The dismal reaction by its investors, however, is a reminder that the principles of sound corporate finance are the same as ever.

The French group justified its splurge on PTC on Monday by arguing that the lines between hardware and software are blurring. Schneider’s electrical equipment generates data that its software tools — including those it will acquire via PTC — can use to automatically tweak designs and make systems run more efficiently. 

This sounds plausible enough. Yet news of the deal wiped about €15bn from Schneider’s market capitalisation. That’s roughly twice the present value of the synergies the buyer thinks it can extract from the deal.

For all the excitement about smart factories and the boom in AI-related infrastructure spending, some things remain true. One is that claims that putting two companies together will generate huge new sales opportunities should be taken with a heavy pinch of salt. Schneider reckons three-quarters of the financial benefits of the merger will come from extra revenue. Only €250mn a year — worth perhaps €2bn today — are from actual cost savings.

But the fall in Schneider’s own market value, far in excess of the premium it is offering over PTC’s undisturbed share price, suggests investors don’t merely think it has overpaid: they think its own business will be less valuable as a result of the deal.

That too speaks to an old-world principle of corporate finance: it is harder to be good at many things than one. Schneider already offers some software products, but its expertise is mainly in electrical hardware. And investors previously seemed quite happy with that. Indeed, analysts expect Schneider’s revenue to grow by more than 10 per cent a year for the next three years, according to LSEG; PTC’s growth rate is not expected to hit double digits.

Branching out into software also leaves Schneider’s stock exposed to a market that has made investors distinctly twitchy this year. Industrial software is presumably less at risk from AI-enabled alternatives than, say, enterprise software. But that doesn’t mean it’s not exposed — or that Schneider’s shares won’t now be pulled into the next software-related market wobble.

In other corners of finance, investors seem surprisingly willing to reward some companies’ long-term visions, however speculative. Think of Elon Musk’s SpaceX and its goal of putting data centres in space, or the looming $2tn initial public offering of AI lab Anthropic. Schneider isn’t getting the same benefit of the doubt, despite making a much smaller bet. Perhaps outside of Silicon Valley, the old standard — near-term profitability matters — still applies.

gaia.freydefont@ft.com

item.content:encoded:
Hat’s on

Louis Ashworth

Last Friday’s charts quiz, as is its wont, tasked you with identifying some charts.

Here’s what they were:

That’s base sponsor income received by Manchester City FC, before the “sham” top-up payments made by its owner Abu Dhabi United Group. With the ADUG payments added, the chart looks like this:

Wow, sure looks like a pattern that will have abruptly ended in 2018!

Chart number two is the real yield (yield minus inflation) on 30-year French government bonds.

Finally, this chart shows Estonia on a split chart of company birth (measure 1) and death (measure 2) rates in Europe. We don’t know why so many Estonian businesses died in 2024, but the comment box is open for your wisdom.
