item.title: Burnham’s Budget must not be overshadowed by the OBR
item.author: Ben Nunn
item.description: Rather than being buffeted by the official forecasts, Number 10 should seek to turn them to their advantage
item.content:encoded:
Rather than being buffeted by the official forecasts, Number 10 should seek to turn them to their advantage

Ben Nunn

The writer is the former chief of staff to Rachel Reeves and senior adviser to Keir Starmer

On the second floor of the Treasury’s vast open-plan office on Horse Guards Parade is a memorial to Britain’s fiscal history.

The front cover of every Budget document for the past four decades or so — the “red book” — is carefully framed and hung across two walls. A sea of red (and some questionable noughties graphic design from the New Labour premiership) hangs over the Treasury’s strategy, planning and budget team, which is responsible for preparing the nation’s annual Budget.

On October 28, a new cover will find its place on the Treasury’s wall as John Healey delivers the first Budget of Andy Burnham’s premiership. But what the new prime minister and chancellor will learn very quickly on the day is that it isn’t the red book that matters, but the numbers in the “blue book”, which is written half-a-mile down the road by the Office for Budget Responsibility.

The OBR’s status in Britain’s economic infrastructure has soared since its creation at the start of the last decade. It looms large as the independent auditor of the country’s economy — from its forecasts on growth, inflation and borrowing costs to picking apart the policy costings and tax measures of successive chancellors.

But it has become more than an economic institution. It is now (whether we like it or not) a major player in the political discourse. The decision of Liz Truss — whose disastrous “mini” Budget in 2022 does not get a place on the Treasury’s wall because it wasn’t technically a Budget — to bypass the institution propelled it to God-like status. The reforms introduced after the 2024 election further strengthened the OBR by preventing future governments from ever sidelining it.

I was in the room for the four fiscal events of the Starmer premiership. I would watch as commentators, journalists and others pored over the OBR’s figures. Hundreds of hours would be spent by officials in the lead-up to a Budget on detailed policy measures and cabinet negotiations on public spending settlements. But on the day, there was less focus on what the chancellor said, and more on what the OBR concluded.

I know we were not alone in feeling politically impotent. When I served in opposition, I never read a single page of the red book. Instead, I spent Budget days photographing pages of the OBR document and pinging them to journalists on WhatsApp in a desperate effort to disrupt the then Conservative chancellor’s message.

In its early days, the new Labour administration has shown competence in using the power of government to tell a story. An initial flurry of announcements has signalled priorities and given voters confidence that the new cabinet “gets it”. This was followed by a successful Labour Party conference. But this month’s Budget will put that storytelling ability under pressure — Burnham won’t be its sole author.

It would be a mistake for Number 10 to think it is a mere observer to the OBR’s dominance. Ministers should not be buffeted by the official forecasts but seek to turn them to their advantage. If the Iran war has pushed up inflation projections, that is why the government has had to prioritise the cost of living. If growth is to be downgraded, then that’s a mandate for further — and more radical — action. And if borrowing costs are rising, then the promise of fiscal discipline is about more than pleasing markets — it is about delivering on the prime minister’s “Makerfield Test” to protect family finances across the country by keeping mortgages and prices down.

The Budget will mark precisely one hundred days since the new government was formed. A symbolic milestone that will prove an early first test: how will it confront the hard economic trade-offs Britain faces? How will it fight to tell a compelling story over the noise and dominance of others?

item.title: The dangerous myth behind AI agent hacks
item.author: Yoshua Bengio
item.description: These are not simply cyber security flaws but problems with the way that models are trained
item.content:encoded:
These are not simply cyber security flaws but problems with the way that models are trained

Yoshua Bengio

The writer is professor of computer science at the Université de Montréal and co-president of LawZero

We now know that leading AI companies are investigating tens of thousands of situations in which agents have undertaken unwanted actions, some of which would be considered crimes if committed by a human.

In the aftermath of the attack on Hugging Face this summer by OpenAI agents and the recent hack of the Australian national healthcare database, a dangerous myth has gained traction: that these incidents are just cyber security problems and that upgrading the security of the sandboxes in which models are trained would prevent future hacks.

This narrow perspective overlooks scientific trends. Weak cyber defences, including the humans involved, are part of the problem and will never be perfect. But unless we address the root causes of the hacks, they are likely to grow in number and severity as AI capabilities advance. 

At the core of all of these incidents is misalignment. AI agents are choosing goals that are misaligned with those of humans, and it is a consequence of their training.

The methodology that today’s leading companies use to train their frontier models is called reinforcement learning. RL trains models to pursue objectives: they get rewards when they succeed and these behaviours are reinforced. It has historically enabled the training of very efficient goal-seeking AIs. But it is also what plausibly leads to unwanted behaviours such as cheating, deception and self-preservation — often violating the moral rules that companies attempt to encode in AI models.

Scientific literature has long shown how misalignment becomes a consequence of RL; it was to be expected based on theoretical arguments and observed experiments.

What we have seen in recent hacking incidents is a tension between the mission given to the AI agents and the safety rules they were trained to follow. In the Hugging Face incident, none of the 1,200 agents involved alerted human engineers of the ongoing cheating and illegal acts, despite knowing these actions went against safety instructions. 

Misalignment tendencies were more benign in the past, when AI had limited capacity and chatbots would struggle to complete a sentence. At its current rate of progress, they are a more serious threat.

This observation contradicts another questionable belief — that improving AI capability will fix misalignment. Past evidence and theoretical arguments suggest that it can instead amplify unwanted behaviours by being too efficient at optimising the wrong goal.

Most people do not fully grasp how far and fast frontier AI companies are pushing the capabilities of their leading models. Since 2024, models have become drastically better at reasoning. This has led to impressive results in mathematics and holds tremendous potential for scientific breakthroughs. The flip side is that it also makes models much more efficient in safety-critical areas such as cyber security and biology (think of an AI system that would significantly lower the barriers to creating, acquiring or weaponising dangerous biological agents). If leading developers continue on this track without fixing the training process that yields such misaligned goals, including allowing catastrophic misuse, their models’ creativity and power will only increase in frequency and impact. 

Of course cyber resilience and monitoring need to be addressed. However, it will always be a cat-and-mouse game if AI companies keep developing increasingly capable models that we do not know how to control reliably.

Organisations will constantly have to adapt to the newest, most sophisticated attacks and react after damage is done. Furthermore, even if a cyber security line of defence is perfect in theory, humans will always be involved, and they can be influenced, persuaded, bought or blackmailed. A recent study by researchers at the University of Oxford, Stanford University, the London School of Economics and Political Science and the UK AI Security Institute found that conversational AI systems were reliably more persuasive than expert humans.

We must therefore address the underlying causes of these rising risks, including possibly disallowing the training of misaligned models by regulating against them until proven safe.

The most powerful AI systems should be approached like other critical technologies including medicine, aviation and nuclear energy.

My work leads me to believe that it is possible to build highly capable AI that is trustworthy by developing systems without any preferences and related objectives. We must refuse to blindly settle for increasingly capable autonomous and uncontrolled AI systems. Burying our heads in the sand is no longer an option.

item.title: Latino Americans are the real swing voters
item.author: Patti Waldmeir
item.description: The ‘moveable middle’ who remain undecided could be unusually influential in next month’s midterm elections
item.content:encoded:
The ‘moveable middle’ who remain undecided could be unusually influential in next month’s midterm elections

Patti Waldmeir

The writer is a contributing columnist

Over 5mn Latino Americans have joined the ranks of US eligible voters since the last midterm elections in 2022 — more than half the total gain in that period. Latino eligible voters are now the second-largest group in the US, after white voters. 

But political experts say they punch well beyond their weight not just because of numbers, but because many Latino voters are in the “moveable middle”: not wedded to either political party. That could make them unusually influential in next month’s midterm elections. 

“Latinos are the only true swing voters in America,” veteran Republican political strategist Mike Madrid, co-host of The Latino Vote podcast, tells me. Latino voters helped Donald Trump win the 2024 presidential election, with their vote nearly split between the two parties at 48 per cent for Republican Trump and 51 per cent for Democrat Kamala Harris. That was a massive shift from the 38 percentage point lead that Democrats commanded among Latino voters as recently as 2016.

But the shift was far from permanent, Madrid says: many Latinos are now telling pollsters they won’t vote Republican again this year. Among those who voted for Trump in 2024, a third now say they are disappointed or regret their vote, according to the Latino-focused polling firm Equis Research. The disaffection was even voiced by a prominent Latina Republican, Congresswoman María Elvira Salazar of Florida. “The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today,” she said, in a widely publicised TV ad campaign.

Altogether, 38 per cent of the Latino electorate is either undecided, independent or has crossed party lines in 2024, according to UnidosUS, the Latino advocacy group. More than two-thirds think the US is headed in the wrong direction, it says, adding that the “moveable middle” of these voters is “big enough to decide who controls Congress”.

But Madrid thinks Latinos are not swing voters in the traditional sense of the word: “2024 was not a shift to Republicans, it was a shift away from Democrats. And right now, the same thing is happening, but in reverse: Latinos are rejecting the Republican Party the same way they rejected the Democratic Party . . . there is nothing ideological about it.” 

“Latino voters are pragmatic,” Ricardo Rauseo Landa of the Latino voter advocacy group Somos Votantes told me. His group’s polling shows that, especially in the Midwest, these voters are “very much focused on the economy and making ends meet”. Immigration, he says, doesn’t really come up in conversations.

In the Latino neighbourhoods of Milwaukee, in the critical Midwest swing state of Wisconsin, the barber shops and bakeries were packed on a recent Saturday. At Rivera’s Western Wear, the pungent scent of real leather greets me as soon as I open the door: shelves stacked with boots, belts and buckles reach to the ceiling as proprietor Alejandro Rivera pauses to talk politics. He is a staunch Democrat but he says that wouldn’t stop him voting for a Republican “if he is aligned with the interests of the community”. And if not? “I wouldn’t vote for him, whether he was a Republican or a Democrat”. 

Nelson Soler, who describes himself as an independent voter, is president and CEO of the Latino Chamber of Commerce of Southeastern Wisconsin. He tells me that most of his members vote by candidate, not party. “Latinos have been underserved by both parties,” he says, adding, “I see more Latinos going from partisan to independent lately.”

Madrid says this is the way elections are supposed to work: the system was designed so that if people aren’t serving your interests, you punish them by voting them out. Instead, he thinks the US is beset by what he calls “paper partisanship” in which voters will not leave their party “no matter how bad it gets economically”. Latinos are the only Americans today who are “voting rationally in an irrational, broken system”, he argues. 

If he’s right, then hold on to your hats: the Latino vote won’t be sitting still any time soon.

item.title: Putin’s nuclear threats no longer work
item.author: Gideon Rachman
item.description: The weakening of Russian deterrence has global implications — and they are not all positive
item.content:encoded:
The weakening of Russian deterrence has global implications — and they are not all positive

Gideon Rachman

Russia has the largest nuclear arsenal in the world — and it wants you to remember that. In a document sent to Nato, the Russian government stated bluntly that it would “be ready to use the entire arsenal of forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons” to defend its territory.

The Kremlin claims to be responding to threats to Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave bordered by Poland and Lithuania. On October 1, Vladimir Putin weighed in personally, stating that if Kaliningrad was attacked, Russia would use “all the weapons” that it has. The Russian leader acknowledged that France and the UK also have nuclear weapons but boasted “in terms of weapons we have, we are unparalleled”.

There was a time when threats like this would have made global headlines. But in Britain, the travails of Manchester City football club were bigger news, while France was preoccupied by rioting schoolchildren.

Some security experts are concerned that Russia may be preparing the ground to take military action inside Nato territory — citing the supposed threat to Kaliningrad. But Putin’s warnings about nuclear weapons are increasingly shrugged off.

The reason for this relative nonchalance is that he has tried to use his nuclear arsenal to intimidate the west ever since he launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Those threats were effective for a while. In the early stages of the war, the US and its allies were very cautious about the military aid they gave to Ukraine — partly because they feared the war could escalate into a nuclear confrontation. But, with the passage of time, it has become apparent that the taboo against the use of nuclear weapons is very powerful. Russia was warned by both China and India not to go nuclear — and the US is also believed to have threatened to intervene directly in the war if Russia used nuclear weapons in Ukraine.

The waning of the deterrent power of the Russian nuclear arsenal has, over time, made Ukraine’s western allies much less cautious about the kinds of weapons they are prepared to provide to Kyiv. Tanks, fighter planes and long-range missiles to fire at targets inside Russia — all once off the menu — have now all been supplied.

In 2025, Ukraine also staged a successful drone attack — Operation Spider’s Web — on Russia’s fleet of strategic nuclear bombers. According to Russian military doctrine, that kind of attack justified a nuclear response. But, again, Russia did not follow through on its nuclear threats.

Observing these developments, Rose Gottemoeller, a former deputy secretary-general of Nato, has concluded “nuclear deterrence is not working”. Nuclear-weapons states, such as Russia, believed that the mere possession of the weapons would protect them against the threat of conventional attack. But that is not what happened.

As Gottemoeller observes, the failure of Russian nuclear deterrence is not an isolated case. Iran has been willing to launch ballistic missiles and drones at Israel, even though it knows Israel has nuclear weapons. India and Pakistan have also struck each other’s territory, despite the fact that both are nuclear-weapons states.

But the failure of nuclear deterrence is a particular setback for Russia. The possession of the world’s largest nuclear arsenal is one of the country’s only remaining claims to superpower status. Building and maintaining its stockpile is also enormously expensive.

Russian pundits continue to fulminate and fantasise about nuclear strikes on Europe — presumably with the Kremlin’s encouragement. But these outbursts no longer make news in Europe. When the threats come from Putin himself, as they did last week, they get more attention. But Nato’s stance on the war in Ukraine remains unaltered.

The diminishing power of Russia’s nuclear threats is mainly good news. But it also creates a new set of problems. The first is that Russia will look for other ways of restoring deterrence. The increase in Russian hybrid warfare in Europe — including sabotage, assassinations and drone incursions — reflects the Kremlin’s desire to find non-nuclear options for intimidating Ukraine’s European allies. But hybrid warfare creates its own risks of accidents and escalation. Russia’s increasing willingness to attack civilian targets inside Ukraine — and the escalating ferocity of its bombardment of Kyiv — reflects its search for non-nuclear forms of escalation.

The second big danger is that the failure of nuclear deterrence makes conventional warfare more thinkable in Europe and elsewhere. With the exception of the UK and France, the European members of Nato are all sheltering under the US nuclear umbrella. The same is true of Japan and South Korea in east Asia.

If potential adversaries of these US allies conclude that the American threat to use nuclear weapons in their defence is not credible, they may be more prepared to launch a conventional war. Indeed, Russia itself may now be less wary of starting a conflict with Nato.

The final danger is that everybody is “learning by doing”. Since the Ukraine war began, both Russia and Nato have had to adapt their ideas about how nuclear deterrence works. The taboo against the use of nuclear weapons is clearly very strong. But is it absolute? Nobody can be sure. That kind of uncertainty is dangerous.

gideon.rachman@ft.com

item.title: Donald Trump’s diesel export coercion will not strengthen the US
item.author: Alan Beattie
item.description: The demand-destroying response to the 1973 Arab oil embargo shows the risk of stopping exports
item.content:encoded:
The demand-destroying response to the 1973 Arab oil embargo shows the risk of stopping exports

Alan Beattie

Welcome to Trade Secrets. The Trump-Xi meeting recedes into the distance leaving nothing but warm words in its wake and the EU-China conflict comes more sharply into view. European trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič is in Beijing this week to see how far things have progressed since both sides solemnly agreed to come up with some rebalancing measures. (My bet: not far.)

I’ll get to that issue in future columns and newsletters. Today I’m looking at the shenanigans of President Donald Trump’s threatened export ban on diesel and the subsequent G7 capitulation. Charted Waters, where we look at the data behind world trade, is on equity prices.

A fuelish endeavour

If you had to design a scenario to show the weaknesses and wrongheadedness of global trade and energy policy at the moment, the diesel saga is it. As Ed Conway, who has just come out with this fascinating book, points out, the global diesel market is much more fragmented and politicised than you’d hope.

Trump’s inane Iran misadventure has driven up global energy prices, with the inefficiencies of the diesel supply chain amplifying that effect. Next, the US president, who never saw a form of intervention that didn’t make things worse in the long run, threatened to restrict diesel exports to drive down the domestic price. As Conway says, it’s not even clear that would work given the fragmentation of the domestic diesel market. For example, the US west coast is quite dependent on imports, so an international diesel shortage might raise rather than lower prices there.

This particular experiment was short-circuited by European governments capitulating — their default response to short-term challenges — by agreeing to release diesel from their strategic reserves. Another win for Trumpian coercion. But in the longer term the US might discover that there is no faster way to encourage your energy customers to diversify than by politicising supply.

Just ask President Vladimir Putin. Western European countries (well, the pivotal ones) thought it was a smart idea to make themselves ever more dependent on Russian hydrocarbons — anyone studying EU trade and energy policy should have this photo as a screensaver — until they realised it wasn’t, whereupon they moved at a speed few had thought possible to wean themselves off. (Of course, one of the things they replaced Russian energy with was US liquefied natural gas which, as they say, is now item two on today’s agenda.)

As my colleague Gillian Tett points out, the US discovered this phenomenon in the 1970s with an ill-fated ban on exports of soyabeans, which merely encouraged Brazil to emerge as a global soyabean superpower. We might add the 1973 Arab oil embargo, a very similar episode around the same time, which aimed to prevent other countries providing military supplies to Israel during the Yom Kippur war. The boycott did not halt those supplies, though it did kick off a decades-long demand-destruction trend towards reducing oil consumption. Such moves can take a long time, but do happen.

Europe’s responses to challenges are often, shall we put it, non-linear. The continent doesn’t move until a problem gets really big and then it shifts fast, for which see former European Central Bank chief Mario Draghi’s “whatever it takes” approach during the Eurozone financial crisis. The EU has a lot on its agenda, but insulating itself from US diesel supplies in the future has just risen up it.

The UK’s post-Brexit trade deals won’t stop ‘Breversal’

I said I wouldn’t write about the UK again for a while. And yet here I am for the second time in two weeks.

I was all ready, along with a lot of other folks, to scoff mightily at new Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s speech to Labour Party conference. He punted off changes to social care and the electoral system years into the future and sounded fairly vague on EU relations, saying he would lay out options at the next EU summit in November. So far, so fudgy. But the next morning Burnham specified that one option was actually joining the EU. (I’m in the camp that it’s “joining”, not “rejoining”; the UK and EU have both changed since 2016, Heraclitus’s river etc.) Suddenly the debate Labour has tried to stifle has burst free.

You can’t really defer relations with the EU, because the economics and politics nip irritably at your ankles. I wrote last week about the bloc applying pressure on the UK over tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. The EU may not be right about that one, but it isn’t going to let up the general idea of a common front to China.

One question: do the preferential trade agreements (PTAs) the UK has done since Brexit make joining harder? There’s no doubt that sabotaging joining the EU was one of the Conservative government’s motives for signing PTAs, because it rather childishly said so.

But I don’t think the attempt to create a poison pill has really worked. The homeopathically small effects of said PTAs — for example, the 0.08 per cent increment to GDP from the Australian bilateral deal — have now become well-rehearsed attack lines by Labour. The boneheaded way in which the Boris Johnson government in particular went about signing deals, for example capitulating to Australia to the fury of British farmers, did its image no favours.

Even before Trump’s second term began, the UK public was firmly in favour of prioritising trade relations with the EU over the US. Unsurprisingly, opinion has moved further in that direction since. And while business organisations cheer-led joining, among other things, the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) — they’ll take any win they can — I’d be very surprised if they opposed joining the EU on fears of throwing those gains away. 

The benefits of buccaneering PTA-signing were always massively oversold. It’s striking and, in some ways, heartening that the UK public wasn’t fooled by the idea. The priority now should be settling on and pursuing a model that works, despite the many challenges that need addressing, such as the euro. I would only beg for some realism. If we end up back in the cakeism of previous governments — and, thus far, Burnham’s too — there really is no point to anything.

There’s a very long way to go before Brexit might be “Breversed”, and a lot of reasons for opposition to it. But the preferential deals the UK has signed are among the weaker objections.

Charted waters

Bond markets are in turmoil and yet equities are . . . fine? Either the bond market isn’t signalling very much about the world economy or stock prices are in their own bubbly world.

Trade links

  • A Centre for Economic Policy Research (CEPR) paper by Sébastien Jean and Jean-Pierre Landau on global imbalances and the China challenge.
  • The FT reports that the use of Arctic sea routes by freight ships has quadrupled since 2022, albeit from a very low number, because of melting sea ice and the Iran conflict.
  • An in-depth look by the FT about China extending its technological and production lead in batteries.
  • Anyone hoping that the EU-China trade conflict might diminish ahead of the forthcoming EU-China summit was disappointed by Beijing launching a bunch of fresh anti-dumping actions against the bloc in retaliation for Brussels doing the same the week before.
  • In light of the Manchester City finances saga and the quasi-state nature of its owners, a reminder from 2020 of how the Saudi takeover of Newcastle United was threatened by a World Trade Organization ruling brought by Qatar that changed the English Football Association’s test for owners and directors.
  • Analysts at ING have published a good piece on the continued vulnerabilities in the US rare earths supply chain.


Trade Secrets is edited by Harvey Nriapia

item.title: One person is now a quorum at the SEC
item.author: Robin Wigglesworth
item.description: The Ankh-Morpork approach to US financial regulation
item.content:encoded:
The Ankh-Morpork approach to US financial regulation

Robin Wigglesworth

Terry Pratchett’s fictional city of Ankh-Morpork is led by Lord Vetinari, who follows a unique approach to democracy: One Man, One Vote; Vetinari is the Man and he has the Vote. The US Securities and Exchange Commission seems to be heading down a similar pathway.

Late last month SEC commissioner Hester Peirce abruptly announced that she was resigning from the US financial watchdog. Her last day was on Friday, and the only two remaining commissioners — the Trump-appointed chair Paul Atkins and the Republican Mark Uyeda — wasted little time in enshrining their ability to keep the agency under their control.

Here’s a new rule that the SEC’s remaining commissioners passed on Friday:

The Commission is modifying 17 CFR 200.41, which establishes the Commission’s quorum requirement. Three commissioners will continue to constitute a quorum of the Commission, with two important exceptions. First, consistent with the current rule, if the number of commissioners in office is two or one, that number is sufficient for a quorum. Second, if the number of commissioners in office minus the number disqualified from consideration with respect to a matter is two or one, then that number of commissioners constitutes a quorum for purposes of that matter.

Some background might be in order. The SEC is supposed to be led by a five-person commission. These commissioners are nominated by the reigning president, approved by the Senate, and appointed in a staggered way to five-year terms to ensure that the agency’s main rulemaking body is full most of the time. No more than three commissioners may belong to the same party to ensure some bipartisanship, but the president gets to choose one to be the commission’s chair.

At least, that’s how things used to work.

The first Trump administration did actually fill three Democrat commissioner vacancies, but the second Trump administration has shown zero indication that it wants to adhere to previous norms. It has let Democrat commissioners Jaime Lizárraga and then Caroline Crenshaw leave without naming any replacements, leaving it with no minority commissioners for the first time ever, aside from a six-month window in 2008.

This matters less for rulemaking — the majority party usually controls enough commissioners to get its will anyway — than it does for transparency and the terms of the financial-regulatory debate. The minority commissioners can and often do use their ability to publicly dissent against SEC rules to help shape the discourse on financial regulation.

In fact, Peirce was a particularly effective SEC commissioner under the Biden-nominated chair Gary Gensler because of her often thoughtful but punchy dissents. Indeed, Alphaville is surprised that someone who clearly valued the role of minority commissioner so highly said so little about the end of dissent at the SEC after Crenshaw had to leave at the start of this year.

But now that Peirce is herself out of the agency, Atkins and Uyeda had to hastily revamp the SEC’s quorum rules to ensure that her swift exit won’t affect their ability to have their way.

The Securities and Exchange Act of 1934 doesn’t actually set out any quorum requirement, but in 1995 the Commission formalised the practice that it took three commissioners to vote on a new rule. It also said that if there happened to be fewer than three commissioners in office at the time then two commissioners could still form a quorum.

However, with now just two commissioners around and it being entirely possible that one of them might have to recuse themselves from an issue (or be otherwise MIA), just one is now enough to pass a formal rule that applies to America’s vast multitrillion-dollar securities markets.

And conveniently enough, the SEC says that since this new “amendment” to its own rules relates only to the SEC’s governance, it doesn’t count as a “substantive rule” — and no opportunity for public comment is therefore required.

The new approach is “designed to promote flexibility and finality of agency rulemaking”, according to the SEC’s statement.

In prior years, the Commission has occasionally been in the position of having fewer than three members and believes it prudent to adapt its quorum rule to further accommodate that contingency. Moreover, the Commission has found that situations often arise in which one or more Commissioners have disqualified themselves or are otherwise disqualified from participating in a matter. When such situations arise, it is important that the Commission be able to continue to conduct business. Accordingly, the Commission is amending the quorum rule to specify that, in a situation in which only one Commissioner is able to participate in a matter because all other Commissioners currently in office are disqualified from participating in that matter, the remaining member would constitute a quorum for that particular matter.

It’s a pretty clear indication that the SEC doesn’t expect any exiting commissioners to be replaced any time soon. But stepping back, this is all very much in keeping with the general vibe of the Atkins SEC, which seems proud of how much it has shrunk, how little action it has taken and how friendly to the financial industry it is.

As Crenshaw warned in her last speech before leaving the SEC at the start of the year: “The darkest depths of winter still lie ahead for America’s capital markets.”

Further reading:
— The giant void of nothingness where US financial regulation used to sit (FTAV)

item.title: Bond turbulence means it’s time for the ECB to put QT on hold
item.author: Lorenzo Bini Smaghi
item.description: Prudence suggests a halt by the central bank until more stable conditions are restored
item.content:encoded:
Prudence suggests a halt by the central bank until more stable conditions are restored

Lorenzo Bini Smaghi

The writer is a former member of the executive board of the European Central Bank and former chair of Société Générale

Long-term rates have been rising sharply over the past few months in most advanced economies. This has triggered concern in financial markets, especially among bondholders, and pushed yields even higher, creating a vicious circle.

In Europe, the shadows of the 2011-12 crisis are emerging again. One of the clearest signs is the widening of spreads between the government bonds of core and peripheral countries, with France being treated by markets as part of the periphery this time.

In many ways, the European economy is in a very different position today. The European Central Bank is much better equipped to address tensions in financial markets that could endanger the integrity of the single currency. It has bond-buying tools and programmes that address spikes in yields.

However, one aspect that is more difficult to understand for observers and market participants is why, in the current stress, the ECB continues to implement its policy of quantitative tightening, the shrinking of its balance sheet by not replacing assets — in particular government bonds — when they mature. This policy means that a larger share of the net supply of government bonds has to be absorbed by private investors, at a time when long-term rates are already under upward pressure.

The policy was launched in March 2023, with a view to bringing the size of the central bank’s balance sheet “back to normal” after the expansion over the previous decade. A similar approach was adopted at the time by other central banks. However, other central banks have subsequently interrupted or modified their approach in light of market developments.

The reason is that the pros and cons of the process through which a central bank shrinks its balance sheet may not have been fully considered and openly debated when the decision was taken. These deserve careful assessment.

Kevin Warsh, the newly appointed Federal Reserve chair, established a task force led by three prominent economists to do just this for the Fed. In the euro area, by contrast, returning to normal has been presented by the central bank as an “obligation”, motivated apparently more by nostalgia for the world that existed before the financial crisis than by rigorous analysis. In fact, there is nothing inherently “normal” about the size of a central bank’s balance sheet, especially when underlying economic and market conditions change in fundamental ways over time.

One example of the changes that have occurred since the financial crisis is banking regulation. Financial institutions are now required to hold much larger amounts of high-quality liquid assets, including government bonds, for prudential reasons. This would put further pressure on yields if banks were again required to obtain liquidity from the central bank by pledging additional collateral.

Another example is the change in the structure of market-making in government bonds with non-banks such as hedge funds taking a greater role. Resulting from post-financial crisis regulation, this exposes markets to stress when liquidity becomes tight, as illustrated by episodes in the US Treasury market.

Furthermore, a system in which banks must obtain central bank liquidity through refinancing operations at a rate above the remuneration of minimum reserves creates a cost for the banking system — which will ultimately be borne by their customers.

It also gives an incentive to banks to hold larger amounts of government bonds, which runs counter to the objective of minimising the bank-sovereign doom loop — where a debt crisis puts pressure on sovereign bonds, in turn destabilising banks and raising the risk of government bailouts.

The ECB’s response has been that the pace of its quantitative tightening is relatively slow and that, while the broad principles of the new liquidity framework have been defined, the precise timing and calibration of the QT transition remain uncertain. This, however, adds additional uncertainty and puts further upward pressure on European long-term rates.

In the current conjuncture, with inflation being the primary concern, monetary policy should be implemented mainly through its traditional instrument, the short-term policy rate.

Changing the size of the balance sheet should be regarded as a secondary instrument. It may actually produce undesirable effects that are not yet fully understood. The principle of prudence would therefore suggest putting QT on hold until a more stable environment has been restored, while taking the time to better understand its implications for financial markets.

item.title: Greens’ anti-Zionism motion narrows potential base of support
item.author: Stephen Bush
item.description: More extreme and divided party could pose problems for Labour and Conservatives if voters take a ‘whole bloc’ view of next election
item.content:encoded:
More extreme and divided party could pose problems for Labour and Conservatives if voters take a ‘whole bloc’ view of next election

Stephen Bush

Good morning from Birmingham. I am at the Conservative Party conference, but the big conference season story today is happening in Brighton at the Green Party’s get-together. Some thoughts on that in today’s note.

Radical position

The Green Party has been accused of racism after passing an anti-Zionist motion that claims “Zionism is racism”. (The full text of the motion is here.)

The motion has a definition of Zionism so expansive as to include functionally every part of Jewish communal life and, in its rejection of a two-state solution, goes further than the Palestinian Authority.

Dave Rich, the Community Security Trust’s policy director, and Lev Saul, a Surrey-based rabbi, cover the motion and its meaning more than adequately on Substack and at Left Foot Forward respectively.

The immediate political impact of the move will, I think, further narrow the Green Party’s potential base of support. At precisely the point when the Labour government’s position on the Gaza war has shifted — partly because of Ed Miliband and others’ sincere conviction, but also because of electoral losses, particularly to Zack Polanski’s party — the Greens are moving away from a position on Gaza that has majority support in the UK to one whose full implications are much more radical, with a motion that defines almost all British Jewish institutions as beyond the pale.

Divisions among the Greens, over this issue in particular but also over their political direction under Polanski more broadly, are going to become louder and more intense, which will only make them seem more extreme and divided. Neither is a quality that makes a party successful.

British politics is now a five-body problem, where the challenge for the two main parties is that they face constraints on their ability to seek supporters directly from each other because of real or perceived threats about losing votes, either to the Greens in Labour’s case or to Reform and Restore in the case of the Tories.

As it happens, I think this fear is misplaced. But that is a topic for another time. What matters is that the parties themselves believe and feel constrained by it. A more polarising Green Party makes Labour’s life easier, thus making it harder for the Conservatives and the fractured right to win elections.

But it also comes with risks for Labour. I suspect that at the next election, some voters will take a “whole bloc” view of where they cast their ballot. For example, they might consider the risk of Reform as a reason not to vote Conservative, or the risk of the Greens as a reason not to vote Labour. A more unattractive Green Party is easier for Labour to defeat directly, but it could also be a drag in seats where Labour competes with the Tories.

Now try this

I had a lovely time at a friend’s wedding party this weekend. The day after, while we recovered, my partner and I played Twilight Struggle, a terrific two-player board game about the cold war in which one of you plays the Soviet Union and the other the US.

Top stories today

  • Regulatory burden | John Healey will this week face pressure from top British lenders to back a cut in their capital requirements, according to Meg Hillier, head of the Treasury select committee.


  • ‘New’ party | Kemi Badenoch has cast aside the Conservatives’ “red wall” focus with a fresh effort to reconnect the party with its traditional supporters in business and affluent Britain.
  • Redeployed | The US withdrew B-1 bombers stationed at the UK’s Fairford air base and returned them to American soil following the suspected terror plot, a US defence official confirmed yesterday.

item.title: The jobs market is still fine
item.author: Robert Armstrong
item.description: But the stock market is losing a lot of weight
item.content:encoded:
But the stock market is losing a lot of weight

Robert Armstrong

Good morning. Diesel prices backed off Friday after the G7 countries’ decision to release 100mn barrels of reserves. Will the effect last, or will the release be added to the list of recent government interventions that show promise, then fizzle? Something has to give: the US retail diesel price is 70 per cent higher than it was a year ago, and the longer this lasts, the greater the economic and political pressure. Email us and let us know how energy costs are affecting you: unhedged@ft.com.

The jobs report (and the economy)

The September jobs report was a little bit softer than expected. In the household survey, the unemployment rate rose just enough to be rounded up by a tenth of a per cent, to 4.2 per cent. In the establishment survey, 29,000 jobs were added, below expectations and the three- and six-month rolling averages. Both the (soft) July jobs number and the (strong) August jobs number were also revised downwards. 

Should we care? Should the Fed? In both cases, some but not much. Fed chair Warsh says he cares about trends, not data points, and the basic trend in the US labour market — a quite slow but steady strengthening — remains in place. Below is total employment. The six-month rolling average still shows a market that bottomed in the second half of last year and has been clawing its way back since:  

The trend is clearer still when you strip out government, healthcare and education jobs to focus on the cyclical part of the economy:

Still, don’t mistake a recovery for a boom. Even in a country with a stagnant workforce and a correspondingly low break-even job creation rate, adding 50,000 or so jobs a month does not speak to a roaring job market. The classic big cyclical sectors — manufacturing, construction, and leisure/hospitality — all added fewer jobs in September than August. And in booming labour markets wage growth does not keep slowing until it falls below inflation:

Despite an incrementally softer jobs report coming on the heels of an incrementally softer PCE inflation report, the bond market got no relief. In fact, both the two-year and the 10-year Treasury yields rose Friday after falling when the jobs numbers first landed. What gives? I’m really not sure. One possibility is that the number that really has the market’s attention is real GDP growth. The second-quarter number was revised higher to 2.5 last week and the third-quarter number looks set to come in near 3. That makes it harder to believe that inflation will take care of itself, especially given the energy backdrop. 

It may also be that bond investors are focusing on the unpleasant fact that two big contributors to demand — the AI boom and the wealth effect from persistently high stock prices — do not seem to be very rate-sensitive. If this remains true, the Fed will have to whack the rate-sensitive bits of the economy (housing, indebted companies and households) even harder to get to its inflation target. It’s not a pretty picture. 

Market narrowness (and the economy) 

Unhedged has an uneasy relationship to market breadth as an indicator. The idea that the proportion of constituents in a stock market or index that are rising or falling is a reliable leading indicator is pretty clearly wrong. The data doesn’t back it up. At best it is (almost tautologically) a coincident indicator. But a rising or stable market that is narrowing at the same time should tell us something, surely? When earnings or valuations are rising at a wide range of companies, that ought to speak to a robust economy or pervasive investor confidence; when the range is narrow, that speaks to fragility. And since about the middle of August, S&P 500 breadth has collapsed on most measures. Here, for example, is the number of S&P companies that are trading above their 50-day moving average:

The difference between the last collapse in breadth in the Spring and the current one is that last time the whole index fell. This time it’s maintaining altitude. That means that a few big stocks are holding up the index by themselves. And it will not surprise anyone to hear that they are tech stocks. In the last month or so in particular, hyperscalers and chip stocks have flexed their muscles again. 

Other sectors are remarkably flimsy. Just a quarter of the S&P 500 rose in price in September. The majority of stocks are falling in 10 of the 11 industry sectors. In utilities, financials, materials, real estate and staples, it’s only a slight exaggeration to say that nothing is going up:

I don’t think this tells us that the sky is about to fall in on the stock market. It is usually the case, to a larger or smaller degree, that a small number of stocks really power markets up. And market gains have been quite concentrated in tech for years now with no ill effects. Still, I think this shows pretty clearly that the fast increase in interest rates is having an effect on the market, despite the stability of the headline indices. Many sectors are acting like they are absorbing a rate shock.

A trickier question is whether the economy of the US is similarly uneven — whether tech investment is keeping the economic music going by itself. I doubt it. Retail sales and personal consumption numbers are firm, and company surveys show activity expanding. Still, there are important data points that stubbornly refuse to fit in with these headline growth indicators: the weak recent report from Walmart (echoed by other staples companies), high wholesale inflation, falling real wages and declining savings make me slightly nervous that thinning markets may be anticipating a shift in the economic trend.   

One good read

Mormon assimilation.

item.title: What’s really going on with AI token price deflation?
item.author: Bryce Elder
item.description: It’s a bit complicated and maybe not that surprising
item.content:encoded:
It’s a bit complicated and maybe not that surprising

Bryce Elder

Chances are you’ve seen this chart a few times, but what does it mean?

Silicon Data’s Token Expenditure Index is a blended dollar-cost benchmark for one million tokens. From a series high of $2.0651 in late May, it’s down 52.4 per cent.

Token price deflation, it’s often argued, is bad for companies that make tokens. The market for units of synthetic intelligence is heading towards commoditisation, because anything that can be mass-produced will be. Most enterprises are still in the exploring stage with AI and they’re already on sale at less than half price.

What the token expenditure index doesn’t show is total token expenditure. It’s a measure of average price that’s weighted by estimated usage and normalised for whether they’re for input or output. (LLM labs routinely charge about five times more for output tokens than input tokens because they want to encourage users to ask a lot of complicated questions, then make the money back by delivering the answers.)

Charles-Henry Monchau, CIO of Syz Group, has a LinkedIn-ish explainer on LinkedIn about why the recent collapse in observed pricing is because token mills are getting more efficient, and because enterprises have been routing lower-priority requests to cheaper open-weight LLMs, causing a bit of a price war:

Technical deflation expands margins and is unambiguously good for the ecosystem. Mix deflation is neutral for aggregate spend but corrosive for the frontier labs’ pricing power. Competitive price deflation is a margin war. The index blends all three into one number and tells you nothing about the composition. Anyone using this chart as a directional signal without decomposing it is trading on noise.

Seaport Research Partners’ tech analyst Jay Goldberg — best known for maintaining a heterodox “sell” recommendation on Nvidia — has tried to build a better mousetrap.

The data he collects shows a similar pattern to the Silicon Data index, with token prices plunging for frontier LLMs from $50 per million tokens in late 2023 to about $6 now. More interestingly, he finds the median token price has held fairly steady at just below $1 per million since mid-2024 as the LLM marketplace became more competitive. A floor price of about $0.11 (basically just the cost of electricity) has barely budged.

The same is true for the ceiling price. Narrowing the sample to the most expensive flagship models, there’s been very little movement in pricing since late 2023. Deflation at the frontier end is mostly just a function of more models launching and dragging down the average.

Pricing data is only so useful without also estimating the cost of milling a token. Goldberg estimates, on what look like fairly typical inputs, that the cost of production is falling much faster than the market price:

(We’re not going to show all the working for this chart, sorry. Stuff like assumed uptime, rental rates and depreciation creates a lot of heated argument more suited to the trade press than a markets blog. Goldberg says his cost assumptions are reasonable and we’ve seen no reason to argue. Also note that the cost inflation forecasts for the 2027 and 2028 hardware are mechanical estimates using what can be extrapolated from pre-release spec sheets, which might not reflect real-world performance.)

What’s revealed is a two-tier market. Gross margins at the (all-American) frontier are about 70 per cent. Meanwhile, the (mostly Chinese) open-weight LLM shops are operating at gross margins of approximately 20 per cent. Profit margin differentials between operators could be disrupted, of course, but appear to have held pretty steady for the past three years.

Training is the elephant in the DCF. Tokens relate to inference alone. Capital requirements for model training are a whole other flaming dumpster. And because the tiers below the frontier are training by distillation, staying first is an expensive race:

All of which leads us back to two fairly simple observations.

The S-1 flotation docs for Anthropic and OpenAI, should we ever be allowed to see them, are going to show some decent operating metrics. There’s a lot to like about year after year of steady gross margins in the 70 per cent ballpark when businesses are doing gangbusters growth.

But to make sense as investments, they’ll need to keep defending competitive leads while somehow calling a ceasefire to the open-model performance arms race. Maybe scaremongering around safety and protectionist cartel formation within national boundaries will do the job. Or maybe it won’t.

This is probably where a majority of prospective investors are already, let’s be honest. It was just nice to see some new data that will confirm a lot of priors.

Further reading:
— AI agents are rewriting the economics of computing (FT)

item.title: The Big Read. Russia’s new drive to crush Ukraine
item.author: Alec Russell
item.description: Moscow’s relentless offensive on cities and ports has stalled the country’s Black Sea grain exports, severing an economic lifeline
item.content:encoded:
Moscow’s relentless offensive on cities and ports has stalled the country’s Black Sea grain exports, severing an economic lifeline

Alec Russell

As a glorious summer draws to a close, across the Ukrainian steppe silos are brimming with a bumper harvest. For farmers such as Volodymyr Varbanets, who has worked the same stretch of land since the 1970s when it was a Soviet collective farm, it should be a season to celebrate. Yet it is not.

Thanks to Russia’s ferocious new bombing campaign against ships on the Black Sea and Ukraine’s cities and ports, the mounds of barley, sunflower seeds and wheat in Varbanets’ giant barn are stranded. Increasingly the grizzled 76-year-old fears his crop will end up rotting where it lies.

“I just cannot sell it,” he shrugs, adding that some farmers in his region are in a far worse plight. “People are storing grain outdoors under tarpaulins or selling it at depressed prices just to survive.”

The scene of thwarted abundance, mirrored at farms across Ukraine, reflects a dramatic shift in momentum in the four-and-a-half-year-old conflict. It has grave implications not just for global food supplies but for Ukraine’s economy, its survival strategy and potentially the course of the war.

Ukraine’s drone strikes on targets in Russia early this year emboldened some of Kyiv’s allies to be cautiously optimistic about the war. But since July Russia has unleashed a furious response: a ruthlessly targeted air offensive that has closed the Black Sea to shipping, blocking Ukrainian exports’ main route to market. Not only has it cut off an economic lifeline to the rest of the world, it is linked to a broader campaign to throttle the economy and crush Ukraine.

Night after night, jet-powered drones and missiles are pulverising infrastructure in the Odesa region — and the capital Kyiv — targeting especially the electricity grid to bring the two cities to their knees.

The devastation underlines Ukraine’s critical shortage of air defences, in particular US-made Patriot missiles, which has left the authorities frequently unable to ward off Russian attacks. Most mornings Odesa awakes to the sight of a plume of smoke in the sky from the latest overnight hit.

Oleh Kiper, head of Odesa’s regional military administration, says they are doing everything they can to repel the attacks and reopen the Black Sea corridor but, he adds bluntly, “pauses and delays” in allies’ weapons deliveries are ultimately responsible for the ports’ closure.

“First the Russians concentrated on substations. Now they have expanded their targets,” says Tymur Samosudov, the National Guard commander in charge of a drone-interceptor unit at the heart of the region’s defences. “They are also hitting storage depots and warehouses to ram home the psychological pressure; and by blocking the grain they maximise economic damage.”

With both Russia’s and Ukraine’s grain exports all but blocked, the world may soon have to take note as food prices rise. Before 2022, according to the UN, Russia and Ukraine accounted for a third of global wheat exports and 20 per cent of corn. Distracted by the war in Iran, world leaders have been slow, Ukrainian officials say, to focus on the coming crisis.

“This affects not just our region’s economy but Ukraine’s and the world’s,” says Kiper, speaking minutes after the latest air raid siren resounded through the city. “We used to supply about 70 countries and 300mn people with our agricultural products. This is a global crisis — and will soon be felt around the world.”

For now though, it is being felt much more acutely in Ukraine.

A calamity for Ukraine’s finances

Ukraine’s Black Sea ports are the traditional beating heart of its economy. Before Russia’s all-out invasion in February 2022, they shipped more than 90 per cent of Ukraine’s overall exports of 60mn tonnes of grain a year. In the three years before the July offensive, several hundred ships a month docked at Odesa’s three deep-water ports.

Now they are motionless — except for a handful of stevedores exploiting lulls in the fighting to patch up the damage and frantically unload cargoes from ships hit at their moorings.

“It’s not just a risk for ships now, it’s a guaranteed risk,” says Kostiantyn Tymoshenko, general manager of the shipbroker Formag, looking out over the burnt-out shell of the Hotel Odesa, which was hit earlier in the war.

Just 12 hours after the interview, a ship carrying the flag of Antigua and Barbuda was hit by Russian drones just outside the Chornomorsk Port, 12 miles south of the city, killing the captain and setting the vessel on fire. Russia’s Ministry of Defence said it had been delivering military cargo to Odesa and was hit as part of its campaign to target ships bringing arms to Ukraine.

July was the most dangerous month for shipping in the Black Sea since February 2022, according to Lloyd’s List in August. The combination of Ukrainian strikes on Russian shadow fleet tankers and naval ships and the Russian offensive on Odesa meant, it added, that the Black Sea and not the Strait of Hormuz was the deadliest theatre for commercial shipping.

This is a calamity for Ukraine’s finances. The huge extra expense of transporting grain by truck means only a trickle will make its way overland to the outside world. Taras Vysotskyi, the minister for agriculture, estimates that if the ports stay closed Ukraine will forfeit at least $8bn between June this year and June 2027. Such a shortfall would amount to 20 per cent of last year’s overall export revenue.

Ukraine would have expected to export 64mn tonnes of agricultural produce this year, he says, but it will be lucky to achieve half that if the ports do not reopen. Some think it will export far less.

Odesa, however, has a more immediate concern. Overshadowing every conversation with officials, businesspeople and residents is the fear that Russia is determined to make this winter, the fifth since the full-scale invasion, the toughest yet.

“I’m worried not only about the winter but the people who live here,” says Kiper, the head of Odesa’s military administration. “The enemy is not waging war against the military but a different kind of war.”

The new urban front line 

In the past three years the fighting in eastern Ukraine has become largely static, with a 20-30km-deep “kill zone” dominated by drones. But in cities far from the trenches, such as Odesa and Kyiv, the front line is more fluid as Russia unleashes jet-powered drones, which are harder for interceptor drones to destroy than the slower models of the first years of the war.

Few have more sobering insights into the raw power of this campaign than Shota Khajishvili, owner of the Risoil terminal at the Chornomorsk Port. He founded his company as a sunflower oil factory after the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991 and has since built up a port empire, which before the war loaded 5mn-6mn tonnes of agricultural goods a year.

Now he presides over a wasteland of crumpled metal that looks as if it has been struck by a series of tornadoes. All his cranes and many of his grain silos have been damaged. Two of his giant sunflower oil containers overlooking the docks were hit, leading to a flood oozing down into the harbour. 

“Nothing is happening here,” he says. “We had a few small six-tonne tankers a few weeks ago, and now nothing. No one will insure people’s lives here now.

“The Russians have changed tactics. They were using single drones. Then three or four at a time. Now sometimes they use many more for a single target. The scariest thing is they have started to bomb us with huge aviation bombs with wings; they are very hard to hit.”

He rebuilt his headquarters after it was blown up by a missile, but soon after the new building opened it too was hit. He still goes to work at 7am every morning, but he has a concrete bomb shelter beside his makeshift office, for when the air raid app on his phone signals an imminent strike.

The day before there were 28 air raid alerts. Such is the damage, Khajishvili says, that if his ports reopened tomorrow they would have only 30 per cent capacity. “We used to be able to have five vessels loading simultaneously. Now we could cope with just two.”

The stoppage is even more acute than in 2022 when the Black Sea was closed after the February all-out attack. Five months later, after Russia’s fleet incurred heavy losses from Ukrainian missiles and drones, Moscow agreed to a UN-mediated Black Sea Grain Initiative, opening the sea to commercial traffic. Russia renounced the deal in 2023 but until July this year Ukraine’s ports have been able to keep operating albeit at lesser intensity than before the war.

A critical difference between 2022 and now, say Ukrainian officials, is that four years ago Russia relied mainly on sea mines for the blockade and did not have drones. So ships were able to ferry cargo to and from freshwater ports in the nearby mouth of the Danube. But now drones are targeting ships there too.

Even if the ports reopen, it is not clear how the cargo will be ferried to the docks. In recent weeks the Russians have stepped up their attacks on trains used to transport the two bulkiest and most valuable exports, iron ore and grain. “We have lost three locomotives in our port area alone,” says Mykyta Hrubov, the executive director of the TIS private port, at the deep-sea port of Pivdennyi, 25 miles east of Odesa. “There is a big shortage now, this is a weak point for us.”

Vysotskyi, the agriculture minister, says they are almost out of reserve locomotives. He is in talks with European allies who have the same railway gauge about providing fresh stock.

All the while port owners — just as the farmers — are running out of money and worried they will have to lay off workers. “The city’s economy revolves around the ports,” says Khajishvili’s son, Tariel, a shipping broker. “When they shut down, much of the population is left without a job.

“The Russians are trying to win the war by hitting us behind the front lines. They are targeting the lives of civilians to force us to surrender by leaving us without heating, water or jobs.” 

The two men fighting to keep Odesa alive

In the coming months of winter, the city will be increasingly reliant on two men: Samosudov, the commander of Odesa’s drone interceptor unit, and Dmytro Hryhoriev, head of the region’s embattled electricity distribution network.

The 36-year-old Samosudov commands a team of 25 young men, veteran drone pilots who have served on the front line and have a record of about 200 hits each. They operate in a secret location in Odesa, dominated by a giant map of the Black Sea, controlling interceptor drone launch pads located across the region. 

In their dark T-shirts they stare at screens; to an untutored eye, they look like video gamers. Their unit logo is a digital mock-up of Themis, the Greek goddess of justice, holding her famous set of scales.

“We have a broad overview of the battlefield in the sky,” says Samosudov. “We can see their missiles and drones being launched. We get around two hours’ advance warning and don’t react immediately because sometimes they just fly around. When they get close to our waters, we act.”

They tend to deploy two interceptor drones for each incoming Shahed, the low-cost attack drone originally made in Iran and now produced in Russia. They claim a 95 per cent success rate in downing Shaheds, but the new jet-powered Shaheds are faster and require fighter jets to shoot down.

“They are a problem,” he says. “We have had instances of hitting them with our interceptors, but it was more luck than anything else.”

His unit is a microcosm of the funding problem facing Ukraine’s defenders. The state provides 40 per cent of its finances and private donors make up the rest, but they are always in need of more. “There is no shortage of drones being produced, we just need the finances to buy them — and missiles to take on jet-powered drones and missiles.”

Their most intense night was September 14 when he says more than 150 Shaheds and Gerberas, cheap Russian drones, entered their airspace. “It was an eight-hour battle without pause.”

But some inevitably get through — and most that do are targeting substations to try to cut the electricity supply.

Hryhoriev, head of the Odesa branch of DTEK, the private company responsible for the electricity network, has possibly the hardest job in the city. He looks and sounds exhausted. Last winter, he says, the Russians attacked more than half the big substations in the region, some two or more times. Fifty transformers were destroyed.

“We have had no let-up in attacks,” he says. “We have done a lot of work to prepare for winter and for now everyone has electricity, but the best protection is air defence.”

Oleksii Miaskovskyi, director of the Port of Odesa, in the heart of the city, says businesses have learnt to adapt but that they all know it will be a “difficult” winter. “We have generators but they are expensive, cannot work all day long and cannot replace the energy system.”

Substations are so huge that you cannot hide them completely, says Hryhoriev. As for replacing destroyed ones, he says even in peacetime it took about two years to build a new one; and mending the damaged ones is out of the question given the constant interruption of air raid sirens and attacks.

“Unfortunately the enemy learns as well. They learn that if the missile they sent yesterday wasn’t effective, they send another one.” He ends the interview vowing to do all he can to keep the power going. The following morning one of his workers is killed by a Russian drone. 

‘We just have to get through this bad winter’

For now the race is on to safeguard the harvest — and see if there is any way of opening up the Black Sea.

Vysotskyi, the agriculture minister, believes as many as 11mn tonnes of crops may lack storage facilities. He has raised $15mn from Ukraine’s allies for giant polymer “sleeves”, which can protect about 200 tonnes of grain and can be erected on fields.

The World Bank is providing a low-interest $250mn loan to help compensate farmers for interest on agricultural loans, but the minister is aware this is just a temporary solution.

As for a repeat of the 2022 grain deal, which opened up the Black Sea, this seems unlikely. Vysotskyi says they are in contact with their allies and the principal buyers of their crops, such as Egypt, Turkey, other countries in the Middle East and India, but Russia has rejected proposals for a maritime ceasefire.

So the farmers of Ukraine’s fabled “black earth” can but pray and wait. Nika Viknianskyi, who oversees a 7,000-hectare megafarm 50 miles north-west of Odesa, has 25,000 tonnes of crops in storage already. This year’s wheat yield per hectare has shot up 40 per cent, he says, but the price has plunged from $220 to $130 a tonne.

“We invested in high tech, but it doesn’t matter how effective you are if you can’t sell your crops,” he says as he conducts a tour of his food mountains — and of the local railway station, which has been hit by Russian drones.  

Remarkably, in Odesa most mornings life seems to carry on pretty much as usual, however disrupted the night may have been. Many businesses in the past four and a half years have been remarkable case studies of stoicism and versatility.

“The new port crisis hasn’t been a crazy shock,” says Katerina Baliutova, the director of a container business. “Our bad experience in 2022 helped us to rethink our business. We were prepared.”

The doughty old farmer Varbanets, too, remains phlegmatic. He disappears into a shed and comes out bearing the remains of a rocket, and some shrapnel. He throws them almost triumphantly on the ground. “Our forces are constantly defending the sky above us. Rockets and drones are falling on our fields, but we have not been harmed.”

Everyone knows, however, that tough times lie ahead. “We just have to get through this bad winter,” says Varbanets. “People will survive in the villages no matter what. Even if the electricity goes, we have wood.

“But in the cities it will be very difficult.”

Data visualisation by Keith Fray and Steve Bernard

item.title: Why a booming economy is not helping Trump
item.author: Ruchir Sharma
item.description: Anxiety about AI and affordability has turned his populist party into a popular target
item.content:encoded:
Anxiety about AI and affordability has turned his populist party into a popular target

Ruchir Sharma

The writer is chair of Rockefeller International. His latest book is ‘What Went Wrong with Capitalism’

An American president’s party normally loses ground in midterm elections but this year is unusual. Economic growth accelerated sharply to near 4 per cent in the third quarter, yet Donald Trump’s approval rating is plummeting, particularly on the economy. His party is haemorrhaging support. Should it lose both houses of Congress next month, which betting markets see as a live possibility, it would be the first such defeat in economic conditions this favourable since the 1950s.

How could this happen? For many Americans, this feels like the wrong kind of boom — marred by a rising cost of living and the fact that growth is driven mainly by the wealthiest consumers and by heavy investment in AI, which the electorate has come to hate and fear more intensely than any previous tech breakthrough.

Frustration with the US economy predates both AI and Donald Trump’s second term. Most Americans have been increasingly dissatisfied about the state of the nation for decades, but the share who say the country is heading in the right direction collapsed over the past year from around 40 per cent to 20 per cent. The big source of dismay: affordability. The share of voters who cite cost of living as the most important issue has risen sixfold in recent years to a record high, over 25 per cent.  

And it is clear which prices are causing the most grievance: housing and energy, with the Iran war restricting oil supplies and AI raising demand for electricity. In the last year, petrol prices are up more than 40 per cent, and overall consumer prices have been rising at well over 3 per cent. With mortgage rates now topping 7 per cent, US housing is less affordable than at any point in the past two decades.

There is a widespread perception that power-hungry data centres are pushing up utility bills. Nine in ten Americans do not want one in their town, and most of these projects face local opposition. It’s hard, however, for Republican Congressional candidates to address these concerns when their president says slowing data centre construction would leave the US “backwards and poor”.  

Unsurprisingly, AI is the first widely hated product of the digital age. In earlier decades, a solid majority of Americans saw computers and the internet as big pluses for society. Now most say they are “more concerned than excited” about AI. Anxiety is rising most sharply among people in their twenties, who are increasingly worried about a jobless future. By asking voters to accept higher prices as the cost of his war in Iran, and AI as the cost of staying ahead of China, Trump is fighting against the national mood.

The consistent message from the White House and many congressional Republicans is: learn to love AI, we need it to compete with China. It’s an odd lecture coming from a party that won the White House and Congress by bashing globalist elites.

Broad GDP growth can fail to capture what people feel on the ground. Popular discontent reflects more granular details, like the fact that wage growth, adjusted for inflation, has turned negative in recent quarters. One key exception is workers with AI skills, who command wages up to 120 per cent higher than their peers.

So the sense of America as a land of haves and have-nots has an AI twist. Investment is growing around 25 per cent a year in AI-related industries, but by less than 1 per cent in other industries. Construction is contracting on average but growing at a double-digit pace for data centre projects.  

This tide of money is lifting other businesses only if they find an AI angle — think of the Japanese toilet manufacturer that saw its stock price jump after it started making ceramics for computer chips. Now, on days when the stock market goes up, nearly half of the stocks go down — an unprecedented phenomenon.

Most voters have reasons to feel left out of the blessed AI circle. The wealthiest own the most stocks, and the mostly AI-driven gains are rising this year, creating a reverse Robin Hood effect. The 0.1 per cent are gaining more than the 1 per cent, who gain more than the 10 per cent, and so on down the income ladder. Similarly, mortgage delinquency rates are rising on a sliding scale, fastest in the least wealthy neighbourhoods.  

Since the second world war, a booming economy has tended to cap midterm losses for the president’s party. Historically, when growth has accelerated towards 4 per cent before an election, the incumbent rarely lost control of either house of Congress and lost control of both just once, in 1954. Should the Republicans get swept aside this year, Trump — who rebuilt the GOP as a vessel of anti-incumbent anger — will have turned his party into a target.

item.title: Letter: How do you price universal extinction risk?
item.description: From Richard Kemmish, Culmhead, Somerset, UK
item.content:encoded:
From Richard Kemmish, Culmhead, Somerset, UK

John Foley’s otherwise excellent “Lex in depth” article on the prospective value of Anthropic surely contains a fallacy about the impact of the extinction of the human race on the valuation (Anthropic at $2tn isn’t far-fetched”, The Big Read, September 21).

If there is a probability that AI is the human race’s last mistake then the shares of Anthropic are indeed worth nothing. But then again, so are T-bills, gold, cash under the mattress and, for that matter, the mattress. No one is left to be better off by not having participated in the IPO. The relevant investment comparison is surely between the pay-offs of investing in Anthropic and of investing in alternative investments in the scenario where there are still people left to enjoy those pay-offs. Universal extinction risk does not belong in one company’s discount rate merely because that company might actually cause it.

Of course, there are reasons that the value may be less because of the perception of that risk — more regulation, litigation, slower roll out of new products, all of which can be priced in a half decent cashflow model. And it is not that unreasonable to have moral concerns about investing in the end of times. But the first of these is about the perception (which is known, ex ante), the latter about the ethics. Neither reflect the probability of the event per se.

There is little point constructing the perfect portfolio for the day after the end of humanity.

Richard Kemmish
Culmhead, Somerset, UK

item.title: Letter: Prediction markets and the wisdom of crowds
item.description: From Neal Kumar, Chief Legal Officer, Polymarket, New York, NY, US
item.content:encoded:
From Neal Kumar, Chief Legal Officer, Polymarket, New York, NY, US

The rapid expansion of prediction markets will naturally prompt debates about the economic, social and institutional utility of this emerging financial exchange.

While David Booth is right to test the merits of platforms such as ours, by conflating gambling and trading event contracts, he fundamentally misunderstands the model (“Beware the false promise of prediction platforms”, On Wall Street, FT Weekend, September 12).

What we provide is true price discovery, offering a platform for event contract trading where users trade on diverse categories like economic releases, commodity and crypto prices and other publicly verifiable events. This helps to forecast future trends, conduct research and assist institutions and investors as well as the general public in making decisions.

On the contrary, while a casino game in Las Vegas is designed so the house wins over time, a prediction market is a mechanism for aggregating dispersed information into a single, continuously updating price.

Traders are not betting against “the house” but trading against each other. Prediction markets such as ours do not set any odds, we do not benefit from customer losses, traders can exit at any time, and orders are matched on a central limit order book by price and time priority.

This is exactly why Polymarket US is licensed by the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission as a derivatives exchange.

Prediction markets are a nascent financial exchange and, just like trading in other markets, there will be attempts at misconduct. We’ve created strong deterrents already — matters are worked by expert investigators with backgrounds including the FBI. When wrongdoing is substantiated, we enforce wallet-level restriction, take legal action, or refer to law enforcement.

And while it is true that prediction markets are a relatively new development in the financial ecosystem that regulators and market participants will discuss and debate, to ignore the information utility of prediction markets as this piece does is to miss the point entirely.

People use prediction markets to gain leverage from the wisdom of crowds to price in the probability of events they care about.

Credible platforms must always monitor user behaviour, but dismissing price discovery on real-world events as gambling misunderstands how these markets function and the participation, transparency and technological innovation that they can offer to financial markets.

Neal Kumar
Chief Legal Officer, Polymarket, New York, NY, US

item.title: Letter: A more immediate threat is the ‘abliterated’ AI models
item.description: From Adam Hadley, Executive Director, Tech Against Terrorism, London N1, UK
item.content:encoded:
From Adam Hadley, Executive Director, Tech Against Terrorism, London N1, UK

Pope Leo is right that the warnings of AI specialists should be taken seriously (“Pope criticises Huang for playing down safety threat”, Report, September 30).

The debate he has joined, which last month also dominated the UN Security Council, remains fixed on the prospect of AI escaping human control.
