However, a more immediate threat to international peace and security receives almost no attention: the malign use of AI by criminals, terrorists and hostile nation states to cause real world harm.

Designated terrorist organisations, including Islamic State, are discussing and, by our assessment, downloading open-weight models whose safety refusals have been deliberately stripped out.

These “abliterated” models are freely available on mainstream model-sharing platforms for anyone to download and use.

Nvidia’s new tools may help developers police their own systems, but anyone who downloads the weights can remove any guardrail a developer builds into an open model.

No one has explained how open distribution of such models squares with the Security Council’s counterterrorism sanctions regime, or with US law on material support to foreign terrorist organisations.

Governments usually struggle to focus on low-probability, high-impact risks. AI has produced the opposite pathology: lavish attention on a speculative catastrophe, almost none on harms already under way.

My organisation, Tech Against Terrorism, has launched a benchmark to test how AI models respond to terrorist requests. We found that all abliterated open-weight models we tested obediently helped with building a bomb.

This is now a non-proliferation problem. A modest start would be for governments to back independent guardrail benchmarking of closed and open-weight models alike, and to curb the spread of abliterated versions, beginning by asking the platforms that host them how this squares with existing counterterrorism laws.

Adam Hadley
Executive Director, Tech Against Terrorism, London N1, UK

item.title: Letter: Clairvoyance or déjà vu?
item.description: From Henk Swarttouw, Domsten, Sweden
item.content:encoded:
From Henk Swarttouw, Domsten, Sweden

French brothers Edmond and Jules de Goncourt must have been tremendously clairvoyant when they devised the eponymous literary prize in the late 19th century as “France’s answer to the Booker Prize” (Report, September 26).

The first Booker was awarded in 1969. So perhaps it’s a case of déjà vu?

Henk Swarttouw
Domsten, Sweden

item.title: Letter: Burnham could take a leaf from Bob Hawke’s playbook
item.description: From John Llewellyn and David Vines
item.content:encoded:
From John Llewellyn and David Vines

You report that the prime minister has ruled out calling an early general election (“No 10 rules out early election as rumours swirl”, Report, September 25).

Yet much of the reaction to Andy Burnham’s speech has been that he will be unable to do much until after he has called (and won) an election, and hence his suggested reforms imply an early election.

But this is foolish reasoning. The proposed reforms are of great potential importance. They need to be reflected on carefully, with all the arguments and counter-arguments heard. Other political parties and many groupings need to be engaged in that debate; and it is essential that the public be, and feel that they have been, consulted.

All this takes time. Too many poor decisions in this country have been caused by ill-thought-out policies, brought in with undue rush from Westminster (think Brexit; water privatisation; HS2; the poll tax; and more).

A model of how to do this properly was provided by the former Australian prime minister Bob Hawke (1983-1991). His series of prices and incomes “accords” with the trade union movement — of which he had until very recently been the leader — were at the core of his success.

They laid the basis of what became the central, and fundamental, achievement of his government, namely the ending of protectionism, the freeing of trade with Asia, and the cascade of internal reforms that this provoked. These reforms stuck; and they have served Australia well.

John Llewellyn
Partner, Independent Economics, London SW1, UK

David Vines
Emeritus Professor of Economics and Emeritus Fellow of Balliol College, University of Oxford, Oxford, UK

item.title: Letter: The case for tax reform
item.description: From Andy Thompson, Worcester Park, Surrey, UK
item.content:encoded:
From Andy Thompson, Worcester Park, Surrey, UK

Martin Wolf argues — not for the first time — that the overall UK tax burden is not currently high, at least by European standards (“A message for the chancellor: the time is ripe for tax reform”, Opinion, September 28).

I am not sure that this would be true if the steadily growing burden of student loan repayments were counted as a tax. Legally they are not quite a graduate tax. Yet their behavioural effect must generally be much like an extra income tax.

The only exception may be when (or indeed if) a full repayment finally comes very close. Then with each extra payment it may perhaps start to feel that it promises an early benefit to the payer.

Wolf has acknowledged in the past that incentives do matter in tax systems. He now endorses the Mirrlees Review of 2011, chaired by the Nobel laureate Sir James Mirrlees, in saying: “do not look at a single tax on its own but relative to the rest [of the tax system]”.

That does not, I think, quite say it all about how fiscal behaviour effects operate. The overall impact of any part of the tax system is of course an aggregate of more primary causative effects, in how all of those individuals subject to it variously react.

I think most people with a current or potential involvement in the UK economy would take a view of those particular taxes likely to affect them most; and of course among all other factors within the whole UK economic and social environment, not just relative to other taxes.

Following a variety of UK personal tax changes targeted at relatively wealthy people in the past few years, I think the evidence is that further tax impositions on the highest earners could now assume quite critical importance.

That is especially (though not exclusively) true for those who were not born here, and others who do not now have all of their roots here, but could nevertheless view the UK as one of quite a number of alternative countries where their ambitions might best be pursued.

Nor would I share Wolf’s confidence in VAT now offering the most effective way to solve large UK fiscal problems. In some commercial sectors, notably building trades and other services direct to final consumers, a VAT rate of much over 20 per cent, on top of all the income and profit taxes, would make cheating an overwhelmingly attractive option.

Andy Thompson
Worcester Park, Surrey, UK

item.title: Letter: Here’s a favourite read from my childhood
item.description: From Anna Kirby, Mallow, County Cork, Ireland
item.content:encoded:
From Anna Kirby, Mallow, County Cork, Ireland

Thank you to Nilanjana Roy (“Children’s books never grow old”, Opinion, Life & Arts, FT Weekend, September 26) for urging us to re-read childhood favourites.

Children’s books that are sadly now out of print, by wonderful writers such as Malcolm Saville, Lorna Hill and Elinor Brent-Dyer seemed absolutely magical to me in the 1960s.

At age 70 plus, I still have a battered copy of The Bookshop on the Quay by the too little known children’s author Patricia Lynch.

Set in Dublin in the 1950s, it is the atmospheric story of a book-mad family surrounded by books for sale, who take in a young Cork orphan in search of his long-lost uncle.

I enjoin your readers to seek it out and read it to their children.

Anna Kirby
Mallow, County Cork, Ireland

item.title: Burnham could learn a thing or two from Thatcher
item.author: Caroline Slocock
item.description: Centralising power may feel like speeding things up but the rest of government actually slows down, waiting for decisions
item.content:encoded:
Centralising power may feel like speeding things up but the rest of government actually slows down, waiting for decisions

Caroline Slocock

The writer is a former senior civil servant. Her latest book is ‘Bad Government (And How to Make It Better)’

Andy Burnham has said he wants to bring about the biggest change in how the UK is governed since Margaret Thatcher, reversing her legacy and healing the north-south divide. But he could still learn from her about how to overturn the status quo, even though it’s her changes he wants to reverse now.

It’s tough inheriting a rodeo ride of a job: the seventh prime minister in 10 years must deal with a faltering economy and multiple international crises. Thatcher’s inheritance was equally challenging, from Heath’s three-day week to Callaghan’s IMF crisis and Winter of Discontent, with the economy in seemingly terminal decline. By the time she left office 11 years later, Britain had changed beyond recognition; she also played no small part in ending the cold war and initiating the European single market that helped secure Britain’s future economic growth.

So how did she master what seemed like an impossible job? I worked for her in Number 10 as her private secretary in her last 18 months and observed her closely, warts and all. Her secret was clarity of vision and purpose, with a determination to get things done. She was across the detail when she needed to be, but her eye was fixed on delivering fundamental change.

It’s so easy to lose your way when you’re prime minister: the vast number of decisions to take, the people to meet, the unexpected events that throw everything out. Bad enough then but more recent incumbents have fallen prey to micromanaging tendencies. Tony Blair started this centralising trend, hugely expanding the political wing of Number 10; Theresa May and Boris Johnson moved even more power there as they tried to deliver Brexit. It may feel like gaining more control and speeding things up, but the rest of government actually slows down, waiting for decisions. Keir Starmer’s Number 10 was more than three times bigger than in Thatcher’s day, and it’s still growing, but few would say it’s more effective.

Add in the 24/7 news cycle and you end up with prime ministers like Starmer who initially promised “country first, party second” then slipped into daily announcements to try to maintain political momentum. As Rishi Sunak wrote after leaving: “You get into this habit — you do an announcement for the evening news, post some things on social media and video, and your team briefs the press. Repeat.”

So many recent prime ministers prefer campaigning to governing, with Boris Johnson first in class. Although Thatcher won three terms through political skill, it was getting things done which she most enjoyed. “The cock crows, but the hen lays the egg,” she said.

Here’s my advice to Burnham if he wants to deliver deep change, drawing on Thatcher’s strengths: delegate, be clear about your purpose, direction and values and empower your cabinet and the whole of government to deliver for you, knocking heads together and joining them up when they don’t. Devolution is a great goal, but you don’t need to do it all yourself through Number 10 North. Instead, invest time internationally solving problems that could otherwise undermine Britain completely — so many clouds are gathering.

But Thatcher lacked a skill essential to Burnham’s success: the ability to inspire and mobilise others outside government, including businesses and civil society, to deliver common goals. On so many issues, government needs others to help it create changes that would reduce public sector costs and promote growth and wellbeing. Burnham demonstrated this skill in Manchester and has promised collaborative, preventive government based on that experience.

Burnham would do well to emulate Thatcher’s clarity of purpose domestically and leadership internationally, but he must also bring the UK together in ways she never did if he is to re-energise the country and escape the cycle of bad government that has dogged it for years.

item.title: The US is looking more like Italy
item.author: Rana Foroohar
item.description: America is not so exceptional any more — and the New World is becoming more like the Old
item.content:encoded:
America is not so exceptional any more — and the New World is becoming more like the Old

Rana Foroohar

There’s an interesting parlour game being played in New York these days: which dodgy economic habits has America picked up from elsewhere? Is it Malaysia’s endemic political patronage? Is it Nigeria’s tolerance of cash bribes as business as usual? Or is it Brazil’s inequality, where the ultra-rich enjoy a life of luxury alongside those living in squalor?

America today has aspects of these and other emerging markets (though that term feels like a misnomer these days, when so many developing nations are besting their rich-country peers in terms of economic performance and governance). But I would make a different comparison. I think that America is starting to look more like Italy, another western nation with a turbulent history.

This is the case for three reasons. While overt corruption may not be as dire in either the US or Italy as in many other frontier markets, both are actively turning away from policing it. Second, populism in politics is showing up in both countries in a similar way. Finally, and most importantly, the labour market in America is starting to look more like Italy’s in one crucial respect: older people are holding on to good jobs, and the young have trouble finding decent ones.

Let’s start with the political economy. Transparency International’s most recent Corruption Perceptions Index gave the US a score of 64 out of 100 in terms of corruption, its lowest to date. Italy was slightly lower, with a score of 53, but the report specifically called out both countries for watering down efforts to fight corruption. Italy’s resistance to criminalising the abuse of power among public officials, for example, and the Trump administration’s weakening of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act belong in the same basket of behaviour.

No surprise then that democracy is weakening in both places. A 2026 report by V-Dem, an academic project that measures democracy, recently identified both Italy and the US as two of the western countries that have had the most democratic backsliding in recent years. Likewise, Freedom House found that the two countries had relatively large swings towards a more autocratic political economy compared with other nations still labelled “free”.

The US is no longer an exceptional nation in any positive sense. I sense my fellow Americans starting to think about corruption as endemic, something ordinary people can’t do much about. This reminds me of the shoulder-shrugging “what can you do?” attitude towards bad political behaviour or black-market economies that you find elsewhere. According to a recent Gallup poll, the percentage of Americans who say corruption in government is widespread has risen from 60 per cent in 2006 to 89 per cent today.

Economic cynicism is growing too, especially among young people. One of the most striking things about the US economy today is how the labour market is beginning to mirror the two-tiered, age-divided system that has dogged European nations like Italy, forcing younger people to live longer with their parents or leave the country for more upward mobility.

The last US jobs report, out in early September, found that unemployment was 7.1 per cent for ages 20-24, as compared to 3.6 per cent for those 25-54 and 3 per cent for those over 55. Youth unemployment in Italy is much higher — a whopping 20 per cent. But the ratios are similar, with unemployment among younger people roughly double that of middle-aged workers.

Some of this two-tiered labour market problem revolves around age, but some of it is about who your parents are. If you are an insider, you have opportunity. If you are an outsider, by race or class, you have less. As academics like Raj Chetty have shown, America is looking much more like Old Europe these days in terms of mobility: where and to whom you are born has an outsized impact on how much or whether you prosper.

These trends may be amplified by AI, which paradoxically seems to be favouring not young digital natives but rather older workers who have the sectoral experience necessary to leverage the technology and do not face the same risk of disruption as those seeking entry-level jobs. In a paper published in September, the Census Bureau estimated that graduates in the most AI-exposed areas would suffer a five-percentage-point decline in the likelihood of initial employment and 13 per cent lower earnings than those going into less-exposed sectors.

While there’s reason to think the technology could benefit younger people in the future, as they move faster into the new jobs and sectors that AI will create, the short-term result is likely to be more disaffected young people.

The result of that would in turn be more of the populism already so evident in the US, Italy and many other European countries. That could in turn slow growth, which would further disadvantage the youngest and the poorest, fuelling the political divides between boomers and younger voters, centrists and extremists.

Italy has, of course, seen this cycle play out many times in its long history, and is right now enjoying a brighter moment, with stronger export and employment numbers. America is only beginning to understand what happens when an empire collapses under its own dysfunctional political economy.

rana.foroohar@ft.com

item.title: In defence of big business
item.author: Tej Parikh
item.description: Despite the lionisation of small companies, prosperity hinges on a handful of large firms
item.content:encoded:
Despite the lionisation of small companies, prosperity hinges on a handful of large firms

Tej Parikh

Small businesses are lionised the world over. Family restaurants, plucky start-ups and independent cafés are routinely hailed by politicians on both the left and right as the lifeblood of the economy. Economists also extol the virtues of backing small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs).

Big business gets a frostier reception. Large corporations are increasingly viewed with scepticism — either as a force to be restrained or a resource to be tapped for tax revenue. The share of Americans with a positive view of them has fallen from close to 60 per cent in the early 2010s to just over one-third today, according to Gallup.

Inequality, high-profile corporate scandals and growing concern about market concentration have all contributed to the souring opinion. Yet, despite the affection lavished on their smaller counterparts, big businesses do much of the heavy lifting in raising economic prosperity.

Globalisation and technological advances have increased the returns to scale, allowing firms to grow larger. Research spanning 10 rich-world economies over more than a century finds that sales, profits and equity capital have become increasingly concentrated in the largest firms within countries. Importantly, significant churn means the largest firms of the past are not the same companies that dominate in the present.

This suggests that big business is not merely a US aberration or prima facie evidence of lax antitrust regulation, but a feature of modern global capitalism.

And firm size matters for domestic economic growth. A study from the World Bank — which has long championed SMEs as engines of development — shows that high-performing economies tend to have a larger share of employment in big, competitive firms. Lower-income countries, by contrast, suffer from a significant shortage of large companies — a “missing top” — with their firms often growing less as they age.

Big companies are both a product of a healthy business environment, which enables expansion, and a key contributor to growth. Scale supports higher wages, better benefits and training, while making firms more likely to export and adopt international quality standards, the World Bank finds. In rich nations, SMEs are on average two-thirds as productive as the largest firms.

In turn, improvements in how big firms operate can ripple through the wider economy, thanks to their large workforces, customer bases and supply chains.

Indeed, large businesses are engines of innovation. Consider Big Tech. In 2024, Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Apple invested $227bn in research and development (R&D), exceeding the US federal government’s non-defence R&D budget as well as the annual R&D spending of most countries, according to the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation.

Deep pockets allow big companies to finance costly research, absorb failures and initiate undertakings whose returns might be years away. For instance, in 2016, Alphabet’s experimental X Development division reported quarterly losses of $859mn pursuing moonshot projects, from internet-delivery balloons to glucose-monitoring contact lenses.

The benefits of R&D are spread widely. A 2004 study by Nobel Prize-winning economist William Nordhaus estimates that innovators captured just 2.2 per cent of the social surplus generated by US technological advances between 1948 and 2001. The rest accrued to consumers via better products and lower prices.

Recent research by the McKinsey Global Institute reinforces the idea that prosperity hinges on a small number of extraordinary companies making leaps rather than incremental improvements across millions of small firms.

The think-tank’s analysis of roughly 8,300 large US, UK and German companies found that fewer than 100 “standout” firms accounted for around two-thirds of the positive productivity gains in each country between 2011 and 2019. Even if the sample included the gamut of smaller firms, a handful of large “standouts” would still account for more than half of productivity growth.

Crucially, these gains need not come from major technological breakthroughs, but bursts of improvements made at scale. Think Tesco embarking on a multibillion-pound cost-cutting programme, United Airlines optimising route networks, General Motors retreating from unprofitable markets or Amazon expanding its fulfilment network.

Indeed, the majority of “standouts” in McKinsey’s sample are large incumbents achieving productivity gains over time, while 20 per cent are scalers, such as Apple and Amazon, and 10 per cent are smaller disrupters.

None of this means bigger is always better. The US productivity advantage over the UK and Germany arises to a large extent because American laggards are more likely to be forced into restructurings or exits. Competitive markets are key.

Size also brings economic and political power that can be abused by suppressing emerging rivals, squeezing workers and suppliers or bending regulation in incumbents’ favour. Competition and regulatory authorities, therefore, have the essential but difficult job of keeping markets open and contestable and technological progress safe.

Still, size itself is too often treated as evidence of market failure. And efforts to address this risk overlooking the economic benefits of scale for productivity, innovation and economic resilience.

Small businesses deserve much of the affection they receive. They experiment, create jobs and provide the pool from which exceptional companies and ideas can emerge. But policy should support scaling and competition, while allowing large standouts to thrive. After all, the most transformative small businesses tend not to stay small.

Send your thoughts via the comments, freelunch@ft.com or on X @tejparikh90.

Food for thought

Do your childhood neighbours influence your career choices and later-life earnings? This study reckons so.

Free Lunch on Sunday is edited by Harvey Nriapia

item.title: EU countries shoot themselves in the foot when they veto sanctions
item.author: Martin Sandbu
item.description: A recent move by France makes talk of ‘strategic autonomy’ look like hot air
item.content:encoded:
A recent move by France makes talk of ‘strategic autonomy’ look like hot air

Martin Sandbu

It is not a pretty picture: the country that has been most insistent that EU member states develop “strategic autonomy” from global powers recently forced the bloc to submit to pressure from a middling Central Asian authoritarian petrostate.

Last month, France held up the six-monthly renewal of sanctions on individuals and companies linked to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s regime. The EU’s foreign policy rules require unanimity for decisions on sanctions. Paris, however, threatened to allow all the sanctions to lapse unless the billionaire Alisher Usmanov was removed from the list. This, it seems, was a condition set by Azerbaijan for the release of French citizens imprisoned there. Luxembourg then followed with a demand to take another oligarch off the hook.

This is not the first betrayal of European solidarity over sanctions. Greece this year held up a previous sanctions renewal to allow a shipping magnate to continue the very lucrative business of shipping Russian gas to non-EU markets. Hungary has long used its veto power for its own benefit.

But for France to behave in this way is a watershed. It is one of the founders of the EU and its second-largest member state. And President Emmanuel Macron’s call for strategic autonomy, at first dismissed as a French idée fixe, had more or less become conventional wisdom in the bloc. Now, however, it looks as though it was just talk.

In the end France — or rather, Azerbaijan — got its way. Baku promptly released one French prisoner after EU governments struck a compromise in which the remaining sanctions were extended for three years rather than just six months. That, at least, means a repeat will not happen any time soon. But what matters more is how much of the EU’s geopolitical influence, such as it was, has been lost in the process.

Paris has in effect put the position of EU capitals on sanctions up for sale to third countries. Quite aside from undermining the “common” in the EU’s common security and defence policy, this further encourages rogue states to hold European countries to ransom, for example by jailing their citizens.

The even bigger loss is the potential for a more strategic sanctions policy, which now seems further from being realised than ever. To give credit where it’s due: the EU has managed to assemble an impressive 21 sanctions packages against Russia. These have hurt the Russian economy and shrunk the resources available to sustain its war effort. But the EU should aim higher than the reactive punishment it has meted out, partially and too weakly enforced.

A truly strategic sanctions policy deliberately links sanctions decisions to demands made of others. That requires the ability to credibly threaten specific sanctions (or the tightening of existing ones) before other states act to harm EU values or interests, and to promise loosening on strict conditions. Such an ability is elusive while 27 veto-wielding member states all pursue their own narrow goals — but it would earn Europe a seat at the table when Ukraine’s future is determined and give it greater influence on Israel’s conduct in the Middle East. On top of boosting the EU’s strategic relevance, that would also serve its economic interests.

The path to achieving this is well known: it is to shift sanctions and possibly other aspects of foreign policy to qualified majority voting (QMV), as provided for in the EU treaties. The last push to do so was a “friends of QMV” group of member states formed a few years ago. Ironically enough, France joined the group, although it is doubtful its heart was ever in it.

Unfortunately, the current prospects for such a move, which itself requires unanimity, are poor. However, now that the existing procedure is being undermined, the need for it is greater than ever.

Some member states fear that their vital interests would be damaged by majority rulemaking. But in a world suddenly more filled with adversaries and enemies, going it alone is to accept being divided and ruled by others — even for the biggest countries, as the French experience shows.

EU countries should remember that it is precisely when majority rulemaking has stopped them from undercutting each other commercially — in trade, competition and the single market — that they have flourished collectively.

Majority voting on sanctions would not by itself improve policy. Brussels’ pusillanimity in robustly using the EU’s anti-coercion instrument, or even conventional trade policy, against the US or China shows that. But it is a necessary condition for progress. Macron could redeem himself by rallying behind a shift now.

martin.sandbu@ft.com

Letter in response:
Sanctions policy sometimes must be compromised to save lives / From Frank Vogl, Adjunct Professor, Georgetown University; Co-founder, Transparency International, Washington, DC, US

item.title: The FT View. Britain’s Budget needs to tame spending and boost growth
item.author: The editorial board
item.description: Chancellor Healey can still make a low-key fiscal event a constructive one
item.content:encoded:
Chancellor Healey can still make a low-key fiscal event a constructive one

The editorial board

The last time Britain had a chancellor called Healey it was grappling with high inflation, an oil shock and a wide fiscal deficit. Today, the pressures facing the latest one — John Healey, the former defence secretary — are similar, if less extreme. The buffer against the government’s fiscal rule has shrunk. Last week, a further sell-off in global bonds pushed UK 30-year gilt yields above 6 per cent for the first time since 1998. Instability in the Middle East, meanwhile, continues to push up fuel prices.

Against that backdrop, Healey and Prime Minister Andy Burnham appear to be planning a largely steady-as-she-goes Budget on October 28. After two years of tax-raising fiscal events and policy rumours, that would be welcome. But mere stability should not be the limit of their ambition. Having set out their long-term vision at last week’s Labour Party conference, they should use the coming weeks to ensure the Budget lays the foundations for sounder public finances and stronger growth in the remaining years of this parliament.

Healey committed to “fiscal discipline” in his conference speech. But that need not mean rebuilding all the headroom the government is estimated to have lost against its rule to balance day-to-day spending by 2030, partly because of global economic turmoil. Restoring too much, too quickly risks sapping growth. The buffer exists to absorb shocks, and gilt investors have signalled some tolerance for a smaller cushion.

Whatever tightening proves necessary, it should come primarily through spending restraint. Further tax rises on employers, investors and wealth creators would be another blow to economic dynamism, making it harder to improve the debt-to-GDP trajectory. Burnham’s pledge to remove the generous “triple lock” on state pensions in the next parliament is promising. But its potential savings will be offset by his costlier plan for a national social care service.

What is needed above all is a credible plan to contain spending in the near term. The government hopes a new apprenticeship programme will get young people into work and ease the burden on benefits. In time, it may. But direct reductions in welfare spending are needed too. Annual expenditure on personal independence payments, which are made regardless of employment status, is forecast to rise from around £30bn this year to £41.5bn by 2031. Significant savings may be unrealistic in this Budget. But Healey can at least spell out how welfare costs will be contained and signal a tougher spending review, slated for next year.

There is also time to be ambitious on growth. Healey and Burnham’s re-industrialisation push has been short on specifics. They should focus on concrete reforms that remove barriers to work and investment. Britain’s tax system, for instance, is riddled with distortions, from income-tax kinks that discourage work to inefficient property levies. An immediate overhaul is unlikely, but the Treasury can set out a roadmap for simplification.

Other measures need not wait. Further liberalisation of planning rules, fast-tracking nationally significant infrastructure projects and grid connections, and slowing plans to raise the minimum wage could all help unlock business activity now. Healey should use the coming weeks to work with businesses and the Office for Budget Responsibility on which reforms would be most fruitful. And even if some measures cannot yet be scored in the growth forecasts, firm commitments to supply-side reform would bolster investor confidence.

A lot can change before Budget day and impact what level of buffer is indeed prudent — so the chancellor should remain flexible. Still, Burnham and Healey can achieve plenty in the coming weeks. By bearing down on costs and doing more to unlock growth, they could deliver a Budget that is not only stabilising, but uplifting too.

item.title: Why the IPO market is booming and busting
item.author: Craig Coben
item.description: Flotations have stalled and returns from new listings have been weak
item.content:encoded:
Flotations have stalled and returns from new listings have been weak

Craig Coben

The writer is a former global head of equity capital markets at Bank of America and is now a managing director at Seda Experts

The initial public offering market right now is booming and busting at the same time.

At one level, investment bankers have reason to rejoice. Proceeds so far this year have reached $147.5bn compared with $44bn for the same period last year, powered by SpaceX’s $86bn IPO and SK Hynix’s $26.5bn offering on Nasdaq. Anthropic waits in the wings.

Yet flotations have stalled of late, with just three US debuts since Labor Day in September. Bamboo Insurance postponed its IPO that month. Just days later Holtec Nuclear pushed back its listing owing to waning enthusiasm towards AI infrastructure. SB Energy, SoftBank’s US data centre developer, has “slowed” its IPO timeline, while fitness wearable maker Oura pulled its Nasdaq flotation last week “due to uncertainty in the IPO market”.

The IPO market and stock market are not the same thing. Investors can gain exposure to companies and sectors through existing listings and do not need to chase the newest thing. And this year’s new issues have disappointed, with more than 40 per cent trading below offer price. Excluding SpaceX and SK Hynix, the weighted average return on IPOs in 2026 is minus 4 per cent, according to Bloomberg, compared with a 12 per cent gain in the S&P 500 index.

Given the weak returns, investors are rebelling over terms. SB Energy was reportedly seeking a $50bn valuation despite not having brought a data centre online yet. Oura sought a substantial valuation premium to peer company Garmin, even though the offering mostly would have cashed out early investors rather than finance investment.

Some of the slowdown reflects the normal ebb and flow in the IPO cycle: money floods in, valuations get stretched, deals trade poorly, and the market seizes up until pricing resets lower and performance improves. This happened last spring with AI-adjacent stocks. Sentiment has since cooled, and companies and boards need time to adjust.

Why does this always happen? A listing often takes at least six to nine months from kick-off. Why doesn’t everyone accept that valuations may fall in the meantime? Part of the answer lies in how mandates are awarded. Bankers resemble politicians who — to paraphrase former New York governor Mario Cuomo — campaign in poetry and govern in prose. The goal is to pitch as credibly optimistic a valuation as possible. You cannot present a ridiculous, unsupported price range, but you are expected to show how you can achieve a premium valuation multiple.

Conversely, every equity capital markets banker has lost mandates to rivals promising a higher valuation. The client tells you: “Other banks seemed to understand our growth drivers better than you guys.” That is vernacular for “your competitors showed a higher number”. Some chastened bankers overcorrect the next time and go into optimism overdrive.

Syndicate structure can aggravate the problem. US IPOs used to be led almost always by a single lead bank, in contrast to European and Asian offerings, which feature joint global coordinators. Today, larger US flotations increasingly have multiple “active bookrunners”, diluting some of the accountability that the lead bank has long held. The banker who pushes for a lower price risks incurring the client’s wrath while other deal “partners” benefit. “ECM used to be held accountable,” a disillusioned former senior banker in New York told me last week. “Now it’s a rugby scrum.”

Once a bank wins a mandate, it is fraught to tell clients that the “comps” with listed stocks have contracted and pricing must come down. No client likes a “re-trade” on a valuation already accepted among early backers, employees and board members.

There is another reason for the logjam. Private equity firms bought assets at nosebleed prices in 2020 and 2021. Going public today risks crystallising a valuation below current marks. That is painful and it partly explains the enormous backlog of unsold private equity-owned assets. Many such companies also do not jibe with the investor zeitgeist: fund managers pay up for go-go growth and scale, not indebted, midsized firms exposed to consumer cyclicality or interest rate risk.

There is a final issue. This year has been a banner year for equity underwriters, but a carpe diem mentality permeates Wall Street: get the deals out while the market is open because next year may be tough. Even as bankers paint sunlit uplands, they are rushing to complete transactions as if the storm could come at any time.

item.title: Lex. Andy Burnham and the art of corporate pitch-rolling
item.description: The UK prime minister has many grand plans, but most won’t kick in until 2030 or even later
item.content:encoded:
The UK prime minister has many grand plans, but most won’t kick in until 2030 or even later

Most executives are familiar with “kitchen sinking”, when a new leader, inheriting a tricky situation, tries to get bad news and tough decisions out of the way as soon as possible. But sometimes, even throwing everything but the kitchen sink at a problem is not enough. That’s when “pitch-rolling” comes in.

This piece of cricket-inspired corporate jargon helps understand the way in which the UK’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham, has described his vision to “put Britain on a new path”. Burnham has many grand plans but most won’t kick in until 2030 or even later. Supporters hope this is long enough to prepare the ground — or “roll the pitch” — for some of the unpopular moves that will be required.

In the business world, pitch-rolling can be a useful tactic for new leaders who are riding high on honeymoon popularity but know that painful adjustments lie ahead. It still takes good execution, though — and sometimes a bit of luck — to see things through.

Look at Citigroup chief executive Jane Fraser. She took over a bank in 2021 that was sprawling, underperforming and had, in her words, avoided making “hard decisions” that would cause “some near-term pain”. Tens of thousands of job cuts later, Citi’s latest profitability targets are still modest by industry standards, but its shares have outpaced most of its rivals’ since she outlined her strategy. 

The art of pitch-rolling is to be realistic without being too gloomy. Go too hard on the warnings, and morale can fall through the floor, as happened in the first months of Sir Keir Starmer’s premiership. Back in the corporate sphere, Boeing boss Kelly Ortberg took the helm of the troubled planemaker in 2024, warning that “tough decisions” and “structural changes” were coming, but that the company would once again become an “industry leader”.

It’s important to act as well as talk. Oil major BP shows what happens when execution doesn’t match rhetoric. Its shares jumped when former chief executive Bernard Looney announced wildly ambitious plans to transform BP into a renewable energy giant and slashed its dividend. But the green initiatives showed little progress. By 2025, Looney had been fired — albeit for bad conduct rather than BP’s performance — and his successor had torn up his entire strategy.

That reversal highlights another warning for Burnham. BP may have messed up, but it was also hostage to fortune. In the case of energy markets, Donald Trump’s return to the White House with a pro-oil agenda dramatically changed the calculus. Preparing the ground is all well and good, but the best leaders also know how to keep playing if their neatly rolled turf gets rudely ripped up.

nicholas.megaw@ft.com

item.title: Today’s youth would like to give back modernity, thank you very much
item.author: Jemima Kelly
item.description: Has any previous generation been so down on the present?
item.content:encoded:
Has any previous generation been so down on the present?

Jemima Kelly

It wasn’t so long ago that acts like Coldplay were actively encouraging audiences to use smartphones during live performances. The band’s frontman Chris Martin would ask crowds to create a sea of phone flashlights during the song Yellow, or to create a “cell phone lights wave”. “Forget cigarette lighters, mobile phones are the new glowsticks!” one of the band’s roadies enthused on their official tour blog back in 2008. 

Perhaps, if we’re being generous, it sounded cool back then. Today, it feels rather depressing — démodé, even. Indeed, these days the band gives out LED wristbands so the crowd can create the sea-of-lights effect without their phones, and Martin routinely asks audiences to put their phones away entirely for a single song. 

Others are taking further the wacky idea that going to see a gig should be about a shared human experience rather than content-gathering. Phoebe Bridgers, a 32-year-old indie-folk singer with a fan base that stretches from young teenager to ageing Boomer, has brought in an all-out smartphone ban for her current tour, requiring audience members to lock their devices in pouches that are magnetically sealed for the duration of the event (also banned are smartwatches, AirPods and Meta glasses). She’s not the only one: Harry Styles and Bob Dylan have recently brought in similar bans, and tech-free events are proving increasingly popular.

You might think it is stodgy old technophobes or techno-incompetents who are driving this trend, but no. A study from gig-booking website Eventbrite earlier this year, which reported a 567 per cent increase in the number of explicitly phone-free events listed between 2024 and 2025, found that 49 per cent of Gen Z and millennial respondents agreed they wanted live experiences “to feel less curated and more real”.

Yet if you look at imagery or footage from live events at which smartphones have not been banned, that 49 per cent is hard to detect. Where there were once mosh pits and dance floors, there are now jumbles of upstretched young arms topped by phones that seem like extensions of their limbs. It appears that even those who would like experiences to feel “more real” still feel the need to capture the moment they are ostensibly living, so that after the event they can show others what a great time they were filming — sorry, having.

A curious paradox seems to be emerging: young people might be the heaviest users of emerging technology, but they also seem to be the ones least positive about it. A recent Pew survey of more than 5,000 Americans found that while 18-29-year-olds were the most likely to use chatbots, they were also the most pessimistic about AI. Some 48 per cent said its impact over the next two decades would be negative for society, while just 14 per cent said it would be positive (compared with 40 per cent and 16 per cent, respectively, for all adults). A YouGov survey in 2023 found that Britons aged 18-24, the heaviest users of smartphones, were the most likely to say they use their phones “too much” and were trying to do something about that.

‘Twas not ever thus. The rate at which young people are falling out of love with technology is striking. An Ipsos survey found there had been a huge increase in people of all ages who agree with the idea that “technological progress is destroying our lives” over the past decade or so, but in the UK the jump was the biggest among 15-24-year-olds. In 2013, only 26 per cent of them agreed with that statement; by 2026, that figure had swelled to 62 per cent. 

So pervasive is the youth’s tech fatigue that many of them wish they had been born in an altogether different era: a large-scale NBC poll released in April found that 47 per cent of 18-29-year-old Americans would, if they had the option, choose to live in the past. (Just 38 per cent said they would rather live in the present, while 15 per cent would like to live in the future.)

Has any previous generation of young people felt this way? Sadly, we don’t have comparable data for earlier cohorts, but the prevalence of this modernity malaise strikes me as unprecedented. Yes, kids in the 1960s and 1970s might have wished the nuclear bomb didn’t exist, but that didn’t mean they wished to be born in the past.

I used to consider it a given that now was the best time to be alive, and that would continue to be the case while we remained at (relative) peace. That this is no longer so is, of course, rather troubling — as is the fact that so many of us seem to be enslaved by technology we resent. But I am reassured, somewhat, by the growing appetite for restriction. As I have written before, if freedom is something we want to be freed from, it’s not really freedom at all.

jemima.kelly@ft.com

item.title: Dear all: how bosses should talk to the troops
item.author: Pilita Clark
item.description: And what they should always try to avoid
item.content:encoded:
And what they should always try to avoid

Pilita Clark

Some chief executives send a weekly email to tell their staff how things are going. Others hold an online Q&A every few months, or post their thoughts on LinkedIn.

I am not sure any do exactly what Greg Jackson does at Octopus Energy, the British household energy supply group he founded in 2015. 

Every Friday at 4.15pm, he encourages Octopus’s 13,000-odd staff in eight countries to join “family dinner”: a mildly chaotic half-hour online session of cheeky, rapid-fire presentations from Jackson and his top managers on the latest company news.

Here’s what happened at one I watched the other week at the group’s London headquarters on Oxford Street. As 4.15pm neared, staff began to log off, grab drinks from company fridges and settle in front of a large screen in an office auditorium.

Jackson soon materialised online to talk about people he had met at Octopus Live customer sessions being held around the country. A couple in Manchester had brought their bills down to £12 a month with a home battery, heat pump and solar panels. A breast cancer survivor had cried as she told him how Octopus had helped her manage bills. 

Then the group’s country heads came on to deliver their news, amid video clips, jokey animations, a stream of online staff comments — and a lot of Jackson interjections.

“Jesus,” he exclaimed as his CEO for Germany reported the company had just swept all 36 categories in industry awards for customer service and innovation. “That is unbelievable,” he said, joking that his Italian equivalent would be furious. 

“Absolutely fucking great!” he hooted, as his man in Tokyo revealed 600,000 Japanese customers.

He liked the news from Japan and China so much he announced that a prize of a free trip to both countries would go to the two employees who could say how many solar panels were installed in China in 2025.

Entries will be “off the charts” by competition cut-off time on Tuesday, he told me later. It’s all part of the effort to entertain staff while reinforcing company priorities such as industry leadership, prices, clean energy and customer service.

The format alternates each week. A global session like that one is followed by a country one, then another global one and then one for individual teams. Jackson hosts all except the team events, meaning he is doing a session three out of every four weeks. It’s time-consuming, he agrees, but crucial “if you want to keep a global company focused on the same objectives and know what we really want”.

A lot of organisations would do well to adopt this type of approach. Too many bosses leave it to managers to do the communicating. Or lumber staff with long, repetitive and widely unread emails that reek of little thought or care. Or livestream rare, stilted and largely uninformative presentations.

Saying that, Jackson is hard to imitate. He has a good sense of comic timing that he can deploy with relative ease since Octopus is privately held, plus a background in tech, where playful online town halls are more common. 

It is more complicated when you run a listed company with more than 200,000 employees in 56 countries and you are axing some of the most expensive ones, as Georges Elhedery is at HSBC. 

He has made internal communication a priority for his senior managers since becoming CEO in 2024 and does plenty of it himself. Along with emails at quarterly results time, he appears at regional town hall meetings and at panel discussions with top executives, and has online chats with outside guests, such as DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis. 

Matt Brittin, the BBC’s new director-general, has taken a similar approach, appearing at online Q&A sessions for the broadcaster’s 20,000-plus staff, hosted by presenters such as Adam Fleming.

At McKinsey, global managing partner Bob Sternfels writes a regular blog about anything from the forces affecting clients to what he has seen on his travels. He also pens less frequent but more substantial letters about news affecting the firm, or ideas he wants everyone to know about.

I know of other bosses who send out videos, or write chatty emails about family holidays, or hold ask-me-anything staff Slack chats.

Ultimately, what matters most is understanding one’s priorities and conveying them as thoughtfully, regularly and non-tediously as possible. Anyone who can do that while making people laugh is well ahead. The rest can gain a lot by trying.

pilita.clark@ft.com

item.title: Chart of the Week: What’s driving the global bond sell-off?
item.author: Hakyung Kim
item.description: Looking at the most cited factors reveals a mixed picture
item.content:encoded:
Looking at the most cited factors reveals a mixed picture

Hakyung Kim

Good morning. Sovereign bond yields have been rising all year, and in the past few weeks the pace has accelerated across most developed markets. But there is not a clear consensus about what’s driving the sell-off. Looking at the most cited factors — inflation and indebtedness — across various countries reveals a mixed picture.

Mapping debt-to-GDP ratios against year-to-date increases in 10-year yields reveals a loose positive relationship. But there are exceptions, such as South Korea, which has a relatively low debt-to-GDP ratio of 52 per cent, but a jump similar to that of Italy, whose public debt sits at a staggering 137 per cent of GDP. Adding inflation rates offers only a little extra clarity. Italy and Spain recently both had annualised inflation readings above 4 per cent, yet their yield increases have lagged behind those of French sovereign bonds, despite France’s tamer inflation rate of 3 per cent.

Growth is another part of the equation. The steady expansion in US real GDP helps explain why its yields have risen more than those of Italy, which has higher debt and more inflation. Finally, there’s the unquantifiable variable: political risk. French bond yields have surged to levels near those of the European debt crisis, as election uncertainty comes on top of a worsening fiscal situation.

The biggest outlier is, of course, Japan. The yield on the 10-year JGB has surged by nearly one percentage point in 2026, an increase comparable to that of Gilts and Italian debt. Yet Japanese inflation came in at just 1.9 per cent in August — the lowest on our list. Historical context is important. While other countries would be pleased with a 1.9 per cent inflation rate, decades of deflation in the Asian nation have made these “normal” inflation levels, alongside a weak yen and energy shock, a bigger jolt to the economy.

Send us your thoughts: unhedged@ft.com.

Good reads from Unhedged

Hakyung: “Almost all writers fade away.”

Rob: a rebirth.

item.title: The right and wrong lessons to learn from Spain’s housing crisis
item.author: John Burn-Murdoch
item.description: Evictions and spiralling rents are the symptom, not the underlying disease
item.content:encoded:
Evictions and spiralling rents are the symptom, not the underlying disease

John Burn-Murdoch

Although housing crises have been smouldering across much of the high-income world for a decade or more, they have generally tended to rank some way down the political agenda.

That may be about to change, with reports suggesting Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez is considering calling an early election in a bid to resolve mounting public and political discontent over spiralling rents and prices after his flagship housing bill was rejected by parliament on Friday.

Mass protests were sparked recently by the case of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal. She was served an eviction notice after her previously rent-controlled flat was bought by a corporate landlord which sought to increase the rent to a level well above her monthly pension income.

Much of the anger has centred on the role of so-called “vulture funds” in the rental market — Sanchez’s party has proposed banning large-scale investors from buying homes until 2028. But if policymakers and tenants alike want to see durable improvements and to avoid unintended negative consequences, it’s worth taking a step back and looking at what is, in truth, a much deeper problem, both in Spain and in other countries.

Consider the many recent cases in the UK and Ireland where protesters have similarly rallied in opposition to evictions — often not by greedy corporate landlords but by local councils seeking to move rent-controlled properties on to new low-income tenants. These happen after the former tenant passes away or moves out but their family members refuse to leave.

The specifics of such cases are very different but they all speak to the same problem: acute housing shortages. A landlord — whether the corporate or “mom-and-pop” variety — increases rents only when they are confident they will find someone willing to pay the higher price. The bidding wars resulting from shortages provide fertile ground. Spain has built fewer homes per capita than virtually any other high-income country over the past 10 years. More than 50 per cent of its young adults now live with their parents, up from 33 per cent in 2005, and rents have risen more steeply than almost anywhere else.

The reason the children of British and Irish social housing tenants are desperate to keep hold of the homes after tenancies expire — and why waiting lists for those cost-controlled homes are so long — is the acute shortage of properties in these countries. The UK and Ireland each lack roughly one in seven homes they need to adequately house today’s populations.

Spain’s problems are on both the supply and demand sides. Its housebuilding crunch has coincided with a population boom fuelled in large part by a conscious effort by Sánchez to boost immigration. On top of that, surging inflows of tourists and digital nomads mean the market-clearing rent is often set not by local incomes but by those of affluent visitors. Courting workers and high-spending visitors from overseas is sound economic policy, but it requires a joined-up approach on the supply side in the form of much greater housebuilding — some of which could be funded through increased tourist taxes.

The government’s proposals so far amount to a patchwork of sticking plasters that address some of the symptoms but not the underlying cause. Stronger protections for existing tenants and bans on investment will not ease shortage-driven pressure on rents and prices. Nor will they house the millions of young adults whose lives and careers are on hold while they are forced to share a roof with their parents.

In this regard Spain may want to look to Ireland, where policymakers last year watered down rent controls over concerns they were contributing to weak rates of new construction in the rental sector, exacerbating the underlying causes of the disease whose symptoms they were intended to treat.

Fixing housing crises is far easier said than done. If mounting costs and worsening shortages were simple to reverse sustainably, they would not be afflicting so many different places with a wide variety of policy and economic environments.

But to stand any chance of lasting success, policymakers must ensure they go beyond shallow and often counter-productive regulations or selective protections for those lucky enough to already be renting, and wrestle instead with the more challenging reforms that could put downward pressure on rents and prices for all and for good.

john.burn-murdoch@ft.com, @jburnmurdoch

item.title: The coming futures market in AI compute
item.author: Marc Rubinstein
item.description: Big swings in the price of chip rentals are spurring the creation of a trading opportunity
item.content:encoded:
Big swings in the price of chip rentals are spurring the creation of a trading opportunity

Marc Rubinstein

The writer is a former hedge fund manager and author of the Net Interest newsletter

You can trade all sorts on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange: soyabeans, precious metals, lean hogs, crude oil, interest rates — all the staples that underpin the world’s economy. Now, CME Group plans to introduce a new commodity to its roster: compute, which it dubs “the new currency for the AI economy”.

“Just as oil fuelled the 20th-century economy and evolved from spot trading into a global derivatives market, our futures contracts will now turn compute into a standardised, tradeable commodity,” said Pete Keavey, the CME executive responsible, when the product was announced in August. Others on Wall Street are equally bullish. “A new asset class will be buying futures of compute,” said BlackRock chief executive Larry Fink in May.

For an exchange, it makes sense to tack on new products, and compute is a potentially large one. Boston Consulting Group estimates that the market for AI compute will climb from $360bn in 2025 to roughly $2.3tn in 2030. If the CME can capture even a fraction of those flows, it will add a lucrative revenue stream.

But just because a market is large doesn’t make it ripe for trading. Research on the origins of futures markets finds that between two-thirds and three-quarters of new contracts fail to attract and sustain a profitable level of trading volume. For compute derivatives to flourish the way oil derivatives have, they must satisfy a number of conditions.

First, underlying prices need to be volatile enough to make hedging worthwhile. Speculators may supply liquidity to a futures market, but it is commercial hedgers that give them their economic purpose. On this test, the case for compute is fairly strong. Long lead times bringing new capacity on stream can make pricing quite volatile.

Oracle’s Project Jupiter data centre build illustrates the point. The facility is due to come online in 2028 but has faced setbacks, ​including delays to a planned natural-gas pipeline and legal challenges over water and air-quality permits. More generally, when chip bottlenecks were tightest at the beginning of 2024, hourly rental rates for one of Nvidia’s H100 chips spiked as high as $8, before falling below $2 in late 2025. That kind of variance is something participants may want to hedge.

Second, participants need to agree on a standardised contract. When oil futures listed in 1983, they were designed to reference West Texas Intermediate, with Cushing, Oklahoma chosen as the physical delivery point. Although WTI accounts for only a small percentage of global crude output, it serves as a pricing benchmark for the rest of the market. In contrast, pioneers of bandwidth trading in 1999 struggled to converge on a standard. Reliability, quality and bandwidth services varied too widely and attempts to fashion a market collapsed with its champion, Enron.

Working with index provider Silicon Data, CME Group has chosen Nvidia’s H100 and B200 chips as the reference for its contracts. According to Silicon Data, capacity on a B200 can be rented for $5.86 per hour; $2.77 on the older H100. CME plans to list contracts that reflect the future value of these rental rates, going out 36 months.

But even a GPU-hour is not fully standardised. Performance varies with cluster configuration, networking, software and location. Rapid obsolescence fragments the market further: an H100-hour is not interchangeable with a B200-hour, which is why CME needs separate contracts for each. Nor is there consensus over how to measure even those rental rates. Another index provider, Ornn, has its own benchmark, and the two do not always align. Until a consensus forms, a derivatives market may be slow to build.

Finally, a vibrant derivatives market requires a diverse group of buyers and sellers. Onion futures were explicitly banned in 1958 in the US after two traders cornered the market. Compute is unlikely to be cornered in quite the same way, but it is already highly concentrated. Nvidia dominates chip supply, hyperscalers control much of the available capacity and a handful of AI laboratories account for much of the demand.

CME Group’s compute futures will attract plenty of attention when they list. The price of compute increasingly bears on the economics of AI, the value of its infrastructure and the vast investment boom surrounding it. This gives investors good reason to want a benchmark for it. Bears may recall the ABX subprime index, which illuminated a previously opaque corner of mortgage finance — and became a focal point for the unwind that followed. Whether it validates the boom or punctures it, compute futures may ultimately matter more as a signal than as a market.

item.title: Lex. The ever-shrinking case for expanding Heathrow
item.description: Need for giant airport hubs is being challenged by rise of long-range narrow-body planes that go to places their bigger predecessors couldn’t
item.content:encoded:
Need for giant airport hubs is being challenged by rise of long-range narrow-body planes that go to places their bigger predecessors couldn’t

To lift his spirits, Hugh Grant’s character in the film Love Actually pictures the joy of those reuniting in Heathrow’s arrivals hall. The UK airport itself is going through much glummer times: its long-discussed £33bn third runway is once again in doubt after Prime Minister Andy Burnham declined to back it last week.

Airports the world over are prone to getting bogged down in arguments over planning, pollution and profit. The debate over the privately funded expansion of the world’s second-best connected airport is all the more emotive because Heathrow is so closely associated with London’s status as a global financial centre. But at this point, whether it goes ahead or not matters more to the national psyche than the UK economy. 

Heathrow still has a case to make in favour of its giant infrastructure project. It would create tens of thousands of jobs. Full-service airlines — and not just British Airways, which operates about half of the airport’s slots — grumble at the cost but really want the additional capacity, particularly for hugely profitable North American flights. The third runway also has wide business support. Airports do add more than tourist dollars to their surroundings: the recovery in corporate travel since the pandemic shows that business cannot or does not want to survive by Zoom calls alone.

Yet the extra £2.6bn, or 0.05 per cent, that the runway would add to the UK’s annual GDP by 2056, according to government estimates, could be considered a rounding error in the grand scheme of forecasting. 

Besides, the need for giant hubs is being challenged by the rise of long-range narrow-body planes that go to places their bigger predecessors couldn’t. Airbus reckons its A321XLRs could open up more than 1,000 currently unserved routes worldwide. The ability to fly direct between, say, New York and Birmingham International — only two hours’ drive from the capital — would be a reasonable alternative for many passengers.

Even that won’t fully remove the bottlenecks at Heathrow, where about 40 additional airlines are at present seeking access. But political capital and planning capabilities are limited, while Heathrow’s relative position in the pecking order has deteriorated.

Love Actually is, by now, an oldie: it was released in 2003. That’s the same year a third runway at Heathrow, which then handled one in three UK passengers and now caters for about one in four, first won initial government backing. Of the two, the Hugh Grant classic has aged rather better.

jennifer.hughes@ft.com

item.title: The Big Read. Does the EU want Britain back?
item.author: Peter Foster and George Parker and Ben Hall
item.description: Burnham has reopened the Brexit debate. That doesn’t mean the UK will be welcomed back on its own terms
item.content:encoded:
Burnham has reopened the Brexit debate. That doesn’t mean the UK will be welcomed back on its own terms

Peter Foster and George Parker and Ben Hall

It was a balmy late September day in New York when Andy Burnham, Britain’s new prime minister, first gave a clue of his plan to reopen the UK’s Brexit debate, 10 years after the country’s vote to leave the EU.

In a private meeting on the margins of the UN General Assembly, Burnham told Ursula von der Leyen, European Commission president, the UK was ready to look again at closer relations with Europe, including possibly rejoining the bloc.

“I think public opinion in Britain is way ahead of the political elite at Westminster,” he said, according to people briefed on the talks. “I’m not sure how far I’m going to get, but I’m going to try to close that gap.”

No one had seen it coming. After years in which Britain’s Brexit negotiations with Brussels have been stuck in a rut, Burnham has dared to reopen the debate on Europe. But EU leaders are clear that any discussion about closer ties will be conducted on their terms, not the UK’s.

A week after the UN meeting, the prime minister received rapturous applause when he told his Labour Party conference in Liverpool he wanted a debate on Britain’s “long-term relationship” with the EU, including possible membership of a customs union and the single market. Or, as he put it later, he would look at going “all the way”.

“Welcome back,” responded French President Emmanuel Macron, breaking into English at a press conference alongside his Spanish counterpart Pedro Sánchez this week.

Sánchez said that “Spain would welcome Britain’s return with open arms”. EU diplomats expressed delight at the new strategic vision from Burnham, even if the final destination remains far from clear.

But Macron was quick to issue a reminder that Europe would still call the shots: “You cannot pick and choose among the Union’s freedoms, nor can you decide to take only what suits you while leaving the rest,” he said, indicating that the fundamental choice remained one of in or out. “So, come back.”

Still to be determined is whether British politics is really capable of accepting that improved access to the EU’s single market will mean opening up to more EU migration, paying money into EU coffers and living under laws made outside Westminster. But finally a British prime minister has got Brussels’ attention.

“It’s a breath of fresh air in a hitherto stagnant debate,” said one senior European Commission official. “But whether the UK can accept the trade-offs, well, that is the billion-euro question. But at least Burnham appears to have the balls to find out.”

Even if agreement can be reached at home, Burnham will also have to convince the EU that he is serious when the bloc is rethinking how to bring its trusted partners closer in an era of geopolitical upheaval.

Some member states would welcome the UK back as a liberal counterweight to France, but Paris itself remains wary of a country with Atlanticist, free-trading, low-regulation instincts.

Since the 2016 Brexit referendum ended Britain’s four-decade membership of the European club, a succession of both Conservative and Labour prime ministers has promised a cherry-picked relationship with Brussels but with very limited success.

“I cannot say to you truthfully that where we are is good enough,” Burnham told his conference, quietly accepting that Labour’s own attempt to finesse the Brexit choices after the election of Sir Keir Starmer in 2024 had hit the same roadblocks encountered by his Conservative predecessors. 

Starmer had promised his party would “tear down” the barriers to trade with Europe while sticking to the same “red lines” that had underpinned former prime minister Boris Johnson’s post-Brexit trade pact with Brussels: no return to the single market, the customs union or free movement of people.

“Starmer thought he could ‘make Brexit work’, but Burnham is saying that he fears it cannot,” says Anand Menon, director of the UK in a Changing Europe think-tank.

But Michel Barnier, the EU’s chief Brexit negotiator, warns that the new conversation will not be fundamentally different from the last — even if the geopolitical landscape of 2026 is very different from a decade ago.

“One thing is sure: the more the UK diverges, the harder it will be to rejoin,” Barnier says. “There will be no cherry-picking. The single market is not à la carte. The British government perfectly knows the rules and the conditions.”

The view from the EU

From the perspective of many in the EU, US President Donald Trump’s antagonism towards Europe, the Russian threat and a desire for like-minded liberal democracies to club together are reasons to bring Britain closer to the bloc.

“There is a strong strategic case for bringing Britain back into the European fold,” says Georg Riekeles, associate director at the European Policy Centre think-tank in Brussels and a former official in the EU’s Brexit negotiating team. 

He adds that a UK decision to drop its red lines “opens the possibility of a much more serious conversation about common interests” but warns that “appetite for closer integration and readiness to reopen membership negotiations are two different things”.

In particular, he thinks that EU governments want reassurance that any UK move would “survive a change of government if negotiations were to be opened”. With the Conservative Party and Reform UK deeply committed to Brexit, “that still seems rather far away”.

Berlin and other northern European capitals have always been open to rebuilding ties with Britain.

But the country that would need most persuading is France, which has long seen Britain as an economic and ideological competitor within the EU.

The UK was traditionally a proponent of widening the bloc to new members rather than Paris’s vision of deeper integration among a core group of countries. Other EU governments saw Britain’s refusal to join the euro as a sign of its detachment from the bloc’s political project; any suggestion of ditching the pound remains political dynamite in the UK.

Over the past decade, the EU has also adopted much of Macron’s thinking on “strategic autonomy” in terms of security, technology and trade, especially with China.

“Since Brexit, the bloc has changed and is more about building its own independent capacities,” says Sébastien Maillard of the Jacques Delors Institute think-tank.

“Member states, especially France in its Gaullist tradition, would test whether a rejoining Britain would fully support this objective or if it just wants to use the EU to boost its own GDP.”

Paris has been the EU government most anxious to prevent the British from selectively enjoying the benefits of membership from outside the bloc.

It has demanded London pay a high price for accessing any EU programmes, such as the EU’s €150bn so-called Safe loans defence scheme — to which London has failed to negotiate access.

Were Britain to rejoin the bloc, it would have to be ratified like any accession by three-fifths of French MPs and senators or in a referendum, a high bar to clear.

Then there is the possibility that far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who has vowed to block further EU enlargement, wins the French presidential election next year.

She plans to confront Brussels by slashing France’s contribution to the EU budget, pulling out of parts of the single market and reasserting the primacy of French over European law.

Conflict with one of its most important members might consume the EU’s bandwidth. It could also give Britain pause for thought about rejoining. 

Hard choices

Philip Rycroft, who served as the top civil servant at the Department for Exiting the EU from 2017 to 2019, argues that the referendum 10 years ago was the worst possible moment Britain could have picked to strike out on its own.

“It turned out that 2016 was spectacularly poor timing for a liberal open economy to launch itself on to the rough seas of the global trading order just at the time it was fracturing and the security situation was deteriorating,” he says.

A decade on, Burnham’s fledgling government has found itself coming up hard against those realities. China is exporting often heavily subsidised goods at a scale, cost and quality that poses an existential threat to some sectors of European manufacturing. In response, the EU is adopting a defensive “made in Europe” agenda that could itself hit Burnham’s own ambitions to “reindustrialise” the UK. 

The fear in London is that new EU rules requiring cars to be assembled in the bloc will stifle investment in an industry vital to the West Midlands and North East regions of the country.

This has helped crystallise the choices facing the UK — as have similar threats to the chemicals, nuclear and green hydrogen industries, according to Anton Spisak, a former UK Brexit negotiator now at the Centre for European Reform think-tank.

It also highlights problems with Starmer’s idea that accepting “dynamic alignment” with some EU rules and regulations would unlock privileged access to the EU single market.

Rycroft argues that the experience of the past decade shows that none of the options namechecked by Burnham at Liverpool this week — a customs union or rejoining the EU single market — are workable.

“Burnham has the credibility to open the debate. And he’s accepted the outcomes range from ‘where we are now’ to ‘rejoin’, but you quickly find the way stations between those points are not very comfortable,” he says.

“The UK is too big an economy to be bound into a reality where it takes trade deals and rules from Brussels with no say over how those deals and rules are put together.”

Changing calculations

Although the 56-year-old Burnham has said he would like Britain to rejoin the EU “in my lifetime”, the European cause has never been a big part of his political identity. Asked whether the prime minister was interested in the EU, one ministerial colleague says: “Not hugely.”

The minister adds that Burnham is worried about Brexit’s long-term economic impact, as well as the China import shock and the EU’s response to it.

Burnham returned to Westminster in June as MP for the staunchly Leave-voting working-class seat of Makerfield near Manchester and told voters in that by-election campaign that he did not want to rerun “divisive arguments about rejoining the EU”.

His calculation appears to have changed. His strategists believe that by flirting with “Rejoin”, Burnham can win back voters from the Green Party, which is responsible for the overwhelming majority of defections from former Labour supporters.

But some colleagues fear the UK prime minister risks playing into the hands of Reform, particularly in working-class seats. The rightwing party’s leader, Nigel Farage, said this week that by reigniting the Brexit debate, Burnham had “opened the door to Reform in the most extraordinary way”.

Another longtime Labour colleague of Burnham says the prime minister is “conflicted” on Europe. In 2019 as Mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham said he would vote Leave in a second Brexit referendum if Labour could secure a better exit deal.

“He understands why people voted Leave. He gets that white working-class alienation,” this person adds. “He won’t want to gift Reform a lifeline by embracing the evangelical crusade to rejoin.”

Stella Creasy, chair of the Labour Movement for Europe, adds that “Labour now has to win the case across the country and with its own membership for why and how to rebuild our relationship with the EU”.

On the face of it, polling is encouraging for pro-Europeans. Since 2021 public hostility to Brexit has grown; YouGov found last month that 59 per cent favoured rejoining the EU with 32 per cent against. However, surveys also suggest that popular support wanes when people are given more details.

YouGov found in June that only 35 per cent favoured Rejoin if Britain had to give up all of its old “opt-outs”, including being required to join the euro and the Schengen passport-free travel zone area.

“People think Brexit has failed, and feel cheated,” says Luke Tryl, of the More in Common think-tank. “They are happy to look at going back in but they are really worried about a return to ‘Brexit wars’ — people are exhausted — and that we end up with a crappy deal.” 

Burnham has developed a habit since becoming prime minister of opening up debates and then quietly retreating in the face of hostile fire, and any reversal of Brexit will require huge amounts of diplomatic acumen and political willpower both at home and in the EU.

A test of his seriousness and of Europe’s response may come next week, when he travels to Berlin for his first meeting with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

“The EU wants a strategic sense of direction,” says Mujtaba Rahman at Eurasia Group, a consultancy, who contrasts Burnham’s bold gambit with Starmer’s incrementalism. He adds that senior figures in Brussels are “all talking about” the British prime minister’s overtures. “There’s no plan, no detail but he has created the political space to have a conversation.”

Data visualisation by Keith Fray and Maxine Kelly

Letter in response:
Recalling the British input to the EU’s single market / From Catherine Stihler, Former MEP for Scotland (Scottish Labour), Carmel-by-the-Sea, CA, US

item.title: Protests from the City about bank tax ring hollow
item.author: Philip Augar
item.description: No one likes to pay more — people or corporations — but this is a time of national need
item.content:encoded:
No one likes to pay more — people or corporations — but this is a time of national need

Philip Augar

The writer is the author of several books on the City and Wall Street

Are banks too big to tax as well as too big to fail? That is the question arising from the industry’s vigorous lobbying of government, hoping to avoid an increase in bank taxes.

The sector’s case as it attempts to head off such a move in John Healey’s first Budget on October 28, is that it is already overtaxed relative to both the rest of the UK corporate sector and global competitors.
