The post-crisis banking windfall tax and UK balance sheet levy, although reduced, remain in place. The banking lobby reckons that the UK’s banks pay 47 per cent in total taxes compared to 28 per cent in the US and under 40 per cent in some EU competitors.

More taxes, this argument runs, would lead to a loss of business to other financial capitals. In what looks like a co-ordinated campaign by global banking chiefs, JPMorgan’s Jamie Dimon warns of “adverse consequences” from further tax increases. Dimon, whose bank is planning a new £3bn head office in Canary Wharf, met Prime Minister Andy Burnham on a recent visit to London. The threat is clear enough.

But it is the British banks that have the most skin in this game — and the most to say. Increased taxes, they protest, would reduce their capacity to fund small and medium-sized enterprises lending, be passed on to customers and impair their own contribution to domestic GDP. The City of London Corporation, the Square Mile’s local authority, urges the Chancellor to “do no harm” to the financial services industry. “That means,” it says bluntly, “no more sector-specific taxes.”

Whether to take this advice requires delicate judgment from Healey, who has a fiscal gap to fill and a growth plan to deliver. Would a populist tax grab really cut the banks’ capacity to lend? Would the cost of loans go up? Or are there other ways the banks could absorb such an increase?

Would more banking taxes really drive business away from London? Perhaps the banks are just playing the Stuart Gulliver card: Gulliver became HSBC chief executive having previously said his bank would consider moving its HQ out of London if retail banks in the UK were ringfenced. The banks were duly ringfenced but HSBC stayed.

The sector’s case is weakened by its extraordinary profitability since the interest rate cycle turned in 2022. Higher interest rates improve banks’ net interest margin (the difference between what they pay to depositors and charge borrowers). The benefits flow through to their UK ringfenced banks, businesses for which Barclays and NatWest reported high returns on equity of over 20 per cent last year.

Together with Lloyds, these three returned nearly £12bn to shareholders through dividends and share buybacks from their 2025 profits. Reducing capital returns to shareholders would give banks the capacity to absorb moderately increased taxation and sustain lending. Bank shares would probably give back some of their recent gains — the FTSE 350 Bank index is up 30 per cent year-on-year — which would increase their cost of capital. But the industry is distributing rather than raising capital at present, so this is a theoretical cost.

Context is important. The banks received a massive taxpayer bailout during the financial crisis of 2008 on the unarguable grounds that a banking failure would be devastating for the whole economy. Arguing that further bank taxation would jeopardise recovery from the crisis that they created looks like a classic “heads we win, tails you lose” scenario, especially since post-crisis policy interventions are currently costing the exchequer dear.

The BoE pays what is known as the bank rate to the commercial banks on their reserves. This rate is now higher than the yield it receives on the Asset Purchase Facility [APF] — gilts bought from financial institutions during Quantitative Easing. This “cost of carry” on the APF is covered by quarterly cash transfers from the Treasury to the BoE, forecast by the OBR to have been an astonishing £11bn in 2025-26 and to be £5bn-£6bn per annum over the next few years, eroding prior gains.

This is a direct cost to the current budget deficit and is in effect an unearned subsidy to banks and other financial institutions. It’s not surprising that the chancellor may be tempted to get some of this back either through direct bank taxes or by engineering a cut in the interest rate paid to banks on part of their reserves.

Burnham has said that the tax burden should fall on those with the broadest shoulders. With the banks enjoying boom conditions, mostly not of their own making, their shoulders are indeed broad. No one likes to pay more taxes, people or corporations. But this is a time of national need. As beneficiaries of taxpayers’ largesse and having already had their say, the banks should now do the gracious thing and back off. Over to the chancellor.

item.title: Letter: Banks are in danger of disenfranchising their older customers
item.description: From Robin Hodgson (Lord Hodgson of Astley Abbotts), Member of the House of Lords 2000-2025, London W8, UK
item.content:encoded:
From Robin Hodgson (Lord Hodgson of Astley Abbotts), Member of the House of Lords 2000-2025, London W8, UK

Claer Barrett’s piece “Are you the ‘digital PA’ for your parents” in last weekend’s FT Money supplement tells only half the story (September 26).

Yes, fast-moving technology has put older customers at a disadvantage. But, more significantly, banks do not really want older people as customers. The elderly do unhelpful messy things like dying, leaving banks with a long tail of business to clear up.

My father opened an account for me at a branch of what is now the NatWest Group in 1959. In the following 65 years my account has never been out of order. Now Coutts (to whom my account was transferred some years ago) has told me that it declines to renew any credit facilities.

It is not a question of lack of collateral. But I have to assume that the bank has made a decision not to lend to people aged over 80.

The bank is careful to say that it is not closing my account. So if I am prepared to leave a £5,000 credit balance permanently in place I can have a checking account. Why should this be to my advantage — in essence Coutts are banking with me rather than the other way round.

Currently, there are 3.3mn people aged over 80 and this number is expected to increase over the next few years. It will not only increase but get older so that, according to the Office for National Statistics, there will be 3mn aged over 85 by 2041.

Older people are increasingly marginalised in a youth-orientated society. Ensuring that they had access to adequate finance facilities would be a good place at which to begin to reverse this trend.

Robin Hodgson (Lord Hodgson of Astley Abbotts)
Member of the House of Lords 2000-2025, London W8, UK

item.title: Letter: How I ended up an extra in Bogdanovich’s ‘Saint Jack’
item.description: From Art Schankler, Belgrade, Serbia
item.content:encoded:
From Art Schankler, Belgrade, Serbia

I very much appreciated the travel piece on Paul Theroux (September 12). Some 50 years ago, I was headed for a teaching job in Singapore. A friend handed me The Great Railway Bazaar — and after reading his four-page description of the city-state, I seriously thought about cashing in my ticket.

But I persevered and found it pretty much as he described — from geckos on the wall to a watchful police state. I even ended up as an extra in the Peter Bogdanovich film of Theroux’s novel, Saint Jack — set in Singapore and banned there for decades.

I also came away with a love of train travel as the best way to get from one place to another — and a few Therouxesque experiences of my own over the years. A priest in Tanzania who asked me to exit our shared cabin so that he could “exorcise” a fellow passenger. A young Aussie on the way to Bangkok who suddenly declared in the middle of the night that she would die for punk rock. And they continue.

Art Schankler
Belgrade, Serbia

item.title: Treasuries are losing their moneyness
item.author: Brendan Greeley
item.description: For four decades, US government bonds have been both securities and money. They may no longer be that special
item.content:encoded:
For four decades, US government bonds have been both securities and money. They may no longer be that special

Brendan Greeley

The writer is the author of The Almighty Dollar: 500 Years of the World’s Most Powerful Money

In 1981 the economists Tom Sargent and Neil Wallace wrote a brief article for the Minneapolis Fed’s Quarterly Review, “Some Unpleasant Monetarist Arithmetic”. Unpleasant, that is, for monetarists. The ideas in the article have become the basis for considering one of the most important trade-offs in political economy: monetary dominance against fiscal dominance.

Under monetary dominance, the government is constrained as it spends money. It can’t sell more debt than the public demands. When the public stops demanding, interest on government bonds rises, and the government stops borrowing. This leaves the central bank a free hand to manage inflation by buying and selling government debt.

Under fiscal dominance, the government simply borrows what it wants, spends what it wants, and leaves the central bank with an unpleasant choice. It can buy bonds, bringing the government’s cost of interest down but risking inflation, as the Federal Reserve did during the second world war. Or the central bank can let the politicians fight it out with the market, risking collapse in the value of the bank’s own portfolio and . . . inflation.

It’s a useful model. But as Sargent and Wallace already hinted in their 1981 article, there’s a wormhole the government can slip through. If the demand for sovereign debt can’t be sated, then the government isn’t constrained. It can borrow and spend and borrow and spend. Its cost of debt remains low, and the central bank holds on to its own discretion to manage inflation.

Since about the time that article came out, the US has been slipping through exactly that wormhole. Washington was both fiscally dominant and not constrained by the cost of debt, a condition so solid and stable it seemed like the result of a physical law, and indeed as it continued it encouraged a new discussion. Were Treasuries debt or money? Did the Treasury sell its bonds, like a security? Or did it simply issue them, like currency?

Certainly Treasuries had what economists call moneyness. They were liquid like money. They were risk-free like money, a stylised fact that became an empirical truth. They were even referred to as money. Traders called them “cash,” historically a maddeningly flexible word that can accommodate anything in any century people think of as money. Commercial banks and the Fed haggled over whether Treasuries had the same secure status as America’s base money, the Fed’s own reserves.

It was difficult to find the limits of global demand for dollar-denominated assets with moneyness, which gave economists and politicians the luxury of treating Treasuries like they were both securities and money, a special phenomenon with its own properties.

The distinctions used to be clearer. In the 18th century, assemblies in the American colonies borrowed directly from their own colonists, paying their debts by issuing small-denomination, liquid bills — currency. Under the Constitution, however, this practice was forbidden. Alexander Hamilton followed by building a liquid market for federal debt, just like the one in the United Kingdom. The early American republic would sell its debt to investors for banknotes and silver, and not issue it to citizens as currency. The Hamiltonian system was built on the assumption that Washington’s debt is a bond, not money.

The idea of government debt as cash money lingered. During the Civil War, Confederate States began issuing their own currencies again, and the Union government began paying for things with greenbacks, paper slips tied to a vague promise that they would be bought back eventually with gold. Periodically during financial crises until the Great Depression, cities would pay for things with their own “hard-times money”, currencies that worked a lot like the old colonial bills.

Each time, however, the old Hamiltonian system reasserted itself: bonds were securities, sold to investors for the ready cash of banknotes and bank deposits. That appears to be happening again. As I write, yield on the US 10-year note is 5.25 per cent. It is not normal to have to add an as-I-write to the 10-year. Not normal, unless Treasuries are no longer special.

There are many explanations for the rise in yields on Treasuries. Yields are going up for government debt around the world. The US has no apparent plans to reduce deficits. A war has raised the price of gas, feeding into inflation. Debt for data centres is competing for cash. All of these are real, but they don’t completely explain the slope of the rise in Treasury yields right now.

One of the things that made Treasuries so money-like is that yields changed slowly, stabilising their value. It’s possible that after several decades, all of these problems together have suddenly eroded the money-like liquidity of US debt; the moneyness is getting squeezed out of Treasuries again.

Sargent and Wallace were always right. Under fiscal dominance, inflation is coming one way or the other, and the central bank has no good choices. America’s Treasuries are just bonds. The wormhole is closing.

item.title: The FT View. Our healthy obsession with fitness trackers
item.author: The editorial board
item.description: Wellness wearables are more than fashion accessories, and that is good for all of us
item.content:encoded:
Wellness wearables are more than fashion accessories, and that is good for all of us

The editorial board

In 2014, Marc Benioff told the World Economic Forum in Davos that his friend, the computer magnate Michael Dell, had called him, worried that data shared from the Salesforce chief executive’s Fitbit monitor showed he had not been working out.

Benioff explained he had skipped the gym because he was suffering from a cold. But his enthusiasm for wellbeing wearables was infectious. Many more people have equipped themselves with Fitbits, Apple Watches, Whoop bands and other trackers since then. 

Benioff and Dell have gone on to invest in Oura Health, maker of a fitness ring that promises in its initial public offering prospectus to “empower people to live healthier, longer”.

Oura this week delayed its flotation, which could have valued the Finnish-American company at about $16bn. The official reason was market uncertainty. But such is Oura users’ devotion to the $400 trackers that it is always possible executives and advisers synced their data that morning and decided to wait until their collective heart rates, sleep numbers and step counts heralded a more propitious outcome. 

The company, and others like it, will be back. Some early leaders in the market, such as Jawbone, have dropped out or been absorbed by rivals, as Fitbit was by Google. But the runners still in the race are part of an overall market for consumer wearables forecast to generate $1tn in revenue between 2026 and 2032.

This is good news, and not just for investors. Healthy life expectancy is the metric that really matters for most people, and if we are to live longer, healthier lives then anything that nudges us to pay greater attention to our wellbeing is worth backing. Our health is our wealth, as the saying goes.

Silicon Valley’s billionaires are not the only ones banking on this connected future. In the US, Oura subscriptions and devices are already part of an insurance package for patients who share their sleep data with doctors, helping them detect, monitor and treat conditions such as obstructive sleep apnoea.

In the UK, insurer Vitality offers points to active customers who share fitness data which can help them qualify for lower premiums. Diabetes sufferers increasingly benefit from wearable glucose monitors, linked to apps. A 2022 analysis in The Lancet Digital Health of multiple studies of fitness trackers found that wearing one increased activity, to the tune of 1,800 extra steps per day.

The list of potential unwanted side-effects is long. As Benioff pointed out in 2014, the shared vital signs of listed company executives could become tradeable insider information. If insurers were to link protection too strictly to fitness goals, the unfit might be unable to buy cover at all.  

The maxim “what gets measured gets managed” also has a flipside. Some important and hard-to-measure areas — mental rather than physical health, for instance — may be neglected, in an example of the McNamara fallacy, named after the bodycount-obsessed Vietnam-era US defence secretary Robert McNamara.

Fitness trackers can focus effort on restrictive targets, such as the quest to clock 10,000 steps daily, while some users’ cult-like dedication to hitting their goals (and bragging about it) could take a toll on their overall health, not to mention the patience of their friends.  

Still, the gap is narrowing between fitness bands as faddish fashion accessories and as the serious healthcare tools some developers and doctors hope they can become. There is much further to go, but, to adapt the Chinese proverb, a journey of 1,000 miles begins with 10,000 steps.

item.title: How to meet Burnham’s ambitions on social care
item.author: Camilla Cavendish
item.description: A radical change in culture and systems will be as important as funding
item.content:encoded:
A radical change in culture and systems will be as important as funding

Camilla Cavendish

The prime minister’s first big speech in the job this week felt more like an election manifesto from a campaigner than an address from the midterm leader of a cash-strapped country. I waited for him to challenge his party, perhaps on welfare. But there was no Clause IV moment to make the hall fall silent: Andy Burnham 2026 is not Tony Blair 1994. He seeks to unite the left with cosy old tunes: nationalisation, municipal socialism and spending, plus electoral reform to woo the Liberal Democrats in case he needs them for a future coalition.

If I sound cynical, then I’m afraid I am. Yet Burnham is right on some things: that vested interests have wielded too much power in Britain, and that short-termist politics haven’t served us well. And he is absolutely right to break the supposedly untouchable triple lock on pensions and link it to social care.

Social care sounds like a sideshow, but is increasingly central in countries with ageing populations. In England, up to a third of hospital beds at any one time are occupied by medically fit people because they can’t go home without support. Meanwhile, the elderly person loses fitness lying flat, ending up with worse mobility.

Burnham’s approach isn’t yet clear: it could either bankrupt the country or usher in a better old age. He seems to want to copy the Scottish model, which makes some services free. But if he can curb his statist instincts and learn from what works elsewhere, he might be able to fashion something genuinely innovative and direct money to staff rather than to complexity and compliance.

Previous attempts to “fix” social care have foundered for three reasons. First, many voters still think social care is free, just like healthcare. When Theresa May tried to level with the public about this during the 2017 general election, she lost the Tory majority. Second, many resist the idea of having to sell their home to pay for care — expecting other taxpayers to magically foot the bill — but no system is sustainable without some kind of call on the main asset. Finally, the Treasury turns down proposals to spend more without any commensurate improvement in outcomes.

It’s also been hard to describe to the public, and to the Treasury, what a better system could look like. Burnham has the communication skills and the understanding of what’s at stake to front up something new where, as he said, “everyone contributes and everyone is covered”. To me, that sounded more like the insurance-based systems of Germany and Japan, which are sustainable and highly popular, than “an NHS-style social care system”. I hope he will allow Louise Casey’s review, which reports next summer, to look at those models.

The current system is an inhumane, bureaucratic mess. People are reduced to units on a spreadsheet by local authority contracts. Agencies bid to provide home visits, sometimes for as little as 15 minutes. You open your door to a revolving cast of strangers, including the council social workers who must do a new assessment even for tiny changes to your “care package”. The workforce is valiant and demoralised, made to clock in even before saying “hello” by public commissioners who don’t trust independent providers.

Care workers, Burnham says, are “invisible to the political class” — and to the NHS, which looks down on them. One of my grimmest experiences during the pandemic was chairing a meeting with very vulnerable people who needed help, when some GPs and councils weren’t even answering the phone. One man in a wheelchair had been saved by two Polish care workers who simply decided to move in with him. As a temporary adviser to the Department of Health at that time, I saw care workers stepping up to manage wounds, give insulin and vaccinations, which they are not usually allowed to do. Yet they still get little recognition.

The conversation always starts with funding and gets stuck there. But what’s as important is a radical change in culture and systems. Good social care is about building relationships. In parts of the Netherlands, Japan and even the UK, much better care is achieved where frontline staff have autonomy to decide what individuals need, helping people maintain independence by “doing with” not “doing to”. A worker who can decide to take Mrs Jones to a lunch club because she’s lonely, or pop back to see Mrs Smith who was tearful this morning, is much more likely to stay in the job. This kind of focus on outcomes also involves staff having support networks outside the rigid boundaries of the state, with their clients’ neighbours, friends and relatives.

Sadly the NHS can’t compute autonomy: attempts to introduce the Dutch model in a few parts of England foundered against bureaucracies, which resisted jettisoning forms or letting teams manage themselves. The idea that the NHS should “take over” social care overlooks the ecosystem of charities, social enterprises and independent providers we need. When these work with councils it means an end to duplication and a big reduction in the amount of data requested, hence real savings. In Wigan, such an approach has improved patient satisfaction while reducing pressures across all public services.

Changing the triple lock on pensions won’t fund a new social care model, not least because the savings in any one year will change, depending on the relationship between earnings and inflation. But it will end the built-in ratchet effect, which is badly needed. And it was deft politics to suggest that money from pensioners will be returned to pensioners, just in a different way. At the very least, Burnham deserves credit for breaking the omertà on that.

camilla.cavendish@ft.com

item.title: The Ellison credit complex gets a bit more complex
item.author: Toby Nangle
item.description: If it wasn’t for the PSKY kid . . .
item.content:encoded:
If it wasn’t for the PSKY kid . . . 

Toby Nangle

We’ve joked before that Warner takeovers are the harbingers of financial apocalypse. So those of a superstitious disposition should mark next week — when the latest takeover is set to close — in their diaries, thanks to the willingness of bond investors to part with their cash.

But Paramount Skydance, the bond issuer and Warner Bros acquirer, is a big investment-grade company, isn’t it? And while $52bn is still a lot of corporate bonds for debt capital market teams to find homes for, big investment-grade companies seem like they sell large slews of bonds on a weekly basis.

S&P Global Ratings, 24th September:

We lowered our issuer credit rating on PSKY [Paramount Skydance] to ‘BB’ from ‘BB+’, as we expect leverage to increase when the acquisition closes shortly.

Wait, what? Double-B flat isn’t investment grade, it’s junk.

Luckily for investment-grade bond investors, Paramount Skydance didn’t let a little thing like being junk-rated get in the way of issuing a monster consignment of investment-grade rated bonds.

Somewhat unusually for a public debt transaction of this size, they threw in extra credit support in the form of a special first-lien charge. And as S&P Global Ratings explains in its ‘recovery rating’ report ($):

Depending on the recovery assessment for a given debt issue, the issue rating is derived by notching up, down, or not at all from the issuer credit rating on the issuer of the debt.

The rating analysts reckon that, in the event of default, noteholders who have the benefit of this first-lien charge will recover 90–100 cents in the dollar. At least this is what they reckon if their 2031 default scenario comes to pass.

The 2031 default scenario imagines a world in which the company runs into difficulty, decides it needs to restructure its debt, but is still churning out $10.2bn of ebitda, giving it an enterprise value of around $63bn (after accounting for all the costs of bankruptcy administration).

Bondholders with the first-lien charge are close to having first dibs on this imagined $63bn enterprise value, and these dibs push the bond ratings up to BBB-, despite being issued by a BB-rated company. Nice.

Are there any other credit supports that help the company squeak over the IG rating line ($)? Our emphasis:

Our ratings on PSKY reflects [sic] the commitment by the Ellison family, the company’s controlling entity, to take all steps necessary for it to deleverage below 3.75x on a net-debt basis (per the company’s definition) by 2028 and to 3.0x by 2029.

Of course.

David Ellison is the CEO of Paramount Skydance. He is also the son of Larry Ellison. And Larry Ellison, according to Bloomberg’s Billionaires Index, is worth $187bn — largely based on the value of his holdings of Oracle Corp common stock. Having the owner of 40 per cent of the global AI hyperscaling heavyweight committed to taking all steps necessary to deleverage has got to be pretty reassuring to credit investors.

We checked in on how investors are pricing the global AI hyperscaler’s creditworthiness. We also threw the new Paramount Skydance bonds, and every other triple-B-rated US corporate bond in the ICE BofA corporate bond index into the chart.

Increasingly, it looks like two large issuers are being priced as having far higher risk credit premia than the rest. Both sit on the lowest rung of the investment-grade ladder, and both are Ellison family companies.

Moreover, as Chris Whittall of IFR noted today, the cost of insuring Paramount debt against default using credit default swaps has skyrocketed. And that Ellison family commitment doesn’t look like it has helped (h/t to Dec Mullarkey, who also flagged this correlation):

Partly, this could be unhappy holders of the new PSKY bonds seeking to lay off risk. An IFR article ($) reports that the new 10-year bonds fell close to five points shortly after issuance, suggesting that maybe not everyone was in it for the long haul.

But, given its long history, the cyan Paramount CDS line most likely references obligations issued specifically by the Paramount subsidiary of Paramount Skydance to whom the commitment has apparently been given. S&P rates unsecured debt from this subsidiary a lowly single-B plus.

Still, if the new PSKY debt doesn’t look like it has been absorbed that well, at least we won’t be muttering about indices being gamed and passive bot-run funds getting stuffed. Because the weird timing of the bond deal all but guarantees that the victims have, so far, all been active human decision-makers.

As MainFT reported Wednesday, Paramount Skydance rushed to sell bonds to close the acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery “before a third-quarter deadline to avoid hefty penalty fees”. And this rush saw them sold on 30th September: not a great day for any wannabe corporate bond index constituent.

The cut-off for inclusion in Bloomberg indices — think the big US and Global Agg indices — is two business days prior to the last business day for the month, so Monday 28th September. For ICE BoA corporate bond indices, the cut-off for month-end rebalancing is three business days ahead of month-end, so Friday 25th September. And the iBoxx USD Liquid Investment Grade Maturity Indices require new issues to settle by the last day of the month. The new Paramount Skydance bonds settle on the 5th October.

So quasi-passive or actual index-replicating investors are unlikely to have piled in. And active managers needn’t have worried about any relative-to-benchmark performance cost of missing out on a deal that performed strongly, at least for the next month.

Further reading:
— Are Warner takeovers the harbingers of financial apocalypse? (FTAV)
— All you never wanted to know about corporate bond market issuance (FTAV)

item.title: Why does Anthropic’s IPO feel so weird?
item.author: Richard Waters
item.description: Compared to other blockbuster share sales, the build-up to the AI company’s stock market debut has felt discordant, even creepy
item.content:encoded:
Compared to other blockbuster share sales, the build-up to the AI company’s stock market debut has felt discordant, even creepy

Richard Waters

For fast-growing tech companies, initial public offerings are an important rite of passage. From Google’s declaration that it wanted to “make the world a better place” to SpaceX’s ambition to “extend the light of consciousness to the stars”, they are a moment to capture the world’s imagination. The best IPO narratives fuse an idealistic vision of the future with a sense of inevitability about why this company will win.

Selling shares to the public for the first time is also seen as a milestone on the path to corporate maturity. There is an expectation that products have been honed and business models perfected.

Perhaps all of this goes some way towards explaining why the looming IPO of AI company Anthropic has felt so . . . weird.

Details from its draft prospectus leaked out this week, suggesting the share sale is close. If it hits the $2tn valuation investors are expecting, it would set a record for a new public company.

Compared to other blockbuster tech IPOs, though, the build-up to Anthropic’s stock market debut has felt discordant, even creepy. What other company, after all, would think to warn shareholders that its main product might go off the rails and resort to blackmail?

The most obvious cause of the weirdness has been the predictions from former and current employees that AI might lead to human extinction. Far from trying to stamp out such talk, CEO Dario Amodei agreed that the technology could cause “catastrophic damage” and regulation was urgently needed.

It isn’t only the doomerism that has struck a jarring note. Like the rest of its industry, Anthropic has struggled to convince the public that its technology is actually going to make the world a better place. AI executives such as Amodei like to talk about the economic “abundance” it will create and the diseases it will cure, but such utopian musings are out of tune with the wariness many people feel.

Then there are the mishaps. The extinction warnings relate to a future version of AI that might escape human control. Even at this stage, though, Anthropic can’t seem to keep a grip on the technology it is already building. Echoing problems at rival OpenAI, it confessed recently to three cases in which its AI had escaped on to the internet and hacked into other companies’ systems.

Ultimately, none of this may matter much to investors, given the company’s astounding growth. Even here, though, things are not straightforward. There is a lively debate among AI investors over whether makers of so-called frontier AI models like Anthropic will be able to maintain any kind of performance advantage. If not, it is likely to struggle to maintain pricing power and be forced into an overhaul of its business model.

To Anthropic’s critics, much of this reflects the immaturity of a five-year-old research lab that has, almost overnight, been propelled to global prominence.

Countering the extinction warnings, tech figures like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, former White House AI tsar David Sacks and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg argue that there is nothing inherently dangerous about developing more advanced AI or releasing the technology to a mass market. It just takes the same kind of engineering experience, product design and quality control that characterise other technologies — disciplines that Anthropic is still learning as it mutates from ambitious start-up into mature product company.

Before it sprang to wider attention, Anthropic was the product of a culture that seems singular even by the standards of Silicon Valley. Its founders were heavily influenced by a branch of the effective altruism movement known as long-termism, which is fixated on the risks of human extinction from technologies like advanced AI. To critics, that has led to a speculative and self-indulgent doomerism that overstates the more prosaic work needed to control AI.

This is certainly how things are seen in Washington. After a lunch at the White House this week, a number of AI executives — including Anthropic’s CEO — signed an “accord on super intelligence” that promises the kind of things you would expect from normal, mature companies: “Robust internal controls”, special board-level committees and outside audits to contain the risks.

It’s hard, though, to see this erasing the weirdness from the Anthropic IPO. Investors still need to grapple with voluminous warnings that take up fully a third of the company’s draft prospectus (including the one about blackmail). There are apparently so many things that could go wrong that Anthropic’s lawyers would be forgiven for suggesting the company instead issue a single, blanket statement: This technology will do crazy stuff we can’t even imagine yet.

Nor has the official line in Washington, exemplified by President Donald Trump’s insouciance, done anything to end the division in Silicon Valley. Technologists without an obvious axe to grind, like Bill Gates, have been sounding increasingly alarmed about AI, which they warn is much too dangerous to be left in the hands of private companies without serious external controls.

As its big moment on Wall Street nears, Anthropic’s unintended IPO narrative is hard to dispel: the hypergrowth AI company which, according to its own employees, might just kill us all.

richard.waters@ft.com

item.title: Lex. Gold miner M&A is finally producing something that glitters
item.description: This time the dealmaking rush looks more disciplined
item.content:encoded:
This time the dealmaking rush looks more disciplined

Energised by rising gold prices, miners are panning for potential takeover targets. Australian producer Northern Star Resources last week rebuffed a $27bn cash-and-share offer from South African miner Gold Fields. Last year, gold miners struck 32 deals amounting to a combined $21bn, the highest value in 15 years, according to S&P Global.

Animal spirits in the mining sector are rarely good news for investors. Executives, haunted by fears that their chosen commodity may run scarce, have been willing to write overly large cheques to obtain their peers’ pipelines of projects. This time, though, the dealmaking rush looks more disciplined.

For starters, buyers are paying in stock, rather than cash. Gold Fields’ bid for Northern Star was roughly three-quarters denominated in shares. That insulates acquirers, to some extent, from the risk that the gold price falls. Excluding China, roughly a tenth of gold-mining deals over the past five years were entirely paid for in cash, according to S&P Capital IQ data, compared with almost a quarter of deals in the previous decade.

Mining acquisitions generally make more sense to investors when there’s a chance to cut costs as well as grab land. Gold Fields and Northern Star, for instance, have neighbouring assets in Western Australia. Predictive Discovery and Robex Resources, which united in April, plan to crunch together some of their projects in Guinea. Genesis Minerals and Vault Minerals expect their merger, announced in July, will mean they no longer need to build a new processing mill.

It helps that larger gold miners are not short of potential targets. After their M&A binge of the 2010s, major producers cut back on exploration, while junior miners kept investing in new discoveries, creating a new generation of mid-cap gold miners. The largest 10 gold producers — think Newmont, Barrick and Agnico Eagle — now account for just a quarter of the global gold mine supply, down from roughly 45 per cent at the turn of the century, on Morgan Stanley estimates.

It is true that discipline in the sector tends to be shortlived. As choice assets run scarce, the willingness to blow through budgets returns. But there is evidence that executives and companies can learn from past mistakes. Think of US shale oil which, in more recent commodity booms, has embraced capital discipline. For the producers of the yellow metal, this merger rush, too, has a chance of actually producing some gold.

gaia.freydefont@ft.com

item.title: My mortgage is a problem for the Fed, and for America
item.author: Robert Armstrong
item.description: Homeowners like me are staying put, the market is frozen and affordability is as ugly as it was in the housing bubble
item.content:encoded:
Homeowners like me are staying put, the market is frozen and affordability is as ugly as it was in the housing bubble

Robert Armstrong

I bought my house in Brooklyn in 2020, using a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage priced at 2.75 per cent. Since then, inflation and a strong economy have driven the average rate for a 30-year fix well above 7 per cent. So I enjoy a big lump of way-below-market financing while the value of my home has kept up with inflation or better, if online valuation tools are to be believed.

I feel very smug about this, but it’s bad for the country, and it’s not all good for me. Unless things change, I’m locked into the place until I die or turn 79, whichever comes first. Downsize when the kids leave? Move for a great job offer in another city? Nope. Both would leave me poorer.

Mortgages like mine are the reason why US home prices are very “sticky down.” When the economy is strong or money is cheap, houses get more expensive fast. When conditions reverse, rather than adjusting to the new reality, homeowners simply refuse to sell, reducing supply. The market, rather than adjusting, freezes. Existing home sales in the US are stuck at about 4mn units a year, the same meagre level as after the housing bubble burst in 2008. At the same time, average home prices have been stable in inflation-adjusted terms since mortgage rates started their climb in early 2022.

As a result, the Atlanta Fed’s home affordability measure, which compares median incomes to median home prices, is as ugly as it was at the height of the housing bubble in 2006. Young people think home ownership is increasingly out of reach, and they’re right. The median age of first-time home buyers has recently hit 40. Looking for an explanation for why consumer confidence surveys have remained weak — the Conference Board’s measure just hit a 12-year low — even as the economy has recovered strongly? Housing is the place to start. A part of the economy we are all acutely aware of is not working.

This is not just terrible for the young. It is a drag on the economy as a whole, both because of forgone activity associated with home sales and because of lost dynamism. People locked into their houses don’t switch to more productive jobs elsewhere (households’ expectations of moving are scraping along at all-time lows). 

High unfulfilled demand might seem like an opportunity for homebuilders, but housing starts have been falling since 2022, and homebuilder confidence is in the dumps. In recent years builders have used subsidised financing to entice buyers, but the latest leg up in rates makes this more expensive. Meanwhile builder input cost inflation leapt to about 8 per cent this spring, and stayed there.

On the labour side, the problem isn’t so much cost as availability. The August homebuilder survey from John Burns Research notes that labour shortages are leading to longer building cycles, a problem many builders attribute to immigration enforcement. “There are a lot of homebuilders that were already on thin ice on profitability,” before rates and costs began to rise again, says Rick Palacios of Burns. “When profit margins get into mid-single digits, that is a natural nudge for them to slow construction.”

Yet despite housing contributing almost nothing to real GDP growth this year and last, the economy continues to grow. In fact, it may be overheating, which is why the Fed just raised interest rates. But there’s a problem. Traditionally, the rate-sensitive housing sector has been a — or the — prime channel for the transmission of monetary policy. As the economist Edward Leamer put it two decades ago, “housing IS the business cycle”: it’s not the biggest sector of the economy, but it is the crucial swing factor. Not so today. Higher rates will only pressure a sector that is already on its knees.

The swing factor today is, instead, tech investment and the stock market wealth it has brought in its wake. On one estimate, AI investment contributed a full percentage point to real GDP growth in the second quarter, a figure that seems unlikely to fall this quarter. And this investment is not — for now — rate sensitive. The richest companies in the world have decided that AI competitiveness is an existential requirement. Additional interest expense pales compared to what they have already absorbed in higher silicon prices. What is the Fed to do? Admit the reduced potency of their primary policy tool, hold rates steady and risk inflation running higher? Or hit housing and other cyclical sectors even harder, creating an even more lopsided economy? Both horns of this dilemma are dangerously sharp.

The prevalence of the 30-year fixed-rate mortgage is, in large part, a policy choice. It is propped up by secondary-market support and guarantees from government-sponsored entities Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. So our housing dilemma is a reminder, if we needed one, that government intervention in financial markets always comes with trade-offs. But whatever its virtues and vices, the 30-year fix is going nowhere; America would sooner abolish fireworks on the Fourth of July.

The only long-term solution is making it cheaper, easier and faster to build homes. This year’s passage of the bipartisan Road to Housing Act added some incentives and cut red tape, but there is much more to do. As election season heats up, voters should be asking candidates what they plan to do to help aspiring homeowners. People like me are lucky enough already.

robert.armstrong@ft.com

item.title: Australia’s ‘postcard from the future’ of big batteries
item.author: Simon Mundy
item.description: Grid storage projects have been reducing power prices and emissions — but ‘cannibalising’ their own revenues in the process
item.content:encoded:
Grid storage projects have been reducing power prices and emissions — but ‘cannibalising’ their own revenues in the process

Simon Mundy

Welcome back.

Large-scale batteries are shaking up the world’s power sector, as I described in yesterday’s FT Big Read — enabling greater use of low-cost solar and wind energy, and eroding the need for fossil-fired generation to keep the lights on around the clock.

But the bigger this sector gets, the harder its developers must work to keep making money . . . 

The promise and peril of the big battery business model

In the second quarter of this year, something remarkable happened in Australia’s main power market.

The average wholesale spot price in the National Electricity Market (NEM) — which covers nine-tenths of the country’s population — was 47 per cent lower than a year before. A key driver: a fall of almost a third in expensive gas-fired generation, due in large part to an explosion in the country’s fleet of power-storage batteries.

Relative to population size, Australia now has the biggest national penetration of large-scale batteries, which have become the world’s fastest-growing power technology according to the International Energy Agency.

The Australian power price decline demonstrates how grid-scale batteries can help lower both electricity costs and carbon emissions by storing ultra-cheap wind and solar power during periods of abundant generation and discharging it later.

For the global power storage sector, Australia offers “a postcard from the future”, says Xavier Barbaro, chief executive of renewable energy company Neoen, which has developed several large battery projects in the country.

But it also offers a warning, he adds — of the risks of “cannibalisation”.

‘Down, down, down’

Battery storage projects have various ways of making money, including providing rapid frequency responses to stabilise the grid. But a grid only needs so much of those so-called ancillary services. So in markets with strong deployment such as Australia, the biggest source of revenue for battery projects tends to be arbitrage: buying power when the price is low (when solar power surges in the middle of the day, for example) and selling when it’s high (typically when household demand spikes in the evening).

As Australia’s battery storage fleet has boomed, it’s smoothed out much of the volatility in the power market. That’s good for consumers; less so for the battery operators themselves, who have been whittling away the spreads from which they gain their profits.

In essence, they’ve been too effective for their own good.

The installed battery storage fleet on the Australian NEM was more than twice as large in the second quarter as a year before, but the sector’s revenue was down 56 per cent.

“When batteries first come into a market, they get paid way too much money,” says Ed Porter, a director at Modo Energy, a research company focused on battery storage and renewable power. That’s because they’re competing head-on with expensive gas “peaker” plants to provide power during the evening demand peak. But once battery storage is deployed at scale, Porter adds, “batteries no longer compete with gas; they compete with batteries, and then the price goes down, down, down”.

Mind your margins

The cannibalisation threat is a serious one for companies and investors in the space — but one they say they’re finding ways to manage.

Barbaro says Neoen has been able to protect its margins in Australia through superior technology and management. “If you have the right bidding strategy, the right algorithms, the right mix of services, you can still be profitable while others are not so able to operate profitably,” he says.

Investors and developers are increasingly focused on safeguarding returns by locking in long-term contracts for battery storage services, says Jeh Vevaina, chief investment officer for energy at the asset manager Brookfield.

They’re now finding especially strong demand for this from utilities in the US dealing with a historic rise in power demand, notably from data centres.

Big tech “hyperscalers” themselves are eyeing direct contracts with battery projects as they look to sustain their power-hungry AI growth. Last month, Amazon signed a deal giving it control of a large new battery farm in Australia’s Victoria state, adding to other contracts with plants that combine renewable generation with battery storage.

The data centre boom will help drive moneymaking opportunities for the battery sector in the years ahead, says Nischal Agarwal, a partner at Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners, which has invested in storage projects from Scotland to South Australia. “The hyperscalers have a huge demand for power, and they will grab whatever source of power they can find,” he says.

For now, he adds, many major markets are in “the very early stages” of the battery rollout, with the available spread for battery projects still looking lucrative. These include Spain, where a huge rollout of solar power has meant that power prices are often negative — meaning storage operators can get paid to charge their batteries, and then get paid again to discharge them.

For big power companies, battery development is a “natural hedge” against low or negative electricity prices, says Pedro Vasconcelos, executive vice-president of renewable power and flexibility at Engie, which provides energy on six continents. But for the battery sector as a whole, he adds, the cannibalisation risk remains a material concern.

“The return expectation is bigger than you would have in wind and solar,” he says. “The thinking of investors is: when [the market] shifts, then we will start to cannibalise each other. So there’s a concern there on how fast you can get your money back.”

Smart reads

  • Lab-grown “cultivated food” — pitched as a humane, low-carbon alternative to animal flesh — is now hitting dog bowls and sushi counters.
  • Can high-end carmakers find a market for luxury electric vehicles?
  • US progressive senator Bernie Sanders has proposed a law that would partly nationalise big AI companies. “The result would be a new form of social and technological imperialism,” writes Evgeny Morozov.

item.title: The Burnham tell
item.author: Jennifer Williams
item.description: The prime minister’s conference speech was authentically Andy
item.content:encoded:
The prime minister’s conference speech was authentically Andy

Jennifer Williams

Good morning from Manchester.

I returned from Andy Burnham’s homecoming conference in Liverpool to find people here mulling the broader reputational impact on the city of the Premier League’s findings against Manchester City. 

The prime minister has been thinking about that too. It was a little surprising to see him highlight Abu Dhabi’s investment in Manchester at this particular moment after tending to sidestep it up to now in his narrative about the city’s growth model.

While Abu Dhabi’s investment here has undoubtedly transformed huge swaths of post-industrial Manchester, it was also contentious long before the Premier League’s conclusions, be it for the price of the homes developed in partnership with the council, the opaque nature of the public-private relationship or general antipathy towards the rights record of the United Arab Emirates.

So it hasn’t always felt as though Burnham particularly wanted to dwell on that aspect of the city’s economic turnaround — until, unexpectedly, the club’s finances hit headlines for the wrong reasons.  

Anyway, with growth models in mind, on to Tuesday’s extraordinary conference speech. 

Authentically Andy

I’ve written before about how responsive Burnham is: you can often spot when someone absorbs a criticism by how often they repeat it back to you.

“He’ll be down in London more than here and his attention will change from Ashton,” said one woman out doing her shopping in Ashton-in-Makerfield the day after the by-election was declared. She had voted Reform in the local elections a few weeks earlier and was yet to be convinced by Burnham.

He responded to such critiques, which were common online, in vox pops and while canvassing, very quickly.

First came the social media videos and posts in which he promised to make Makerfield the most important constituency in the country; then there was the “Makerfield Test”; and finally there was the linguistic tell: over and over again, including in his acceptance speech, he stressed that the by-election was no “stepping stone”.

By his conference speech, he had a new tell.

Manchester doesn’t quite answer enough questions to function as a national growth narrative, and it isn’t apparent what philosophy is likely to guide any painful fiscal trade-offs coming down the track at this month’s Budget.

Why do we know Burnham has clocked this? Because he’s already told us.

“I have to evolve it,” he told the New Statesman of “Manchesterism” in an interview published a few days before conference. “It was right to . . . localise it when I was the mayor of that area, but now I think you can broaden it out . . . it is about broadening it out into a theory of growth.”

Less than a week later, he told conference: “I have a theory of growth.”

He repeated, later in the speech, that he and other mayors had a “theory of growth”, after telling chief executives the same thing at Monday’s business day. 

According to his remarks this week, his theory starts with public control and devolution. 

Burnham believes that only strong institutions on the ground can understand what makes a place tick and therefore create the necessary conditions for growth and investment, whether that’s skills or housing or infrastructure; and that privatisation and deregulation have resulted in an extractive economy that gives the taxpayer and communities poor returns, leaving the country overexposed to the whims of bond markets.

I think he probably knows that this is only a partial answer, though. Repeating “I have a theory of growth” feels like the September version of May’s “this isn’t a stepping stone”, almost as though he is trying to convince himself as much as his audience.

One government figure agrees. “That is absolutely his tell,” they say, admitting that he still needs to fill in some “blanks” on the economy.

One such opportunity may arise at a Gordon Brown-organised summit on innovation in Manchester next Friday, at which Burnham is set to speak. Brown is keen to see the agenda promoted ahead of the Budget.

Watch this space. We’ve heard little from the prime minister so far on innovation (or indeed competition), but under Burnham there was nonetheless a significant agenda in Manchester on that front.

He worked closely with universities, including on a reciprocal research and development partnership between Manchester and Cambridge; Jim O’Neill, his erstwhile informal adviser, has a successful venture capital outfit busy investing in university spinouts across the north of England. 

Indeed the original “northern powerhouse” agenda that gave birth to the mayoralty, of which O’Neill was an architect, had R&D at its core. Immediately prior to Burnham’s arrival as mayor, George Osborne seemed to be here every five minutes opening a new advanced materials institute. 

Burnham himself published Greater Manchester’s new growth strategy last year — “a concrete plan to reindustrialise the birthplace of the Industrial Revolution” — outlining the city-region’s existing and emerging growth clusters.

Some of this was very much focused around the strengths of the Oxford Road research corridor, even if the vibes imply a new era of mills and factories.  

Nonetheless, he still always seemed more at home, to me, selling Atom Valley on the edge of Rochdale and Bury. This vast brownfield site is his vision for how Oxford Road’s growth can reach out into the former mill towns on the fringes of Manchester, translating the city’s abstract but fast-growing knowledge economy into tangible change in places much like Makerfield, where he instinctively wants to revive the sort of employment that anchored those communities when he was growing up. 

That is probably more what he feels in his political bones than the whizzy economy of the university ecosystem, even though he knows its value on an intellectual level. 

Tuesday’s speech was therefore authentically Andy: more the stuff of emotional instinct than of growth theory. It was partly why it jumped out of the TV screen and transfixed the conference hall.

It was also so well delivered that its strengths went a long way towards masking its weaknesses — even as the prime minister himself subconsciously signposted where they were.

Now try this

You can’t actually try this until they next go on tour, but the highlight of my conference was watching the Sugababes do a brief turn at a Labour Students event at Camp and Furnace, just over a year after I saw them at the Salt and Tar in Bootle (which was right up there with the most fun I’ve ever had at a gig).

Back with the original line-up, in my view they have more than stood the test of time, quietly packing out bigger and bigger stages at Glastonbury, and they are one bit of 1990s nostalgia I am more than happy to indulge in.

Top stories today

  • It’s not easy being green | Green leader Zack Polanski faces two critical tests that will define his grip on his party: the conference in Brighton, where an anti-Zionism motion risks turning off many moderate voters, and the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, where bookmakers say he is likely to lose to Labour’s candidate.
  • Alternative suppliers | The government is searching for a UK alternative to Palantir as part of the prime minister’s “Buy British” push.
  • ‘Saviour of steel’ | Ministers are resisting union and industry demands to take control of Liberty Steel Dalzell, which is part of Sanjeev Gupta’s faltering steel empire, amid concerns about the cost of recent nationalisations, according to two people close to the situation.

item.title: Donald Quintin: ‘We’re entering a different market now’
item.author: Robert Armstrong
item.description: The Lone Star Funds CEO on value investing, higher rates and the credit cycle
item.content:encoded:
The Lone Star Funds CEO on value investing, higher rates and the credit cycle

Robert Armstrong

Good morning. The S&P 500 has been all but unchanged for four months. Look under the hood, and you will find that earnings expectations for the coming year have risen 7 or 8 per cent over that period — but that this has been neatly offset by the price/earnings ratio index falling from 22 to 20. This is exactly what one would expect to happen in an environment where a combination of real economic growth and inflation are driving interest rates up: future earnings increasing while the valuation of those earnings falls as the discount rate rises. Once in a while, markets make sense. If you spot anything else making sense, email us: unhedged@ft.com.

Friday interview: Donald Quintin

Donald Quintin joined Lone Star Funds in 2010 and became its CEO in 2024. Previously, he worked at Merrill Lynch and Salomon Brothers. Lone Star, founded in 1995, invests across private equity, credit, and real estate. Headquartered in London, the group has offices around the globe, from Dallas to Tokyo. It had about $36bn in assets under management as of the end of 2025, according to regulatory filings.

Unhedged: How do Lone Star’s three strategies — buyout, commercial real estate and credit — fit together?

Donald Quintin: The fund started in commercial real estate during the savings and loan crisis, and pivoted through time to respond to the Japan banking crisis, then moved to Europe. As investment opportunities expanded it made sense to break the fund into commercial real estate and an opportunistic strategy, which we did during the early stages of the financial crisis. Subsequently, we took the opportunity strategy and split it between credit and traditional buyouts. But across all those strategies we remain dedicated to value investing.

Unhedged: What do you mean by value?

Quintin: We focus on transactions where there is a preponderance of asset backing or some sort of reliable cash flow. So, being disciplined on entry price and looking at the companies where there are opportunities to make changes — where the return is predicated on what you can do to improve the business, rather than on market growth or multiple expansion.

We tend to focus on those situations where there could be, for example, a corporate carve-out, or you have a global corporation that is looking to shed a business. These are complex situations — they require a lot of work desegregating that business from the parent. Those situations require a lot of muscle memory, setting up new management teams, addressing technological shortfalls and really trying to define what the business should look like on a standalone basis.

Unhedged: Is it too crude to say that where a lot of buyout shops think about revenue growth, you think more about margin or return on capital?

Quintin: The broader market has historically focused on either revenue growth or multiple expansion. How we think about investing, that is really a small part of the value proposition. The real alpha is coming from either improving the underlying margins of the business, or focusing on the cash flow.

Unhedged: The last time we spoke you talked about how you made your bones picking through the wreckage of the great financial crisis — loans in distress, CDOs on the rocks. What did that teach you?

Quintin: Having gone through the financial crisis gives you an appreciation for things like excess leverage, and focusing on how things can go wrong . . . I started my career at Salomon Brothers in fixed income, in the mortgage division as a trader. I moved to Merrill Lynch just at the onset of the financial crisis and worked closely with management there — John Thain, Greg Fleming — culminating in the sale to Bank of America. That was a huge learning opportunity, with many sleepless nights and difficult situations during the day. 

Unhedged: We’ve seen lower returns and longer hold times in the buyout industry. Are industry returns permanently lower now?

Quintin: I think what’s happening is a separation in the market, which will force a return to what private equity was in the beginning, in the nineties — where the quality of the business, the quality of the management and a realistic view as to what one can do to improve that business are really important. A respect for how you’re going to exit that business before you ever buy it. When money is cheap, rates are low and multiples are expanding, that kind of stockpicking attitude isn’t as relevant because a rising tide raises all boats. Now we have high interest rates relative to recent history, and those rates are likely going to be higher for longer. That puts pressure on the assumption that growth is what’s going to drive your returns . . . We’re entering a different market now.

Unhedged: 2021 was a euphoric peak in private equity. That’s five years ago now — time for that vintage of buyout to grow up and move out. Are they going to struggle to do so? And does that create opportunities for Lone Star — helping with companies’ balance sheets or on the equity side? Are you licking your chops? 

Quintin: I think we are. It will create opportunities. Broadly, I agree with your timeframe, 2021, that period had really kind of peak multiples. And you had post-pandemic inflated Ebitdas, you had a significant amount of cheap debt available that wasn’t hedged at the operating company level from floating rate to fixed rate. Because nobody was anticipating that rates would go up — they’d only seen them stable to down. Those situations are now manifesting themselves into credit opportunities. You have good businesses that are under capital structure pressure . . . with companies where the purchase prices were elevated, the challenge is really if those positions haven’t been marked low enough. I’m struck by the fact that we’re in a time now where you have a huge amount of debt capital available through private credit and through the bank market. You have a healthy banking system, generally. And there’s a lot of dry powder. So you have the tools for transactions, right? You are starting to see asset-by-asset transactions happening, but you’re not seeing portfolio sales, and a lot of it is because those companies didn’t grow into the elevated prices they were acquired at, they didn’t hit their growth projections.

Unhedged: So if they mark to market, it crystallises a bad return. 

Quintin: You could make that argument. If they’re willing buyers, and transactions don’t happen, it’s often because the expectations are not being met by the seller. 

Unhedged: What about retail distribution of private equity investment? Lone Star hasn’t done it, but what do you think? Where is it appropriate? Is there an opportunity here? 

Quintin: It’s not something we anticipate doing in the future. Raising money in the retail space requires a significant apparatus. And I think where you’re seeing a prevalence of that is in those institutions that have become quite large and they have many different channels for fundraising. It’s not something that we have spent time thinking about. 

Unhedged: What’s the best deal you ever did? 

Quintin: I feel quite proud of the Novo Banco transaction, which was the acquisition of the good bank from Portuguese central bank Fundo, the rescue vehicle. At the time, there were those calling for the liquidation of the bank, and the Portuguese state had difficulties selling the bank. It was a very complicated transaction. It required a significant amount of work on the balance sheet, the structure and the needs of the state. We presented them with a very novel proposal that enabled the state to sell the bank, and we bought a 75 per cent stake. What I’m really proud about is that we really refocused the bank, we improved the governance, we introduced technology, we expanded its lending footprint in Portugal. When you are buying a bank, particularly post-financial crisis, you have a lot of stakeholders, whether it’s the ECB, the Central Bank of Portugal, the Portuguese government. And an incredibly important stakeholder in the citizenry of Portugal. We successfully exited the bank, selling it to BPCE, a French bank. And I think it was a great success story for Portugal.

Unhedged: Lately there has not been a lot of distress in the credit world. So what’s keeping you busy in the credit business? 

Quintin: Credit is something that we do on an opportunistic basis, and it hasn’t really been a big focus of ours given where we are in the cycle. That being said, there are opportunities coming up because some of it is a situation you described before — the high prices paid and the excess debt used in the 2019 to 2021 timeframe. I also think the elevated rates are creating issues . . . there are operating businesses that didn’t hedge their debt and where things were priced to perfection. Debt starts to impact cash flow. That’s something that we’re clearly seeing. Also, private credit has been a complement to the existing bank loan market and it complements private equity very well, but when you start to enter a credit cycle, if there’s an element of bad underwriting, you can’t escape that. And we’re starting to see instances of that crop up. But I still think it’s early days.

I do think that the market will start to separate between those that have experience handling stressed and distressed credit. Private credit that’s been assembled without proper workout teams, anticipating potential issues, will have to scramble to catch up, just to find the expertise. 

Unhedged: Where are we in the credit cycle?

Quintin: It’s early days, but we are starting to see a trend. I think the reported figures from folks like Fitch and others are starting to increase. I think it is different than the financial crisis . . . to this point the economy has continued to do well, and in the industrial manufacturing space order books are still holding up fine. But there has been an impact from the prolongation of a higher-rate environment. 

Unhedged: Turning to the real estate business, rates were nothing and now they’re 5 per cent. How does that change how you manage that business? 

Quintin: We’re obviously not immune to the higher-for-longer interest rates. But I think those also create opportunities for investors in that opportunistic space, as higher rates put pressure on individual situations. In the financial crisis, we had a concentration of large pools of assets that are under stress at the same time. Now you have more idiosyncratic situations, and those in and of themselves are creating opportunities for investors. You also have a different banking environment, and private credit. The positive side of private credit is that it’s very patient capital.

Unhedged: When asset values are high and rates are rising, everybody wants to know, is there going to be a big dislocation? I’m not going to ask you that, but I will ask: if there is a dislocation, where will the opportunities be?

Quintin: I think it’s about being very disciplined, pragmatic and able to move quickly and handle complex situations. You don’t want to be learning on the job in those types of markets. You want muscle memory to kick in. That’s where experience comes into play. It prevents you from making decisions that you will come to regret later.

A correction

In yesterday’s letter we incorrectly stated that the 10-year Treasury yield was 4.29 per cent, rather than 5.29. This was a careless error — and one committed by Rob, not Katie, despite Katie’s byline being at the top of the letter. Rob regrets both misleading readers and damaging Katie’s reputation.

One good read

A tough guy.
