item.title: Lex. IPO hopeful Zilch needs to prove it’s one of a kind
item.description: Listed peers of the UK fintech are ailing, so comparisons are likely to hinder rather than help in gauging a valuation
item.content:encoded:
Listed peers of the UK fintech are ailing, so comparisons are likely to hinder rather than help in gauging a valuation

Part of valuing any company when it goes public is working out which existing stocks it most closely resembles. Investors gauge valuation multiples for the so-called peer group, add a discount or maybe even a premium, and presto — an IPO share price emerges. For Zilch, a UK fintech preparing for a London listing, this simple-sounding process poses a grave problem.

Zilch’s main product is a cheaper alternative to credit cards, offering customers a competitive interest rate that is, in effect, subsidised by selling advertising. Five years ago it was valued in a fundraising at $2bn. Peers included Sweden’s Klarna, which had rocketed to a $46bn valuation. But the peer group has gone from help to extreme hindrance: Klarna has shed 90 per cent of its value since then.

Value Zilch next to its Swedish counterpart now and it would be worth, well, close to zilch. True, Klarna had its own idiosyncrasies. But it’s not like other comparisons are less awkward. Affirm, a buy-now-pay-later specialist, still trades above its IPO price but is down 42 per cent from where it closed the day it went public, and 9 per cent this year. Upstart, which focuses on personal loans, has fallen 92 per cent over five years and halved this year so far.

What about earlier generations of consumer finance companies that Zilch hopes to usurp? There’s Vanquis, a subprime credit card lender that has been restyling itself as a fintech, but has been around in various forms since the 1800s. No luck there either: its shares are down almost 40 per cent over the past 12 months, and 80 per cent over five years.

Zilch may argue it isn’t really like any of these. It aims to mix the low interest rates and convenience of companies such as Klarna with the stickier customer relationship of credit card lenders. Since its service can be used anywhere — unlike products that are offered by retail partners at the checkout — it should not be reliant on a handful of large merchant partners, while the quick turnover of its loan book makes it less exposed to interest rate moves.

Its finances do seem to be on the up, too. Zilch reported a net loss of £10.5mn in the year to March 2025, but showed a route to profitability. Revenue nearly doubled, massively outpacing the mere 7 per cent growth in operating expenses, creating what financial analysts call “positive jaws”.

Zilch would be one of a kind in one important way: by listing in London. The City has not always been welcoming for tech groups, but scarcity can be a virtue. The listing of Raspberry Pi in 2024 with a valuation of just over £500mn would barely have registered in the US, but created a sizeable stir in the UK. Its shares have risen almost 150 per cent since.

By the same token, Zilch would be assured attention from exchange executives and politicians desperate to liven up the long-quiet IPO market. And other fintech IPO hopefuls such as Zopa are watching closely. If Zilch can secure a better reception than its ailing listed peers, it may not be a one-off for long.

nicholas.megaw@ft.com

item.title: No, AI is not similar to the Manhattan Project
item.author: Adam Tooze
item.description: What is singular and novel about the current threat is that it was born out of the private sector
item.content:encoded:
What is singular and novel about the current threat is that it was born out of the private sector

Adam Tooze

The writer is an FT contributing editor and writes the Chartbook newsletter

To describe the current AI race, the historical analogy of the moment is the nuclear arms race. Trump’s White House has directly tied its Genesis Mission for AI to the precedent of the Manhattan Project — the effort during the second world war to develop the original atomic bombs. This historical association is intended to sound urgent, dramatic and reassuring all at the same time. And that is also why it is unhelpful. As serious as it may sound to invoke Los Alamos, the analogy in fact presents a sanitised image of the drama we find ourselves in.

For those pushing the urgency and national importance of AI, it is obvious why the Manhattan Project is attractive. A spectacular scientific breakthrough owed to the greatest minds of their generation was put at the service of winning the war against fascism. The ethical dilemmas were real, but in figures such as Oppenheimer they can be portrayed as morally serious.

This is not the world that we are in.

For one, the early atomic bombs were comparatively modest explosive devices, suitable for destroying individual cities not entire civilisations, let alone humanity. The sort of apocalyptic risk fitfully debated in Silicon Valley right now did not appear in the nuclear arms race until the advent of the thermonuclear age in the 1950s and the development of the hydrogen bomb.

If you are looking for a narrative from that period, the urtext is Stanley Kubrick’s satire, Dr Strangelove. Tellingly, in that version of nuclear disaster it is rogue agents — not software but actual humans — who take it upon themselves to launch a first strike and thus provoke the Soviet doomsday machine. The analogy is not edifying. Kubrick’s point was to highlight the obvious insanity at the heart of deterrence doctrine. From the cigar-chomping cold war cowboy to the not-so-ex-Nazi ruminating lasciviously about the sex ratios in the atomic bunker, every manner of ideological fixation was mixed into an annihilatory logic of tit-for-tat.

But dark and funny as Dr Strangelove may be, our situation is even more delirious. We have the old framings of autocracy vs democracy and China vs US. We have dark rumours of the antichrist. But this time, the central actors in our drama are not scientists, soldiers or civil servants but businessmen with huge conflicts of interest. When the bosses of OpenAI and Anthropic took it upon themselves to warn of existential risks and to call for “pacing the frontier”, the immediate suspicion was that they were talking their own book. They were seeking to stir up a panic so as to provoke regulation and thus stabilise their precarious oligopoly. “Rocket-makers in clash with Wall Street over nuke safety worries” is not a headline even Kubrick would have dreamt up.

What separates us both from the Manhattan Project and from Dr Strangelove is political economy. Between 1940 and 1996, a Brookings study estimated that the US spent $5.5tn in 1990s dollars on the nuclear arms race. A substantial slice of that went to private contractors, who no doubt did their best to keep the foreign policy “blob” in Washington DC on high alert and the dollars rolling in. But in its overall architecture the Manhattan Project was the paradigm case of technocratic, government-led industrial policy. It inaugurated the era of publicly funded “big university” research, to which the Trump administration and the likes of Elon Musk are so deeply opposed.

What is singular and novel about the current AI threat is that, for all its profound geopolitical implications, it was born out of the private sector, out of the technologically and commercially driven logic of search engines and advertising algos. It is a product of Silicon Valley after the end of the cold war, when R&D budgets had substantially shifted from the public to the private sector. At first it could be funded in-house from the cash-rich tech balance sheets. But in the hyperscaling race for AGI, existential technological risk has been hooked to Wall Street and financialisation.

The world we are in is not that of ascetic bombmakers wrestling with their souls. It is both darker and more mundane. Today’s world-threatening technologies are fuelled by trillionaire greed, junk bonds and jerry-rigged financial engineering. In filmic terms, think Dr Strangelove mashed up with Gordon “Greed-is-Good” Gekko and a dash of The Big Short. If this is the way the world ends, it will be not with a bang or a whimper, but in a whirl of tech jargon, Californian lifestyles and financial engineering.

item.title: Trump’s short-sighted diesel gamble
item.author: Gillian Tett
item.description: Yes, Nixon’s export ban did briefly suppress domestic prices but it had a huge long-term cost
item.content:encoded:
Yes, Nixon’s export ban did briefly suppress domestic prices but it had a huge long-term cost

Gillian Tett

Cometh the hour, cometh the panic — and the performative politics. This autumn Chuck Grassley, the longest-serving Republican senator, has watched in dismay as his party’s polling numbers have wilted amid popular anger over inflation and the Iran war. 

So, with the midterm elections looming, he and other Republican leaders have been urging President Donald Trump to ban exports of US diesel, in a bid to stop record-high prices squeezing voters. 

“Why doesn’t Pres Trump put an embargo on diesel exports like presidents in the 70s put embargoes on ag[ricultural] products bc food prices were inflated,” Grassley wrote in a recent social media post, referring to President Richard Nixon’s 1973 embargo on soyabean exports. “High diesel prices ARE KILLING FARMERS INCOME.”

The prospect of a ban has sparked debate in the White House. Chris Wright, the energy secretary, lobbied against one, as did American energy executives. Trump himself said that he was “very seriously” considering embracing a ban, although one person close to the debate admitted to the FT earlier this week that “we don’t have a firm sense of what he’s going to do” because “this is all about Trump.” Welcome to how Washington works today.

Nonetheless, the presidential threats seem to have paid off. On Friday, they prompted — or bullied — G7 leaders into dipping into their reserves to lower prices.

Amid all this, however, there is a bitter historical irony at play. In the Trump administration, it seems almost natural for Republicans to embrace trade controls as nationalist economic tools in order to appease populist political forces.

But for 1980s Republican president Ronald Reagan — who men such as Grassley revere — such trade meddling was anathema. And if you dig into the history of that 1973 soyabean embargo, it was anything but a success.

Yes, Nixon’s export ban did briefly suppress domestic prices; hence why Trump might still be tempted to emulate it for diesel. But it also “raised questions about the US as a reliable supplier of staple commodities”, as Jonathan Coppess at the University of Illinois wrote in a 2019 paper.

The Japanese government, which relied on US soyabean imports, was so furious that in 1974, Coppess says, the Japan International Cooperation Agency began a large-scale investment in the development of the Cerrado region in Brazil for soyabean production.

That worked remarkably well. Indeed, by 2015 Brazil was exporting more soyabeans than America — and, somewhat remarkably, Brazilian sales last year were nearly twice those from the US.

More recently, the US has scored another own goal. Today China is the world’s biggest source of soyabean demand. However, Trump’s US-China trade war has hobbled American sales there, and Chinese purchasers buy from Latin America instead. When Trump met with Xi Jinping, his Chinese counterpart this month, soyabeans were notably excluded from the $30bn worth of tariff-cutting trade deals that were announced — much to American farmers’ fury.

“Trump has been very good for the Brazilian soybean business,” one Chinese importer joked to me last week; he now buys most beans from non-US sources. Or as Philip Verleger, an American energy economist, wrote in a recent Substack: “[In 1973] Richard Nixon sacrificed the US farmers’ future for a few months of lower consumer prices.” 

Would a diesel ban have repeated that? White House officials tell me not, because America is now so dominant in fossil fuels, and it is harder to switch diesel suppliers. They also insist that fuel supplies will soon move freely through the Strait of Hormuz. Maybe so.

Friday’s move from G7 leaders has relieved the pressure for now. But what is more notable is that during the recent meeting of the UN General Assembly in New York I heard non-American executives and government officials outlining plans to protect themselves from the fossil fuel squeeze by “diversifying”, ie embracing renewable energy.

That might create new vulnerabilities: renewable energy can be intermittent, and China dominates the green tech supply chain. But these risks look less daunting when set against the dangers of being a hostage to capricious US trade policy or wars in the Gulf.

As Verleger tells me: “What country is going to want to rely on the US for natural gas exports now, if America might suddenly cut these off?” To put it bluntly: one consequence of Trump’s Iran war is an acceleration of the green transition that the president loves to hate — and which will make others less exposed to the US.

The White House should be paying attention. Yes, a putative diesel ban might have scored short-term political points. But all this furore may also prompt US energy groups to curb production, thus boosting prices in the medium term. And insofar as this will make America seem (even more) unreliable to allies, there will be big long-term costs. Just look at that humble soyabean to see what happens when politics ignores the power of unintended consequences.

gillian.tett@ft.com

This article has been updated to reflect breaking news

item.title: Lex. Paramount picked a bad time to fund a $110bn leveraged buyout
item.description: David Ellison’s media company sold $52bn in debt and got an investment-grade credit rating — albeit the lowest available
item.content:encoded:
David Ellison’s media company sold $52bn in debt and got an investment-grade credit rating — albeit the lowest available

This may not be the absolute worst moment to fund a highly leveraged acquisition, but it’s certainly not the best. Treasury yields are hitting multi-decade highs; risk appetites are wavering. Paramount Skydance, which has a $110bn purchase of Warner Bros Discovery to finance, is forging ahead anyway. It has little choice.

David Ellison’s media company sold $52bn in debt on Wednesday. Paramount won an investment-grade credit rating — albeit the lowest one available — but money managers buying the bonds seem sceptical. Ellison ended up offering yields higher than comparable investment-grade bonds. The same was true of the riskier “junk” part of the offering, sold with a yield of 9 per cent.

It’s not hard to see why. Fixed income buyers are being asked to finance a media company that, for all its streaming ambitions, relies for cash flows on a legacy TV business in long-term decline. The combination has annual ebitda of roughly $12bn, before factoring in cost savings resulting from the deal, compared with net debt of roughly $80bn.

And while the projected cost savings are substantial at $6bn a year, Ellison can’t count on the company keeping them all for itself in what remains a very competitive industry. Netflix chief Ted Sarandos vowed on Wednesday to make his own streaming giant grow faster, suggesting the prospect of a new round of expensive “content wars”.

A downturn in Paramount’s prospects could get messy, quickly. Investment-grade funds would have to sell out of the company if its credit rating fell to junk. And if things get even worse, Paramount’s creditors include some tough negotiators. A big portion of the new debt is held by huge firms like Apollo, Pimco, and Man Group according to a person familiar with the situation.

Ellison can take some comfort from the fact that those funds did not wring out particularly tight covenants, potentially as a trade-off for relatively generous yields. The tighter the covenants, the more protection investors have against borrowers getting creative in order to skirt bankruptcy.

Ideally such protections won’t be put to the test. Paramount certainly isn’t starting from a position of strength, though. Ellison has already come through a series of battles, first with WBD’s board and then with US states that tried to block his deal. A balance sheet laden with debt that is both copious and costly pretty much ensures struggle will be the Paramount chief’s new normal.

sujeet.indap@ft.com

item.title: The Big Read. When luxury cars turn electric
item.author: Kana Inagaki and Christian Davies
item.description: Ferrari is selling its priciest models to tech millionaires. But it’s a hard playbook to follow
item.content:encoded:
Ferrari is selling its priciest models to tech millionaires. But it’s a hard playbook to follow

Kana Inagaki and Christian Davies

Two months after motorsport grandee Luca di Montezemolo deemed Ferrari’s new all-electric Luce model unworthy of the marque’s prancing horse emblem, the group’s chief executive had the last laugh.

“I would not change anything in the launch of the Luce,” Benedetto Vigna told reporters on an earnings call. “We are very pleased about what has been done.”

When the vehicle was unveiled in May, social media exploded with criticism of its design, the work of former Apple designer Sir Jony Ive rather than renowned automotive studios such as Pininfarina or Bertone. The group’s Milan-traded shares fell 8 per cent as di Montezemolo, a former Ferrari chair, witheringly described the Luce as “a car that at least the Chinese won’t copy”.

But by July, Ferrari had already achieved this year’s internal sales target of just under 500 units, according to people with knowledge of the matter, despite the Luce’s €550,000 base price tag. Todd Blue, a California luxury car dealer, adds that demand for the Luce has been “tremendous”, with his salespeople selling out their allocation.

The new car did not just deviate from Ferrari’s historic design ethos. It was part of a strategy to win over completely new clients that allowed the Italian group to tap into a new generation of young and wealthy buyers, particularly in China and in technology hubs such as Silicon Valley.

“For me, this car has an important meaning for Ferrari but also for the European world and for the western world,” Vigna says of the Luce. “Why not believe that we can do it?” He has previously remarked that the surge in wealth creation due to AI is “a good opportunity for us”.

But it is not a playbook that other luxury manufacturers can easily follow, as they contend with the Trump administration’s hostile stance towards EVs and China’s slowing economy.

Many renowned marques are finding it difficult to decide whether to focus on electric or combustion engines, pushing up their costs and complicating longer-term strategic choices. It is a problem for a sector of the industry that is often at the forefront of advances in design and technology, and in which European manufacturers still enjoy almost total dominance, even as cheap Chinese-made cars flood into the mass market.

“There is a small market for luxury EVs, but it’s a very different market from your usual luxury or supercar buyer,” says Scott Sherwood, an independent analyst of luxury car brands. “And that’s where Ferrari got it right with the Luce. They targeted a completely new group of consumers.” 

In Ferrari’s wake, Bentley has rolled out its first all-electric model and Jaguar will do so next week. Porsche is also going ahead with an electric version of its 718 two-seat sports car.

All are hoping that a foray into EVs could open up a new and younger client base with different tastes for design and personalisation. They, like Ferrari, intend to target the beneficiaries of the tech wealth being generated across the US.

But it is a difficult balancing act. Manufacturers need to navigate their costly transition to EVs while ensuring that combustion-engine loyalists are not left alienated and that profits from higher-margin petrol cars are not eroded.

Sherwood argues that the difficulty in replicating Ferrari’s success comes down to scale and brand strength. “Ferrari doesn’t need to sell 10,000 units to be successful. They can sell 1,000 to 1,500 and declare victory,” he says.

“The problem for Porsche is that they’d need to sell 20,000 or 30,000.”


For decades, the US has been the most attractive market for luxury-car makers because of its deep pool of millionaires and the resilience of its economy.

In 2008, when most Americans had never even seen an electric car, Tesla targeted its two-seater Roadster electric sports car at a small cohort of rich tech entrepreneurs and environmentally conscious celebrities. Early owners included Google co-founder Sergey Brin and film star Leonardo DiCaprio.

That playbook is increasingly being revisited as demand in China, now the world’s largest car market, falters. Overcapacity in the country has led to a flood of exports, but ultra-high tariffs and a ban on Chinese software have kept them out of the US market.

The total US market for luxury vehicles and exotic cars is likely to expand to as much as $215bn by 2035 from $110bn at present, according to recent analysis by Boston Consulting Group and duPont Registry.

Demand is expected to be weaker for higher-end luxury EVs due to the reversals in US climate policy under Trump and concerns about the resale value of battery-powered models.

Separate data from Cox Automotive shows that electric cars accounted for roughly 6 per cent of the overall new vehicle market in the US in the third quarter, down from a peak of 10.6 per cent a year earlier.

BCG and duPont Registry expect the internal combustion engine will continue to dominate sales in the “ultra-luxury” and “hyper-luxury” segments, which include vehicles priced at more than $170,000.

But Felix Stellmaszek, BCG’s managing director, says there is still a market for luxury electric cars, in part because of their exclusivity. “Everyone has his or her car collection in the garage, but if you have something that is electrified, it’s actually quite different from the rest of the buyers and collectors that you meet at the car shows.”

He adds that “range anxiety and all the factors preventing broader adoption of electric vehicles across North America in particular don’t really matter much” in the luxury sector, since high-end cars tend to be bought for personal enjoyment or scarcity value rather than daily use.

Blue, the Californian dealer, adds that what really matters to his customers is “a visceral [driving] experience in a world where we all live on these screens and on our phones”.

Jaguar Land Rover, which like Ferrari was excoriated on social media after a rebranding exercise, is targeting the US as a core market for the $130,000 Jaguar Type 01 electric vehicle due to launch in October. Range Rover’s first electric SUV appeared in September at a starting price of $140,450.

“The amount of wealth transfer that’s going to happen [in the US] over the next five to ten years is . . . by far the biggest [in the world],” says PB Balaji, the UK-based carmaker’s chief executive who has been tasked with reinventing Jaguar as an all-electric brand. “Therefore, we are giving it everything.” 

Vigna has expressed confidence that the Luce will be profitable from the start, largely thanks to its high sticker price. But Ferrari is not setting high ambitions for EVs overall. It aims to make 20 per cent of its models fully electric by 2030, half of its original target, while its industry-beating operating margin of 30 per cent will be protected by continuing sales of petrol models and limited edition models such as the €3.6mn F80 supercar. 

Bentley, the UK-based carmaker owned by Volkswagen, is also hoping to take advantage of vigorous US economic growth, and broaden its appeal to younger drivers, with its Torcal electric SUV.

“The strength of the US economy is unbeaten in the world,” says chief executive Frank-Steffen Walliser. “The West Coast is a very natural area and we expect that we could definitely grow there.”

But it has taken a different approach to pricing; the Torcal will start at a comparatively modest £173,300, less than half the price of the Luce. At that price point, analysts say Bentley will need to sell large numbers to generate profits, and warn that the Torcal targets the same buyers as the Bentayga, another Bentley SUV that is available in petrol or plug-in hybrid versions. The company argues there will be no cannibalisation, given the Bentayga’s slightly higher pricing.

Walliser has described the Torcal’s debut as “one of the most important product launches in our 107-year history”. It comes as Bentley’s operating profit margin in the first half fell to 4.5 per cent while vehicle deliveries declined 13 per cent to 4,211 units, partly due to its ageing product line-up and the downturn in China.

For all the recent activity in the sector, the car industry remains deeply divided on how much actual demand there is for high-end battery-powered sports cars. 

Product launches so far have tended to be saloons, SUVs or so-called grand tourers — cars designed for luxurious long-distance travel. Jaguar’s Type 01 and the Rolls-Royce Spectre both belong in this category.

Beyond a few models from Lotus and Rimac, a Croatian start-up often compared to Tesla, an all-electric hypercar has proved challenging because of the adverse effect of the battery weight on performance and handling, and the perceived lack of connection between car and driver.

Porsche is busy recalibrating what some regarded as an overly bullish EV strategy. While it enjoyed initial success with the Taycan saloon and could start selling electric 718 models next year, it also plans a new combustion-engine version of its best-selling Macan SUV in 2028.

Michael Leiters, the former boss of British supercar maker McLaren who took over as Porsche chief executive in January, says he still has reservations about the readiness of EV technology for high-performance sports cars.

“There won’t be a 911 electric,” he says, referring to Porsche’s legendary rear-engined model. “The advantages of the technology depend a lot on the customer profile and the use of a car.” 

Others have pivoted to hybrid cars as an interim measure, and to offset the thin margins on pure electric models. McLaren is developing its first hybrid SUV, even though it merged with EV start-up Forseven Holding last year.

Michael Straughan, McLaren’s chief operating officer, says the luxury sector’s transition to electric propulsion is “inevitable” over the long term but cautions that for now, its customers were not “crying out for EVs”. 

“The trick is timing it so that the product development start matches the time when EVs are accepted,” says Straughan, who was previously the chief operating officer at Aston Martin. “For a small maker, if you select the wrong technology, it has a dramatic effect on the business.”

Italian rival Lamborghini, another Volkswagen brand, has abandoned plans to launch its first fully electric car by 2030 and will instead roll out two plug-in hybrid models, while Lotus, the Chinese-owned marque known for lightweight and agile sports cars, has also pivoted from an EV-focused strategy to one more focused on hybrids.

“We have very good technology and architecture for both battery EVs and plug-in hybrids. So we are going to do both,” says chief financial officer Wang Daxue. He adds that the US will be “a very important market” for its upcoming Type 135 hybrid supercar, though the vehicle’s Chinese technology content means Lotus will need regulatory approval to sell it in America.

Consumers are warming to EVs at different speeds in different markets, say industry executives. The rise in fuel prices amid war in the Middle East has sparked a surge in sales in Europe, contrasting with the EV slump in the US.

“There was a pendulum that was going back to the internal combustion engine and now it’s coming back because of high petrol prices and subsidies by governments [in Europe],” says Leiters.

“You have to be very careful . . . so we have all the tools we need to react to the markets.” 

In addition to correctly predicting the pace of the electric transition, luxury car brands need to ensure that they do not leave their existing clients behind in the pursuit of new technology and design.

“We as a company have the responsibility to move forward the flag of innovation [while] respecting the values of the past,” says Ferrari’s Vigna.

Two months after unveiling the Luce, the company launched the 12Cilindri Manuale. With its massive V12 petrol engine and a transmission system that mimics the feel of a mechanical gearbox, the limited edition model is red meat for traditionalists. “A manual transmission is the ultimate emblem of the ability to reconnect to actually living,” says Blue, the car dealer.

Even the Luce’s design nods to tradition. Its interior features physical dials and buttons, in addition to a modern touchscreen panel. A vibrating sound from its motors and components inspired by an electric guitar compensate for the lack of traditional engine roar.

For the Torcal, Bentley’s engineers tried to create an emotional connection with a propulsion sound handcrafted by musicians and featuring a blend of percussion, crystal glass, birds and the tapping of leather.

“The consumer choice is very different in the acceptance of electric cars,” says Walliser, the Bentley chief executive, adding that this is why he and others will keep offering petrol and hybrid models as well as EVs.

Ed Kim, chief analyst at AutoPacific, an automotive market research group, does not expect combustion engines to leave the ultra-luxury segment in the foreseeable future.

“We should remember that there are still plenty of those traditionally minded old-money buyers left,” he says. “My hunch is that the ultra-luxury segments will be one of the last to let go of combustion.”

But while western carmakers deliberate over the pace of the electric transition and continue to develop models for petrol devotees, Chinese EV makers such as BYD, whose mass-market models are already making inroads in key European markets, are now setting their sights on the premium segment.

At the Goodwood Festival of Speed in July, BYD unveiled its new Denza Z electric supercar, which is capable of more than 320km/h and will have a starting price of £142,900 in the UK.

Asked why BYD was entering the premium segment, its top international executive Stella Li says: “It is natural, since we have the technology. Why not?

“Then, we need to make it super successful.”
