item.title: Lex. Europe should take Trump’s diesel ban seriously, if not literally
item.description: Even if the president backs down, his threat should prompt Europe to be more energy independent
item.content:encoded:
Even if the president backs down, his threat should prompt Europe to be more energy independent

President Donald Trump’s threat to stop exporting diesel is a terrible prospect for other countries that rely on the critical fuel. For Europeans, the stand-off is particularly tense, because Trump has delivered an ultimatum: dig deeper into your own reserves, or everyone will end up with less.

It is not surprising that the White House wants to turn the screws on European countries. Record diesel prices in the US are becoming a political flashpoint ahead of the midterm elections in November. The reason is brisk demand in the global market, which sets the US price too because exporters can choose where to sell.

Europe isn’t the only region where US diesel flows, but it is one that sits on quite sizeable stocks, at least based on the patchy data that’s available. In June the EU27 held 32mn tonnes of “emergency” road diesel for a rainy day, according to Eurostat data, as well as some commercial stocks.

All told, Europe’s diesel inventories are equivalent to between two and three months of demand, Lex calculates. The Trump administration has asked for it to release 120mn barrels over six months, Reuters reported, which looks equivalent to 40 per cent of the bloc’s stockpiles.

Before acceding to this demand, the question for Europe is how credible Trump’s threat really is. Blocking diesel exports would be disruptive to the US too, because it has finite room to store the surplus that would soon result.

Because of the quirks of the refining process, reducing diesel refining would mean cutting back on other kinds of essential fuel too — including gasoline. Besides, some US-based industrial consumers actually import their diesel, and would have to pay the higher global price.

Even without a full ban on exports, Trump may have other tricks up his sleeve that mean Europe can’t stand too firm regarding its stockpiles. A US cap on exports, say, or a tax, might cut the price of domestic diesel compared to that in the rest of the world without going as far as a full ban, even if these measures would be hard to implement.

Happily for Trump, Europe has some reasons of its own to release more of its diesel back into the market. Current high prices are a political issue everywhere, not just among Americans, and the region has in the past weathered lower stocks than it has today.

But whatever the White House does next, Europeans should take this threat seriously, as a sign that they can no longer rely on the US being an unconditional supplier of energy to global markets. Having already been scorched by a reliance on Russia, the case for pursuing energy independence — meaning more nuclear, renewables and drilling — is now even stronger.

camilla.palladino@ft.com

item.title: The FT View. France meets fiscal reality with a crunch
item.author: The editorial board
item.description: A surge in borrowing costs leaves the country on the edge of a debt spiral
item.content:encoded:
A surge in borrowing costs leaves the country on the edge of a debt spiral

The editorial board

“Reality is catching up with us,” French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu warned this week on the eve of presenting the 2027 budget. Lecornu was referring to this year’s surge in government borrowing costs which aggravates France’s fiscal woes just as it enters the presidential election campaign. Amid a broader debt market sell-off, France has become a focal point of investor jitters about debt sustainability.

France’s debt-to-GDP ratio now stands at 119 per cent. Its 10-year bond yields this week climbed above 4.9 per cent, the highest in the Eurozone, from 3.6 per cent in early July. The premium that Paris must pay compared with German debt has risen sharply to more than 125 basis points, the highest level since the peak of the Eurozone crisis in 2012. A country that has not run a budget surplus since 1974 is now paying dearly for its profligacy.

The draft budget would make total savings of €54bn next year, including €43bn of new measures, in a mixture of tax rises and spending cuts. That should be enough to trim the deficit from 5.4 per cent to 5 per cent, a target France was supposed to hit in 2026 but, as in so many previous years, has missed. Lecornu’s minority government could push the budget through by decree, at the risk of being toppled in a censure vote, but the plan will soon be overtaken by next spring’s presidential vote. Investors are paying less attention to a temporary fix at the tail-end of Emmanuel Macron’s presidency and more to the political and fiscal developments that follow. They don’t like what they see.

The first concern is the structural deterioration in the public finances. On current policies, the deficit would hit 6.8 per cent by 2030, according to a government-appointed commission, as spending is driven up by population ageing and rising interest costs. Debt servicing would eat up €124bn in 2030, the commission estimated, 60 per cent more than France’s defence spending.

The second worry is the inability of France’s political class to find some kind of majority for fiscal retrenchment. As the election campaign begins, the populists have the momentum while a divided centre is struggling to gain traction. It has become impossible for candidates to ignore France’s debt problem, but their answers mostly lack credibility. Whoever wins the presidency may not secure a majority in follow-up parliamentary elections, meaning more political deadlock.

The worst-case scenario for debt investors would be a run-off between the far-left Jean-Luc Mélenchon and the far-right Marine Le Pen. Mélenchon has proposed cancelling government debt held by France’s central bank, which would send fear rippling across debt markets. Le Pen has committed to a 3 per cent deficit ceiling but lacks anything like a serious plan for the €140bn or so in annual savings needed to get there by 2032.

The centre-left wants to pile more taxes on businesses and the wealthy despite the inevitable hit to investment and jobs. Thankfully, Édouard Philippe, the leading centrist candidate, injected some sanity into the race this week by proposing to raise the retirement age to 65 and the contribution period for a full pension to 45 years. It is only a start, but a bold gamble in the current climate.

Since France is too big to fail, investors expect the European Central Bank to eventually intervene in case of crisis, keeping a lid on yields. The ECB has the tools and could step in to prevent contagion to other Eurozone sovereigns. But it would also face stiff opposition in other capitals to bailing out a country that has repeatedly failed to get its house in order, especially if led by a president who is at loggerheads with the EU on other fronts. The market squeeze and France’s fiscal pain could get much worse before any rescue.

item.title: Dealmakers line up to test EU’s appetite to create European champions
item.author: Barbara Moens
item.description: As Brussels opens the door to bigger deals within industries, companies look for a test case of the new approach
item.content:encoded:
As Brussels opens the door to bigger deals within industries, companies look for a test case of the new approach

Barbara Moens

For companies, bankers and corporate lawyers around Europe, there is a sudden scramble under way to recast how they pitch a series of big mergers and acquisitions to regulators.

The EU is signalling that it is opening the door to bigger corporate mergers, allowing European companies to gain the scale needed to compete with Chinese and American rivals.

So in response, companies and their advisers are framing their planned deals as test cases for this new approach, betting that arguments about the need for European champions, resilience and investment will help win approval.

Several potential contentious transactions in industries ranging from mining to elevators — and one including a satellite tie-up between Airbus, Thales and Leonardo — are set to provide first indications in the coming months of whether the change in language translates into a more permissive approach to consolidation.

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen has emphasised the need for European champions and cast competition policy as an important part of the bloc’s competitiveness agenda. Meanwhile, her competition chief Teresa Ribera has been explicit in saying the new approach does not amount to a blank cheque for consolidation.

For businesses, that unusual divide over policy leaves one crucial question: how much will actually change?

“Businesses and investors need to see a body of coherent precedent showing how the framework will operate in practice, and it’s for businesses and advisers to work constructively with the commission to achieve this,” said Rafique Bachour of law firm Skadden Arps.

That body of precedent does not yet exist. So, as one Brussels-based M&A-lawyer, points out: “Every big case will now be packaged differently and presented as a test case to create a European champion.”

There is no shortage of candidates. The proposed joint venture between paper manufacturers UPM and Sappi has left the commission concerned it will restrict competition in the markets and give the companies the ability to increase prices. However, the companies argue the deal is the only way to stay competitive and maintain the security of supply in a shrinking industry grappling with excess capacity.

Anglo American’s planned sale of its Brazilian nickel assets to China-backed MMG is seen as a test of how far Brussels is willing to go in its stronger China policy. The case ticks boxes for both resilience and security of supply.

Further down the pipeline is a bid by Finnish lift maker Kone to buy its rival TK Elevator, a deal that from a traditional antitrust perspective would be seen as a steep uphill battle. Whether European competition officials will now assess it through a different lens will be closely watched by dealmakers.

But the clearest test of Brussels’ new philosophy is emerging in space. Airbus, Leonardo and Thales want to combine their satellite business in a venture designed to create a European player capable of better competing with Elon Musk’s SpaceX. Its competitors warn it would weaken competition, ultimately increasing costs for taxpayers.

The mix of traditional merger policy, industrial policy and geopolitical competition makes the joint venture, dubbed Project Bromo, “the obvious test case and a no-brainer”, another lawyer said.

In unusually public remarks about an upcoming antitrust review, von der Leyen referred to the Bromo merger in a recent speech and said “these are the types of industrial champions we need if Europe is to lead in the space economy of tomorrow”.

Ribera subsequently defended the independence of European antitrust officials, many of whom are already nervous about the new political winds. The Spanish competition commissioner made clear that von der Leyen’s comments did not mean “we are not going to apply and to enforce our own regulation”.

Some antitrust experts argued von der Leyen should have given her political steer more subtly. But for companies and deal markets, more clarity is welcome.

That is acknowledged by some European Commission officials, well aware their in-tray is being closely watched. “We need one deal that shows we are serious about the shift,” said one.

barbara.moens@ft.com

Letter in response:
A warning not to push EU merger law too far / From Tomás Espuny Carreño, Barcelona, Spain

item.title: Do US lawmakers finally have capital in the crosshairs?
item.author: Oren Cass
item.description: With a metastasising financial sector and declining business investment, action is essential
item.content:encoded:
With a metastasising financial sector and declining business investment, action is essential

Oren Cass

The writer is an FT contributing editor and chief economist at American Compass

Greed is so often the undoing of an otherwise brilliant scheme. Never satisfied, people become overconfident, push the envelope too far. And everything comes tumbling down. The high-flyers of finance seem headed towards a similar fate, as capital’s share of US income continues to rise, its share of tax payments continues to fall, inequality worsens, wealth concentrates and deficits become unsustainable. All the while the financial engineering gets ever more absurd.

For just one example, take AQR, the hedge fund behind a fairly recent innovation in tax avoidance called the “tax-aware long-short” account, which wraps leveraged, straddled portfolios around conventional equity indices or established fund strategies to generate large harvestable losses and indefinitely defer taxation on gains. Close to $200bn has poured into the strategy at AQR and its imitators such as Quantinno, which welcomes investors “to the next evolution of tax-loss harvesting” and has seen its assets swell from $2bn to $70bn in just a few years. 

Such elaborate gamesmanship helps some of America’s highest earners to reduce taxes on even their wage income. The Financial Times reported earlier this year that fathers at a local sports game in Greenwich, Connecticut, “were fixated on AQR’s Delphi Plus fund, which specialises in ordinary income losses”.

The extraordinary wealth that these individuals and their money managers had already accumulated wasn’t enough, nor was the favourable tax treatment afforded to their capital gains, which in effect meant they might be able to pay a lower share of their income in taxes than their secretaries did. They had to avoid paying taxes altogether, and then claim this as the righteous course.

AQR chief Cliff Asness has said that the moral issue here is that of working for a client’s interests. But things are surely not that simple. A fiduciary duty to a client requires putting his interest above any other, but it does not require pursuing every potential action or developing every potential product.

The ethical business owner or manager operates within not only the letter but also the spirit of the law. It is the letter that determines whether a punishable violation has occurred. But as Milton Friedman observed in his famous essay arguing that “the social responsibility of business is to increase its profits”, the “basic rules of the society” include “both those embodied in law and those embodied in ethical custom”. Ethical custom may be a more subjective matter, but a good place to start is with the easily discernible intent of the laws established through the democratic process.

The defenders of the latest “tax-aware” funds make a comical effort to equate the exotic manoeuvres with garden-variety deductions and retirement saving. But the exercise must be enormously complex to justify the huge fees that the funds charge, allowing the financial wizards to pocket a good chunk of the revenue they divert from the public purse. Clearly, they are embarrassed by all this, or at least nervous about the potential consequences.

They should be. The political winds are shifting and even a business-friendly Republican administration is fed up. On Monday, the US Treasury department issued a notice of plans to scrutinise a range of schemes. “Treasury is serious about cracking down on transactions designed to dodge taxes or exploit our federal tax code,” warned Treasury secretary Scott Bessent in a social media post.

Beginning in the 1980s, the US tax code was rebalanced in favour of capital, in the belief that creating better conditions for its holders to deploy it and reap the rewards would ultimately redound to the benefit of all. The theory required some trust that the capitalists would indeed pursue their profit in ways that would be broadly beneficial. Instead, we got a metastasising financial sector dedicated not to productive investment but to helping the rich get richer by moving money in circles, extracting wealth from the real economy and then paying no taxes at all.

The central argument against wealth taxes, high marginal tax rates and taxes on mobile capital is that they will merely fuel avoidance and push productive activity away. But if we get the same with low tax rates, what then? The US is now in a fiscal crisis and capital should expect to find itself in the crosshairs. If the financial sector is determined to be a socially corrosive drag on the economy, then it is going to have to be taxed that way.

item.title: Australia’s banks show how to prepare for cable blackouts
item.author: Elisabeth Braw
item.description: The country is making its financial system resilient enough to withstand the cutting of undersea lines
item.content:encoded:
The country is making its financial system resilient enough to withstand the cutting of undersea lines

Elisabeth Braw

The writer is the author of ‘The Undersea War: The International Battle for Supremacy at the Bottom of the World’. She is a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council and advises M&C Saatchi World Services

Australia is connected to the rest of the world by a rather small number of subsea data cables. Those cables efficiently transmit all the connectivity the country needs; they even offer spare capacity. But if the cables were damaged, Australia would struggle. Now the country is creating a backup that would thwart the worst harm — and other countries should learn from the Australians’ pragmatic take.

Earlier this year, executives from National Australia Bank sat down with managers from other leading financial institutions and government officials. The purpose of the gathering was to simulate what would happen if the country’s subsea cables suddenly became unavailable. “In the first stage, we hypothesised that the cables on the east coast, where most of our cables run, were cut,” Brad Carr, NAB’s executive in charge of geopolitical risk, who conceived the simulation exercise, told me. “And then we assumed the cables on the west coast were cut too.” The teams switched to satellite communications, only to discover that this transmitted a minuscule portion of the data — that is, money — they needed to send.

On their own, satellites won’t save banks or anyone else if cables suffer a massive outage. The Australians realised that they needed to plan for a situation in which their country found itself cut off from the rest of the modern world. Repair ships and their crews excel at their task, but they need time to get to the fault site, and malicious actors could obstruct them. Then there are administrative delays. Repairs to cables that travel through Indonesian waters — including the crucial links that connect Australia and Singapore — require Indonesian permits, which can take over a month to obtain.

For all these reasons, Australia needed a backup plan, the exercise demonstrated. Its major banks had already, together with the government, begun developing a plan that would allow the financial system to work in a mostly offline situation. “If we have a major incident, how can we make sure that our customers can pay for groceries?” Carr explained.

In parallel, the government has launched CI Fortify, guidance for infrastructure operators “in preparation for instances of crisis or service disruption”; it also expects operators to be able to isolate their infrastructure from other networks and systems for up to three months to be able to provide critical services to Australians.

If the cables were cut, the country would have to become digitally self-sufficient, relying on its domestic connectivity. In a crisis Australian consumers would be able to use their debit cards and withdraw cash from ATMs, and banks would be able to make necessary transactions, though without access to international bank-clearing systems. “It’s like field surgery, not a complete hospital,” a person familiar with the efforts told me. “There will be blood, but it will save the patient.”

Finland is making similar advances. And this summer, Sweden’s central bank teamed up with retail banks and payment cards “to enable card payments to be made even in the event of disruptions in data communication lasting up to seven days”.

Australian leaders are acutely aware of China’s fast-growing submarine fleet and the mysterious visits paid by Chinese research vessels to nearby waters. It could be nothing — but if it’s not, Australia will weather the storm a whole lot better than the countries that treat the risk of a major cable incident as unlikely. In August, Vietnam — which was less prepared — faced a major subsea-cable crisis when four of its eight major cables were damaged and connectivity dropped by 30 per cent.

Much of modern life would come to a halt without undersea cables. Planning for the turmoil that would hit the financial system if they were cut creates resilience at little expense.

item.title: Is circular financing in AI a problem?
item.author: Toby Nangle
item.description: Only if the wheel stops spinning
item.content:encoded:
Only if the wheel stops spinning

Toby Nangle

There are lots of ways in which circular financing among AI companies can be organised. A new report from a team of Bank for International Settlements researchers lists three.

First, there are those tech firms who receive both financing and business from another tech firm; so, maybe including Amazon pouring billions into Anthropic while also supplying the Trainium chips used to train Claude.

Second, suppliers could be financing customers to stimulate demand for their products, a bit like old-fashioned vendor financing. Nvidia’s pivot to providing ‘balance sheet as a service’ comes to mind — along with numerous reports of the giant chipmaker pumping cash in the direction of its financially more precarious customers so that they can buy more chips.

Or the flow could run the other way: customers financing suppliers in order to secure critical inputs. And finance can take many forms, from straight-up loans and equity injections through to forward compute contracts. So maybe the $300bn of business with which OpenAI is backstopping Oracle’s data centre build-out counts, even if OpenAI doesn’t actually have the $300bn and is relying on current or future investors to supply it.

Third comes everything else: reciprocal commercial relationships where goods or services flow both ways.

Looking at a universe of 1,246 AI firms split across compute, infrastructure, data tools, models and applications, the report’s authors — Jon Frost, Rudraksh Kansal, Kumar Rishabh, Vatsala Shreeti and Leanne Si Ying Zhang — found, perhaps unsurprisingly, a lot of circular relationships.

Totting up all the incoming investment flowing to AI firms between 2021 and 2025, they reckon more than half came from other AI firms. And looking just at this lump of AI-to-AI deals, almost half of these were between firms that shared some commercial relationship, suggesting “that a significant portion of financing and commercial relationships in AI are self-referencing.”

But is it a problem?

... circular relationships make reported demand partly endogenous to firms’ own financing decisions. For example, when a supplier finances a customer, part of the supplier’s revenue growth reflects its own capital investment, rather than organic final demand. This makes it harder for investors, lenders and supervisors to gauge what part of the current AI boom is based on organic demand.

Beyond making analysts’ lives a bit tricky, are there real-life problems for the rest of us?

The parallel with the telecommunications boom of the late 1990s is instructive: upstream equipment vendors such as Lucent and Nortel financed network operators so that the operators could buy the vendors’ equipment. This meant that part of the equipment vendors’ reported sales was being funded by the vendors themselves. For a time, as operators expanded their networks, equipment orders also expanded and vendors booked both the sales and loans as assets. However, when operators’ own revenues failed to materialise or slowed, they could neither repay the loans nor sustain the equipment purchases. Equipment vendors then sustained both financial losses and a loss of sales. Such dynamics may also play out in AI if revenue growth and end user demand fall short of firms’ expectations.

We couldn’t find a market cap series for Lucent, but the Nortel market cap chart suggests circular financing can be a problem. But is it a problem this time?

...these circular arrangements tend to be opaque, making monitoring and supervision difficult. Many of the firms involved in AI are private and may disclose limited information. Even where firms are publicly listed, deal terms can often be complex, mixing cash investments with long-term purchase commitments and guarantees on the value of the underlying assets. Residual value guarantees (RVGs) are one example, where the guarantor pledges to cover any shortfall in an asset’s worth (such as chips or data centre equipment) after a fixed period. These contingent commitments sit off balance sheet and only materialise during a downturn – when a guarantor is least able to absorb them. As such, reported deal values may not capture the whole picture, and headline figures can differ substantially from disbursed amounts. Moreover, many of these firms reside in different sectors and jurisdictions, making it difficult for a single supervisor or regulator to monitor these risks.

Hmm. Without the necessary disclosures to pore through, even the hardest-working supervisor or investor is going to struggle to know whether it’s a problem until after the fact.

But there is a silver lining. If it does turn out to be a problem, the BIS reckon that at least we’ll all know about it. Not only through a public equity market swoon, and upending of macroeconomically significant investment. But also because they reckon risks will be magnified by hidden leverage and interconnected exposures across private credit and special purpose vehicles used to finance AI infrastructure. 😬

Further reading:
— Joining the dots between big AI (FTAV)
— Nvidia’s $200bn ‘balance sheet-as-a-service’ (FTAV)
— The US economy is running hot (FTAV)

item.title: Burnham’s wake-up call for the right
item.author: Robert Shrimsley
item.description: Opponents of big-state socialism have never been more in need of a strong Conservative Party and rarely further from having one
item.content:encoded:
Opponents of big-state socialism have never been more in need of a strong Conservative Party and rarely further from having one

Robert Shrimsley

Timing is everything. The Labour Party has waited nearly 20 years for the type of leader Andy Burnham revealed himself to be this week, someone who could bury Blairism and still look like a winner. 

There have been several false steps on the way. Gordon Brown remained troublingly committed to economics. Ed Miliband and Jeremy Corbyn could not convince the country. Keir Starmer won but then turned on the left. Burnham was rejected (twice) for still seeming too New Labour. But the pattern has been consistent: members have been willing the way back to the land before the hated neoliberalism took hold.

Now Labour has the leader it wants and at an opportune moment. Burnham can, quite clearly, do the politics and is also determined to wind back the clock. A leader who believes in higher spending, more public intervention and stronger trade unions; a leader committed to undoing Thatcherism. And above all they have him when his political opponents are in chaos.

What his bravura party conference speech ought to have rammed home to opponents is that Burnham presents an existential threat to the right of British politics and to the economic liberalism it espouses. New Andy is unapologetically old Labour and he is taking the argument for municipal socialism to an enfeebled right. And the peril for them is larger than a mere election defeat.

Alongside Burnham’s policy platform is a shrewd political strategy, calculated to rebuild the electoral coalition on the left and then drive through voting reform in the explicit belief it will keep the right out. He is planning this when, for the first time in modern politics, there is a clear split on the right which could gift him a return to Downing Street.

Consider his headline announcements of what he would do after the general election. He wants to reopen Brexit, tantalising pro-Europeans by not ruling out rejoining the EU. No doubt he is sincere, but this and his commitment to electoral reform are also calculated to tempt Lib Dems, Greens and others to lend Labour their votes. 

Burnham has not committed to a specific voting system, so it is impossible to judge the impact of that intended reform. Anything close to a proportional model would mostly throw up European-style coalitions, potentially bringing left and right extremists into governing blocs.

He has spoken favourably of the supplementary vote system under which he was elected Manchester mayor. This gives voters a second preference and requires the winner to secure 50 per cent support; in many instances it will still benefit the front-running parties.

But we can be sure of two things, whatever version of electoral reform goes forward. It will not be designed to disadvantage the left and it will entrench multi-party politics, cementing the split on the right and permanently diminishing the Conservatives.

And layered on top is an economic and political argument which derides the market-based model. Perhaps this will prove mere rhetoric but the Burnham offer is to wind back the clock and, through electoral reform, to keep it there.  

So his ascent should be a wake-up call to Conservatives — and all who believe in a lower-tax, smaller-state model. Labour has found a leader with the personality to offer up a left agenda to voters desperate for dramatic change and receptive to a rose-tinted view of the world before Thatcher (which three-fifths of the country will not remember). 

There are two problems for Burnham. The first is that even as Labour returns to the comfort zone of what it believes to be working-class politics, the party has rarely been more middle class. A recent study showed nearly two-thirds of its voters are now economically middle class and higher. Meanwhile, working-class and non-graduate voters are moving rightward, a trend crystallised by Brexit.

The bigger obstacle is that he is still presiding over high taxes, high debt and hard times. He admits that rising energy bills will lead to a “tough winter”. Bond markets remain volatile and there is no sign of a serious plan for growth or a real roadmap to his new economy. While presenting himself as a change agent, Burnham has deferred his most transformational promises till the next election, which he claims is not soon. His gamble is that voters will keep faith till then. 

But what this week has shown the right is that they now face a man who, unlike Starmer, may have the clarity of purpose and political skills to win. Burnham may still stumble. But his opponents cannot count on it. 

Were they different, this would be a spur to Reform and the Tories to co-operate, but that seems highly unlikely. There is evidence it would alienate Conservative voters. With Reform a threat, left and centrist voters will bunch around Labour to stop them.

This is the reality for Kemi Badenoch as the Tory leader heads to her own party conference. Those who oppose big-state socialism have never been more in need of a strong Conservative Party and rarely further from having one. Badenoch must somehow lead an intellectual political revival with a badly discredited brand and convince voters her party is the viable alternative to Labour. This means broadening support rather than spurning liberal-minded voters.

Burnham is now offering the UK a real political fight about its future. If the right cannot regroup before he shifts the electoral rules, it will be a long road back.

robert.shrimsley@ft.com

item.title: An AI sovereign wealth fund isn’t progressive — it’s techno-imperialism
item.author: Evgeny Morozov
item.description: Accruing income at home from land and power abroad has an old name: empire
item.content:encoded:
Accruing income at home from land and power abroad has an old name: empire

Evgeny Morozov

The writer is the author of ‘The Net Delusion’ and ‘To Save Everything, Click Here’

A growing number of Americans dislike AI so Washington is trying to change their minds the old-fashioned way, with a stick and a carrot. The stick was on full display on Tuesday. President Donald Trump, with tech executives at his back, told voters that if they refuse data centres, companies will “be forced to go overseas” — and, as he put it, “whoever wins superintelligence wins . . . you’re probably not gonna have a second place” implying that detractors would be handing China victory in the AI race. 

The carrot comes in the form of a dividend. In July, Sam Altman proposed that leading US AI labs each hand 5 per cent of their equity to a public fund. And Senator Bernie Sanders has introduced a bill for a national fund with 50 per cent ownership of the AI giants, with citizens entitled to a stake in their profits.

The stick, on inspection, is flimsy. The two are perfectly compatible: US-aligned data centres can go overseas while AI profits still accrue to Americans. Most of AI’s power goes into training models. This can happen wherever electricity is cheap; only the systems answering users in real time must stay near them. That means data centres can leave US soil and US companies still gain, while citizens with a stake in them are paid no matter where the machines run. For shareholders, it’s the best of both worlds: no data centre next door and a cheque in the mail. 

But the machines still stand somewhere, on someone’s land, guzzling someone’s water, straining someone’s grid. Income at home from land and power abroad has an old name: empire. What’s new is the idea, shared by Altman and Sanders, of enrolling every US citizen. The result would be a new form of social and technological imperialism.

Pax Silica, the state department’s AI supply-chain club, has barely concealed its aim: to lock members into America’s compute and out of China’s. The Pentagon’s new Economic Defense Unit has even invoked the East India Company — a firm whose shareholders drew dividends from conquest — as its model. Pax Silica’s first outpost is a 4,000-acre “economic security zone” in the Philippines. Washington reportedly sought US jurisdiction and immunity for its personnel there; Manila said no twice and insists the zone will stay under Philippine law (the project is proceeding). Just as Detroit in its heyday ran on Liberian rubber and Chilean copper, San Francisco’s AI glory could run on Philippine land and other people’s megawatts.

The imperial ambition behind such initiatives has provoked discontent in host nations. In Kenya, a $1bn data centre stalled after Microsoft and its Emirati partner asked the government to guarantee purchases of its computing capacity. Mexico’s president said her country need not become the data centre of the world. What other countries cannot stop is America’s use of sanctions to lock out China by rationing advanced chips. With the US’s chips and open markets, China would crush Silicon Valley’s valuations. Shutting Beijing out allows US AI companies to capture enough profits that a public fund would be able to redistribute them. Such a fund would be no custodian of collective intelligence but a collector of geopolitical rent: the yield on keeping China’s AI down and the world’s AI bills up.

The US left seems not to have noticed. Gavin Newsom waxes lyrical about “universal basic capital”, Sanders about a Norwegian-style sovereign wealth fund. Yet, there’s a difference. Norway’s wealth comes from its own seabed, while America’s would come from a chokehold on chips and bullying weaker countries for resources. Sanders’s bill lets this slip: it traces AI’s value to humanity’s “collective intelligence”, then pays out only to Americans.

For Maga, local tribute flowing to the all-powerful centre is a cause for celebration. Not so for the left. When Edwardian social imperialists promised to fund welfare out of Pax Britannica, old socialists, from Engels to Lenin, derided workers who took the money as the labour aristocracy. Their point stands: a public that lives off the rent acquires a stake in whatever protects it.

For now, AI’s expansion abroad is a freelance affair, as individual companies cut deals that host nations can still refuse. However, once the US state clears the ground and the American public draws a dividend from it, a refusing government will find itself up against not only Washington but every American with a payout to lose.

Critics from Sanders to Steve Bannon are right about the disease: AI breeds oligarchy. But a dividend funded by flexing American muscle while underdeveloping the rest of the globe would not cure it. It would solve one injustice by hiding another, and give oligarchs what they’ve never had: a public with a stake in looking away.

item.title: We have forgotten what budgets are for
item.author: Martin Sandbu
item.description: The biggest problem with public finances is when they cease to be tools for governance
item.content:encoded:
The biggest problem with public finances is when they cease to be tools for governance

Martin Sandbu

Here, at last, is a Brexit benefit of sorts: UK chancellor of the exchequer John Healey’s in-tray contains only one impossible budgeting task rather than two. EU governments have not only their national budgets to worry about but face pressure to make progress on the next seven-year common budget for the bloc as a whole. This week I want to highlight a parallel between the two challenges.

The parallel is that both the UK and the EU budgets are failing badly to deliver what they are supposed to. To be sure, both public finance arrangements sustain long-established patterns of redistribution. But neither does a good job of newer and more urgent needs: in the UK, to promote higher and more productive private investment and growth, and across the EU, to fund agreed new priorities on defence, energy, industrial policy and digital technology.

The ultimate reasons for this are also similar: a set of political constraints that together make any significant change to the allocation of resources seem out of reach. In the UK, the constraints combine stultifying fiscal rules (here is my longer take on that) and a government that thought, to be elected, it had to promise not to raise income tax, national insurance and VAT. It is therefore reduced to tweaking along the edges (and yes, I count the decision to slightly weaken the “triple lock” on state pension as no more than that).

In the EU case, the constraint takes the form of a political war of attrition. States that receive more out of the budget than they put in want to maintain the programmes that secure this. Net contributors, meanwhile, want a larger relative share to fund new priorities such as defence and energy, without increasing the overall size. Every time in the past, the result has been stalemate, last-minute brinkmanship and an outcome that only marginally changes the status quo ante. For example, researchers from Bruegel have just found that the budget currently being negotiated will only fill a small fraction of the widely recognised investment gap for European public goods. 

What I think the two situations (and no doubt budgeting in many other polities) have in common is that they largely undermine the ability to use budgets as tools of governance. When politics locks public finances into at most marginal departures from the status quo, budgets cease to be tools of governance. Yet the time has long since passed when public policy could largely be left to autopilot and market equilibria.

Something has to give, and if it’s not the budgeting process, it’s most likely a crisis that ultimately forces politicians’ hands. The much better alternative is to find a way to deliberately unlock the political economy of budgeting. That is easy to say, of course, and harder to figure out how to do. But if we know that moving incrementally means hardly moving at all, then it’s at least clear that much bigger steps are needed: these are chasms that cannot be crossed in many small leaps. So what might this entail for the two cases I have mentioned?

In the UK, it is surely a comprehensive reform of the entire tax system. My colleague Martin Wolf wrote this week that: “The important challenge is to improve the efficiency of the fiscal system . . . [D]o not look at a single tax on its own but relative to the rest. The time now is ripe for such reform.” What sort of reform? He rightly points out that a comprehensive overhaul needs to be done with deliberation and care, and mentions the 2011 Mirrlees Review, which remains as good a place as any to start.

But it is possible to state straightforwardly what one thinks should be the main steps of a good reform. As I have written before, I think a lot would be gained from fully harmonising the taxation of income, replacing the current income tax and employers’ national insurance, as well as capital income taxation, with a single new tax that would cover all sources at the same rates for the same levels of income. This would have some obvious losers: those with non-labour income, where national insurance is not paid today, and those with capital gains, who would no longer pay lower tax than wage earners. But that could in return pay for noticeably lower rates.

For example: based on Resolution Foundation research, shifting 2 percentage points from employee national insurance (which is not paid on pensions and investment incomes) to income tax (which is) would raise £6bn. So a rough estimate is that folding the entire 8 per cent national insurance into income tax would give the government roughly £25bn to play with. New research from CenTax, meanwhile, finds that taxing capital gains like other sources of income would raise an additional £20bn. Add in other, smaller effects, and the amounts raised easily surpass £50bn a year. And that is before even contemplating similar simplifying reforms to VAT or property taxation.

The point is not that taxes should rise by that amount, but to underline just how much political room for manoeuvre comprehensive reform buys you. With these sorts of resources, a lot of taxes can be cut. For about £10bn a year, the threshold for paying tax on income at all could be unfrozen, along with that for the higher rate. For about the same amount, you could cut all income tax rates or VAT by 1 percentage point, or corporation tax by 2.5 percentage points. (All of which should be good for growth.) It would be a poor politician who could not marshal that kind of largesse into political support. As an added benefit, if income tax and national insurance no longer existed in their previous forms, it’s not clear how Labour’s manifesto pledge not to raise their rates would continue to bind.

One could mount all kinds of objections. But the question really is: who can honestly say the current marginalist approach to budgeting is delivering?

What about the EU? There, the political economy deadlock may seem deeper than in the UK. It is caused not by the self-imposed strictures of an otherwise all-powerful one-party government, but by the irreconcilable policy positions of many veto players. Not literally irreconcilable — every seven years, EU leaders somehow hammer out a compromise and pass a budget, but always involving very small changes. Irreconcilable, then, in that it seems impossible to get much past the status quo ante.

Here too, it is useful to think about how root-and-branch reform could change the political economy of budgeting. How, when unanimity is so hard to get to? But this objection assumes that a budget must be agreed. That is not true. EU law provides that without a budget agreement, previous spending decisions are carried on. The nominal spending limits follow a fixed 2 per cent inflation adjustment — so as long as nominal growth exceeds that, the share of the budget to GDP will keep shrinking.

So consider a radical rupture with current procedures, in which EU leaders simply decided not to agree a new budget. (Unanimity means it only takes one brave leader to impose this on the rest . . . ) The status quo ante would prevail, but be eroded by inflation and growth over time. That erosion is sizeable. (For illustration: in the soon-to-be finished seven-year budgetary period, EU nominal GDP has gone up by about 40 per cent. Against a 2 per cent per year inflation adjustment, that sort of increase would shrink the budget as a share of GDP by more than one-fifth.) In isolation, this is a double win for the net contributors, who would contribute less and less overall, and in particular cut the size of the traditional transfers they most object to. That alone should concentrate the minds of net recipients.

Another consequence, however, would be resources falling even more glaringly short of what is required for new, geopolitically important spending. So in this hypothetical world where budget talks both consumed a lot less political attention and evidently did not address agreed priorities, the pressure would rise to come up with other solutions — parallel budgets, as it were.

The EU has a good record of coming up with these quickly when needed. Most notable is NextGenerationEU, agreed within months during the Covid-19 pandemic and largely matching the normal seven-year budget for size. Sure, an unemployment reinsurance scheme, Safe, a fund for joint defence procurement, and the Ukraine Support Loan as well as earlier facilities to fund Kyiv through joint debt, together committed nearly another seven-year budget’s worth of resources. The USL even pioneered a way to borrow jointly against the EU’s creditworthiness while leaving some unwilling countries off the hook through side payments.

This is beginning to look like a political economy to produce a shrinking traditional budget coupled with more — and more debt-funded — new budgets for specific purposes. Does anyone think the current model — which wastes enormous amounts of time and effort and by common consent fails to address the most urgent priorities — is preferable?

Other readables

● My colleague Soumaya Keynes has a very thoughtful conversation with Jenny Bates, a senior British civil servant who has reflected hard on how the UK must change its way of doing things in the new era of geoeconomic rivalry.

● The return on East German industrial espionage in the west was astonishingly high, new research finds.

● Is quantum computing becoming reality?

● The Syrian government has unleashed a free-market experiment on the previously closed and protected economy cultivated by the Assad regime.

item.title: Four potential positives from higher bond yields
item.author: Ian Harnett
item.description: The sharp rise in borrowing costs has raised justified alarm but there are benefits too
item.content:encoded:
The sharp rise in borrowing costs has raised justified alarm but there are benefits too

Ian Harnett

The writer is co-founder and chief investment strategist at Absolute Strategy Research

The alarm over the rise in the benchmark US bond yield above the 5 per cent threshold has been dominating financial markets in recent weeks and not without reason.

US 10-year Treasury yields have jumped more than 0.5 percentage points in the past month and 1.3 points since the start of the Iran conflict to levels not seen since 2007. Indeed, today’s levels of US Treasury yields have only been higher since 1900 during the inflationary mid-1960s to mid-2000s, and at the end of the first world war. And importantly, yields on inflation-linked bonds have been rising around the world.

But the move in bond yields has not been without potential positives for investors.

First, we suspect that stronger growth is driving yields higher rather than increased inflation risk or policy uncertainty. For us, real yields — those adjusted for inflation — simply reflect the true cost of capital. Accelerating AI-related capital expenditure is both boosting economic growth and, likely, pushing real yields higher. Increased government spending on areas such as defence and infrastructure may also be boosting real growth and real rates — especially as some of this economic growth is coming from falling household sector savings across the G7 group of nations.

 Second, investors should welcome the fact that higher real yields are a source of capital discipline on both governments and corporates. Moreover, this additional discipline need not necessarily constrain the level of capex. Despite what economic theory would suggest, real yields and corporate capex have tended to broadly rise and fall together over the past 40 years. More importantly, these higher real yields are also likely to lead to more productive capex. One of my gripes about the impact of central bank bond-buying programmes known as quantitative easing was always that the resulting low rates didn’t boost capex but reduced it. Companies were rewarded by investors for providing yield via dividends and buybacks, rather than investing in new capacity and processes.

Third, higher real yields will probably see less financial engineering driving markets, which should boost investor and policymaker confidence in the longer-term stability of the financial system. Non-bank financial institutions such as private capital firms were key beneficiaries of the QE period, in part because cheap funding facilitated increased financial engineering. This helped NBFIs to displace the more regulated, traditional bank lending.

We are already seeing a reversal in the fortunes of listed US non-bank stocks compared with US bank stocks, as real rates have normalised. While this may be a coincidence, we suspect that if real yields continue to rise, the business models of some of these new NBFIs, which have been based on low rates, plentiful liquidity and a dose of financial engineering, could be challenged. 

Finally, higher bond yields may create more options for long-run asset allocators. The AI bubble has meant that, for many, investing in US equities has been the “only game in town”. This could be changing. Rapidly rising bond yields have often been a precursor to market corrections, as they expose the extent to which the gains in the stock market have been driven by higher valuation multiples, rather than the growth in earnings, or dividends. 

Take a look at the gap between US Treasuries and US markets earnings yield — the earnings per share of companies divided by the share price. While the US 10-year yield is up to more than 5 per cent, the equity market has an earnings yield of only 3.9 per cent, and the dividend yield is back to its 2000 lows at 1.1 per cent. Even if you include buybacks alongside dividend income, the total equity yield is just 2.6 per cent — again, close to the 2000 lows.

But it is also this divergence in relative valuations where the investment opportunities arise for longer-term investors with patient capital. While bondholders can now get a 5 per cent return if they hold their 10-year Treasuries to maturity, the kind of returns that equity holders might expect over the same 10-year period is close to zero, based on historic precedent as indicated by the cyclically adjusted price-earnings model developed by economist Robert Shiller.

While this still may not be enough of a return premium for some investors, given the excitement surrounding the prospects for AI-related stocks, it does create more optionality for long-run asset allocators to invest in something other than equities.
