item.title: An optimist’s guide to the bond market
item.author: Katie Martin
item.description: It could be a lot worse. Really!
item.content:encoded:
It could be a lot worse. Really!

Katie Martin

Good morning. What does a country gotta do to get lower bond yields around here? The US personal consumption expenditures inflation index — the Fed’s preferred measure — came in softer than expected in August, at a 3 per cent annualised rate, excluding food and energy. More important, perhaps, the prior two months’ readings were revised down, leaving the three-month rolling average (the pink line below) at 2 per cent, the central bank’s target:

Cue celebrations in the bond market? Umm, no. The 10-year Treasury yield rose four basis points, to 5.29 per cent, yesterday. What gives? Well, part of the decline in PCE (just how much is unclear) was down to a change in how the index handles financial services prices. And, as the chart above shows, the longer-term trend still looks more sideways than down. Most important, though, the growth story is rocking and rolling: second-quarter real GDP was revised up from 1.5 per cent to 2.2 per cent yesterday. A good reminder that the bond market story is not just about inflation. Email us: unhedged@ft.com

This is fine?

Dear oh dear, what a month September was in the rates markets. US benchmark 10-year yields gained half a percentage point, with some rather gut-wrenching days in the mix that have, I gather, hammered some hedge funds. You have to go back to 2022, a proper bond bloodbath, to see that kind of action. And the pain has been pretty widespread, with US yields making life difficult for everyone else. Check out Norway, for example: its debt-to-GDP ratio is a little over 50 per cent — rookie numbers by developed-world standards — and its yields are still getting dragged higher.

We asked the other day whether hopping into bonds now would represent a savvy bit of dip-buying or the investment equivalent to jumping into a meat grinder. Most respondents opted for meat grinder. However, it is still possible to turn that frown upside down. 

The first reason to be cheerful is that, thankfully, this is not 2022, when bonds and stocks both tumbled together. Sure, it looks like the ascent in bond yields is keeping a bit of a lid on the stock market, but the latter is not in distress.

As Jurrien Timmer, director of global macro at Fidelity Investments, pointed out in a LinkedIn post the other day, the secret ingredient is earnings.

if the 10-year yield rises to 6%, that suggests an equity P/E ratio of 16x. [The S&P 500] is currently 19-20x. A 4-point drop in the P/E ratio is a 20% valuation haircut, but if it’s offset by 30% earnings growth, we could be spared the kind of drawdown we experienced in 2022. Maybe a 2022 echo or aftershock.

Second, this is what bonds are supposed to do in a growth-y environment. We’ve all had our brains scrambled by the quantitative easing years. Yes, this shifts the burden from central banks to governments, and it will all impose some tough political choices on countries like the UK and France that rely heavily on borrowed money. But maybe it is time for us all to take that medicine.

Third, a related point, this is not a solvency crisis or anything like that. It is the effluent coming off a massive repricing on the path ahead for the Federal Reserve. We all had our doubts that the Fed would be able to stick to the script and raise rates to tackle inflation. Chair Kevin Warsh put those doubts to bed in Jackson Hole and forced the market to flip expectations. Bear in mind at one point last year, the market was pricing in five interest rate cuts from the Fed in 2026. Now it is pricing two rises — one done, one to go.

Fourth, and OK maybe this is not exactly a reason for normal people to pop the champagne, but this is a nice set-up for hedge funds, or at least for the hedge fund managers who have not already been carted out by the rates market in September.

As UBS Wealth Management said in a note yesterday:

Major central banks [have] made clear that interest rates will need to remain high in the near term amid sticky inflation and resilient economic growth.

Historically, such a global policy environment has been favourable for hedge funds. They generated positive cumulative returns during every Federal Reserve tightening cycle since 1994 and generally outperformed global bonds. In the most recent cycle, global bonds fell by around 12%, while hedge funds ended the period with positive returns.

Fifth, we all know that markets are prone to overreaction. It’s possible this is that overshoot at work, especially now that the rates markets are dominated by more price-sensitive buyers. Reasonable people can disagree here, but the market is pricing in a further four rate rises from the Fed in this cycle. Really?

Olivier de Larouzière, chief investment officer of fixed income at BNP Paribas Asset Management, is saying “non.” He reckons there’s maybe one more rise to come. The shorter end of the market has been “brutal”, due to that rates repricing, he says, but “apart from that, nothing much has happened”, and as such, he’s a buyer of G-4 rates out to a maturity of five years. “The macro is stronger than expected,” he said. “Bond markets are supposed to suffer.”

Pain and suffering are how fixed-income people enjoy themselves, and hey, maybe there’s more of that to come. But if this is an excessive market response to the Fed, he could have a point.

One good read

Syria’s free-market experiment

item.title: Why we can thumb our noses at AI
item.author: Elaine Moore
item.description: Our sense of smell helps us to keep a few shreds of privacy intact and maintains a dividing line between real and virtual worlds
item.content:encoded:
Our sense of smell helps us to keep a few shreds of privacy intact and maintains a dividing line between real and virtual worlds

Elaine Moore

If you are the sort of person who worries about privacy, the AI doomers probably have you in a headlock right now. OpenAI contractors are reading ChatGPT conversations and Meta’s cutesy AI agent Muse is reported to be skipping past permissions. What you look like and sound like can already be replicated with ease. Anonymity is starting to seem like a quaint idea. 

But it turns out there is still one — rather niche — identifier that remains yours alone. The way that you smell is, in technology terms, a data modality into which AI has made relatively little headway. 

Does this seem like clutching at straws? Maybe. When a technology writer told me last month that, in all seriousness, they now regarded smell as one of the few bright spots in a world of surveillance, it sounded like the sort of thing someone would say when they’d run out of normal ways to be cheerful. What is there to gain from being undetectable and unreplicable in this way? What sort of aroma-based resistance can you mount?

Yet in the world of olfactory neuroscience there are some who take the idea of not being sniffed out by AI seriously. “I have attributes not digitally coded,” says Barry Smith, director of the Institute of Philosophy at the University of London’s School of Advanced Study. “And I’m happy about that.”

Smith spends a lot of time thinking about senses. Smell tends to be the most neglected — or it was until Covid knocked it out for millions of people. And it was an academic backwater for so long that there is relatively little data available for AI models to ingest.

Keeping this sense beyond the bounds of AI is good not just because it helps us to keep a few shreds of privacy intact but because it maintains a dividing line between real and virtual worlds.

“No matter how good the visuals and sounds — no matter if you can move around a virtual world — we will never be really immersed in a digital world if we cannot smell it,” says Smith. That goes for the notion of uploading ourselves on to the cloud by digitally recording our experiences too. Even if you can see and hear every memory digitally, without taste and smell they won’t be as vivid as the real thing. 

If AI could log, identify and recreate scents, there would be obvious commercial gains beyond sci-fi memory devices. A machine that can smell disease could become a medical tool. One that was able to detect rotten produce could be used by food manufacturers or agricultural companies. 

But it is proving to be a difficult process because smell is such a physical experience. When we sniff something (or someone) we are inhaling tiny little pieces of them. “The smell which is in me is the fusion of the other person’s body with my body,” was Jean-Paul Sartre’s poetic description. This is either comforting or gross, depending on your mindset. But while large language models can simulate other cognitive faculties, smell is, for now, the outlier.

Whether it will stay this way is debatable. Alex Wiltschko, a neuroscientist and AI researcher who spun his start-up Osmo out of Google Brain, says no. He compares olfactory intelligence (aka OI) to the early days of photography, when different methods of capturing images were being tested. “How do we quantify the ephemeral?” he asks. “We know it is possible, but there are different ways to go about it.” 

The barrier standing in the way of a perfectly accurate AI nose is, Wiltschko says, data. For this, Osmo is building data labelling infrastructure — “a Rosetta Stone from the world of molecules”. MIT researchers did something similar with SmellNet, a database of real-world smells.

It is an enormous job. Research by Rockefeller University’s Laboratory of Neurogenetics and Behavior suggests that humans can sift between molecule combinations to detect more than a trillion different scents. Compared to vision, audio and language processing, our understanding of how we perceive those molecules is limited. We can know that a rose contains over 400 distinct odour molecules in various sizes and configurations without knowing exactly how we register its smell.

The last memorable attempt to reproduce real-world smells was Smell-O-Vision, a 1960s cinematic experiment involving puffs of scent that tended to linger and mingle in unpleasant combinations. Making a more sophisticated AI version is still a work in progress. Digital reproduction of the way that we smell remains a philosophical question mark. For now, only the human nose knows.

elaine.moore@ft.com

item.title: How Europe can stall Russia’s hybrid war
item.author: Alexander Gabuev
item.description: Enhancing domestic security, using new technologies and negotiating guardrails could lessen the risk of mass-casualty events
item.content:encoded:
Enhancing domestic security, using new technologies and negotiating guardrails could lessen the risk of mass-casualty events

Alexander Gabuev

The writer is the director of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center in Berlin 

European policymakers are scrambling for a response to deter Russia’s escalating hybrid campaign. Unfortunately, there is virtually no way to fully discourage the Russian security state from trying to hit targets on the continent that are linked to military support of Ukraine. What Europe needs is a defensive toolkit to disrupt the attacks, clear thinking on how to build leverage vis-à-vis the Kremlin, and a path to establish guardrails with Russia.

From the Kremlin’s viewpoint, there are at least three reasons for intensifying its hybrid war against Europe. First, many European arms producers are working to supply Moscow’s enemy, and some facilities bolstering Ukraine’s defence-industrial base are located on the continent. This has turned Europe into Kyiv’s secure rear. The Kremlin wants to remove this safety margin.

The second reason is revenge. The Russian state is aware that hundreds of thousands of its servicemen have been killed by weapons and munitions supplied or paid for by Europe, and using intelligence supplied by Nato. On top of that, Ukraine has been intensifying its campaign against Russia’s war economy and supporting infrastructure. All these losses are ultimately the result of Vladimir Putin’s own senseless decision to invade Ukraine but leaders in Moscow do not take this into account for obvious reasons. Instead, there are myriad bureaucratic incentives to show Putin that his secret services are busy making Ukraine and Europe pay.

Finally, there is hope in the Kremlin that the Europeans will eventually abandon Ukraine because their governments will be put under pressure by voters who are agnostic about Kyiv’s fate. So far, these hopes have proved futile. But even if Russia’s hybrid campaign doesn’t ultimately engineer a change of sentiment towards Ukraine, attempts to disrupt European military supplies and revenge are strong enough motivations for the Russians to carry on.

Some European policymakers are calling for direct offensive responses to all this because, they say, Russians only understand the language of force: if they are hit hard enough, they will back off. This logic mirrors the Kremlin’s understanding of the west, which means that both sides may find themselves on a path of uncontrolled escalation in a domain where language for escalation management does not exist — unlike the cold war’s nuclear or conventional domains. Both sides would then be just one mass-casualty event away from a different world.

But there are other ways Europe can manage the Russian challenge in an effective, resolute and careful manner. Nato is already doing a good job of disrupting the Russian attacks. However, Europe can step up its efforts to boost domestic security tools. As the continent embarks on a generational investment in its security and military capacity, some of these resources should be spent on domestic needs: beefing up under-resourced police, counter-intelligence and counterterrorism agencies and enabling closer co-ordination between these three branches. 

Europe is entering a dangerous period in which many of its younger citizens may be organically radicalised by the images continuously coming out of the Middle East and Africa — and then exploited by terrorists or adversarial states like Russia and Iran. The continent did a good job tackling this in the wake of 9/11, and a similar generational effort is needed. Modern technology, particularly AI, will be a powerful ally, and if policymakers are concerned about the reliability of the US, Europe has its own companies that can help to make it safer.

Focusing on defence doesn’t preclude sharpening the offensive toolkit. Europe can discreetly signal to Moscow that every hostile action will have a price — and that every Russian attack will result in additional European support for Ukrainian operations. Europe can try to use that as leverage to bring the Kremlin into a discussion about guardrails in the hybrid domain. While it’s unlikely that the Russians will abandon their attacks altogether, they may be pressed into discussing sets of civilian targets — for example, purely civilian airports — that should be off limits for all sides. This would reduce the potential for mass-casualty events.

Scepticism is understandable among Nato professionals who may believe that such discussions would be a waste of time given the Kremlin’s disregard for human life, and the low level of trust between intelligence services. But trying to talk the Russians into limitations from a position of strength must be explored despite the risk of failure. It may save lives.

item.title: Lex. UBS should make the positive case for staying Swiss
item.description: Too much doom-mongering may be bad for the bank’s business
item.content:encoded:
Too much doom-mongering may be bad for the bank’s business

It’s as predictable as Switzerland’s famous clocks. Last week UBS lost its latest battle with Swiss politicians over strict new capital rules. Within days came reports that the giant lender might move abroad, or even receive a merger proposal from any number of large international rivals. But for the bank itself, focusing on what Bern stands to lose is the wrong approach.

The bank is right to consider all options. Moving headquarters could be doable, though the benefits of lighter regulation from doing so would have to be weighed against the costs of losing customers who prize a Swiss bank — or at least a non-American one. However, insofar as any threat to leave would mostly be a negotiating tactic, executives should remember to make a more positive case alongside it.

For one thing, the idea of UBS decamping might not have the desired effect. The next group to vote on its fate — politicians in the National Council, the Swiss parliament’s lower house — skews more leftwing than the upper chamber. They are less likely to be upset by the idea of losing a pillar of Swiss high finance. And too much doom-mongering may be bad for UBS’s business. Wealthy individuals and corporate executives read the news: rumours of disruption and wailing about a lack of competitiveness hardly encourage new clients to join the bank.

Better, then, for chair Colm Kelleher and chief executive Sergio Ermotti to focus on the benefits their institution brings to its home country. The bank funds about a quarter of domestic loans and is the country’s third-largest private employer. It previously commissioned economists to study how higher capital requirements would damage the economy; it shouldn’t be hard to show the wonderful things UBS could do if it were to win a compromise.

For tips they could also look to JPMorgan Chase in the US. Chief executive Jamie Dimon isn’t afraid to complain when he has issues with regulators, but has also made moves to win over politicians and style his bank as a national champion, with initiatives such as a $1.5tn “Security and Resiliency Initiative” supporting some of President Donald Trump’s priorities. UBS has struggled to balance vinegar and honey in the same way.

Executives are understandably wary of following the US playbook too closely. Appealing directly to the public with heart-wrenching TV adverts depicting sad farmers and crying babies, as US banks’ trade groups did when fighting against new capital rules in 2024, might backfire in a country with less tolerance for explicit corporate lobbying.

But the current approach is clearly not working: UBS is at present set to be saddled with rules that are only marginally better than its worst-case scenario. At the very least, a shift in tone would reduce the reputational risk for the Swiss bank. Ending up in a position where it either has to decamp or look like it has made empty threats would not be its finest hour.

nicholas.megaw@ft.com

item.title: The Big Read. China’s bigger, better batteries
item.author: Simon Mundy
item.description: It’s the world’s fastest-growing power technology — and Beijing is dominant
item.content:encoded:
It’s the world’s fastest-growing power technology — and Beijing is dominant

Simon Mundy

On a production line in south-east China, machines paste a black slurry of electrode material on to a copper ribbon just five microns thick — one 20th of the width of a human hair.

Further down the line, a team of robots monitored by an AI quality inspection system will turn the strips into battery cells by cutting them with lasers, winding them into rolls and pressing them with a force equivalent to a 23-tonne weight.

The factory is at the Ningde headquarters of CATL, the world’s biggest battery producer and a goliath in the electric car industry.

But the large-scale storage batteries these cells will go into are destined not for the world’s roads but for the energy sector. They represent the fastest-growing power technology today, according to the International Energy Agency, the world’s energy watchdog.

By driving down battery costs and improving the underlying technology, CATL and other Chinese manufacturers have provided an answer to a longstanding problem with solar and wind energy: their intermittency — or, simply, the fact that they only generate power when the sun shines or the wind blows.

Systems using Chinese batteries are now able to store solar power long after sunset, for example, eroding the need for fossil-fuel generation that until now has ensured round-the-clock electricity supply.

“This is the big one,” says Michael Liebreich, a veteran energy analyst and consultant. Reliance on intermittent wind and solar power for the majority of electricity supply seems implausible, he says, “until you realise you have cheap batteries”.

The cost of battery packs used in grid-scale storage systems fell by 45 per cent last year alone, according to think-tank Ember. This year, prices have edged upwards because of tight global supplies of lithium. But the storage capacity of large-scale batteries installed around the world is today 11 times greater than the level five years ago, says the IEA.

Momentum around renewable energy investment has quickened as countries smart from the soaring cost of natural gas due to the US war with Iran and in anticipation of demands from data centres. This year, 40 per cent more large-scale batteries are set to be installed than in 2025, according to analysts at S&P Global.

But the power storage boom has brought energy security worries of its own. Governments from Washington to Brussels are wary of their reliance on Chinese-made equipment. Chinese producers account for 95 per cent of large-scale storage batteries, says Benchmark Mineral Intelligence.

The sector’s rapid growth is strengthening China’s position as the dominant force in low-carbon energy, compounding opportunities for Chinese companies in adjacent markets such as wind and solar generation equipment.

It is also changing power systems around the world. “We see, in all our scenarios, transitions towards systems based on renewable energy,” says Brent Wanner, head of the power sector unit at the IEA, whose long-term energy market modelling is closely watched by governments and investors. “Battery storage is kind of the glue that can hold [such systems] together.”

China’s battery surge

The seeds of China’s battery storage boom were sown in the years after Xi Jinping took power in 2012, with his pledge to build an “ecological civilisation”.

The government increased support for renewable power investment in an effort to boost energy security, tackle urban pollution and gain a strategic advantage in a sector with global growth potential. Solar and wind generation duly soared, supporting manufacturing capacity gains and cost declines that fed a global rush of renewable technology installations.

At the same time, China’s government started giving out hefty subsidies for electric vehicles, aiming to capitalise on the country’s battery prowess and to build strength in the automotive sector, where it had long struggled to compete.

This fuelled the rise of CATL, a company established in 2011 to make batteries for EVs, based in Ningde, an obscure fishing town close to where founder Robin Zeng grew up.

Today, the company produces 40 per cent of the world’s EV batteries. Plug-in vehicles now account for nearly two-thirds of new passenger car sales in China.

But that is only one part of the batteries sector. By 2021, it had become clear to the Chinese state that a vast amount of renewable power was being wasted, with solar and wind plants often generating far more electricity than the grid could absorb.

So it launched a strategic push to deploy battery storage on the grid at large scale. Across much of the country, developers were required to build or commission large-scale storage as a condition of approval for new wind and solar plants.

Again CATL has been at the forefront of this effort. Its fastest-growing business line today is the production of cells for large-scale energy storage systems. The company accounted for 22 per cent of cell sales for these systems globally in the first half of the year, making it the market leader in China and abroad.

As a result of the state’s drive, China’s battery storage capacity expanded from 2.4 gigawatts in 2020 to more than 140GW at the end of last year, according to the Energy Institute, an industry membership body. In the first half of this year, coal’s share of Chinese power generation fell below 50 per cent for the first time ever.

Exports of China’s large-scale battery technology have also surged. Researchers at BloombergNEF estimate that new battery storage capacity of 84.6GW will be added outside China this year — 65 per cent higher than last year.

“It is absolutely a global trend,” says Jeh Vevaina, chief investment officer for energy at the asset manager Brookfield. “We’re seeing it in all our markets, be that in Europe, the US, Asia — really everywhere we do business.”

On a vast stretch of sun-baked desert south of Abu Dhabi, construction is under way on a $6bn power plant designed to provide a power output of 1GW — equivalent to the average demand of more than 2mn European homes — around the clock. A huge battery array, installed by the Chinese companies BYD and Sungrow, will soak up excess solar power during the day from millions of panels stretching over 90 square kilometres, discharging it after dark.

The plant’s developer, state-owned clean energy company Masdar, is presenting it as a blueprint for similar projects elsewhere — opening the prospect for a greater uptake of low-cost renewable power than had previously seemed possible, and weakening the case for continued investment in fossil-fired plants to provide 24-hour “baseload” power.

“We have always been challenged, as an industry, by the fact that renewables are intermittent,” says Masdar chief executive Mohamed Jameel Al Ramahi. “This project demonstrates the ability for renewables to become a baseload solution.”

In May, the International Renewable Energy Agency, an organisation with more than 170 national governments as members, found that the cost of hybrid power plants that combined renewables and storage had fallen so much that in many parts of the world they could provide a “firm” round-the-clock power supply, matching the typical level of reliability achieved by fossil-fired plants at an equivalent or lower cost.

In India, the government in August held an auction for renewable power delivered round the clock, with bidders required to match the typical supply of coal plants. It secured 1GW of solar and storage capacity at a lower cost than recent coal power contracts.

Chinese-made batteries are now being deployed en masse in the country, which in the first half of this year added seven times as much new power storage as it had in total at the end of 2025, according to energy research company Mercom India. Much of the rise comes from a single huge solar and storage project built by the Adani Group, whose founder Gautam Adani has pledged to support Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s clean energy drive. 

The government is now planning regulation that would require storage to be installed alongside new solar and wind power plants — similar to the rules that drove China’s storage lift-off. Climate advocates hope this will reduce the country’s heavy reliance on coal, the most carbon-intensive fossil fuel.

“Give it another two or three years . . . when all this gets set up, then you can start seeing a decline in the requirement for coal-based power,” says Sumant Sinha, chief executive of ReNew, one of India’s largest green energy developers. 

‘The equipment is safe’

China’s battery makers are now firmly in the ascendancy.

Ningde came third this year in a UN World Intellectual Property Organization ranking of the world’s most “innovation-intensive” places, sandwiched between the UK’s Cambridge and the Boston-Cambridge cluster in Massachusetts. The accolade reflects the more than 60,000 patents filed by CATL, exceeding the combined total of its biggest rivals. Zeng, meanwhile, is China’s fourth-richest person with a fortune of $50bn.

Yet CATL and others now risk becoming victims of their own success. As the technology has seemed increasingly crucial to the renewables transition, officials in major markets have grown alarmed by the dependence on supply from a single country — and the potential for interference from Beijing.

Early in September, Ford chief executive Jim Farley received a strongly worded letter from US transportation secretary Sean Duffy, voicing “profound concern” over the carmaker’s partnership with CATL. 

During Joe Biden’s presidency, Ford had started investing heavily in EV technology, only for Donald Trump to return to power and scrap Biden’s industry-supporting policies.

In December, Ford announced that it would use its idle car battery capacity as the foundation for a $2bn push into a new business line: stationary battery storage systems, which it would produce under a licensing agreement with CATL. “There is no doubt that the growth for battery storage . . . is exploding,” Farley said in August.

Ford’s strategy has now run into government opposition. Duffy’s letter warned against “reliance on technologies of foreign adversaries”. It is the latest instance of Washington’s resistance to the incursion of Chinese technology, following prior crackdowns on companies from telecom infrastructure provider Huawei to the social media app TikTok.

In August, Trump authorised the energy department to block Chinese-linked battery storage equipment from the US grid on national security grounds. Washington has also revised the rules around tax credits for battery storage, in effect limiting the amount of Chinese equipment American companies can use.

Some US officials say that Chinese-made storage equipment could potentially contain chips enabling it to be controlled or switched off remotely. Similar worries have emerged in the EU, where the authorities have moved to restrict public funding for storage projects using certain key components from “high-risk” countries including China.

Such concerns are baseless, says Cao Renxian, the billionaire founder of Sungrow, one of the world’s biggest providers of large-scale battery systems. “It is a trade issue, not a safety issue,” Cao says, at his headquarters in China’s eastern Anhui province. “We all know that the equipment is safe.”

Like battery sector peers including CATL and BYD, Sungrow is seeking to address European worries of excessive reliance on imports from China by building up large-scale manufacturing operations on the continent. In the US, however, it is forecasting a gradual decline in sales as restrictions tighten.

The US crackdown will force a growing reliance on kit made by alternative suppliers such as South Korea’s Samsung SDI and LG Energy Solution, whose storage batteries are significantly more expensive, says Anna Darmani, a battery storage analyst at Wood Mackenzie.

The US government’s Energy Information Administration still forecasts that battery storage capacity in the country’s grid will continue to soar, doubling between 2025 and 2027, as utilities try to meet rising power needs from data centres. Battery storage is “the main lever left to pull to meet new demand”, says Andy Bowman, chief executive of Jupiter Power, one of the country’s biggest storage project developers.

The AI power rush has exposed the limitations of today’s battery storage technology. US data centre developers are also investing in on-site generation — most of which is in the form of gas power, despite the falls in the cost of renewables and batteries.

“Not everywhere do we have the right combination of renewable resources and land footprint that’s required to build out large amounts of renewables plus storage,” says Lucia Tian, Google’s director of advanced energy technologies.

Another concern is the fact that lithium-ion battery storage systems are typically designed to provide power for only several hours at a time — meaning it can be “economically challenging” to build enough capacity to fully guard against periods of unusually weak solar or wind generation, Tian says.

All the same, Tian adds that Google will use renewable and storage plants to provide much of the power for its new data centres. It will also invest in alternative “long-duration” storage technologies that could provide power for much longer periods. It has commissioned storage projects from Form Energy, which uses reversible iron rusting to store energy for up to 100 hours at a time, and Italy’s Energy Dome, whose system uses compressed carbon dioxide.

China’s battery makers, however, insist that some of their biggest advances are still to come.

Last month CATL began commercial deliveries of power storage units with batteries that use sodium — an abundant mineral — instead of lithium. “When the production volume goes up, we expect it will be much cheaper than lithium,” says Ni Jun, CATL’s chief manufacturing officer.

Improvements in lithium-ion technology are also increasing the duration for which storage systems can provide power.

In June, the Shanghai-based Envision Group launched a new system designed to provide up to 16 hours of storage, compared with the roughly four-hour capacity that is currently standard on the market. The company is developing in Inner Mongolia what it says will be China’s largest AI data centre, to be powered by on-site renewable energy and battery storage. 

Envision founder Zhang Lei argues that such projects provide a model for the rest of the world — if it can overcome what he sees as an irrational fear of reliance on Chinese-made equipment.

For creating energy technology that is “not only sustainable but also extremely cost competitive”, Zhang says, “China deserves respect”.

item.title: Lex. Australia’s housing slump could have a silver lining for its banks
item.description: Housing slowdown could result in lenders directing capital to more profitable places
item.content:encoded:
Housing slowdown could result in lenders directing capital to more profitable places

The UK isn’t alone in wanting to help new homebuyers clamber on to the first rung of the property ladder. But rather than writing newbies helpful cheques, as Prime Minister Andy Burnham plans to do, Australia has opted to chill activity in the rest of the property market to increase their relative purchasing power. The resulting slump in house sales has rattled its mortgage-laden banks.

Shares in the country’s lenders have slid almost a tenth in the past six months. Sharply higher interest rates — four quarter-point rises this year to 4.6 per cent and counting — are good for their profit. But rising debt costs had dented the mood in the housing market even before the government in May scrapped longstanding tax incentives on existing homes for buy-to-let properties, which included lower capital gains levies as well as the ability to offset rental losses against tax.

That hurt house sales. Commonwealth Bank of Australia, the country’s largest lender, said mortgage applications fell 15 per cent in the three months that followed the tax changes. House prices in Sydney fell 5 per cent in the three months through September, according to property data provider Cotality, while country wide, they’ve slipped more than 5 per cent from their March peak.

Australia’s banks are particularly reliant on housing, with mortgages making up between roughly half and two-thirds of their total loan books, compared with closer to a quarter for most European and US lenders. So the property slowdown leaves lenders scrabbling to find businesses to lend to instead.

There are helpful pockets of growth. Even before Australia began attracting AI data centres, local utilities were rushing to shift from coal towards renewable energy sources. Generally, businesses are investing the equivalent of 25 per cent of GDP, according to government data, the highest level in more than a decade. That must be funded somehow: business credit is expected to grow at 7 per cent or more for at least the next two years, reckon analysts at Citigroup, well above the 4-5 per cent average. 

For the banks, this is a useful opportunity to rebalance their activities. CBA’s corporate lending, for example, makes up just a quarter of its loan book but generates two-fifths of adjusted earnings and is growing much faster than its giant mortgage operations. The housing slowdown has taken the shine off bank shares, but it isn’t so bad if it results in them directing capital to more profitable places.

jennifer.hughes@ft.com

item.title: Don’t own bonds and be cautious with stocks
item.author: Bill Gross
item.description: Balance sheets have become unbalanced and growth in turn may suffer the consequences
item.content:encoded:
Balance sheets have become unbalanced and growth in turn may suffer the consequences

Bill Gross

The writer is a philanthropist, private investor and co-founder of Pimco

“Neither a borrower nor a lender be,” wrote William Shakespeare, who was one of history’s greatest authors but obviously ill-versed in economics. Without lending or borrowing, our modern economic society wouldn’t grow very much, AI or not.

That is another way of saying that credit expansion is a fundamental and necessary condition to foster nominal GDP growth, here in the US and everywhere else in the world. Just doing the equivalent of trading seashells back and forth does not do much for that. Economic growth requires seashell/balance sheet expansion in order to promote long-term growth.

Milton Friedman’s work may have confirmed this with his “money matters” thesis, which argued that money supply is the primary driver of inflation. But his definition of “money” was always missing a link to my way of thinking. It is better to look at total credit in the US. This category includes government, mortgage and corporate credit and is now in the vicinity of $84tn, according to the US Federal Reserve. It has been expanding recently at an acceptable 5.9 per cent, just enough in a world of nominal US GDP growth of 8 per cent or so to stabilise asset prices or propel them higher given AI euphoria pricing GDP growth at higher-than-historic levels.

This is what is responsible for current equity levels. Should credit growth slow to 4 per cent or so, financial markets will probably feel the tightening.

But expanding balance sheets, whether they be personal, corporate or government, must in the medium/long term be balanced. Too much debt can lead to too much risk and too much equity can lead to less earnings per share growth under certain underperforming productivity cycles. Move them both at the same pace consistent with industry standards and economic growth more than likely expands as well.

Although hard to measure because of reporting lags, personal, corporate and government balance sheets have become unbalanced and growth in turn may suffer the consequences. Recent AI expansion financed in debt markets is anomalous by historical standards. Hundreds of billions of hyperscaler borrowings to finance data centre expansion are presumably a good bet on future growth promotion, but if not — “Houston, we’ve got a problem.”

The $1tn of AI-related investment that has been forecast for 2027 is likely to be funded by debt alone now that positive cash flow has disappeared.

It’s on the government balance sheet where risk is just as significant. Even the most optimistic economist must begin to recognise US debt levels are reaching “peacetime” peak levels with a net debt-to-GDP ratio of around 100 per cent. And boomer cohorts in populations will cause future social security, Medicare and Medicaid costs to swell. The transition to a future populated more by younger generations is years ahead.

What this implies for prospective financial markets is commonsensically apparent. Uneven balance sheet growth through taking on more debt has led to growth now, but likely lower later. Likewise, it has led to higher inflation now with little future respite absent global containment in fiscal/debt markets.

In such an environment, my view is: don’t own bonds, with the exception of one-year Treasury bills, which are now at 4.55 per cent. Be cautious with stocks at record levels as higher yields over time will contract profit margins. Be prepared for the end of “what you are used to” stock markets and higher volatility in prices for the benchmark 10-year Treasury bonds.

In terms of specific sectors, I am leery of hyperscalers unless they have price-earnings ratios of less than 20. And while I don’t own these stocks, the decent yields of Verizon and AT&T might be attractive for some conservative investors in the US market — though their businesses are threatened now by SpaceX’s Starlink Mobile in terms of mobile telephone markets.

There might also be opportunities in income funds trading at a discount to net asset values. Nuveen Preferred & Income Opportunities Fund, to cite an example where I don’t have a holding, is trading at about an 8 per cent discount to NAV and yields 11 per cent. However, like others in the sector, it would suffer if short rates move higher than expected.

Preserve and protect is my current investment motto.

Letter in response:
An American investor ‘ill-versed’ in Shakespeare / From Vipin Bharathan, New York, NY, US

item.title: The UK needs to do more to support its own AI companies
item.author: David Lammy
item.description: The prime minister needs a plan to avoid a US ban on Chinese models that would divide the world
item.content:encoded:
The prime minister needs a plan to avoid a US ban on Chinese models that would divide the world

David Lammy

The writer is a Labour MP and former foreign secretary

As foreign secretary, many of my counterparts would come to me saying they wanted to “do AI with Britain”. At the time I was only able to direct them to the AI Security Institute, a state research organisation. This was in sharp contrast to how the Americans or the French handle such a request, which is by pointing people straight to companies like Palantir or Mistral.

It was thus an astute move by Andy Burnham to announce at the United Nations last week that he wanted to put AI at the heart of Britain’s chairing of the G20 next year.

But to do so will be a challenge. Despite the smiles at the recent US-China state dinner in the White House, geopolitical tensions are rising. One looming flashpoint comes from reports that the US plans to ban cutting-edge, open Chinese AI models, citing security concerns and IP theft, and thus force its allies to follow suit. 

This would knock the legs out from under the European AI start-up scene and foreclose the faint hope of a genuine breakthrough in diplomacy on the subject at the G20. Martin Casado, a partner at Andreessen Horowitz, has said that when entrepreneurs walk through the VC firm’s doors there is a high chance they are using a Chinese open-weight AI model. The reason is cost. According to Vercel’s AI Gateway Production Index, these models cost roughly one-tenth of their average American counterparts. 

China is also aggressively promoting them. Knowing full well that every technology of tomorrow, from autonomous cars to automated factories, will be running on AI, the Chinese want to become the default model provider around the world. This will allow them to escape US export controls on critical components like chips by binding allies more closely to the Chinese stack. 

There are genuine security concerns about these Chinese open-weight models such as DeepSeek’s or the Alibaba Qwen series, and US agencies allege that many Chinese companies have inappropriately trained their models on American AI at industrial scale, using proxies and fake accounts to breach their terms of service. 

But they are also a commercial threat to the US. Why pay for an expensive American AI company subscription if you can just use a cheap Chinese model, as Airbnb does, or adapt one, as Thomson Reuters has? According to OpenRouter, a service used to access AI models, Chinese models have sat above 30 per cent of US companies’ token usage since February 2026.

The risk is mounting. All the White House has to do is decree that American software and cloud providers cease working with Chinese AI models and every British company that relies on some aspect of Microsoft, Google or Amazon — which is pretty much all of them — and is also trying to use Chinese AI will struggle to operate. Such a ban would be an immense setback to the European tech sector, where many companies use Chinese open-weight models, including frontier AI developer Mistral.

That is why Burnham needs a plan to avoid a US ban on Chinese AI that would divide the world. This requires a three-part strategy. 

First, the prime minister should develop a diplomatic plan with our allies to present to President Donald Trump, as we did in developing the Coalition of the Willing for Ukraine. Taking the Americans at their word about security and IP concerns, such a coalition should propose turning the UK’s AI Security Institute into a collective allied regulator that can assess whether Chinese open-weight models pose a threat, with a transparent, mutually designed process about the repercussions of a ban.

Second, we need to invest more in British AI so that we are not vulnerable to external pressure. There are extraordinary companies like Fuse, which is working on our energy grid, Era4, which is building data centres, or Fractile and Olix, which are building chips. The government needs to do more to support existing companies.

Third, we’ve made huge strides in launching the UK’s Sovereign AI fund this year, which has invested in 18 companies, including the British AI giant Demis Hassabis’s AI drugs venture, the efficient-compute company Callosum, and the new AI lab Ineffable Intelligence. These companies are building sovereign British AI capacity and the Foreign Office must promote them. 

As I saw in government, when the US abruptly banned the use of Anthropic’s latest models, the White House can take us by surprise. A ban on Chinese open-weight models would be far more than a temporary suspension of access. Burnham can get ahead of this by proposing a way to address security concerns while also building up a British technology stack that leaves us less vulnerable to coercion by either friend or foe.

item.title: Lex. Novo’s weight-loss deal highlights its weakness and the seller’s strengths
item.description: Hengrui deserves attention because it has not had much of late
item.content:encoded:
Hengrui deserves attention because it has not had much of late

Investors barely blinked at Novo’s deal, announced on Tuesday, to license an experimental weight-loss pill from China’s Hengrui Pharma, worth up to $2.6bn. They are right to be sceptical: it will take more than that for the rapidly shrinking Danish drugmaker to regain its dominance in the burgeoning GLP-1 market. But the deal highlights the significant potential of the HK$333bn ($42bn) Chinese biotech that developed the drug in the first place.

In common with other groups operating in the country, Hengrui has turned itself from a maker of cheap generics into a research and development powerhouse. Its R&D spending is healthy, equivalent to 23 per cent of sales in the first half of this year or broadly in line with innovative European pharmaceuticals groups such as AstraZeneca.

On top of that, it is good at turning ideas and money into pills and shots. It has attracted acclaim for treatments aimed at cancer and type 2 diabetes and is planning to launch more than 30 new innovative drugs between 2026 and 2027. At least part of its ascent reflects home advantages: operating in a nation where research and development capabilities are vast, clinical trials speedy and manufacturing efficient. 

One thing that sets Hengrui apart from its domestic peers is that it has reached escape velocity. It has cut 13 international licensing deals since 2023, worth $42bn, including treatments to Bristol Myers Squibb and GSK. These tend to bring in relatively modest upfront fees which ratchet up as milestones are met, though Novo’s $300mn upfront payment is on the generous side. Depending on terms, royalties on international sales can flow in after that.

Consensus analyst forecasts collated by Visible Alpha call for a near-doubling of Hengrui’s revenue by 2031, while operating profit is expected to rise even faster to $2.7bn. Government policy is conducive. Beijing has bold plans for the sector, aiming for China to produce at least a quarter of first-in-class drugs, and is targeting 20 per cent annual growth. It is also liberalising — at least slightly — tough curbs on pricing. Top innovative drugs should henceforth be able to charge prices that at least partially reflect their investment in R&D.

Finally, Hengrui deserves attention because it hasn’t had much of late. Its Hong Kong-listed shares have virtually halved in the past year, falling on earnings misses and a bulky but declining legacy generics business that makes up about a third of revenues. In an industry blighted with false hopes and drugs that fail to live up to their promise, Hengrui has the ingredients to perk up its own jaundiced investors.

louise.lucas@ft.com

item.title: Bond investors 💔 OATs
item.author: Toby Nangle
item.description: Sacré bleu
item.content:encoded:
Sacré bleu

Toby Nangle

Ruptures in US bond markets have, understandably, been taking up quite a lot of headspace lately. Continued bond market woes are important, and the US Treasury market is the most important of them all. Unless you’re French.

Because it won’t have escaped any French bond-type’s attention that the market for OATs is having a moment. And by moment we mean a bad one.

As MainFT writes today:

The government has said the deficit will widen to 5.5 per cent of GDP this year, well above target. Slowing economic growth — France now lags its neighbours — has also complicated efforts to improve its finances.

We know what you’re thinking. A 5.5 per cent budget deficit looks a little weedy compared to the Americans’ whopping 6 per cent of GDP. And pictured next to the rise in US yields, things really don’t look exceptionally awful:

But this is to compare apples and pears.

US Treasury prices are sinking/yields are rising for some combination of reasons (a higher expected path for Fed funds, rising term premia, higher breakeven inflation expectations), and while some of the rise in French bond yields is going to reflect Eurozone versions of these, these should be captured also in changes in German bond yields.

Unfortunately, if you compare French and German bond yields then it’s hard to escape the idea that it’s specifically French debt that investors really don’t like holding:

Never in the post-Whatever-It-Takes- era have 10-year and 30-year French bond spreads traded as high as they do now over their German equivalents.

Are investors spooked by polls showing that the Eurosceptic far-right Marine Le Pen is on track to win the presidency next year? Or by leftist challenger Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s idea to cancel some of France’s debt? Or maybe just by the seeming inability of the current minority government to win any kind of support from left or right to shrink next year’s budget deficit down to a mere 5 per cent of GDP?

Alphaville had been warming up for possible French debt fireworks in 2027, given all the exciting things scheduled to happen, but it’s increasingly looking like that timeline is being brought forward.

item.title: How to escape the low-pay, low-productivity jobs trap
item.author: Sangheon Lee
item.description: Informal employment may absorb surplus labour in developing countries but it can also weaken skills and economic resilience
item.content:encoded:
Informal employment may absorb surplus labour in developing countries but it can also weaken skills and economic resilience

Sangheon Lee

The writer is chief economist at the International Labour Organization

The broken link between economic growth and employment is now widely recognised. Too often, structural transformation has failed to create enough work, especially for young people in developing countries such as Rwanda and Ethiopia, who are having a tough time gaining a foothold in the labour market.

The problem is not just that there are too few jobs but that too many are low quality: informal, unprotected, low productivity, low pay, offering little opportunity to learn or move up. Some 2.1bn workers (around 58 per cent of the global workforce) remain in informal employment. More worryingly, research indicates that the gradual reduction of informal jobs associated with economic growth has stalled in recent years. 

There is a common assumption that when jobs are scarce, countries must choose between more jobs and better ones. Job quality, it is argued, can come later. But this mistakes short-term necessity for strategy. 

Low-quality jobs may absorb surplus labour but they can also weaken skills, productivity, demand and resilience. In so doing, they diminish the foundational capacity to generate more and better jobs.

This poorly understood dynamic is clearest when it comes to education and training.

Economic transformation requires workers to keep improving their abilities. But they are more likely to do so when new skills are rewarded through better pay, greater security or prospects for advancement. When this link is fragile, workers have less incentive to invest in training, companies have less pressure to upgrade and economies risk being stuck in low-productivity competition. 

Once again, this is a particular problem for young people whose first jobs often shape not only their income but their expectations, abilities and trust in the future. AI and other new technologies only make the issue more urgent. Without better jobs that allow workers to learn, adapt and share in productivity gains, tech advances may end up deepening existing divides.

Similarly, workers with protection against health and income risks can better cope with shocks and remain in the labour market.

There is therefore a strong economic case for investing in job quality through skills, social protection and support for productive small and medium-sized enterprises as part of strategies to avoid the low-pay, low-skill, low-productivity trap. 

But decent jobs also create social and non-financial value for workers, families and communities. They shape personal identity, stability, health, education and trust. Poor-quality jobs, by contrast, can impose wide-ranging hidden social costs. Markets may not always recognise all of the positive externalities that come from high-quality employment, so it must be a job for policymakers.

This echoes Indian economist Amartya Sen’s idea of development as the expansion of people’s real freedoms and capabilities. Work matters because it can enlarge (or restrict) people’s ability to plan, learn, participate and move forward. These capabilities can only be cultivated by systematic and sustained investment in job quality.

The renewed focus on employment by global financial institutions, such as the World Bank’s jobs agenda, is therefore a real opportunity.

But it should not stop at counting jobs. Development finance needs to ask sharper questions: whether the jobs it supports raise productivity, improve pay and prospects, build skills, strengthen workers’ voices and eventually create social returns.

Development policy should be built on the real possibility of progress, not desperation. Continued reliance on poor-quality jobs will ultimately weaken the very process on which future economic growth depends.

item.title: Trump’s coal drive plays into Beijing’s hands
item.author: Simon Mundy
item.description: Agreement on Chinese coal purchases reflects the administration’s misplaced focus
item.content:encoded:
Agreement on Chinese coal purchases reflects the administration’s misplaced focus

Simon Mundy

Welcome back.

The US government is on a mission to revive the country’s ailing coal industry. That may be good news for fossil fuel financiers at the biggest UK banks, which have reportedly bucked a European trend of cutting back support for the carbon-intensive fuel. It’s less good news for the US itself, as I explain below.

Trump’s eyes are on the wrong energy prize

Donald Trump spared no effort in his hospitality for Xi Jinping last week, meeting his Chinese counterpart’s plane on the tarmac and throwing him a black-tie dinner party studded with tech billionaires.

For all the pomp and ceremony, the meeting produced little in the way of solid agreements — with one interesting exception. “China will import at least 10 million metric tons of coal from the United States in 2027 and again [in] 2028,” the White House announced on Friday, trumpeting “President Trump’s revival of the US coal industry”.

That industry has rarely had such a supportive political champion as Trump — and has never needed one more. US coal production has fallen by about half since 2000. Over the same period, its share of national power generation has declined from 51 per cent to 17 per cent, and is set to keep falling inexorably over the years to come, according to forecasts from Trump’s own energy department.

Coal has been the single biggest driver of global warming, accounting for 46 per cent of fossil fuel carbon dioxide emissions. It also has a disastrous effect on the health of local communities, contributing to nearly 1mn deaths in 2021, according to a study published in The Lancet.

The main driver for coal power’s decline in the US, however, is not environmental but economic. The levelised cost range for new coal generation is significantly higher than that of gas power, and far above solar and onshore wind, according to a recent report from investment bank Lazard.

Trump’s administration has gone into battle with the laws of energy economics, issuing a string of emergency orders to block planned retirements of coal plants — despite resistance from state governments and the plants’ own operators. This month a federal appeals court struck down one of these orders, ruling that Washington had acted beyond the scope of its powers.

The government has separately announced more than $1bn in planned financial support for the coal sector, while cutting back the Biden administration’s fiscal incentives for clean energy investment.

The energy department insists that coal power is needed to meet the country’s rising electricity demands, and that coal exports will form an important part of its “energy dominance” agenda.

In the short term, Trump has boosted those exports by entering a conflict with Iran. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has sent natural gas prices soaring, prompting some Asian economies to lean more heavily on their coal power fleets. US coal exports rose 19 per cent in the second quarter of this year, according to researchers at S&P Global.

But the conflict has strengthened those same economies’ push for low-cost renewables, which are set to keep eroding coal power demand. The International Energy Agency projects that global coal generation will decline over the next four years even as total electricity demand continues to rise strongly. It estimates that coal’s share of global power generation will drop from 34 per cent in 2025 to 27 per cent in 2030, and keep falling thereafter.

That declining trend is now conspicuous in China, where the fuel’s share of power generation has fallen below 50 per cent for the first time.

China is still by far the world’s biggest coal market: its total consumption, including for power and other uses such as steel production, was nearly 5bn tonnes last year, more than half the global total. With domestic production squeezed after a major mine accident, the resumption of US imports — which had been in effect suspended amid the two countries’ trade dispute — will be a small but useful addition to its supply.

But the vast majority of new power, in China and internationally, is now coming from renewable sources, which accounted for nearly 86 per cent of global power capacity additions last year according to the International Renewable Energy Agency. China’s domestic surge in clean energy deployment has provided a springboard for global leadership in a huge and growing market. Chinese clean tech exports exceeded $220bn last year, estimate researchers at Ember.

Judging by the White House announcement, Xi agreed to the coal purchase pledge without getting any sort of firm US commitment in return. But if Trump’s government wants to focus on resisting the decline of coal — instead of competing in the low-carbon technologies of the future — Beijing has no strategic incentive to interfere.

Smart reads

  • Coffee-shop chain Starbucks — once one of the most prominent corporate ESG champions — has scrapped green goals and fired sustainability staff as part of a $2bn cost-saving drive.
  • Australia’s attempt to tax nicotine into extinction has fostered a giant black market controlled by organised crime, Nic Fildes reports from Sydney.

item.title: At least Burnham doesn’t pretend to care about growth
item.author: Janan Ganesh
item.description: Unlike his predecessors, Britain’s prime minister is a fairly honest stagnation-ist
item.content:encoded:
Unlike his predecessors, Britain’s prime minister is a fairly honest stagnation-ist

Janan Ganesh

The prime minister breaks the omertà at last. It is a brave act. He tells an ageing nation that pensions are too expensive at their current rate of increase. How true and how overdue. Here is a chance to lighten the tax burden on those in work. Andrew Murray Burnham, man of destiny, governing from the world’s first industrial city: unchain Britannia.

Oh. The cash is going on social care, specifically for the elderly. This will be a fiscal transfer from the retired to the retired. Burnham envisages a whole new arm of the welfare state for them, modelled on the NHS. (That is the NHS which is forever in need of being “saved”, according to Labour. A perverse thing to emulate, but there we are.) As the pension reform is small and the social care plan big, there is an implied tax rise, not a cut.

As ever with Britain, the wonder is not that it grows at just 1.3 per cent per year but that it manages even that much.

What is there to be said for Burnham? At least he does not pretend to care about growth. There is a refreshing candour about his indifference to this (admittedly paramount) issue. Sir Keir Starmer felt the need to pretend, which led to extreme disillusion when he raised taxes and red tape on business. The last few Conservative prime ministers extolled economic dynamism in the abstract while favouring pensioners, gumming up the planning system and spurning the vast single market on Britain’s doorstep.

Burnham is a fairly honest stagnation-ist. Until such time as Britain suffers an acute economic crisis, he would rather pursue left-liberal aims than growth, which might after all entail deregulation and other forays outside his comfort zone. Besides social care, a big item in his speech in Liverpool on Tuesday was reform of Britain’s majoritarian voting model. A man who spends scarce time and political capital on this while his country borrows more expensively than Greece is letting you know who he is. Even when he argued for unpicking Brexit, he framed it as a means of controlling immigration as much as a spur to trade.

Asked about a third runway at Heathrow, which could be an economic tonic, Burnham’s line is that it is “a matter for London”, as if he were not prime minister for London. He still says things like “UK plc”, which is the kind of 1990s flannel that someone of a certain age with nil interest in business would rote-learn to get through a speech or interview. What he calls his “theory of growth” is so sparse that I double-checked the transcript of the speech for a missing page.

This is just not what moves him. His inner self comes out in blurted, half-withdrawn remarks. Britain should rejoin the EU. A group called the Waspi women, who were unprepared for a rise in the pension age, deserve compensation. Britain should not be “in hock” to bond markets, whatever that means. National security must not come before social security. Football fans should be free to take beers to their seats. Burnham is pragmatic enough to let these statements die a natural death when critics poke holes in them. But notice the theme: not one is to do with growth. (Even his case for the EU was that he liked “unions of all kinds”: togetherness was the point, not wealth.) What was until recently seen by all as Britain’s central problem is not that much on his mind.

Of course, Burnham would rather that GDP expanded at 3 per cent per annum. But whether a government wants growth is never the question. The question is whether it wants growth more than it wants other things: equality, sovereignty, climate goals, low immigration. The US, a dynamo this past decade, does not have a growth strategy. What America has, when it is faced with trade-off after specific trade-off, is a growth preference.

If Britain’s answer is that other things matter more, there is no dishonour in the choice, as long as people accept the consequences of economic torpor. The dishonour is in the pretence: in the decade-long sham of prioritising growth but not really. It wasn’t even good for the governments who practised the deceit, as it deprived them of strategic direction.

So welcome the new candour. A Labour government exists to steer cash to its own people until the economic waters close over it. Burnham, unlike Starmer, hardly pretends otherwise. His relaxed charisma, which was not there earlier in his career, might even come from being open about his tribalism. (As a normal bloke, Burnham does normal things, such as join professional Labour politics at 24 and remain there at 56.) He hasn’t the shiftiness of someone feigning interest in people unlike himself. It is for Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch and others to build a winning coalition out of the voters he is taxing. Some will ask her what the hardest of Brexits has gained them.

The telling phrase in Burnham’s speech was “good growth”. Notice that qualifier, for there are two decades of national economic decline contained within it. A country that has underperformed since the financial crash is open to growth — how gracious of us — as long as it is not distasteful or unjust in some ill-defined sense. The growth must also touch “every postcode”, as if that ever happens anywhere. The hauteur, the almost regal choosiness, is majestic. And they say that Britain has lost its pride.

janan.ganesh@ft.com

item.title: Andy Burnham’s courageous speech had one striking omission
item.author: Stephen Bush
item.description: Prime minister touched some of the most controversial policy areas, but said nothing about Budget or spending review
item.content:encoded:
Prime minister touched some of the most controversial policy areas, but said nothing about Budget or spending review

Stephen Bush

Good morning from Liverpool. Andy Burnham delivered his first conference speech as prime minister yesterday.

Courage under constraints

Burnham used a wide-ranging, policy-rich speech to announce that Labour will, after the next election, scrap the “triple lock”, deepen EU-UK relations, change Britain’s electoral system and introduce a comprehensive social care model.

In the more immediate term, Labour will seek to unpick Margaret Thatcher’s economic revolution by increasing “public control” over more services and utilities, and to unwind her administrative revolution by increasing the power of local government.

In terms of its depth and engagement with some of the biggest issues facing the UK, for good and for ill it was the most serious speech delivered by a British prime minister since Theresa May left office. Burnham was willing to touch some of British politics’ most controversial policy areas: England’s social care crisis, relations with the EU and the pension triple lock. He deserves credit for doing so, because each of the debates that will spring up about his proposed solutions could derail his premiership.

There was, however, a striking omission. He said nothing at all about how the government is going to navigate its biggest immediate challenge, the Budget in October and the comprehensive spending review next year. Burnham has concluded that while the country wants change, he can’t deviate from the promises and manifesto he inherited from Keir Starmer this side of an election. The logic of his speech is twofold: first, the next election will not take place until 2029. And second, that until then he will remain bound not only by the real fiscal constraints the country is operating under, but the ones Labour has imposed on itself. Whether his programme and popularity can survive that remains to be seen.

Now try this

No trip to Liverpool is complete without visiting one of its many excellent museums and art galleries, so I’m off to potter around the Walker Art Gallery for a bit.

Top stories today

  • ‘Substantial increase’ | The energy price cap is forecast to rise by 16 per cent in January to nearly £2,000 because of the impact of the Iran war, further squeezing households.

item.title: ‘Big names in AI like Kyndryl’
item.author: Louis Ashworth
item.description: Love me tendril
item.content:encoded:
Love me tendril

Louis Ashworth

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham gave a big speech in Liverpool yesterday in which he laid out certain plans. Here, via the official speech, are some things he said:

The Mayor of the Liverpool City Region should not have had to fight Whitehall as hard as he did to get a new ferry built on the banks of the River Mersey.

And what a job he is doing.

Liverpool growing faster than the UK economy.

How often have we been able to say that in our lifetimes? What a brilliant thing to be able to say.

Places written off by the powers-that-be in the past now proving them wrong.

Bringing big names in AI like Kyndryl into the city.

Ah yes, big names in AI like … Kyndryl.

You know, Kyndryl.

Without googling, try to guess what Kyndryl is and what it does pic.twitter.com/mcodBgRvqm

— Tom Gara (@tomgara) December 7, 2022

Kyndryl:

“Kyn” comes from “kinship.” It represents the strong bonds we form with customers and with each other. Our people are at the heart of our business. “-dryl” is coined from “tendril,” evoking new growth and connections. By working together, we are growing.

New growth and connections between people are two of the core principles that make up our identity at Kyndryl. These principles are closely linked with our desire to provide oxygen to innovation, energy to change the world over, and to further human progress every day. The work we do at Kyndryl reflects these principles.

Come on. Kyndryl.

As the world’s largest provider of IT infrastructure services, Kyndryl is committed to the health and continuous improvement of the vital systems at the heart of the digital economy. With our partners and thousands of customers worldwide, we co-create solutions to help enterprises reach their peak digital performance.

Kyndryl:

Reuters, February 9 2026

Kyndryl’s shares plunged 53% on Monday after the software provider delayed the filing of its October-December report, made several management changes, and launched an accounting review over potential weaknesses found in its internal controls.

Kyndryl? Really? Nothing?:

The Company’s senior finance executives failed to set an appropriate tone at the top based on the principles associated with the control environment component of the COSO framework. Specifically, there was a lack of transparency with the Company’s Chief Executive Officer, the Audit Committee of the Board and the Board, such that disclosure processes, including with respect to cash management practices regarding deferring vendor payments quarter to quarter, were impacted. Additionally, the Company lacked an appropriate complement of finance personnel with sufficient understanding of their responsibilities as Disclosure Committee members and with adequate competency in their responsibilities regarding disclosure controls.

Look us in the eye. Kyndryl?

Trust fuels our purpose, frames our promise and focuses our mission

Nah, you’re having us on. You must have heard of Kyndryl — it’s a big name in AI:

Before the Court are competing motions to appoint lead plaintiff and lead counsel under the procedures set forth in the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995 (the “PSLRA”) in a putative securities class action against Kyndryl Holdings, Inc. (“Kyndryl”) and its executives.

item.title: Midterms and the market
item.author: Hakyung Kim
item.description: How much will it matter?
item.content:encoded:
How much will it matter?

Hakyung Kim

Good morning. The 10-year Treasury yield has been stable-ish at 5.25 per cent for a couple of days now. Have we all acclimated to the higher altitude? Stocks look steady and gold caught a bid for the first time in a while yesterday. Today we get the final revision to second-quarter GDP, the August PCE inflation numbers and Micron’s earnings report. Enough to get everyone excited again? Email us: unhedged@ft.com 

Midterms

The US midterm elections are in a little over a month. Currently, Republicans control both the House and the Senate; the consensus among Wall Street policy analysts is that the Democrats will retake the House while the Republicans will hold on to the Senate. Meanwhile, on Kalshi, the betting is that Democrats will win a clean sweep. 

We’re not in the business of political forecasting, but we are interested in the market implications of the likely scenarios — particularly the fiscal implications.

Republican control of the Senate, Democratic control of the House. In this case, there wouldn’t be much change to the fiscal backdrop, given the greater friction involved in the legislative process. Here’s EY-Parthenon’s Gregory Daco: 

Whenever we have a split Congress, that tends to lead to less [action] on the fiscal front — unless of course there is a recession — in which case, generally speaking, policymakers gather and promote support for the economy. But in the current environment, we’re not anticipating a recession, and so any form of stimulus would likely be just a reconciliation package

The caveat Daco mentions is as such: if the Republicans do lose their unified control of the House, then they could pass a reconciliation bill, focused on defence spending, in the window before the new Congress is sworn in. President Donald Trump has asked for $350bn in reconciliation. Even in the unlikely event his full demands are met, Elias Haddad of Brown Brothers Harriman notes, that increase amounts to only about 0.3 per cent of GDP annually, a small increase to the fiscal impulse: 

It’s unlikely going to be something to shift the dial on Fed rate expectations . . . Even if Reconciliation 3.0 gets approved and [comes] close to the president’s request, the gridlock within Congress means that we’re not going to have more fiscal spending in the pipeline, and that means fiscal policy will be a drag to growth 

A Republican sweep. The least-expected outcome. In this case, there could be another large reconciliation bill topping $1tn next year. Trump’s proposed $5,000 per adult payouts alone would come to $1.3tn. The sweep scenario “would likely support growth, pressure rates higher, and create the most risk-on outcome for credit”, according to Michael McLean at Barclays. That strikes us as an understatement.

Full Democratic control: A similar scenario of a Republican president paired with a Democratic Congress played out in 2006. What’s notable about that case, according to Haddad, is that “the political gridlock didn’t lead to fiscal gridlock”. In the first year following the midterm elections, fiscal policy was loosened while the Federal Reserve cut borrowing costs amid housing and credit pressures. 

But the comparison is imperfect. For one, signs of a weakening economy, and then an impending crisis, spurred bipartisan action. “Generally speaking, we see Congress act in a bipartisan way whenever there is a crisis,” says Daco. Barring a recession, a significant further increase in bond yields could lead to a bipartisan effort to cut spending, such as the (failed) Simpson-Bowles plan in the early 2010s. But we’re sceptical.

More broadly, the Trump administration has shown repeatedly that it doesn’t follow political convention or wait for congressional support before taking action. There’s no reason to expect Trump will behave differently in his final two years in office. “I’ve been telling clients — think about the way we’ve experienced lame duck presidencies in the past and throw that out the window,” says Ed Mills of Raymond James. He adds: 

Donald Trump is going to be unlike every other lame duck president we’ve had in history. He does not spend any time on defence. He always goes on the offence. And the biggest market impacts of his presidency have been when he has taken executive action. And my expectation is executive action, especially if there is a Democratic Congress, is going to become an even greater feature of his presidency, and [he will push the limits] further. 

One further twist: how might the election results affect AI investment, the key marginal source of GDP growth? AI data centre build-out has been increasingly contentious. “One of the takeaways from the elections is likely to be: if you oppose data centres, you win; if you support data centres, you lose,” Mills points out. The big economic legacy of this election might be local AI policy, not national fiscal policy. 

One good read

“One who is on his first journey.”
