item.title: Self-fulfilling bank runs just aren’t really a thing
item.author: Toby Nangle
item.description: Or, at least, that’s what the data seems to suggest
item.content:encoded:
Or, at least, that’s what the data seems to suggest

Toby Nangle

A few weeks ago we presented you with what we thought was an amazing animated history of global bank runs, backed with over 17,000 words of pop-up text. Oh how innocent Alphaville was back then.

Shortly after, we were contacted by Professor Emil Verner, one of the authors of some of the work ultimately backing the bank run data. It turns out we’re not the only fans of animated bank run maps.

Along with collaborators Sergio Correia of the Richmond Fed and Stephan Luck of the New York Fed, Verner has built what looks like the mother of all interactive databases of US bank runs, including an animated map of his own that plots bank runs and suspensions in the US all the way back to 1800.

Along the way you can pause their animation and click a dot. We haven’t replicated it here, but this is what it looks like:

Click here if you’ve had enough of reading this post and want to go play.

Their site allows you to click through to not only get a timeline for each bank run and what ultimately happened to it, but also access the archive of newspaper clippings attached to each episode.

So if you want to read about how Chicago bankers blamed Communist plotters for systematic attacks on the Stock Yards National Bank in 1933, how the Bank of Zapata was shuttered after its president mysteriously vanished in 1961 leaving a note in the window that the bank was “closed for an audit”, or check out the run on the Bank of Yolo, you can. 😊

Professor Verner told Alphaville that an extended team had built the database by running word searches for things like ‘bank’, ‘run’, and that kind of thing on 380mn newspaper reports scanned as part of the Library of Congress’s Chronicling America project, ultimately whittling it down to a mere 800,000-ish articles. Then they used LLMs to sift these articles further to find pieces about actual bank runs rather than, say, stuff about boats running into river banks, or the local bank manager running for mayor, and to match each report to individual banks.

Apart from making a monster resource that can be used for free by the world as a time sink that will sabotage the productivity of any self-respecting finance nerd to pursue further research, are there any quick takeaways?

Yes! According to Verner, the research reveals that the idea that runs kill solvent banks is dramatically overstated. It turns out that depositors are actually pretty good at working out how dodgy a bank is, generally making runs on banks that are insolvent or very close to insolvent.

Moreover, looking at recovery values on the banks that do fall over after a run, they find that banks that can’t take the heat of a bank run are almost always very insolvent. Receivers on average collect around 50 cents in the dollar on failed banks’ asset book value.

However, most bank runs didn’t actually result in bank failure. Surely the mere process of a run on a healthy bank wreaked havoc on their local economy? Apparently not.

Cross-referencing each bank’s financial strength, the researchers trace the local economic impact of each bank run using Bradstreet’s contemporary reporting. They find that a run on a strong bank doesn’t really impose any economic cost at all on the local economy. Yet runs on banks whose fundamentals are awful are followed by major lending contractions that can cause all sorts of spillover problems.

So, sure, bank runs are bad for local economies, but only if the banks that are being abandoned have been making bad loans, a big borrower defaults, or something like that.

That said, they do find a handful of seemingly irrational bank runs — runs they term “non-fundamental”. Out of 3,984 bank runs on individual US banks from 1863–1934, the authors identify 53 that look like they’re based on “misinformation” or “depositor confusion”, which reads as academese for “blind panic”.

Of these 53 oddities, six banks failed, which sounds like maybe six too many. But the researchers argue that the historical data indicates that “strong banks (fundamentals in the upper tercile) subject to non-fundamental runs have a zero probability of failure”. And one of the footnotes indicates that at least one of these failed banks had basically committed massive fraud, which was only uncovered by their so-called irrational run.

So where does SVB’s face-palm fit here? Surely a modern-day example of a self-fulfilling panic? Not so fast, reckons Verner.

At close to $20bn, the loss absorbed by the FDIC was pretty much the industry’s largest ever, even though this hit represented only 9 per cent of pre-run assets, or just a few billion dollars more than its equity capital. Running on a basically insolvent bank therefore looks legit. This is not to say that SVB couldn’t have got lucky and survived if it had never suffered a run. But then the same could maybe be said of FTX.

This is all pretty interesting, not least because Douglas Diamond and Philip Dybvig won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences, along with Ben Bernanke, for their fascinating work showing why banks are vulnerable to self-fulfilling runs.

And the ideas that the Nobel winners formalise are really the ones sitting behind the rationale for bank deposit insurance.

Further reading:
— Historical bank runs database
— 140 years of banking crises and bailouts (FTAV)
— Visualising US bank failures (FTAV)

item.title: Lex. The crucial things Anthropic’s jumbo ‘risk factors’ won’t tell you
item.description: The real question for those considering buying stock is whether it will make money
item.content:encoded:
The real question for those considering buying stock is whether it will make money

Depending on the kind of person you are, the “risk factors” section of a company’s initial public offering document is either the first place you look or the last. Anthropic’s will be more readable than most, thanks to its stark warning that the AI lab’s products could extinguish humanity. But some more salient information will almost certainly be absent.

The practice of itemising risks to a new stock in its pre-IPO filing, and thereafter in annual reports, is a classic example of good intentions gone awry. Such disclosures have been mandatory in the US since the 1960s. But through a combination of regulatory diktat and fear of lawsuits, they have multiplied. Microsoft in 1986 offered fewer than two pages. SpaceX this year stretched to 38. Uber, in 2018, filled 50.

Anthropic might be the first to warn of human extinction as a potential input into a $2tn valuation, but weird warnings are not unknown. Lab testing firm Charles River advises of the risk of transmitting “new pathogens”. President Donald Trump’s media group TMTG warned in 2024 that the company could be “significantly disadvantaged” were its founder to wind up incarcerated. Nuclear energy firms, naturally, have to nod to the unthinkable.

Is obliterating all humans a risk worth elucidating? If it happens, there will be nobody left to sue, so perhaps not. But noting AI’s apocalyptic potential is still helpful, because if lawmakers impose stringent, profit-sapping curbs on Anthropic’s business model because of such existential fears, lawsuits may fly.

The real question for those considering buying Anthropic stock is whether it will make money. On that, the IPO filing is, at best, only moderately useful. Anthropic, like all companies, is likely to refrain from sharing its executives’ forecasts of revenue and profit. Instead, it will report backwards-looking figures, which are next to useless because of its rapid rate of change. Last year’s revenue was $4.6bn, the FT has reported; already this year, its run rate in July was $65bn.

This lacuna is the result of a legal quirk: companies enjoy protection from legal liability if they disclose forecasts once they’re public, provided they do so in good faith, but not before. Researchers at Arizona State University, University of North Carolina, the University of Washington and the University of Michigan found that one-third of listing companies tackled this problem by giving verbal guidance in their pre-IPO “roadshow”, but even they mostly stick to broad strokes on steady-state profit margins.

Other insights investors might want but are unlikely to get: who are the two customers that made up a quarter of Anthropic’s revenue last year? And if there really is a risk of AI apocalypse, how risky is it exactly? Anthropic could report its view of P(doom), the mathematical probability of mass destruction. It could even provide a table showing what happens to future earnings if the number goes up or down — as banks often do regarding interest rates.

Instead, expect Anthropic to provide the worst of all worlds: fuzzy estimates of its “total addressable market”. It may even try to outdo rival SpaceX, which touted $28.5tn in its IPO filing — an astronomical 600 times the revenue analysts expect Elon Musk’s rocket maker to generate this year. The real risk factor is the likelihood that investors are too easily impressed and end up dramatically disappointed.

john.foley@ft.com

item.title: Is the world really drowning in debt?
item.author: Martin Wolf
item.description: We may not be on the eve of disaster but room for manoeuvre is shrinking for major economies
item.content:encoded:
We may not be on the eve of disaster but room for manoeuvre is shrinking for major economies

Martin Wolf

Gross global debt reached $365tn, or 311 per cent of global GDP, in the first half of 2026, according to the latest Global Debt Monitor from the Institute for International Finance. Should we be worried? The IIF thinks so, pointing out that “Mature market governments now spend more on interest expense than the world invests in either AI, defense, or energy” and “Debt has become more a political issue than a macro-financial one — creating a vicious cycle between elections and short-term quick fixes, and a long-term vulnerability as the marginal utility of higher debt diminishes.” What is still more striking, is that the IIF worries more about high-income than developing or emerging economies.

Yet the IIF also shows that between 2018 and June 2026, the rise in the ratio of global debt to output was less than 10 percentage points. That hardly sounds so bad. The story is striking: the ratio reached a post-Covid peak of 337 per cent in early 2021, before falling by 27 percentage points by the end of 2023. What was this magical “debt-buster”? Good old-fashioned (and supposedly “unexpected”) inflation. This is — to put it mildly — not the first time inflation has wiped out debt. It was, to take one of countless examples, an important part of the UK’s elimination of its post-second-world-war debt. For countries able to print the money in which their debt is denominated, that is often what happens. (See charts.)

Yet inflation leaves a legacy. It is one of the reasons interest rates are now much higher than pre-Covid. Interest costs have soared for governments in mature economies: between December 2021 and the end of August 2026, these jumped by 1.5 percentage points, to reach 3.3 per cent of GDP. The US is a good example: as a share of GDP, interest costs rose 1.6 percentage points between January 2021 and 2026.

What is happening with the level and costs of government borrowing is central — but it is not everything. The IIF also notes the huge recent rise in issuance of AI-linked corporate bonds. It estimates that this will reach $541bn in 2026, up from $90bn three years before. The associated investment boom is also a driver of the higher interest rates and so an indirect cause of the higher cost of government debt.

Remarkably, AI-related corporate debt is issued at far longer maturities than US Treasuries: in 2026 so far, the average maturity of the former reached 13.4 years (from 11.5 years in 2024) against a mere 2.5 years for US Treasuries (down from 6.1 years in 2024). Interest on corporate AI-related debt is also only a percentage point higher than on Treasuries. While US government borrowing is strikingly short term, other high-income governments are not far behind.

The IIF indeed seems more relaxed about private than government debt and that of emerging economies than of high-income ones. It notes, for example, that private credit, about which there is some concern, “accounts for only around 5 per cent of outstanding non-financial corporate debt”. On the latter, it points to the record pace of sovereign Eurobond issuance in 2026, adding that “stronger fundamentals have helped”. It also stresses the health of “ESG lending”, with year-to-date lending of $1tn.

In sum, the IIF’s view is that the recent inflation-induced fall in debt ratios has created a “deceptively benign picture”. With structurally higher interest rates than a few years ago and governments without the will or the mandate to impose pain on voters, public debt will continue to accumulate in supposedly mature countries at a rapid rate. Meanwhile, the shift to shorter maturities, notably in the US, flatters to deceive. The risk is that there could be a sharp jump in these yields, with dramatic results for the cost of debt service. A possible trigger might be sharp depreciation of a vulnerable currency.

There are also political risks. War is one. Energy shocks are another. Bigger trade conflicts are yet another. It is also not hard to imagine outright internal conflict in the US or a breakdown of co-operation in the EU. If the far right were to become a dominant political force, the implicit support of, say, France by Germany, might even be in question.

My take from the IIF’s report is not that we are on the eve of disaster but that important countries are losing room for manoeuvre on an unsustainable long-run path. As the late economist Herbert Stein famously said, “If something cannot go on forever, it will stop.”

Huge accumulations of public debt cannot be justified forever, particularly when there is no crisis to justify them. But there is also a corollary to Stein’s law by the late economist Rüdiger Dornbusch, who said that: “crises take longer to arrive than you can possibly imagine, but when they do come, they happen faster than you can possibly imagine.” His expertise was Latin America. Many must have noticed the growing similarity between that region and the US.

In emerging countries that rely on borrowing in foreign currencies, the crises Dornbusch had in mind tend to require a foreign rescue. That is not the case for countries able to borrow in their own currencies. The latter can also play all sorts of games with their lenders, be they domestic or foreign. One is “financial repression” in which lenders are forced to accept lower interest rates or, in other ways, lend to governments on unfavourable terms. The US is powerful enough (the UK most definitely is not) even to coerce foreign lenders. But such tricks never work forever.

Dornbusch’s law still applies: it can merely take a long time to get there. Maybe even the free capital flows we are so used to will be sacrificed. But inflation is almost always the first resort. Why else does Trump want the Fed to put rates at 1 per cent?

martin.wolf@ft.com

Follow Martin Wolf with myFT and on Twitter

item.title: Time for some DIY LDI
item.author: Robert Buckland
item.description: The spread between equity and bond valuations has narrowed to the point where government-guaranteed real cash flows can finally be bought at reasonable prices
item.content:encoded:
The spread between equity and bond valuations has narrowed to the point where government-guaranteed real cash flows can finally be bought at reasonable prices

Robert Buckland

The writer is senior adviser at Engine AI and Investa, and former chief global equity strategist at Citigroup

For the first half of my career, UK equity valuations closely tracked the yields on the type of gilts where returns are linked to inflation. The 2000–03 bear market broke that neat relationship, but it is making a comeback.

As a green young strategist in the early 1990s, I asked my boss how to value the UK stock market. His gruff reply: “It’s simple, equities trade on the same yield as linkers.” That rule of thumb worked for many years. If real yields rose, as in 1994, then equities derated. If real yields fell, as in the late 1990s, they re-rated.

There is a simple logic behind this. Both assets offer an inflation hedge, albeit of different quality. Index-linked gilts adjust principal and coupons in line with the Retail Prices Index. Equities pay dividends that should, theoretically, rise in line with nominal corporate revenues.

However, during the early 2000s bear market, the relationship broke. Index-linked prices rose relentlessly, driving the benchmark real yield below zero in 2012 and down to almost minus 3 per cent in 2021. Meanwhile, equity dividend yields drifted higher, including spikes as shares fell during the 2007–09 financial crisis and 2020 Covid pandemic panic. Having matched index-linked yields for the 1980s and 1990s, equities paid a yield premium of 3.3 percentage points on average between 2001 and 2021.

To explain this profound change, I could use technical terms such as equity risk premia, terminal growth, natural rates and the like. But let’s keep it simple. It was about buying and selling.

The 2000—03 bear market in stocks left deep scars, especially among UK pension funds. Falling equity prices depleted assets while lower bond yields increased future liabilities. Defined benefit pension funds fell into deficit and many closed to new entrants. New accounting rules encouraged fund trustees to match assets against liabilities more closely. Many adopted liability-driven investment (LDI) strategies. 

The impact of this on asset allocation was stark. UK pension funds held roughly half their assets in UK equities in 1999. That weighting fell below 1 per cent in 2025 for defined benefit schemes, according to the Pension Protection Fund. As they sold UK equities, these funds bought into liability-matching index-linked gilts, pushing the weighting up to 31 per cent in 2025.

This was like pouring a gallon into a pint pot. The UK equity market (currently worth some £4.9tn) is much bigger than the linker market (currently about £688bn). And the big move in linker prices was not just happening for domestic reasons. The bond-buying programmes by central banks known as quantitative easing contributed to negative real yields everywhere.

This relative valuation shift encouraged the “de-equitisation” of the UK stock market. Listed companies issued debt to buy back shares. Others delisted via debt-financed mergers and acquisitions.

But things started to reverse in 2022. Central banks hiked interest rates and began to unwind QE, driving real yields up everywhere. In the UK, the September 2022 mini-Budget spooked the markets and savaged leveraged LDI strategies. Index-linked prices collapsed, pushing real yields back into positive territory for the first time in 10 years. They are still rising amid fiscal concerns and fears of rate hikes. The 15-year real gilt yield is now 2.3 per cent, not far below the FTSE dividend yield of 3.0 per cent.

What does this all mean? First, it reduces the financial logic behind de-equitisation. The giant spread between equity and bond valuations has narrowed. To use financial jargon, the UK equity risk premium is normalising.

It also has important implications for those, like me, approaching retirement age. I have been saving into equities my whole life. I can now sell these at all-time highs and, finally, buy reasonably priced government-guaranteed real cash flows to cover my future spending needs. If I wait, maybe those cash flows will get even cheaper but, if I’m holding the bonds to maturity, then I don’t really care. This retirement trade looks even more attractive in the US. Investors there can currently sell the S&P 500 on a 1.1 per cent dividend yield to buy future real cash flows via 10-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities yielding a real 2.9 per cent.

For much of this century, selling equities to buy an index-linked annuity became prohibitively expensive. That has now changed. The strategy, of course, is not for everyone — circumstances vary and professional personal advice should be sought. But for me it’s finally time for some DIY LDI.

item.title: Lex. Armani’s last wishes may sell his fashion empire short
item.description: The fashion house is set to kick off a three-way process with LVMH, L’Oréal and EssilorLuxottica for the sale of a minority stake
item.content:encoded:
The fashion house is set to kick off a three-way process with LVMH, L’Oréal and EssilorLuxottica for the sale of a minority stake

Successful dealmaking is all about reading the moment and the room. This is particularly hard to do, though, from beyond the grave. That’s a problem for fashion house Armani which, in accordance with the instructions left by its founder, is poised to kick off a three-way process with LVMH, L’Oréal and EssilorLuxottica for the sale of a minority stake.

In principle, Giorgio Armani’s request makes sense. His fashion group is potentially attractive to an outside investor. As one of the first movers in a now crowded space, it boasts strong name recognition and a classic look that appeals to a large audience. And, while one might quibble with the choice of “preferred buyers” — two out of three aren’t even in the fashion business — any one of them would help steady the ship upon its captain’s departure.

Trouble is, this isn’t a good time for Armani — which Lex has in the past calculated could be worth €6.5bn — to sell. The luxury slump has pushed LVMH’s share price down nearly 40 per cent this year and the sector bellwether has been trimming its portfolio, offloading Marc Jacobs earlier this month. Meanwhile, EssilorLuxottica has gone all in on Meta’s smart specs and L’Oréal has recently written a big cheque to Kering, potentially making them even less likely to want to leap into the fray.

Hence the idea currently doing the rounds of the preferred buyers splitting the 15 per cent of Armani on offer three ways. For a few hundred million euro each, EssilorLuxottica and L’Oréal would protect their licences for Armani glasses and beauty respectively, while LVMH, perhaps aided by the judicious use of call options, would stake out its territory for a potential future acquisition.

But while such a patchwork solution might suit the buyers and comply with the founder’s last wishes, it is by no means clear that it would be best for the company. Armani’s revenue declined 2.8 per cent in 2025 and, over time, the group has sprouted a whole host of more-or-less affordable sub-brands. It could do with some vigorous remodelling, which a consortium of heirs and minority investors is unlikely to deliver.

That’s a reminder to entrepreneurs the world over that being a visionary businessman and actually being able to see into the future are two very different things.

camilla.palladino@ft.com

item.title: The Big Read. The risks of HSBC’s return to its roots
item.author: Arjun Neil Alim and Ortenca Aliaj
item.description: Doubling down on Hong Kong offers a way to capitalise on wealth flowing out of China, but increases the risks of confrontation with Beijing
item.content:encoded:
Doubling down on Hong Kong offers a way to capitalise on wealth flowing out of China, but increases the risks of confrontation with Beijing

Arjun Neil Alim and Ortenca Aliaj

When Thomas Jackson worked as chief manager of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation in the British territory in 1899, he and the institution were so integral to the region that a letter addressed simply to “T.J., China” was duly delivered to him.

In the century that followed, HSBC leveraged this dominance of a remote outpost of Britain’s empire to expand across the world. Acquisitions in the Middle East, the Americas and Europe helped make it one of the world’s largest banks by assets.

But over the past five years, outbound investment into new markets and businesses has been thrown into reverse. The company that until recently marketed itself as “the world’s local bank” is now firmly staking its future on Chinese wealth flowing out of the country, rather than western capital flowing in.

HSBC, comfortably Europe’s largest bank by market capitalisation, “is now a bet on China outbound”, principally from its base in Hong Kong, says a former senior executive at the bank. Its presence in China itself is much smaller, while the UK, its other major profit centre, is a much slower-growing market.

“[Chinese wealth] is a once-in-a-lifetime structural growth opportunity . . . We are best placed to capitalise on that,” says another senior HSBC banker. Executives at the bank believe there are 73mn people in the country who could potentially be interested in offshore wealth services — a number that has more than doubled since 2022, according to internal presentations.

Capturing a bigger slice of that could generate fee income that tends to grow with assets under management, is less vulnerable to interest rate movements and also does not require much regulatory capital.

But the strategy comes with risks. A slowdown in China’s economy could affect its rate of wealth creation, while managing assets from Chinese offshore leaves HSBC exposed to crackdowns by Beijing — such as the “common prosperity” campaign against capitalist excess that started in 2021, or more recent investigations into historical foreign capital gains.

There is also the long-held fear that China’s leaders may try to assert more influence over the bank, either through regulation or by acquiring shares. Some suspect Beijing may have tacitly supported an attempt by Chinese insurer Ping An in 2022 to force the bank to spin off its Asian entity into a separate business — though HSBC has said it saw no evidence of this and Ping An has always declined to comment.

Even so, Georges Elhedery, appointed chief executive two years ago, has accelerated the rush to the east. He has largely withdrawn HSBC from helping companies raise equity and providing M&A advice in many markets, split the bank’s operations into eastern and western spheres, and spent over $13bn acquiring full control of Hong Kong-based Hang Seng Bank.

“Increasing exposure to Hong Kong and capturing growth from wealthy Chinese clients has worked reasonably well,” says one top-20 shareholder in HSBC. “On the other hand, clearly, this has also come under [Chinese] government scrutiny.” 

HSBC’s co-CEO for Asia, Surendra Rosha, said in a statement that the bank is “delivering focused, sustainable growth across our four businesses in line with our strategy”. Hong Kong, he added, “is far from the only opportunity we see. We are investing to capture structural wealth growth and connect Asia to the world for our clients.”

Unassailable in Hong Kong

Even before Elhedery’s latest pivot to Asia, Hong Kong was HSBC’s biggest source of both revenues and profits. According to an FT analysis of first-half results, the territory plus China accounted for almost half of group pre-tax profit.

The Hong Kong business unit also generates the highest returns, as measured by return on tangible equity, at an annualised 44 per cent in the first half. That is more than double the 21 per cent recorded in the UK.

Comparisons with previous eras can be challenging due to frequent restructurings, but Hong Kong and China combined accounted for 40 per cent of HSBC’s total revenues in 2025.

Asia accounts for almost 70 per cent of HSBC’s global wealth balances with $1.1tn managed in the region, while almost $9 in every $10 of new inflows in that business during the first half of 2026 came from Asia.

China-related business also accounts for a significant portion of the bank’s corporate and institutional banking arm. Hong Kong is the only place where HSBC has maintained a competitive equity capital markets division, and bankers say that bringing companies to market there generates windfalls for founders that represent another wealth management opportunity.

Hong Kong overtook Switzerland last year as the world’s largest cross-border wealth hub, according to the Boston Consulting Group, with $2.9tn of non-local assets.

In retail banking, HSBC reinforced its longstanding dominance of the Hong Kong market earlier this year by acquiring the 36 per cent of Hang Seng Bank that it did not already own, allowing it to upsell premium and wealth services to Hang Seng’s 3.3mn customers.

Alex Potter, global financials analyst at shareholder Aberdeen Investments, says the deal was on the expensive side but adds that “increasing your profit contribution from Asia, when it is growing incredibly fast, is a brilliant thing to have done”.

One of the largest components of HSBC’s wealth-related income in 2025 was insurance, driven by Chinese visitors to Hong Kong. Many mainland Chinese buy non-renminbi insurance policies in person, allowing them to legally diversify their currency exposure and place assets beyond China’s capital controls.

Such policies tend to pay out an annuity-like income and their holders will often open HSBC bank accounts to pay premiums or receive dividends. There are 7.3mn HSBC and Hang Seng accounts in a city of 7.52mn people and HSBC is on track to add more than 1mn new customers in Hong Kong for the second year running, according to its investor presentations.

“A lot of new customers in HSBC Hong Kong are non-residents,” says Kathy Chan at Morningstar, the investment research firm. “[Although] they do not disclose where the non-residents are from, we do believe HSBC is benefiting from the China wealth flow.”

Insurance purchases hit an all-time high in the first half of 2025, the last available figures before the territory’s Insurance Authority stopped disclosing the proportion bought by mainland visitors, in a sign of the sensitivity of the metric.

The bank’s hiring also indicates an institution pivoting to China. Although a snapshot of current vacancies may not provide an accurate picture of hiring across a full year, an FT analysis of current job openings at the group shows almost half of vacancies are in Hong Kong and China, with 29 per cent in the mainland.

This build-out has its challenges, particularly for the group’s focus on scaling up in China. “Getting good relationship managers in [mainland China] . . . is not a given,” says one senior HSBC banker.

Benefits and perks for senior HSBC employees in Hong Kong are increasingly aligned with those of Hang Seng bankers, who are mostly recruited locally. An institution that once dispatched cohorts of “international officers” from the UK to occupy key roles abroad has recently cut back on perks such as private school fees and club memberships for expatriate staff.

“All senior [local] roles have to be Mandarin speakers in Hong Kong and China,” adds one person familiar with the bank’s hiring in China.

The contrast with HSBC’s UK business, its other single big profit centre, is striking. Just 3.3 per cent of open jobs are in the UK. Revenue growth in the UK is slower, while profit growth in recent quarters has been driven mostly by a widening spread between what the bank pays depositors and what it receives from borrowers or investments, rather than fee income.

Exposed to risks

HSBC may have a dominant position in Hong Kong, but it is yet to translate into a commanding market share in mainland China, despite heavy investment in the country.

The bank acquired Citigroup’s retail wealth management portfolio in China in 2024, adding approximately $3.6bn in deposits and assets and giving it an established client base of affluent customers across almost a dozen cities.

“HSBC’s ambition is to be the leading international wealth manager for mass affluent and high-net-worth individuals in mainland China,” Nuno Matos, who was then head of wealth and personal banking, declared at the time.

But it is a long way from achieving that goal. HSBC booked more than $200mn of profit from wealth management in China in the first half — a significant increase from just $8mn in the same period last year, but still small in relative terms. The city-state of Singapore made the bank $346mn on the same measure in the same period. 

HSBC boasts a strong position among foreign banks in the mainland market and is one of a few to wholly own its onshore insurance business. But the big four state-owned banks still dominate the market.

“They are not competitive in the domestic Chinese market,” says one former HSBC executive in Hong Kong. “HSBC doesn’t have retail distribution, a branch network or brand awareness [in mainland China].”

Elhedery has since expanded the network of so-called wealth centres, where advisers can court affluent clients, across Beijing, Chengdu, Hangzhou, Ningbo, Shanghai, Shenzhen and Wuxi. HSBC executives also gathered this summer in Nansha, a ferry ride from Hong Kong, where the bank has established a training centre for over 14,000 employees.

Matt Choi, analyst at Fitch Ratings, says the bank is playing to its strengths. “In onshore China, investment mainly went into wealth management in previous years, but demand has been stronger for cross-border flows,” he says, “[The] Hong Kong business has been the key beneficiary.”

Meanwhile, HSBC’s growing emphasis on Chinese wealth moving abroad inevitably exposes the bank to more policy risk from Beijing.

Over the summer, its share price whipsawed after the FT reported a fresh tax crackdown on insurance and offshore trusts, the latest in a series of measures to prevent wealth leaving the country.

China has moved more broadly to regulate outbound investment flows and close loopholes used by wealthy individuals to shelter overseas assets from tax liabilities, spurred by the need to raise tax revenues and a desire to limit capital flight, according to analysts at Barclays.

As a bank created to facilitate trade between east and west, HSBC has long had to navigate geopolitics along with the varying regulatory hurdles of different markets.

The FT spoke to one member of a wealthy Chinese family and HSBC premier client, who praises the bank’s global transaction network and ease of use but bridles at what he regards as an intrusive onboarding process. “Are they making opening accounts easier for Chinese people?” he asks.

But the geopolitics can be extremely delicate. In 2021, HSBC found itself caught in the tussle between US authorities seeking the extradition of Meng Wanzhou, the chief financial officer of telecoms equipment group Huawei, and a Chinese government seeking to protect a national champion.

After the bank handed over records related to the case to US prosecutors, Beijing threatened to add HSBC to its “unreliable entity list” while Huawei took it to court in the UK.

Some fear that HSBC’s continued shift towards Asia could give Chinese partners, regulators or policymakers more leverage. Ping An’s attempt to split the bank up was fended off at the time by Noel Quinn and Sir Mark Tucker, then chief executive and chair.

Neither is still at the bank, and not everyone is convinced the current senior leadership team has the depth of experience needed to navigate its increasingly consequential relations with Beijing.

During its search for a new chair, HSBC struggled to find executives with sufficient Asia and China experience. It considered former UK chancellor George Osborne and Kevin Sneader, president of Asia ex-Japan at Goldman Sachs, but ended up appointing Brendan Nelson, a well-regarded former KPMG executive who has had little direct involvement with China.

It said at the time that Nelson had demonstrated “excellent leadership capabilities backed by strong banking and governance credentials”. But one former executive still questions whether the bank has “the right people in the right roles to deal with the geopolitical situation they are in now”.

Additional reporting by Emma Dunkley in London. Data visualisation by Haohsiang Ko in Hong Kong

item.title: FT Weekend Fest: How AI is really changing jobs
item.description: Sarah O’Connor on the impact AI is already having in the workplace
item.content:encoded:
Sarah O’Connor on the impact AI is already having in the workplace

Murad Ahmed speaks to FT journalist Sarah O’Connor about her new book ‘We Are Not Machines’, which explores the impact AI is already having on workplaces. They discuss how Swedish miners dealt with the introduction of AI-powered vehicles, and how Czech translators found AI stealing the most creative part of their job. Recorded live at the FT Weekend Festival.

item.title: The Lady Gaga moment for corporate Japan
item.author: Leo Lewis
item.description: Recruitment ad by megastar points to the mounting labour problems and misallocation of human capital
item.content:encoded:
Recruitment ad by megastar points to the mounting labour problems and misallocation of human capital

Leo Lewis

The new staff recruitment campaign by FamilyMart is striking. Global megastars, however sincerely they worship your fried chicken tenders, do not come cheap: hiring Lady Gaga to dance for 30 seconds and ask “Why not work for FamilyMart?” marks a distinct new episode for corporate Japan.

Superficially, the company’s need to spend big and raise its game on recruitment is clear enough. But the timing is especially revealing. 

Japan, out of deflation and in labour deficit, now offers fewer cushions between companies and reality. The prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, has an investment-driven growth agenda that threatens to narrow the padding even further. The pressures of monetary normalisation, after years of ultra-loose central bank policy, demand increasingly abnormal thinking from corporate leaders.

The labour-shortage implications of Japan’s shrinking, ageing demographics are not new, but have thoroughly caught up with it. In July, across all industries, the ratio of jobs-to-applicants was almost 1.2 times, while in parts of construction it was as high as 7.9. 

Even with a sustained availability of immigrant workers, businesses like FamilyMart have few places to hide: self-checkouts, robot shelf-stackers and AI-powered tech will go a long way, but keeping such full-spec, high-quality retail running 24/7 still requires people, and lots of them. 

FamilyMart is currently advertising for about 10,000 part-time staff for its domestic network; its larger rival 7-Eleven is looking for around twice that number, and is doing so without the star power of Lady Gaga.

More and more companies, say advertising agencies and consultancies, are diverting larger slabs of budget into recruitment campaigns. They are doing so with a sense of urgency — not in a hunt for raw staffing numbers but for a suite of skills and a likelihood of loyalty that are in even more acute scarcity. Japan has a crisis of misallocation, say company HR departments.

As Japan entered the millennium, a series of unspoken pacts were in place. The Bank of Japan had begun what would become a quarter-century experiment with ultra-low interest rates; companies, for their part, would spare the country mass unemployment by avoiding the most brutalising version of creative destruction; investors, by and large, would not make too great a fuss. 

Companies that might not have survived in another environment muddled through, delaying consolidation and favouring sprawl. The labour market, in industries that thrived in other countries on liquidity, became viscous. People who might otherwise have retrained and moved elsewhere stayed put, bloating the workforce in non-useful places. Equity was not called upon to work its socks off for returns. 

All of this was a recipe for a protracted, double misallocation of financial and human capital that has been exposed by two changes. The first has been the push for greater governance reform — a process that started with Japan’s first corporate governance code in 2015. Early iterations of the code provided the basis on which investors could more effectively push Japanese companies to change their behaviour — primarily by focusing more sincerely on shareholders, thinning their flocks of non-core businesses and improving the independence of boards. But the most recent revision, in July this year, calls on companies to continuously review and explain allocation of resources, including human capital.

The second major change has been the normalisation of monetary policy by the Bank of Japan, which has raised its target interest rate to 1.25 per cent. That level is still low enough to be entirely manageable. But the psychological nudge, say executives, is starting to have an impact: even if they are not doing so yet, the prospect of a higher cost of money is creating an expectation that capital allocation will, eventually, become a more existential activity than it has been in Japan for over two decades. That should drive companies to become more active participants in job markets, in turn providing far greater social licence for people to change jobs and reskill for deployment where the economy most needs them.

FamilyMart has recruited Lady Gaga to its recruitment drive because it needs lots of younger people who can be rapidly trained up to work with whatever new technology the company employs to keep itself in business. But her appearance signals the start of a much broader recruitment arms race in a Japan where corporate survival is no longer guaranteed.

leo.lewis@ft.com

item.title: Lex. Shein’s pain is high street retailers’ gain
item.description: UK’s imminent end of duty-free loophole for low-cost imports will benefit Hong Kong-listed company’s rivals
item.content:encoded:
UK’s imminent end of duty-free loophole for low-cost imports will benefit Hong Kong-listed company’s rivals

Shein, the ultra-cheap fashion machine that delivers clothes to customers’ doorsteps, is finding growth hard to come by. That, at least, is the message from its maiden set of results as a Hong-Kong listed company, which knocked 12 per cent off its stock. While Shein’s investors reach for their cash flow models, its cut-price rivals will be reaching for the champagne. 

The juggernaut’s business model relied on offering infinite choice while undercutting rivals on price. But that cost competitiveness is coming undone as a growing number of countries join the US in putting an end to duty-free treatment for low-value imports, prompting Shein to raise prices. Its sales in Europe, where the “de minimis” loophole recently closed, were down almost 14 per cent in the second quarter.

That creates an opening for local fast-fashion groups. In the US, the beneficiaries from Shein’s retreat included Gap-owned Old Navy, Ulta Beauty, Nordstrom Rack and thrift store chain Savers Value Village, according to data provider Consumer Edge. With the rules now in effect in Europe, cheap online retailers such as German operator Zalando have reason to cheer. 

The glad tidings are soon to reach the UK high street, with the de minimis exemption scheduled to be scrapped in late 2028. The country’s low-cost fashion operators have a lot of ground to reclaim: UK consumers spend an estimated £4.7bn a year on Chinese ultra-low-cost platforms such as Shein and Temu, equivalent to roughly 5 per cent of the country’s non-food online sales, according to consultancy Retail Economics.

Potential beneficiaries of a UK rule change include Asos, Debenhams Group — owner of Boohoo and PrettyLittleThing — and ABF-owned Primark. And the bonanza from also hobbling Temu, which sells tools, tech, home furnishings and virtually anything in between, would extend to non-fashion groups such as Currys, Argos and car parts provider Halfords.

Of course, it is just about possible that, over the next two years, Shein will tweak its customer proposition so that it is less dependent on simply being super cheap. One idea is that its customers may be willing to pay more for products if they have to spend less time waiting for them to turn up at the door: the company is therefore building local warehouses, including a recently opened facility in Birmingham, to cut shipping times. Its plan to move upmarket might help too: plenty of Chinese-manufactured products initially attracted customers by being cheap and then became cool in their own right.

But all that is as yet untested. The likeliest outcome of Shein’s retreat is a redistribution of fast fashion’s spoils and one that consumers, deprived of the lowest-cost provider, will partially pay for too.

gaia.freydefont@ft.com

item.title: The FT View. Andy Burnham’s ‘jam tomorrow’ vision
item.author: The editorial board
item.description: Speech was more a bold manifesto for the next election than an urgent action plan
item.content:encoded:
Speech was more a bold manifesto for the next election than an urgent action plan

The editorial board

In his 10 weeks as UK prime minister, Andy Burnham has proven he is among the most gifted communicators of the current political generation. His speech to the Labour conference, complete with jokes and tears, demonstrated he can do the “vision thing” and rouse the party faithful in a way his ousted predecessor Sir Keir Starmer never managed. The new Labour leader also showed he is prepared to think boldly and take risks — in his readiness to unlock the triple lock on pensions, to go into the next election pledging electoral reform, and to seek a new post-Brexit relationship with the EU. Yet his often worryingly Old Labour speech was more a manifesto for a poll that may not happen until 2029 than an urgent action plan for the years in between.

One reason for shifting some of his boldest initiatives into the future is that Burnham is hemmed in by the Labour manifesto and by straitened public finances — and his necessary pledge to maintain fiscal discipline. Nowhere are those tensions more apparent than in the decision to postpone until a putative second Labour term the prime minister’s intended flagship measure: setting up a national care service in England.

Burnham’s stated goal is a system as comprehensive as the National Health Service. But that looks hard to afford even in a best-case scenario. A preferable option would be a phased approach that starts by setting a lifetime cap on individuals’ contributions to care costs — opening the way for private insurers to start offering policies consumers can take out to cover costs.

Burnham’s readiness to loosen the pensions triple lock — which ensures the state pension rises each year by the highest of inflation, earnings growth or 2.5 per cent — to help fund his social care plan is welcome. But this will be nowhere near sufficient in itself to fund even a slimmed-down version of Burnham’s care service. And by tying the move to a costly future extension of the welfare system, the prime minister could squander the credit the restive bond markets might have given him had he scrapped the triple lock now.

The prime minister is also sticking with Starmer’s manifesto commitment to maintain the pensions lock for the rest of this parliament. If he is to fulfil his second bold pledge — to find a better UK relationship with the EU — he will need to be more flexible about Labour’s red lines from 2024. The Starmer government bound its hands too tightly by insisting on no return to the EU’s single market, customs union or freedom of movement.

His third eye-catching gambit, to press for electoral reform, could help to better align the UK’s anachronistic electoral model with an increasingly multi-party system. There are more pressing priorities, though, including developing the government’s strategy to get more of the 1mn young people who are not currently in employment or learning into work. Chancellor John Healey outlined a promising apprenticeship scheme this week; the final Milburn Review will shortly recommend further measures.

For Burnham’s programme to be affordable, growth will need to be quickly rekindled. After doubling down in his speech on a model that emphasises public control over utilities and a bigger public role in housing, Burnham still has to reassure business that he cares as much about unleashing the animal spirits of enterprise as he does about rebuilding the power of the state.

The most immediate imperative, however, is to show that Burnham and Healey have credible plans to control spending rather than pile yet more taxation on business and the wealthy. The Budget on October 28 is shaping up as a moment that will reveal whether Burnham’s expansive vision of social democracy represents a credible plan that can be funded, or an unsustainable clash between Downing Street ambition and the hard realities of fiscal arithmetic.

item.title: Snoop-and-scoop poses a real threat to science in the AI age
item.author: Anjana Ahuja
item.description: Establishing attribution in research has become harder in the age of AI-assisted breakthroughs
item.content:encoded:
Establishing attribution in research has become harder in the age of AI-assisted breakthroughs

Anjana Ahuja

The writer is a science commentator

Mario Rodríguez Mestre and colleagues heard on the rumour mill that a scientific paper was about to drop, containing work very similar to theirs. “We were actually joking about it and making bets about which lab it might be,” Mestre, a computational biologist at the University of Copenhagen, told me, adding that being scooped was common.

What happened next, however, floored him: “What we absolutely did not expect was . . . that it was not another academic lab, but one of the largest AI companies in the world, presenting the result as an autonomous AI discovery.” Last week, scientists at Anthropic claimed its AI agent Claude had independently found a new type of enzyme and associated molecules — the same ones that Mestre had himself been exploring with the help of Claude.

The episode follows the controversy about an OpenAI breakthrough on a famous mathematical problem, the Navier-Stokes theorem. New York University mathematician Tristan Buckmaster claimed that the company’s calculations bore a striking resemblance to the unusual approach that he and colleagues had been taking, using OpenAI’s tools to help them.

We might term these experiences WTAF (What The AI Found) moments — a feeling of shock and suspicion by scientists seeing their own work mirrored, even claimed, by AI. But these episodes raise profound questions: who owns and controls scientific data; what counts as autonomous discovery by an AI agent, especially when scientists are feeding in unpublished ideas; and what does attribution look like in an age of AI-assisted breakthroughs?

Mestre studies a class of enzymes called reverse transcriptase, which read the sequence of an RNA molecule to make a corresponding DNA molecule (RNA, like DNA, is an essential molecule for life). Bacteria use them to detect invading viruses, and they are seen as promising biotech targets. Mestre, who was using Claude to write code and draft an unpublished manuscript, believes Anthropic has not adequately shown that its agent reached its finding independently, rather than through rediscovery (Mestre is cited, with others, in the references).

“Some of the systems highlighted include exactly the same genes, from the same phages [bacteria-eating viruses], that we had previously identified,” he said, pointing out that the systems were unusual.

Mestre admitted the overlap could be coincidence; he has no evidence that his unpublished work was used directly and has had no communication with Anthropic. But he is now urging clearer standards for establishing provenance and attribution in AI-assisted research. Claims of autonomous AI breakthroughs should come with full documentation of the information accessed, the tools used, any human guidance and how prior work was accounted for. Mestre is now moving away from Claude and developing alternative AI tools for biologists.

A spokesperson for Anthropic told the FT it was not aware of any previously published work describing the same biological finding, and Claude’s distinctive contribution was to identify that the reverse transcriptase concerned was part of a larger system. The spokesperson added: “Claude was also not trained on any user transcripts, and our molecular biology team has no such access either.”

Mestre is already known in his field, with fellow biologists vouching for his research. Other academics, though, could be pipped to the post before they have even begun.

The vulnerability comes from external reviewers uploading confidential grant proposals to AI models to assess and rank them. Major funding bodies in the UK like Wellcome now forbid this but there are suspicions it still happens. One policy analyst told Science Business that peer review reports and funding recommendations have “suddenly become much longer, more detailed and complex”. Revealing a truly novel scientific idea before a researcher can claim it theoretically presents AI companies with a snoop-and-scoop opportunity.

Attribution can be contentious when many minds chase the same goal, as we may discover when the Nobel Prizes are awarded next week. Autonomous AI discovery is not yet figuring prominently in those discussions, a spokesperson from the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences told me, partly because the awards generally recognise pre-AI research and partly because the rules state the prizes must go to a person or people.

Given that all of AI, whether in literature, art or science, is trained and built on the wealth of human knowledge, that is how it should remain.

item.title: Who is driving the massive surge in repo borrowing?
item.author: Robin Wigglesworth
item.description: You can probably guess this one
item.content:encoded:
You can probably guess this one

Robin Wigglesworth

Some people spend their time thinking about the nature of the divine, the singularity, geopolitical fragmentation or how to cure cancer; others spend their time pondering the repo market. Alphaville is in the latter camp.

In case you missed it, here’s a 4k word deep-dive into the repo market’s origin story that ran in the FT Magazine earlier this month. If that doesn’t float your boat, the tldr is that repo is short-term collateralised lending that helps grease the wheels of the financial system’s machinery.

And repo is huge. The Financial Stability Board estimated earlier this year that the global government bond-backed repo market stood at approximately $16tn at the end of 2024.

Given the FSB’s estimate that sovereign debt-linked repo accounts for about 80 per cent of the total (and assuming that ICMA’s latest European growth estimates are broadly representative) that would make the global total about $22tn today.  

But who uses the repo market? Who are the biggest lenders and who are the biggest borrowers? What has driven the big upswing we’ve seen over the past decade.

Unfortunately, repo is a remarkably opaque industry, but analysts at several US bodies — like the Federal Reserve System and Office of Financial Research — have been digging a lot into it in recent years. And yesterday the NY Fed published a new report looking at the identity of the main repo market players in the US.

Anyone who has read Alphaville will probably be unsurprised at their findings:

The main borrowers have long been hedge funds, but their dominance has become incredibly stark over the past decade. They do also lend (to the tune of $1.3tn in late 2025) to squeeze returns out of any cash they hold and to turn cash into securities, but this is dwarfed by their now $3tn of borrowing as of January 2026.

For the sake of clarity, FBOs are the US branches of foreign banks, USDIs are US-based deposit-taking banks, and REITs are real estate investment trusts.

Note that this data is derived from certain US reporting forms, and Alphaville suspects that they only capture some of the multi-faceted repo market. That’s not to say that hedge funds are the biggest actors across every corner of the repo market — banks also use repo to fund their internal trading desks, for example — but this can safely be assumed to be a conservative estimate.

That hedge funds are big repo market borrowers and money market funds are big money market lenders has been known for a long time. But the scale of the recent increase — the Fed’s estimate for hedge fund repo borrowing has nearly trebled since October 2022 — piqued Alphaville’s interest. In fact, this data indicates that most of the growth in repo has been solely driven by hedge funds.

At the same time, as Adam Josephson at Sakonnet Research has highlighted, non-Treasury collateral has become far more common lately, at least in the triparty repo market.

And in case you’re curious, this massive pile of short-term leverage is one of the main reasons why the Federal Reserve had to start increasing the size of its balance sheet again last year. After all, when so much financial activity relies on a short-term debt market then you have to do what it takes to avoid any jitters.

It will be interesting to see if Fed chair Kevin Warsh ever actually tries to do something about the central bank’s balance sheet. Given how tricky it could prove we suspect not, but there’s an argument that introducing some volatility in repo could be a healthy thing in the longer run.

item.title: John Healey failed to truthfully articulate causes of Britain’s problems
item.author: Stephen Bush
item.description: Inability to acknowledge the financial crisis or credit New Labour’s inheritance illustrates wider issues among politicians
item.content:encoded:
Inability to acknowledge the financial crisis or credit New Labour’s inheritance illustrates wider issues among politicians

Stephen Bush

Good morning from Liverpool. John Healey delivered his first speech to the Labour Party conference yesterday. Some thoughts on it in today’s note.

A spoonful of sentimentality makes the medicine go down

Healey’s speech yesterday was peppered with overtures to the left. There were references to Labour’s 1990s Treasury team and lengthy sections on mining. His opening greeting featured a shout-out to the two trade unions he is closely affiliated with, the GMB and Community. He also namechecked the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), which currently faces threats for its work saving people from drowning at sea. A lot of his speech was about gesturing: “conference, I’m one of you!”

He did that partly to smuggle in two more difficult messages. The first was on welfare spending:

The Tories let the number of young people in this country not in employment, education or training rise to nearly one million.

Two-thirds have never worked.

Potential wasted. Ambition frustrated. Opportunity closed.

Signed off, written off.

And I know it’s tough for young people today.

Some find it hard to face the world.

And I hear the fear in their mums’ and dads’ voices when they talk about their kids’ futures, when they talk about the dark forces on the internet.

And our social security system must always be there for those who can never work.

But for everyone else, benefits should be a bridge to work, to wider participation, to a better life, not a trap that people can’t escape.

And conference, it is simply not progressive to allow a bigger and bigger benefits bill and a system which offers an income but doesn’t offer a future.

The important thing here is in the detail. One problem for Labour on welfare reform is that the party is trying to serve two imperatives. The first is about creating a better, more effective system. The second is about making savings that the Office for Budget Responsibility will score favourably to give the government more breathing space against its fiscal rules. The difficulty is that it’s not clear these two aims can really be reconciled.

The second difficult message, albeit heavily coded, was that the economic boom New Labour inherited from John Major is not “here now”:

I know the nineties is having a bit of a revival,

To Andy’s excitement, Oasis are going back on tour.

To Angela’s joy, Gladiators is back on Saturday night TV.

But I have to level with you, conference.

The money New Labour had in the nineties is simply not there now.

Economic growth under Gordon was more than double the Tory years that followed.

And Britain has it harder now.

We had 14 years of flatlining Tory growth and living standards.

On the one hand, it’s good that Healey is acknowledging the most important fact in British politics: our economy has not recovered from the global financial crisis. (It’s time to roll out my favourite chart again.)

On the other hand, I think it actually does matter that strong economic growth did not start when New Labour took power in 1997 and that it came to an end with the global financial crisis rather than because of anything the Conservatives did in 2010.

A government can only find solutions if it can truthfully articulate a problem’s size and causes. It may seem like a small thing that Labour politicians cannot talk about the UK’s economic record without saying a kind word about Major, or that they talk about the problems since the financial crisis without referencing the financial crisis. But it illustrates a wider inability among politicians to talk about the real causes of the country’s challenges, whether that is the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets), the drivers of increased welfare spending or the absence of growth.

Now try this

I mostly listened to Anna Phoebe’s Divergence while writing my column this week.

Top stories today

  • ‘Start it now’ | Andrea Egan, the general secretary of trade union Unison, has attacked Andy Burnham for delaying any firm decisions on setting up a new social care system until after the next general election.
  • ‘Very serious situation’ | The suspected terror plot near RAF Fairford “clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor”, US secretary of state Marco Rubio has said.
  • £1.5bn is not enough | Northern Ireland’s Stormont is facing a crunch week following a demand from the UK government to agree a “final offer” for a financial bailout. The deadline comes at a time when tensions between the executive parties are high owing to contentious protests last weekend.
  • Prime minister’s prospectus | Andy Burnham is expected to discuss welfare reform, social care, Thames Water nationalisation and the pensions “triple lock” in his speech to Labour Party conference today.
