item.title: Rethinking the dollar
item.author: Katie Martin
item.description: Strong and stable, somewhat surprisingly
item.content:encoded:
Strong and stable, somewhat surprisingly

Katie Martin

Good morning. Bonds are still getting chewed up and spat out, with the rising oil price doing a lot of the chewing. The 10-year US yield touching 5.27 (!) per cent on Monday was something to behold. After a stinker of a month, though, is it time to pinch your nose and buy the dip? It certainly looks like the market is getting ahead of the economists on the likely path of the federal funds rates this year and next. For investors who can stomach the volatility, these are starting to look like juicy rates to lock in. Buying on the sounds of cannons, or catching a falling knife? Tell us what you reckon: unhedged@ft.com

Smile, and the dollar smiles with you

Markets analysts in general, and analysts at investment banks in particular, are generally decent human beings but they are almost all guilty of a great sin: not admitting when they’ve screwed up.

They publish new and updated forecasts on stocks, bond yields or whatever, but often fail to spell out what the previous forecast was or fess up to clients that their previous forecast suffered an unfortunate collision with reality.

This has long been a bugbear of mine. It’s not dishonest, as such, but it misses out an important process that can be very valuable to clients: explaining what went wrong and why. It also creates the ridiculous expectation that sharp-suited analysts are always right when in fact, everyone is feeling their way around in the dark to some extent. As Dan Davies wrote on Alphaville the other day, it’s actually fine to admit it when you don’t know something.

So the other day it was nice to see a Morgan Stanley note titled “We Were Wrong About Dollar Weakness”. The bank now thinks the DXY dollar index will end the year at 102 (previous forecast: 96, now 101), with the euro at $1.12 (previously $1.20, now $1.13) and sterling at $1.30 ($1.38, now $1.32). It has a small upwards revision to the yen exchange rate too, but that’s a bit of a special case.

The bank had previously thought the Federal Reserve would keep rates on hold and other central banks would be catching up. This would have exerted pretty mechanical pressure on the dollar, and also make it much cheaper to hedge dollar risks away, amplifying the downdraft. Nope. “We were wrong,” the team there said.

Instead, we all know what has happened to the dollar:

Hedging levels have dropped substantially, too. Morgan Stanley chart:

It is not just the turn in the dollar’s fundamentals doing the damage here. Instead, investors are getting increasingly jumpy about France, given the widening yield gap with Germany, adding a big risk factor to the euro over the next few months.

So the result is that the bank is now neutral to positive on the dollar, if not all-guns-blazing bullish (observant readers will note its forecasts are not a million miles away from today’s spot prices.)

It adds (our highlight):

We can’t help but remember price action over the past 18 months. At various points in time, unexpected ‘unknown unknown’ dollar-negative shocks have weighed on the dollar, such as after liberation day, the ‘rate check‘ in January, concerns around the composition of the FOMC, and most recently the announcement of larger than expected Treasury buybacks. These increases in dollar-negative risk premium haven’t been long lived in many cases, but they represent a key risk to holding dollar long trades. We’re worried that dollar longs may be ‘stopped out’ by an unexpected shock down the line, even if the fundamental case for dollar strength is greater and the most likely outcome is a stronger dollar over time.

Fool me once, I guess.

This way of thinking is very much in line with other currency pointy-heads, including Steve Englander at Standard Chartered, who wrote earlier this month that the hawkish pivot from the Fed was a game-changer that removed some of the big doubts over the buck but di not leave the currency entirely out of the woods. Bond yields will probably be the driver of the dollar’s value for now “provided there are no fiscal dominance or default concerns” (the latter of those two feels like something of an understatement.)

For now, the famous “dollar smile” (up when the US economy is leading the world, up when the US is in trouble, and down in between) is undefeated.

The other big theme in currencies at the moment, which I addressed in this newsletter the other day, is that they are so quiet, as this chart from Goldman Sachs demonstrates:

The fact that growth has been quite synchronised in major economies means there’s just not enough divergence for currencies to feed on. 

As Goldman says, it’s just hard at the moment to take a strident view:

On the one hand, downside risks to the dollar stem mostly from policy risks in the US and beyond, which have been the catalyst for most dollar downturns over the past 18 months. On the other hand, we see risks to the upside from more pronounced inflation pressures or a more prolonged capital expenditure cycle that would require stronger policy steps to tighten financial conditions.

Keep calm and carry on.

One good read

How the hyperscalers are shaking up corporate bond markets

item.title: Lex. Why a £10bn Monzo takeover could be good for the UK
item.description: Brazil-based Nubank has considered moving its legal domicile to the City
item.content:encoded:
Brazil-based Nubank has considered moving its legal domicile to the City

Monzo may be a household name in the UK but in much of the world it is probably known only — if at all — as the sponsor of football club Coventry City. While the digital bank, like Coventry, has done a good job of fighting it out as a small team in the big leagues, a potential takeover bid from Brazil’s Nubank could create a more level playing field.

Nu, an online lender listed in New York, has approached Monzo about an acquisition valuing the British business at £8bn to £10bn, according to people familiar with the matter. Separately, Monzo has spoken with private equity firms about raising cash to help go it alone.

The big challenge is that Monzo’s easiest wins are behind it. True, it has amassed up to 16mn UK customers and about £26bn of deposits as of March, and its pre-tax profit is growing smartly. But only a minority of customers consider it their main bank. Its loan book was just £2.3bn in March, and building it will require a lot of time and patience.

There is also a huge gulf between the UK’s traditional big four lenders — Lloyds, NatWest, Barclays and HSBC — and the rest of the sector; the only bank that has closed the gap is Santander, a global group which made a series of acquisitions.

Teaming up with Nu could provide resources and offer a straightforward exit for Monzo’s existing venture capital backers. The Brazilian bank’s US-listed shares trade at roughly 5 times book value, based on S&P Capital IQ data. An £8bn price for Monzo would imply the same multiple, plus a 30 per cent takeover premium. That said, the UK bank might be able to argue for more because it has an EU banking licence, which gives it options for future growth.

Nu also has an incentive to pay a healthy price — even if the 8 per cent drop in its shares on Monday morning suggests investors will take some convincing. While it’s far more profitable than Monzo, thanks to a $39bn lending portfolio, it is also riskier. Adding a stable, deposit-driven UK business might counter the volatility of its Latin American markets and thus reduce its implied cost of capital. That’s similar to the model Spain’s Santander and BBVA have pursued.

Any potential takeover of a UK company tends to provoke hand-wringing about the future of the country’s financial markets. Monzo, long seen as a potential candidate for a London listing, would no doubt renew anxieties about the City’s status. Yet such fears may be misplaced. Nu chief executive David Vélez has previously considered moving the group’s legal domicile to the UK; buying a British bank would give him more reason to do so.

Monzo’s tie-up with a Premier League football team could be apt in that regard. The league is seen as an English success despite an influx of foreign money over the years. Why shouldn’t the City be the same? Being small and scrappy has its charms, but sometimes it’s nice to actually win for a change.

nicholas.megaw@ft.com

item.title: Lex. Private equity wrestles with its own generational wealth gap
item.description: Joe Baratta of Blackstone will retire a billionaire, but future up-and-comers will struggle to match his record
item.content:encoded:
Joe Baratta of Blackstone will retire a billionaire, but future up-and-comers will struggle to match his record

Today’s youth complain, not without reason, that Gen X had it best. It’s true in private equity too. Joe Baratta, about to retire from Wall Street investment colossus Blackstone, is a good example of how the cohort that entered private equity at the end of the last century timed the market perfectly.

In its early days, Blackstone struggled to get traction. But by the 1990s, co-founder Stephen Schwarzman had hit a sweet spot. His industry had become credible, yet was still growing at warp speed, thanks to declining interest rates and globalised capital flows. Baratta, who joined in 1998, was instrumental in bringing the concept of the leveraged buyout to Europe.

Now, only in his mid-50s, he is stepping back. Despite not being a founder of Blackstone, Baratta has shares worth nearly $900mn. Last year he took home more than $30mn in dividends on those shares; his cut of performance fees known as carried interest snared him another $28mn. His next move is, so far, unknown; politics or public policy are not out of the question.

The retirement of a senior executive is always a good opportunity for up-and-comers to flex their skills. But the buyout trade isn’t what it was. Blackstone’s success — it now manages $1.3tn in assets, roughly 90 times what it did in 2001 — has inspired a flood of competitors. Returns have moderated sharply: even at Blackstone, several funds have recently fallen short of the 20 per cent annualised return that a top-tier private equity firm ought to deliver.

One problem is that interest rates have risen since 2022, and may stay elevated. The industry’s dealmaking machine, which involves buying businesses and selling them on eventually to public markets, is jammed. And politicians are taking aim at “vulture capitalists” who have burrowed their way into every industry from hospitals to youth sports — and, of course, housing.

Moreover, it is harder these days for large buyout firms to take big swings. With a large asset base, more than 5,000 employees and, since 2007, a share price to think about, playing it safe and steady has become the better course.

Where does that leave a 20-something would-be Baratta today? Potentially looking at other kinds of private capital that have emerged as growth areas, from so-called secondaries to “net asset value “loans. Further afield, there are cryptocurrencies and digital assets, AI infrastructure and sports deals, though none are likely to experience growth quite like Blackstone’s since 1998.

Meanwhile at the top of the Wall Street tree, boomers still reign. Schwarzman remains CEO of the empire he built. Peers from BlackRock’s Larry Fink to JPMorgan’s Jamie Dimon and Apollo’s Marc Rowan seem in no rush to vacate their posts, and shareholders are by no means eager to see them do so. When it comes to generational inequality, high finance looks a lot like everywhere else.

sujeet.indap@ft.com

item.title: The Big Read. The booming business of insuring against US gun violence
item.author: Lee Harris
item.description: Companies, political campaigns and even schools are taking out policies to shield themselves from litigation that can follow attacks
item.content:encoded:
Companies, political campaigns and even schools are taking out policies to shield themselves from litigation that can follow attacks

Lee Harris

The fatal shooting of conservative influencer Charlie Kirk at a Utah university last year convulsed national life in the US and was widely seen as a grim new benchmark for political violence.

For the state of Utah, the killing sent officials looking for ways to guard against the risks of further violent attacks — the physical threat to its citizens, as well as the potential financial hit from future lawsuits.

Despite President Donald Trump labelling Kirk’s shooting an act of terrorism, it was not clear that the state’s terrorism insurance policy would cover its losses from the attack.

And so, two months after Kirk was killed, Utah bought a new product to shield its university campuses, schools and state agencies from damages: active-assailant insurance.

The fast-growing product, also known as deadly weapons or malicious attack insurance, covers businesses against losses from violent acts such as trucks being driven into crowds and active shooters.

Schools, local governments, private equity real estate trusts and political campaigns are among the groups buying billions of dollars of cover against the financial risks posed by gunmen.

US buyers are now paying more than $100mn in premium each year for standalone active shooter insurance, up from half that amount in 2020, according to brokers and insurers. The broader market for insurance against violence is one of the fastest-growing segments of the sprawling US liability insurance industry and a stark measure of the growing price of American violence.

A culture of litigation, which sets many of the boundaries of ordinary American life, has prompted victims to take to the courts. As a result, companies, governments and even schools are seeking to shield themselves from the financial penalties they can face in the wake of tragedy and disaster.

Shootings are often regarded as a signal of the need for greater regulation or legal change. But in the US, and in some other countries, the risk of such calamities is increasingly managed as a cost of doing business, a hazard whose financial implications can be passed on to others.

Because the US political system is subject to “extreme limitations on legislative action”, says University of Kansas public policy professor Charles Epp, pressure from social issues “is channelled into the courts”.

In response, property owners and businesses that might be accused of negligence are buying policies to cover future claims, which can also give employees access to emergency-response services.

Months after Kirk was shot, says Rachel Terry, who was Utah’s head of risk management at the time of the shooting, the state had already found occasion to use its new active assailant policy. Employees became concerned about a colleague’s suspicious behaviour and phoned a crisis hotline covered by the insurance.

Access to private security services has given “a sense of comfort”, Terry says, to state employees such as schoolteachers worried about violent attacks.

Beyond reassuring employees, the insurance has allowed investors and property owners to offload their exposure to American violence and civil unrest. Many have also bought coverage for incidents such as “strikes, riots and civil commotion”.

Active-assailant insurance is a “sleep-easy”, says one insurer in the UK, where many of the top providers are based. 

Many of the premiums flow back to London, the world’s biggest speciality insurance hub, where discreet English insurers have helped businesses to quantify and manage the risk of violence.

Blackstone, Brookfield, and sports stadiums hosting this year’s Fifa World Cup are among the growing number of buyers of active assailant insurance, according to people familiar with these policies — as are high-profile political campaigns at national and state level.

“The better question is who doesn’t buy it,” says Peter Bransden, head of US crisis management at broker Willis. Clients, he adds, are “a who’s who of the American economy”. 

The buyers

The grim rise in deadly shootings in recent years prompted Tony Giles, who leads a California government agency that buys insurance on behalf of more than a dozen cities, to buy an active assailant policy. 

“Almost every time you turn on the news, there’s another shooting somewhere — not always on public property but often,” he says.

This year, the California Joint Powers Risk Management Authority he runs paid $63,000 to cover its members — which include police departments, city halls and libraries — for payouts of up to $1mn per shooting.

The premium is “incredibly affordable”, Giles says, because his organisation has never filed an active assailant claim.

His group is one of hundreds of government authorities, towns and school districts across the US buying similar cover, worried that they could be held liable for future attacks taking place on their property. 

The city of Shreveport, Louisiana, for example, which has fewer than 200,000 people, has paid a $48,200 annual premium for its active-assailant insurance. A primary school district in Montana — Cascade Elementary — recently renewed a $122,451 insurance package that included deadly weapons coverage among its “key risks”, along with conventional coverage for buildings and vehicles.

Political campaigns, too, are increasingly buying policies, insurers say, with demand picking up ahead of November’s midterm elections.

Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign submitted an inquiry with London-based active-assailant insurance providers about buying a policy to cover attendees of his rallies against a potential attack, people familiar with the discussions say. The inquiry was made before Trump was shot in Pennsylvania, they said, and it was unclear whether the campaign had ultimately purchased the coverage. The White House did not respond to requests for comment.

It was once rare for event organisers or property owners to be held liable for shootings, since courts treated such events as unforeseeable tragedies for which businesses were not expected to prepare.

But the risk of attack has become harder to ignore. More than 13,000 people have died from shootings in the US every year since 2016, not including gun deaths from suicide, according to the CDC. Other groups, including the Gun Violence Archive, an independent data collection and research group, have had similar findings.

In response, judges have begun to find businesses responsible for failing to identify or stop a shooter, according to research published by the American Bar Association. 

Insurers have sometimes been stuck with large losses. After a 2017 mass shooting in Las Vegas that killed 58 people, the deadliest in modern US history, MGM Resorts, which owned the hotel from which the gunman fired, agreed a settlement fund. Its insurers, including Chubb and AIG, were on the hook for more than $735mn.

Worried about their exposure, insurers have begun to carve exclusions for assault and battery out of general commercial liability policies that cover businesses against all manner of legal damages.

Over the past five years, active assailant insurance has boomed, promising to cover the gaps. Policies cover victim compensation and counselling, funeral costs and private crisis response companies that can advise on threats and help gather evidence for the police. Some policies also cover legal liability, property damage and business interruption costs.

For Giles, the insurance is not only a way to cover losses. Being able to offer help in the wake of an attack could also stave off bigger lawsuits and bigger payouts, he says.

“Calling and saying, ‘We know you’ve had this tragedy, and we’d like to help you with the funeral expenses’ — the way that can bring the temperature down is very valuable,” Giles says. “It helps preclude, hopefully, a liability claim.”

Insuring against terrorism

Specialist coverage for large-scale acts of violence already exists in the form of terrorism insurance, a market that grew rapidly after the September 11 attacks on New York’s World Trade Center. 

From 2003 until 2023, the US Treasury found, insurers were paid some $68.3bn in terrorism premiums. But very little has been paid out.

This is because such policies typically cover damage to buildings and property, brokers say. Attacks have also often proved hard to link to a political ideology or specific motive, which can be required in contract language to trigger a terrorism insurance payout.

Utah, which is now being sued by Kirk’s family, is a typical example. The state had a terrorism policy in place when the activist was murdered last year, but it was unlikely to cover damages, according to insurance broker Jonathan Stutz, who has advised the state.

“That policy is very much tied to property damage, and in the Charlie Kirk matter, there was very little property damage,” Stutz says.

This holds beyond the US, brokers say. In Europe, businesses are buying active assailant cover against vehicle attacks — cars being driven into crowds — and knifings.

But more than half of global demand comes from the US, brokers said, where active assailant coverage has become the newest layer of the American business sector’s vast spending on legal liability. US insurers were paid $163bn in liability premiums in 2024, data from S&P shows, or about 0.5 per cent of national GDP.

The risks faced by small-town America are underwritten thousands of miles away by specialist providers in London.

Charlie Hanbury, a London crisis insurer, spends much of his time travelling across the Deep South and Midwest, where he has become familiar with the rhythms of violence and litigation often present in American life.

To price an active-shooter insurance policy, his Samphire Risk group looks at dozens of risks, ranging from whether a state has “open carry” gun laws that allow people to visibly carry firearms in open spaces to whether a high school has public footfall on their premises.

“Open carry” states are not always more expensive, since their politics are typically more rightwing and the tort law that governs personal injury litigation is often more business friendly.

By contrast, Hanbury says, California has tighter gun laws but a more challenging legal environment. Jury verdicts against companies in the state have stretched into the billions of dollars, driving up the price of insurance.

He adds that Samphire has experienced a rise in business demand from political campaigns in the months before November’s midterm elections. He says such groups are seeking active-shooter insurance to cover plans ranging “from large events to little fundraisers to dinners”.

Buyers of active-shooter insurance tell the FT that one of the main selling points is the access it provides to private crisis-response companies.

Such companies can help a business check whether a threat received on the internet is credible or whether it is “just trolling”, says Thea Grootenhuis of London brokerage Blackthorn, which sells active-assailant insurance globally. “The crisis responders want to be there pre-incident, to prevent things from escalating.”

A North American client of Blackthorn recently became concerned about an employee facing “personal issues” whose behaviour had become “erratic”, she says. After the employee posted threatening pictures online, the organisation contacted law enforcement and the crisis response company under its insurance policy, she says, and agreed to close their two flagship offices for the rest of the week.

“Everyone’s scared with insurance that if you trigger the policy you’re going to get a higher premium next year. This doesn’t work that way,” she adds.

While many people associate US gun violence with mass shootings, Department of Justice data shows that the vast majority of firearm homicides had one victim. Hanbury also works with public housing complexes, selling insurance against domestic violence and gang disputes.

Hanbury dislikes “European intellectual snobbery”, he adds, or people who lecture Americans on their gun laws. “You should never sell on fear or ambulance-chase,” he says, adding that selling policies only takes “pointing out the facts”.

Reform through litigation

These kinds of policies are a hallmark of an American system that gives citizens more ability to take risks, so long as they shield themselves financially against the potential fallout in the courts.

“The tort system is our populism,” says University of Virginia law school professor Kenneth Abraham. “In this country, what we’ve chosen to have is less regulation . . . and more freedom of action on the part of potentially regulated parties.”

For example, political funding vehicles such as Super Pacs — campaign organisations that can take unlimited money from donors to spend on elections — are increasingly purchasing not only active-assailant insurance but also media liability policies. These offer protection against defamation claims for campaign advertisements later deemed libellous.

Filings show that America Pac, Elon Musk’s Super Pac, has spent more than $85,000 on insurance payments to Three Arbor Insurance, an Alabama-based group offering political and liability insurance.

But liability policies also fuel a cat-and-mouse game between insurers, investors and plaintiffs seeking to use the legal system to pursue social reform or obtain multimillion-dollar payouts.

In the 1980s, for example, police officers faced a wave of legal claims over police violence, leading the cost of liability insurance for departments to soar.

Epp of the University of Kansas says there was “almost a panic among police chiefs” as they struggled to pay damages and afford insurance. He adds that pressure had “some reform-oriented effects on police”.

But what he calls “the American model of reform by piecemeal litigation”, including the role of soaring insurance costs, was less effective at reforming US police behaviour, he maintains, than centralised national oversight has been in other countries.

Abraham of the University of Virginia says he believes the American system of regulation after the fact — by costly litigation — has contributed to a more dynamic and entrepreneurial economy, and supported Americans’ “assumption of risk”.

He acknowledges, however, that the American tort system is costly. “It’s a very expensive system — it’s not an efficient way to resolve disputes.”

Insurance is a product that is rarely beloved, and buyers of insurance products — even large companies and governments — often report feeling frustrated at paying upfront for a service that may offer them little.

But buyers of active-assailant insurance say it offers a measure of reassurance and relief as once unthinkable events become commonplace.

“It shocks people, the amount of guns we have, and the amount of violence,” says Giles. When the product was presented to his board, he says: “Everyone just said, ‘Obviously, yes, we should have this.’”

item.title: Lex. BASF should take another crack at chemicals M&A
item.description: Evonik, governed by the RAG-Stiftung foundation, may find it hard to turn up its nose at a higher number
item.content:encoded:
Evonik, governed by the RAG-Stiftung foundation, may find it hard to turn up its nose at a higher number

For companies in shrinking industries, the question isn’t whether to band together through mergers — but how to share the resulting gains. German chemicals group BASF, whose €10.3bn bid for rival Evonik was rebuffed despite being pitched at a sizeable 29 per cent premium, should consider trying again.

BASF was already making a big bet: including debt, the deal would have cost around €14bn. Evonik is undergoing its own cost-cutting and restructuring programme. And BASF’s shareholders clearly aren’t thrilled by the prospect of a deal. Its shares fell 4 per cent on initial news of the approach last Friday.

But the benefits from putting together the two companies are such that BASF has room to push the price a bit higher. Overlapping areas — where either both companies make the same products, or one makes the raw materials that the other buys — represent about a third of BASF’s sales, and two-thirds of Evonik’s, according to Deutsche Bank analysts, leaving lots of room to combine plants and remove duplication.

And even assuming that BASF only managed to cut costs equivalent to 7.5 per cent of Evonik’s sales, which is typical for the sector according to Bernstein analysts, that would imply €1bn in annual savings for roughly €8bn of equity value today, Lex calculates. By comparison, the €2.3bn premium BASF offered on Friday looks positively meagre.

For its part, Evonik, governed by the RAG-Stiftung foundation, may find it hard to turn up its nose at a higher number: analysts are not expecting a rapid recovery in its prospects, and are pencilling in 2030 operating profit below that forecast for this year, according to Visible Alpha.

Meanwhile, both companies’ shareholders should bear in mind that consolidation, in Europe’s chemicals sector, is a strategic imperative. Amid rising competition from China, almost a tenth of production capacity has already been scheduled to close, according to consultancy firm Roland Berger. A less fragmented chemicals sector could find its return on capital improves through higher margins, or perhaps even growing sales if lower costs are passed on to struggling industrial customers.

Having scale could also help beyond the factory gates. A large European chemicals champion would have more clout in Brussels as the industry lobbies for greater protection from cheap imports and looser environmental regulation.

And if Evonik proves too resistant, BASF need not abandon the hunt. Europe has no shortage of midsized chemicals companies, including Arkema, Syensqo and Lanxess. An ample supply of struggling rivals should provide BASF with the motivation to keep knocking on doors.

gaia.freydefont@ft.com

item.title: The FT View. Russia’s escalating hybrid campaign against Europe
item.author: The editorial board
item.description: European countries need a robust response to Moscow’s increasingly brazen actions
item.content:encoded:
European countries need a robust response to Moscow’s increasingly brazen actions

The editorial board

In August came an attempted Russian drone attack on a Ukrainian cargo plane used to transport military aid at Germany’s Leipzig-Halle airport; then, this month, a drone hit a train close to Ukraine’s border with Poland moments after another train carrying European officials including former UK prime minister Boris Johnson had passed through. In these and a string of other incidents, Russia appears to be stepping up its “hybrid” attacks on Ukraine’s European partners — from lower-level sabotage to more brazen operations with a potential to cause serious casualties.

European leaders including France’s President Emmanuel Macron and Polish premier Donald Tusk are sounding alarms that Moscow could escalate further. Tusk told Poland’s parliament Moscow might launch drone or missile attacks on Nato members, claiming they were accidental, to test the bloc’s collective defence. Danish intelligence last week made public its assessment of a “low but growing risk” that Russia could launch a limited military attack against a Nato country within months.

While western leaders are right to level with the public about the imperative to strengthen defences, such warnings should not shade into hysteria. Some longtime Russia experts are dubious that President Vladimir Putin would take the huge risk of testing Nato’s Article 5, which treats an attack on one member as an attack on all, with a large-scale assault. Donald Trump’s erratic nature has dented Nato partners’ confidence that America would come to their aid if Russia attacked — but means Moscow cannot be certain it would not.

Yet Russia seems intent on raising the costs and risks for European countries supporting Ukraine — and Putin would surely like little more than to humble and paralyse Nato, upturning the European security order. The less pushback he gets on his lower-level attacks, the greater the chance that he might just gamble on probing Article 5. European countries need a better strategy.

First, they have to respond rapidly and robustly to Moscow’s provocations. That can be hard; European capitals need to be pretty sure of Russia’s involvement before going public, but its interventions are intended to be deniable, sometimes contracted out to third parties. But European countries should be quicker to point the finger where evidence is compelling. Germany took nearly four weeks before formally accusing Moscow over the Leipzig incident, where the drone thankfully failed to detonate.

European capitals need to gauge responses carefully to signal deterrence to Moscow without triggering escalation. But they should do the most they can below the threshold of direct military action — from closing consulates (as Germany did over Leipzig) and expelling diplomats, to tightening or imposing new sanctions or doing more to clamp down on Russia’s “shadow fleet” of oil tankers.

Such measures could be more effective if multiple countries imposed them simultaneously, should a Russian operation against any one country exceed a certain level. Some capitals suggested Berlin should have invoked consultations under Nato’s Article 4, permitted if a country considers its “security is threatened”. EU defence ministers on Monday debated new collective ways to answer Russian aggression. Establishing rapid-response protocols would be desirable — though the EU should be wary of overlapping with Nato and causing confusion.

European countries need, too, to step up preparations to counter any Russian effort to challenge Article 5 — with the aim of deterring it. The evidence of Putin’s 27 years as Russia’s paramount leader is that he respects strength but penalises weakness. As the Kremlin steps up its greyzone attacks, failure to make a firm response risks only emboldening it to go further.

item.title: Why the EU fears Britain becoming a back door for Chinese cars
item.author: Alan Beattie
item.description: Brussels is urging UK tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, but it might take more than that
item.content:encoded:
Brussels is urging UK tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles, but it might take more than that

Alan Beattie

Welcome to Trade Secrets. The big Xi-Trump showdown was as content-free as I predicted, though that wasn’t a terribly long shot. The alleged US-China trade truce has been extended until January, when it will of course be extended again. The supposed October deadline for the EU and China to agree some kind of rebalancing deal will similarly recede into the future.

Meanwhile, the real action is the three big trading powers trying to insulate themselves from each other by building that supply chain resilience everyone talks about. Today’s first piece is on some collateral damage (the UK) of the EU’s attempts to do just that. Charted Waters, where we look at the data behind world trade, is on liquefied natural gas (LNG) prices.

The UK ‘aircraft carrier’ launching Chinese cars into the EU

Playing its now familiar role as the nation giving its body to economic science — just what does happen when a medium-sized economy loses its senses and wrenches itself out of a densely woven trading area? — the UK now has some exciting new issues to deal with. Nothing major, just industrial policy, protectionism, electric vehicles and relations with Brussels and Beijing.

These challenges have been around for a while but are becoming acute. Briefly: the UK is desperate to be inside the “made in Europe” procurement and subsidy tent. In return, the EU wants the UK to impose tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles and has even mooted Britain joining the bloc’s customs union. It would be an unorthodox way to accelerate the turgid process of unpicking Brexit, but there you have it. It’s an exaggeration to say “it’s a world of blocs, Britain — pick one”, but certainly it’s hard to replace a large neighbour’s supply chains if you’re knitted into them.

You’ll never guess which country (clue: Roquefort) is most sceptical about bringing the UK inside the fold. It was, of course, the same nation (another clue: pétanque) that objected when the UK invited Nissan in 1986 to invest in the north-eastern city of Sunderland, comparing it to a “Japanese aircraft carrier” aiming cars at the EU market.

Indeed, tariffs are one thing, but I can’t help thinking that Chinese investment inside the UK ought to be worrying the EU more. Rules of origin should prevent Chinese EVs imported to the UK from being reimported to the EU, or the final assembly of almost-finished cars being passed off as having had substantial value added.

The real difficulty comes if Chinese car companies invest in large-scale UK production and then those Britain-made vehicles are sold into the EU at subsidised prices. Intriguingly, Chery is looking at having Nissan build cars for it in Sunderland. Brussels does have tools to address this. It can bring anti-dumping and anti-subsidy actions against products made in third countries, an instrument it pioneered a few years ago by going after Chinese glass-fibre manufacturers in Egypt. But the difficulty of building a case means the tools are hard to use and have barely been employed since.

Within the EU itself, such companies are subject to the Foreign Subsidies Regulation (FSR), an even newer tool whose efficacy is also uncertain and with which China has told its companies not to co-operate. This might lead to a peculiar situation where Chinese companies invested in both the EU and UK markets are competing against each other, or even against other units within their own company, while being regulated by different pieces of legislation. The winner, perhaps, is whichever company or subsidiary best wriggles out from under the rules. That is, of course, until the EU starts to push the UK to adopt the FSR, and another precious, precious Brexit freedom comes under threat. Just rejoin the bloody EU and have done with it, Britain. Honestly.

Detroit watches nervously as Trump leans towards China

As my FT colleagues put it, US President Donald Trump has caged his China hawks and was in full-on emollient mode when he met Chinese President Xi Jinping. In fact, perhaps more than emollient. My former colleague Phil Coggan absolutely nailed it by describing Trump as the Basil Fawlty of international diplomacy: “He only has two modes: unctuous flattery and petulant aggression”.

Being in the former mode this time, Trump also repeated something he’s gone back and forth on over the years. On September 11 he mused on Fox News that allowing Chinese car manufacturers to set up in the US would be fine as they employed American workers. The remark predictably prompted fierce reactions from Detroit auto unions and Michigan politicians, including Trump’s best friend (irony alert!) Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic candidate for senator. 

Trump’s rationale would, of course, be wildly different from those of the EU and UK. He might dislike EVs’ climate-saving qualities, but he likes the idea that the technology is advanced and he admires China.

But would it be a good idea? Here is a truly splendid expostulation of the case against by Michael Dunne of Dunne Insights, a consultancy for the auto industry.

China’s scores of automakers are currently engaged in a fight-to-the-death price war at home. There’s red ink everywhere. Access to the US, by far the most lucrative car market in the world, is like a giant tank of life-saving oxygen. President Xi cannot believe his good luck. 

I’m not sure about this bit. It’s certainly true that there is ferocious competition in the Chinese market, but that’s a fight to the death between different companies, not something that will threaten the whole industry. More convincingly, Dunne argues that China will bring in its own suppliers rather than boost the wider US industry, and that connected cars installed with Chinese software are a security risk.

If President Trump is still hell-bent on letting the Chinese enter, he should require them to form joint ventures with majority American ownership and subject the Chinese partner to quarterly audits on their investment and technology transfer progress. 

Insisting on technology transfer is a laudable goal, and we should all be watching the Chery-Nissan Sunderland tie-up with interest. But if China can’t convincingly promise it, and Washington keeps blocking Chinese software and investment, the US will find that its neighbours Canada and Mexico continue to welcome Chinese EVs and capital, and North American supply chains will degrade. Those trading blocs are hard to manage on both sides of the Atlantic.

Charted waters

It’s not just US diesel: LNG prices in Asia have surged, partly because of competition with European buyers.

Trade links

  • The Net Zero Industrial Policy Lab at Johns Hopkins University has created a great data source that maps clean-energy investments around the world. The paper explaining it with some results is here. 
  • A play about inept economic coercion in three short acts. Act One: Trump threatens to buy potash (used in fertiliser) from Belarus instead of Canada because Prime Minister Mark Carney has annoyed him. Act Two: Belarus says it doesn’t have enough spare potash to sell. Act Three: Trump continues to buy Canadian potash. Curtain.
  • Relatedly, the FT’s Swamp Notes newsletter argues that Trump is not going to drop Canada as a partner, the other half of my contention that Canada won’t, indeed can’t, drop the US.
  • In economic security news, the EU has urged Trump to keep diesel supplies flowing in response to talk of US export restrictions.
  • The FT’s Unhedged podcast looks at the tumultuous bond markets.
  • It’s mainly about the security angles, but this Carnegie Endowment piece on the Houthis’ expanding area of control in the Red Sea also covers energy shipments and the effect of maritime security problems on freight costs.

Trade Secrets is edited by Harvey Nriapia

item.title: A faintly hopeful mood at Labour conference
item.author: Stephen Bush
item.description: Most party MPs think Andy Burnham’s government is handling politics better, but manifesto and fiscal constraints remain
item.content:encoded:
Most party MPs think Andy Burnham’s government is handling politics better, but manifesto and fiscal constraints remain

Stephen Bush

Good morning from Liverpool. All changed, changed utterly . . . at least in terms of the Labour Party’s mood. But some things remain the same and those continuities are more important. Some thoughts on that in today’s note.

Second chance

The mood at Labour conference is undoubtedly transformed from this time last year. Then, the government was reeling from what one senior figure described as the most politically inept reshuffle they had ever seen. Even the beneficiaries of it were unimpressed by how it was handled politically and uncertain how long Keir Starmer’s government had left to run.

A year later, the country has a new prime minister and the Labour Party a new leader. But not everything has changed: after “Change Begins” in 2024 and “Renew Britain” in 2025, Labour’s conference once again has a slogan that reads as if it progressed from client brief to printer without anyone sprucing it up: “Hope Again” is the message of the week.

You don’t need to be Hercule Poirot to detect a barbed commentary on Starmer’s premiership in that “Hope Again” slogan. And it’s true to say that most Labour MPs think the government’s handling of politics has improved. Don’t forget that most MPs want to be loyal to the government when their party is in office. They become fractious and annoyed when the line from the top changes frequently or is unclear such that they don’t know what to be loyal to. Now they have a leader whose personal project is clear and a government with direction. Even MPs with doubts about the party’s trajectory in the main concede that the political handling has improved under Andy Burnham.

But beyond the mood, the self-imposed constraints in the last Labour manifesto and the very real fiscal constraints facing the government have not changed. The geopolitical backdrop has shifted, but not for the better. As John Plender set out at the weekend, the parallels between now and the 1976 IMF crisis are striking indeed. “Hope Again” might yet give way to “1976 again”.

One change that matters more than the mood is that Labour MPs believe very strongly that they can’t switch leaders again — that the Burnham project has to succeed because there is no alternative. “We’ve been given a second chance,” one cabinet minister observed to me. “We aren’t going to be given a third.”

That gives Burnham more power to be radical and do things Labour MPs might not like — if he is willing to take that opportunity.

Now try this

I mostly listened to Michael Nyman’s music for Peter Greenaway while writing about the “7 Up” series for FT Weekend.

Top stories today

  • ‘New age of industrialisation’ | Chancellor John Healey will confirm a £6bn plan to build three new floating docks at the Royal Navy’s submarine base on the Clyde in Scotland in a speech to the Labour Party conference today.


  • RAF Fairford ‘major incident’ | Counterterror police said yesterday that they had arrested five men on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act after three “suspicious” vehicles were seen being driven towards a US air base.
  • ‘Genuine refugees’ | Shabana Mahmood will today announce plans to reopen the UK’s resettlement scheme under which around a quarter of those accepted are expected to be either Afghan women and girls or Palestinians.

item.title: Helen Thompson: “I don’t think we’re ever going back.”
item.author: Daire MacFadden
item.description: Geopolitical phase change
item.content:encoded:
Geopolitical phase change

Daire MacFadden

Good morning. So far, a 10-year Treasury yield of 5.2 per cent doesn’t bother US stocks. The S&P 500 rose Friday and remains right in the trading range it has been in since the beginning of August, when the yield was 4.6 per cent. That economic growth is a major driver of the yield increase certainly helps. The big risk, as we described on the podcast last week, is that the rapid rise in yields causes some sort of financial accident. But maybe we’ll get lucky!

Usually we run interviews on Fridays but the bond market excitement disrupted our plans. Email us: unhedged@ft.com.

Monday interview: Helen Thompson

Helen Thompson is professor of political economy at the University of Cambridge and the author of Disorder: Hard Times in the 21st Century. Her work focuses on energy, geopolitics and the economic pressures reshaping western democracies. She spoke to Unhedged earlier this month about the latest energy shock, China and US energy power, high debt levels and the politics of central bank independence. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Unhedged: During the post-pandemic inflation surge, people reached for historical analogies to understand that moment. What analogies explain the current energy shock?

Helen Thompson: In the 2021-22 energy shock there were some parallels with the 1970s. In both periods western countries had become accustomed to relatively low oil prices and experienced considerable domestic problems that arose not just from the high energy prices but also from the geopolitical conditions that caused it.

But the parallel that should have been drawn was to the oil price shock from 2005-08, which I think is underestimated in the history of the past couple of decades. A great deal of that was China’s demand for oil. Likewise, the beginning of the gas shock in 2021-22 wasn’t Russia’s invasion of Ukraine but China’s demand for liquefied natural gas which surged in the autumn of 2021. So actually the parallel is one of western countries having to adjust to China’s energy demand, which they haven’t been very good at over this century.

Unhedged: What makes the latest energy shock structural rather than temporary?

Thompson: From the late 1970s the US took responsibility for guaranteeing maritime navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and out into the Persian Gulf. While the US had problems projecting military power in the Middle East, it has not had a problem acting as that guarantor. Now we’re seeing the US willing to accept turmoil around transit through the Gulf for months on end and, to some extent, being part of the reason why, given the blockade it imposed on some ships coming out of the Gulf.

I don’t think we’re ever really going back to a world in which the US acting as a guarantor of passage through the Strait of Hormuz can be taken for granted. And you can see that in the way in which various Arab states, including Saudi Arabia, are working on the presumption that they need pipelines. You are going to see Arab states really trying to move as far away as they can from reliance on maritime passage through that body of water.

Unhedged: Why has the global economy proved more resilient to the oil shock than expected?

Thompson: First, I think a large part of it is China’s demand destruction. China, in some sense, did prepare, if not exactly for this war, then for a similar war, given the amount of oil stockpiling that it did. The Chinese leadership have a quite good understanding of the geopolitical risks around their energy security and have taken that a lot more seriously than European countries have.

Second, the drawdowns from the US shouldn’t be underestimated in the explanation. But something that has surprised me is the ability of US producers to supply European countries with refined petroleum products. I think it suggests there’s more flexibility in the shale industry than might have been expected.

Unhedged: Many of the advanced economies are facing extraordinary debt levels and high borrowing costs. Do you think this will lead to financial repression?

Thompson: I think that’s been the direction of travel for some time. In a way, quantitative easing is a form of financial repression. It’s obviously very different from trying to directly cap yields but you’re still using the power of the central bank to support debt and keep yields low. QE has gone away but the need to sustain high levels of debt hasn’t gone away and in some cases it has got worse. So you are going to have something to replace what QE was doing.

The more formal ways of doing financial repression are just harder than they were before. They run into the hard constraints that international capital flows have imposed on the world economy since the 1970s — 1980s. We’re in quite uncertain territory because the ways in which the problem [of high debt levels] has been dealt with in the past are not really workable any longer. So I think we’re going to see lots of improvisation to achieve the same ends, which is sort of what Bessent has been trying to do.

Unhedged: Do you see any overall coherence to the Trump administration’s economic policy?

Thompson: I think that there is actually more rationality than there may seem. What I think is clear in the US, and what you can see in [Stephen Miran’s] Mar-a-Lago accord paper, that for some of the people who have been economic advisers to Trump is the idea that US has a fundamental debt problem, the trajectory of the debt is unsustainable, and one of the reasons it’s unsustainable is because the interest on it is too high. I think we can see that they want to make the US debt more sustainable by paying less interest on it. And they will try to go about that through different means, some more strategic, some tactical. Whether that can succeed is a whole other question.

Unhedged: Is the 1990s conception of central bank independence still suited to the current political and economic challenges?

Thompson: It seems to me that you get a change in what the relationship is between politics and monetary policy at different economic and political junctures. 

Central banks like the BoE were given independence against a relatively benign international monetary background. If you told them to keep inflation to 2 per cent or lower, that was both doable and didn’t come with hard trade-offs. I think that era ended with the crash. And, actually, we did get a political version of monetary policy. It just didn’t look how it had looked in the past because it was QE. But once QE has become so hard, what do you do now? I don’t think anybody really knows the answer. But I think [political monetary policy] is what you would expect once you’ve gone back to an underlying international monetary and financial order that is much less benign than the one that prevailed when the BoE was given its independence.

There’s almost a kind of “end of history” — type argument around the BoE’s independence. It was somehow the liberal thing to do. It’s what competent technocratic politics was when big ideological conflict was over. But it’s just as historically specific to that time period as the whole universal liberal democracy argument.

One good read

Madame Ambassador and friend.

item.title: The Big Read. AI hyperscalers are transforming debt
item.author: Euan Healy and Emily Herbert and Michelle Chan
item.description: The sector’s huge capital needs are forcing companies and countries to rethink how they borrow money
item.content:encoded:
The sector’s huge capital needs are forcing companies and countries to rethink how they borrow money

Euan Healy and Emily Herbert and Michelle Chan

As Silicon Valley’s tech giants fan out across the world in search of cash, often changing the economic facts of life in the process, Europe’s debt markets are set to welcome a new borrower.

Meta will tap the European bond market for the first time this autumn to raise funds for its AI expansion, according to investors familiar with its goals.

It is due to be the latest stop in the sector’s record-breaking hunt for funds from new and old sources alike — a headlong rush with big implications for other borrowers during the current AI investment supercycle.

“The overarching narrative is — anywhere and everywhere,” says Greg Peters, co-chief investment officer of asset manager PGIM’s credit business. “The quantum of debt that is hitting the marketplace is historic. The numbers are just absolutely enormous. It’s transformational.” 

The fundraising binge is changing the way the world borrows money, affecting where, when and at what cost companies and governments issue debt. Some have said it could be the biggest shift since the creation of the Eurobond market in the 1960s.

Many companies are now being forced to tiptoe around hyperscalers, timing their bond issues to avoid clashing with those of the tech giants and, investors say, often borrowing for shorter periods to avoid the market’s glut of long-term debt.

Even the very biggest financial players say they are affected.

Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh and US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent argue that the hyperscalers are competing for capital with the $31tn US Treasury market, where last week 10-year borrowing costs hit their highest since 2007.

Staff at the European Central Bank have expressed concern that “the surge in big tech borrowing could make it harder for other companies and other economic sectors to access finance.” In a blog post last month, they asked: “Can euro area financial markets smoothly handle such large and concentrated debt inflows?”

The scale of the borrowing has shattered precedents. Last week Japan’s SoftBank raised more than $11bn of debt in the biggest junk bond issue in history to finance an investment in ChatGPT creator OpenAI.

Overall, according to Goldman Sachs, investors have provided about $500bn of financing to AI-linked groups so far this year.

The hyperscalers — Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle — account for about $200bn of the total, and are expected to issue more than $1tn of new debt over the next few years to finance their vast investment in the infrastructure needed to power AI.

Meta did not respond to a request for comment about its plans to raise funds in Europe.

Such outsize demand has created credit markets that can support larger and longer-term debt issues than ever before. But it has distorted pricing, with highly rated bonds sometimes trading at discounts to lesser-quality issues because of the sudden glut in supply.

It also brings new risks. Chipmakers, data centre operators and their power providers are all borrowing from public and private credit markets as well as financing each other, making it hard for the pension funds and insurers who buy their debt to assess their true level of exposure to the sector.

The interconnections between borrowers, in a new sector whose long-term trajectory is still unclear, have sparked concerns that if one falters, others could be dragged down with it.

“Inevitably, this is a one-way bet,” says Scott Schulte, global co-head of investment-grade debt syndicate at Barclays. “As long as everything goes right, it’s good. But the minute there’s a problem anywhere . . . the ecosystem is so intertwined.”

‘How much can we issue?’

In 2025, when hyperscaler debt issuance was just beginning, the tech giants set their bankers a challenge.

The question, according to Schulte, was: “How much debt do you think that we can issue over the course of the year?” They did not just mean in their home market, the world’s largest, he adds. They wanted to know how much they could possibly borrow “across currencies, globally”.

Their bankers spent that year “putting pencil to paper, and working out what [they] think the actual capacity is in any given market”, he says.

Then they acted, beginning with the market they know best, the $12tn US corporate bond market.

Fraser Lundie, global head of fixed income at Aviva Investors, says the ensuing “supply shock” quickly overwhelmed investors. With so much debt on offer, they were able to demand lower prices, meaning higher yields, or borrowing costs, for hyperscalers.

Lotfi Karoui, multi-asset credit strategist at Pimco, adds that the “repricing” in hyperscaler bonds — in some cases, close to levels of junk or lower-quality bonds — is occurring “because the pipeline is too unpredictable right now”.

During the second-quarter earnings season, Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Meta increased their projections for this year’s capital spending to a combined $745bn. “We haven’t found a landing zone for capex and supply . . . the pace and magnitude of revisions to capex are quite significant,” Karoui says. 

So far, this repricing has mostly been confined to the tech names themselves. “At the moment you’ve almost got two credit markets, the AI-related issuers and everyone else,” says Andy Chorlton, chief investment officer for fixed income at M&G. But he is concerned that, over time, borrowing costs for all high-grade corporate issuers will be dragged higher. “That is something that we are certainly focused on.” 

There have been few signs that higher financing costs are deterring the tech giants from issuing more debt, however. “Elon Musk is endeavouring to colonise Mars,” says PGIM’s Peters, referring to SpaceX’s ambitions to build data centres in space. “It doesn’t matter to him if a bunch of bond investors charge an extra hundred basis points.”

To avoid overwhelming the market, some hyperscalers have given investors assurances, for instance, that they will not issue debt in two consecutive quarters.

But companies in other sectors are still growing concerned that they will be crowded out by hyperscalers’ massive debt offerings. Coming to market at the same time as Oracle or Amazon could mean higher costs as bond buyers hold back cash to deploy in the AI-related issue.

David Brown, co-head of global investment-grade fixed income at asset manager Neuberger Berman, says that when a large AI issuance is coming to market, “we will definitely prepare . . . We will hold off or make sure we have capacity to add that issuance.”

Hyperscalers on tour

The magnitude of the borrowing, and its impact on pricing even in the highly developed US bond market, has led the tech giants and their bankers to travel the world.

Records have tumbled as a result. In June, Amazon sold C$14bn ($10bn) of debt, smashing the Canadian currency’s previous record of C$8.5bn set by Alphabet just a few weeks earlier.

Canadian borrowers now have to make sure that they “are not going head to head with some of the bigger deals that are out there”, says Abeed Ramji, head of Canadian debt capital markets at TD Securities. “The windows of access matter so much more than they used to in the past.”

Ramji adds, however, that Canada’s ability to absorb large deals has helped promote the country as a strong credit market and encouraged other companies to increase the sizes of their own debt issues.

“I don’t think this takes away from any demand,” he says. “The pie is just getting bigger.”

Last month Alphabet issued a record A$5.5bn ($3.9bn) bond in Australia, more than twice as large as the previous biggest. The group also holds the record for the largest Swiss franc bond issue, having raised SFr3.1bn ($3.7bn) there in February. Amazon’s SFr2.8bn offering in May is the second-largest.

The deluge of debt in hitherto less sought-out markets is pushing up borrowing costs for other companies and prompting them to shift the timing or duration of their deals, investors said.

Barclays analysis of the European credit market found that non-hyperscaler bonds were underperforming in parts of the market where hyperscaler issuance has been heaviest, such as longer-dated, higher-rated bonds.

The same appears true in Canada. Since Amazon and Alphabet’s record deals, the country’s highest-quality AA corporate credit index — where both hyperscalers sit — has traded at a discount to the equivalent index of A-rated bonds.

Even though hyperscaler deals can represent a meaningful share of current issuance in individual foreign-currency markets, their overall outstanding debt is a relatively small component of bond indices.

“When we look at the percentage of outstanding debt across the different markets, the euro capacity for hyperscaler debt is still untapped,” says Rehan Latif, global head of credit trading at Morgan Stanley.

The new deals have revitalised some of the smaller markets, say bankers. Adam Bothamley, global head of debt capital markets at HSBC, says there had been a slower pipeline of companies seeking to borrow in pounds this year, until the hyperscalers stepped in. “Having these sizeable transactions has been really helpful and has increased interest in and focus on the sterling market,” he adds.

Alphabet sold £5.5bn worth of sterling bonds in February, part of a $31.5bn package that included a rare 100-year £1bn bond that some say rekindled interest in long-maturity sterling debt. Amazon also raised £4.25bn earlier this month, its first-ever sterling issue.

The unknowns of gobbling up new debt at such a long maturity are huge, some investors warn. “If you just take it at its face value, investors are buying up to 100 years of unsecured debt in a transformational technology,” says Peters of PGIM. “Not to overly simplify it, but 100 years is a long time. I don’t think it’s good risk reward . . . it’s unknowable.”

Christian Hantel, head of global corporate bonds at Swiss bank Vontobel, highlights the practicalities of piling into smaller debt markets. “Those local markets will be filled quicker than the dollar market,” he says. “In some smaller markets like Swiss, sterling, Canadian, the market is getting close to its limit soon.”

The Treasury effect

The AI debt spree comes at a fragile moment for bond investors globally, as borrowing costs for governments in mature economies such as the US, UK, Germany and France rise to levels last seen in the late-2000s.

Whether investors have cashed out of government debt to buy into bonds issued by tech giants, as some credit-watchers have asserted, is a hot debate on Wall Street.

“We can see clearly . . . [hyperscaler debt] competes with government bonds,” says Marion Le Morhedec, chief investment officer for fixed income at Fidelity International.

“As a portfolio manager . . . that question about whether to invest in a 30-year bond from a hyperscaler versus a government is relevant, where it wasn’t before,” she adds. The hyperscalers offer an attractive “pure credit story”, as investors grow less tolerant of governments’ inability to rein in deficits and spending.

Others are less sure, arguing that the sell-off in government bonds has principally been due to macroeconomic factors such as inflation and fiscal deficits.

“The numbers we are talking about on the sovereign side are so much higher,” said HSBC’s Bothamley. “It’s a stretch to say that . . . hyperscaler issuance is causing any sustained increase in [sovereign] yields.”

It is difficult to prove that investors are ditching government bonds for corporate debt. But markets have nevertheless been jolted by the arrival of such large and relatively price-insensitive sellers of debt, at a time when some traditional bond buyers — notably central banks and defined-contribution pension funds — have reined in their purchases.

“As heavy government borrowing collides with growing AI financing needs . . . persistent demand for capital is one reason we think borrowing costs can stay elevated,” BlackRock analysts wrote last week.

Matthew Hornbach, global head of macro strategy at Morgan Stanley, adds that part of the sell-off of US Treasuries that has pushed up yields could be down to banks or brokers hedging their hyperscaler credit exposure. When such companies provide liquidity for investors to buy and sell previously issued bonds, they are known as primary dealers.

“We can find a small amount of evidence, through US primary dealer balance sheet holdings of corporate bonds”, that hyperscaler issuance is having an effect on US Treasury yields, Hornbach says.

Even so, some investors think the authorities in charge of governments’ debt-issuing plans are having to think harder about when they conduct debt auctions, to avoid competing with a popular hyperscaler deal.

“We are starting to see countries thinking about AI issuance, going shorter or avoiding timing when they think there will be AI issuance,” says Henrietta Pacquement, chief operating officer for fixed income at Allspring Global Investments.

What if something breaks?

As the AI-related share of credit markets grows around the world, so do the risks associated with a downturn in the sector that now influences all other capital markets to some degree.

Although the majority of AI’s debt needs are being met in the safer investment-grade market, the sector’s more speculative names such as cloud-computing company CoreWeave have been venturing into the market for junk debt.

Such riskier issuers are deeply intertwined with the rest of the AI ecosystem. “If something did break in the below-investment-grade market, either a credit or a specific data centre, that would not play well in investment grade,” says Brown, at Neuberger.

With tech giants tapping all corners of the financial market for capital, assessing the overall exposure to individual borrowers has also become increasingly difficult.

Meta, for instance, has issued various bonds through its corporate balance sheet and via special-purpose vehicles tied to individual data centre projects.

Loren Moran, fixed-income portfolio manager at Wellington Management, says that “people have crept higher on single-issuer limits than they’ve really accounted for” and that close monitoring is needed across asset classes to avoid being unintentionally overweight on a single name.

With so much money committed to the bet that AI will transform the global economy to the benefit of the hyperscalers and their investors, a sector slowdown could come with huge financial consequences.

“The credit story in hyperscalers rests on a single consensus assumption, that operating cash flow triples from $600bn to $2tn,” Apollo’s chief economist, Torsten Sløk, wrote this month.

“If this doesn’t happen, then the risk is that the AI trade weakens, with credit spreads widening, capex plans getting cut and ultimately US GDP growth slowing,” Sløk warned.

Leading AI labs Anthropic and OpenAI have already talked of slowing development after rogue AI agents hacked into websites. Popular opposition to power-hungry data centres is growing, especially in the US. It is far from clear what the long-term financial returns from AI will be, or which companies will reap them. Analogies with the bust that followed the railway boom of the 19th century, which was also capital-intensive and largely debt-financed, are commonplace.

In the wake of mounting worries by equity investors that the world’s stock markets are dangerously tied to the fortunes of AI, the same risk is creeping into the bond market — risking an even bigger fallout if cracks emerge.

“New bonds . . . are increasingly a claim on the same AI investment cycle that has been driving equity return,” says Lucas Baynes, a senior investment strategist at Vanguard. In other words, the places investors can hide from the financial consequences of AI are getting fewer and further between.

Letter in response:
The globalisation of AI borrowing is a problem / From Edoardo Porrato, Turin, Italy

item.title: The India shock: exporting workers to the world
item.author: Tej Parikh
item.description: Emigration has helped New Delhi manage its labour surplus, but the strategy has limits
item.content:encoded:
Emigration has helped New Delhi manage its labour surplus, but the strategy has limits

Tej Parikh

India has its own version of the “China shock”. Instead of exporting high volumes of competitive manufacturing goods across the globe, the world’s most populous nation sends millions of workers abroad.

India churns out roughly 5mn graduates each year and around 1mn people enter its workforce every month. But just as the Chinese economy lacks the demand to absorb more of its industrial production at home, India’s cannot produce enough suitable jobs to employ its expanding labour supply. Youth underemployment is rife, despite the country’s rapid growth rate.

As a result, many Indians, often well-educated and English-speaking, move abroad to pursue careers. The country is the world’s largest source of international migrants, with an estimated 18.5mn living abroad in 2024. The Anglosphere and United Arab Emirates are common destinations.

Indeed, over the past decade, Indian nationals have accounted for the vast majority of approved H-1B petitions, a US visa for global professionals in selected fields. In the UK, about 1mn Indian nationals arrived between 2021 and 2025. Meanwhile, last year Indians overtook the English for the first time to become Australia’s largest overseas-born group.

Under Prime Minister Narendra Modi, the country has positioned its large labour force — which includes the world’s second-biggest pool of science, technology, engineering and mathematics (Stem) graduates — as an answer to skills shortages and ageing demographics abroad.

S Jaishankar, India’s foreign minister, recently said the country had signed labour-mobility pacts with 26 countries, with more in the pipeline. Such arrangements have been a central pillar of India’s bilateral trade negotiations. An overseas mobility bill also aims to help Indians access the “global workplace”.

This strategy has several upsides for New Delhi. At around $150bn last year, 3 per cent of its GDP, the country is by far the largest recipient of remittance payments. Returnees and the overseas community are sources of foreign exchange, investment and knowhow for the country. This summer, domestic banks raised more than $50bn by encouraging the diaspora, the world’s largest, to shift savings to India as part of measures to shore up the rupee.

Crucially, as with China’s overproduction, overseas markets provide a release valve. The export of workers enables the Indian government to ease socio-economic strains at home, where frustration abounds over the lack of good job opportunities.

But there are drawbacks to the worker-export model. For example, one estimate suggests brain drain costs India between $35bn and $50bn per annum, owing in part to lost productivity growth. Many Indians end up settling abroad.

And just as China is experiencing a worldwide backlash against its exports, India faces one as well.

Scepticism about immigration continues to animate politics in the rich world. And the recent surge in arrivals from the subcontinent, who join historical waves of emigration, puts a growing spotlight on people of Indian origin abroad.

Relative to native-born citizens and other migrant populations, Indian-born migrants and people of Indian heritage tend to obtain higher levels of education and earnings. Their rising prominence in public life — as chief executives, politicians and heads of prestigious organisations — can drive animosity. And though Indian nationals often dominate high-skilled immigration routes, family members and less-skilled individuals have emigrated too, in some cases by abusing the rules. This all provides fuel for anti-immigrant narratives.

Indeed, anti-Indian sentiment is on the rise. Just this month, the Republican nominee for a seat on Texas’s oil and gas regulator sparked allegations of racism for a social media post aimed at South Asian students. Last year, Indian-origin migrants were explicitly targeted in “March for Australia” rallies. Anti-South Asian slurs in online spaces in the US have also surged. The backlash could hinder the Modi government’s strategy. As it happens, US President Donald Trump has raised scrutiny of and fees for H-1B visas.

The “India shock” has implications for both sides. Rich economies need talented young workers. But a policy of immigration warrants robust administration, investment in housing and public services and initiatives to encourage integration and cohesion. Otherwise it won’t be sustainable.

India, meanwhile, cannot rely on remittances and its diaspora alone. The worker-export model reflects a deeper challenge facing New Delhi, which must strive to create enough productive work to better harness the country’s demographic dividend. China lacks consumer confidence. India lacks jobs. Neither can export its way out of domestic problems.

Send your thoughts via the comments, freelunch@ft.com or on X @tejparikh90.

Food for thought

How do recessions influence the flow of doctors into different practices of medicine? A recent US study explores.

Free Lunch on Sunday is edited by Harvey Nriapia

item.title: The FT View. The EU needs a clearer strategy for partners like Canada
item.author: The editorial board
item.description: Bloc should define what it can offer to prosperous fellow democracies
item.content:encoded:
Bloc should define what it can offer to prosperous fellow democracies

The editorial board

There was one message the leaders of Canada and the European Commission were keen to hammer home in their back-to-back speeches earlier this month: they are not going to take the dismantling of the rules-based international order lying down. In Strasbourg, Mark Carney and Ursula von der Leyen vowed to create a deeper alliance to make their economies more resilient and their sovereignty more effective. It was enough to rile up Donald Trump — but what it all means has yet to be decided.

In October, an EU-Canada summit is set to put policy flesh on the rhetorical bones. The two sides should set their ambitions high: they complement each other in so many areas that there are big benefits to be reaped. Energy resources and critical raw materials are in great demand in Europe and in ample supply in Canada. The large EU market offers much-needed diversification for a country badly buffeted by its neighbour’s erratic and domineering trade policy. Both sides have great capacities in technological development that they want to make less dependent on the US or China. They share geopolitical interests in the Arctic, and could collaborate more in defence industrial policy. Progress on any of these would make for a worthwhile summit.

Still, the potential should not be overhyped. Von der Leyen misjudged by inviting Canada “to be the first associate member of the EU”. No such thing exists, and the mention unwisely took capitals by surprise (Berlin had even been promoting an entirely different proposal with the same label as a way to gradually absorb Ukraine into the bloc). More importantly, it suggests a much deeper degree of integration than Canada is contemplating.

Any notion of EU membership inevitably comes with pooling of sovereignty to benefit from strictly aligned policies. Canada is not interested in the former and cannot go very far on the latter — joining the EU’s single market, for example — without raising trade barriers with the US that would be so costly they would make Brexit look like a walk in the park.

A more modest but more realistic partnership would be enough. Beyond the substance of any collaborations that might be agreed, it would show success for Carney’s “middle powers” agenda. It would also undo some of the damage sustained to the EU’s credibility from its members’ failure to fully ratify a decade-old EU-Canada trade agreement.

At the same time, the EU must see its evolving relations with Canada in the context of what it can offer to a broader range of countries, such as the UK, Norway, Switzerland and Turkey, where membership is not on the horizon but where closer co-operation is imperative. The EU’s approach instead seems to be ad hoc bilateralism with each of them. This risks missing the opportunity for more deliberate strategic leadership. 

If the EU wants to shape the changing economic world order, it should clarify the collaborative benefits it is willing to offer — from more ambitious access to the single market to more modest inclusion in its emerging “made in Europe” policy for preferential subsidies and public procurement. It should clarify, too, what reciprocal, legally binding commitments it expects in return.

None of this, moreover, should overshadow the crucial task of bringing in those countries that do want to become members. That means Ukraine above all, as well as nations such as Montenegro that are doing all they can to meet the EU’s strict accession criteria. This is harder than finding common ground with partners such as Canada — but also a greater test for the EU’s strategic relevance.

item.title: The Big Read. Tourist taxes on the march
item.author: Stephanie Stacey and Barney Jopson and Leo Lewis
item.description: Some governments want to fight back the hordes
item.content:encoded:
Some governments want to fight back the hordes

Stephanie Stacey and Barney Jopson and Leo Lewis

From the ancient city of Kyoto to Barcelona, Malta and the Maldives, countries and cities around the world are increasing taxes on tourists.

France and Italy now raise more than €1bn a year apiece from such duties and last year Greece’s tourist tax receipts rose by almost two-thirds. England said this month it was giving mayors powers to raise potentially unlimited levies.

The tourist tax drive is gaining steam, as hard-pressed local and national authorities seek voter-friendly ways to raise revenues and exert a measure of control over a tourist boom that is regularly breaking records.
