Mateu Hernández, director-general of Turisme de Barcelona, which promotes the Catalan city, emphasises the positive effects of its tourist tax, which since April has been set at a nightly rate of as much as €12 per person, one of the highest in Europe. He depicts the levy, which helps fund air conditioning in sweltering public schools, as part of a shift in tourism from “quantity” to “quality”.

Some areas want taxes to curb crowding even more sharply, as post-pandemic tourism surges to new heights, with a total of 1.54bn international overnight visitors last year according to the World Travel & Tourism Council.

Venice, which imposed overnight accommodation duties in 2011, brought in precedent-setting fees for day trippers in 2024. Other cities and regions, including San Diego and Columbus in the US and Manchester in the UK, invest the funds in marketing to attract still more guests.

So far, experiences across the world indicate that the duties are proving more efficient at providing a fiscal fillip than at keeping the waves of tourists in check in the world’s most famous destinations.

But some worry that the hospitality industry will end up paying the bill or that they will divert travellers from less glamorous locations.

Scottish Ballet has cancelled plans to extend a Christmas run of Cinders! — its gender-swap retelling of Cinderella — in Edinburgh due, it says, to soaring accommodation costs, exacerbated by a new tourist levy in the Scottish capital.

“Local authorities are strapped for cash and this kind of seems like a hack: a way to raise money without taxing your voters,” says Dan Neidle, founder of UK-based think-tank Tax Policy Associates. “But we’re not seeing realistic analysis from government of where the cost will actually fall.”

While not all countries have nationwide figures on tourism tax receipts, in a report this summer the OECD group of rich countries noted that New Zealand, Japan, Malta, Greece and the Maldives have all increased tourism-related taxes over the past two years.

At a city level, Kyoto increased its maximum accommodation taxes almost 10-fold in March, while Amsterdam laid out plans in June to charge a 20 per cent levy by 2030, the steepest in Europe.

“It’s a fashionable time for taxing visitors,” says Jan van der Borg, a professor of tourism management at Leuven Catholic University who cautions that governments should not mistake the levies for “a magical instrument”.

If, like the UK, governments want simultaneously to bring in more tourism and more tax revenue, they have to find a Goldilocks rate. Set it too low, and you lose out on valuable income. Set it too high, and you risk eroding the tourist economy that pays the tax.

Van der Borg warns that for those looking to curb crowding and cut tourist numbers, “ill-targeted” overnight levies — the most common form of visitor tax in Europe — risk hitting the most lucrative visitors while sparing day trippers who do not contribute as much to the local economy.

In Amsterdam, which has tied its visitor charges to a target of keeping annual tourist numbers under 20mn, he says applying the levy to accommodation rates “hurts the most interesting type of visitor: the people that want to spend several nights in your place, see the hidden gems, and spend money locally”.

Bears among us

Italy introduced one of Europe’s earliest modern tourism levies in 1910. Initially targeted at spa towns and health resorts, the taxes spread across the country under Benito Mussolini’s fascist regime in the 1930s.

The levies were scrapped nationwide ahead of Italy’s 1990 World Cup but made a comeback in the 2010s and are now a mainstay of more than 1,000 municipalities, according to Italian tourism consultancy JFC. They are an important source of funding for local governments, bringing in a total of close to €1.19bn in total in 2025.

In Japan, where a long-running campaign has boosted international tourist numbers from 7mn in 2005 to 43mn in 2025, the taxes have also become an important source of revenue.

Japan started charging a nationwide tax in 2019, while some cities have also imposed extra levies on hotel stays, with rates varying depending on the room cost. Kyoto’s tax is notably high, at up to ¥10,000, while in Tokyo even stays in tiny capsule hotels are now taxable. Other quasi-tourism taxes imposed in recent years include new fees for climbing Mount Fuji, which was free until 2024, and a ¥2,500 fee for non-residents to visit Himeji Castle.

For tourist hotspots, the funding opportunity is clear, but there is less evidence that the taxes help combat overtourism. Kyoto has become one of the most popular destinations for tourists in Japan, attracting 13mn overseas visitors last year, placing strain on the city’s infrastructure and overcrowding its once-tranquil temples and streets.

This July, Japan tripled its international tourist tax to ¥3,000. The revenue from the additional tax is supposed to fund countermeasures against overtourism, such as promoting the attractions of places outside the core tourist magnets of Tokyo, Kyoto and Osaka, as well as improving tourist infrastructure.

Part of the budget for the current fiscal year was allocated to controlling the wild bear population in rural areas and funding the war against parasites afflicting the country’s famous cherry trees.

Similarly, visitor levies have been proliferating in Spain alongside mounting angst about overtourism in what is now the world’s second most visited country after France.

Revenue from the Balearic Islands’ “sustainable tourism tax” — introduced a decade ago in Mallorca, Menorca, Ibiza and Formentera — is channelled into investments for what the regional government calls “the structural needs of residents”. This month it approved a new €200mn spending package dedicated to projects ranging from desalination to video surveillance.

But that money has not quelled complaints from some locals that tourism is pushing the islands to breaking point by driving up housing costs, straining public services and degrading the environment. In July, police fired rubber bullets and struck protesters with batons after thousands took to the streets in Palma de Mallorca to demand curbs on tourism.

Nor has Venice’s day-tripper levy stopped the city from setting new visitor records. Officials are now exploring raising the fee, which was previously set between €5 and €10 but lapsed in July, to as much as €30, according to Reuters.

Stealth taxes

Tourist taxes are not exactly popular with the sector tasked with actually collecting the levies — hospitality.

Normally they are applied to hotel rates. So as not to put off prospective customers, accommodation providers typically absorb a proportion of new levies and end up taking home less than before, says Kelsey Fenerty, manager of analytics at hospitality data tracker CoStar. They may also feel unable to push through annual rate increases.

Studies of levies applied in recent years suggest that, “generally speaking, it takes about a year” before hotels can start increasing their take-home rates again, says Fenerty. Occupancy is usually unscathed — in part because hoteliers tend to absorb much of the new costs.

The way the rate is applied can make a big difference. Many cities in Europe — including Barcelona, Lisbon and Rome — allow hotels to exclude tourism taxes from the headline online price, adding the levy only once guests arrive at the property. By that point, “it’s kind of too late to impact guest demand”, says Fenerty, adding that this might explain why hotels in Barcelona have been able to keep pushing up their take-home rates in tandem with increases to local levies.

In the UK, by contrast, anti-drip pricing rules mean that hotels will have to advertise the total price including all mandatory fees and charges upfront, making the tourist tax “more visible here”, says Neidle of Tax Policy Associates. That could increase the chance of would-be travellers looking elsewhere.

The UK government has said it expects local authorities to levy only a “modest charge” that will have “minimal impact on visitor numbers”. But lobbyists warn that raising taxes could backfire by denting demand, ultimately curtailing hoteliers’ ability to stay in business, pay further taxes and employ locals. UKHospitality, an industry body, says a 5 per cent tourism levy could cost as many as 33,000 jobs in the UK.

Almost a fifth of respondents to a February survey by the World Travel & Tourism Council said that existing tourist taxes had already caused them to visit a different destination than they had originally planned.

“Travellers experience the total cost of a trip rather than its individual components,” says Marriott’s Europe president Neal Jones.

Taxes are also split into percentage levies and flat fees. England has gone with percentage fees — the precise rate of which can be defined by local mayors. Ministers say this will limit the pain for budget travellers while maximising returns from the wealthy.

Hoteliers, however, say they would prefer a flat fee. A fixed charge would have saved a “huge” administrative burden for Jackie Innes, an Edinburgh landlord who says it has been “impossible to figure out” how to calculate the right charges to apply to the two apartments she rents out.

Places like Edinburgh and London might “get away with” raising levies, says Alan Glen, a partner at accountancy Azets. Tourists will always want to visit places with the unique stature of Venice. But seaside UK towns, or second-tier Italian cities, could struggle to compete.

This could raise the prospect of local tax wars, particularly among rural and seaside towns. Researchers in Italy have in the past found some evidence of “substitution” towards resorts with lower taxes.

Not all markets are created equal. “Blackpool is not Venice,” Neidle says.

Letter in response:
Greece’s tourist levy is too blunt, says Mykonos DJ / From Nikolaos Iatrou aka ‘Nixxie’, Mykonos, Greece

item.title: The FT View. What an AI maths breakthrough means for human discovery
item.author: The editorial board
item.description: In solving complex problems, process can be as important as the final result
item.content:encoded:
In solving complex problems, process can be as important as the final result

The editorial board

Albert Einstein described the harmony of pure mathematics as “in its way, the poetry of logical ideas”. Yet the field that underpins science and all it describes is now in uproar, after OpenAI produced a proof of a high-profile maths problem.

The turmoil over the AI lab’s intervention and its wider impact shows how maths is on the frontline of the possibilities and perils of the technology. While headlines focus on the risks that AI will cause mass unemployment, accelerate global heating or even destroy humanity, its impact on scientific discovery is also fundamental.

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, announced this month that it had developed a solution for the Navier-Stokes maths problem set 26 years ago as a Millennium Prize challenge with a $1mn reward (which the company has said it won’t take). The news sparked dismay from many leading mathematicians over how OpenAI obtained its result and what it means for maths’ future. Some fear it will open an era of computational brute-force shortcuts to solutions, shunning crucial insights that humans would have gained along the way.

On one level, the story highlights familiar concerns about AI exploiting human intellectual property. OpenAI’s announcement prompted a New York University mathematician, Tristan Buckmaster, who had been working on related research with Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, to raise questions about possible foul play. OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman rejected what he called “unfounded accusations of plagiarism”.

The incident caused a deeper unease in the global community of mathematicians. In an open letter, 27 winners of the prestigious Fields Medal argued that the goals of AI companies and the maths community were “severely misaligned”. Solving problems should be “only a tool and proxy for achieving the primary goal of conceptual understanding and insight”, driving the formulation of new questions and ideas, they wrote.

The stakes are much higher than esoteric discussions about theories very few people on Earth understand. Maths is the foundation of our understanding of the natural world and human civilisation. The patterns it reveals are crucial to billions of years of evolution and to the latest technologies, including AI.

The idea that humans should be central to mathematical discovery is not a misplaced argument against digital progress. AI has a potentially exciting and constructive role in mathematics, just as in the physical sciences in areas from medical imaging to understanding the origins of disease, which could transform healthcare.

There is, though, a long history of mathematical understanding gained from being a person moving through the material world. From the (embellished) stories of Archimedes leaping from his bath to Newton being hit on the head by a falling apple, physical observations have long been linked with sparking transformative chains of thought. The Navier-Stokes problem itself relates to the flow of fluids such as water and air.

There are powerful arguments that skipping to the solution of a maths problem in an opaque way could deprive us of essential knowledge that humans might have discovered. For example, Fermat’s Little Theorem, along with Euler’s generalisation of it, underpins modern cryptographic methods that protect data across the globe. More broadly, maths and its pursuit by thinkers over millennia have had a profound role in grappling with great philosophical questions relating to the human condition and the world around us.

The maths dispute is a powerful reminder that in the pursuit of progress, human-led processes matter as well as outcomes — for hard-nosed practical reasons as well as romantic ones.

item.title: The world’s 80mn-kilometre power grid problem
item.author: Simon Mundy
item.description: Huge rise in infrastructure investment needed to meet energy access and climate goals, UN says
item.content:encoded:
Huge rise in infrastructure investment needed to meet energy access and climate goals, UN says

Simon Mundy

Welcome back.

Considering that it ranks among humanity’s most complex and sophisticated creations, and has been core to the creation of the modern world, the electric grid has long been rather unfairly taken for granted. Now it’s getting an overdue — and urgently needed — burst of global attention, as I explain below. Have a good weekend.

Grappling with gridlock

Eighty million kilometres is more than half the distance between the Earth and the Sun. It’s also the length of global power lines that António Guterres wants to see added or replaced by 2040 to support the clean energy transition.

This week the UN’s outgoing secretary-general launched a new scheme, the Global Grids Accelerator, aimed at galvanising investment in power transmission and distribution infrastructure. “Renewables are booming, but the grids that carry clean power are not keeping pace,” Guterres said, calling grids the “arteries of the energy transition”.

The official announcement pointedly noted that this initiative will “not create a new financing institution”. Instead, it’s intended to bring together governments, investors and technical experts to drive deeper collaboration around grid investment, with an initial focus on Africa and south-east Asia.

This reflects a wider shift in the energy transition conversation — from lofty pledges of eye-watering green energy capacity to a less glamorous stage of wrestling with the raw mechanics of how a low-carbon energy system will work. This has brought a new focus on the world’s grid infrastructure, which has now emerged as a major constraint.

As of last year, renewable projects with a capacity of 1,700 gigawatts — nearly 50 times the UK’s average power demand — were stuck in grid connection queues, as were 600 gigawatts of battery storage, according to the International Energy Agency. Meanwhile, many wind and solar projects that have managed to secure connections are finding that the power they produce is often “curtailed” — wasted — because of inadequate transmission capacity, forcing the system to call on more expensive fossil power.

One factor behind this is the fact that permitting and other bureaucracy for new grid infrastructure tend to take a very long time — completing these projects often takes more than a decade, according to the IEA. Another is the new technical challenges facing grid authorities, who have been used to designing a system around a relatively small number of thermal power stations rather than a larger, widely dispersed number of variable renewable plants.

Still another is cost: prices for key grid infrastructure components such as transformers have rocketed in the past five years as the investment drive runs into manufacturing capacity limits. Here’s a useful chart from new research by JPMorgan’s Derek Chollet and Sarah Kapnick:

Annual investment in grid infrastructure has risen from about $300bn in 2020 to about $400bn in 2025 — but will need to rise by a further 50 per cent by 2030 to meet projected global electricity demand, says the IEA (which is also the original source of that 80mn km figure, its estimate of the length of new or refurbished grid infrastructure required for countries to meet their national clean power goals — roughly the total length of all the world’s grids today).

The issue has taken on a particular salience in Europe, where the continent’s high electricity prices are fuelling concerns about its economic competitiveness, and in the US, where grid operators are struggling to keep up with a huge rise in demand from data centres to power AI. Yesterday, the Trump administration announced a $1.9bn federal funding package for 31 projects to improve US grids, through refurbished power lines and the deployment of “grid-enhancing technologies” including AI tools.

But the challenge is still more urgent in many developing countries — notably in Africa, where more than 500mn people still lack access to electricity — which are forecast to account for most of the world’s future rise in energy demand. During more than a century quietly underpinning the workings of modern civilisation, the world’s power grids have rarely been so starkly in the spotlight.

Smart reads

  • Brussels has urged the UK to raise tariffs on Chinese cars, as the continent’s carmakers struggle to cope with competition from Chinese-made electric vehicles.
  • The rise of AI is likely to worsen, not reduce, worries about economic inequality, writes Adair Turner.

item.title: The dangers of devolution dogma
item.author: Jennifer Williams
item.description: Viewing decentralisation as a silver bullet could lead to an unthinking rush to pass down power as fast as possible
item.content:encoded:
Viewing decentralisation as a silver bullet could lead to an unthinking rush to pass down power as fast as possible

Jennifer Williams

Good morning from Manchester. Andy Burnham has often spoken with antipathy about the SW1 bubble, complaining that it misunderstands and misconstrues what he says. 

Back in Manchester, there is a small army of people who have worked on the regional growth, post-industrial turnaround agenda for decades, latterly alongside Burnham, who now hope that such endeavours will be given a fair wind from central government. 

But that does not mean the current devolution rhetoric has been accepted completely uncritically. 

No silver bullets 

“I think people need to understand this is probably the deepest thing he and his team really believe in,” said Jim O’Neill earlier this week of the new prime minister’s focus on English devolution, adding that most observers still didn’t seem to have recognised that. 

For “those few” like him who have been pushing the agenda for years, “this is like Christmas Day”, O’Neill told the think-tank Centre for Cities.

Nevertheless O’Neill — who advised Burnham in recent months, albeit informally — sounded notes of caution. Devolving to places that are not ready could be a recipe for disaster, he said.

“This is probably the single most immediate challenge they’ve got,” he added of Burnham’s team. “With a lot of local areas putting their hands up saying ‘what about me, me, me’, they’ve got to be tough about it.”

That could indeed be a challenge, given the level to which expectations have been raised. I sighed a little in relief at his remarks, though, because for some time I’ve worried that there seem to be only two permissible positions in this space. 

One is scepticism about the entire idea of decentralisation, sometimes in tandem with the perennial refrain that “there is no point trying to grow the regions”. The other seems to view decentralisation as a silver bullet.

The former view is now in its box under this government. But the latter risks turning into blind dogma if it becomes an unthinking rush to pass down power as fast as possible, particularly if it isn’t anchored in local reality or a national theory of growth.

Michael Heseltine, an ardent devolutionist, is fond of noting that MPs don’t like devolution because turkeys don’t vote for Christmas: they’re not going to actively hand power away. The same is true in reverse. Mayors will never reject more power. 

But it has been a long time since Britain put a premium on strong local institutions, and when they have failed in recent years central government has been slow to notice or learn lessons. They falter not because Whitehall inherently knows better, but because their foundations are weak. So piling more on top of them at pace is a risk. 

That the local level lacks capability has not been missed in Number 10 North. One of the government’s first announcements this summer was for a mass civil service relocation to the regions.  

Mancunian economist Mike Emmerich, who worked with O’Neill on Manchester’s Independent Economic Review in 2009, elaborated further in a paper published in August. 

The problem, he wrote, is not that the landscape of mayoral authorities is currently uneven, since by its nature they will vary and take time to mature. “The problem is . . . that the ambitions now being placed upon [them] are growing more quickly than the institutional and financial foundations available to many of them.”

Places will need to build a host of strengths, including an understanding of the local economy, strategic decision-making, credible projects, finance assembly, strong partnerships and relationships with other organisations.  

O’Neill advocates a staged approach similar to the view taken by his old boss, George Osborne, in which the most advanced areas are granted powers first, while some powers are granted to places on the rise. Otherwise there is no incentive for the rest to get to an appropriate point, he argues, recounting 37 devolution submissions from local areas during his time as a minister, only four of which were credible.

“There was one place in particular . . . where the Treasury had to basically rewrite and tell them what they were asking for.”

This is not the dead hand of centralising Whitehall talking, but a longstanding advocate of the opposite.

Property developer Mike Ingall, whose outfit Allied London built Manchester’s Spinningfields central business district in close partnership with the city council in the 2000s, is blunter still.

“My fear is if we devolve to all the mayoral departments, towns, cities, are they good enough?” he queried, speaking to me yesterday at a Place North conference on urban regeneration. 

“That’s not a criticism of everyone, it’s just a question. Will we have to go through a process of educating these other local government officials? Because my experience elsewhere is not good.”

It is a delicate message to convey to other places from Manchester, which tends to think it can do things not only differently, but better than everywhere else. Mayors reading this will doubtless find some of these observations irritating or condescending. 

All three men have nonetheless been involved in this agenda longer than Burnham or any of the regional mayors. None are in the business of talking down places outside London, all wish the new prime minister well in his endeavour and all have experienced the cold maths of trying to get investment into difficult areas. 

They were all also at a charity fundraiser in Manchester’s Soho House yesterday, an event perhaps best summarised as “getting the old band back together”. This fragment of the “Manchester mafia”, the power brokers during the late Howard Bernstein’s era who skew towards the property sector, gathered to discuss Emmerich’s forthcoming book on Bernstein and the city’s journey. 

The dinner was an echo of the days when deals in this city were cut in a different part of Heron House, the building that now houses Number 10 North. Wing’s, the Chinese restaurant next door, was a favoured Bernstein haunt.

To those inside that court, Manchester’s tight ecosystem of key players was the secret sauce. To its fiercest critics outside, it was a cabal, a closed shop. 

Others pressed their ears up against the metaphorical door, trying to work out how much of the prevailing orthodoxy to believe and how much to treat with caution. Often, in reality, it was a bit of both.

No ruling class is perfect, after all. Power is seductive, wherever it is, and all orthodoxies are worth challenging, even when they’re made in Manchester.

Top stories today

  • Up in the air | Andy Burnham has cast doubt on the plan for a third runway at Heathrow after privately telling MPs he has always opposed the project.
  • ‘Turkey-across-the-Channel’ | The EU has warned that Britain would need to raise tariffs on Chinese cars if it wants to avoid “made in Europe” barriers that would threaten key exports.
  • Does Burnham mean business? | Devolving power appeals to corporate leaders, but the government’s fiscal room to manoeuvre is limited, writes John Gapper in today’s Big Read.
  • Opinion | Is the UK electorate fragmenting? Not so fast, write Marta Miori and Jane Green of Nuffield College, Oxford.

item.title: Bonds can keep falling
item.author: Robert Armstrong
item.description: Easy to explain, hard to live with
item.content:encoded:
Easy to explain, hard to live with

Robert Armstrong

Good morning. However badly your week has gone, and no matter how much the mean old bond market has hurt you, you are unlikely to have had a worse time than the Morgan Stanley employee who, as Bloomberg reported, accidentally emailed a list of the bank’s real and prospective investment banking deals to a wide distribution list. This is the stuff of nightmares. It makes our toes feel funny. Our friends on Alphaville unpacked it all here. Rival bankers are wincing and chuckling at the same time, but they should remember: next time it could be you. Tell us about your daft email mistakes, ideally with the subject line “the sender wishes to recall this message”: unhedged@ft.com.

Are we there yet? (Spoiler: no)

On Wednesday, the US 10-year yield rose by 14 basis points, which is a lot. On Thursday, the yield stayed stubbornly above 5.1 per cent, dragging borrowing costs in the rest of the world up with it. This has painful implications for the fiscal situation of many countries, and it might have painful implications for markets more broadly. But keep in mind: it is not surprising. There are very straightforward reasons for bond yields rising right now. And there is no particular reason to think that we have seen the top in yields.

Start with the fundamentals — that is, the basic factors that are pushing yields higher (and bond prices lower) over the long term.

Fundamental #1: Inflation is above target. US PCE inflation is at 3.6 per cent and trending the wrong way. We have been slicing and dicing the inflation numbers in a zillion different ways for five years now, but we are where we are. Higher oil prices don’t explain all of this, but they sure don’t help. If the US bans diesel exports — an absolute lock for the bad policy decision hall of fame, if it happens — that will cause inflation to rise globally almost immediately, and in the US eventually. Tariffs are a very small part of the story, but probably not nothing. But whatever the list of causes, we are where we are.  

Fundamental #2: US economic growth is accelerating. The labour market is clearly getting stronger. Consumer spending, although there are some weak data points, is robust at the headline level. The AI data centre spending boom continues apace, and business investment more generally is strong. Corporate profits are booming. If inflation is what happens when demand outruns supply, the demand side is set to be a bigger problem in the near term.

Fundamental #3: The Fed is credible. Fed chair Kevin Warsh walks and talks like a hawk, and the market is starting to believe he is a hawk. The Fed will raise rates, which may cool the economy eventually, bringing rates down, but in the short term the increases add to the upward pressure on rates.

Given all this, there is nothing particularly surprising about Treasury yields above 5 per cent. Indeed, on the fundamentals, one can imagine them being higher. In a rough way, the 10-year yield tracks nominal GDP growth — with the yields a percentage point or so lower than GDP growth under normal conditions. Well, nominal GDP growth was over 6.5 per cent last quarter and, at the current rate, could be higher still this quarter. Five per cent yields, if anything, look a shade low in that context.

Move beyond these fundamental points, and the picture doesn’t get any better. The fiscal situation in the US is poor, and a load of Treasury supply is on the way. Competition from massive hyperscaler debt issuance can’t help. And finally, the buyer base for Treasuries seems to have become flightier. With impeccable timing, the New York Fed put out a paper earlier this month stating:

the Treasury market has become increasingly price-sensitive over time, driven by the declining participation of less price-sensitive foreign official investors and the rising role of more price-sensitive hedge funds and other private investors 

This is ageing well, and it raises a really interesting/scary question: what happens when the market’s pre-eminent marginal buyer, Joe Hedgie, falls into a blender?

As our excellent colleague on the news side, Ian Smith, pointed out yesterday in our Unhedged podcast, we have seen this movie before. When the war with Iran started, hedgies got hosed on short-end UK and European debt. Now they seem to be having a rough week in Treasuries. From the NY Fed paper:

In normal times, the presence of highly elastic investors such as hedge funds dampens yield responses to supply or demand shocks — small yield changes are sufficient to induce these investors to adjust their portfolios. However, this also creates fragility risk: if these elastic investors become impaired or step back from the market during stress periods, the market becomes suddenly much less elastic, and shocks can generate large yield movements.

The speed of Wednesday’s ascent in yields certainly suggested there was some forced selling in that mix. This is a perfect environment for some kind of accident.

One good read

Oops, they did it AGAIN.

item.title: The Big Read. What Burnham means for business
item.author: John Gapper
item.description: His core message of devolving power from London appeals to corporate leaders. But his government has limited fiscal room to manoeuvre
item.content:encoded:
His core message of devolving power from London appeals to corporate leaders. But his government has limited fiscal room to manoeuvre

John Gapper

When chief executives and business leaders journey to Liverpool for Labour’s annual conference this month, they can be sure of at least one warm welcome. Steve Rotheram, the northern city’s metro mayor and a close friend and ally of Andy Burnham, prime minister, is seeking £11bn of private investment for its continued regeneration.

The gathering of Britain’s governing party, which begins on Sunday, will take place in a conference centre next to the River Mersey. The city’s ambitious plans for the revival of its historic docklands include a 70-storey tower with a luxury hotel and apartments. They echo Burnham’s strategy as mayor of Greater Manchester to bring growth to neglected towns and cities with business backing.

But Liverpool also symbolises a Labour Party with far less sympathy for capitalism. In the mid-1980s, it was controlled by the hard-left Militant Tendency faction, which halted the city with strikes. Neil Kinnock, Labour’s former leader, dramatically denounced its tactics at the party conference in 1985, and it took a long struggle to haul the party back from socialist purity to electability under Tony Blair’s New Labour.

So it raised disturbing memories when Burnham used his first speech as leader in July after ousting Sir Keir Starmer to promise a return to the past. He criticised “four decades of the neoliberalism that began in the 1980s” for taking the UK in the wrong economic direction. The speech was rich in nostalgia for the period before both Margaret Thatcher and Blair, although Burnham served as a junior minister in the latter’s government.

Burnham’s speech was partly a people-pleaser’s tactical nod to his leftwing base. But it alarmed business leaders, who fear that Labour’s attitude to private enterprise is ambiguous at best. Starmer took office in 2024 courting the corporate elite with promises of investment and relief from bureaucracy. But his chancellor Rachel Reeves scotched their hopes with a £25bn annual increase in employer national insurance in her first Budget.

Now, they hope for easier treatment from Burnham, who has emphasised his “pro-business” stance in Greater Manchester. His core message of devolving power from London has corporate support, and Labour has a long tradition of moderating in office. But the fiscal pressure on Reeves’ successor John Healey will make it hard to offer companies relief from their tax burden.

Healey has said he wants the UK to be “a country of wealth creation”, but many are sceptical: “They all want to promise growth and they’re not the people who create it,” says one entrepreneur. Andy Haldane, president of the British Chambers of Commerce and an FT contributing editor, noted last week that markets suspect this of being “a traditional tax-and-spend socialist government with better TikTok videos”.

Labour itself has become less enmeshed in business since the mid-1980s, when its party base was rooted in the working-class industrial sector. About 60 per cent of trade union members now work in the public sector, and many Labour MPs have come from charities, think-tanks and public sector bodies, rather than the private sector. Although Healey hopes to reduce the burden of business regulation by 25 per cent by the end of parliament, there are no plans to reverse extensive new employment rights for workers.

Despite this, the mood among some business leaders heading to Liverpool is cautiously positive. Regardless of Burnham’s early rhetoric, they regard him and Healey as more interested in economic growth than progressive ideology. “We have a prime minister with political nous and charisma who could get things done . . . Our message has been ‘We can help you,’” says Rick Haythornthwaite, chair of NatWest Group and the business-led 2030 Prosperity Alliance.

Rain Newton-Smith, director-general of the CBI business group, says that Burnham is “clearly bringing” a similar approach to national government as he did to the Manchester region. “He is pragmatic and wants to roll up his sleeves and turn problems into shared challenges.” Another leader contrasts Burnham’s tone approvingly with attitudes to big business of recent Labour and Conservative governments. “The vibes are encouraging. They now need to be turned into actions.”

Chief executives tend to be optimistic until proved wrong, but those close to Burnham suggest they are not deluded. “Andy is far more likely to quote from a homeless person he’s met than a political theorist he’s read. He’s a man of lived experience,” says Danny Sriskandarajah, chief executive of the New Economics Foundation, a progressive think-tank that has been influential on Labour policy. The prime minister wants “a more interventionist state”, he says, “but not an anti-business one”.

Burnham is not the first Labour leader whose radicalism is hard to assess. Inspired by socialism, the party’s 1918 manifesto promised the “immediate nationalisation and democratic control of vital public services” but its commitment to common ownership of the means of production became diluted from the 1950s onwards before finally being rewritten under Blair.

“I don’t see Labour as ever having been primarily an ideological party,” says Mark Wickham-Jones, a political science professor at Bristol University. But Burnham’s mention in his first speech as leader of the movement being “forged” in steel and iron works, coalfields, mills and shipyards fitted with the party’s nostalgic nature. “Labour is extraordinarily attached to its past,” notes Wickham-Jones.

Having paid tribute to that history, Burnham has since become harder to pin down. He indicated during the by-election in Makerfield in which he was re-elected as an MP that he backed public ownership of privatised industries such as water. He has since moderated his stance, talking only of “public control”. After being a Blair minister, he moved to what is broadly characterised as the party’s “soft left” wing.

He defines his programme as “Manchesterism”. As mayor of the city region, he adapted a strategy pioneered by Sir Howard Bernstein, former chief executive of the city council. Investment in transport and infrastructure was used to lure private investment. Greater Manchester’s economy is estimated to have grown by 3.1 per cent a year in the decade leading up to 2023, double the national average.

Many of the city’s new jobs are in financial and business services, rather than in the old industries that he eulogised but “Andy believes in whatever works and makes him feel good”, says one adviser.

Like Starmer, he has an overarching faith in public intervention to boost private sector investment. But there are significant differences. Labour’s 2024 manifesto emphasised its national “missions”, notably the drive by Ed Miliband, former energy secretary, to turn the UK into a “clean energy superpower”.

Burnham, however, is more focused on restoring local economies by devolving power and control of public investment from Whitehall to metropolitan regions. Harry Quilter-Pinner, executive director of the IPPR think-tank, says the prime minister has “a theory of the state and power that most politicians don’t”.

Yet private and public aims can conflict, as with the UK’s pivot from North Sea oil and gas to renewables. Despite hopes for a smooth “green new deal” transition, a target for Scotland to have 28,000 offshore wind jobs by 2020 was missed by 80 per cent, according to the Resolution Foundation. Burnham wants fewer “job-deleting metropolitan projects”, one adviser says. He appointed Miliband as foreign secretary rather than chancellor, as some on the party’s left wanted.

One lingering symbolic question is whether the government will approve more drilling for North Sea gas and oil in the Jackdaw and Rosebank fields, despite opposition from environmentalists. The projects would bring a combined £11bn in investment and Jackdaw would reduce the UK’s reliance on gas from Norwegian fields. Unions criticised long delays in approving the projects and Michael Marra, the newly elected leader of Scottish Labour, backs both.

The larger problem facing many businesses, particularly those in the manufacturing industries close to Burnham’s heart, is that the UK’s industrial energy prices are about a third higher than the European average. This has accelerated the deindustrialisation that he laments in ceramics, chemicals and energy-intensive sectors. Although oil prices have been raised by the Gulf war, businesses also face high levies to pay for the energy transition.

“We have the highest industrial electricity costs in the world and that is a choice of government, not markets. We love his narrative about re-industrialisation but you need to fix the cost base,” says Stephen Phipson, chief executive of Make UK, the manufacturing trade group. Reeves provided some targeted relief for energy-intensive industries, but the CBI said it still leaves some 2.7mn British companies facing higher bills.

Electricity prices are part of “a tsunami of costs facing businesses”, says Shevaun Haviland, director-general of the British Chambers of Commerce. It says official policies have added 70 per cent to the costs of the average small and medium-sized business in the past decade, including increases under Starmer in employer NI and the statutory National Living Wage. The latter has risen by 11 per cent for adults in two years, above general average wage growth, and by much more for young workers.

A second challenge is the expansion of business regulation. Reeves and Healey have accepted that excessive regulation can limit economic growth. Healey has blamed this on “a thicket of arm’s length bodies and regulators” and set his target for cutting it back by 25 per cent. But others such as Angela Rayner, Labour’s former deputy leader whom Burnham has reappointed to his cabinet, back new union-backed restrictions, notably in the new Employment Rights Act.

The act makes it easier for unions to be recognised in workplaces and gives workers on zero- and low-hours contracts rights to guaranteed hours. It became law last year despite business opposition and the government is consulting employers and unions on its detailed implementation. Burnham has given no indication that he will retreat. “We are not asking for a bonfire of rules, but we want it to be proportionate,” Newton-Smith says.

Apart from the details, the way this is being implemented by the government with input from employers and unions echoes “tripartism” under governments in the 1970s. The principle of the three sides “sitting together round the same table”, as the Tory prime minister Edward Heath put it in 1972, was dismantled by Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s. That was the start of the “neoliberalism” that Burnham decries.

Whatever the hopes of business leaders for the new government, it will be extremely constrained, politically and fiscally.

Cutting regulation aggressively would sit oddly with a prime minister who blames UK society’s ills on liberalisation. Meanwhile, it would be expensive to offer broad relief on business costs. It would cost the Treasury about £5bn a year to shift energy policy levies to general taxation, although the CBI argues that it would raise growth.

Healey could yet be forced by the fiscal squeeze to impose further tax increases that affect business and investment. Jamie Dimon, chief executive of JPMorgan, has warned against a putative windfall tax on banks, saying that it would affect inward investment. Some ministers back the idea of pushing capital gains tax closer to levels of income tax, arguing that wealth has been undertaxed. Reeves made some increases in capital gains taxes in her first Budget.

A further rise in capital gains tax would affect family businesses and employee share schemes, as well as carried interest income of UK-based private equity partners. “Our members are 100 per cent against it,” says Haviland of the BCC. Burnham has blamed private equity-backed chains for having raised the cost of care for the elderly and hopes to create a public alternative, like the National Health Service. “He hates a lot of what private equity stands for,” one adviser says.

The prospect of higher taxes sends shivers through the City of London. “I hope we’ve learnt that some things that work politically do not work economically . . . A lot of investors say that they like the UK and want to invest here but the government makes it damn hard,” says one financier. These fears have had an effect. Chris Rokos, the hedge fund billionaire and one of the country’s largest taxpayers, is moving residency to Greece.

It does not help that neither Haldane nor Lord Jim O’Neill, former Goldman Sachs chief economist, have joined the administration, despite having advised Burnham before he became prime minister. Varun Chandra, former managing partner of the consultancy Hakluyt, has remained in Downing Street as chief business adviser and Jonathan Reynolds has returned as business secretary. Company leaders respect them both, but now depend heavily on Healey’s restraint.

Even next month’s Budget may not provide clarity on the prime minister’s attitude to business and government. That must wait until the publication of a white paper on devolution, setting out the implications and how much power will be given to mayors. But a trip to Liverpool to see the changing city will offer some clues. If Burnhamism exists anywhere apart from Manchester, it is on this waterfront, from his football team Everton’s new stadium to its development plans.

Here is a hopeful vision of a new economy replacing one that foundered, along with Britain’s northern industrial might. “The government must look at what the world will want in 10 years and work from there. You cannot look back,” says Newton-Smith. Despite Labour’s habit of doing so and the nostalgia of its leader’s first speech, that is good advice.
