item.title: The FT View. Russia’s $6.9bn sanctions evasion scheme
item.author: The editorial board
item.description: Western punitive measures have forced Moscow into costly workaround efforts
item.content:encoded:
Western punitive measures have forced Moscow into costly workaround efforts

The editorial board

Before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Russia was so worried about the economic toll of being cut off by western partners from the Swift interbank messaging system that it warned it would consider this an “act of war”. Four years after Russia’s major banks were cut off, an FT investigation has exposed how a vast document forgery operation nonetheless enabled a Kremlin-backed fintech company to funnel more than $6.9bn through the global banking system in about nine months — some of it used to buy sensitive military supplies. It is bad news that Russia has managed to evade sanctions by using old-school money laundering techniques. The good news is that it has been unable to create any viable alternative to the traditional cross-border payments system.

One big lesson is that despite years of tightening controls on money laundering, the correspondent banking system is only as strong as its weakest links. It relies on assumptions that each bank is doing proper due diligence on its own clients. But when those banks are in jurisdictions with weak sanctions enforcement or poor know-your-customer controls, the whole system is vulnerable. By using front companies to funnel payments through jurisdictions such as Kyrgyzstan, Russia’s A7 fintech in effect created a back door into big clearing banks such as Standard Chartered, Citigroup and JPMorgan Chase.

When western correspondent banks raised suspicions about money flows through banks in Kyrgyzstan, where the authorities are pro-Moscow, A7 routed more payments through the United Arab Emirates, where it beat the banks’ controls. Trying to track such shifts leaves banks and regulators playing whack-a-mole.

Anti-money laundering controls also still rely heavily on verifying documents such as invoices. The A7 case shows how an industrial-scale forgery operation — using thousands of fake stamps and software to strip out Cyrillic lettering — was able to spoof the system. The fintech also created a shadow foreign exchange swap network. Foreign-currency export earnings from the state-controlled oil company Rosneft and others were deposited into front-company accounts abroad and used to settle payments; oil traders in Russia received payments in roubles.

Clampdowns on money laundering over the past 10 years have increased frictions and inconvenience for law-abiding countries, banks and customers. So banks and regulators must be wary of using blunt-edged tools to curb Russian sanctions busting that could have further side effects. But banks ought to be able to do more to track and question suspicious patterns in documents and payments.

Most effective in tightening up sanctions would be to find ways to pressure Russian allies and laxer jurisdictions to enforce them properly, including by using secondary sanctions. The US has the biggest stick here, but has been more reluctant to wield it in Donald Trump’s second term. The EU is wary of using broader secondary sanctions but could expand its use of entity-specific listings of companies that facilitate sanctions evasion.

Yet the fact that Russia has found ways to skirt around sanctions does not mean they are pointless. Indeed, the fact businesses are being forced into expensive workarounds is a sign they are working as intended: to throw sand in the gears of Vladimir Putin’s war economy. Despite China’s cross-border interbank payment system (Cips) launched in 2015, Russia’s efforts to create something similar and the rise of cryptocurrency, Rosneft CEO Igor Sechin has blamed the lack of a viable alternative for a “manyfold increase in total payment and conversion costs”. The response to the A7 revelations should not be despair over sanctions’ shortcomings but a redoubling of efforts to close the loopholes.

item.title: Notes on living in a dangerous world
item.author: Martin Sandbu
item.description: Central banks and state-directed capital; Europe and great power rivalry
item.content:encoded:
Central banks and state-directed capital; Europe and great power rivalry

Martin Sandbu

I hadn’t thought of my last two pieces in the FT as connected. One was on how central banks face pressure on their independence as governments care more and more about who gets the capital on offer from investors; the other was on the EU and Canada’s fumbling towards a joint approach to great power geopolitics. But they are both really about how to react to a world where states and their leaders take their gloves off in using power to direct the global economy rather than let markets run their course.

And that is what everyone is thinking about, in one way or another. Since many of those thoughts have been sent my way, I decided to feature some of them, and my reactions, in this week’s column.

I received quite a lot of correspondence on how central banks can navigate the new era where governments are no longer happy to let markets determine what investments available capital is going to fund (and where!). Some readers hold on to old principles, pointing out (rightly) that if politicians want certain investments, they have plenty of budgetary tools to achieve that without enlisting central banks in their efforts.

Others take seriously the possibility that conventional “neutrality” doesn’t quite cut it anymore. Sushil Wadhwani has penned a thoughtful list of recommendations on how central banks’ asset purchase policies — should they be needed again — could be made more aligned with government policy priorities. What he says about quantitative easing applies more generally:

[T]he [Monetary Policy Committee] can achieve the inflation target in multiple ways, and differences in the level of expected losses [on the unwinding of QE] can help them choose between these alternative strategies. For example, the MPC could choose to buy UK equities instead of gilts . . . 

Expected fiscal losses are not the only legitimate policy concern. As I wrote last week, it is also possible to treat different sources of demand (including different types of investment demand) differently within an overall stance for average monetary conditions for the economy.

Central bankers themselves are coming up with ideas that, with some further development, play straight into the state-directed capital game. Last week I argued for reducing remuneration paid to banks on reserves deposited with the central bank. And right on cue, my colleague Chris Giles highlights an interview with European Central Bank vice-president Boris Vujčić, who wants to require banks to hold more compulsory reserves. Reading his words closely, his goal is to mop up excess liquidity. But since required reserves are uncompensated in the euro system, it would also increase profits for central banks and eventually their governments.

Matthew Klein, ex-FTer who now writes a must-read newsletter, points out to me that if things really go in this direction, then the Swiss central bank and the People’s Bank of China are the pioneers to watch.

And David Skilling, whose thoughts on “capital wars” I mentioned two weeks ago, writes:

[M]y starting point is that central bank operational independence around a price stability target is relatively recent (thanks NZ . . . ), and is state-contingent — in particular, it was politically feasible in the context of a range of structural disinflationary forces from the 1990s. In a world where structural inflationary pressures are building, as well as strategic policy imperatives (military, industrial policy, etc) . . . I don’t see how the current institutional set-up remains a political equilibrium. 

I took a sceptical view of last week’s speechmaking love-in between Canada and the EU. In my column earlier this week, I highlighted that Prime Minister Mark Carney’s vision of an alliance of middle powers is in contradiction with the EU rising to become a power bloc in its own right. If the world really needs “a great-power rival — only with better manners”, which Carney rejected, then Canada’s approach really amounts to free riding.

As Mario Draghi pointedly said after Carney’s January Davos speech, middle-power alliances can only be a holding strategy for Europeans, who “alone have the option to become a genuine power” . . . Many useful deals can be struck between Brussels and Ottawa but they will not change the geopolitical weather. Only the EU can do that, and only if it assumes its role as a protector of the order it so benefits from.

Many will disagree (let me know how: freelunch@ft.com). But it is welcome that quite a serious debate is now brewing about how the EU should deal with friendly and like-minded countries.

I tried to make two points in my piece. First, that there is a difference between liberal democracies forging tighter networks of equals, and for some of them — those pooling sovereignty within the EU — to cultivate great power status to preserve and protect some form of liberal democratic world order. Second, that the EU, as it ponders how to deepen links with like-minded others, ought to think of this systematically, and develop a template for deeper association that can be attractive for many non-members, rather than the current ad hoc bilateral approach.

On the first question, I recommend a very interesting new contribution by Daniel Gros and Nathalie Tocci. They propose what I interpret as a compromise: that the EU should see itself not as a great power or just one of many middle powers, but as a “central power” or first among equals. A leader then, in the new liberal democratic front, but not a “hegemon”.

But why not a hegemon? It depends a bit on what you mean by that word. I take Gros and Tocci to say the EU should not aspire to play the role of the US for the postwar world order. But some would argue — probably overly generously — that the US’s success in creating a world order to its benefit came precisely from its willingness to refrain from hegemonic behaviour and at least pretend to be “primus inter pares”. (Of course, only vis-à-vis western Europe and Anglo-American allies. There was no such pretence in Latin America, Asia or Africa.)

It’s also not clear that you can even have “leadership without domination”. Surely the European Economic Area, where Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein tag on to the EU’s single market, is a relation of domination. Any alliance of liberal democracies that meets two conditions — it includes the EU and involves serious and deep commitments to policy alignment — can hardly avoid aligning more or less around EU preferences, given that the EU would be by far the largest member.

This is not a reason to dislike Gros and Tocci’s idea of a “Compact for Open and Resilient Economies”. It just doubts that such a compact could be consequential without being dominated by the EU. For example, they want the compact members to “pledge to consult each other” on trade and industrial policy. “The EU in particular would promise . . . to allow others the right to participate [in] working expert groups that thrash out the details of proposals.”

It’s not clear if this is supposed to be a political or legal promise. If political, how much is it worth? If legal, what is the quid pro quo legal commitment from the non-EU members? Either way, “the final decision would be taken following exclusively internal EU procedures”. So wouldn’t it be hegemonic after all?

In the debate over industrial protectionism, the authors endorse “made with Europe” over “made in Europe” — ie public subsidies and procurement demand should not just be reserved for EU producers but a wider set of friendly countries. Their “compact” would require other countries to pledge similarly to extend “any national preference . . . to other members of the group”. But this makes it sound optional to have any industrial preference at all. That is not good enough: if another country wants to benefit from a policy designed to build a domestic supply chain, surely it needs to commit itself to the same project.

All these thoughts go to the same point: can you really have a meaningful deepening of relations with the EU without converging around the EU agenda, however it happens to evolve? If not, it is better to be explicit about this from the outset as we think about new models for keeping the “rest of the west” together.

Which leads to the second part of the debate. Should this effort be pursued systematically or with ad hoc bilateral approaches? I noticed this statement by the Austrian foreign minister after Carney’s speech to the European parliament:

We need to think about partnerships that go beyond EU membership. Not as a loose network of neighbours, but as a kind of European extended family. Countries that share our values and whose interests are closely aligned with ours should be able to work more closely with Europe — without having to become EU members . . . The partnership we are now forging with Canada can serve as a model . . . for the future — one that Europe can also offer to other partners: Norway, Iceland, Japan, South Korea and New Zealand.

I think this more structured approach is right. But it also means you shouldn’t think of these partnerships in terms of what makes bilateral sense. You need to create models that fit a larger group — and “you” must be the EU. So we come back to the first point, on whether the EU can (and should) avoid being dominant or hegemonic, or had better embrace the greatness that is being thrust upon it.

Something else

Now for something completely different. I have long admired my colleague Stephen Bush’s sharing of a cultural highlight in his newsletter. In the spirit of “good artists copy, great artists steal”, I will give it a try as well. (Free Lunch readers will no doubt let me know at freelunch@ft.com whether this idea is good, bad, or plain ugly.) Which brings me to the Bayeux Tapestry, which I went to see with the family last weekend.

The museum event of the year, if not the decade, in London, the exhibition has already been a fount of middle-power diplomacy and oligarchic controversy — appropriately enough for an object that was arguably commissioned to impose a certain narrative on the public debate (on how to assess the Norman invasion), as we would say today. The British Museum, meanwhile, has defeated the purpose of imposing timed visits by letting viewers wait in an antechamber after admission for nearly an hour before getting to the tapestry itself.

So, is it worth it? Of course it is. The tapestry is one of the most spectacular objects of European cultural history. Once the wait is over, the British Museum’s bespoke gallery and perfect lighting really do it justice, more than I remember from seeing it in Bayeux in the past. Presumably, its home will be suitably upgraded when it returns. So if you don’t manage a visit during the London run, do plan a holiday to the pleasant town of Bayeux in future years.

Other readables

● The ECB’s Pontes project has gone live, so euro central bank reserves can now be used to settle tokenised securities trades on the blockchain. The head of the ECB’s digital agenda explains why this matters in an essay for The Economist.

● Politically, eastern Germany is still a different country.

● The Institute for Fiscal Studies uses clever economic techniques to find large positive effects on childhood mental health of a movement to delay giving children smartphones.

● The Centre for European Reform looks at how the EU’s next budget can protect democracy and the rule of law.

item.title: Flattering the forecast should not be John Healey’s priority
item.author: Stephen Bush
item.description: Labour should aim to run a day-to-day surplus sooner rather than seeing how little fiscal headroom it can get away with
item.content:encoded:
Labour should aim to run a day-to-day surplus sooner rather than seeing how little fiscal headroom it can get away with

Stephen Bush

Good morning. A scoop from my colleagues: John Healey may opt to accept a smaller amount of headroom against his fiscal rules to limit any tax rises at next month’s Budget. Some thoughts on that below.

Getting away with things

Whatever happens next month, Healey is going to have to either raise taxes, cut spending or do a bit of both to keep to his fiscal rules, given the various negative shocks that have taken place since Rachel Reeves’ previous Budget.

But by how much? That’s the debate within Downing Street and the Treasury at the moment. Here’s our story:

The Treasury and Number 10 are actively debating whether to set a lower buffer in the Budget than the government’s fiscal watchdog forecast in March, according to people familiar with the discussions. Such a move would allow them to temper the tax increases and spending cuts needed on October 28.

The government’s key fiscal rule requires day-to-day spending to be covered by revenues by 2029-30.

The Office for Budget Responsibility predicted in March that then chancellor Rachel Reeves would reach that target with a buffer of £23.6bn.

But many gilt investors now argue that the surge in yields fuelled by the Iran war has made it unrealistic for Healey to build the government’s headroom all the way back to that level. The fiscal buffer could fall to about £14bn without sparking a gilt sell-off, according to the average of eight estimates provided to the FT by market participants.

I’m not going to comment on what the government can get away with on the markets side, because it’s not my field.

The government ought to ask what it gets out of doing things this way. One reason why I am a stuck record on the need for Labour to breach its manifesto pledges on income tax and the triple lock is because I think there are benefits to showing that it really is getting spending down and running a day-to-day surplus sooner than at the end of the parliament.

The UK can have a better, cheaper working-age welfare system. That said, I don’t really buy that there are large upfront savings to be had because of the record of the past 20 years. Instead, I think the government should prioritise actions that get real savings, such as moving from the triple lock to an “earnings lock”.

Now, if you think that actually all that matters is flattering the forecast at the end of the parliament, then going for as small an amount of headroom as you can get away with makes sense. But if you think headroom is worth pursuing in itself, then “getting away with things” is the wrong priority for the government.

Now try this

I had lunch at Quo Vadis, a really lovely restaurant which, by happy coincidence, is one of the restaurants offering up a free lunch with an FT journalist in aid of Flic, our financial literacy charity. (You can bid to have lunch with me as part of the campaign at another great restaurant, Noble Rot.)

Top stories today

  • Data dashboard | FT journalists compile the key fiscal numbers facing the chancellor ahead of next month’s Budget.
  • Radical overhaul | Reform UK said it would shrink the civil service to about 300,000 employees from more than 520,000 today if it won power in a bid to streamline the operation.
  • ‘Not good enough’ | The UK will review its deal to transfer sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius after Donald Trump pressured Andy Burnham on the proposal.

item.title: The SVB postmortem continues
item.author: Robert Armstrong
item.description: Plus: quality
item.content:encoded:
Plus: quality

Robert Armstrong

Good morning. Bonds just cannot catch a break, with higher oil prices and strong US business survey data triggering another leg up in yields yesterday. This is bad (mkay), and if for some reason you don’t believe us on that, then the OECD is also banging the same drum, urging governments to “contain and reallocate” spending. Good luck with that one.

Today, I pick the scab off SVB (yes, again) while Hakyung writes on value stocks. Tell us we’re right/wrong on these matters: unhedged@ft.com.

The SVB failure files

Silicon Valley Bank went to pieces in 2023 because it had:

  • A lot of long-term debt on the asset side of its balance sheet, and
  • A lot of uninsured deposits on the liability side of its balance sheet

There is more to the story (I wrote rather a lot about it at the time), but it’s all just detail. Long-term debt assets bring interest rate risk without a bit of hedging: when rates rise, the debt’s value falls, threatening insolvency. While this is happening, you do not want liquidity risk: the possibility that deposits suddenly depart. Uninsured deposits can depart fast. Do not mix rate risk and liquidity risk in large quantities. The end.

The hard question, then, is not what happened but how it was allowed to happen. Call me old-fashioned but if the bank’s problem can be described in two bullet points, a regulator or a supervisor should have noticed and stepped in before the failure.

The first big report of who messed up and why landed with a thud in May 2023, just a few months after the bank itself did. It came from Michael Barr, then the Federal Reserve’s vice-chair for supervision and a Joe Biden appointee. He linked the supervisory and regulatory failures involved to the easing of Dodd-Frank bank regulations during Donald Trump’s first administration.

The second big report landed, in draft form, this week. It was written by the Starling Advisory Group — but commissioned by Michelle Bowman, the current Fed vice-chair for supervision and a Trump appointee. You’ll never guess what, but the Starling report does not think Trump’s deregulation was part of the problem.

I’ve argued that the role of deregulation in Trump’s first term on SVB’s failure is ambiguous, and probably turns on attitudes and culture more than hard rules. And I fearlessly predict the Starling report will not make it any less ambiguous.

There is another, somewhat sharper point to make, however. It has been raised by Jill Cetina, an academic and former bank regulator. (Our recent interview with her about banks and quantitative easing is here.)

Cetina points out the remarkable fact that, at the time SVB hit the rocks, there were no “hard quantitative guardrails” for interest rate risk in the Fed’s bank supervision manual. Nor was there, or is there, a capital surcharge in US banking regulation for interest rate risk as other countries have adopted under Basel guidelines. “If there is no accounting for interest rate risk in bank capital regulation, what is going to happen? SVB,” she says, “regulators need some bright lines”. She points to this telling quotation from a Fed staffer in the Starling report:

Silicon Valley Bank, everybody knew, ex ante, there was a lot of interest-rate risk going on there but no one knew if the amount of interest-rate risk that was going on there was exceeding some risk tolerance threshold, because I don’t think we really had adequately set one.

In financial regulation we are always fighting the last war. All the same, maybe introducing a hard guideline and capital charge for interest rate risk would be a good idea?

What’s a quality investor to do?

Quality investing — buying shares in companies with wide competitive moats, high and steady profitability, and strong balance sheets — is having a difficult run.

Like any other investment “factors” (value, growth, momentum and so on), the precise definition of quality is debated. And because many of the names that dominate the S&P 500 are quality stocks too, the quality benchmark indices often track the wider index quite closely. But this hasn’t been true lately. Below is the S&P 500 Quality Index, which is weighted by return on equity, cash conversion and low financial leverage, charted against the plain old S&P 500, which is weighted by market cap:

On other measures, quality’s underperformance goes further back. Data from David Souccar at Vontobel shows how from July 2017 to June 2025, half of quality stocks in the S&P 500 beat the overall index, compared to about 47 per cent for non-quality stocks. The difference is bigger for international and emerging markets.

But starting from July 2025 to last month, a much bigger share of non-quality stocks (37 per cent) are beating the market than the quality basket (22 per cent).

Chris Osmond at Fifth Third Wealth Advisors argues that in an era of AI dominance and fast earnings growth, the market overwhelmingly rewards high-growth, high-beta names:

Resilient growth in the economy removes quality’s defensive premium … Momentum is given more of a premium than quality and profitability. The market is not rewarding low leverage as a risk-reduction attribute. Instead, investors are chasing earnings growth and cyclical exposures.

Souccar argues market concentration is the problem:

The extreme market concentration in AI names means that the chances of a manager picking 40 to 60 quality stocks across a range of sectors, to reduce correlation and to maintain downside protection, and still beating the market has become extremely low.

The problem is wider than just quality. Investors of any flavour seeking diversification from the AI “everything trade” and looking to beat the market at the same time are struggling.

But that doesn’t mean this is a bad time to own quality companies. In fact, the opposite might be true. Chris Rossbach of J Stern & Co sums this up: “People are thinking there’s a secular problem with quality, and there isn’t. There’s a cyclical issue with quality.”

Quality companies are generally more sensitive to events in the real economy, which, while still strong overall, is facing crosswinds from inflation, rates and tariffs. AI, meanwhile, looks like a one-way bet, whatever the economy does. We don’t think that perception can last for ever, and when it changes, we expect quality investors to be rewarded.

(Kim)

One good read

Martin Wolf on Trump vs the Fed

item.title: Trump’s tariff war is clobbering the Hanks of America
item.author: Alan Beattie
item.description: The end of the ‘de minimis’ exception can inflict major damage on niche companies
item.content:encoded:
The end of the ‘de minimis’ exception can inflict major damage on niche companies

Alan Beattie

Want to meet a victim of Donald Trump’s tariff war? Let me introduce Hank, a figment of my imagination. Hank is a retired machinist from Indiana. He now has a successful business as a sole proprietor importing tabletop war-gaming figures from China, modifying them using his metalworking skills, sending them to Spain’s world-class figurine-painting industry for decoration, bringing them back and profitably selling them. You might not think of someone like Hank as a hero of globalisation, but he totally is.

Until Trump (for whom Hank voted) came along, Hank’s imports from China and then Spain came in under the $800 “de minimis” exception to tariffs. Since Trump abolished de minimis, his business has been in turmoil. 

The unprocessed imports from China now attract tariffs. For the figurines returning from Spain, the tariff will partly depend on whether the product is treated as originating in China after Hank has done his alterations to it. (Like the fictional Hank, I’ve done all this without professional customs advice, so tell me if I’ve got it wrong.) But regardless of whether he’s only liable for duties on the value added in Spain or on the whole value of the reimport, Hank must fight his way through the thicket of Customs and Border Protection regulations on “goods for repair or alteration”.

He’ll have to file a complex declaration signed by himself and the company doing the painting, and pay tariffs on return. If he’s particularly unlucky, the goods will be deemed incomplete when they leave the US — whether an unpainted figurine is a finished or unfinished product would seem to be a marginal case depending on past CBP rulings — and therefore subject to full tariffs on the way back. Hank might just give up his business altogether. Hank is planning to vote Democrat in November.

Trump removed de minimis on imports from China in May last year and from all countries in August; other trading powers including the EU have done similar. In recent months the US elimination was made permanent and certified as constitutional by a ruling from the Court of International Trade.

The move was supposed to hit Chinese companies like Temu and Shein, which sold directly to individual American consumers. It’s certainly not been great for them: the profits of Temu’s parent company dropped sharply after de minimis was removed. But both companies have adapted by shifting towards a warehouse model and using Chinese-owned delivery companies in the US. Getting rid of de minimis was intended to clobber Temu, but it’s inflicted collateral damage on many thousands of Hanks.

“Sounds good, but what about the paperwork?” is evidently not the kind of pettifogging woke technocratic objection given much shrift in the Trump administration. The abolition of de minimis has required a new system to be created for small-value parcels. It’s intended to simplify the process but still requires declarations of tariff classification, origin and valuation, and creates more work for customs professionals.

The typical effect of tariffs and trade restrictions — indeed regulation in general — is to advantage larger companies with more capacity for compliance. Trade is already heavily dominated by big business, which accounts for around two-thirds of US goods exports by value. Even they are feeling the strain: an industry survey by the American Association of Exporters and Importers and the supply chain company Altana says more than half of large-turnover companies don’t feel “trade ready” when it comes to dealing with the bureaucracy.

The more that exporters are swamped by successive waves of paperwork, the more that large companies get an advantage. Preferential trade agreements routinely contain chapters on small and medium-sized enterprises — which enable ministers to chunter about the importance of enabling the nimble minnows to swim the limpid waters of international commerce alongside the stately whales and so on — but these are widely and correctly regarded as primarily for show.

Research on the effect of Trump’s first-term tariffs on global production networks has added more detail to what we know about how companies respond. Chinese exports were routed through third countries, sometimes with some production moving too, and multinationals with flexible affiliate networks did the bulk of the work in rejigging supply chains. Domestic companies couldn’t do much more than let the shock hit them.

The Trump administration is now proposing yet another bureaucracy-creating wheeze in the form of increased reporting requirements to stop shippers mislabelling the origin of imports, an attempt to solve a problem it itself created. Experts in the industry are sceptical it will ever happen, given how overloaded the administrative system already is. Whether it does or not, one thing is absolutely clear: any time one of these initiatives is created, it favours the multinationals over the Hanks.

alan.beattie@ft.com

item.title: The Big Read. Syria’s unfinished reckoning
item.author: Malaika Kanaaneh Tapper
item.description: Many citizens are desperate to see past crimes punished. Others worry about reigniting violence
item.content:encoded:
Many citizens are desperate to see past crimes punished. Others worry about reigniting violence

Malaika Kanaaneh Tapper

When rebels took power in Syria two years ago, Othman began to hunt for the man who had broken all his teeth.

He could see his former captor’s face in his mind, knew the way his body moved as he meted out electric shocks. But he needed to know the name of the man who had tortured him in the air force prison.

Othman, who gave only his first name, tracked another former officer from the prison down in a small Shia town. “He was the one who gave us his complete CV: name, description, where he lives,” says the former rebel, now an industrial painter, from the Bayada neighbourhood in the central city of Homs.

He let the officer go and rode to the hills north-west of Homs in pursuit of the man who had abused him. “We went to his village. We tried to catch him,” he says. “If I caught him, I would not leave him, I would not hand him over to the security services. I would hand him over to the graveyard.” 

His deep sense of aggrievement is shared by many ordinary Syrians desperate to see justice done for the crimes committed under the regime of Bashar al-Assad, the dictator who ruled for almost a quarter of a century until he was ousted in 2024. The challenge is how to find accountability without tearing the country apart.

Other countries, such as Chile and South Africa, have struggled to balance truth, reconciliation and justice after a regime change; in Syria, where the judiciary is broken and many cities are still in ruins, the task is yet harder.

Damascus’s new leaders say they are anxious to turn the page on 14 years of one of the world’s most brutal civil wars.

Mass trials may be impossible to hold fairly and the risk of sectarian strife is rarely far away after the shift of power to the country’s Sunni majority from the Assad regime, which was dominated by his Alawite minority. The lesson of neighbouring Iraq, which was plunged into strife after the 2003 US invasion precipitated the fall of Saddam Hussein, is all too clear.

At the same time, the new government, led by former Sunni Islamist militants, knows that if the people who suffered under Assad do not feel that justice is being served, they may take matters into their own hands. Civil unrest would weaken the new state at a moment when it is seeking international legitimacy and threaten the country’s fragile transition out of the Assad era.

The nature of the former regime meant that many victims experienced violence at the hands of people from the same town or who seemed familiar.

Yet in the two years since the new leadership took power, there have been few trials, and prosecutions have mainly been limited to those who held the most senior positions within the Assad regime.

Periodic sweeps of lower-level regime loyalists have resulted in an incomplete round-up of perceived perpetrators. Some 5,000 remain in detention with little progress in trials, which has deepened mistrust in Alawite communities.

“The challenge is that your average person . . . would feel a sense of reparation when these big names are arrested and tried,” says Zahra al-Barazi, vice-president of Syria’s National Transitional Justice Commission, “but the person living opposite them who is an informant is actually what creates the bigger issues.”

Since the authorities did not seem to be going after his abusers, Othman sought retribution himself. But by the time he arrived at his alleged torturer’s villa at the edge of town, he found it empty. The officer was said to have fled to Lebanon.

The aliases of others who had abused him during his two stretches as a political prisoner rushed through his head. Friends in the new security forces offered him tips. He would drive through the Alawite districts of Homs, scanning for a face he recognised.

Still, not a single person responsible for his pain has been caught. He says: “I feel pressure closing in on me.”

Haunted by the mistakes of Iraq

At the end of 2024, a rebel offensive led by Ahmed al-Sharaa, a former militant who led a group that had once been affiliated with al-Qaeda, advanced from the north towards Damascus. Assad’s army folded, its ranks dropped their weapons and deserted.

In a matter of days, the regime’s detention facilities closed and its vast web of informants disintegrated. Details of the regime’s crimes poured into view as prisons were opened and mass graves investigated. Many regime members fled, including to Lebanon. Assad and his family escaped to Moscow. But others seemed to melt back into obscurity in Syria.

Sharaa was named as president. Disparate rebel factions, including Islamists with hardline, anti-minority views, began integrating into the new state forces. The rebels who were suddenly in charge focused on keeping basic stability in the shattered nation. Faced with immense competing priorities, progress on justice has been slow.

For the residents of Deir al-Asafir, a village in the countryside of Eastern Ghouta, near Damascus, painful questions remain unanswered. During the civil war, the area was subjected to a five-year siege. Trapped in Ghouta, Sherifa Hezbar learnt to eat grass and bitter corn, and to take higher ground when she smelled the chlorine of a nearby chemical attack.

When rebels in Ghouta surrendered in 2018, Hezbar and her family left on green buses for regime-run shelters. There was fresh food there. Hezbar recalls that her husband, Bassel, cried when he realised their daughter, raised in the siege, did not know how to peel an orange. 

Shortly after they arrived, Assad’s forces took Bassel from the shelter to prison. Over 100 people from Deir al-Asafir were similarly detained, according to the European Institute of Peace. In total, 215 people from the village remain forcibly disappeared, according to a union of their relatives. Hezbar never received official confirmation, but she believes Bassel probably died in detention.

Now, Hezbar is part of a coalition of families of the missing in Eastern Ghouta. They want the truth, reparations, and cards for their children certifying their parent was a martyr, a matter of honour. They also demand that those responsible — many of whom they say they knew personally — be held to account.

“I’m in a constant battle with my son . . . trying to keep him in check,” Hezbar says, adding her son was livid each time he saw a former regime collaborator in the village who had taken their land. “I’m trying to convince him that there’s a state that will bring justice for him, let it take its course, OK, and if the state doesn’t act? He will repeat [the violence].”

Even before the rebels took Damascus, Sharaa was aware of the very real threat of civil unrest, according to four people who described meetings with him during the preparation for and aftermath of the offensive. 

Wary of triggering a sectarian conflict, Sharaa argued that only the most senior figures and those behind the worst massacres should be tried, the people say.

The great majority of those who staffed the regime’s security apparatus and fought in its affiliated militias would not face criminal investigation. Some bureaucrats and public employees would even be kept. People would have to move on.

Syria’s new leaders say mass trials could be felt as collective punishment of Alawites. “The mistakes of Iraq” loomed large, says Ibrahim Khalil al-Hassoun, head of the Ministry of Justice’s Higher Judicial Institute.

After the 2003 invasion that helped bring that country’s Shia majority back to power, an American-designed process disbanded the army and culled people from the state based on their membership in Saddam’s Ba’ath Party.

It disproportionately affected the former Iraqi dictator’s Sunni sect and led to a sense that Sunnis were collectively guilty, deepening sectarian grievances. In the years that followed, Iraq was torn apart by social and political conflict, the rise of Sunni Islamist militancy and armed Shia factions aligned to Iran.

Sharaa disbanded Assad’s security forces, mirroring what the US did in Iraq, and many former state employees were dismissed, leaving huge numbers of Alawites out of work.

Regardless of his Syrian government’s rhetoric of inclusion, a streak of Sunni revanchism has manifested itself in violence since it took power, from insults to evictions to killings — deepening mistrust and fear among minorities.

In the first year of Sharaa’s rule, tensions twice turned into full-blown sectarian slaughter. In March 2025, an attack by Assad loyalists in Syria’s coastal Alawite heartland triggered sectarian violence that resulted in the deaths of about 1,400 people, mainly civilians. An investigation by the UN Syria Commission of Inquiry found that massacres were carried out in part by members of armed groups under the control of, or nominally affiliated with, Sharaa’s government.

A few months later, in July, clashes between Druze militias, Bedouin fighters and government forces left 1,700 dead, according to the UN. The majority of those killed were from the Druze minority.

Unfurnishing

Distrust between neighbours is acute in Homs, the bastion of a 2011 uprising against Assad and the site of some of the former regime’s worst brutality.

When Tarek Baderkhan, a former activist in those 2011 protests, returned to his home in the Sunni-majority Khaldieh district in 2025, having been displaced for a decade, he found the furniture was gone, the doors were missing and the light switches were stripped.

Like the rest of the neighbourhood, his home had been subject to “taafish” — unfurnishing — a systemic looting by Assad supporters during the civil war of opposition areas in Homs. Paint was peeling off the walls. On one, an intruder had written in black ink: “We will not have mercy and we do not ask for anyone’s mercy. [His name], Homs, al-Zahraa, Abu Jaafar Special Forces”. 

Baderkhan went to look for him in al-Zahraa, a nearby Alawite-majority district, hoping to bring a legal complaint. “I asked the local leader, but he acted like he didn’t know who he was,” he says. 

In Homs, instead of reconciliation, there has been retribution. Alawites and Shia have sold their homes cheaply out of fear or had their properties seized.

There have also been shootings. Armed men driving through Alawite neighbourhoods on motorcycles. In some cases, the attacks seem to be targeted acts of revenge; in others, they appear to be a form of collective sectarian punishment, according to residents and a report by the Syria Justice and Accountability Centre, a non-profit human rights organisation.

Officials claim they are holding perpetrators of sectarian vigilantism to account but analysts say they need to do more to break the sense of impunity.

Despite the lack of prosecutions so far, Syrian officials publicly insist that all those reliably accused of “grave violations” during the Assad regime fall within the scope of criminal trials. Some of the 5,000 regime suspects in custody were detained in sweeps in the weeks after the regime fell, based on their military or security rank.

The number of suspects is far higher than the judiciary has the capacity to handle. If all “grave violators” were prosecuted, it would probably mean the kind of mass trials that the state deems risky. Hard evidence of crimes is often missing, complicating prosecutions.

“Alternatives to criminal accountability” are needed to address the vast number of violations, Barazi of the transitional justice commission says. These could include confession, moving city or asking for forgiveness. But those methods have to be determined on a local level, she adds.

Assad’s foot soldiers

This summer, former rebels aligned to the administration organised demonstrations demanding more accountability.

Alarmed, authorities quickly held the first batch of trials for high-profile regime figures. Bashar al-Assad and his brother Maher were sentenced to death in absentia, while Atef Najib, a security chief whose crackdown on protesters in Deraa helped spark the wider revolt, was also given the death penalty and is currently in custody. A handful of notorious regime figures have been convicted since. Many Syrians celebrated.

Some rights groups criticised the rushed and theatrical nature of the trials, saying they should have waited until Syria passed its Transitional Justice Law.

But Hassoun, of the Justice Ministry, says the government realised it could not afford to wait for that legislation, which is still under consideration by parliament. Noureddine al-Baba, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Interior, says the “threat” of public anger and mistrust of the security and judiciary apparatus has declined since the rulings.

For many of the people who worked for the regime at the lower levels, legal stasis has descended.

Under Assad, many residents of the quiet Alawite village of Nawa, east of Homs, worked in the regime’s security forces or as public employees. Since his downfall, many have fled or have tried to emigrate. Others lined up at the village school in January 2025 to hand over their weapons and regularise their status as part of the new authorities’ settlement process.

That day, a group of men was separated based on their military rank and taken to prison, where they have remained since. Similar sweeps happened in Homs’ Alawite districts.

Syria’s justice ministry is ill-equipped to process so many cases. Its new leaders have dismissed around 300 judges but retained some from the regime era to keep the institution running. Recruitment and training of replacements could take years, says Hassoun, who is overseeing the process.

Um Aziz used to run a grocery store in a windowless room on Nawa’s main road. But since she ran out of money to source products, she distributes only bread. Her son, who was in air force intelligence, and her son-in-law, who was a lieutenant colonel, never came home after they left to normalise their status, Um Aziz says. Instead, they were taken to a prison and remain in detention.

Like many in Nawa and Homs, the men had volunteered to join Assad’s security forces out of economic need, she says. Often the families of former soldiers — even those who served over a decade and reached middle ranks — recognise regime violence occurred but cannot contend with their relatives taking part and claim they were merely couriers, drivers or cooks.

After the regime fell, the demobilisation process was the priority of the new security forces, says the interior ministry’s Baba. “The fundamental choice [was] a push towards settlement and handing over weapons, rather than arresting them,” Baba said.

But Baba added that the process, which he said included some 250,000 people, had also been useful for gathering information about regime suspects.

Abu Ali, a former internal security officer who did not wish to give his real name, was detained when Sharaa’s forces came to his house in Homs’ Zahraa district in January 2025, days after he began his settlement process. He echoed others in calling the process a “trap”.

Like several other detainees whose families spoke to the FT, he was held in Homs Central Prison then transferred to a prison in Hassia, where a large portion of regime detainees are held, according to a justice ministry employee with knowledge of the cases.

Abu Ali says he was interrogated at least four times. After over a year and a half, he was released in the late summer without ever facing trial. Since he has no documents proving he has already been investigated, Abu Ali is afraid of being arrested again and claims he now hardly leaves the neighbourhood. 

‘Insufficient evidence’

As people rejoiced at the convictions of Assad and Najib this summer, Amer Zaidan, a former resident of the Damascus suburb of Jobar, was organising a protest.

Almost every week, Zaidan marches with other Jobar residents through its chalky streets. In the shells of their homes, the sky is visible from the ground floor because of how the ceilings have been removed for the metal inside.

After Assad’s trial in August, Zaidan’s target was the luxurious home of Mohammad Hamsho, a businessman close to the regime accused of destroying Jobar to extract its steel. This year Hamsho cut a settlement deal with the new government.

“Shame, shame! He’s the one who plundered the country,” the protesters clapped in rhyming Arabic. 

In January, the National Committee for Combating Illicit Gain said its official settlement with Hamsho was part of a programme of deals that would allow businesspeople to regularise their legal status and present accurate information on their assets. 

Defenders of the deals suggest it is the only way of getting access to information on the funds of regime cronies and that they do not preclude future criminal prosecution. 

But for many, deals with alleged collaborators like Hamsho have undermined the government’s promises of justice.

“You convicted Atef Najib and sentenced him to death. Great job, now what are we demanding?” Zaidan says, adding that people like Hamsho should also face justice. “He’s still there and everything’s going well for him,” he adds. 

He scrolls through his Instagram, staring at pictures of one man he says was a regime informant in Jobar, looking at posts of the man supporting Assad before his fall and newer ones where he had photographed himself with new government officials.

Zaidan says that he reported the man to the authorities and this twice led to his arrest. But on both occasions the suspect was released without charge. The cause, Zaidan says, was “insufficient evidence”.
