item.title: The FT View. Britain’s union reforms are a risk to business dynamism
item.author: The editorial board
item.description: Labour’s expansion of workers’ rights adds to pressures on the private sector
item.content:encoded:
Labour’s expansion of workers’ rights adds to pressures on the private sector

The editorial board

Britain’s newish prime minister, Andy Burnham, faces an uphill battle in his efforts to mend the Labour government’s relations with business. On October 28, with companies still reeling from the previous two tax-raising fiscal events, another difficult Budget looms. Then just a few days later, trade unions will gain intrusive new powers to access workplaces — one of the most far-reaching changes in the government’s flagship workers’ rights reforms.

The rule will enable qualifying trade unions to use premises and digital platforms in companies with 21 or more employees to communicate with workers. It comes alongside a raft of new worker protections established in the Employment Rights Act. Earlier this year, as part of the legislation, the threshold for unions to gain recognition in organisations was reduced and some Tory-era strike restrictions were also eased.

The influence of unions in Britain has waned considerably over recent decades. Today just 12 per cent of private sector employees have membership, compared with much higher levels in the public services. But unions are finding their voice again under Labour, with private sector membership rising by 76,000 last year. Unions can, of course, play a constructive role with employers in supporting pay and working conditions, particularly as AI threatens to displace white-collar work. But the government’s reforms risk shifting the balance of workplace power too far away from businesses at a testing time for Britain’s private sector.

Boardrooms are rightly concerned that the new powers, which enable unions to convene employees on a weekly basis, could create regular distractions and disruptions. Many smaller organisations, with little or no historical union presence, currently lack the internal protocols to handle access requests, which could come at short notice. In time, greater access would widen unions’ ability to secure recognition agreements and represent staff in consultations on wages, working conditions and redundancies.

The prospect of more time-consuming run-ins with trade unions only adds to the rising cost of doing business under Labour. The private sector is already contending with higher payroll taxes, steep increases in the minimum wage and a growing regulatory burden. These measures, alongside continued fiscal and global economic uncertainty, have contributed to a drop in payrolled employees since Labour came to power.

There is a broader risk to competitiveness too. Since April, when barriers to submitting applications were lowered, the UK’s Central Arbitration Committee has experienced a surge in unions seeking formal bargaining rights, including in fast-growing sectors such as technology. Just this week, Meta agreed to give the Prospect union access to its 5,000 UK employees.

Much will depend on how unions use their new powers. Stronger workplace representation could encourage closer co-operation between employers and staff. But right now, business groups are pressing ministers to moderate further minimum wage rises and slow the rollout of employment reforms. This would give them more scope to protect existing workers. Unions, meanwhile, see such calls as an attempt to weaken workers’ rights. Given the limited business experience in Labour’s cabinet, the unions may well have the government’s ear.

Burnham has pledged to roll back four decades of “neoliberalism” ushered in by Margaret Thatcher, but the 1970s were a time when the nation was sapped by frequent strike action, led by powerful trade unions. As the latest tranche of Labour’s workers’ rights reforms comes into effect, businesses fear the prime minister’s nostalgic vision will come one step closer.

item.title: Just how much power will AI need?
item.author: Simon Mundy
item.description: Rise of agentic AI could supercharge the electricity demands of data centres
item.content:encoded:
Rise of agentic AI could supercharge the electricity demands of data centres

Simon Mundy

Welcome back.

Staff at leading AI companies and institutions are showing worsening signs of mental strain due to worries about the dangers presented by the latest models, the FT reported yesterday.

What about the climate implications of this sector’s breakneck growth? Angst-ridden AI engineers may want to look away now . . . 

AI’s growing power problem

How big a deal are the carbon emissions from the AI boom? It depends which high-profile climate advocate you ask.

“Energy-guzzling artificial intelligence is driving up planet-heating pollution from coal, oil and gas,” UN climate change head Simon Stiell told a New York audience on Monday, urging AI companies to power their proliferating data centres with renewables instead of fossil fuels.

A few days earlier, former US vice-president Al Gore told me and my colleague Attracta Mooney that AI emissions “should be put in perspective”, noting that their greenhouse gas impact was still well below that of the world’s uncovered landfills.

Gore has a point: power usage by data centres currently accounts for well below 1 per cent of global emissions, according to the International Energy Agency.

Unfortunately, so does Stiell.

Enter the agents

Tech evangelists like to point out that posing a question to a chatbot like ChatGPT uses far less energy than charging a phone or boiling a kettle. This is true; in fact, the amount of power needed to address a basic AI query has been declining impressively through efficiency gains in both hardware and software.

Yet the aggregate power consumption of data centres has kept rising fast — by 17 per cent in 2025 alone, says the IEA, which projects that the figure will double from that level by 2030.

The rise of agentic AI — through which autonomous bots can perform highly complex tasks without direct supervision or guidance — is now threatening to make that rise even steeper (on top of the fears it’s creating around cyber security and potential human extinction).

In a July paper, researchers at the Korea Advanced Institute of Technology found that an agentic AI system comparable to current commercial services used up to 136.5 times more energy per query than a basic chatbot session.

Last month Zeke Hausfather, climate research lead at payments company Stripe, calculated that his own use of Anthropic’s agentic AI system (he averaged about 20 prompts per day) consumed about a tenth of the power demand of an average US household.

Here’s a very useful chart from Hausfather that puts this in a broader context, and highlights the massive difference in energy demands between this kind of work and a modest ChatGPT habit:

As Hausfather pointed out, he uses “the latest AI tools more than most people”. But his usage pales by comparison with the growing number of businesses that are beginning to deploy agentic AI at an industrial scale. And tech companies are now on a drive for mass consumer adoption.

See, for example, Meta’s launch this month of its “Muse” agent, which will be made available through WhatsApp, Instagram and Facebook. Meta suggests users try asking it to sell their personal belongings or process their medical records, adding: “As you get comfortable, the tasks you hand over can get larger.”

Really large-scale adoption of agentic AI would have big implications for the global energy system. The KAIST team modelled a scenario where the number of daily AI agent requests rises to 13.7bn, roughly the current daily number of Google searches. That would create new power demand of just under 200 gigawatts, the model showed — about half the average load for the entire US power grid today.

That is an illustrative scenario, not a forecast. The crushing failure of Mark Zuckerberg’s previous “metaverse” strategy shows his company can’t be relied upon to identify the next big thing.

But data centres’ rising energy demands have already been pushing electricity prices higher in parts of the US, creating a major political backlash. Rather than be slowed down by the struggle to secure grid electricity, US data centre developers have resorted to commissioning their own power plants at a huge scale. And despite a growing body of research showing that much of this need could be met by systems combining renewable generation and battery storage, they’ve chosen to embark on a gas power procurement frenzy.

Gas is back

Growth in the overall US power sector has shifted overwhelmingly towards low-carbon sources: last year the country’s capacity in renewables and battery storage grew by 51.7GW, compared with a net gain of just 2.7GW for fossil-fired power. Big Tech is now riding to the rescue of the fossil fuel power industry, with announced plans for 189GW of gas generation tied to data centres, according to a report last month by think-tank Global Energy Monitor. Meanwhile, utilities are cancelling planned retirements of coal and gas plants in response to the surging AI demand for grid power.

Analysts at Morgan Stanley this week estimated that annual emissions from data centres — including those linked with their buildings and equipment as well as power usage — would quadruple between 2025 and 2030 to reach 1.2 gigatonnes. That’s more than the annual emissions of Japan, the world’s fourth-largest economy.

While he acknowledged these emissions are “a cause for concern”, Gore — whose asset management firm Generation counts hyperscalers Amazon, Microsoft and Alphabet among its largest shareholdings — pointed to “very persuasive” research on the future emissions reductions that might be driven by advanced AI.

A paper published in Nature last year, by authors including prominent climate economist Nicholas Stern, suggested that these potential savings — through, for example, more efficient transport and advances in alternative proteins — could be as high as 5.4 gigatonnes, well over 10 times this year’s forecast global data centre emissions.

Perhaps. For now, it’s impossible to know whether the climate benefits of AI will materialise at anything approaching that scale. The rapid emissions growth from this sector, in contrast, is already very real.

Connect with 300+ senior delegates and hear from 60+ speakers — including 20+ CEOs — at the Energy Transition Summit in London, 19–20 October. As a Premium subscriber, you will receive a 20% discount on an in-person pass with the code FTpremiumsub.

Smart reads

  • A Kremlin-backed fintech moved $6.9bn through global banks including Standard Chartered and Citigroup through a massive forgery operation, the FT has revealed.
  • A UK appeal tribunal has struck down a previous ruling against retailer Next for paying workers in its shops less than those in its warehouses. Rightly so, writes John Gapper, arguing that equal pay law cannot ignore the labour market.

item.title: The Liberal Democrats’ unserious tax cut pledge
item.author: Stephen Bush
item.description: An unlikely plan to fund increased tax thresholds with extra growth from EU deals will turn away target voters
item.content:encoded:
An unlikely plan to fund increased tax thresholds with extra growth from EU deals will turn away target voters

Stephen Bush

Good morning. Ed Davey has unveiled his big offer to Conservative voters in his speech to Liberal Democrat conference: a £17bn tax cut. Some thoughts on that below.

Seriously?

A Lib Dem government would increase the tax-free personal allowance to £15,000 and the higher-rate income tax threshold from £50,271 to £56,000 by the end of the next parliament using the proceeds of the extra growth unlocked by rejoining the EU single market and customs union.

The political logic is, on paper, pretty sound. Since the 2024 general election, Davey has tried to signal to moderate Conservative voters that they should give his party a go. Labour will almost certainly have to raise taxes at the Budget in October or as part of the comprehensive spending review next year. Increasing the personal allowance is one of the tax cuts that it is easiest to get past the Lib Dem rank and file and polls well because you can describe it as “taking the poorest out of tax”.

But the policy logic is pretty lousy. A tax cut paid for by the proceeds of growth from a treaty as yet to be negotiated with 27 EU member states, all of which have their own elections and internal politics . . . This is the fiscal policy equivalent of me asking to borrow money from you by saying “don’t worry. A friend of a friend is sharing a room with someone who’ll invent the next Facebook and will grow rich on the lawsuit and they’ll pay you back.” It’s a nice idea. It could happen. But it is not particularly likely.

I think in practice the risk is not that people look at this policy and go “great! A tax-cutting offer!” It is that they hear an awfully big promise with a deeply convoluted method of paying for it and conclude that the Lib Dems are not serious. And while not being serious is not a drawback for many political parties in the UK, it is a drawback for the voters the Lib Dems are seeking.

Now try this

I watched the concluding episode of Up, ITV’s remarkable 63-year documentary that has caught up with its participants every seven years since the age of seven. It really is an astonishing achievement — one of the greatest bits of television, I think. Gabriel Tate’s brilliant piece on it is here, while readers in the UK can watch the whole thing on ITVX.

Top stories today

  • Revenue reaping | How could John Healey raise tax in the Budget? FT reporters explore the various channels the chancellor could pursue.
  • ‘Globalist scheme’ | Donald Trump has rejected the idea of international co-ordination to control AI, in a blow to Andy Burnham’s plan to develop G20 global guidelines for the technology.
  • ‘Tipping point’ | Banking executives have warned that they will divert investment away from Britain if taxes on the sector are raised at next month’s high-stakes Budget.

item.title: Private credit’s “soft” defaults
item.author: Katie Martin
item.description: How the can gets kicked, and why
item.content:encoded:
How the can gets kicked, and why

Katie Martin

Good morning. Is the stock market setting up for another AI scare? Yesterday excitement about Meta’s new AI model/personal assistant Muse sparked a sell-off in banks, brokers, financial advisers, insurance distributors and travel sites. The idea is that Muse, or in any case AI, could displace all the financial intermediaries in our lives. Maybe it will, and maybe that would be a good thing. But it is probably worth remembering that “we cut out the middle man!” has been a marketing slogan at least since Rob was watching ads for discount furniture outlets on UHF television in 1970s Boston. Let us know what, if anything, you were watching 50 years ago: unhedged@ft.com.  

Private credit: a bit of a wobble

It’s weird how even the supposedly clever people in markets — and, to be fair, the supposedly semi-clever people in markets journalism — can only concentrate on one or two things at once. Right now, that’s the wobbles in interest rates and the little possibility that the robots will kill us all. This time a year or two ago, the only thing anyone could think about was private credit. Well, if you can be bothered to pay attention, there are signs that not all is going perfectly there, either.

A note from rating agency Fitch last week said the US private credit default rate was running at 6.3 per cent for the 12 months ending in August — the highest level in the three years Fitch has been tracking the space, and a notch up from 6.1 per cent in the previous month. Fitch said it recorded 14 private credit default events in August, the highest monthly tally in the past year and up from three in July. 

If the loans involved are private — rather than, say, standard tradeable syndicated loans — how is it that Fitch has visibility into their performance? Fitch monitors two portfolios of private debt. One consists of middle-market loans originated by private credit managers and placed with insurance company clients, who require ratings for regulatory reasons. Another consists of loans that have been bundled into tradeable collateralised debt obligations, which in turn disclose the performance of individual constituents. Together, the two portfolios represent more than 1,650 borrowers.  

It is important to point out that, in private credit land, default is often not followed by legal action, change of control or bankruptcy. As Randy Schwimmer at Churchill Asset Management puts it, in private markets “a default isn’t the end of the story, it’s often the start of negotiation”. He adds:

Restructurings nearly always happen around a conference table, not in front of a judge . . . Private credit can also have a long runway before a loan ever reaches a true default. Amend-and-extend agreements, PIK toggles, and equity cures all give companies lifelines to address underlying issues . . . A covenant trip can give managers the ability to get “back to the table” to negotiate a better outcome. Examples include pushing for a sponsor cash injection, tightening credit agreement provisions/baskets, increasing reporting/transparency, requiring sale of non-core assets for debt repayment or pressing for a change in management and/or governance while there’s still time to right the ship.

Fans of the asset claim that this flexibility contributes to better risk-adjusted returns than public credit. A bilateral relationship between lender and borrower, the story goes, increases recoveries when companies run into trouble by reducing the chance of a destructive fight among multiple creditors ending in an inefficient liquidation.

Whether that’s true or not, the existence of a large and flexible private credit industry is likely one reason why the plain vanilla corporate bond and loan markets are so well-behaved lately. M&G has described the high-yield market as a honey badger, because as every connoisseur of internet frippery knows, honey badger don’t care. Wars, rate hikes, whatever. The private credit industry may have taken on some of the more, erm, challenging credits and is propping them up when they stumble.

Fitch, however, includes “soft” defaults, such as “payment in kind” equity-for-interest swaps and negotiated extensions, in its private credit index. Lyle Margolis of Fitch told Unhedged that “the bottom line is pressure building in these portfolios and that is manifesting as higher defaults . . . the default rate is dominated by soft defaults, but it’s still a sign — if everything was fine, you wouldn’t be seeing this”. The rate is rising for three reasons, Margolis says: a wave of loans reaching maturity, higher interest rates and a slowing market for middle-market M&A. He notes that many private credit borrowers use five to seven turns of leverage, all of which often carries floating rates. And in the past, a company with a difficult capital structure could sell itself without much trouble; it’s harder now. 

The loans Fitch tracks may not be perfectly representative of the $2tn private credit industry. And because the industry, in its current form, is new, it is hard to know what a moderate but rising default rate portends. Are other, larger horrors being worked out behind closed doors? Watch this space. 

One good read

Meanwhile, in Maine.

item.title: The Big Read. Mark Carney and the limits of defying Donald Trump
item.author: Ilya Gridneff and Andy Bounds
item.description: Canada’s PM has become a rallying figure against the US president. But is the country’s economy too exposed to break away?
item.content:encoded:
Canada’s PM has become a rallying figure against the US president. But is the country’s economy too exposed to break away?

Ilya Gridneff and Andy Bounds

Standing in front of lawmakers almost 4,000 miles from his own parliament, Mark Carney set out his goal of helping create “the next just, stable and prosperous world order”, even as his native Canada reels from the actions of Donald Trump.

The Canadian prime minister, rapturously received by the European parliament in Strasbourg last week, called for an alliance with the EU to serve as “a beacon for other democracies” — in vivid contrast with his talk the month before of being “at war” with the US.

Carney does nothing to hide his belief that trade and political tensions with Trump’s US create the opportunity — indeed, the responsibility — to fashion a new global order to address problems such as climate change, the erosion of democratic standards and an unnamed but all-too-identifiable “hegemon”.

“My experience in crises is that fortune favours the bold,” he tells the FT in an interview this month. “Canada has what the world wants — and particularly in a world where sovereignty is under pressure.”

He adds that “we are about what we’re for, not what we’re against”. But few other western leaders have based their domestic and international appeal so clearly around their opposition to Trump.

Carney based his Liberal Party’s triumphant campaign in last year’s general election around the idea of fighting back against the US president.

He also electrified the World Economic Forum in Davos in January with his vision of “middle powers” co-operating in a world that superpowers would otherwise dominate. Canada is so far the only country other than China that has retaliated against Trump administration tariffs with concrete, rather than threatened, countermeasures of its own.

Yet Ottawa is also almost uniquely exposed to a vengeful US — because of the depth of integration between the two states’ economies, the limits of co-operation with other countries and the vulnerabilities of Canada’s own model.

Trump elicited Carney’s “war” remark last month by imposing 50 per cent tariffs on C$28bn ($20bn) of Canadian exports to the US, ranging from electronics to alcohol to tulip bulbs.

Since the US accounts for two-thirds of all Canada’s exports, the country’s economic health is at stake as the two governments step up the trade conflict.

“A trade relationship that was once a great strength has now become a serious vulnerability,” Carney himself noted this year, adding that 60 per cent of Canadian-made car parts and 90 per cent of finished vehicles were exported to the US, while components could cross the border “up to eight times before landing on a showroom floor”.

By contrast, even as Carney and European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen speak of making Canada an “associate member” of the EU, a decade-old trade deal between the two jurisdictions has yet to be fully ratified.

Some EU officials make clear their view that, despite Carney’s call for middle powers to work together, a bid to strike a new deal with Canada would be a diversion from bigger issues.

“The Canadian economy exports the majority [of goods sold abroad] to the US, so does Canada actually have an interest in aligning with EU regulatory frameworks and the internal market?” asks an EU diplomat, who considers von der Leyen’s idea of associate membership as a “distraction” from more concrete goals. “Does Canada understand what this would entail?”

In turn, Trump, who regularly posts “WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US” and similar sentiments, suggested the country’s putative association deal with the EU could be considered a “hostile act” provoking a wave of new tariffs.

At present, Carney is pursuing his battle on two fronts.

He has continued his predecessor Justin Trudeau’s tactic of imposing countermeasures to Trump administration tariffs at almost every turn, ramping up economic disruption ahead of the US midterm elections in November, even as Washington seeks to use its much greater economic weight — its GDP is 13 times Canada’s — to push Ottawa into compliance.

The prime minister has also sought to reduce Canada’s dependence on the US as best he can — not just by seeking to deepen ties with the EU but also by holding a high-profile investment summit and by criss-crossing the world looking for new trade.

Canadians have signalled they favour his course of action. One poll this month, by Spark Insights, reported a record approval rating of 70 per cent — above any previous prime minister’s.

International elites — groups in which the former central banker has long moved — have also proved appreciative.

Marco Mendicino, Carney’s former chief of staff, says Carney “has developed relationships around the world that are anchored in trust”.

Barclays chief executive CS Venkatakrishnan, who attended last week’s summit, described Carney’s efforts at attracting investment as “heroic”, while Deutsche Bank chief Christian Sewing said Canada was “now on the map, far more important than ever before”. 

Other leaders are taking pains to indicate their affinity with Carney. France’s President Emmanuel Macron met him on Sunday on French territory off the coast of Newfoundland. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham hailed him as a “great progressive leader” when they saw each other in Liverpool last week. 

The question is whether, faced with the ire of his neighbour to the south, Carney’s attempt to set out an alternative to Trump can prosper.

“He is taking the risk, because the relationship is so important, that the US will not shoot itself in the foot,” says Inu Manak, at the Washington DC-based Peterson Institute for International Economics.

Bilateral trade in goods and services totalled $870bn last year and Carney says some 80 per cent of Canadian exports remain tariff-free. But there is room for the trade war to spread, not least because Trump has opted against a long-term renewal of the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement he himself renegotiated in his first term — he says it unfairly favours America’s neighbours.

Manak adds: “If the United States turns its back against one of its oldest allies and trusted partners, then I think we’re in a very different place.”

From banking to politics

In some ways, Carney is an unlikely rallying figure for those seeking to break out of Trump’s influence.

The 61-year-old economist is a 13-year Goldman Sachs veteran who steered the Bank of Canada through the financial crisis and led the Bank of England in the aftermath of the 2016 Brexit referendum.

He has built his political identity on being more than a career politician, a background that some commentators say has given his pronouncements greater weight.

Canadian historian JDM Stewart argues that the prime minister’s more combative approach to the US has revived a national narrative that had been largely dropped from public discourse.

For much of the 19th century, Canadians feared a US land grab, as American politicians expressed their interest in taking control of their northern neighbour.

“We’ve had the ups and downs of the US relationship, but there’s been nothing as caustic and disrespectful and egregious as this president’s treatment of Canada,” Stewart adds, referring to Trump’s talk of US annexation of what he calls the “51st state” and moves such as this month’s rebranding of Lake Ontario as “Lake America”.

As for the international stage, Carney says his Davos speech “resonated because it said what a lot of people were thinking independently anyway . . . a number of us are thinking the same way and working together to build together”.

He adds that other countries’ trading ties with the US are not what they were — even if they are not caught in the same spiral of measure and countermeasure as Canada.

“Everybody’s access to the US market has changed,” he says. “Everybody is having to pay, and this is, in the words of the president, a price for access to the US market.” 

In a sign of the continuing tensions between Ottawa and Washington, Trump posted on his Truth Social network on Monday that the US now planned to buy the agricultural fertiliser potash from Belarus, Russia’s ally, “for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada”.

Canada is the world’s largest producer and exporter of potash; Belarus is the target of international sanctions, including by the EU.

Carney’s middle-power rhetoric has won favourable reviews from other governments that have found themselves on the receiving end of Trump’s mercantilist foreign policy. His next challenge is to convert that goodwill into more trade.

The Canadian prime minister claims that the country had previously leveraged its position “into free trade agreements that access 1.5bn consumers”, telling the FT that “we will double that in the next six months to 3bn”.

But trade experts warn that building an alternative economic order, in which Canada no longer depends so heavily on the US, could take decades.

The EU is a case in point. Von der Leyen’s support for associate membership for Canada has gone down well in a country where 71 per cent of people have a “favourable” view of the bloc.

But it is far from clear what associate membership would bring.

Péter Balás, a former head of the Commission’s trade department who now advises law firm Covington and Burling, says the EU’s much larger population “shows who has to adjust to whom”.

Canada has already paid to become the first non-EU country to enter into the bloc’s €150bn loan scheme to fund defence. Carney also wants Ottawa to join the Erasmus+ student exchange scheme, increase its role in the next stage of Horizon Europe, a research programme, and secure a deal allowing young people to work in each other’s countries. 

It would have to pay to participate in these programmes as well, says one EU diplomat. “There is no such thing as a free lunch.”

The economic impact of such a deal would be minuscule. The UK, a bigger economy located on the EU’s doorstep, is negotiating a similar youth mobility scheme, aligning its animal health and food standards with the bloc and connecting its energy markets. Yet that package would increase GDP by just 0.3 per cent by 2040, according to the British government.

Most of the bloc’s governments have also shown themselves to be much less keen than von der Leyen on formal ties with Canada, with Germany calling for the term “associate member” to be “reconsidered”.

Such caution is all the greater, given the EU’s failure to fully ratify the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement it signed with Canada in 2016.

Ceta has been provisionally in force since 2017, meaning tariff cuts, customs rules and market access for goods and services already apply. In that period bilateral trade has risen by more than 80 per cent.

But France, Italy and Poland are among 10 countries holding out against full ratification, citing sovereignty concerns, environmental regulations and technical objections to Ceta’s investment court mechanism.

Greece and Cyprus will not ratify the deal because Canada insists on producing its own feta and halloumi, cheeses that are geographically restricted in the EU.

Even with Ceta provisionally in place, Canadian beef remains barred from Europe because its cattle are fed growth hormones, a practice that is permitted in the US.

A more dangerous world

Obstacles remain for Canada in other markets, such as Mercosur, the South American trade bloc that counts Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay as full members.

Canadian beef producers raised concerns this year that Ottawa’s plan for a free trade deal with the grouping would lead to a flood of cheaper imported meat that could devastate their industry.

Canada wants to double bilateral trade with India, and has talked of a deal by the end of 2026. But relations between the two countries are only just starting to normalise after a diplomatic spat in 2023, when Ottawa accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government of complicity in the killing of a Sikh activist in British Columbia.

Rapprochement with China is also delicate, not least because Canadian intelligence services deem Beijing an “enduring threat” and one of the “main perpetrators of foreign interference and espionage”.

“There is a legitimate role for the Chinese capital in Canada,” says Vina Nadjibulla, an Asia policy expert and founder of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft. “But pragmatism cannot mean treating all capital as strategically neutral.”

Meanwhile, other supposed middle powers such as Australia and Japan have signalled interest in building coalitions and supply-chain resilience — goals Carney set out in his speeches at Davos and Strasbourg. But their direct geographic exposure to China and heavy reliance on US security guarantees limit how far they can pursue strategic autonomy.

Even if relations with major powers could be repaired and trade agreements concluded, the spoils would still be relatively minor compared with the scale of Canada’s trade with the US.

Carney plans to combine his overtures to other trading blocs with an investment blitz at home, focusing on infrastructure and natural resources and taking advantage of Canada’s relatively strong public finances.

“We are an energy superpower in both clean and conventional. We are going to act like one and develop that to the full potential,” he says, adding that the country is also “one of the largest critical minerals providers” and is active in AI and space technology.

But the limits to Canada’s economic autonomy are clear.

The Bank of Canada said this month that while the economy was in a “broadening recovery”, “uncertainty is high and new US tariffs and threats of further action pose risks”.

The country also suffers deeper structural problems, notably regulation and barriers to trade between Canada’s 10 provinces and three territories. 

Leading industrial groups complained in April that the country’s red tape cost it billions more in trade losses than Trump’s tariffs, partly because of national and provincial regulations that can overlap with each other. Productivity growth has slowed to a virtual halt over the past five years, as the gap with the US has increased.

Taxes as a proportion of GDP are lower than in much of western Europe but higher than the US. Peter Howitt, a Nobel Prize-winning Canadian economist, has argued that the country’s tax system favours small and medium-sized enterprises rather than more productive businesses.

Carney says Canada has “one of the most tax-competitive environments for business investment” and will “look for ways to enhance that”. He adds: “One of the things we’ve really been working on is predictability [and the] speed with which we approve [new projects].”

He emphasises that Canada has slowed growth in public spending, has often had the lowest deficit in the G7 and has relatively low core inflation. “We’re going to get the macro fundamentals right in a world that is increasingly looking at those,” he says.

The political test is not whether Carney can outmanoeuvre Trump on the world stage or wow attendees at Davos, but how long Canadian voters are prepared to endure the painful process of reducing the country’s economic dependence on the US. 

For now, he is making full use of his domestic approval rating, which stands in stark contrast with Trump’s domestic unpopularity. 

But even as he makes his pitch for investment and international co-operation, Carney acknowledges the scale of the challenge — a challenge he sees as a call to action but which may instead unseat his ambitions. “The world’s becoming more dangerous, divided,” he says. “Everyone understands that.”

item.title: The FT View. How China and the US can work together on AI security
item.author: The editorial board
item.description: Xi-Trump meeting should build on plans for dialogue on shared risks
item.content:encoded:
Xi-Trump meeting should build on plans for dialogue on shared risks

The editorial board

It may turn out that the most significant development linked to this week’s summit between President Donald Trump and Xi Jinping happened days before the Chinese leader’s scheduled arrival in Washington on Wednesday night. US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent and China’s vice-premier He Lifeng last weekend agreed to establish a formal US-China dialogue on AI. The US has also proposed a mutual notification mechanism about AI incidents serious enough to raise national security concerns — reminiscent of the nuclear hotline set up between Washington and Moscow after the Cuban missile crisis. Together these could mark first steps, however tentative, towards applying some guardrails to the world’s most perilous technological race.

Recent apocalyptic warnings have focused on the risk of AI turning against its human creators. But the fierce competition between the US and China for AI leadership means that agreeing on ways to slow the development of cutting-edge models — however desirable — is likely to be the most contentious issue between Washington and Beijing. Trump has dismissed AI doomsday scenarios as a “hoax”. Beijing sees any US talk of curbing frontier models as an attempt to lock China into second place in the AI race — although since Chinese open-source models have now become a major export, it is in Beijing’s interest to reassure over AI safety. (US officials suggest China seems less concerned about AI’s risks to humanity than about its risks to Chinese Communist Party control).

Yet for all the suspicion, Washington and Beijing have shared vulnerabilities on which it would be in their interests to co-operate and which could form the basis of the AI dialogue. The first is the risk of highly capable AI falling into the hands of non-state actors. Advanced AI is making it potentially much easier for terrorists, rogue non-state groups or even organised crime to engage in activities ranging from developing bioweapons to launching cyber attacks on telecoms, energy or transport networks or financial markets.

An associated danger is the risk of AI agents escaping testing environments and themselves conducting hacks of foreign companies or infrastructure. Agreeing baseline standards for controlling access, identifying customers, testing models and establishing containment mechanisms could begin to reduce risks. The speed with which an AI-directed incident could unfold, compressing the time available to work out who or what was responsible, also risks triggering an escalatory spiral of retaliation. That makes the US AI incident “hotline” idea one that would make sense for Xi to endorse in his meeting with Trump.

Clear rules of engagement are similarly needed on AI in weaponry and nuclear arms systems. Here, an important foundation already exists: Xi agreed with US President Joe Biden in November 2024 that humans should retain control over nuclear weapons use. But no progress has been made since then, even as AI technology has made giant leaps. Security experts from both sides have since 2019 been developing recommendations that should feed into the AI dialogue. They include “absolute” red lines prohibiting AI systems from making autonomous decisions to launch nuclear weapons; mandatory human authorisation for any AI-driven cyber attack on an adversary’s nuclear control network; and agreeing precise definitions of what counts as “meaningful human control” over weapons systems.

The first US-Soviet nuclear hotline was a response to a stand-off that pushed the world to the brink of conflict. The task for US and Chinese AI negotiators is to put a safety framework in place before any such near miss — or actual cataclysmic event — caused by a technology that is developing at breakneck speed.

item.title: The divide that defines the Liberal Democrats
item.author: Stephen Bush
item.description: Members in seats where the party is not competitive feel poorly served by its leadership and strategy
item.content:encoded:
Members in seats where the party is not competitive feel poorly served by its leadership and strategy

Stephen Bush

Good morning from Brighton. The dispute among Liberal Democrats over their party’s direction is partly political, but it also has a geographical component. Some thoughts on that in today’s note.

Different perspectives

One reason why the Lib Dems’ conference always has a good atmosphere is that the party’s activists are enjoying a rare experience: being in rooms in which the majority of people are Lib Dems.

For most Lib Dems involved with politics, their everyday experience is of being a minority on their local council, sometimes not having any council members at all, and not being in contention for their local parliamentary seat. But at the Lib Dem conference, they are one big community.

While the party has its ideological splits, broadly speaking, what defines the divide at the moment is whether or not members are part of the minority of Lib Dems who are not in a minority in their local areas. Lib Dems with a sitting MP, who have seen the party make successive gains at a local and parliamentary level, are much more likely to think the political operation is well led and going well. That is particularly true after recent changes within Lib Dem HQ: the appointment of Ruth Younger as chief of staff and James Holt as political director are both favourably cited by MPs. And, of course, the mood among MPs matters most when it comes to the leadership.

But then there are Lib Dems who don’t have an MP and are not likely to. They don’t feel well served by a message and strategy largely geared around the 72 seats the party holds and the 30 or so others for which it is competitive. What these Lib Dems want is something that will help them win.

There are exceptions, of course. But broadly speaking, the best predictor of where a Lib Dem stands on their party’s direction is whether they live in a place that got a Lib Dem MP in 2024 or if they are in a part of the country where Lib Dems are squeezed out and likely to remain so.

Now try this

This week, I listened to Chloe Qisha while writing my column.

Top stories today

  • Blow to John Healey | UK government borrowing rose more than expected to £18.3bn in August, in a challenge to the chancellor ahead of a high-stakes Budget next month.
  • ‘Honest broker’ | Andy Burnham will claim that Britain can co-ordinate global efforts to contain threats posed by AI at a speech to the UN General Assembly today.
  • Escalation of involvement | The prime minister has approved a request from Saudi Arabia for the UK to provide the kingdom with military support in its fight with Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.

item.title: Quiet please, the currencies are sleeping
item.author: Katie Martin
item.description: Plus, the end of stocks’ summer of ‘meh’?
item.content:encoded:
Plus, the end of stocks’ summer of ‘meh’?

Katie Martin

Good morning. I just dropped off Kid B at university, and it occurred to me that the freshers now entering higher education are the cohort made around 2008 — the GFC Generation. They will have the same non-memory of that as their parents have of, say, the oil shock of the 1970s or the UK’s 1976 IMF bailout (Rob, who is very old, remembers the oil shock). Given that the seventies generation is now replaying expensive petrol, inflation and big deficits, should we worry about the youngsters rerunning the financial crisis in a few years’ time?

Please remind the youngsters in your life that they can often get the FT for free at school or university. And let us know how to make history stop repeating: unhedged@ft.com

FX: shhhhhhhh

For all the excitement in global macro this year, major currencies are largely asleep at the wheel.

Deutsche Bank points out that if the euro stays in the $1.13-to-$1.20 range it has inhabited since mid-2025, that will make for the tightest range on record for the world’s most actively traded currency pair. On the euro specifically, you can see why this is happening. Inflows are helping the currency. . . 

. . . while rate differentials are hurting it:

But more broadly, it is rather odd. Sterling is, if you believe, er, certain publications, in the grip of some kind of crisis. Take a look at the exchange rate, however, and . . . crickets. Meanwhile, Canada is in a full-blown trade/diplomatic spat with the US, not that you can tell from looking at the currency. The only excitement really, among the majors, is in the Japanese yen, and even then, the decline has been mostly orderly.

I’m yet to speak to anyone in the market who has a really good answer as to why this is happening (or rather not happening). Some of it must have to do with the US dollar still being the world’s cleanest dirty shirt. We are all very familiar with the threats facing its dominant reserve currency status, but this stuff moves very slowly — a point emphasised in a recent note from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. 

As Goldman Sachs’ analysts put it the other day:

We think FX should remain in a low volatility regime under a range of likely economic scenarios. On the one hand, the dollar should be supported by solid US economic performance and bright prospective investment returns, and it is on the right side of the energy and carry themes that we think are key to the current backdrop. On the other hand, negative dollar impulses have come mostly on the policy side. We think this back-and-forth can continue.

No one would wish for an outbreak of currency volatility for its own sake — our nerves are already tested enough by rates and energy markets, thank you very much. But a bit more excitement would help out Scott “The House” Bessent.

That’s because the carry trade just loves a couple of things: decent growth (check) and low volatility (check). This basic formula (sell low-rate currencies, buy the higher yielders) is one of the things helping to waft the dollar higher against the yen even despite the joint US-Japanese interventions and Friday’s rate rise from the Bank of Japan. The same force — comparatively low rates — is also gradually depressing the likes of the Swiss franc and the Swedish krona.

Your thoughts on what, if anything, will break the calm, are welcome as always.

Is US stocks’ summer of ‘meh’ finally over?

The past few months have featured an odd combination: lots of talk about how the US stock market is unsustainably exuberant, while that market moves sideways rather than up. Between the start of June and last Friday, the S&P 500 has been rangebound between 7,266 (the June low) and 7,798 (the August peak). The only move of note was a sharp leg up in the first few days of August, which proceeded to peter out: 

Only three sectors have risen over the whole of that period, and no, tech is not one of them. The summer stalwarts have been healthcare, energy and financials:

With energy and financials, the reasons for the prosperity are easy to explain: higher oil prices and higher interest rates, respectively. As for healthcare, pharma companies seem to have become a popular way to hedge the AI trade. 

But despite the sideways aggregate trend in the S&P, there has been at least one big change beneath the surface. A bit over a month ago, leadership in the market shifted decisively back to tech, while healthcare and financials fell away:  

In fact, most things fall away: since August 18, 392 of the components of the S&P 500 are down. It’s a thin market again.

Astute readers will have noticed that I did not include yesterday’s quite lively price action in any of the above. Oil fell hard on Monday, energy stocks got whacked and tech exploded upward. It felt like something different — an inflection point. But volatile days always do. Let us know how it feels to you. 

One good read

Korea risk.

item.title: The Big Read. Betting on the yen: the risks of the carry trade
item.author: Leo Lewis and David Keohane
item.description: As the country’s central bank tightens monetary policy, investors who leveraged its currency for higher yields may be forced into a sell-off
item.content:encoded:
As the country’s central bank tightens monetary policy, investors who leveraged its currency for higher yields may be forced into a sell-off

Leo Lewis and David Keohane

In early September, the top foreign exchange experts at Japan’s biggest banks started taking calls from investors and regulators with two big questions: how big is the yen carry trade, and how close is it to unwinding?

The short answers from the Tokyo forex gurus — “nobody exactly knows” and “a lot closer than we would like” — were of little comfort to them.

The yen carry trade is the term for when hedge funds and others use Japan’s currency to access low-cost financing to make bets in markets across the world. For almost 30 years, investors have borrowed the cheap, stable yen in order to fund higher-yielding investments elsewhere, exploiting differences in interest rates and, in particular, the fact that until this month the central bank benchmark rate had not risen above 1 per cent since 1995.

But every so often, those differences threaten to shrink, or the value of the yen shifts with unexpected speed. Investors exit carry trades and dump the acquired assets — fuelling spectacular spasms in global markets from emerging economy debt and Nasdaq stocks to cryptocurrencies and luxury property.

For this reason, the health of the global economy is deeply connected to the state of the yen, making the carry trade a proxy — albeit an opaque one — for risk. “The yen carry trade is one of the main potential sources of market instability,” says Masayuki Nakajima, a senior strategist at Mizuho Bank, reflecting the concerns of foreign regulators.

The most recent major ruction in the carry trade was in 2024, immediately after the Bank of Japan raised interest rates definitively above zero for the first time in well over a decade. It helped send global markets into a tailspin.

This time around, the damage could be much further reaching.

Even though its true size is extremely hard to gauge, the current value of the carry trade may far exceed $2tn, making it probably the biggest it has ever been, the world’s regulators heard from the experts in Tokyo.

The concern that the cheap yen may be anchoring US Treasuries and may have helped inflate a bubble in AI-related shares, they added, leads the list of worries. Many strategists now say that one of the top risks for the year is the danger that the carry trade unwinds.

Of investors and regulators who have been in touch in recent weeks with numerous analysts, Nakajima says: “Their main focus is very clear, whether an unwinding of the yen carry trade could lead to a global sell-off.” And while an unwind, unruly or otherwise, is not the base case of most analysts, many see it as a far more pressing threat than it was as little as six weeks ago.

US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent warned last month that “disorderly yen markets can trigger forced unwinds, which could destabilise global markets”, setting out his justification for a historic joint Japan-US intervention to support the yen at the end of July. The intervention helped to stabilise the currency, which had hit a 40-year low with short-term traders heavily positioned against it.

But some now worry that further interventions and hawkish pressure from the US on the BoJ to accelerate its rate increases — which may continue, even after Japan raised rates to 1.25 per cent on Friday — could lay the conditions for the very unwind that policymakers are trying to avoid.

Mizuho’s Nakajima and others say there is more to the unwinding risk than the market has yet appreciated. The image that investors and regulators may have had about the trade, about who was using it and about how it has been inflated over recent years, was incomplete.

The yen carry trade in 2026, say Nakajima and others, should be considered in much broader terms: it is fuelling not just leverage but also real economic strategy. Once, it had indeed been the preserve of fast-moving speculators. A version of the trade had also long been a favourite of “Mrs Watanabe”, a shorthand for Japanese retail investors whose response to ultra-low interest rates at home has been to swap their yen savings for riskier but more lucrative investments abroad.

But they have been joined by the mammoth of corporate Japan: hundreds of major companies that have staked their future outside the shrinking home market and are funding a $2tn transformation, much of it with cheap yen.

“Japan is by far the biggest source of foreign direct investment into the US. So if those flows reversed, it would probably have a significant effect on global markets as well as the global economy,” says Nakajima.

That dynamic, and Japan’s newly “normalised” monetary conditions after decades of abnormality, is in the process of fundamentally changing the yen carry calculus. The yen carry trade has long tracked and fuelled the megatrends in global markets, say investors. Now a new era may be dawning.

The yen carry trade is perfect until it isn’t, say some investors. Borrowing at reliably low rates in one place and investing at reliably higher rates of return elsewhere is global finance 101.

But it requires careful attention. It is vulnerable to currency volatility, to government intervention and to sudden market fears of a change in central bank policy direction. For much of the past couple of decades, Japan has provided a sweet spot.

The carry trade does not normally appear to worry financial regulators or major institutions until its fragility is laid bare.

In the most striking cases, the build-up for an outright collapse has been rumours about central bank moves and a single, data-driven trigger. Conditions, say traders in Tokyo, London and New York, that seem applicable now.

When the carry trade has unwound, it has left collateral damage. It was a key factor in the crash that took down hedge fund Long Term Capital Management in 1998. It was a pivotal factor in the “quant meltdown” in 2007, which many see as the precursor to the global financial crisis a year later.

But in the summer of 2024, in an incident that has since been minutely studied by the Bank for International Settlements for its global impact and the potential lessons for regulators, the fragility of the carry trade became especially clear.

The first half of July that year saw a long phase of yen weakness begin to reverse, as the market traded on rumours of potential interventions by the Japanese authorities. That altered the incentives for many leveraged speculators, the BIS later said in its report.

Turbulence in markets became noticeable. By July 24, after months of rallying, AI and technology stocks crashed, in a rout that wiped billions from the market. The yen surged, creating the perfect conditions for a sudden unwind of the carry trade. The ultimate triggers were a hawkish-sounding rate increase by the BoJ and a relatively minor, somewhat disappointing data point from the US labour market.

“The [US labour market] news could hardly be taken as an unequivocal sign of a deteriorating outlook, let alone a looming recession,” said the BIS report. “Yet, markets had become hypersensitive to any signs of a change in growth momentum and in the associated monetary policy outlook.”

What followed is precisely what regulators and investors now fear: massive unwinding of leveraged positions and carry trades, rippling out through global markets. The broad Topix index of Japanese stocks lost 12 per cent in a single session. US, European and Asian markets plunged. Bitcoin, as an indicator of the yen carry trade’s infiltration into all corners of global risk trading, fell 16 per cent over a few days’ trading. The Mexican peso, along with other emerging market currencies that have long been a destination for yen-funded bets, lurched violently as those bets were removed.

By the end of the week, some of those markets had recovered: the fear this time is that the rebound may be more elusive.

So how extensively has the speculative, leverage-seeking side of the carry trade been reinflated since 2024 and how precarious is it now?

The size of the carry trade remains notoriously difficult to measure. Hedge funds often trade with off-balance-sheet derivatives which can stay mostly hidden from the eyes of regulators, while yen borrowing can be visible without it being clear where that money is being put to work.

According to US Commodity Futures Trading Commission data, which gives only a limited view into the market, short positions on the yen surged in 2021, both outright and as a share of overall positions, before unwinding in late 2024 and early 2025. They were rebuilt in 2026 and only began to unwind again over the past fortnight.

“The low in dollar-yen volatility . . . tends to suggest we’re in the early stages of an unwind,” says Kit Juckes at Société Générale.

Shrikant Kale, a quants analyst at Jefferies, estimates that outstanding cross-border yen borrowing — from hedge funds but also the likes of banks, corporates and households — increased by 67 per cent to ¥360tn ($2.3tn) between December 2021 and March 2026.

That surge, Kale said in a recent note, suggests a substantial build-up in yen-funded leverage and means that “the current cycle is by far the largest carry-trade build-up of the past three decades, highlighting the potential vulnerability of global markets to a disorderly unwind”.

The only two comparable historical moments, adds Kale, took place between 2003 and 2007 and between 1995 and 1997 — both periods that ended with sharp, painful carry trade unwinds.

What is different this time is the part that corporate Japan is playing. In previous reckonings of the carry trade, the overseas investments of Japanese companies were rarely considered.

But because the companies have long been able to rely simultaneously upon an ultra-low cost of funding in yen and a consistently strong US dollar, they have had no reason to hedge their overseas investments, which have built to unprecedented levels.

According to data from Citi, the total outstanding Japanese stock of foreign direct investment, incorporating equity capital, reinvested earnings and debt capital, reached ¥384tn in 2025, meaning it has increased from 20 per cent of GDP in 2014 to more than half today.

Citi estimates that non-financial corporations in Japan now hold more overseas assets than banks, pension funds and insurance companies.

“This is structurally a type of [yen carry] position, and the building of the position puts downward pressure on the yen,” says Citi’s chief FX analyst Osamu Takashima.

The yen carry trade holds the potential for global trouble in the short and long term, analysts say.

In the short term, the risks are clear. First, that this summer’s $96bn intervention by the US and Japan in the dollar-yen rate could be a turning point for the yen. And second, that the BoJ could raise rates even faster than the market is expecting, strengthening the currency far beyond the current level of around ¥157 to the dollar and undermining the logic of the speculative carry trade.

The longer-term risks are more nuanced, but once set in motion, say analysts, could be much more profound. Japan is emerging from decades of deflation and the BoJ is normalising its policy after years of fuelling the belief that the yen could permanently be used to fund risk at a knockdown price.

Japan’s current policy rate of 1.25 per cent, and headline inflation of 1.7 per cent, may seem low by global standards, but the sense of divorce from years of expectation, say traders, is palpable every day.

This normalisation of monetary policy means that rates are likely to keep rising for at least a while longer, increasing the attractiveness of Japanese assets to the masses of companies and financial institutions that have bought into dollar assets in search of yield.

For years, the speculative carry trade and the enormous underlying outflow of corporate Japan’s investment created downward pressure on the yen. Now, analysts are wrestling with the prospect of that being reversed - even if many believe that Japanese households and companies are too conservative to move with speed.

The mere fear of such an outcome could start a carry trade unwind in motion as investors rethink how safe their current positions really are.

“Once doubts arise about their dollar positions abroad,” says Citi’s Takashima, “hedging transactions and repatriation [of capital] this time could be unprecedentedly severe.”

A new factor in assessing the risk of a carry trade unwind, say analysts, is the intense interest that Bessent has shown in the level of the yen, in BoJ policy and Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s attempts to reinflate the domestic economy.

High on Bessent’s apparent list of fears is that the carry trade has been, over a now protracted period of years, a huge contributor to holding down yields on US government debt as lower-risk players of the strategy bought US Treasuries.

A sharp carry-trade reversal, or a massive but gradual repatriation of Japanese capital taking advantage of decades-high yields on domestic bonds, could prove extremely painful to Bessent and other finance ministers across the world.

During its era of rock-bottom yields at home, Japan has been a reliable source of demand to absorb record levels of rich-world sovereign borrowing.

Some analysts viewed the US motivation behind its yen buying in July as a desire to help stem a combined currency and bond slide that could prompt Japan to sell its Treasury holdings, or for domestic investors to bring money home.

Bessent upped the stakes earlier this month, warning speculative investors not to bet against the yen, saying “I am the house now”, and adding that he had a “pretty good insight into what the Bank of Japan is going to do”.

Some believe that the normalisation in Japanese interest rates will erode the yen’s longtime role as the funding currency for the world’s trades. Another popular funding currency, the Swiss franc, has tumbled in recent months as the Swiss National Bank has kept interest rates rooted at zero while other big central banks hike rates.

As Barry Eichengreen, professor of economics and political science at the University of California Berkeley, puts it, the yen’s “funding currency days are over now that Japanese interest rates are finally beginning to normalise”.

But plenty will make the opposite case. The Japanese economy is still beset by myriad weaknesses, most strikingly demographics, that argue against fast interest rate rises.

It is probable that a significant gap will remain between interest rates in Japan and the US. Last week, the US Fed raised rates for the first time since 2023, to 3.75-4 per cent, and signalled that it was prepared to take further steps to curb inflation.

The fragility in sentiment was evident as the yen tumbled even after the BoJ raised rates on Friday, and signalled more rises to come. Investors spoke of a “rate hike race” as the two central banks tighten policy.

As Bessent’s comments and the joint intervention fade from memory, the fundamentals of the carry trade will remain, say some analysts.

“I just found it odd that people came out [after the yen strengthened following the intervention] saying the yen carry trade was dead,” says Shoki Omori, chief rates strategist at Deutsche Bank in Tokyo. “It’s not going to be easy to change the structure of the market.”

Additional reporting by Ian Smith

Letter in response:

Yen carry trade and those laconic Wall Street adages / From Desmond Lachman, Washington, DC, US

item.title: The FT View. Merz’s last chance to reform Germany
item.author: The editorial board
item.description: After regional election disaster, the chancellor is living on borrowed time
item.content:encoded:
After regional election disaster, the chancellor is living on borrowed time

The editorial board

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz spoke candidly about the state of his Christian Democratic Union after terrible results in regional elections. The CDU on Sunday was wiped out altogether in the north-eastern state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the first time it has failed to win seats in a regional parliament since the founding of the Federal Republic in 1949. It was, Merz said, a “dramatic” outcome with long-lasting repercussions for his party.

The CDU also lost power in Berlin, which is now likely to be led by the far left. The double defeat followed a crushing loss to the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month. Christian Democrats “no longer have satisfactory answers to far too many questions”, their leader conceded. The once mighty party of Konrad Adenauer, Helmut Kohl and Angela Merkel was “only in some respects” still a broad-based people’s party.

In Germany’s decentralised system, regional elections are never solely about national politics. But widespread dissatisfaction with Merz’s unwieldy coalition of Christian Democrats and the Social Democratic Party and the record-low popularity of the chancellor himself were important factors behind the CDU’s drubbing. Party knives were already out for Merz this summer after a botched cabinet reshuffle seemed to confirm his weak political skills.

The AfD’s stunning victory in Saxony-Anhalt sparked feverish speculation about a leadership battle. This time Merz promptly set out to pre-empt any revolt, combatively insisting he would carry on as chancellor with the support of party barons. In truth, he looks like a condemned man politically. Any reprieve is likely to be shortlived.

In Merz’s favour there is no party consensus on who should succeed him: a moderate like Hendrik Wüst, the premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, or a conservative like Markus Söder, the Bavarian leader. But this may not last long. If Wüst can steer his party to victory in elections in his home state in April, his claim would be hard to fend off. It seems hardly conceivable that the CDU would want Merz to serve another term as chancellor. So sooner or later a succession plan will become unavoidable. Pressure may also grow for Merz to give up the chairmanship of the CDU and focus on his chancellorship just as Merkel did three years before leaving office. But Merkel was far more popular at that point than Merz is now and had 13 years as German leader under her belt. Giving up the party leadership might just hasten Merz’s demise.

Merz said the election disasters were a “profound turning point” for his party. But there are no new easy directions in which to take it. Ending the coalition and running a minority centre-right government, as some in his party have suggested, might look appealing. It is fanciful to think, however, that it could govern without compromising with its opponents. The firewall policy of excluding any co-operation with the AfD has failed to curb the latter’s rise while depleting support for the CDU. But working with an increasingly radical far right, even within strict red lines, would be a massive step that could break the CDU apart.

Merz’s answer, for now, is rightly to double down on economic and welfare reforms. Steering through important reforms to pensions, out-of-work benefits and employment rules would be a service to Germany but will be difficult. Some Social Democrats and many voters now want them watered down, and Merz is short on the dexterity and salesmanship needed to push them through. But he should expend whatever time and political capital he may have left to put the country on a better footing.

item.title: Donald Trump’s crusade against tariff cheats may tangle up trade in red tape
item.author: Alan Beattie
item.description: Yet another US customs initiative will strain an overburdened bureaucracy
item.content:encoded:
Yet another US customs initiative will strain an overburdened bureaucracy

Alan Beattie

Welcome to Trade Secrets. I’m old enough to remember a time when Canada was a North American country and part of a highly integrated regional trade bloc. Those were the days.

I was sceptical of Canada’s EU ambitions in last week’s newsletter, when the news of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s overture to Brussels was just breaking, and remain so now. Before I explain why, I first look at the US government’s creation of even more work for its customs authorities and whether it will have the desired effect. Charted Waters, where we look at the data on world trade, is on the travails of German industrial bellwether Volkswagen.

The trouble with ‘transshipment’

The thing about announcing big sweeping trade policy changes is you have to implement them. And when you’re an administration like President Donald Trump’s, which is better at saying stuff than doing it, or indeed better at saying stuff that sounds good than stuff that makes sense, that’s a problem.

Earlier this month Customs and Border Protection (CBP), which is a part of the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), announced its intention to create rules to allow it to poke around in supply chains to try to find goods that are cheating customs law by evading rules of origin. It’s the implementation of something I wrote about before, a crusade against what the Trump administration wrongly calls “transshipment”. (That term instead simply means goods being dropped off and picked up en route to their final destination.)

The burden of complying with this is going to fall on customs brokers and other intermediaries, who will be legally liable if found to be facilitating the transport of fraudulently labelled goods. But is this really going to happen?

Jonathan Colehower, head of global operations and supply chains at the technology company UST, works with big retailers and other companies that depend on international supply chains. He reports quite a lot of scepticism. “Clients of mine are hedging and saying, you know, I think that DHS is so screwed up right now that they couldn’t pull this off if they tried to,” he told me.

It’s quite a thing to suggest of US federal bureaucracy that it is in too much disarray to implement a major policy initiative, and yet here we are. The administration reckons that between $19bn and $26bn in federal revenue is lost because of mislabelled or otherwise illicit trade. The higher end of that is about the same as CBP’s entire budget, suggesting enforcement could pay for itself.

Colehower remains to be convinced. “It’s going to be technically hard getting this done, getting suppliers to comply with the documentation requirements,” he said. The numbers involved are vast: he has one client who receives 10,000 containers a month. Chinese contract manufacturers in particular are notorious for sending product loose in containers that then has to be sorted and accounted for at the receiving end.

We have, of course, seen an increasing amount of supply chain scrutiny. US rules against imports from China’s Xinjiang region and goods made with forced labour; EU laws against products from deforested areas. The pressure on shippers and freight forwarders to examine and regulate vastly complicated global value networks has created an awful lot of jobs in compliance.

CBP has also had to take the strain of Trump’s decision to abolish the $800 tariff-free de minimis exemption for a single consignment. It hasn’t been fun: international postal services have struggled with the tariff requirements and a whole new administrative system has had to be created. The situation has become more manageable since the policy was announced last year, but largely because of a massive drop-off in small parcels: the number of such shipments between September and November last year after the exemption was removed annualises to 29.1mn, compared with 74.8mn in the previous fiscal year. It is always easier to regulate trade if you simply choke it with red tape.

Putting substance behind Canada’s rhetoric

And so to the alleged Canada-EU initiative. I’m only talking here about the trade and economics, which in any case are the most developed bits of what the EU does. You’ll need to ask others about defence and security (this is what I think of whenever I hear that).

First, agriculture will be a massive block on trade integration in more ways than one. The grumpiest Canadian farmers are in the country’s most rebellious provinces, Quebec (known for dairy) and Alberta (known for cattle). Dairy and beef are, by unhappy coincidence, some of the most sensitive sectors in EU farming. Beef in particular is one of the reasons that the EU-Canada Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (Ceta) still hasn’t been ratified by several EU member states.

Single market regulation isn’t going to happen either, not least because food pops up again as a problem. For example, Canadian cattle farmers have blocked the updating of a bilateral trade deal with the UK because, ambitiously, they want London to drop its objection to beef raised with growth hormone, as is standard practice in the US. A similar demand will not go down well with Brussels. The highly polluting extraction of crude from oil sands, a big industry in Canada, will also be unpopular in the carbon-pricing EU. 

What else? A youth mobility scheme? Fine by me: I well remember the nice Canadians on the European interrailing circuit with maple leaf flags on their backpacks so no one mistook them for Americans. An innovation would be an EU-wide scheme, not member state by member state. This is the model the UK’s painfully slow negotiations with the EU are striving for. But still, a youth mobility scheme is not general freedom of movement.

At the higher end of the labour market, there’s a mechanism in Ceta for mutual recognition of professional qualifications. But the first such deal, regarding architects, only came into force this year after eight agonising years of negotiation. Qualifications in other professions could be agreed, but will require an increase in political will to accelerate the process. A step beyond the Mutual Recognition of Professional Qualifications (MRPQ) mechanism would be creating a general skilled-worker programme, similar to the EU Blue Card scheme, which would give individuals a national but potentially transferable work permit if they get a qualifying job offer.

These are the substantive things to watch for, the fine detail of skilled-worker permits and mutual recognition of qualifications. Ignore the empty bureaucratic edifices built with prefabricated slabs of abstract verbiage and watch what they’re doing with visas.

Charted waters

If Volkswagen is emblematic of German export manufacturing, the travails of the automaker’s share price have made it clear that German industry, particularly cars, is seriously struggling to compete with China in both its domestic and foreign markets.

Trade links

  • FT reporters give five reasons why the Iran oil shock is different from what we’ve seen in the past.
  • World Trade Organization director-general Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala tells the FT that the boom in AI products is masking deeper problems in the global trading system.
  • Speaking of the WTO, its annual report assesses how global trade is performing overall.
  • Trump has reacted in his usual calm and measured fashion by describing Canada’s overtures to the EU as a “hostile act”.
  • Scott Kennedy, senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, says that this week’s US-China summit will reveal a vacuum of global leadership.

Trade Secrets is edited by Harvey Nriapia

item.title: Ed Davey leads Liberal Democrats with firm hand
item.author: Stephen Bush
item.description: Public opinion on the party remains pretty constant, while other parties rise, fall and change leaders
item.content:encoded:
Public opinion on the party remains pretty constant, while other parties rise, fall and change leaders

Stephen Bush

Good morning from Brighton. The Liberal Democrats’ conference is under way, and with it a fierce debate over the party’s leadership and direction. Some thoughts on both perspectives in today’s note.

Britain’s least disliked party

On the one hand, the Lib Dems’ performance in the opinion polls is pretty much normal for the party outside of general election time. Their support remains pretty constant, even as all around them other parties rise, fall and change leaders.

Thanks to a series of reforms to the party’s selection and other processes, the Lib Dems have selected many more candidates much earlier than usual in their target seats. As Paula Surridge, political sociology professor at the University of Bristol, sets out on Substack, their underlying political position is not bad.

Ed Davey doesn’t get enough credit in my view for what hasn’t happened at any point during his six-year leadership. The Lib Dems have not ended up with an ambitious policy designed to outflank Labour that ended up hurting them in their own target seats, like their disastrous mansion tax in 2010. Nor have they made a host of eye-catching promises that they couldn’t possibly deliver in a hung parliament (a mistake that contributed to their rout in 2015).

Paddy Ashdown said the Lib Dems were like a car that required a firm hand on the wheel to stop them drifting too far to the left, and part of Davey’s success has been providing that firm hand. They remain Britain’s least disliked party. This makes them well placed to make gains in the seats they are targeting — a small but vital group of 30 seats largely held by the Conservatives — and to consolidate power in the 72 they already hold. Taken together, that could make them influential in a hung parliament, which they could then use to secure the change to our electoral system they badly need to achieve their broader ambitions.

On the other hand, while the Lib Dem position is actually pretty good, the past two years have been pretty bad ones for liberal democracy. The party is a bit worried because it hasn’t had the sugar rush of a winnable by-election or a big win recently. But another more important cause for concern is that the Lib Dems’ political success is coming at a time in which the party’s values and ideals are under profound threat.

Now try this

If you’re in Brighton, try Cin Cin.

Top stories today

  • Closer access | Lobbyists, media outlets and communications consultancies are beefing up their operations in Manchester as Number 10 North becomes a new front door to power.


  • The president and the prime minister | Andy Burnham’s previous criticisms of Donald Trump have been dismissed by a UK cabinet member as just “politics” as the two leaders prepare to meet for the first time in New York this week.
  • ‘Electoral suicide’ | Labour MPs have warned against cutting a planned “mansion tax” threshold to £1.5mn, with one fearing the consequences of such a policy for the party in its central London strongholds.

item.title: Nepotism at Berkshire
item.author: Robert Armstrong and Daire MacFadden
item.description: Plus, fear gives gold a boost
item.content:encoded:
Plus, fear gives gold a boost

Robert Armstrong and Daire MacFadden

Good morning. On Friday, the Bank of Japan raised interest rates, and the Bank’s governor signalled that more increases may be on the way. But the vote for the increase was not unanimous, and the yen fell sharply — until a BOJ “rate check” alerted the market to possible intervention in the currency. Scott “the house” Bessent may have work to do if he remains concerned that an aggressive response to a weak yen by Japanese officials might put upward pressure on Treasury yields. Are you betting with the house or against it? unhedged@ft.com. 

Nepotism at Berkshire

Warren Buffett’s son, Howard, has been the chair of Berkshire Hathaway since Friday and has long been chair-in-waiting. He should not have the job.
