The paper’s authors — Michael Callen, Saipremnath Muthukumaran and Noam Yuchtman (London School of Economics), Gregory Levy (University of Oxford) and Jonathan Weigel (University of California) — scrutinised the widely accepted argument that institutional change often comes about at critical junctures, “moments where multiple institutional futures are possible, including a return to the status quo”. They scrape through nearly 12mn articles from the Times of London, from 1800 to 2019, to see if they can identify these critical junctures before and while they unfold, rather than only in retrospect, as we generally do.

Obviously, this throws off big moments that do not fundamentally rewrite institutions, such as the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre, the 2011 Arab Spring and the 2014 Umbrella Revolution in Hong Kong. But it still recognises that these were critical junctures, or CJs for short. Newspaper text, the researchers say, provides a useful window into these moments when the rules of the road are in question.

Thanks in no small part to the Scottish independence referendum of 2014 and the Brexit vote of 2016, the CJ index for the UK looks like this:

Now, the gradual increase in sensationalisation in the news over recent decades, driven first by rolling television news and then by the web, may be playing a role here, as the authors suggest. But if they’re right that these measures have some kind of predictive function and provide warnings of incipient ruptures, then that feels like something investors should take seriously.

On that note, see if this line from the paper sounds familiar to you (with our highlight):

When the rules of executive succession, electoral competition, civil liberties or judicial authority are thrown into question — when no one is quite sure who will rule, by what means, or under what constraints — we argue a polity is at a critical juncture.

Hmmm. And right now:

We remain agnostic on exact thresholds that define a critical juncture, [but] the index surfaces moments when core political and economic rules were deeply contested, offering both expected and unexpected insights into Britain’s turbulent 20th century. We reproduce similar analyses for the US, France and India — which have the next four largest shares of articles in the Times. Strikingly, in most of these countries, the CJ index estimates a current level of institutional uncertainty comparable to that in the early 1940s, during World War II.

We are, the authors conclude, “well into an era of substantial uncertainty”, and it’s worth noting that this is looking at a dataset that ended in 2019, before Trump 2.0 and Covid-19, and well before the masters of the AI universe realised that — oopsie — they may accidentally have created the Torment Nexus. If this is an early warning system, then maybe we’re already living through the subsequent turmoil.

The other obvious question here is whether this is as scary as it sounds. I’m minded to think it is, because I lean more into the idea that institutions matter than some of my colleagues do (hi Rob), but one thing that has stuck out from the past few years is the impressive ability of markets, particularly of risk assets, to shrug off a series of pretty big shocks.

The genuinely, admirably, permanently optimistic multi-asset team at HSBC pointed out recently that markets have weathered a “breathtaking” series of blows in the past five years, and they see no reason to think that will change. Reasons to be cheerful include vibrant earnings, even outside of tech and AI, enhanced firefighting skills at central banks since the crash of ‘08, much lower sensitivity to oil prices than in the ‘70s/‘80s, relatively low corporate leverage and so on.

There’s an element of cynicism, even moral hazard, here. As the team points out:

Particularly in the US, equities, wealth effects and financial conditions have become so intertwined that it’s hard to imagine that central banks wouldn’t intervene if equities were indeed to drop sharply and sustainably. We’ve seen this time and again in the last 16 years.

Maybe the new normal is an era of critical junctures in institutions and rock-solid resilience in markets. Funny old world, although I have my doubts that central banks can QE their way out of a robot apocalypse.

One good read

(Almost) everybody loves the sunshine

item.title: The Big Read. Britain, Burnham and tax: the walls close in
item.author: George Parker and Sam Fleming
item.description: The new prime minister wants a feelgood factor. But tax rises look all but inevitable — just to stay still
item.content:encoded:
The new prime minister wants a feelgood factor. But tax rises look all but inevitable — just to stay still

George Parker and Sam Fleming

John Healey, Britain’s chancellor of the exchequer, was until June in charge of the country’s defence: a deadly serious politician known for his sombre statements on national security. Now he is the man in charge of talking up the UK’s economy.

The shift in tone has not come easily. In his first major speech this month as chancellor, with two mildly sinister robotic arms stationed behind him, Healey declared Britain was “turning a corner” but was largely focused on reassuring markets he was not going to do anything reckless. Critics said he sounded as if he was preparing the country for war. One government insider acknowledged: “It didn’t scream positivity.”

The chancellor and his boss, Prime Minister Andy Burnham, took office in July determined to project optimism. But ahead of a crucial Budget next month, the economic walls are closing in.

The UK government’s room for manoeuvre has been dramatically cut by the continuing fallout from the Iran war and a global bond sell-off that has forced up Britain’s borrowing costs to levels not seen since before the 2008 financial crash.

Now an administration seeking to provide the feelgood factor that eluded its predecessor faces pushing through yet more tax rises when the government’s take of national income is already approaching a postwar high. 

More than that, Burnham and Healey appear to have been taken by surprise by just how precarious Britain’s fiscal position has become. 

“Core to this fiscal crisis is the seeming inability of the government to recognise it,” says Stephen Jones, chief investment officer at Aegon Asset Management, who describes the government’s “current inability to act [as a] simple denial of the hard reality, versus a market all too well aware of the delicacy and unsustainability of the UK situation”.

Healey discovered he would become chancellor just days before he entered the Treasury, giving him no time for the customary meetings with officials to see the state of the government’s books ahead of taking power.

“I don’t think John Healey knew; I don’t think Andy knew,” says a senior Labour official. “Until you get the proper briefings you can only know so much. John was not in access talks with the Treasury until it was way too late.”

Ahead of replacing the unpopular Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister, Burnham had hinted at big spending plans: ending a freeze on the tax-free personal income tax allowance, nationalising troubled Thames Water, compensating women affected by the rising state pension age and a big increase in council house building. So far none has happened.

Burnham also famously declared last year that he wanted Britain to “get beyond being in hock to the bond markets”. But those markets are the ominous backdrop to Healey’s first Budget.

Healey’s predecessor Rachel Reeves pushed through hefty tax increases in November 2025, in large part to replenish the government’s fiscal buffer — its margin for manoeuvre. But by the time Healey gives his own budget on October 28, half or more of the £24bn buffer bequeathed by Reeves could be wiped out because of higher borrowing costs.

That raises the prospect that the UK government may have to increase taxes just to stand still. Treasury insiders admit to being glued to market screens.

“I think everyone shares Andy Burnham’s desire not to be in hock to the bond market,” says Rupert Harrison, senior adviser at asset manager Pimco and former chief of staff to Conservative chancellor George Osborne. “But in this environment it’s the bond market that’s defining his Budget choices.” 

Successive Labour and Conservative chancellors have been faced with the same bleak fact: Britain’s economy is not growing quickly enough to fund an ageing population, defence, housing, creaking infrastructure or welfare. Government finances are, as a result, deeply reliant on debt.

UK growth outpaced that of other G7 nations in the first half of the year and there are signs of improving business confidence. But the economy still bears the scars of the global financial crisis and the pandemic. 

GDP per capita would be 30 per cent higher today if the pre-2008 trend had continued, according to the Office for Budget Responsibility, the country’s fiscal watchdog. Then there is the legacy of Covid, which has pushed up debt still further. In real terms, per capita GDP has barely increased since the eve of the pandemic: in 2019 it was around £40,100 — seven years later it is about £40,500. 

While the government has not balanced its budget since the dawn of the century, public spending has surged to 45 per cent of GDP, around its highest levels for five decades outside the financial crisis and the pandemic.

In recent years governments have shied away from cutting big areas of public spending, notably the welfare bill — now £333bn a year — including the rising cost of the state pension. Adding to the pressure is debt interest — currently being driven up in the bond market sell-off — which at £110bn is more than the government spends on the military.

Healey quit Starmer’s government in June in protest at Reeves’ failure to find the extra £10bn a year needed to take defence spending to 3 per cent of GDP in 2030, claiming that the then chancellor had failed “to commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country at this time of rising threats”.

But he has now been forced to delay any decision on when to reach the 3 per cent target until a spending review next year — when defence will be jostling for cash with other priorities. In response to Healey’s discomfort, an ally of Reeves just texted “Lol”.

Britain is far from alone in being hit by the fallout of the global bond rout. But the country is especially exposed. Amid the UK’s structural fiscal and economic problems, the yield on its benchmark 10-year bonds has been the highest in the G7 since early 2025, making the financing of new debt more costly than for its peers.

Healey has blamed the past Conservative government — including former prime minister Liz Truss and her market-spooking 2022 “mini” Budget — but investors have also been concerned about Burnham’s apparent instinct to spend money that does not exist.

“The biggest lesson of the last few weeks is that if there are different messages coming from Number 10 and Number 11, the markets will listen to Number 10,” says Sir Jeremy Hunt, former Tory chancellor. “Unless there is a united message when it comes to discipline on spending, the UK premium on bond yields will stay.”

If he was not alive to the need to manage the bond markets before he became prime minister, Burnham is now. In the past few weeks both he and the chancellor have given interviews to the FT stressing the need for fiscal discipline as the “bedrock” of their growth strategy.

Wile E Coyote and the flame of optimism

In some ways, Burnham has made a propitious start as prime minister. 

His cheery demeanour and ability to speak directly to voters about the concerns of their daily lives have gone down well with voters — as have his pledges to ease costs for households and businesses. Labour has now moved ahead of Nigel Farage’s Reform UK in the polls, as the rightwing insurgent party has been hit by a series of financial scandals.

But Rob Ford, professor of politics at Manchester university, speaks of a “Wile E Coyote moment”, when the prime minister’s favourability ratings, shored up by low-cost giveaways such as a reduction in VAT on energy and a cap on bus fares, come up against the laws of political and economic gravity. 

“He has been selling a politics of hope over the summer, but that is not cheap,” says Ford. Labour’s people-pleasing prime minister may have to “make difficult decisions that let people down”.

The fiscal picture has darkened since the early days of 2026, when Reeves hoped that Britain was about to bounce back. Treasury officials had been feeling increasingly optimistic in February as they watched the 10-year bond yield heading down towards 4 per cent for the first time since the lead-up to Reeves’ first Budget in 2024. 

The Bank of England appeared to be on course to hit the 2 per cent inflation target, opening the door to a seventh interest rate reduction. Instead, the war has confounded those hopes, with the oil price exceeding $100 this month. 

Amid a global bond sell-off spurred by inflation fears linked to the Iran war, the UK’s 10-year yield this month hit 5.4 per cent, the most since 2007, while an auction of 30-year debt last week was priced at the highest interest rate on any gilt issuance in almost three decades.

Such shifts are enormously consequential for the UK’s Budget arithmetic given that the country spends £1 in every £10 on debt interest. 

Indeed, the surge in yields comes as the OBR is preparing its estimates of government borrowing costs — a key part of economic forecasts by the fiscal watchdog that will underpin the Budget. 

The prime minister and chancellor have sought to distinguish themselves from the unpopular Starmer and Reeves, who introduced £68bn of tax rises in 2024 and 2025, the biggest pair of revenue-raising Budgets, when adjusted for the size of the economy, in more than half a century.

The political danger for Burnham is that his political momentum will be sapped by a tax-raising Budget focused not on raising money for Labour’s policy priorities but on repairing fiscal damage stemming from a war not of Britain’s choosing.

Andrew Goodwin, chief UK economist at Oxford Economics, says that any fiscal loosening — more borrowing or a smaller buffer — in the Budget “would likely cause markets to react badly”.

Among the more eye-catching measures in the Budget will be a “road map” towards devolution of a share of income tax and business rates to local areas. But while this plan dovetails with Burnham’s decentralisation agenda, the move was originally launched by Reeves and is likely to be fiscally neutral. 

“This government has inherited a lot of the challenges and constraints that the last government faced,” says Isabel Stockton, an economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies. 

“We have to get used to a level of debt interest servicing costs that we were not used to throughout the 2010s,” she adds. “And on public spending there are these big defining changes: we are in a situation where we are trying to bring up defence spending when we are spending a lot more on healthcare and welfare including pensions.” 

Mahmood Pradhan, a former IMF official who is now a non-resident fellow at the Bruegel think-tank, says the Treasury will have to face fiscal trade-offs given the limited buffer or headroom against the government’s self-imposed borrowing rules. 

“It would not be comfortable for Healey to live with headroom that is half the levels forecast in March,” he says. “If there are to be tax increases I suspect he will be inclined towards higher taxes on capital, potentially combined with some welfare savings — though these would take time to deliver.”

Business, banks and the wealthy are already braced for the government to turn to them — again — for the tax revenues needed to patch up the public finances.

JPMorgan Chase chief Jamie Dimon has warned of “consequences” of another tax raid on the banks and saw both Healey and Burnham in Downing Street last week.

Meanwhile Chris Rokos, a hedge fund billionaire who paid £330mn in taxes a year, has become the latest high-profile financier to decide to leave the UK. Burnham insisted in his FT interview he did not want to drive the wealthy out of Britain.

Healey has spoken of the need for the Budget to maintain “confidence” in the British economy and is acutely aware of the risks of damaging fragile business sentiment with more tax rises.

But staying on course when it comes to deficit reduction will also be critical if the chancellor is to avoid giving the BoE further reason to raise borrowing costs. 

Already, BoE Governor Andrew Bailey looks like an international outlier as the Monetary Policy Committee prepares to decide whether to keep rates at 3.75 per cent on Thursday even as other central banks — notably the Federal Reserve — consider rises. 

“It would not take much to swing the MPC in favour of a rate rise, and looser fiscal policy in the Budget would be one trigger,” says Pradhan. 

Under the fiscal rules, Healey needs to bring the difference between tax revenues and day-to-day spending into surplus by the end of the parliament. While estimates of that headroom vary, the Resolution Foundation think-tank created a stir last week by predicting it had dropped to just £5bn. 

That would be a similar level to the OBR forecast ahead of Reeves’ last Budget — a margin so thin that she considered a politically hazardous plan to increase income tax before ultimately raising revenue through other changes.

Healey’s task in the Budget is not to snuff out any economic optimism.

One huge question is whether he will focus on restoring the government’s fiscal buffers or whether he will seek higher tax increases to fund its longer-term goals.

If the chancellor concentrates on repairing the economic collateral damage from the Iran war, it will leave open how he pays for Burnham’s priorities in areas including defence and social care. 

Asked by the FT in the interview whether he would need a spring Budget given the big decisions that loom in next year’s spending review, which will lay down day-to-day departmental expenditure plans until the end of the parliament in 2029, Healey declined to outline any timetable. 

It remains a mystery how he will make the sums add up. Previous chancellors have tested the limits of the public’s and markets’ tolerance for higher taxes and borrowing, while Labour MPs have shown no appetite for big spending cuts, especially to welfare.

The election option

Burnham will set out his longer-term objectives for government in a 10-year plan after the Budget — probably in November — and Healey will then be given the unenviable task next year of working out how to pay for them. Government insiders allow themselves to hope that rising productivity and growth will come to the rescue, plus perhaps some luck: notably if the Iran conflict finally ends. 

There is an alternative scenario, increasingly discussed by Labour MPs: could Burnham postpone the agonising tax and spending choices looming in 2027 by holding an early general election in the hope of winning a new mandate to address the long-term issues facing the country?

The argument runs that if Burnham could persuade the country to endorse a plan to bolster the country’s defences, tackle the welfare bill and sort out its social care crisis, he might also persuade voters to accept the need for tax rises or spending cuts to pay for it.

Ending Britain’s costly “triple lock” mechanism for increases to the state pension, building a closer economic partnership with the EU and dropping the promise not to increase the main personal taxes have all been floated as Labour manifesto offers. Why not go to the country while Burnham is popular and both Reform UK and the Conservatives are struggling?

But there are big problems with the idea. Burnham has a massive Labour working majority in the House of Commons of 166 and can continue governing for almost three years before he needs to go to the polls again. Even in the best-case scenario, the prime minister would return from an election with a shrivelled majority and hand Reform a parliamentary breakthrough.

And would voters really reward a party campaigning for a mandate to put up personal taxes, cut future pensions and reopen some of the traumas of Brexit? “The potential for losing their majority altogether is pretty big and the case for an early election is pretty weak,” says Ford, of Manchester university. “So far nothing in Andy Burnham’s agenda is something that requires an election to get a mandate for.”

Some Labour MPs acknowledge the temptations of going to the polls rather than actually confronting hard economic choices next year. “The whole spending review doesn’t add up,” says one. “That’s why people talk about an early election.”

In any event, cold economic reality is about to intrude on the Burnham honeymoon when Healey delivers his first Budget next month. As a former Labour minister put it: “The world is the world, no matter how optimistic or happy you are.”

Additional reporting by Ian Smith

Data visualisation by Keith Fray

item.title: AI leaders call for slowdown
item.description: Trump rejects calls from tech bosses for AI slowdown Rivals Altman and Musk rally behind Dario Amodei’s call for an AI slowdown
item.content:encoded:
Trump rejects calls from tech bosses for AI slowdown
Rivals Altman and Musk rally behind Dario Amodei’s call for an AI slowdown

item.title: The FT View. Time for a pause on cutting-edge AI
item.author: The editorial board
item.description: The most advanced models are starting to escape human control
item.content:encoded:
The most advanced models are starting to escape human control

The editorial board

There is a Jekyll-and-Hyde quality to the world’s most powerful AI bosses. The same executives now talking about slowing the pace of work on cutting-edge models given the risks to humanity have been competing hell-for-leather to advance AI, chasing trillion-dollar flotations. But the backing of two AI titans — Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of SpaceX — for the slowdown call by a third, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, ought to become a watershed moment for the industry.

President Donald Trump dismissed the calls as “negative forces”, insisting the US must beat China in the AI race. But as Trump’s techno-libertarian former AI tsar David Sacks pointed out, since these companies dominate cutting-edge AI they can “pace the frontier” themselves, without waiting for regulation. Such co-operation has seemed unlikely, but the slowdown calls suggest companies realise it is time to act. They should use their power to slow, or better still pause, development of the most advanced frontier models until the risks can be understood and contained.

Such calls are not made lightly. The extraordinary potential benefits of even more powerful AI should not be forgone. Hundreds of billions of dollars are being sunk into AI development that underpins the value of the US stock market. There are indeed risks of the capabilities falling first into the hands of an authoritarian China. But, even setting aside insider warnings that AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”, some models are clearly starting to escape control.

The hack of Hugging Face during an OpenAI model test showed AI agents working in a swarm to escape guardrails and cover their tracks. Whether or not this meets industry definitions of “artificial general intelligence”, it looks like human-level reasoning abilities. The big labs are also racing towards using AI to help create more advanced AI, known as recursive self-improvement. As Amodei noted, left unchecked, this could “outrun our ability to understand and control these systems”.

Even in a best-case scenario, legislation could not keep up with the current pace of AI’s advance. That makes it incumbent on the top labs to pause sensitive research and model testing. They need to come up with standards and best practices on AI safety, talked about for years with scant progress. Amodei’s promise to embed independent researchers working alongside staff and reporting publicly is a start, but outside audits will quickly need more teeth.

A more responsible US administration than Trump’s would already be using existing regulation to strengthen guardrails. Lina Khan, the former Federal Trade Commission chair, argues that law enforcers already have the powers to charge companies and CEOs for creating and releasing dangerous or defective products. Companies whose agents hack into other businesses could also face civil liabilities, though criminal charges are harder to bring.

Companies will always be tempted to depart from voluntary agreements if they can grab share, making a legislative framework necessary longer-term. A political shift at the US midterm elections might yet ease the path. One law that would concentrate minds would be to make top executives criminally liable for harm caused by their models.

US tech bosses warn that a slowdown in the US alone would be ineffective if China or others push ahead. Chinese companies’ heavy reliance on US research means a US pause would slow the entire industry at least for a time — though, like the US ban on advanced chip exports, it could be a spur and an opportunity for China to catch up. AI safety and security issues are on the agenda when President Xi Jinping visits Washington this month. The Chinese leader sees AI as a crucial tool of economic and military modernisation. Ultimately, however, unconstrained AI escalation is no more in Xi’s interests than it is in Trump’s — or the interests of the rest of us.

item.title: The Saudi relief valve is being closed
item.author: Alan Beattie
item.description: The Houthis’ Red Sea blockage is still largely an oil shock rather than a general threat to trade
item.content:encoded:
The Houthis’ Red Sea blockage is still largely an oil shock rather than a general threat to trade

Alan Beattie

Welcome to Trade Secrets. It’s nice to know that it’s not just the trade world where President Donald Trump is capable of causing alarm by sounding off about things he manifestly does not understand, and Saturday’s declaration of support for the rapid unification of Ireland was a corker. (I’m now visualising actual Irish people patiently explaining to Irish Americans that this isn’t the great idea it might seem.) More constructively, he followed up by promising to cut tariffs on Irish whiskey, as he has already done for Scotch.

Today’s newsletter is on Houthi action in the Red Sea and the Brics countries’ summit. Charted Waters, where we look at the data behind world trade, is on oil prices.

Red alert

Just when you thought it was safe, by which I mean highly dangerous, to go through the Red Sea, our old friends the Houthis pop up again to make it even more hazardous. 

It was a seriously bad week for global oil supply. Following drone attacks by militias backed by Iran, Saudi Arabia on Friday said it would be shutting the East-West pipeline from the oilfields in its east to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea. The Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen have been battering oil facilities in the south of Saudi Arabia and recently extended their control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.

Oil prices have now popped up above $100, as they did briefly in July (see Charted Waters below), and this time might stick there for a while. How worried should we be from the perspective of global trade?

It might seem like I’ve written this a thousand times, but the answer is much the same as since the US attacks on Iran began. The wider threat to shipping and trade isn’t dramatic. The container industry has shown for several years now that it can cope with the blockage of the Red Sea and Suez Canal by going round Africa. Even if the Houthis consolidate control over both ends of the Red Sea, that pattern won’t fundamentally change.

This is really about the shock to oil and associated products. The Saudi pipeline is the main relief valve for oil supply given Iran’s control of the Strait of Hormuz, and closing off Bab al-Mandeb would be a serious problem. US diesel costs hitting an all-time high show that being a net energy exporter doesn’t shield a country from oil shocks and that refining capacity can be as important as global prices. The fact that Trump is reportedly considering weighing in with the Defense Production Act to boost diesel supply shows he’s worried. 

But a quick check round the rest of the global trade and food supply dashboard doesn’t show a lot else flashing red. Fertiliser has been surprisingly abundant, with China releasing supply on to world markets. Some types (phosphate) are scarcer than others (nitrogen), but the World Bank’s overall fertiliser price index is essentially where it was before the attacks started in February.

The Food and Agriculture Organization food price index is higher than a year ago and heightened Russia-Ukraine hostilities in August pushed up grain costs, but current prices and commodity futures prices into next year remain well short of the peaks of 2022. The invaluable Agricultural Market Information System (AMIS) monthly global commodity monitor shows there have been good wheat harvests in Canada, Morocco, Russia and Ukraine that more than outweighed the effects of drought in Europe. The global maize production forecast is down a bit, rice up a bit, soyabean kind of stable. Really nothing dramatic.

It’s all worth closely monitoring, especially as the El Niño episode strengthens. But still, the problems in the Gulf and Red Sea are essentially a classic oil shock rather than a general crisis of trade.

Trump gives Brics a common enemy but not a common purpose

It was the Brics emerging market countries summit this weekend in New Delhi. No googling: what happened?

Well, you can read the 140-paragraph communiqué if you have a mind to do so, though it weighs in at nearly 18,000 words and for that length you’ll get more intellectual nourishment from one of Henry James’s finest novellas. The Brics thought that the war in the Gulf was bad, that the World Trade Organization was good, that unilateral tariffs were not on and that both fossil fuels and renewable energy were important, so that’s all fine.

My FT colleagues laid out at length ahead of the meeting the potential for the 11-nation emerging-market grouping to have a big effect on global governance and the constraints which stop it doing so. Essentially the same problems have been there since the original four members (Brazil, Russia, India and China) decided they were going to form themselves into a diplomatic bloc more than a decade ago. India and China are economic and geopolitical rivals; the members are disparate in size, income and alignment; the group doesn’t have binding mechanisms of co-operation.

The main reason for Brics coherence at the moment is the eccentric destructiveness of Trump. Whatever the countries think of each other’s geopolitical positioning and trade policy — emerging markets are worried about imports from China hollowing out their manufacturing industry just as advanced economies are — it’s pretty easy to unite in opposing US tariffs and the bombing of Iran.

Those shared concerns created sufficient Chinese-Indian rapprochement that President Xi Jinping made his first trip to India in seven years to attend the meeting. The grouping even managed to incorporate leaders of countries on opposing sides of the Middle East conflict, Iran and the United Arab Emirates, by dint of keeping the wording about the Gulf vague. Russian President Vladimir Putin turned up for his first Brics summit since his invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

But, in reality, the Trump-induced solidarity only goes so far and is largely rhetorical. It’s producing warm words and nice photo-ops, not the basis of a new international economic or geopolitical order. China will have whatever relationship with, say, Iran and Russia that it deems to be in its best interest, not be bound by a united Brics strategy.

In November 2024, even before taking office, Trump directly threatened the Brics countries with 100 per cent tariffs if they tried to undermine the dollar. He needn’t have bothered. The bloc’s work on alternative payment systems is a long way from creating a rival currency: the communiqué talked with magnificent woolliness of “respecting national priorities and acknowledging that there is no one-size-fits-all approach”.

In other words, as you were. Trump makes the Brics a comfy club to be in, but not a lot more than that.

Charted waters

As noted above, global oil prices have gone above $100 a barrel for the first time in a couple of months, when conflict in the Red Sea also disrupted supply.

Trade links

  • Global goods trade continued to strengthen in mid-2026 despite persistent geopolitical and policy-related uncertainties, according to the WTO.
  • Trump’s new retaliation against Canada, involving bans on imports of dairy and motorcycles and other restrictions, will not have a huge impact on the Canadian economy, CBC reports.
  • Speaking of Canada, the Wall Street Journal says Prime Minister Mark Carney is exploring “associate membership” with the EU, though I doubt that means joining the single market, given the vast rewriting of Canadian manufacturing and food regulations it would entail. Carney is also signalling distance from the US by telling financial executives they should invest in Canada as a hedge against Trump’s volatility.
  • A group of economists has filed an amicus brief in the case against the Section 301 tariffs on goods from countries that are purportedly weak on enforcing rules against forced labour.
  • The Economist argues that Trump’s recent bizarre threat to the US Federal Reserve, which stipulated that Washington would cut off trade with some countries if the central bank did not lower rates, provides a strong reason to raise borrowing costs to signal political independence.
  • The EU’s resolve in insulating its supply chains from China is being tested by a request from the China-backed metals company MMG to buy the Brazilian nickel assets of Anglo American, a purchase which could give Beijing influence over European steel production.

Trade Secrets is edited by Harvey Nriapia

item.title: Reform’s windfall changes the mood music
item.author: Stephen Bush
item.description: Donations will not solve everything but they will strengthen Nigel Farage’s party in the fight against Tories to lead Britain’s rightwing bloc
item.content:encoded:
Donations will not solve everything but they will strengthen Nigel Farage’s party in the fight against Tories to lead Britain’s rightwing bloc

Stephen Bush

Good morning. Reform has had a big weekend — in which Nigel Farage’s party received a combined £72mn in gifts from two crypto billionaires. Some thoughts on some of the implications of that in today’s note.

Crypto cash

Money isn’t everything in politics — the better-funded campaign doesn’t always win and the mere possession of money doesn’t guarantee you will spend it well.

But it helps a great deal, not least because it makes it easier to hire more staff, print more leaflets, pay for more advertising on Meta and Google’s platforms (in terms of swing voters, those are the two venues that really matter online), and so on.

It also changes the mood music around a political party — it will shift some of the chatter around Reform from their decline in the polls to new talk of their continued ability to pull in record-breaking donations (for context, either of the £36mn donations Reform received from Ben Delo or Christopher Harborne is more than Labour and the Conservatives have raised combined this year).

On the left, it will make the debate within the government over party funding and regulations on what parties can do with their money fiercer.

On the right, while none of Reform’s difficulties — Farage’s polarising nature, the damage that the undeclared £5mn gift continues to do — can be magicked away with money, it does make it harder for the Conservatives to knock Reform out of contention and to demonstrate that they are the main and most viable option on the right of politics. A split rightwing vote is more likely to become a semi-permanent feature of British politics for the foreseeable future.

Now try this

I went to see Tate Britain’s excellent Whistler exhibition — it only has a few weeks left to run and is well worth seeing if you are able.

Top stories today

  • Stunning sums | Yesterday Angela Rayner left the door open to the government imposing a cap on political donations after the news of Reform’s record-breaking donations. As the i paper’s Caroline Wheeler explains, Andy Burnham previously signalled his support for a £500,000 cap on individual donations. But his government rejected a proposal from Labour backbencher Stella Creasy and other MPs to bring in the limit earlier this month.


  • Infrastructure gap | Every adult in Britain would have to pay an extra £590 a year in tax to fund the £258bn of public investment needed to build planned reservoirs, prisons and schools, according to a new report on the state of Britain’s infrastructure.
  • ‘The UK cannot just hope for the best’ | Martin Wolf kicks off his series of pre-Budget analysis by setting out the challenges that John Healey faces — and the glimmer of positivity in productivity performance. How can the chancellor nurture confidence in our economic stability?

  • Break-up deal? | The first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland will meet in Cardiff today to discuss “working more closely” including on constitutional issues, the BBC reports. All three want their countries to leave the UK, but their short-term demands are different. “Across these islands, we are seeing a new political landscape emerge, with a growing recognition that the Westminster model is no longer working,” said Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Plaid Cymru leader elected in May.

item.title: High inflation or low credibility?
item.description: Making sense of the Fed’s next move
item.content:encoded:
Making sense of the Fed’s next move

Good morning. This time last week, AI was a miracle technology and we were encouraged to look beyond the rogue agents and focus on the glorious future just over the next hill. Now the big dogs in big tech have agreed it is sufficiently dangerous that we need to take time out and make sure it doesn’t destroy humanity. Three possible interpretations spring to mind: either the tech oligarchs knew weeks ago that this is a menace but did nothing about it, or they did not realise what they had created and we’re all doomed, or this is all a load of nonsense. None of these sounds great, to be honest, but it all points to fun times for markets that are highly reliant on the whole thing working out fine. Human readers, let us know what you think while you still can: unhedged@ft.com

What kind of rate increase?

After Friday’s CPI inflation report, the odds that the Fed will raise interest rates this week rose to 86 per cent, from 72 per cent the day before. One might think, then, that the inflation debate is more or less closed — there is a firm consensus that inflation is stubbornly above target and the central bank needs to act. But it isn’t so.

Within the majority that foresees a rate increase, there are two factions. One thinks tighter policy is needed to stamp out rising prices. The other thinks that a rate increase is coming, not because inflation is too high, but because the new-ish Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, has “painted himself into a corner” and has to drag the Open Market Committee into a rate increase just to maintain the bank’s credibility.

Recall Warsh’s speech at Jackson Hole two weeks ago

I am impressed by the overall performance of the economy, which appears to have strengthened . . . The jobless rate, at 4.1 per cent, remains low by historical standards …

But on the price-stability side of our mandate, the numbers are more concerning . . . The Fed’s preferred measure of inflation, the 12-month change in the PCE price index, stands at 3.7 per cent . . . And while this summer’s PCE and CPI readings were better than expected, they do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved . . . 

That muscular talk is the context for August core CPI rising at 2.4 per cent from a year ago, or 3.5 per cent month-over-month annualised: 

On a year-over-year basis, the August reading is (by a hair) the lowest reading since Covid, so there is some recent improvement here, albeit glacial. And as many observers pointed out, there was a large — anomalously large — increase in wireless services prices, in the absence of which the reading would have been a tenth of a percentage point lower. Here is how Frederik Ducrozet, strategist at Pictet Wealth Management, summed up in a tweet:

Crazy how Warsh backed himself into this. Without a one-off adjustment to wireless telecom services . . . the Fed could have paused

Albert Edwards of Société Générale took a similar line: 

It would be criminally stupid for the Fed to hike rates when YoY core CPI is within 1-3 per cent range and decelerating — as are wages. Plus core CPI ex shelter is smack bang on 2 per cent (and close to 2 per cent for three full years).

Before the CPI report landed, Stephen Miran, former chair of Trump’s Council of Economic Advisors and (briefly) Fed governor, said that:

The Fed has backed themselves into a place where policy is ultimately going to be a function of the next inflation print . . . I don’t think hiking rates is the right move; I think the inflation data have been coming down every month for the last few months 

I don’t think an increase this week would be a mere “credibility hike” as some are calling it. I think inflation is too high and not improving fast enough, and policy should be tighter.  

Let’s start with the obvious point: the Fed measure of inflation is PCE, not CPI, which is weighted differently (notably, housing is a lower weight in PCE). Not only has PCE been higher lately, but the August reading is expected — based on the price data underlying CPI — to remain at or above 3 per cent. This is not an improving trend. 

Furthermore, striking out unpleasantly high numbers, like this month’s wireless services reading, is risky. Price rises are lumpy and if it’s not one thing it’s likely to be another. And the economic context suggests we should expect more inflation “lumps”. We are all familiar with the increase in oil, petrol and diesel prices and the possibility they infect other prices. But that is not the end of the story. The cyclical parts of the job market are heating up in a way that is notable, given a flat or shrinking workforce:  

The tightness of the job market may be showing up in higher wage growth, which tells you something about current conditions even if (like Warsh and Daire) you don’t think wage growth is predictive of future inflation:

In another indicator that the economy is approaching capacity constraints in some areas, several consumer goods companies have recently complained that higher freight costs — as distinct from fuel costs — are affecting their margins. The producer price index for trucking services is near 14 per cent; sea freight prices are rising even faster.

It is important that inflation gets all the way back to 2 per cent and stays there. That is not happening right now and there are enough indications of tightness in the economy overall to suggest that the trend is not about to improve. A rate increase makes sense.

One good read

The Ritz-Carlton purge, a $1.3bn demand and nine years trapped in Saudi Arabia

item.title: The Big Read. ‘Offensively cheap’: solar power is looking up
item.author: Rachel Millard and Humza Jilani and Monica Mark and Krishn Kaushik
item.description: Chinese-made panels on rooftops across the world are changing the facts of life for big utilities
item.content:encoded:
Chinese-made panels on rooftops across the world are changing the facts of life for big utilities

Rachel Millard and Humza Jilani and Monica Mark and Krishn Kaushik

In the badlands of Chakwal, in north-central Pakistan, Bestway Cement is transforming plots of dry earth and olive and peach groves into a forest of solar panels.

Its efforts will add 6.34 megawatts of generation capacity by the end of the year, the company says, in addition to the 26MW of photovoltaic cells currently in place. Already, solar generates over a quarter of the electricity powering its cement plant. 

“It’s the only way we can compete,” says Abdul Waheed, the general manager at Chakwal, which produces over 3mn tonnes of cement per year. “Our rivals have already gone in this direction.” 

Bestway and its competitors are among millions of businesses and households around the world that have installed solar panels on roofs, in yards, gardens and other land, helped by a flood of cheap components from China.

At the end of 2025 such capacity totalled almost 1.2 terawatts worldwide, according to the Energy Institute’s Statistical Review of World Energy. While the nature of solar power, which depends on the availability of sunlight, means it only produces a fraction of its theoretical potential, that total equates to roughly three times the size of the global nuclear power fleet.

The solar revolution made possible by cheap Chinese photovoltaic panels — and the rise of small-scale, individual power generation — is transforming energy in the developing and industrialised world alike. Millions of people in poorer countries now have more reliable access to electricity, often through their own endeavours rather than massive installed infrastructure.

And across the globe, consumers are using cleaner energy and bringing down their bills at a time when the cost of living is a constant concern, not least because of the Iran and Ukraine wars.

But such a massive, ungovernable influx of energy carries risks too — the world’s power infrastructure was not designed for solar self-generation — and investment, pricing models and even the security of supply could be affected as a result.

In some countries, the rise of such domestic generation is starting to undermine the economics of power generation and distribution — just as utilities need to invest heavily in re-engineering grids to allow power to flow both to and from consumers.

The UK and several US states have now approved the sale of the low-cost “plug and play” solar panels already widely available in other parts of Europe. Some fear such equipment, which simply plugs into domestic wiring, will introduce yet more unpredictability to the already complicated task of forecasting and managing overall power demand.

That challenge was dramatically illustrated last year by a day-long blackout across much of Spain and Portugal. Professor Janusz Bialek, an expert in power systems at Imperial College London, said in a recent paper that while solar and other renewables did not directly cause the outage, Spain had failed to sufficiently adapt its power system to reflect their growth.

“The rapidly increasing share of renewables in many power systems causes a profound change in the way power systems behave which we do not yet fully understand,” he wrote.

Josefin Berg, research manager for solar and energy storage at S&P Global, says the growth of solar is “completely transforming the system from the centralised structure to something where anyone can produce power”.

“Distribution grids may not always be prepared to take a big influx of electricity . . . and if you have more and more solar and batteries, reducing the sales of electricity for the grid, who is paying for the grid charges?” she adds.

Syed Muhammad Taha, the chief executive of K-Electric, is all too aware of this issue. For the power utility that serves 20mn people in Pakistan’s coastal metropolis of Karachi, solar panels are a “curse and a blessing”, he says.

The concrete villas in Karachi’s wealthy Defence Housing Authority neighbourhood below his office are covered in photovoltaic panels. “These are my best customers,” he laments, “and they’re opting for solar.”

At the turn of the millennium, solar panels cost $5-$6 per watt of generation capacity. Today, they sell for around 12 cents per watt, a level described as “offensively cheap” by Dave Jones, co-founder of think-tank Ember.

That reduction is entirely the result of an explosion in China’s production capacity, which, according to research firm Wood Mackenzie, stands at roughly 1.36 terawatts, even as Beijing tries to rein in output to combat price deflation. 

Cheaper panels enabled a vast rollout in China itself and helped solar generation evolve from a subsidised technology deployed mostly in markets looking to decarbonise to a vital source of electricity in areas where power is scarce, expensive or unreliable. That process started in countries like Pakistan, Brazil and South Africa and has now spread to other parts of Africa and the Philippines.

Based on analysis of customs data, Ember estimates that Africa will install around 17 gigawatts of new solar this year. It believes most of that will be small-scale installations at factories or other businesses. “If you’re a business, you’re using electricity during the day — it’s a natural fit for you to use solar,” says Jones.

But solar is also a boon for households. “A home goes from burning two or three kerosene lanterns to a light that is 20 to 40 times brighter, [turned] on every day,” says Anish Thakkar, co-founder of Sun King, a Kenyan business which lends families money to pay for solar and battery installations.

In the Philippines, Ember estimates rooftop solar capacity may have almost doubled over the 12 months to April and its calculations suggest residential solar panels can now pay for themselves in just over three years. Meralco, the country’s electricity distributor, said rooftop solar generated 372 gigawatt hours in the first six months of the year.

The Indian government’s national subsidised rooftop solar programme, launched in February 2024 with a budget worth nearly $8bn at current exchange rates, has so far put solar panels on over 5mn homes and is adding roughly 500,000 per month, according to Praveer Sinha, chief executive of Tata Power. “It’s a democratisation of the use of electricity,” he says. 

The fallout from the US-Iran war has led to more interest in rooftop solar in Britain, where since the end of August households have been able to buy 800-watt solar panels in supermarkets or DIY stores to plug in at home, a move the government says will give them “breathing space” on bills.

Several US states have also been making it easier for households to do the same, with New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill saying she was “laser-focused on driving down energy costs” as she exempted the devices from metering requirements. Plug-and-play panels are proving popular in the US despite President Trump’s general antipathy to renewables and his decision to eliminate a tax credit for rooftop solar systems.

Sanjeev Raghubir, head of sustainability at Shoprite, Africa’s biggest supermarket group, says the company could “power an entire suburb” with the panels it has been installing on its roofs and trucks in South Africa and Namibia since 2015.

But what has been good for Shoprite, which now has around 43MW of peak capacity at its disposal and is looking at battery storage, constitutes a problem for state power utility Eskom.

It estimates that rooftop solar panels and batteries, mostly installed by businesses and wealthier customers in response to years of rolling blackouts, were responsible for around 7 per cent of the 11.7 terawatt-hour reduction in its electricity sales for the year ending March, compounding a sharp fall in industrial use exacerbated by high prices.

The lower revenues come as Eskom needs to fund the upkeep of the grid, which allows households to export electricity during the day, and the power stations that fill the generation gap when it’s dark or cloudy, or when power stored in batteries is insufficient to meet demand.

“Everyone who has rooftop solar in any major city, they are still connected to the grid,” says its chief executive, Dan Marokane. “Three weeks ago . . . the whole country had to rely on Eskom generation for three days,” he adds, due to prolonged cloudy weather slashing output from rooftop panels.

The company is redesigning tariffs to distinguish between network and energy costs, which analysts hope will make pricing more efficient and help the market adapt to the shift in supply. But its overriding task is to avoid the kind of “utility death spiral” seen in Pakistan, where poorer people end up shouldering a greater proportion of the cost of power infrastructure.

Those customers not using solar panels in Karachi’s Defence Housing Authority are more likely to live in the poorer parts of town such as Lyari, a densely populated borough where the rates of non-payment are so high that KE loses Rs30-Rs40 for every Rs100 it spends supplying the locality.  

Customers like Azem Baloch, a mechanic living in Lyari, face rising power bills as utilities across the country attempt to recoup the cost of a previous poorly planned build-out of centralised generation capacity. Baloch and his family rent a flat in a rundown tenement where it is difficult to install panels on the roof. “I am spending more than half of my income on power,” he says. 

Tata Power’s Sinha acknowledges that “if paying consumers are going and the non-paying consumers stay with you, then it becomes a problem”. But he says India has reduced that risk by focusing support on lower-income households, while the company generates additional revenue from installing solar panels.  

The growth of rooftop solar in Africa raises broader questions about the wider role of utilities and grids in its future energy infrastructure. “What should your grid look like in five, 10 years if you suspect that more demand is going to go ‘behind the meter’?” wonders Berg, at S&P.

“Everyone is talking about the huge need for electricity grids,” says Jones, at Ember. “But in a distributed [energy] world, you would need less.”   

The challenges of solar power are practical as well as financial. In Australia, operators of the high-voltage transmission system have grappled with too little demand as consumers draw power from their rooftop panels rather than the grid.

Very low demand can make it harder to run certain power plants needed to keep the whole system stable. Electricity supply and demand have to be constantly matched, and energy groups in some states are having to literally give away excess power generated during the middle of the day. 

Power flowing from local distribution networks into transmission grids can cause voltage increases, limiting the amount of power that households can put into the grid.

Predicting output from thousands of solar panels bolted on to rooftops around the vast country is complex at best — and the risks of getting it wrong grow with the number of installations.

“Perth, for example, is covered in rooftop solar,” says Pierluigi Mancarella, chair professor of electrical power systems at the University of Melbourne. “If you have a massive cloud formation, the rooftop PV production can drop by so much that it looks like you have lost basically almost a nuclear power station.”

Australia has developed a sophisticated database to match weather forecasting with other system data, he adds. But he questions the merits of adding plug-and-play panels to this already unwieldy mix. “This is not a good idea,” he says, highlighting the cumulative effect of, say, one million consumers each adding a kilowatt’s worth of panels. The system operator has very little visibility over the aggregate gigawatt of generation capacity thus created, he says. In most jurisdictions, plug-in solar panels have to be registered, but research in Germany has shown many installations are not.

Household batteries, which allow some of the power generated by rooftop panels to be stored rather than fed back into the grid, are also falling in price and will help ease the problem.

So too would better visibility over supply, with many companies and governments turning to AI to help with this. Lucy Yu, the UK government’s AI champion for clean energy, said in a report published last week that AI can learn the “underlying structure of the grid” and help speed up calculations to measure supply and demand. UK Power Networks has just finished a £389,000 study to develop machine-learning models that can better estimate the solar generation capacity connected to the network.  

Jon Ecker, general manager for Europe at solar forecasting company Amperon, says the company’s machine learning models retrain every hour, assessing changes on the grid to get the most accurate forecasts. “They know that in springtime, they’re going to need to weigh what has happened over the last hour more heavily than in the last year,” he says.

New technology developed in Australia can increase the amount of power that grids absorb from households. “Engineers are moving very fast to respond [to the changes]. But the major lesson is: don’t wait until the last minute — you know this is coming,” says Mancarella.  

In Pakistan, utilities plan to deploy large-scale solar and wind plants along with battery storage infrastructure to mitigate the high cost of using oil and other fossil fuels to generate power after sunset. The country has also slashed the amount grid operators pay households to buy back surplus solar power.

Eskom chief Marokane says he is looking to heavy electricity users such as data centres and bitcoin miners to help reverse falling power sales, while introducing a new pricing policy aimed at helping lower- and middle-income households and businesses. But he warns that the cost of investment in the network to support renewables “is going to find its way into the electricity price”. 

In the meantime, Eskom has waived registration fees for new solar installations, in part to give it more visibility over new installations. “I think we will see more uptake [of solar],” Marokane says. “It’s not going to stop.”

item.title: Why teenagers are doing worse at school
item.author: Tej Parikh
item.description: Falling global test scores underscore the importance of core knowledge, attention and mindset
item.content:encoded:
Falling global test scores underscore the importance of core knowledge, attention and mindset

Tej Parikh

Artificial intelligence is getting smarter. Human intelligence, however, appears to be going the other way — at least among teenagers.

The performance of students in science, mathematics and reading has plunged to record lows across developed nations, according to the OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), which tests 15- to 16-year-olds roughly every three years.

Many glanced at the most recent data release and reached for simplistic explanations in an attempt to interpret the decline. But this only risks obscuring the problem and the solutions.

One frequently cited culprit is the Covid-19 pandemic. Lockdown measures disrupted learning across the world and contributed to steep drops in PISA scores between 2018 and 2022. Pupils sitting last year’s tests would have been around 10 years old in 2020. School closures might have hit younger students harder, coming at a more formative stage of their education.

But zooming out, OECD-wide PISA scores have been falling since the early 2010s, which means broader underlying factors are also at play. This has put the spotlight on technology. The use of AI by students has surged in recent years. In science, pupils who use chatbots every day for tasks such as summarising and drafting text tend to underperform those who barely use it by the equivalent of about one year of schooling.

While offloading cognitive tasks to AI can atrophy processing skills, much depends on how the technology is used. Indeed, students who use it daily to aid, rather than replace, thinking perform better than those who use it less frequently. (Students with opportunities to develop AI literacy skills at school also perform better.)

Besides, chatbots are a more recent phenomenon and the beginning of the decline in PISA scores coincides with the proliferation of smartphone use among teenagers. Digital devices distract and endless content absorbs mental bandwidth. It is telling that many Silicon Valley executives limit their own children’s screen time.

Still, some nations have managed to avoid notable declines in attainment amid the pandemic and technological shifts. This has led some to advance policy-based explanations. For instance, students with access to high-quality teachers tend to outperform, and schools that place restrictions or guidelines on phone use report lower distraction rates on average, according to PISA.

More broadly, nations that have leaned into educational fads, which generally involve placing less emphasis on a core knowledge framework, have experienced more notable drops in long-term performance. Average scores in Finland, once the darling of supposed innovative teaching practices involving play-based learning and less testing, have declined the most among rich nations since 2006 across all three subjects. Shifts to less rigorous teaching methods in Sweden in the 1990s and in Scotland’s Curriculum for Excellence in 2010 have been linked to subsequent declines in student outcomes, too.

By contrast, countries that have retained an emphasis on foundational subject matter, such as England and Estonia, as well as nations in east Asia, have stemmed declines. The share of “low performers” across science, mathematics and reading — that is, those achieving below baseline proficiency — is also well below the OECD average in many of these countries, suggesting that with patience, repetition and support, most students can achieve a functional understanding of core concepts.

Progressives too easily dismiss the value of traditional teaching, but facts are the building blocks of critical thinking and tackling repeated algebraic problems, for instance, hones abstract reasoning. (PISA assesses pupils’ application of skills to real-life problems, not purely mastery of knowledge.)

This does not mean non-traditional forms of teaching have no merit. For instance, high-performing Estonia and Singapore embrace technology and autonomous and interdisciplinary learning. And in both, use of AI is well above the OECD average.

Finally, some blame immigration for dragging down national scores. Immigrant students are more likely to come from disadvantaged backgrounds or speak a language at home that differs from the language of the test, which can contribute to weaker performance. But non-immigrant students’ average reading, maths and science scores have also fallen over the past decade across the OECD, implying that broader forces are at work.

Rapid immigration can certainly stretch local education systems, but it can raise performance, too. On average, countries with a larger share of immigrant students tend to perform better in science. In some countries, including the UK, Australia, Canada and the United Arab Emirates, immigrant students outperform those from non-immigrant backgrounds. Studies show exposure to immigrant students with a particularly hard-working ethic can drive up the performance of native students.

This highlights another important factor in learning outcomes: the home environment. Parents’ education and involvement in their child’s learning, as well as their attitudes towards education and command of the teaching language, can shape how well children perform, regardless of the system.

There are then myriad, interlinked reasons for the decline in PISA scores. But beneath the grim numbers lies an empowering lesson: a good education still appears to rest on some enduring principles, such as attention, core knowledge, quality teaching and a culture that values learning. The use of technology and liberal teaching practices ought to complement these foundations, not displace them.

Send your thoughts in the comments, to freelunch@ft.com or via X @tejparikh90.

Food for thought

The first large-scale economic study of workplace meetings concludes that they resemble broccoli — widely disliked, but probably worthwhile.

Free Lunch on Sunday is edited by Harvey Nriapia

item.title: The FT View. The coming robotaxi revolution
item.author: The editorial board
item.description: Self-driving cars could transform urban transport, if they can win public trust
item.content:encoded:
Self-driving cars could transform urban transport, if they can win public trust

The editorial board

Fifteen electric Ford Mustangs have begun steering themselves around London this month as the capital’s first commercial self-driving taxi service. For now, a licensed driver still sits ready to seize control in case of mishaps, and this partnership between Uber and the UK-based AI start-up Wayve is hardly the first such service: autonomous “robotaxis” — many without safety drivers — operate in more than 20 cities in the US, China and the Middle East. Yet London’s narrow streets, teeming with pedestrians, cyclists and double-decker buses, present a special challenge. To borrow a phrase associated with another great world city, if robotaxis can make it here, they can make it anywhere.

Many residents are not convinced they should. YouGov in July found 42 per cent of Londoners opposed autonomous passenger vehicles, with only 29 per cent in support. Concerns ranged from safety to job losses. Still, more than 140,000 people have registered to try out Uber’s AVs. Robotaxis deserve to succeed, in London and elsewhere.

Despite some unfortunate and highly publicised accidents, data suggests the best AVs are already a lot safer than human drivers. Nearly 1.2mn people die globally every year in road crashes; human error is a contributing factor in the vast majority. An independent analysis found driverless vehicles from Alphabet’s Waymo in four US cities were involved in 68 per cent fewer crashes per vehicle mile than human drivers — though this is human drivers generally, not just professional ones.

Driverless vehicles can struggle with “edge cases” ranging from snow to traffic light failures. But they may become better at handling such situations over time as the technology evolves. Rather than relying on their training on high-definition maps, the latest “vision-language-action” models, developed by companies including Wayve, use cameras paired with language-based AI to improve their ability to interpret unfamiliar situations.

For now, robotaxis are costlier to operate due to development costs and extra kit. But Goldman Sachs says operational and scale efficiencies could cut costs sharply, and projects a $415bn global robotaxi market by 2035. As costs fall, driverless vehicles could start to displace driver-operated taxis and, in big cities, even private car ownership (the RAC found the average personal car in England is parked for 96 per cent of the time). AV evangelists suggest that could open the way, longer term, to their vision of “shared mobility”, easing congestion and cutting emissions — provided cheap AV rides do not encourage more journeys and lots of unnecessary miles by loitering vehicles.

News of cabbies losing their livelihoods could fan disquiet among a public already worried about the wider impact of AI on jobs. Cab drivers in many cities are understandably polishing their stories of emergency dashes to maternity units and touting their driving prowess, local knowledge and ability to help with bags or keep an eye on vulnerable passengers. Some human-driven taxis will always be needed. But provided serious safety issues are avoided, many consumers may be won over by AVs’ convenience and potentially lower fares.

Fragile trust means the robotaxi revolution will need careful handling by regulators and operators alike. The UK’s 2024 Automated Vehicles Act, which sets demanding safety requirements and makes operating entities liable for how AVs drive, could be a useful model. Some in the industry who have spent years trying to build trust worry about the re-entry of Travis Kalanick, the pugnacious former Uber chief, and Elon Musk’s aggressive promotion of controls-free Cybercabs. When it comes to acceptance, the pioneers of “AI on wheels” could learn from the backlash being felt by their cousins in frontier AI.

item.title: Chart of the Week: the long shadow of quantitative easing
item.author: Daire MacFadden
item.description: Central bank balance sheets will stay large
item.content:encoded:
Central bank balance sheets will stay large

Daire MacFadden

Good morning. As a percentage of nominal GDP, the balance sheets of the Bank of England, the European Central Bank and the Federal Reserve are now at levels not seen since before the era of Covid-19 expansions. But the central banks’ experience of shrinking their balance sheets — a process known as quantitative tightening — suggests they may not be able to go much further, and nor do they really need to.

The Fed was the first to start normalising its balance sheet in 2017. Its first attempt ended in August 2019, only for a repo-market blow-up the next month to reveal that it had gone too far. Its second attempt has been more orderly, but to avoid another “repocalypse” it ended QT late last year.

The BoE’s approach has been the most controversial. Unlike the Fed and ECB, it has shrunk its bond portfolio through maturities and outright gilt sales. As a share of GDP, its balance sheet has fallen by just over half from its 2022 peak. But this may also have pushed up UK borrowing costs, with some estimates putting the effect as high as 0.7 percentage points. The BoE will decide on September 17 how much further to shrink the balance sheet over the coming year.

The ECB was the last to start quantitative easing and has also been the slowest to unwind it. Its balance sheet was shrinking before it began QT, but mainly because banks were repaying crisis-era loans and nominal GDP was rising quickly. Its caution reflects the challenges of maintaining financial stability across a 21-country currency union.

The era of large-scale asset purchases may be over, but large central bank balance sheets are probably here to stay.

Send us your thoughts: unhedged@ft.com.

Good reads from Unhedged:

Hakyung: Haute cuisine in Saudi Arabia

Rob: America lost sight of other threats

Daire: The decline of non-fiction

Katie: Mario Draghi on difficult choices

item.title: The Big Read. Britain thinks twice about free museums
item.author: Franklin Nelson
item.description: The UK government is considering charging tourists entry fees. The sector is vehemently opposed
item.content:encoded:
The UK government is considering charging tourists entry fees. The sector is vehemently opposed

Franklin Nelson

At the British Museum last week, King Charles was taken aback by the climactic scene of the 70-metre Bayeux Tapestry.

“Oh dear,” he said, coming to the embroidery’s depiction of the death of England’s last Anglo-Saxon ruler, Harold Godwinson, by an arrow to the eye at the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

“You killed our king!” a British official scolded Emmanuel Macron, who was alongside the King and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the grand unveiling of the near 1,000-year-old work in London. “I won’t do it again,” quipped France’s president, according to a person present at the exchange.

To see the tapestry, which is billed as a “special exhibition” and open to the public from this week, adults must pay up to £33. Access to the world’s first public national museum and its 8mn-strong permanent collection is otherwise free. The same is true for England’s 14 other national museums and galleries.

But the future of the universal free admission model — which costs taxpayers about £485mn a year — is in doubt after UK ministers proposed in March to make overseas visitors pay at the front door.

The British government is now formally exploring the policy alongside the group of 15 museums, which welcomed 19.4mn overseas visitors and 22.6mn domestic visitors in 2024-25.

At a time when the UK’s public finances are squeezed, the government is looking to the tourism industry as a means of raising revenue. This week, it said mayors and council leaders in England would be able to charge unlimited taxes on overnight stays.

Ministers said in March that charging could support the “long-term financial resilience” of the 15 institutions. Yet the proposal is roundly opposed by museum chiefs. They argue that free admission has widened access to culture and that fees risk leaving them worse off if foreigners holidaying in an already expensive country decide against a visit.

Nicholas Cullinan, director of the British Museum, says free entry “changed my life [as a child]”. Roland Rudd, chair of the Tate network of galleries, thinks “putting up barriers to entry is ultimately self-defeating”. The move “would be extremely short-sighted”, according to Lord Tony Hall, chair of the Natural History Museum. Nat Edwards, director-general and master of the Royal Armouries in Leeds, calls it “small-minded and frankly xenophobic”. 

Although some smaller museums in Britain do charge, its best-known venues are outliers. The Louvre in Paris asks adults from inside the European Economic Area for €22 and, as of January, for €32 from others, to help fund a major renovation. A trip to the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam costs €25. The Met in New York charges $30. To see Botticelli’s The Birth of Venus at Florence’s Uffizi, visitors pay €29.

In England, in lieu of admission fees, “self-generated income” from special exhibitions, events and gift shop sales has become increasingly important for the 15 national institutions, which are directly supported by the state.

Government funding fell by 16 per cent in real terms between 2021-22 and 2024-25 — although it remained 12 per cent above the average in the three years before the pandemic — while the museums’ expenditure rose by 18 per cent over the same period, says the National Audit Office, the public spending watchdog. 

Some sector veterans and donors back a change. Sir Mark Jones, who stepped down in 2024 as interim head of the British Museum, where visitors are mostly from outside the UK, says “at a time when government money is relatively short it would be a good thing to consider charging tourists” so museums can “invest and enlarge what they do”. 

Sir Peter Bazalgette, former chair of Arts Council England, the arm’s-length funding body, says “it makes sense to reciprocate; people quite happily pay for museums across Europe”. In London, tourists are used to paying for access to historical sites and attractions such as Hampton Court Palace and the Tower of London.

But, given the broad funding pressures, most museum leaders believe that charging tourists would be a sticking-plaster solution for only a small portion of the sector.

Laura Pye, chair of the National Museum Directors’ Council, which speaks for museum leaders, says that beyond the practical difficulties of identifying an overseas tourist at the door, the idea poses “philosophical challenges”.

“How do you make someone from Greece pay to see the Parthenon Sculptures?” she says, of the contested artefacts kept in the British Museum. “If the government wants a thriving museums sector, what we need is more money into the whole system. Robbing Peter to pay Paul isn’t the answer.” 

‘Somebody has to pay’

When the British Museum was founded in 1753 to house Hans Sloane’s vast collection of objects from around the world, lawmakers said entry should be free for “all studious and curious persons”.

Distinct though they are in focus and size — the Natural History Museum has more than 1,000 staff versus roughly 60 at the Museum of the Home in Hoxton, east London — that sentiment has served as a blueprint for all of England’s national museums and galleries since. 

It also inspired the US Congress when, almost a century later, the Smithsonian Institution was set up “for the increase and diffusion of knowledge among men”. Today, 20 of its 21 museums — including all those in Washington DC — offer free admission.

On the first day of 1974, Edward Heath’s Conservative government ended the tradition in England, bringing in a standard entry charge for all adults of 10p, about £1 in today’s money. The experiment was brief — it was scrapped in March 1974, after Labour returned to power the previous month. But it was impactful. 

Across the board visits declined, in some cases sharply. The National Portrait Gallery, for instance, welcomed 14,006 people in January 1974, down from 30,750 in January 1973. In three months, the gallery generated £2,310 but spent more than twice that sum on staffing and ticket machines. 

In the 1980s, Margaret Thatcher’s Tory government gave museum trustees the option of levying charges. While the British Museum and the National Gallery stayed free, the Victoria and Albert Museum and the Science Museum were among those to require entry fees or impose a “voluntary donation”. In December 2001, universal free entry was reintroduced by Lord Chris Smith, then Labour culture secretary.

In the years since, as demands on the public purse have grown and competition has increased internationally, the group of 15 has had to embrace mixed-income models.  

Exact figures vary, but in 2024-25, 46 per cent of their income on average came from the government, according to the audit office. Self-generated income, which also includes donations and legacies, soared 53 per cent to £563mn between 2021-22 and 2024-25.

Last December, an independent review of the Arts Council by former culture minister Baroness Margaret Hodge said ministers should look at charges for international visitors. When it responded in March, the government accepted her proposal.

Hodge’s suggestion was predicated, she wrote, on digital ID cards “achiev[ing] universal coverage”, in a move that “would align the UK with other countries, such as New Zealand and Singapore, that charge an entry fee to international visitors whilst retaining free entry for citizens and residents”.

Sir Keir Starmer’s government made no mention of digital ID cards in its response to her review, and Burnham has since abandoned them. “Without IDs, it’s absolutely not feasible. It will be discriminatory,” Hodge says. 

Smith, the former culture secretary, says the push for charging “has come from the Treasury . . . They thought it would be an easy and attractive way of raising money, given the difficult fiscal picture. 

“But of course for the museums that did charge, the Treasury would just claw back a portion of the grant-in-aid that they give them,” he adds. “So we would not see a new dawn for the sector, just a fall-off in visitors, reputational strength and soft power.”

The Louvre is the most visited museum in the world despite its entry fees, which date back a century. A 2016 study by consultancy DC Research for the Association of Independent Museums found that institutions in the UK “that do currently charge for admissions most commonly report that this has no impact on visitor numbers”.

Nevertheless, many national museum chiefs are concerned that “friction” on arrival could deter domestic visitors who are not habitual museum-goers and that charging would undermine the country’s attempt to tell global histories through its collections.
