Caro Howell, director-general of the Imperial War Museums, says the credibility of her institution’s focus on “stories of service, sacrifice and resilience by nations and individuals from the Commonwealth as well as Britain” rests in part on ensuring “as many people as possible can access them”.  

“The idea of charging a Holocaust survivor to visit the Holocaust Galleries is grotesque,” she adds.

Government officials have already told Pye, who is also director of National Museums Liverpool, that if overseas visitors were forced to pay for entry, the city’s International Slavery Museum would be exempt. “The suggestion that I’d be charging visitors from the Caribbean feels very wrong,” she says. 

But Jones, who previously ran the V&A and proposed the “heretical idea” of an entry fee of £20 per head when he left the British Museum, believes there is “something a little bit unattractive about the kind of idea that Britain is rendered morally superior” by its aversion to tourist charges.

“It’s no more outrageous that the Louvre, whose collections also come from a wide range of countries, should charge than the British Museum should charge,” he says. “Somebody has to pay. Who is that going to be? What conception of equity leads one to the conclusion that British taxpayers, many of whom are not museum visitors and many of whom are less well off than foreign tourists, must subsidise foreign tourists?”

Bazalgette, who cautions that decisions on charging should be down to museums, maintains that the system of free entry “wasn’t fashioned for visitors to the country; it was fashioned for Brits”.

Of similar mind is Dame Vivien Duffield, who has donated about £185mn to arts institutions and charities around the UK, including 14 of the 15 national museums. “With everything else the government has to pay for, especially the NHS . . . I simply don’t understand why foreigners shouldn’t pay, and I really don’t see why well-off Brits shouldn’t pay either,” she says.

“If I thought even fewer people could come to museums [with the introduction of charging], I would pay for the people who really couldn’t afford to go.”

Modelling by the culture department forecasts that several bigger museums in London stand to gain financially from charging international visitors, say three people familiar with the data.

But it also projects a decline in the number of domestic visitors if entry fees for overseas visitors come into force.

Sir Nicholas Serota, who stepped down as chair of the Arts Council this summer, says charges risk hurting the wider museum ecosystem. “If national museums start to charge, then many local authority museums, which are struggling badly, might feel the need to follow suit,” he says. “That would shut people out.”

The UK culture department had no comment.

Tourist pounds

With sources of self-generated income “vulnerable to wider economic factors”, according to the audit office, many museum leaders have backed another charge: a levy on overnight stays in England, part of the government’s push for fiscal devolution.

V&A head Sir Tristram Hunt told the FT in January that 80 per cent of revenues from “tourist taxes” in London should be ringfenced for the cultural sector. 

The levy — which mimics charges in cultural hubs including Paris, Amsterdam and Florence, whose big museums also charge — would raise more than £1.2bn a year if set at 3 per cent of the average room rate, according to research by the Cultural Policy Unit, a think-tank that wants to see universal free entry maintained. 

But mayors and council leaders will decide how money raised from the levy — which will not be capped — is spent in their areas, meaning cultural organisations may lose out to high streets and local transport.

Bernard Donoghue, head of industry body Alva, says both the levy and the museum charging proposal have been put forward “in complete isolation from a comprehensive tourism strategy by the government” and would compound the end of VAT-free shopping for tourists, which was phased out in 2021. 

“Culture, heritage, visitor attractions are the integral heart of the UK tourism visitor economy. Hotels are built next to museums and galleries, not the other way around,” he says. “Any rise in the cost of visiting puts people off the UK.”

In her review, Hodge urged the Arts Council to work with ministers to “create a specific long-term plan for museums”. Burnham’s appointment of Baroness Ruth Mackenzie, a former theatre director, as arts minister has boosted hopes that he is serious about the sector.

Smith, the former culture secretary, is somewhat optimistic. He recalls that when he was seeking to reinstate free entry in the late 1990s, Mackenzie and Burnham were among his special advisers. In fact, they shared an office. At the same time, in Downing Street, James Purnell was working on the policy. He went on to serve as culture secretary and is chief of staff in Number 10 these days.

“Although Ruth Mackenzie and I led on the policy, Burnham was an enabler, and the three of them now form a powerful trio with a commitment to culture at its heart,” Smith says. “I very much hope they will do the right thing and get rid of this really stupid idea.”

Letter in response:
Merseyside’s solution to free museum access / From JAB Joll, Chairman, Museums and Galleries Commission, Pewsey, Wiltshire, UK

item.title: Time to start taking AI risks seriously
item.author: Simon Mundy
item.description: Governments promise a light-touch regulatory agenda amid growing threats
item.content:encoded:
Governments promise a light-touch regulatory agenda amid growing threats

Simon Mundy

Welcome back.

Anthropic’s new report on “misuse” of its technology gives a sobering overview of the dark ends to which cutting-edge AI can now be applied — most strikingly, in citing five instances where scientists circumvented controls to use its models “in ways that could support biological weapons development”.

Tackling these risks, according to Anthropic’s boss and hundreds of others at leading AI companies, requires serious co-ordinated action from global governments. As things stand, the prospect of such action seems more distant than ever.

‘No one is prepared’

If AI ends up wreaking catastrophic damage on humanity, we won’t be able to say its creators didn’t warn us.

Much attention has been given this week to the parting shot from Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old researcher who quit Anthropic, warning that “the people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.”

This might look like a hysterical outburst from a disgruntled ex-junior employee. But in its warning of AI’s increasingly severe, potentially existential risks, Coxon’s message is broadly in line with repeated warnings from people at senior levels of leading AI companies, who remain very much in post.

Just three days before Coxon’s public statement, in a blog post entitled “An Alien Mind”, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki warned of the “clear new dangers” from what could become “an alien intellect exceeding our own”, threatening humanity’s control over its future.

“I am concerned no one is prepared for the consequences of a continued rapid rise in machine intelligence,” Pachocki wrote, noting that the most advanced AI models were becoming increasingly hard for their builders to control.

Alarming proof of this came in July when a large number of AI “agents” created by OpenAI broke free of their controls and launched a co-ordinated attack on the tech company Hugging Face without any human instruction to do so.

Separately, the arrival of an age in which nation states make use of these technologies for cyber warfare was illustrated by a reported Chinese attack on Taiwanese digital infrastructure using autonomous AI agents.

Pachocki urged governments to introduce “shared safety bars” to mitigate the worsening risks presented by advanced AI. “The idea of racing forward at all costs seems absurd once one internalises the seriousness of the stakes,” he wrote.

This follows a string of similar calls from leading AI executives and experts. In July, over 1,300 employees of advanced AI companies — including Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei and senior figures at OpenAI, Google DeepMind and Meta — issued a statement urging the US government to support an international effort to develop “technical and governance tools” that could control the pace of this technology’s development, and “buy time to address emerging risks”.

In the absence of such international controls, they argued, “each company — and country — is under intense competitive pressure” to keep up with that dangerous acceleration, rather than unilaterally slow down and drop out of the race.

At a G20 meeting in North Carolina last week, the US indeed pushed through an international agreement among major economies — one seemingly aimed at impeding, rather than enabling, regulatory action to slow the pace of AI development to a safer level. This fits with the Trump administration’s broader approach to AI, which is heavily focused on promoting US companies’ leadership in the sector and minimising obstacles to their growth.

By signing up to the “Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies” — which are clearly about AI but shy away from using the term — major economies have in effect thrown their weight behind what is known in the industry as the “accelerationist” AI camp. The document heavily emphasises various measures that governments should take to minimise the regulatory burden on AI developers, including by providing exemptions from rules and streamlining permitting procedures.

Governments should aim to rely on existing regulations where possible rather than creating new ones, the document says, stressing that any evaluation of AI regulation should “consider the opportunity cost of delayed or forgone adoption”. True, it nods to the idea that AI experimentation should be “responsible”. But the thrust of the document is squarely in favour of speeding things up. The verb “accelerate” appears seven times in this 1,200-word text, which makes heavy mention of the positive impacts of these technologies and none at all of the negative ones.

The communiqué will have pleased the likes of Elon Musk and Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, both of whom urged the G20 meeting against undue regulatory barriers to AI. “Don’t regulate hypothetical, theoretical harm,” Huang told the gathering.

It will have been less welcome to Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey, who currently chairs the global Financial Stability Board. On the eve of the meeting, he issued a letter to G20 ministers warning that the most immediate concern for the global financial system was the risk that “frontier AI” posed to cyber security.

“Many jurisdictions do not have the protocols in place to manage the development, release and deployment of advanced frontier AI models, heightening risks for the financial sector and beyond,” he wrote, warning that these risks “could undermine market confidence system-wide”.

Bailey’s warning — while severe by central bankers’ standards — seems tame when set against some of the language coming from AI developers themselves. Earlier this year, Anthropic’s Amodei published a long essay warning of a panoply of potentially catastrophic risks presented by the AI models that his company and its competitors are developing.

To give you a flavour, here is Amodei on just one of those risks, biological weapons:

I am concerned that a genius in everyone’s pocket could . . . essentially mak[e] everyone a PhD virologist who can be walked through the process of designing, synthesizing, and releasing a biological weapon step-by-step . . . To put it another way, renting a powerful AI gives intelligence to malicious (but otherwise average) people. I am worried there are potentially a large number of such people out there, and that if they have access to an easy way to kill millions of people, sooner or later one of them will do it . . . I am concerned that LLMs are approaching (or may already have reached) the knowledge needed to create and release [biological weapons] end-to-end, and that their potential for destruction is very high.

Some dismiss such warnings as a weird form of marketing. Musings on existential risk, the argument goes, are a way for people like Amodei to hype the power of their technology and thereby attract ever more interest from amoral investors; to simultaneously burnish an image as empathetic, thoughtful business leaders; to distract attention from other problems like embedded bias and racism in AI models.

This analysis has become increasingly fashionable as the warnings from within the AI sector have become more severe. There’s surely some substance to it. But with every new piece of evidence of this technology’s growing power — and of its creators’ limited ability to control or even understand it — that comforting narrative looks ever more fragile.

Smart reads

  • Obstruction by some governments is threatening the crucial work of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, writes Pilita Clark.
  • The oil sector is no longer seen as a pariah by young people seeking well-paid work, with big tech companies now seen as “the villains”, according to the boss of one of the largest US shale oil producers.

item.title: The FT View. The day that blew America and the world off course
item.author: The editorial board
item.description: A quarter of a century later, the consequences of 9/11 have reshaped the global order
item.content:encoded:
A quarter of a century later, the consequences of 9/11 have reshaped the global order

The editorial board

Twenty-five years ago as the smoke and dust rose from the ruins of the World Trade Center after the devastating 9/11 attacks, much of the world rallied to America’s support — and rightly so. It was a shocking assault that even then seemed to draw a line under the post-cold war decade and the attendant hopes for a more peaceful, just and stable world. 

Nearly 3,000 people were killed when 19 members of the Islamist terrorist group al-Qaeda hijacked passenger airliners and flew them into the Twin Towers and the Pentagon; a fourth plane, probably intended to target the US Capitol, crashed into a field after the passengers fought back against the hijackers.

Le Monde memorably encapsulated the stunned sympathy of American allies in a front-page editorial under the headline: Nous sommes tous Américains. Nato invoked its collective defence clause for the first and only time since it was founded more than five decades earlier.

Strikingly, old enemies too rushed to show support. Russia’s then relatively neophyte president, Vladimir Putin, was the first world leader to call the US president, George W Bush. He followed through by supporting the use of former Soviet bases in central Asia to help the US-led coalition in its offensive against Afghanistan’s ruling Taliban, then sheltering al-Qaeda’s leader Osama bin Laden. 

It says much for America’s can-do spirit that New York recovered remarkably quickly. Many of the worst fears circulating in America in the bleak days after 9/11 were also not realised: there were no further large-scale terrorist attacks on US soil for more than a decade. To that extent Bush’s “war on terror” was a success.

But unfortunately, America’s broader response to 9/11 casts a deep shadow over the world. The politics of revenge, and the hubris in Washington that followed the rapid initial overthrow of the Taliban for the loss of just 12 US military personnel and a CIA officer, led to a series of calamitous mis-steps and misjudgments, most of all the decision to invade Iraq in 2003.

The US raced to war barely going through the motions of seeking UN backing, and with what even at the time seemed the flimsiest of evidence to back up its claim that Iraq had weapons of mass destruction. (It did not.) The invasion and the sectarian conflict and insurgency that ensued cost hundreds of thousands of mainly Iraqi lives. They also gravely damaged America’s standing, as did the revelations over the torture of prisoners at Abu Ghraib and other human rights abuses by US troops.

The failed 20-year campaign to dominate Afghanistan, which ended in 2021 with the Taliban’s return to power, further weakened America’s reputation — and also cost hundreds of thousands of lives. 

The global sympathy was long ago squandered, as was America’s massive pre-9/11 budget surplus; debt this year surpassed $40tn. The financial crisis and Covid-19 bailouts all played major roles, but so did the dizzying cost of the wars.

Even without 9/11 and the US overreaction, it was perhaps inevitable that the 21st century would see a weakening of the US-led world order against the backdrop of a rising China, and other aspirant powers. Ultimately Putin might well have always gone his own way, turning away from the west and pursuing imperialist ambitions.

But it is hard to escape the conclusion that a post-9/11 desire for vengeance led America to be distracted from focusing on how to approach its primary rival, China, and an increasingly revanchist Russia, as it fruitlessly unleashed its might on the world.

Bush’s successor, Barack Obama, tried to repair some of the damage to America’s standing in the world. But the post-9/11 spirit of muscular US interventionism has been revived by President Donald Trump in his second term. Trump has succumbed to his own bout of hubris in launching his ill-conceived war on Iran, albeit without the deployment of ground troops. At home, he has pushed to accelerate a worrying centralisation of power from the federal government to the executive that began after 9/11.

In a characteristically scattergun speech ahead of this poignant anniversary, Trump said that the US was “bigger, better, stronger than before”. Sadly, much of the rest of the world that stood with America 25 years ago would find it hard to agree.

item.title: Andy Burnham’s blind spot
item.author: Jennifer Williams
item.description: Prime minister risks forgetting ‘flyover states’ in the Midlands that have huge growth potential
item.content:encoded:
Prime minister risks forgetting ‘flyover states’ in the Midlands that have huge growth potential

Jennifer Williams

Good morning. Greetings from Manchester, Andy Burnham’s “North Pole” to London’s traditional southern centre of national power. 

If you’re sick of hearing about the city — and especially if you happen to hail from the Midlands — you’re in luck. Because that is what I want to look at today.

Turn the page

John Healey’s speech in Coventry on Monday instantly brought to mind a conversation I had already been having with grumpy friends and contacts from the Midlands. Having chosen the city’s Manufacturing Technology Centre as his stage, he proceeded to announce a series of investments and policies almost exclusively for the north of England. There was nothing in it for the Midlands at all. 

If that complaint sounds parochial, bear in mind the second-biggest city in the country is in the Midlands and that the region’s economy, as the latest Jaguar Land Rover episode demonstrates, is not inconsequential.

We in the north have the highest propensity to get annoyed at this stuff and, indeed, the prime minister himself used to regularly capitalise on that sense of grievance. He knows exactly the risks of appearing to prioritise one part of the country at the expense of others. 

Take the growth speech Rachel Reeves made 18 months ago, which featured a series of major economic priorities for the Golden Triangle connecting Oxford, Cambridge and London, as well as the wider South East. She chucked in a (flawed) proposal for Manchester United’s home ground as a gesture. It did not go down particularly well here, never mind elsewhere. 

Now the tables have turned. It is Burnham who must be alive to such risks, having spent the last few weeks and months emphasising the northern narrative, sometimes deliberately but sometimes seemingly out of reflex. 

It’s in the name, Number 10 North, and it is in the fact that the most advanced mayoralties cover most of the northern map. Those two things can be excused to some extent. Wherever you put your second prime ministerial base, somebody will complain and the devolution map is what it is at present. 

Other things can be helped. “I am probably not renowned for spending much time on farms,” he began in response to a question about farms. “I am more likely to be found in the Northern Quarter of Manchester.” 

Every single person I discussed that remark with in Manchester cringed. The city is fast losing the underdog status that characterised Burnham’s own brand of politics here and indeed the era that spawned the bands he so often references. That’s the trade-off. We are the new London.

“I love New Order and the Smiths, but every time he opens his mouth and says these things, he loses votes,” reflects one West Midlands business leader. “Someone needs to tell him that.”

Manchester and the North are not interchangeable, of course. Other northern places get at least as irritated by the Manc shtick as anywhere else, but at least they’re getting some political love. By contrast, businesses I’ve spoken to in the Midlands are beginning to get irritated.

Some of this narrative will be for the Midlands itself to fix. Bluntly, Manchester had to think its own way out of the doldrums — aided by receptive Conservative ministers — to get to here. Prolonged financial, political and bin-related chaos at Birmingham City Council hasn’t helped the wider region and neither does the reality of its location, trapped between what remains a largely London-authored public discourse and the north’s periodic noisy rejoinders. 

But there is so much existing activity and so much potential.

Almost a year ago I sat in the audience at the government’s regional investment summit in Edgbaston, already intending to write an article highlighting that this was the one place already benefiting from HS2. (The viaducts that will carry HS2’s trains into the city from the south-east are literally there, in the centre of the city, and investors know it’s coming.) Yet Reeves herself expressed surprise that, once complete, the journey from London to the Birmingham Interchange would take just 38 minutes. 

Birmingham City FC’s billionaire owner Tom Wagner, on stage with her, knew it full well. It would be easier for him to get to the West End for a night out than from his New York base to downtown Manhattan, he pointed out. How on earth, I wondered, could the finance minister holding the purse strings on this endlessly beleaguered project not at least have a sense of the ultimate end destination?

So national politics can and should think more carefully about those “flyover states” — not my own phrase, but that of a born-and-bred Midlander I have discussed this with — through which, for example, the HS2 line northwards would also once have run. More than one person has suggested to me that any revived version of a future line serving Manchester should, particularly if it is no longer prioritising speed, include Black Country and Staffordshire stops if it is to get political buy-in. We shall see.

In the meantime, the new prime minister is instinctively responsive, instinctively able to read the room. But he does have a blind spot. It isn’t the Midlands, so much as Manchester itself.

A fanboy-level of enthusiasm for the city works well as mayor, but he is now PM. Manchester is busy adjusting to this strange new experience of being on top. If Burnham’s narrative is to reach every postcode, then it will need to adjust too.

Now try this

After a very fun day at the FT Weekend Festival I had hoped that maybe a Sunday trip to the Bayeux Tapestry might be in order, before I realised it did not open for another four days and there are no more tickets to be bought until October 21 anyway. 

So I went to the National Portrait Gallery. For ages I’ve wanted to go to look at their Tudor paintings and wasn’t disappointed, although I remain puzzled by the fact that everyone in the 16th century apparently had such identically small mouths. 

Then again, I studied Thomas Wolsey’s machinations at A-level, not the painterly depictions of the period, and I think we can all agree it’s just as well I’m not the FT’s cultural critic.

Top stories today

  • ‘It’s simply common sense’ | Laila Cunningham, Reform UK’s candidate for mayor of London, said the previous Conservative government “should have borrowed and borrowed and borrowed” more money. Her stance appears to put her at odds with Nigel Farage, who has slammed the previous Conservative administration and the current government for failing to tackle the national debt.
  • In it for the long run | Alan Milburn, who is leading the government review of Neets, said it will not produce savings fast enough to avoid painful decisions on tax and spending as he prepares to recommend that mayors should get a share of long-term welfare savings if they boost youth employment.
  • Lindy hop to the top | Lindy Cameron, Britain’s high commissioner to India, will become the first female top civil servant at the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office.


  • Andy expected at Antigua event | Andy Burnham is under pressure to confirm he will attend the Commonwealth summit in November amid increasing Caribbean demands for slavery reparations. 


Letter in response:
The benefits of HS2: a sceptical northerner’s take / From Peter Hardwick, Manchester, UK

item.title: Oil is scary again
item.author: Hakyung Kim
item.description: Plus wage growth and inflation
item.content:encoded:
Plus wage growth and inflation

Hakyung Kim

Good morning. The European Central Bank raised rates to 2.5 per cent yesterday, moving its policy stance into restrictive territory. President Christine Lagarde said the bank believes “inflation will be longer-lasting than we anticipated”.

On the other side of the Atlantic, the pressure is on the Federal Reserve to follow. Oil prices rose to $109 per barrel in late trading on Thursday and the 10-year Treasury yield rose sharply again, hitting 4.95 per cent — a whisper away from a 19-year high. The futures market now prices in a 70 per cent chance the Fed moves rates higher next week, up from 50-50 a week ago. If this morning’s CPI inflation report comes in hot, it will look like a lock. Stocks, notably, are responding to all the excitement by continuing to do nothing whatsoever. The major indices have been going sideways for four months now. Tell us how long that can last: unhedged@ft.com.

Oil: yikes

The US-Iran “memorandum of understanding”, signed in June, was flaky from the get-go. So it is not surprising that the war is escalating again. Brent crude prices are back at $109 per barrel, right up against the peaks hit this spring:

Bring out the forecast revisions: Goldman Sachs has bumped up its forecasts for the end of the year by $5, to $85 for Brent and $80 for West Texas Intermediate Crude. That doesn’t sound like much and is well below the spot price, but a lot of these spikes get smoothed out in monthly averages; it’s a decent step higher, as you can see in the chart below. And the new estimate comes with a warning of “significant upside risk”.

It is also not a huge surprise to see that Treasury yields, particularly on the short end, have climbed since the new wave of attacks:

Oil markets have proven more adaptable than feared when the war began. Crude oil prices haven’t reached the levels — $150 or so, according to most analysts — where US growth starts to slow in earnest. But the market is on borrowed time. “Complacency would be the wrong lesson to take from the more modest price increases over the last several months,” says Jason Bordoff at Columbia University. Most of the buffers that have kept crude oil prices lower than expected — such as inventory drawdowns, low Chinese import levels, pipelines bypassing the Strait of Hormuz — are not perpetual.

Ship-to-ship transfers have also allowed quite a bit of oil to pass illicitly through the strait. Hamad Hussain at Capital Economics estimates this let as much as 12mn barrels a day slip by, as opposed to 20mn or so prewar. The latest round of fighting makes this harder. Bordoff says we’ve essentially run out of cushion for oil prices:

The only alternative to more supply coming out of inventories or floating Iranian oil is demand going down. And the only way to make demand go down is for prices to go up. And I think that’s where we’re headed for the remainder of this year, unless we get flows through the strait rising quickly and substantially.

Refinery capacity is also tight, driving up petrol, diesel and other consumer-facing prices. Crack spreads (the premium on refined products over crude) are rising to fresh highs. Chart below courtesy of Hussain :

Even if crude supplies and transit normalise, the war has resulted in much damage to refineries. The remaining functional ones, such as in the US, are already operating at maximum capacity. With critically low refined product inventories, there’s very little give in the system. For consumers, we expect higher petrol prices, just in time for the US midterm elections.

(Kim)

Wage growth and inflation

A Federal Reserve decision should never turn on a single data point. But Fed chair Kevin Warsh struck such a hawkish posture in his Jackson Hole speech that every economic report since is treated as a yea-or-nay referendum on tighter policy.

But Warsh, in that speech, said Fed watchers should ignore one particular data point: wage growth. Drawing on a large body of the US central bank’s research on the topic, he claimed “wage growth has not proven a reliable indicator of future inflation for a very long time”. Is he right?

He is, and there’s a relatively simple way to show it. We can plot the relationship between wage growth and changes in core inflation a year later:

If wage growth were a reliable indicator of future inflation, the crown of dots would form an upward slope — rising inflation following faster wage growth. But they don’t. In fact, since the early 1980s, periods of high wage growth have tended to be followed by lower core personal consumption expenditures inflation over the next year. That’s because wages are often catching up to a price shock, rather than prices resetting to capture higher wages.

This doesn’t prove wage growth is irrelevant. High wage growth is positively correlated with periods of high inflation. But by the time it shows up in the data, it is unlikely to be an indicator of underlying inflationary pressure.

(MacFadden)

One good read

A dying power.

item.title: The Big Read. Brics on the rise
item.author: Michael Stott and Andres Schipani and Joe Leahy and Michael Pooler
item.description: The grouping accounts for a bigger share of the world economy than the G7
item.content:encoded:
The grouping accounts for a bigger share of the world economy than the G7

Michael Stott and Andres Schipani and Joe Leahy and Michael Pooler

They represent nearly half the world’s population and will dominate the global economy this century. They include some of the planet’s most powerful leaders and its biggest militaries. They reject a US-dominated world and aspire to remake the international order.

This should be a moment for the Brics bloc of developing nations. Their economic heft is undeniable. The US has stepped back from global leadership and Europe is in decline. The multilateral order is in need of friends.

But 25 years after then Goldman Sachs economist Jim O’Neill coined the original acronym for the bloc comprising Brazil, Russia, India and China, internal divisions could yet prevent it coming of age.

Brics leaders will aim to present a united front when they meet for their annual summit in New Delhi this weekend. The bloc has expanded out of all recognition since the heads of government of the initial four countries first met in Russia in 2009.

Today Brics includes South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, the United Arab Emirates, Iran and Indonesia as full members, and another 10 “partner nations” as observers, several of whom will send presidents. (Saudi Arabia was invited to join and attends meetings but has not formalised accession).

Chinese President Xi Jinping will be in attendance for his first visit to India in almost seven years, state media confirmed, a gesture that signals a thaw in relations between the bloc’s two most populous nations after several frosty years.

Brics leaders will contemplate a global economic picture that they have done much to create over the past 25 years. The expanded bloc now accounts for around 40 per cent of the world’s economy at purchasing power parity.

Yet the build-up to the New Delhi summit has been low-key. Officials emphasise “people-centric” and “development-oriented” outcomes, rather than grand geopolitical aspirations. Talk about challenging the dominance of the US dollar, a pet topic of some Brics leaders, has been suppressed.

Host premier Narendra Modi and his top officials have said little about the event and only a smattering of Brics posters adorn the streets of the Indian capital, a sharp contrast to the lavish festivities surrounding New Delhi’s hosting of the G20 three years ago.

The modest approach partly reflects a desire to avoid provoking US President Donald Trump, officials say, but it also reflects tensions within the bloc, which has admitted members as diverse as Iran and Indonesia, and in particular a battle over who should lead it.

While western powers readily accepted US leadership in the post-1945 international order, some Brics members, notably India, resist submitting to a new world led by Beijing. Also in dispute is whether the 10 countries under the Brics banner can unite around common economic and diplomatic goals when geopolitical ambitions are discordant.

Sarang Shidore, who heads the global south programme at the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft in Washington, sums up the dual challenge facing Brics. “Suddenly the world is more opportune for them to create alternative institutions. But on the other hand, the diversity and heterogeneity and the squabbling we have seen of late internally means that they’re not ready to fully seize the moment.” 

Just after Brics leaders met in Rio de Janeiro last year, Trump tried to impose a price for membership of the bloc.

“They have to pay 10 per cent [tariff] if they’re in Brics because Brics was set up to hurt us,” he told reporters in Washington. “Brics was set up to degenerate our dollar and . . . take it off as the standard.”

As so often in his second term, Trump did not follow through. But his warning was a reminder of the growing clout of the grouping of nations, and its capacity to unsettle some in the west.

“This is the first time where you have the president of the United States making explicit threats [about the costs of Brics membership],” says Mihaela Papa, director of the Brics Lab research project at MIT’s Center for International Studies. “That gives you a sense that Brics . . . is actually perceived as a threat.”

It’s a far cry from when O’Neill dreamt up the original Bric moniker in 2001 while head of global economics at Goldman Sachs. “I never dreamt there was going to be any Brics political club,” he tells the FT. “My thing was based on each of them individually, just that they were very important economic powers.”

Over the past quarter century, the economic performance of individual Brics has diverged sharply. “China and India have vastly outperformed any of the projections we had in the early days, but the others [Russia and Brazil] have badly underperformed,” he says.

Nonetheless, the basic concept — that key emerging markets would grow faster than the west and dominate the 21st-century global economy — remains intact.

Goods trade between Brics nations has jumped more than 13-fold since 2003, according to UN data, with intra-Brics exports hitting $1.2tn in 2025.

Some of the causes long espoused by the Brics, such as seeking an alternative to a US-led world, defending multilateralism and open trade, are newly fashionable amid Trump’s disruptive diplomacy.

Matias Spektor, dean of international relations at the Fundação Getulio Vargas, a private university in São Paulo, argues that the Brics should not be judged on whether they act cohesively like the EU, because that was never their aim.

“The original objective of the Brics was to show that another world was possible outside the unipolarity of the United States and its selective use of international law,” he says. “That message is a message which is mainstream today, so in that sense the Brics have been a resounding success.”

Yet scepticism about the bloc persists, particularly in the west.

For Yun Sun at the Stimson Center, a Washington-based think-tank, “there is a perception” that groupings like Brics are “nothingburgers, right? That they don’t produce concrete collaboration mechanisms. But . . . if there’s no benefit provided to these member states, why do they want to join?”

Officials from Brics countries point to a range of concrete achievements. One is the creation of a lending institution intended as an embryonic rival to the World Bank, the Beijing-based New Development Bank. Since its founding in 2015, the NDB has approved $43bn in lending, according to bank figures from early 2026, versus almost $600bn globally from the World Bank.

Less visible is what officials describe as an extensive web of intergovernmental Brics collaboration. Diplomats say it now extends to 20 separate negotiating tracks, focused on co-operation in areas ranging from space technology to green energy. 

Among the latest initiatives: Moscow has suggested exploring a Brics digital platform for leading food exporters Russia, India and Brazil to trade grains and challenge the dominance of western commodity trading groups such as Cargill or Bunge.

Mauricio Lyrio, a Brazilian diplomat who acted as his country’s Brics “sherpa” — a senior official who lays the groundwork for meetings — highlights technical co-operation in areas like health.

“There have been important advances, such as Brics research centres for vaccines and socially determined diseases,” he says. China, Russia and India have combined on domestic tuberculosis vaccine research and development, for example.

For newer members such as Ethiopia, the main attraction of the bloc is economic. “The core objective of Brics has always been our development,” says Mamo Mihretu, Ethiopia’s former Brics sherpa and central bank governor. “We want secure and predictable access to markets in trade, finance and investment and a genuine voice in global institutions.”

On the economic co-operation agenda, Brics nations are looking at ways of linking up digital instant-payment systems, such as Brazil’s widely used Pix or India’s pioneering UPI, which would allow them to bypass the dollar-based international payments system.

“Practically every country in the world outside the US . . . would like to disentangle itself from the dollar-dominated financial system and would like to see a world in which the dollar is less dominant as a payment currency and as a reserve currency,” notes Eswar Prasad, a trade professor at Cornell University.

Although China, Russia and Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva have a long-held ambition of reducing dependency on the greenback, senior Indian representatives made it clear that there is “no de-dollarisation agenda” at this year’s summit, partly because, at least from New Delhi’s perspective, “we have to be sensitive” to Trump.

Despite the bloc’s progress, Brics nations are wrestling with growing geopolitical tensions that have accentuated their differences.

The most fundamental is over the role of China — whether it is a mere participant or de facto leader.

Like the G7, the Brics has no permanent secretariat and its chair rotates annually. Decisions must ostensibly be reached by consensus but in reality, Beijing’s status as the group’s sole superpower gives it huge weight.

For Xi, multilateral organisations such as the Brics are a critical platform for his ambitions to create an alternative global order that is more amenable to the Communist Party than the US-led model.

Through programmes such as China’s Global Development Initiative, which it espouses at forums such as the Brics, Beijing sells the idea that Chinese-style development and poverty reduction contribute more to human rights than universal suffrage and western rule of law.

Yu Jie, senior research fellow for China at Chatham House, says China’s aspirations are now becoming reality. “China has become a world order shaper,” she says. “What Beijing says is not just diplomatic rhetoric, but also it has begun to tentatively fill that space.”

Brazil and India, on the other hand, resist Chinese domination. “For the Indian government in particular, the sense that the Brics agenda sometimes turns into China’s agenda is a worrying prospect,” says Prasad.

Brasília and New Delhi want to position Brics as an alternative to the western-led world order, but not as anti-western — a position supported by the UAE. China, however, “wants to turn this into an anti-western forum,” says Amitabh Kant, India’s former G20 sherpa, speaking in a personal capacity. “India should ensure that the grouping does not become an anti-western grouping.”

Relations between China and India, which have periodically clashed over their contested border, became hostile again in 2020, when at least 20 Indian soldiers and an unknown number of Chinese troops were killed in clashes in the Himalayas. Economic rivalry adds another complication. Beijing is wary of India becoming an alternative for export manufacturing to compete with China, such as by wooing Apple to assemble iPhones or by producing semiconductors. 

“India is cautiously re-engaging with China out of pragmatism, but deep mistrust persists,” explains Manoj Kewalramani, a China expert at Takshashila Institution, a research centre in Bengaluru. “Beijing today views itself as a great power, and India as an inferior regional power,” he adds.

Russia adds further complication because its invasion of Ukraine has made it a pariah in the west. Its Brics partners are engaging with a country under heavy sanctions by Europe and the US.

Yaroslav Lissovolik of Brics+ Analytics, a private consultancy in Moscow, estimates that just over half of Russia’s foreign trade is now conducted with core Brics partners, twice as big a share as before the Ukraine war. “The global south is becoming the key partner in the global economy for Russia,” he says. “It’s a significant shift in terms of economic alliances.”

As the economic heft of the Brics has grown, so has the appetite of some of its members to wield greater military power. China, Russia and India are among the world’s top five defence spenders, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (Sipri).

This has led to tensions over whether the Brics should remain focused on economic development and trade, as India and Brazil prefer, or pursue more explicit security goals, as favoured by China.

A naval exercise this year off the coast of South Africa, championed by China’s ministry of defence under the label of “Brics Plus” and given the name “Will for Peace”, created acrimony after Brazil and India declined to send ships and host President Cyril Ramaphosa unsuccessfully tried to stop Iran from participating.

Beijing’s state media touted its goal as ensuring “the safety of relevant maritime trade routes” among the Brics — a reference to China’s preoccupation with keeping shipping lanes open in the event of a conflict with the US over Taiwan. 

The big Brics expansion of 2023-24 — opposed by Brazil and India but pushed through by China — proved especially problematic this year because new members Iran and the UAE are on opposing sides in the US-led war.

A Brics foreign ministers meeting earlier this year in India struggled to reach consensus as tempers flared between UAE and Iranian representatives.

Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi told reporters at the time, without naming Abu Dhabi, that the final statement was “blocked” by a “member state” with a “special relationship with Israel”. The UAE representative, minister of state Khalifa bin Shaheen Al Marar, later accused Araghchi of “attempts to justify Iranian terrorist attacks” against the UAE.

Nonetheless, the UAE’s foreign ministry says it views Brics as “a platform for dialogue and practical co-operation”.

Seyed Emamian, co-founder of the Governance and Policy Think-Tank in Tehran, says what binds the members is more important than what separates them: “Everyone is looking for an alternative to US unilateralism. So Iran is looking for powerful alternative collaborative frameworks, like Brics.”

Some say Brics ought to stick to areas where they are already aligned, rather than trying to find common political ground. A senior Brazilian diplomat describes the Brics as “completely good news” on economy, science and technology, and international co-operation, but cautions: “The idea of the Brics as a political grouping is very artificial.”

But as the group looks at the next 25 years, it will face an intensifying gravitational pull from China.

“The Chinese view . . . is that the wind is blowing in our direction right now on the Brics, in large part because the west is making a hash of it,” says Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, south Asia head at the consultancy Eurasia Group. “India is putting up at best a valiant rearguard action but will struggle.”

Chatham’s Yu says: “Not only does China want to have a decisive vote in the game, but it also wants to design how the game is now played.”

Additional reporting by Nicolas Parasie in Dubai. Data visualisation by Keith Fray and Haohsiang Ko

item.title: The FT View. Burnham’s devolution project needs strong local media too
item.author: The editorial board
item.description: Regional leaders have to be held accountable to their voters
item.content:encoded:
Regional leaders have to be held accountable to their voters

The editorial board

When Britain’s ousted prime minister Sir Keir Starmer decided last week to stand down as an MP, he gave the scoop to the local newspaper, the Camden New Journal. It recalled an era when local papers were central to their communities. As Starmer’s successor Andy Burnham plans to devolve some powers and tax revenues from Westminster to England’s regional mayors, something is missing from his vision: a robust local media sector that can hold local officials to account for their decisions and spending.

Burnham wants to turn back the clock on the centralisation of power since the Thatcher era. Back in the 1980s, though, an estimated 1,600-plus local daily and weekly newspapers in the UK supported tens of thousands of journalists. Local reporters made it their business to track local movers and shakers, sit through council committees, follow court cases and monitor services.

But the digital revolution hit regional media especially hard. Local paper circulations dipped and print advertising that supplied much of their revenues plunged by more than two-thirds between 2007 and 2017 as ads migrated online. Readers turned to Facebook and WhatsApp groups for local news.

Regional newspapers consolidated and slashed costs and newsrooms. Press Gazette, a trade publication, found that the three publishers dominating UK local print and online news by 2022 employed only about 3,000 journalists, down from 9,000 in 2007. By 2025, according to the Public Interest News Foundation, one in 10 UK local authority districts, covering 4.4mn people, were “news deserts”, with no dedicated local outlet.

The licence fee-funded BBC still operates 39 local radio stations in England plus regional TV and online services, and after standards were previously loosened, from 2027 local commercial radio stations will have to carry a mandatory amount of local news.

Some successful new online outlets and reporting projects have also sprung up, especially in cities, though they often struggle financially. A core of local journalism survives. But the broad decline of local media matters for Burnham’s project. The point of devolution is to make local decision makers both more responsive and more accountable to their voters. Authorities including Nottingham, Liverpool and Tees Valley have experienced financial or governance issues in recent years that more robust local scrutiny might have identified earlier.

Journalists can in turn help local leaders by alerting them to issues ranging from potholes to problems in care homes. A government study found that during urban riots in summer 2024, trusted local journalists — where they existed — helped to counter online misinformation and to de-escalate tensions by amplifying community leaders’ and police voices. Research has also found a link between strong local media outlets and local election turnout.

The old local press cannot be recreated and building more viable local media ecosystems will be a long process. Alternative funding is hard to find. Several of the big US tech companies, which absorbed so much local advertising, fund local reporting initiatives through grants or philanthropic programmes, but their aims and approaches vary widely. Other forms of philanthropy could play a role, though wealthy donors would need convincing of the merits. A BBC scheme funds 165 journalists to do public-interest reporting at local news organisations, but the BBC’s own funding is severely squeezed.

The Starmer government launched a local media action plan earlier this year including £12mn of grant funding over two years. But Burnham wants to go much further with his version of devolution. If he is committed to regenerating local governments and communities, reviving local media has to be part of his strategy too.

item.title: The capital wars are coming
item.author: Martin Sandbu
item.description: Expect more intense competition for the world’s savings
item.content:encoded:
Expect more intense competition for the world’s savings

Martin Sandbu

In perfectly normal, move-along-nothing-to-see-here news, President Donald Trump has referenced military intervention in a discussion about managing bond markets, and the Dutch central bank is moving its gold out of the US, just in case of “geopolitical unrest”. Oh, and US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent tells foreign exchange traders that “I am the house now”. Are we at the phoney war stage of some global financial conflict?

As my colleague Katie Martin recently wrote, the view that we are heading for an era of financial repression (where governments regulate financial markets to ensure low borrowing rates for themselves) is increasingly becoming mainstream. I am neither shocked nor surprised, since I warned about this more than a year ago. But I think the discussion is still too focused on the national, domestic dimension of this and not enough on the international aspects.

In an analyst note from Landfall Strategy Group, David Skilling writes:

. . . to a greater extent than domestic financial repression, the likely preference will be to undertake international financial repression by coercing foreign investment into long-dated Treasuries . . . [T]he US will try to fight and win capital wars to secure foreign financing of US borrowing by leveraging US geopolitical, technological and financial advantages.

I think this is right, and “capital wars” is a good term. It echoes “trade wars”, and is built on the same belief in zero-sum relationships in capital flows as trade warriors see in trade flows.

As my slightly glib news references at the top were meant to suggest, this may already have been bubbling away under the surface for some time. Skilling includes the below chart of the share of US Treasuries held by foreign investors: it has been on a downward path since the 2008 financial crisis.

And the need to finance a stubbornly high US government deficit, as well as similar needs elsewhere, is raising more and more concern both with investors and with the officials who need to secure borrowing at reasonable cost. (Related to that, also read Katie’s thoughtful take on the Norwegian sovereign wealth fund’s intention to reweight its bond investments from sovereign to mortgage-backed and corporate bonds.)

Skilling references the “Mar-a-Lago accord” ideas of Stephen Miran, a Trump economic adviser who served a limited period on the Federal Reserve’s board; the use of trade conflict as leverage to extract investment promises from, most notably, Japan and South Korea; and the politicisation of dollar swap lines. These are all indeed signs of a desire to politically steer cross-border capital flows.

I would add to this the stablecoin agenda. The Trump administration is determined for the US to lead this phase of financial innovation. There are several motives for that, but an important one is, no doubt, to trap a source of captive demand for US Treasuries as the reserves backing dollar-denominated stablecoins. (The cross-border dollar-based payment system, too, has long since been weaponised.)

So there is every reason to think that we are heading into capital wars which could make the last year and a half of trade wars look like child’s play. If so, what do you need to know to prepare yourself?

First, it’s going to mightily complicate economic diplomacy by and with the US. Not just because the US is likely to be one of the most aggressive capital war belligerents (but that too). It’s also that the US presents a unique contradiction in its policy objectives as well as in the demands it makes of others. On the trade war side, it wants to get rid of its trade deficit. On the capital war side, it wants to maintain (and who knows, maybe increase?) its capital account deficit — that is what it means to have foreigners invest more capital in your economy than you invest in theirs. But, of course, the difference between what you produce and what you consume simultaneously determines both your net exports and your net savings.

Second, even so, it is not all about the US. Others, too, are looking hard at the flows of capital in and out of their economies. The EU sends large savings surpluses out of the bloc even as it needs to raise investment at home, something pointed out by both Enrico Letta and Mario Draghi in their influential reports on the EU’s single market and productivity. Political leaders now consistently echo this point. Japan’s government is pressing pension funds and households to invest more at home. China, so far, has been defensive about its structural surplus in the face of loud criticism from others. But as I and many others have argued, it too could benefit from rebalancing its external account so that it could raise either consumption or investment at home.

If history is any guide, it is the surplus economies that have the upper hand once capital wars get hot. When it comes down to it, you have more room for action if you have capital to spare than if you want others to lend you theirs. A corollary is that any deficit country that is not the US should realise how vulnerable it is and try to become less so (Britain, I am talking to you).

A third thought: this is not all or even mostly about government debt. In the US, the enormous amounts being invested in data centres and AI development are facilitated by the large imports of capital. In every other advanced economy, governments’ policy objectives are not just to fund their budgets but to increase private investment in similar sectors, as well as climate change, energy and defence-related activity. A big question, therefore, is what will happen to US private investment if Washington succeeds in strong-arming global investors into funding the US government more cheaply than they would like. It could very well crowd out other US-destined capital flows (ie to private investments). If so, it will be hard to prevent.

What is going to transpire when the phoney capital wars become serious? Skilling offers three scenarios. The US might get its way and impose a global “tribute system”. For the reasons set out in the previous paragraph, I think this will be harder to achieve than it might seem. Or the capital wars may rupture traditional western alliances. Finally, they could lead to outright global fragmentation, a financial de-globalisation.

None of these, unfortunately, feels like a remotely attractive future.

Other readables

● After the results of Iceland’s referendum, I argue that the EU must articulate a clearer vision for how it sees long-term relations with the prosperous, like-minded, but non-member neighbours to its north.

● School students’ performance has plunged across the OECD. The policy research organisation suggests passive technology consumption is to blame.

● The BBC’s Steve Rosenberg notes how the Russian press is increasingly reporting about serious economic problems inside the country.

● How will Ukraine’s innovative but contested military doctrine evolve after the dismissal of the country’s top commander and defence minister?

● Seafaring nations warn that maritime trade is threatened by a breakdown in global shipping rules.

item.title: Doubts about Reform and Labour benefit Kemi Badenoch
item.author: Stephen Bush
item.description: Nigel Farage’s party is losing credibility as a viable option for voters, to the advantage of the Tories
item.content:encoded:
Nigel Farage’s party is losing credibility as a viable option for voters, to the advantage of the Tories

Stephen Bush

Good morning. Today’s newsletter is on two things that are together greatly to the advantage of Kemi Badenoch: Reform UK and Labour, which are both, in different ways, having difficulties with the law.

The anti-Labour, anti-Reform alternative

The Metropolitan Police has expanded its investigation into Reform’s financial affairs after a Channel 4 undercover sting alleged that senior party figures had sought illegal funding from overseas.

This matters in its own terms, and also politically because it adds to the swirl of stories around that party that make it look sleazy in the eyes of most voters.

This is one of the biggest problems for Nigel Farage and Reform. It is also one of the Conservative Party’s biggest assets. Yes, it’s true that thus far, the Conservatives’ poll position remains dire and their electoral position in actual contests is worse, for the most part.

But when people vote, they are largely making a judgment call not just on “how they feel about a political party” but “do they feel that party is viable”, and I just don’t think that Reform, which most voters think is sleazy and scary, is going to pass that viability check. Some Reform voters will stay the course. Others will move further to the right with Restore. But if the government gets into real trouble, the party best placed to benefit and become the “get rid of Labour” option is the Conservative Party, for want of anything better.

And Labour may well get into trouble. After the police were caught flat-footed by masked vigilantes over the weekend, a group of masked men with the same ringleader — Daniel Thomas, the far-right activist who claimed credit for Saturday’s events — stood outside the west London offices of the Mail newspaper, to register their objection to its coverage.

As of this year, it is illegal to use a mask to hide your identity at a protest. It has been illegal for a lot longer than that to blockade critical infrastructure — like a port, say — and it is corrosive to the foundations of liberal democracy to turn up in masks outside a newspaper’s HQ because of a legitimate story you don’t like.

Tackling this stuff is the bare minimum of what we should expect of any government. An administration that appears incapable of arresting the ringleaders or the attendees of such a protest is one that is visibly failing to do the basics of being a government. It feeds into a general narrative of malaise — that whether it is bike theft or responding to tricky geopolitical issues, Labour cannot govern. Taken together with Reform’s difficulties, it is a gift for the Conservatives — if Kemi Badenoch can seize it.

Now try this

My mother came to stay yesterday evening, so I cooked dinner from Sabrina Ghayour’s marvellous book Persiana, with some potatoes from Claudia Roden’s Med, which is also terrific. Neither will be as good as the food at Noble Rot, which is kindly auctioning off a lunch with me for the FT’s financial literacy charity Flic. I am currently the cheapest lunch, which is severely testing my faith in the power of free markets. The full roster is here.

Top stories today

  • ‘Constraint on belonging’ | The UK charges three times as much as any other G7 country for citizenship, shutting many long-term residents out of full participation in civic life, according to new research. 
  • TUC talk | Paul Nowak, head of the Trades Union Congress, told the FT that Andy Burnham should raise taxes on wealth to fund cuts to household energy bills, arguing there was “no evidence” that this would drive rich investors to leave the UK. Separately, in his interview with the Guardian, he urged Burnham to overhaul Shabana Mahmood’s migration reforms that would impose tougher settlement rules. “I think it is fundamentally unfair to change the rules when people came to this country with one set of expectations,” Nowak said.


  • RNLI volunteers targeted | A police investigation has been launched after two Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) volunteers were branded “traitors” online and had their photos, full names and home addresses leaked in the wake of anti-migrant protests in Portsmouth on Sunday night, the Independent reports.
  • Row with hospitality over tourist levy | Council leaders and mayors in England will receive new powers to impose unlimited taxes on tourists for overnight stays. Allen Simpson, chief executive of UK Hospitality, suggested the levy would add over £100 to the cost of an average family holiday in England.

item.title: Must high bond yields crack stocks?
item.author: Robert Armstrong
item.description: It’s mood first, then maths
item.content:encoded:
It’s mood first, then maths

Robert Armstrong

Good morning. Oil passed $100 yesterday, for the first time since July. Perhaps as a result, a $6bn Treasury buyback announcement from Scott “I am the house now” Bessent was not enough to keep Treasury yields from rising. Perhaps Bessent, the US Treasury secretary, is only “the house” in Japan, where the yen has risen since the US and Japan intervened in that market? Does this make him more of a vacation house? Or perhaps an Airbnb? Send your thoughts: unhedged@ft.com.

Yields up, stocks down?

The 10-year Treasury yield, at 4.85 per cent, is now just a few basis points from its 2023 highs and the symbolically important 5 per cent level. This has the punditocracy asking, when do yields crack the stock market? Here is Michel Lerner of the UBS Holt team:

History suggests bond vigilante episodes rarely remain contained given the challenges of curbing deficits without weakening growth or fuelling inflation. Among highly indebted economies, US equities appear particularly vulnerable to a spillover.

And here is Ruchir Sharma in the FT this week:

Going back 300 years, every major bubble ended only when borrowing costs rose significantly for the companies at its core . . . the marker to watch is the yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds . . . When it decisively breaches 5 per cent, the upper end of its range since the dotcom period, the AI bubble could pop.

On to Freya Beamish and Davide Oneglia of TS Lombard:

While we don’t think there is any magic number that tips over equities, we stand by our long-held view that macro fundamentals suggest the US 10-year should be at least 5% to compensate for this environment . . . term premium in the US still looks too low to compensate for the loss of hedging capacity for equities . . . eventually these things have to come back into line and compression of US equity premium does not look sustainable.

I share the feeling that something is wrong about the combination of high yields and high stock prices. But what is the causal mechanism by which high yields force stocks down? I can think of four possibilities:

  • High rates slow the economy by raising the cost of financing for cyclical business sectors, profits fall and stock prices follow.
  • High rates — a higher discount rate — reduce the present value of companies’ future cash flows, making stocks less valuable.
  • High rates pull capital flows away from stocks by offering more attractive prospective returns.
  • High rates force governments to cut deficits, and the reduced deficit spending is balanced — as it often has been historically — by lower corporate profits.

Consider each in turn.

On #1, the traditional view is that the crucial sector is housing. Higher rates make mortgages more expensive, fewer houses get bought and all the activity that goes into residential investment — construction, renovation, transport, furnishings and so on — slows. This activity is the key “swing factor” for the economy. Or as Edward Leamer put it 20 years ago, “Housing is the business cycle.”

But the housing market is already bad! More precisely, it is frozen, with moderate new home sales, existing home sales at historically low levels, and residential investment low and falling as a share of GDP:

Why is the economy humming along when housing is persistently weak? Ajay Rajadhyaksha of Barclays says data centre construction has taken up the slack:

US data centre construction spending has reached $85bn in 2026, up from $45bn just two years earlier. By our estimate, 74 new facilities have broken ground this year across 28 states . . . When a hyperscaler builds a data centre complex a quarter the size of downtown Manhattan — and several are doing exactly that — it hires roofers, electricians, plumbers, steel workers, concrete crews and general contractors . . . This is why the traditional rate transmission mechanism has not worked.

And hyperscaler spending has not been rate sensitive, or indeed sensitive to anything at all. The Big Techs see themselves as fighting for survival, so no price is too high. But data centre spending isn’t perpetual, Rajadhyaksha points out: after they are built, data centres are not big employers. If and when we have built enough compute capacity, old cyclical forces will be relevant again.

It is not clear to me that investors in data centres will remain rate insensitive forever, however. At some point, returns on the trillions of dollars in AI investment will become salient to decisions about further investment. At that point, discount rates will matter, possibly a lot. One might argue that it is already happening to the financially and/or technologically weaker AI players such as Oracle, for whom the question of returns on investment are already pressing.

On #2, the net present value maths works, but reality does not always co-operate. In 2021-2022, when rates rose with inflation, equity valuations duly fell — but rates stayed high and valuations bounced right back:

Part of the rebound is due to profit growth, which is the other component in net present value calculations. Still, we are not talking about an “automatic” process, where higher rates force valuations down if growth is constant. Animal spirits are involved. Human beings have to decide, en masse, that stocks are just too expensive given the opportunity costs. Moods before maths.

Putting it that way shows how mechanisms #2 and #3 are closely related. The old “Fed model” said that when the forward earnings yield on the S&P 500 (currently about 4.6 per cent) was below the 10-year Treasury yield (4.85), stocks are too expensive — the intuition being you should get a higher yield on stocks, which are riskier than bonds. How big the gap should be is disputed, of course. In a moment when inflation uncertainty looms large, you’d think everyone would demand more return from bonds (but it is worth noting that inflation-adjusted Treasury yields are near long-term highs, too). Again, animal spirits are a factor: investors have to care about relative valuations for the numbers to matter, and a lot of the time they just don’t.

If flows into US investment funds are any indication, we are not seeing signs of a reallocation towards bonds and out of stocks. Equity flows spiked this summer, and have come down recently. But bond flows are softening too.

Of course, the mechanism may take time. As bond prices fall and investors with fixed allocations rebalance, there could be a drip-drip move away from equities, at least until stocks fall too.

As for #4, I am confident that significant government austerity would crack the stock market. The federal deficit in this fiscal year will be about $2tn. To scale that, total US after-tax corporate profit is $4.3tn. If the borrowed government money were to stop flowing, the shock to the economy and stocks would be huge.

But I don’t think austerity is going to happen any time soon. My guess is that rates will have to go quite a bit higher to change the federal government’s habits. So I’m more concerned about the first three mechanisms, but as I have indicated, “mechanism” may be the wrong word. The emotions of data centre investors and equity portfolio managers will be decisive, and emotions follow no law.

One good read

Look how they massacred my deli.

item.title: The Big Read. Milei’s great free trade experiment
item.author: Geoff Dyer and Ciara Nugent
item.description: First came budget cuts. Now the president is embracing foreign competition — ahead of his re-election bid
item.content:encoded:
First came budget cuts. Now the president is embracing foreign competition — ahead of his re-election bid

Geoff Dyer and Ciara Nugent

Standing outside a giant tyre factory on the outskirts of Buenos Aires that shut down in February after 86 years, trade union leader Alejandro Crespo warns that this is the end of an era for Argentina.

“We have an epidemic of factory closures,” says Crespo, blaming surging imports. “This is a government which is not at all interested in factories.”

Javier Milei, the political outsider elected as Argentina’s president in 2023, agrees that it is the end of an era — but he sees it as something to be welcomed. For the man who named his four dogs after libertarian economists, the closure of the factory, run by a company called Fate, is part of the transformation of the country’s economic model that he is trying to orchestrate.

Rather than propping up inefficient manufacturing companies, Milei wants to spark a boom in the export sectors where he believes Argentina can compete globally, including energy and mining.

“We think it is a good thing that the factory closed,” says Federico Sturzenegger, the minister for deregulation and one of the architects of the plan to liberalise the economy. “This is a company that for 40 years exerted political pressure in order to keep the tyres that we use three times more expensive than the world price.”

For many, the idle factory is a symbol of the rapid opening up being pushed by Milei, whose firm belief in free markets sets him apart from US President Donald Trump and the other rightwing populist leaders with whom he is often bracketed.

Influenced by his admiration for Margaret Thatcher and Milton Friedman, his plan for Argentina resembles the neoliberalism that swept across Latin America in the 1990s — and which is now vocally repudiated by other populists.

The first part was to subdue runaway inflation through dramatic budget cuts, symbolised by Milei waving around a chainsaw — a stunt later copied by Elon Musk when he was looking to slash US public spending last year. The inflation rate has duly fallen from 289 per cent in early 2024 to 34 per cent.

The second phase entails exposing Argentina to a sharp burst of foreign competition, which is creating winners and losers across the economy just a year ahead of Milei’s bid for re-election. Many of the losers are concentrated in the populous area around the capital.

For much of the last century, Argentina sought to build its own domestic market behind a wall of tariffs and subsidies — a project spearheaded by Juan Perón, the former military officer turned populist pioneer who first came to power in 1946.

Instead of selling beef to the rest of the world, Perón prioritised making tyres and other goods for Argentines, creating a new elite of homegrown industrialists and an urban working class led by government-aligned trade unions. Founded in 1940, the Fate factory was closely connected to that project: José Ber Gelbard, one of the company’s main shareholders in the 1960s and 1970s, served as Perón’s last economics minister.

Milei wants to dismantle the web of Peronist corporatism rather than promoting its national champions. In the process, he is also trying to redraw the economic map of Argentina.

Perón’s model was focused on Greater Buenos Aires, which has a population of about 17mn. But the sectors Milei champions are in some cases more than 1,000 miles away — mining in the far north, or oil and gas production to the south in Patagonia. The government talks about millions of workers moving out from Buenos Aires to outlying provinces in the coming decades.

“Argentina was one of the most closed economies in the world,” he said in a recent speech in which he used Joseph Schumpeter’s famous term “creative destruction” three times. “In the 100 years before we came to power, Argentina was a declining country.” For Milei, the domestic-led model was the root cause of decades of economic instability and a source of massive corruption.

However, his bet on free trade is starting to face significant economic and political opposition. Last week’s nationalistic speech on the Falkland Islands, a popular rallying cry in Argentina, is partly a reflection of how he is on the defensive politically.

Complaints from manufacturers, which have been shedding jobs in the face of surging imports, are growing louder. Some claim the currency is overvalued in order to curb inflation; others say Chinese producers are using Argentina as a dumping ground for their surplus output.

With real incomes being squeezed in part by government austerity, public opinion has also started to turn against the government, creating a potential opening for a challenger to Milei.

In common with other liberalisation drives over the last eight decades, Milei’s project is running into the economic and political heft of Buenos Aires, where almost 40 per cent of Argentine voters live.

“There are no other jobs at the moment,” says Rodrigo Ambrosio, 56, who worked in the Fate tyre factory for 23 years. He is surviving through occasional painting jobs and driving for Uber. “Oil? Mining? They don’t create many jobs.”

But Milei is digging in. He claims that much of the criticism comes from either his Peronist opponents or vested interests that expect the state to keep bailing them out.

As he bluntly put it last month: “The son-of-a-bitch crony capitalists need to go bankrupt.”

From beef to oil

Until the 1930s and the Depression, Argentina was primarily an agricultural exporter, famous for its frozen beef.

Under Milei’s plan for a new export-led model, agriculture is still important — in addition to cattle, the country is one of the world’s biggest producers of soyabeans. But two other export sectors are also now beginning to boom: oil and gas and mining.

In April, Congress passed a law that could provide a major impetus to the mining sector by reducing what the government says were excessive restrictions on projects near the country’s many glaciers.

Environmental groups say the new law could endanger the water supply to a number of cities. However, local politicians and mining executives say it lays the groundwork for a wave of new investment.

“Argentina has a lot of the resources that the world needs at the moment,” says Carlos Sadir, governor of Jujuy, a province high in the Andes on the border with Bolivia that has rich deposits of copper, silver and lithium.

Martín Pérez de Solay, head of the mining conglomerate Glencore in Argentina, says the country has seven mining projects under way that are “world-class” and believes the country could bring on new annual supply of 1.5mn-2mn tonnes of copper over the next decade — about a third of the output of neighbouring Chile, which is the world’s largest producer.

The boom in oil and gas is already under way. The US government estimates that Argentina has the second-largest reserves of shale gas in the world, most of it in the Vaca Muerta formation in the Neuquén Basin in the south of the country.

Investment is accelerating sharply, partly as a result of a new legal framework introduced in 2024 that provides tax breaks and other incentives. Wood Mackenzie, the energy consultancy, estimates that the pipeline of new projects now exceeds $100bn. “Argentina is on the cusp of a shale revolution,” it says, comparing the atmosphere to west Texas in the early 2010s, at the start of the US shale boom.

Exports in mining, energy and agriculture have already increased to record levels under Milei, beginning to ease the dollar shortage that has underpinned Argentina’s chronic economic instability.

Sturzenegger says that the cumulative impact of recent investments will allow Argentina to triple its exports in the next five to six years. “For the first time in my professional life I see Argentina starting a growth process that is export-led,” he says.

Back to the provinces

The excitement among resources companies, however, is mirrored by rising pessimism among the domestic-facing industries that employ millions of Argentines.

Manufacturing, construction and retail have all contracted or stalled under Milei even though economists surveyed by the central bank predict the economy will grow 2.1 per cent in 2026.

According to government figures, about 3,400 manufacturing businesses have closed since late 2023 — more than 10 per cent of the total. In the formal labour market, over 240,000 jobs have been lost, a fall of nearly 4 per cent, although this drop has partly been offset by growth in the informal labour market where employees have minimal protections.

Textiles have been one of the hardest-hit industries, as Milei’s tariff cuts open Argentina to a flood of cheaper foreign clothing, including via Chinese ecommerce sites such as Shein and Temu.

Will Der, which used to make clothes for brands such as Adidas and Puma, closed its two factories in August. The company had been so desperate for new customers that it offered to make overalls for the new mining companies.

“The orders just disappeared,” Santiago Phelan, a former captain of the Argentina rugby team who was president of the company, told local media.

The owner of a large textiles business in Buenos Aires says the government has set companies like his up to fail by opening them to competition from imports without dismantling the high taxes and cost structures put in place under the protectionist Peronist model.

“My factories are competitive, it is the taxes that are killing us,” says the executive, who did not want to be named for fear of attracting the wrath of Milei, who has clashed with a number of business owners. He has cut his staff by half over the past year, he adds. “We’re just hoping Milei’s government ends before we die off completely.”
