Martín Rappallini, head of the Argentina Industrial Union, says that Argentine companies face an annual tax take equivalent to 56 per cent of the formal economy, the highest burden in Latin America. A surge in contraband and dumping by other countries and limited access to finance are adding to their problems.

He is urging the government to construct a “bridge” that will allow manufacturers to survive the transition to the new free-trade model. “We want Argentina to have a more normal, open economy and we are not asking for protection, but we have been left carrying all the stones from the past,” he says.

Many industrialists argue that the government is still in the game of picking winners but this time favouring industries such as energy and mining. “It is not economic liberalism for a government official to decide — ‘no, this sector is not going to work, but this other one will’,” says Rappallini. “Give us the conditions to compete on equal terms and then the market will decide who survives and who does not.”

The government sees many of these complaints as special pleading. Milei is particularly dismissive: “You have to be very stupid to say that investment is taking place in sectors that do not generate jobs,” he says, because money earned by workers in Vaca Muerta will be spent in the wider economy.

Sturzenegger says that access to cheap energy from shale oil and gas will lead to a new “industrial boom”, which could include sectors such as fertilisers and petrochemicals. “Just as the US reindustrialised as a result of the Permian Basin in Texas, there is no reason not to think that something similar will happen here,” he says.

In the long run, he estimates that about 4mn people will leave the Buenos Aires area over the next 30 years — with 2mn decamping to the oil and gas region in Patagonia and another 2mn heading for the mining region in the north.

“In the second half of the 20th century, there was a big migration from the interior to Greater Buenos Aires at a time when Argentina was one of the most closed economies in the world,” he says.

“This process is exactly the opposite; it opens up the economy and generates competitiveness from exports and the population gradually reverts to the interior.”

‘Worst is still to come’

To secure such a long-term agenda, Milei needs to win re-election in October 2027. His big advantage is that the Peronist opposition remains in disarray and there is no obvious challenger to take him on.

But political analysts are picking up alarming signs of pessimism among many voters. According to a recent poll by Trespuntozero, 77 per cent of voters believe the country is still in an “economic crisis”. Even worse for the government, 84 per cent believe “the worst is still to come”.

“The mood among voters today is in favour of a change of government,” says Shila Vilker, director of Trespuntozero. “The government can shift that sentiment, but they need to do something and they need to hurry.”

Real wages have failed to fully recover from a sharp drop in 2023, when inflation surged into the triple digits. Disposable incomes have fared even worse as Milei has scrapped subsidies for energy, water and transport, falling 17 per cent in real terms since early 2023, according to think-tank Equilibra.

Milei, determined to protect his flagship progress on inflation, has ruled out any fiscal measures to boost the economy ahead of next year’s election, saying in August that “populism isn’t defeated through populism”.

Some analysts believe Milei’s confrontational style, which worked so well for him as an insurgent challenger, could become a liability as people start to blame the government for hardship. At an event in August he mocked his critics, putting on a taunting voice to repeat the often-used phrase “people can’t make ends meet”, which he called “stupidity”.

The impasse between Milei’s vision for Argentina and the stubborn reality of the economy today is on full display at the Fate tyre factory, where some of the 920 workers who lost their jobs have maintained a constant vigil since it closed in February.

Their aim is to keep the possibility of a reopening alive, since the union believes the factory has been profitable and only closed as part of a wider dispute between the government and Fate’s owner.

Crespo, the union’s leader, doubts that Milei’s plan can replace the jobs being lost. “Industrialisation should generate lots of skilled, manual jobs with respectable salaries . . . what Milei is suggesting is not sustainable,” he says.

Even Milei himself sees the trade-off. Speaking about the factory, he said: “If you look at it in utilitarian terms, I have 47mn Argentines who are benefiting and I have 920 who are losing out.” But he also acknowledged that this was not necessarily “fair” on those workers.

One of them is Carlos Romero, a 59-year-old who spent 30 years working at the factory and now helps maintain the vigil there. He says he and others have nowhere else to go.

“Are we really expected to migrate with the whole family, to move 800km or more,” he asks, “to look for work somewhere where there might not be any jobs?”

item.title: The FT View. The lessons of LIV Golf’s failure
item.author: The editorial board
item.description: Saudi Arabia has found it is easier to buy into existing sports franchises than to create a new one
item.content:encoded:
Saudi Arabia has found it is easier to buy into existing sports franchises than to create a new one

The editorial board

Four years ago, LIV Golf promised “golf, but louder”. Protracted 72-hole tournaments would be swapped for higher-octane 54-hole team events with shotgun starts — simultaneous tee-offs at different holes — blaring music and huge payouts for players. Backed by $5bn-plus of investment from Saudi Arabia, it was an attempt to disrupt the sedate world of golf and build soft power for Riyadh. After the Saudi Public Investment Fund said in April it would pull funding, LIV Golf filed for bankruptcy protection this week. It hopes to launch a “LIV 2.0” backed by buyout firm BC Partners. But LIV 1.0 is over, along with Saudi hopes of building a rival power centre in golf — though not Riyadh’s newfound clout in many other sports.

LIV Golf was the flagship of a broader Saudi sports investment strategy. This was often justifiably portrayed as an exercise in “sportswashing” the kingdom’s record of human rights abuses. But there was something more to the investment. It was another way to diversify the economy away from oil, and hosting sports events could help make the kingdom more attractive to tourists. And it was intended to get young Saudis off their couches — but involved in pursuits not connected to politics.

Saudi Arabia learnt the hard way, however, that unless a new entrant can identify a specific structural gap or market failure, disrupting existing sports franchises is hard. Sports incumbency is extremely powerful — through control of existing structures, tournaments and ranking tables. LIV Golf was able to win over some top players with a fat cheque book. But while it enjoyed considerable success in Australia and South Africa, it struggled elsewhere to attract a critical mass of fans and viewers, and the major TV deals that could have made it viable.

LIV Golf’s rivalry did trigger reforms by golf’s dominant PGA Tour, including new tournaments and bigger prize money. But its fate has quietened murmurings about possible Saudi-funded breakaway competitions in everything from tennis to cycling to rugby league. It joins other failed attempts at sports disruption, such as football’s European Super League, which suited top clubs but was strangled at birth by angry fans. A striking counter-example is the Indian Premier League, which brought the pacy T20 game to cricket-mad Indians underserved by existing formats and shifted the game’s global balance of power, though this was led by India’s existing powerful cricketing authority.

Yet while LIV has been a hubristic misfire, the Saudi effort to use sport to burnish its brand more widely has not failed. Before and since its splurge on golf, Riyadh has found it is cheaper and more effective to buy into existing sports structures. Saudi entities are today key sponsors of Fifa, Formula 1 and the men’s and women’s pro tennis tours, and have partnerships with numerous football federations as well as in wrestling, mixed martial arts and boxing. The kingdom has also become a force in video gaming.

These ventures have not necessarily delivered big returns, but Riyadh has parlayed them into hosting events ranging from the Saudi Arabian Grand Prix to tennis tournaments featuring top players and boxing title fights. Its biggest coup was securing the 2034 men’s Fifa World Cup. Though mired in controversy, as previous Fifa hosting decisions have often been, this offers the Saudis a place in the global spotlight similar to neighbouring Qatar in 2022.

While Saudi Arabia has failed in its effort to build a new sporting institution, its riches have enabled it to become embedded in the governance and commercial architecture of global sport. But the abruptness with which it pulled the plug on LIV Golf funding may be a warning for global sports against becoming too financially reliant on the whims of an autocratic state.

item.title: Mariana Mazzucato: ‘I’m not talking about utopias’
item.author: Simon Mundy
item.description: Economist calls on governments to ‘shape’ markets for the common good
item.content:encoded:
Economist calls on governments to ‘shape’ markets for the common good

Simon Mundy

It’s easier to imagine the end of the world, the late philosopher Fredric Jameson suggested, than to imagine the end of capitalism.

Maybe so. But one thing that’s certainly possible is to imagine the next stages in the evolution of capitalism — how today’s prevailing systems can be refined and improved.

For today’s edition I spoke to economist Mariana Mazzucato about her latest book on this theme, built around the vision of a “common good economy”. Let me know your thoughts on her arguments — or other work on these questions that you think we should explore. You can reach me at simon.mundy@ft.com.

A different way of doing capitalism

“What I’m talking about is very practical,” Mariana Mazzucato tells me. “I’m not talking about utopias, I’m not talking about socialism, you know, regardless of whether I think a socialist system would be better. What I’m trying to do is say: capitalism can work in a very different way.”

Since her breakout 2013 book The Entrepreneurial State, Mazzucato has become one of the world’s most publicly influential economists with her arguments for governments to take a more hands-on, ambitious approach to national goals.

Political leaders have been paying attention to the work of Mazzucato, a professor at University College London, where she leads the Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose. She advised Joe Biden’s administration on its Chips Act for the semiconductor sector, has counselled Brazil’s government on areas including social service provision, and influenced the UK Labour Party’s successful 2024 election manifesto built around national “missions”. (Sir Keir Starmer’s team then “lost the plot” in office, neglecting those missions for a focus on narrowly conceived economic growth, she laments.)

In her latest book, The Common Good Economy, Mazzucato takes these ideas a step further, sketching a framework through which all actors in the economy — governments, businesses, workers and communities — could be organised around a shared conception of the greater good.

While she’s broadened her lens beyond governments, they remain at the centre of the picture. She complains that they tend to view their job as merely monitoring markets that work according to the rules that happen to prevail, stepping in only to fix major problems when things go wrong. Instead, she says, they must work to “shape” markets in line with major national objectives.

Beyond laws and regulations, she argues, governments have a range of potent tools at their disposal. These include public procurement, which commonly accounts for about a quarter of government budgets, and which she says should come with far more conditions attached in order to influence corporate practices. “When you just give Palantir access to the [National Health Service] data as we do in the UK — it’s ridiculous,” she says. “They’re laughing at you.”

Then there’s the potential for more strategic deployment of funds through publicly owned banks and financial institutions, with tens of trillions at their disposal globally — “a lot of money to be wasting”. She wants governments to focus more on investing for the long-term flourishing of their societies through state-led investment, rather than cutting this back (as in the UK) in the name of fiscal responsibility. And by treating tax systems more as a means of shaping economic behaviour — rather than just a source of revenue — governments can align private sector activity with good outcomes for society.

What exactly the common good is, Mazzucato does not specify (though she writes at length in the new book on the need to tackle problems such as climate change and economic inequality). This was intentional, she says; instead, she wanted to paint a picture of how governments can build their own picture of the common good, and then pursue it.

Crucial to that first step, she says, is much greater engagement and consultation with citizens on an ongoing basis, rather than just on the election campaign trail. This, she argues, will tackle the sense — palpable among many of those who voted for Donald Trump — of “the elite telling them what’s good for them”.

Many free-market advocates, I point out, will balk at Mazzucato’s prescriptions, worrying that such an expanded role for government will result in inefficient bloat and reduce the space for productive competition and innovation in the private sector.

Adam Smith’s seminal conception of the free market, she retorts, was of a market free from excessive economic rents — a small number of participants using privileged market positions to capture an unduly high share of income — not from government involvement.

Those rents have been mushrooming under the current market structure, she contends. “The number of billionaires has now passed 3,000,” she says. “That is not about economic incentives. That is about huge rents being extracted.” The answer, she argues, is not for government to suppress markets, nor to leave them alone, but rather to “tilt” them to reward and incentivise the sort of innovation and business practices that drive better outcomes for society as a whole.

The obstacles to Mazzucato’s agenda are huge and conspicuous — not least the political clout of vested interests that might stand to lose out. There are some “huge profits being made”, she acknowledges, “by not having the common good”. And the book’s vision of heightened intergovernmental efforts towards the global common good, notably on climate change, seems optimistic at a time of increased nationalism and Trump’s attacks on multilateral collaboration.

But Mazzucato insists that her ideas are eminently workable, with a tad more ambition from leaders. “I think sometimes we forget,” she says, “that there are very different ways of doing capitalism.”

Smart reads

  • The Brent crude oil price has risen above $100 a barrel for the first time since July — a reminder that the Hormuz crisis is continuing to shift the economics of energy away from fossil fuels.
  • The lack of a clear rulebook for sovereign debt restructuring is worsening problems for heavily indebted developing countries, writes Reza Baqir. “This current system is not sustainable and must change.”

item.title: China’s giant trade surplus has an increasingly geopolitical twist
item.author: Alan Beattie
item.description: Partners are faced with a model that combines export-led growth with tech supremacy
item.content:encoded:
Partners are faced with a model that combines export-led growth with tech supremacy

Alan Beattie

It takes quite a lot for a group of nations to line up with Donald Trump’s rogue US administration, but current account imbalances as a result of China’s surplus and competition from Chinese companies have pretty much managed it.

At last week’s meeting of the G20 group of finance ministers, there was widespread agreement about the risk to the world economy and trade imbalances from “non-market” policies. Governments say China’s return to an aggressive export-oriented growth model in recent years is hollowing out their manufacturing.

There are just two tiny problems with fixing this. First, China doesn’t agree, and vetoed the attempt at a G20 communiqué on this. Second, there are two increasingly intertwined issues — macroeconomic imbalances on the one hand and China’s drive for technological supremacy on the other. China’s trading partners are attempting to resolve the first with (generally uncoordinated) industrial policy that is only suitable to address the second, and which in any case is struggling for impact.

Rich countries in general, and the US in particular, have been complaining about imbalances and unfair competition from China since the early 2000s. But in the 2020s, the Chinese property bust and weakened domestic demand have caused China to embrace export-oriented growth with ever greater fervour. As David Lubin of the Chatham House think-tank points out, Chinese export growth has often exceeded world import growth for a while, after which the gap generally closes as Chinese domestic demand recovers and absorbs more of the output. But since the early 2020s there has been a large and sustained rise in Chinese export growth relative to world import growth.

The Chinese vice-premier He Lifeng has repeatedly talked about boosting consumption, but the government has veered instead towards investing in yet more supply-side technological innovation and infrastructure. The underlying cause of imbalances is macroeconomic, but it’s tied up with an aggressive campaign of domination of world markets in electric vehicles, semiconductors and the like.

As Lubin notes, China increasingly sees surpluses as complementary to controlling global supply chains and technological chokepoints. It’s not essential to have the surpluses to have the tech — the US was at the forefront of global technological development for decades while running trade deficits — but that seems to be the belief in Beijing.

It’s almost nostalgic that the term that prevented consensus last week was a reference to “non-market” economic policies. A decade ago there was a long and determined diplomatic and legal battle at the World Trade Organization over designating China as a “non-market economy”, partly because the designation made it easier for authorities like the EU to impose protective anti-dumping duties. In the end, the EU simply abolished the distinction between market and non-market economies in its trade defence law.

It was a neat solution, but one that merely underlined the fuzziness of attempts to categorise China and use traditional trade tools against it. US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent last week repeated a line he had used before: the Chinese company BYD, he said, made “the best $70,000 car that $35,000 can buy”. It’s a cute turn of phrase, but the Rhodium Group consultancy estimates that only about 5 per cent of BYD’s cost advantage over Tesla cars made in China is because of subsidies. Much of the rest is a genuinely low-cost base created through years of ferocious domestic competition. Simply using tariffs to correct that distortion won’t make a critical difference.

The EU claims to be gearing up to take on China’s industrial might. It used to be said that the bloc’s trade policy was essentially set by Volkswagen, which was generally in favour of trade. But the company is now haemorrhaging jobs and has called for trade measures against China. The EU is, however, up against an opponent who doesn’t mind playing dirty. Beijing recently said it would block the EU from gathering information in China to use in official investigations into Chinese subsidies.

As for solving the imbalances with purely macroeconomic policy, it’s as hard as ever to imagine co-ordination. The US can’t credibly claim it’s trying to reduce imbalances while pushing the fiscal deficit ever higher with tax cuts and spending.

China generally doesn’t like being isolated in international forums, but it’s highly resistant to joining a consensus that is hostile to its growth model. Beijing’s attachment to export promotion has always been about growth and jobs. It is now increasingly about projecting technological supremacy as well.

alan.beattie@ft.com

item.title: Lessons from England’s school success story
item.author: Stephen Bush
item.description: Its latest PISA scores have bucked the OECD’s downward trend in performance and we can learn a lot from the top-performing examples
item.content:encoded:
Its latest PISA scores have bucked the OECD’s downward trend in performance and we can learn a lot from the top-performing examples

Stephen Bush

Good morning. This year’s PISA scores are a reminder of a neglected policy story about what was probably the biggest success of the last Conservative government: state schools in England are really very good nowadays.

Some thoughts on that below.

Why England stands out in a world of slumping scores

The 2025 PISA scores of performance in reading, maths and science make for grim reading across much of the developed world, as the post-pandemic decline in educational outcomes continues to make itself felt.

England remains one of the exceptions.

A couple of things worth noting. First, the UK has hosted a neat experiment: Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland have all gone in different directions and they have all produced sharply different and worse results compared with England. Northern Ireland’s continuing use of grammar schools is a useful advert against restoring those in England, while Wales’ fall down the ranking is essentially the product of a big bet on “skills” as a driver of education policy rather than “knowledge”.

Thanks to the changes made by successive education secretaries from the late 1980s onwards, but particularly by Michael Gove and his schools minister, Nick Gibb, from 2010 to 2014, schools in England have vastly improved.

A common myth that needs scotching here: a frequent thing some readers write in to say is that the “real reason” why schools in England have stronger outcomes is because of the children of immigrants, who are more driven. This is not the case! In fact one measure of just how good England’s schools are is that we are one of the few places in the OECD where second-generation immigrant pupils outperform natives in reading and maths: that is in and of itself a consequence of our school system succeeding, not a cause.

What underpinned it? What do we mean by “knowledge-rich” curriculums? Well, in the subject of English, for example, the aim isn’t that students leave knowing some disconnected facts, like who Elizabeth Bennet ends up with or who kills Macbeth, but that they are able to: write for a range of purposes; speak clearly; understand and participate in spoken debates and generally have all of the abilities necessary to flourish in life. The best way to instil those skills is to teach knowledge, as both research and outcomes across the developed world show.

(As I have written before, there are important lessons here for how to use AI in classroom settings, which is that for the most part, we should not seek to bring AI into classrooms all that quickly.)

One read of this is that Labour should refrain from big experiments or structural changes to primary and secondary education (particularly given that both further and higher education badly need ministerial attention — frankly just leaving schools alone for a bit is not a bad policy right now).

I disagree. I think there is a useful new question in schools policy. There are a handful of schools in England that are performing incredibly well even by the standards of their peers. They are getting top grades and doing even better on “Progress 8” scores (that’s how we measure how well pupils are doing once we account for their start in life, and other academic and demographic factors). What are these schools doing well and can we scale that up across the education system? One thing we’ll be doing in this newsletter is reporting from some of those schools and discussing what can be scaled and what can’t.

Now try this

(Georgina writes) A lovely interactive story about Asian names and conventions in the Singaporean data journalism outlet Kontinentalist.

Top stories today

  • Gilt trip | The UK has paid the highest borrowing cost on a sale of its debt in almost three decades, as the global bond sell-off intensifies the pressure on public finances ahead of a crunch Budget.
  • End of the ultimatum | In June Keir Starmer gave tech companies a three-month deadline to voluntarily introduce device-level protections that stopped children from taking or sharing nude images or face legislation. Now Andy Burnham is going ahead with the government’s plans to introduce these laws. (For more on the practicalities of this, see Georgina’s investigation into SafeToNet, the British company featured in the government’s June press release).
  • Police had tip-off about far-right agitators | Police were told the night before far-right agitators blocked roads into Dover that those involved had converged on a village 18 miles away, the Guardian reports, raising questions about Kent police’s handling of the agitation which the force described as “spontaneous”. At least one person is understood to have sought to pass on details to counterterrorism police after people heard the far-right activists boasting in the local pub that they intended to go to Dover and “attack Muslims”.



Letter in response:
Here’s a different way to measure success in an English school / From Chris Tooley, Principal, The Netherhall School, Cambridge, UK

item.title: Norway’s oil fund says what everyone is thinking
item.author: Katie Martin
item.description: Sovereign debt ain’t what it was
item.content:encoded:
Sovereign debt ain’t what it was

Katie Martin

Good morning. Sorry for the Groundhog Day vibes, but we are up at about $100 oil again, and analysts are warning of another creep up to $120 a barrel if attacks on ships keep on intensifying as they have been. Andrew Bailey, governor of the Bank of England, is warning of upside risks to inflation, and the UK is paying up handsomely for new debt sales. The beatings will continue until morale improves. Cheer us up: unhedged@ft.com.

Our friends in the north

Readers of Unhedged love a bit of asset allocation discourse. A week after Hakyung wrote about the challenges facing the classic 60/40 portfolio model, and followed up with a selection of the correspondence this provoked, she is still getting loads of emails about it. Seriously, loads.

But you don’t often get live conversations on this topic at big investment houses aired in public. Step forward Norway’s super-huge oil fund, all two-and-a-bit trillion dollars of it, the biggest single investor in the world, practically visible from space. Last week it proposed chopping the weight of government debt in its bonds portfolio from 70 to 50 per cent (if you missed it, the news story is here).

This is a big deal. As Shreyas Gopal and George Saravelos at Deutsche Bank wrote, it is potentially the biggest shake-up in the oil fund since it was founded more than three decades ago, and:

While the sums involved are small relative to the size of global fixed-income markets, we believe the change in the investment strategy of one of the world’s largest and most successful sovereign wealth funds offers powerful signals as to the slow-moving but persistent shifts in global capital flows and portfolio allocation currently taking place in markets.

There’s lots of scope for confusion here. The fund is not proposing pulling back from fixed income altogether. It looks like it’ll stick at today’s split of 70 per cent stocks, a bit over 25 per cent fixed income, and the rest still in renewables and real estate. But within that fixed income slice, it’s talking about going from 70/30 government debt/corporate debt to more like 50/50. And yes, Treasuries are likely to take the strain here, but still, this is not a rejection of US assets as such, and though it is tempting to read a political snub into all this, that really isn’t what’s going on.

With admirable transparency, the fund explains its thinking in a lengthy letter to the government here.

The killer line in the letter is:

The degree to which bonds will contribute to dampening volatility in future crises will depend on the nature of the crisis. For example, one might expect government bonds to not have the same volatility-dampening effects in a government bond crisis.

Probably not! Also:

High government debt has gone from being a distinctive feature of individual countries, particularly Japan and some euro area countries, to becoming a more general characteristic of developed economies.

Mic drop there from the Norwegians. This is an articulation of something that, deep down, we all know to be true. Government debt, including US government debt, is just not the pristine risk-free asset we’ve all pretended it is for the past few decades. Sure, defaults in developed-market debt just don’t happen. But the volatility is high, persistent inflation is a pain, and the sheer amounts that governments are borrowing amplify a range of problems. To have the world’s biggest investor say this out loud feels like a moment.

By contrast, as the fund says, corporate and, for example, mortgage-backed bonds, make it worth your while and often perform at least part of the same safety-net purpose. They are not necessarily as liquid in a crisis as government bonds, but a fund the size of this is not exactly short of liquid assets. And at least this kind of debt pays the holder something of a premium.

In addition, the fund proposes switching away from a model that penalises governments with high debt-to-GDP levels and switching instead to size-based allocations. This is big news for Japanese government bonds.

In summary, the fund says:

The most important changes from today’s index are a considerably lower share of government bonds and the inclusion of mortgage-backed securities, which account for around 13 per cent of the recommended index against zero today. Government-related bonds increase from around 4 to around 11 per cent. The currency distribution is close to unchanged, with the exception of the Japanese yen, which increases from around 5 to 8 per cent. The US dollar is by far the largest currency, with a weight of just over 50 per cent. The largest difference in the dollar market is that the share of US government bonds falls, which is offset by a roughly corresponding increase in other US bonds.

In chart form, from Deutsche Bank, that is:

And:

Obviously, the Norwegian oil fund is pretty big. Not every investor has this kind of liquidity profile in its existing holdings, and few operate on these kinds of time horizons. But this real-life example of a serious fund thinking very differently about what its bond holdings are really for is catnip for the asset allocation nerds out there and, we hope, the first of many.

One good read

Lagarde’s memoir

item.title: The political challenge of Britain’s mounting debt costs
item.author: Stephen Bush
item.description: The government was right to protect infrastructure spending but tweaking the fiscal rules comes at a price
item.content:encoded:
The government was right to protect infrastructure spending but tweaking the fiscal rules comes at a price

Stephen Bush

Good morning. The UK faces a tricky combination of more borrowing, higher borrowing costs and nervous markets that are narrowing chancellor John Healey’s room for manoeuvre. Some thoughts on the politically fraught levers for tackling the issue.

We are looking for savings in the wrong place

The UK has three overlapping problems selling its debt. As a result of the Liz Truss experiment, the country faces a higher premium on selling its debt relative to even similarly indebted peers. Under Keir Starmer, we consciously increased the amount of borrowing to pay for more infrastructure, and now actions by the US and its own spending habits are sending debt costs rising across the world.

In short, our debt has become less attractive, we are selling more of it and there are signs of a flight to safety in debt markets at a time when the UK is increasingly not seen as a safe bet.

Like most wonks I support the changes Rachel Reeves made to treat infrastructure spending differently from day-to-day spending in her fiscal rules, because it prevented her from doing something British chancellors have long done in order to get out of a hole domestically: slashing infrastructure and capital expenditure.

But the change has come at a cost, in that essentially nobody really talks about it, and it has made the government blind to the fact that this borrowing still comes at a cost. It really does mean we are selling more gilts. It really does mean that we are diverting the UK’s real resources from consumption to investment — I’m not saying this is a bad thing in policy terms, but it does come at a political cost, because broadly speaking, households like consumption.

It does also further limit what the chancellor of the exchequer can do at a time of rising debt costs to reassure bond markets — Healey can’t take an axe to future infrastructure spending to meet his fiscal rules (this is a good thing) but it means his actual options are more politically fraught.

The consensus at Westminster across almost all parties is that he should tackle the “spiralling welfare bill”. There are two problems here — the first, as Chris Giles set out recently, is that the welfare bill is not spiralling, ballooning, skyrocketing or anything like that. The change in composition in UK welfare spending should really worry us in my view. Although we spend about the same amount, we spend less of it on support into work and less of it on in-work welfare. But we should be clear on what the actual problem is, which is that we spend money poorly, not that spending has got out of control.

The second is that in recent decades, essentially everything successive governments have done on welfare has been a) designed to cut costs and b) has failed to do so. (I argued a while back that the current mess is itself the product of a desire to prioritise headline savings over designing a well-thought-through benefit system. Neither has been fruitful.) The Office for Budget Responsibility has many strengths, but on welfare spending, it has consistently costed measures that have not actually delivered savings in practice.

Announcing yet another round of changes to welfare eligibility and thresholds for support will probably make the light go green in the next OBR report, but recent history suggests that it will not actually lower spending.

I know I am a stuck record, but if you want to get control over government spending, the bit of welfare spend you would really look at is the triple lock. Second, you would be open to changes to how the UK pays for healthcare.

That is not what Healey is currently minded to do, and in any case the government’s Plan A is to implement a “steady as she goes” Budget ahead of a more far-reaching settlement in next year’s comprehensive spending review, which will include some (theoretical) reductions in in-work welfare spending.

The risk is that events get ahead of the government and that Healey’s ability to deliver a steady-state Budget in the autumn vanishes.

Now try this

This week, I mostly listened to berlioz’s 2024 record open this wall while writing my column.

Top stories today

  • Calming markets | Budget speculation is heating up as Healey races to reassure bond markets and protect his fiscal “buffer”. The OBR will gauge the fiscal impact of movements in market interest rates during an observation “window” in the lead-up to the Budget. One government insider said the chancellor was pushing hard on the “fiscal discipline” message because he has to create a “more positive backdrop” before this window closes — there is no word yet, though, of where he would be making early cuts to public spending.
  • Ed Miliband intervenes | The UK government is set to announce that it will ban trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, according to people familiar with the matter.
  • Trading places | Hedge fund billionaire Chris Rokos, one of the UK’s biggest taxpayers, is moving his residency from the UK to Greece, amid fears of tax rises in the Budget.

item.title: Canada is fated to try to do deals with Donald Trump
item.author: Alan Beattie
item.description: Ottawa has no alternative but to keep the door open to negotiating the best possible access to the US market
item.content:encoded:
Ottawa has no alternative but to keep the door open to negotiating the best possible access to the US market

Alan Beattie

Welcome to Trade Secrets and a happy Labor Day (US) and Labour Day (Canada), the difference in spelling serving to remind everyone that despite Donald Trump’s best efforts, they are in fact different countries.

Today’s newsletter is on how Canada, like everyone else, has to get the best deal it can from the US president whether it likes him or not (it doesn’t). I also do one of my occasional drop-ins on the UK to see if it has got its trade, aid and immigration acts in gear. I won’t give away the ending. Charted Waters, where we look at the data behind world trade, is on US stock prices.

Dealing with the Donald

It has been a couple of weeks since the big US-Canada blow-up over trade. My views at the time are here and here, and if you prefer me in audio form I’m on the excellent Unhedged podcast here. The dust kicked up by the confrontation is a long way from settling. Apart from the many memes about renaming lakes and so on, there is ongoing sniping between the countries and a load of speculation about how much the negotiation’s outcome owed to having two principals, US trade representative Jamieson Greer and US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick, who may not have been completely aligned. Prime Minister Mark Carney has refused to compromise, and the Canadian retaliatory tariffs are set to go ahead tomorrow.

Of course no deal will be possible on anything like the lines the US was demanding. But the one thing the Canadian government hasn’t done is declare the talks dead. Even as they broke down, Carney said: “The bonds between Canadians and Americans remain strong. A mutually beneficial trade agreement is possible.” Since then, Janice Charette, the chief Canadian negotiator, coined a rather nice expression: “the pens are down but the door is open”.

Within a few days of telling Trump to “kiss my ass”, the pugnacious (that adjective is compulsory, remember) Doug Ford, premier of Ontario, admitted that the rhetoric had got a bit heated on both sides. He called Canada and the US “allies” and “best friends” and said “I just think that we need to focus on a free trade agreement.” 

Despite all his talk about becoming more independent of the US, Carney knows Canada doesn’t have a credible alternative that could remotely replace it as an export market in the foreseeable future. I’ve heard it argued that the Canadian prime minister mistimed his strategy by fighting the US alone rather than with the middle-power alliances he talked about at Davos in January. That’s putting way too much weight on an alliance’s potential: disparate geographies, economies and political orientations meant middle powers were never going to form a solid negotiating bloc.

Remember that Carney was sounding much more emollient about a deal in the early summer before the US decided to give him an offer he could only refuse. It’s best to see all this back and forth between the US and Canada as part of an ongoing negotiation, each side jockeying for position and claiming that it doesn’t need a deal but that the other does. It’s not an irrevocable break at this moment, and it’s not likely to become one.

As you were in the UK

It’s time to drop in on the UK to discover what it (I guess “we”, given my nationality and domicile) is doing in aid, trade and immigration. I was pretty savage about Sir Keir Starmer’s Labour government earlier this year, which was absurdly restrictive on immigration, performatively destructive on aid and far too timid on integration with the EU. 

So what’s the UK up to now? It’s been seven weeks since Andy Burnham took over as prime minister. In an appropriately football-related (soccer-related, whatever) metaphor, that’s enough time on the ball to see how he’s doing.

Burnham has more room for manoeuvre than Starmer because people like him and he appears to be capable of doing politics. In theory, he should also get some slack on the immigration front from a sharp drop in recent arrivals, including the small-boat migrants with whom the UK public is utterly obsessed.

Last week was the big chance for rapprochement with France, habitually the main sceptic within the EU of doing the UK favours: the meeting between Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron, the unveiling of what King Charles correctly called the “Canterbury Embroidery” (it’s not from Bayeux and it’s not a tapestry), and so on.

Any serious change? No. As my colleagues reported last week, the red lines stay in place regarding the EU. No membership of the single market or customs union. No freedom of movement. Instead desperately minor stuff, such as haggling over university fees in a youth mobility programme, and entitled behaviour, such as demanding special treatment in the EU’s “buy European” rules. Nor does the wider security relationship change much. As a Chatham House study (usual disclaimer: I’m an unpaid associate fellow there, though wasn’t involved in this paper) points out, any idea of trading off market access for closer defence co-operation is a non-starter.

Progress on aid? Also no. Having inherited a policy of slashing official development assistance to fragile conflict-affected states, Burnham announced a frankly offensive plan to increase UK bus subsidies by converting grants to help low-income countries combat climate change into loans, thus possibly cutting off some nations from help at all. I wonder how this policy resonates in flood-ravaged Nepal or how it will look as the El Niño weather system sweeps through poor countries. Burnham also appointed an aid minister experienced in international development issues but then stopped her attending cabinet. This is poor stuff.

On migration, it would take a heart of stone not to laugh. Labour has spent so long distorting reality that it’s getting no credit at all now the net figures are actually falling. The public has largely not registered the decrease in migration levels and still thinks immigration is the country’s number one issue. In any case, the core beliefs remain in place. Even if the government gets more political room for manoeuvre to back away from its absurdly restrictive plans, it won’t use it unless its own backbenchers force it to.

So, there you have it. As you were. I won’t be rushing back with an update soon.

Charted waters

Despite everything — despite the trade war, despite Iran, despite Trump’s attempts to bully the US Federal Reserve — stock prices continue to rise. There is a great deal of ruin in a nation.

Trade links

  • The FT reports on how the once-thriving port of Jebel Ali in Dubai is threatened by the Iran war. (I’d add that Jebel Ali’s transhipment business shifted rapidly to other ports after the Strait of Hormuz was blocked, defying fears that dependence on it would materially affect world trade.)
  • Scott Lincicome of the Cato Institute looks at the underwhelming reality of Trump’s coercive bilateral deals.
  • A trio of stories on the world’s dependence on US data and tech services: First, a column in the Toronto Star on how Google Maps going along with Trump’s renaming of Lake Ontario as “Lake America” shows the true allegiance of US tech and the threat Washington poses to Canadian sovereignty.
  • Second, EU defence officials are warning against Europe trying to develop its own tech to compete with the US, saying such de-risking is not realistic and creates more problems than it solves.
  • Third, an op-ed in the FT argues that other countries building data centres consolidates rather than challenges the US’s lead in AI.
  • The FT reviews a new book by Ed Conway of Sky News on the resilience of global trade and the threats to its future.

Trade Secrets is edited by Harvey Nriapia

item.title: Port demonstrations prompt questions for authorities and government
item.author: Stephen Bush
item.description: Concerns over police response to Dover protest and Portsmouth blockade will dog Westminster this week
item.content:encoded:
Concerns over police response to Dover protest and Portsmouth blockade will dog Westminster this week

Stephen Bush

Good morning. The police and the government are facing questions after a gathering of up to 500 masked activists on Saturday brought parts of Dover to a standstill and a group blockaded a second port on Sunday evening.

Some short thoughts in today’s note.

Caught unawares

Both the police and the government look to have been caught flat-footed by anti-migrant protests this weekend after masked protesters brought the Port of Dover to a halt for several hours on Saturday and a group blockaded the port of Portsmouth yesterday.

No arrests were made on Saturday. As I have explained in previous emails about other protests, arresting demonstrators is something police officers are often reluctant to do, because the act of performing an arrest reduces the number of police on the scene and can make any confrontation worse. Small-scale protests, such as the 2020 anti-lockdown demonstrations or gatherings of environmental campaigners who block motorways, will attract immediate arrests. But arrests relating to criminal behaviour at larger-scale protests — such as the far-right march last year or the various pro-Gaza marches — will usually take place after the fact.

The relevant question here is why the police did not have the numbers on Saturday to make arrests at the protest and indeed why it seems to have come as a surprise. Its organisers are not a new group and warnings had been raised. Moreover, there are questions for the government to answer about why a subsequent and similar blockade on Sunday seems to have caught the authorities unawares. Those questions are going to get louder and louder this week at Westminster and within the government, I suspect.

Now try this

It was lovely to meet and talk to so many Inside Politics readers at the FT Weekend Festival and to see some great talks. My highlight was Paul Smith in conversation with Peter Capaldi, and you can watch back all of the events you might have missed and register for the 2027 festival here.

Top stories today

  • Jobs jump | UK hiring picked up for the first time in four years in August, according to an employment survey, adding to evidence of a tentative improvement in economic confidence under Prime Minister Andy Burnham. 


  • Contentious contracts | More than one-quarter of police forces in England and Wales are involved in pilot contracts with Palantir of the same kind that prompted London Mayor Sir Sadiq Khan to order the Metropolitan Police to sever its links with the company, FT research shows.

item.title: Britain is a factory for ideas applied elsewhere
item.author: Tej Parikh
item.description: Barriers to development at home push the upsides of UK research abroad
item.content:encoded:
Barriers to development at home push the upsides of UK research abroad

Tej Parikh

Britain excels at producing ideas and advice for others, but it is much less effective at putting them to work at home.

Take the country’s comparative advantage in professional services. The UK is the second-largest exporter of business services, advising boardrooms around the world on how to run their organisations. And yet studies show that British companies have weaker management practices than those in peer nations on average, which contributes to the country’s lagging productivity performance.

Then there is Britain’s excellence in higher education and research. The UK ranks in the top five worldwide for total publications in high-quality journals across applied, natural and social sciences, according to the Nature Index. But it underwhelms at turning this research into industrial and technological output.

For measure, since 2012, 80 per cent of initial public offerings by UK university spinouts have occurred overseas — and between 2012 and 2021, the majority achieving exits through acquisitions were sold to foreign suitors.

Britain’s entrepreneurial activity reflects this dynamic, too. The country does not lack the laboratory breakthroughs to start businesses, ranking only behind the US and China for number of unicorn start-ups. But beyond a few sectors, it often lacks the infrastructure and capital to scale them, fuelling fears that it has become an “incubator economy”.

Indeed, research-intensive UK firms have played a foundational role in many of today’s critical technologies. But commercialisation has predominantly taken place abroad. DeepMind, a London-based AI pioneer, was bought by Google in 2014. Cambridge-based semiconductor designer Arm was acquired by Japan’s SoftBank in 2016.

There is a similar pattern in the public sector. UK research is cited in policy-related documents twice as frequently as the global average, according to analysis by publishing company Elsevier and trade group Universities UK. However, British governments have not been standard bearers for good policymaking.

In this way, Britain has come to resemble a factory for ideas that are mostly capitalised on elsewhere.

The speed of the country’s economic transformation is one explanation for this mismatch. The decline of manufacturing and rise of the services and knowledge economy have taken place faster in the UK than in other advanced nations. Strong universities, advantageous geography and the English language positioned the country, and London in particular, to specialise in higher value-added service and quaternary sectors as global trade and industrial supply chains developed.

But this shift has become self-reinforcing. As Britain’s industrial ecosystem — ranging from manufacturing knowhow to component suppliers and testing facilities — has withered, it has become harder to develop research beyond the ideas stage.

In turn, talent and capital have gravitated towards higher returns in knowledge-intensive sectors. This has contributed to the dearth of practical and technical skillsets across UK business, industry and government. Compared to the OECD average, the country produces a significantly lower proportion of graduates in degrees such as engineering, manufacturing and construction.

The policy environment hasn’t helped either. High energy costs and restrictive planning regulations have made scaling business ideas at home less attractive. Last month, Chris McDonald, UK science minister, lamented that a lack of “industrial laboratory space” was pushing the country’s innovators abroad. Uncertainty, high property taxes and steep labour costs have also undermined the ability of domestic companies to invest and boost productivity.

A lack of capital as companies grow is another factor. Seed-stage companies attract close to three-quarters of their funding at home, but less than one-third at the scale-up stage, according to data from the UK government’s council for science and technology. This, in part, reflects risk aversion and fragmented funding pots among domestic institutional investors.

The UK’s knowledge sector is a boon for the rest of the world and a strength the country should reinforce. But if too many barriers remain between the ideas and the company, factory or infrastructure they could create, other nations will continue to capture the upsides of British intellect.

Send your thoughts in the comments, to freelunch@ft.com or via X @tejparikh90.

Food for thought

Beyond easing traffic jams, a recent study of New York City’s congestion pricing system finds that the policy has improved emergency medical service response times.

Free Lunch on Sunday is edited by Harvey Nriapia

Letters in response:
UK’s frontier AI strategy is aimed at the wrong target / From Alexander Kardos-Nyheim, Founder & CEO, Safe Sign Technologies, London E14, UK

‘The most valuable cargo ever brought to US shores’ / From Roger Gill, Cradley, Worcestershire, UK

item.title: The 1.5C climate goal is dead
item.author: Simon Mundy
item.description: Focus must turn to limiting the ‘overshoot’ — and managing its consequences
item.content:encoded:
Focus must turn to limiting the ‘overshoot’ — and managing its consequences

Simon Mundy

“We have kept 1.5 degrees within reach, but its pulse is weak,” COP26 president Alok Sharma said at the close of the 2021 climate summit in Glasgow. “It will only survive if we keep our promises; if we translate commitments into rapid action.”

That was an optimistic diagnosis even then. Five years on, it’s clear that the last chance of holding global warming below 1.5C has been lost. Welcome to the age of the overshoot.

Time for a reality check

For more than a decade, a good deal of humanity’s effort on climate action has been guided by a single number: 1.5, the number of degrees Celsius by which the global average temperature must not rise.

Now that goal has been declared out of reach in a major UN report — and not a moment too soon.

Ahead of the UN Paris climate summit in 2015, a group of small island nations spearheaded a high-profile push for a deal to limit global warming to 1.5 rather than 2 degrees. The latter level, they pointed out, would have catastrophic consequences for them and other vulnerable developing nations.

The Paris Agreement ultimately included both numbers in the following crucial clause, which committed nations to:

Holding the increase in the global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and pursuing efforts to limit the temperature increase to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, recognizing that this would significantly reduce the risks and impacts of climate change

Initially, limiting temperature rise to 1.5 degrees looked conceivable — just. In 2018, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change estimated that, for the world to have a two-thirds chance of keeping warming below 1.5 degrees, future carbon dioxide emissions must be limited to a grand total of 420 gigatonnes, or about 10 years’ worth at the prevailing annual level. That would be possible, the body said, with rapid action to cut emissions.

But as the years passed, global emissions instead kept rising, depleting the remaining “carbon budget” at an accelerating rate. The emissions cuts needed to stay within it became increasingly hard to imagine, even for the most enthusiastic climate warriors. In 2022, more than 1,000 scientists and academics signed an open letter stating that “there is no plausible pathway to 1.5C”, and that pretences to the contrary were undermining serious climate action.

This week, a publication from the UN Environment Programme, co-authored by dozens of climate scientists from around the world, arrived at a similar conclusion, stating that the “overshoot of 1.5C” is now “inevitable”. The carbon budget for even a 50 per cent chance of staying below that ceiling has now been depleted to just 130 gigatonnes.

At our current rate of emissions, the world will exhaust it in roughly three years. Put another way, to stay within it, “global CO2 emissions would need to decline linearly from 2025 levels to zero in just over six years.”

Talk of abandoning the 1.5C goal has long drawn accusations of defeatism. A decade ago, or even later, that might have been fair. But to keep pretending that warming can be kept below that level is now perverse — a denial of the true scale of this global problem; a disservice to those most vulnerable to its impacts; a gift to those who argue that the entire effort to tackle it is based on starry-eyed wishful thinking.

The UNEP report stresses that the imminent breach of the 1.5C warming level is reason to strengthen, not give up on, work to mitigate and respond to climate change. It calls for expanded support for the “many nations and communities [that] will face irreversible losses and permanently changed conditions” at these higher temperatures. As the Alliance of Small Island States — the original force behind the 1.5C push — put it in response to the report, “overshoot cannot become an excuse for further inaction”.

And while we’ll soon crash through that 1.5C threshold, the UNEP report recommends the world keep it as a different sort of long-term goal — one that “must now be approached from above”. In short, the focus should be limiting the extent of the overshoot through large-scale emission cuts, and eventually bringing temperatures down below the 1.5C benchmark through carbon dioxide removal. Here’s the UNEP vision of what that could look like:

UN report: temperature overshoot requires urgent action to keep warming in line with Paris accord
Data is indicative and does not represent precise warming magnitudes, rates or probabilities — Source: UN Environment Programme

Hopes of a near-term decline in global carbon emissions — so brutally disappointed in the years after Paris — are starting to look more realistic. The vast majority of the world’s new power generation capacity is now renewable. Sales of electric vehicles are booming while those of combustion-engine cars slide. There are signs that emissions may now have passed their peak in China; the global figure rose by 0.2 per cent in the first half of this year, well below the average pace of recent years.

In their 2024 book Overshoot, Andreas Malm and Wim Carton noted an “irreal” quality to governments’ approach to the 1.5C goal: enthusiastically cheerleading for it while failing to take anything close to the measures needed to implement it. “At a certain point,” they wrote, “this optimism bid farewell to the reality of the crisis.”

The opportunity to limit global warming to 1.5C, with no overshoot, has gone. Yet the prospect of getting emissions on a downward trend — and thereby limiting the extent of further warming — has never looked more feasible. This would be a good moment for governments, and the rest of us, to connect with that reality.

Smart reads

  • Anthropic’s public listing is driving scrutiny of the AI company’s unusual governance structure, with most of its board controlled by an external group of trustees prioritising the long-term interest of humanity.
  • Volkswagen is set to lay off up to 50,000 workers as it struggles to respond to competition from Chinese electric cars.
  • Devastation from the new El Niño weather event — likely to be the strongest in living memory — can be limited if governments “allow international markets in food to function”, writes Alan Beattie.

item.title: Latest allegations make Reform look ridiculous
item.author: Stephen Bush
item.description: Accusations of racism and corruption threaten party’s image as a serious prospect for power
item.content:encoded:
Accusations of racism and corruption threaten party’s image as a serious prospect for power

Stephen Bush

Good morning. Reform UK has kicked off its conference, and conference season as a whole, by being mired in accusations of racism and allegations of deep-seated corruption. Some short thoughts on the political implications of that in today’s note.

Orr! What is he good for?

A 30-minute undercover investigation broadcast by Channel 4 News apparently shows Nigel Farage celebrating with a purported donor and key members of his inner circle discussing how to circumvent campaign finance laws. (One of the members of that inner circle, James Orr, is the subject of a fascinating profile by Helen Warrell and Ramsay Hodgson in this weekend’s FT Magazine.) Orr and Reform deny any wrongdoing. Reform this morning said that Orr and Dan Jukes, another figure featured in the undercover footage, had stepped down while the party conducts its own investigation.

Separately, Zia Yusuf, another senior Reform figure, has been accused of racism after attacking Sagal Abdi-Wali, the leader of Camden Council, a Somalia-born British citizen who is one of the contenders to be Labour’s candidate in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election. On X, Yusuf posted: “The front runner being foisted on the people of Holborn by Labour to replace the former Prime Minister Keir Starmer in our Parliament was born in Somalia. Do you understand what’s happening?”

Individually, these accusations are deeply damaging, but together they are even more so. In addition to the serious evidence that Channel 4 has uncovered, the manner in which Reform’s bigwigs conduct themselves in the video makes them look a bit ridiculous. A political party can survive being seen as mean or soft-hearted or a number of other things. But if it is seen as silly it cannot be a serious prospect for power.

Add that to the allegations of racism — something beyond the pale for many British voters — and the party is fishing in a small pool indeed. There are people who will vote for a ridiculous party. There is a smaller number who will vote for a party facing allegations of racism. But the number who will vote for a party that is both ridiculous and facing allegations of racism is smaller still. Ditto the number who will vote for a party that is ridiculous, facing allegations of racism and committed to the socially conservative agenda Reform has increasingly adopted (and to which the likes of Orr are firmly committed).

I return to what I think is the single most important bit of research for understanding the current political situation in the UK, Jane Green and Marta Miori’s analysis into the factors that make voters switch within blocs. They identified two: intensity of preference (how much you prefer, say, Reform to the Conservatives or the Greens to Labour) and assessment of viability (whether you think that voting for Reform is a waste of time in your constituency and that you are better off backing the Tories, for example).

What these accusations all do, in my view, is damage the sense that Reform is a viable option. That the party’s record in parliamentary by-elections is, frankly, terrible only compounds the problem. It can only be described as a terrific start to conference season for Kemi Badenoch and the Conservatives.

Now try this

I’ve just finished The Husbands by Holly Gramazio, a terrific novel about dating, relationships and love. It starts when Lauren, the heroine, finds a stranger in her flat who claims to be her husband. Then another stranger with the same story appears. Her attic, she realises, is creating an endless supply of husbands. How can she find the right one? What even is the “right one”? It’s a brilliantly constructed read for the end of the day or for a holiday, and one I cannot recommend highly enough.

I’m at the FT Weekend Festival this weekend and will be in the subscriber tent at about 3.30pm. Whether you’re there or elsewhere around the festival, do say hi, and however you spend it, have a wonderful weekend.

Top stories today

  • ‘Brussels over America’ | Britain’s alignment with the EU is a “problem” for a US trade deal and the country has failed to capitalise on Brexit, said US trade representative Jamieson Greer.
  • Sting operation | FT reporters break down the latest claims against Nigel Farage.
  • ‘We will prevail’ | Argentine President Javier Milei cited what he called the UK’s “migration, demographic and economic crises” in an address in which he dialled up his country’s claim over the Falkland Islands.
