On the off chance you haven’t already read them, here are Peter’s discussion of EU trade policy and defence of plurilateral deals, and Aime on President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

OK, so what’s new? The Gulf is in the same partly open state it has been in for months, and oil prices remain at manageable levels. The searingly hot northern hemisphere summer may be causing wildfires and damaging crops, but global food prices remain quiescent. Today I look at the Trump administration adding to its follies with a long whine about what it wrongly calls “transshipment”, and also add a note of scepticism about the new ice-free Arctic shipping passage. Charted Waters, where we look at the data behind world trade, is on gold prices.

Transshipments passing in the night

A big old whinge came out of the US administration last week, stamped with the indelible mark of White House trade adviser Peter Navarro. The report was a bit like anger therapy, lashing out at trading partners for not doing enough to stop what it wrongly calls “transshipment” but which is actually country-of-origin fraud. That is, goods from a highly tariffed country (eg China) falsely labelled as coming from a low-tariff one (eg Mexico) or wrongly reported as having undergone “substantial transformation” in a second country to qualify for preferential treatment.

While the nomenclature isn’t the most important point, “transshipment” is actually a simple technical term for drop-off and pick-up en route to a final destination, reasons for which could be entirely legitimate. Using a neutral descriptor as a pejorative, it’s hard to escape the conclusion that Navarro just doesn’t like modern trade.

Anyway, what’s the administration going to do about it? One of its more constructive ideas is to estimate the extent of rules-of-origin (ROO) evasion using AI to spot patterns of suspected cheating. It’s hired the data company Altana to do just that. Altana reckons that after last April’s “liberation day” tariff increases, the shipments that its systems flagged as transshipped quintupled from $5bn to $25bn a month, in particular by exploiting the low-tariff US-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) route through Mexico. 

The administration wants to tighten ROO in the USMCA review to make evasion harder, but higher hurdles aren’t much use if products can sidle round them. As Evan Smith, Altana’s chief executive, pointed out to me: “Rules only work if the authorities inspecting the goods can verify what’s upstream. These behaviours migrate to whichever declared field is easiest to falsify.”

But it’s one thing to estimate this at a macro level. How do you fix it shipment by shipment? Naturally, at this point I turned to Trade Secrets favourite Ryan Petersen, chief executive of the global logistics technology company Flexport. He applauds the principle but notes the limitations of attempts to infer country-of-origin fraud by looking at available data such as “dwell times”, which reveal only how long a shipment stays in one place, not what happens when it’s there. “Without officers doing inspections all over foreign ports, it will be hard to detect fraud just by looking at data for physical flows of goods to prove that products haven’t undergone substantial transformation,” Petersen told me.

Unless the administration can (extremely improbably) train a global task force of Customs and Border Protection officers and persuade China to embed them in its ports, the burden will be shifted to companies such as Flexport to assess non-compliance and attest that they’ve done so. This will be a festival of paperwork, raising prices for customers. “The administration is going to lean heavily on customs brokers to drive compliance and fight country-of-origin fraud,” Petersen said. “We will have to do a lot more know-your-customer vetting work, somewhat like in banking, which will push up costs.” 

Here’s the thing: it’s very likely true that there is a lot of cheating, not just rules-of-origin evasion but the simpler frauds of mislabelling or misvaluing consignments. I’ve written before about the latter issue in the context of foreign companies acting as “importers of record” in the US. 

But the reality is that the more tariffs you impose, the higher the incentive is to cheat. Poisoning consumers with bathtub gin is not a good thing, but Prohibition made it profitable. The administration evidently did not see widespread evasion coming. It’s a bit like Brexit. Navarro is fulminating at the subversion of his plans by a world he did not understand and therefore did not plan for. It’s not something to be celebrated as an outcome of public policy, but then again, you have to admit it’s pretty funny.

Ice ice baby

There is some excitement over the announcement that Chinese container lines will now be operating a regular service through the Arctic during the increasingly ice-free months of summer, showing that it’s an ill wind — or, in this case, ecologically disastrous global warming — that blows nobody any good.

So, a new era of global freight, Asia-Europe shipping times halving, the Suez Canal (or, these days, the round-Africa) route falling redundant, the Houthis gnashing their teeth, the Malacca Strait silent and abandoned save for the lonely cries of seagulls? Not quite yet. There are a bunch of reasons why the move at this stage is more to do with Chinese geopolitical manoeuvring than a big structural change, certainly as far as container shipping is concerned.

My colleague Richard Milne does a great job here of laying some of them out. The service will be open only for three months in the summer; there will be extra costs for icebreakers to offset the fuel savings; there are considerable reputational risks to European and US shipping lines from environmentally damaging accidents in the Arctic. Also, the route is under Russian control, so it substitutes one political chokepoint for another, and the entry from the east is the Bering Strait, with Russia on one side and the US on the other. As Flexport’s Petersen pointed out to me: “Companies using the Arctic route will have to sign contracts with the Russian ice-breaking company Atomflot, which is sanctioned [by the US and Europe], so we can’t and our customers can’t, but it will be interesting to see who does.” 

More generally, imagining that it will suddenly displace existing routes misunderstands the nature of container shipping. Paul Taylor, senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre (EPC) who wrote a report on the subject, says the China-Europe route isn’t a nonstop sprint. Container vessels on the conventional Malacca Strait route generate value by servicing consumer markets along the way and stopping off at ports for transshipment (in the correct sense of the term). There are no such opportunities in the frozen wastes of northern Russia.

The seas are also too shallow towards the eastern end of the Arctic passage to allow through the giant 20,000 twenty-foot equivalent unit (TEU) container vessels that are the workhorses of modern container shipping. Ice-class container ships currently using the route have one-tenth of that capacity.

Certainly it is useful for China to show it has other options than the Malacca Strait route, which it has long feared the ability of US naval power to block, but for now they are symbolic as much as substantive. The EPC’s Taylor says: “From a Chinese perspective, given the geopoliticisation of chokepoints, it makes sense to show the US that they have alternative shipping routes to Europe. But the problems with lack of infrastructure, absence of drop-off ports on the way and shallow draft mean the northern route is going to struggle to become a widely used passage for container ships.”

Charted waters

It is the perennial market narrative: gold prices rise because of inflation and general geopolitical risk. But as usual the story doesn’t fit the facts. The big run-up in bullion in 2025 and early 2026 has reversed, despite inflation and uncertainty being very much alive.

Trade links

  • Mike Froman, former US trade representative and now president of the Council on Foreign Relations, argues that the next economic crisis might come from China.
  • The FT reports that the price of a niche rare earth has jumped on fears of renewed Chinese rare earth export controls, underlining that the tensions over minerals trade are very much in place despite the supposed ceasefire between the US and China.
  • A piece published by research group Official Monetary and Financial Institutions Forum looks at the implications of not extending USMCA.
  • The academic Dennis Snower looks at strategies for rebuilding the world economic order.

Trade Secrets is edited by Harvey Nriapia

item.title: How economics is changing
item.author: Harvey Nriapia
item.description: The subject is becoming more inventive and empirical, but questions about reproducibility and AI abound
item.content:encoded:
The subject is becoming more inventive and empirical, but questions about reproducibility and AI abound

Harvey Nriapia

In 1849, Scottish essayist Thomas Carlyle was feeling rather glum. A half-century earlier, Thomas Malthus had suggested humanity was caught in a crunch, where any time there was a bright spot — say, a bumper harvest — the subsequent boom would quickly be snuffed out by population pressures. Put differently, bad times followed good as night did day. Economics, Carlyle concluded, was the “dismal science”. Or so legend has it.

Two centuries on, the dismal science is anything but. Modern-day economics is a Cambrian explosion of new methodology and research subfields. Thousands of papers in the subject are published each year, many of which weave in insights about human behaviour and social norms. Indeed, it is now the fifth most popular A-level in England. And researchers in the field are increasingly stretching into more exotic areas and collaborating across boundaries. 

A research paper by Tom Harris, an economics PhD student at the London School of Economics, bears this out. Aggregating the literature published in 24 leading economic journals between 2000 and 2025 and NBER working papers between 2021 and 2025, he found the share of papers written by teams spanning different fields had jumped 16 points to 35 per cent between 2000 and 2025, while solo-authored papers fell as a proportion of the literature from 34 per cent to 15 per cent.

Subfields whose researchers reach furthest into distant areas of study tend to gain share of the literature in subsequent periods, according to the paper. “Intellectual distance seems to matter, not collaboration as such,” says Harris, adding that “reaching into a distant part of economics predicts growth; reaching into a neighbouring topic within the same superfield does not”.

The mechanism, he suggests, is people rather than papers. And some economists, such as Daron Acemoglu and Sendhil Mullainathan, bridge disparate fields across a particularly wide intellectual territory.

The dominant research fields across the 21st century seem to have shifted, too. As a proportion of the literature, research about econometric theory, monetary policy and corporate governance has slumped. Meanwhile, papers on development, crime and gender are on the up. This could perhaps be because of changing intellectual interests, or maybe demand-side pressures, such as policymaker priorities and external funding.

The other explanation is the “credibility revolution”, a phenomenon whereby economists began eschewing theoretical models in favour of empirical approaches. As methodology such as difference-in-differences and randomised controlled trials cemented their place in the literature, applied work expanded so fast that theoretical fields were outgrown rather than abandoned.

Empiricism helps economists make causal inferences. Research from Prashant Garg, a postdoctoral researcher at Bocconi University, and Thiemo Fetzer, economics professor at Warwick University, finds causal claims in economics have jumped. In 1990, 7.7 per cent of claims made in the literature were causal. In 2023, that hit 32.6 per cent. Additionally, papers with more causal claims are more likely to receive citations and wind up in top five journals, the research suggests. By this measure, economics is increasingly resembling a hard science.

But that scientific turn has brought consequences. Results derived from real-world data and experiments are hard to replicate under the same conditions and methodology, with research suggesting that up to 70 per cent of recently examined economics papers contain some results that cannot be reproduced. Sometimes this is simply because the data is broken or otherwise unavailable to other researchers, although other theories abound: pressure to publish, data manipulation, patterns of funding and structural incentives in the academy, for instance. There are also cynical explanations, such as questionable research practices or fabricated data sets.

AI is the next frontier. At a recent academic conference, I was baffled by how economists were deploying the technology to process and gather data, contracting tasks that previously would have required teams of researchers and weeks of time into a few hours’ work. Moreover, some practitioners are embracing machine learning to process non-text data, such as images and sounds, or to capture non-linearity. That said, AI is also creating low-quality content, straining the capacity of editorial teams at prominent journals.

Larry Katz, economics professor at Harvard University and editor of the Quarterly Journal of Economics, told me that although he had noticed an uptick in submissions, AI-generated papers “are easily spotted from a quick skim and can be rapidly desk-rejected by human co-editors at this point”. And even though editorial workloads have increased, with the QJE planning to onboard another co-editor to handle the additional capacity, the global growth of economic researchers, especially in China, could also be playing a role, he added.

“The number of high-quality submissions we are getting appears to be rising as well in my view,” adds Katz, perhaps as AI polishes text irregularities and formats copy in the right style. The technology is also good at identifying small technical mistakes, he says.

As long as the academy keeps a close eye on rigour, especially as economists embrace frontier technologies and methods, the future of economics looks dynamic. Not bad for a subject once thought so dismal.

Send your thoughts to freelunch@ft.com.

Food for thought

Cultural shifts towards patience, openness and individualism were major drivers of economic growth in the early modern period, new research suggests.

item.title: All aboard the wind power rollercoaster
item.author: Simon Mundy
item.description: Vestas share price surge highlights wild swings in investor sentiment
item.content:encoded:
Vestas share price surge highlights wild swings in investor sentiment

Simon Mundy

Welcome back.

Shares in Danish wind turbine producer Vestas, which have spent much of the past few years taking a hammering, jumped by more than 20 per cent after the company’s quarterly results statement on Wednesday.

Are the boom times back for this sector? The answer is complicated — and it highlights some of the most important current trends in green energy, as I explain below.

Have a great weekend.

Winds of change

Vestas’s stock chart is starting to resemble the blueprint for a fairground rollercoaster.

The market value of Europe’s biggest wind turbine maker tripled in less than nine months to reach a record high in January 2021, amid feverish investor excitement about green energy growth. It went on to give up all those gains and more, as the wind sector was hit by rising financing and component costs — and then by Donald Trump’s return to the White House.

Now it’s soaring skywards again. Vestas shares gained more than a fifth on Wednesday after it announced strong second-quarter earnings growth and gave a bullish forecast for the rest of the year. The shares are now up over 150 per cent from their nadir in April 2025. Shares in smaller German rival Nordex have done even better, tripling since the start of last year.

This comes amid some real grounds for bullishness in their home European market. Governments — keen to reduce exposure to fossil fuel price shocks such as the Strait of Hormuz crisis — have been strengthening the systems through which wind farms can receive guaranteed prices for the power they generate, reducing investment risk. Countries including the UK, Germany and France have all held successful large-scale wind power auctions in recent months.

Trouble in America

Overseas, however, the outlook seems shakier. A casual glance at this week’s earnings statement might suggest that Vestas’s US business is in fine fettle. It delivered 1.1 gigawatts’ worth of wind turbines to US power projects in the second quarter — comfortably more than to any other country, and a nearly 50 per cent year-on-year rise.

But that flurry may be followed by much leaner times in the US market. Developers have been rushing to take advantage of the green energy tax credits introduced in Joe Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act. The Trump-backed law phasing them out stipulated that wind power projects must start construction by July 4 this year (or enter service by the end of 2027) to be eligible.

Trump will fall short of his goal “not to let any windmill be built”. Surging electricity demand in the US, particularly among big tech companies, is driving a desire for “more of everything”, as Vestas chief executive Henrik Andersen put it on Wednesday. See, for instance, Google’s February announcement of a deal to support 1.4GW of new wind capacity to power a new data centre in Minnesota.

The US administration’s anti-wind crusade has also been running into legal hurdles — notably last week, when a judge ordered the Pentagon to stop stalling onshore wind projects by refusing to process once-routine approvals.

But the policy environment has still had a damaging impact on developer appetite for new wind projects — particularly offshore ones, which have been the biggest target of the government pushback. “For offshore wind, besides the projects under construction, you will not have any new project development [under the current administration], for sure,” says Tancrède Fulop, an analyst at Morningstar.

Competitive threat

Elsewhere, the big problem for Europe’s wind turbine producers, which also include Siemens Gamesa and Enercon, is Chinese competition.

Chinese groups, led by Goldwind, now account for all six of the world’s biggest wind turbine producers in terms of new capacity installed last year. The vast majority of that was delivered to domestic clients. But they offer export prices 30 to 40 per cent lower than their European rivals who once dominated the sector, according to an analysis last year by Rystad.

Chinese competition, at least, is one thing European turbine makers don’t need to worry about too much in the US. In their home market, they may get a boost from regulatory scrutiny of Chinese rivals over concerns about security and unfair competition. The obliteration of Europe’s solar manufacturing sector is an unnerving precedent.

Some in the sector want the EU to go further and bend its merger control rules to allow Europe’s wind producers to consolidate and gain the economies of scale needed to compete globally. Vestas boss Andersen backed that idea this week, warning: “Size matters and that’s the only thing.”

Globally, the outlook for wind power growth looks robust. China — which installed nearly three times as much wind capacity last year as the rest of the world combined — is targeting a massive further expansion under a five-year strategy unveiled last month.

Economics should keep things moving forward. The levelised cost of onshore wind is substantially lower than that of fossil-fuel power, according to analysis by BloombergNEF, and falling battery storage costs continue to boost the case for intermittent solar and wind power. The International Energy Agency reckons global wind generation will increase 65 per cent from the 2025 level by 2030. But Europe’s turbine makers will have to fight hard for their share of that action.

Smart reads

Effective altruism went into reverse after the downfall of crypto baron Sam Bankman-Fried. Now the philanthropic movement has fresh momentum, thanks to the rise of ultra-wealthy AI developers.

Investors should wake up to the risk of “an emerging climate-sovereign doom loop”, writes Simon Nixon.

item.title: Alarm bells are ringing for investors on climate
item.author: Simon Nixon
item.description: Damage wrought by wildfires in Europe should be a wake-up call to pay more attention to environmental risk
item.content:encoded:
Damage wrought by wildfires in Europe should be a wake-up call to pay more attention to environmental risk

Simon Nixon

The writer is the publisher of the Wealth of Nations newsletter

Many investors have taken a sceptical view of ESG investing in the past few years, and governments have been scrambling to retreat from climate commitments — particularly now there is a climate-change denier back in the White House. But if this summer’s extreme weather in Europe has served any useful purpose amid the death and destruction, it should be to force a rethink.

The damage wrought by the wildfires that have engulfed parts of France, Spain and Greece will probably be huge — as much as €3bn according to an FT analysis. Nor is it unusual. The European Environment Agency reckons that between 1980 and 2024 extreme weather events, including floods, storms and droughts, caused €822bn of damage, a quarter of it in the past four years alone. And that is only the direct cost. The indirect costs include higher inflation, not least through food prices and disruption to supply chains; weaker productivity as working time is lost and infrastructure damaged; and stranded assets as businesses close and regions depopulate.

What should worry investors is the effect these events may have on the finances of highly indebted sovereigns as they grow more frequent. During the Eurozone debt crisis, markets rightly feared a sovereign-bank doom loop. As the Brussels-based think-tank Bruegel warned in a recent report, the danger now is an emerging climate-sovereign doom loop. Rising climate costs erode sovereign creditworthiness, which in turn limits the fiscal capacity to spend on adaptation and mitigation, leading to still larger costs in future.

These are neither trivial nor distant concerns. EU member states are collectively spending just €29bn a year on climate adaptation and mitigation, compared with the €70bn annually that the European Commission has estimated they need to spend between now and 2050. According to a recent study by the World Resources Institute, every euro spent on adaptation is estimated to save €10 of future damage. Meanwhile, in a heat-stress scenario in which each country’s hottest recent years are replayed over the remainder of the decade, Europe’s most exposed economies could suffer an aggregate loss of between 5 and 7 per cent of GDP, reckons the insurer Allianz. France alone could be hit by about €210bn of costs by 2030, adding 2.2 per cent of GDP to its deficit.

Already there is a clear link between higher physical climate risk and higher sovereign borrowing costs even after factoring in standard macro-debt variables, notes Michael Penn, a climate analyst at Absolute Strategy Research.

He estimates that as many as 60 countries could face climate-related downgrades by 2030, with the most vulnerable to default risk including Egypt, Pakistan and Nigeria. Conversely, some countries could see climate-related improvements in their ratings, whether because, like Chile, they have strong renewables potential or, like Argentina, have abundant resources needed for the transition.

Europe, though, is particularly exposed, Penn notes — not just because its banks tend to be large holders of sovereign debt, but because they increasingly hold diversified portfolios of other member states’ bonds. This raises the risk of contagion should climate stress trigger a financial crisis in any one country. Little wonder the European Central Bank has been flagging these risks for years, urging governments to work with the private sector to widen climate insurance. With about 20 per cent of losses currently insured, falling to as low as 1 per cent in Romania, the rest is more likely to end up on the sovereign balance sheet, the state serving as insurer of last resort.

But while the European institutions are showing some welcome vigilance, the same cannot be said of the US. That is especially troubling because, as David Owen of Saltmarsh Economics has noted, America may be even more vulnerable than Europe. The Saltmarsh Economics Climate Index, established over a decade ago, shows the US scoring worse on both emissions and the estimated economic costs of climate-related disasters. Indeed, the latter are averaging about 0.5 per cent of GDP in the US, more than double that of Europe — with much of that risk concentrated in a handful of states.

This is precisely the sort of thing US regulators ought to be tracking closely. That they no longer do makes it all the more important that investors pay attention themselves — ready for the day when an extreme weather event triggers an extreme market event.

item.title: How will El Niño hit the world economy?
item.author: Simon Mundy
item.description: Disruptive climate event is likely to be one of the strongest on record
item.content:encoded:
Disruptive climate event is likely to be one of the strongest on record

Simon Mundy

Hello from London, where glimpses of green grass have become a rarity as the UK enters the fifth heatwave of a drought-ridden summer, prompting new Prime Minister Andy Burnham to call a meeting today of the Cobra emergency committee.

Extreme heat has ravaged much of the northern hemisphere over the past couple of months — a stark reflection of the onward march of climate change. (FT climate experts Attracta Mooney and Pilita Clark will be holding a live Q&A on the subject tomorrow: sign up here.)

Now global temperatures are in line for a further boost from a major episode of the naturally occurring El Niño phenomenon, which threatens wild weather and increased heat across much of the world over the coming months. How bad could things get?

Markets brace for El Niño

Investment firm Moreton Capital Partners is raising money for a new fund with an unusual focus: profiting from the El Niño cycle of temperature changes in the Pacific Ocean.

The hedge fund wants to exploit what it reckons is a failure by other investors to appreciate the market implications of the El Niño event that started in recent weeks and is expected to drive extreme weather events across multiple continents.

But Moreton is far from alone in paying attention to this issue. Prices of commodities such as coffee and cocoa have been soaring in recent weeks as traders anticipate blows to harvests in Asia and Africa. Investment banks have been publishing primers for clients on how to navigate the market impacts, and the World Bank is warning that the event may push up international food prices.

The back story

El Niño got its name from Peruvian fishermen, who were aware since at least the 19th century of a recurrent warming of the coastal ocean that drastically reduced their catch. They named it after the infant Jesus because the effects typically hit them around Christmas.

The cause, we now know, is a cyclical interaction between the Pacific Ocean and the atmosphere above it, involving the dominant trade winds that normally run strongly from east to west across the Pacific, driving warm water with them.

Every two to seven years, these winds weaken (or even reverse), allowing the waters to get warmer in central and eastern sections of the ocean — interfering with atmospheric circulation and disrupting weather patterns across much of the world.

But while El Niño events are nothing new, this year’s looks set to be unusually severe, judging by sea surface temperatures and atmospheric indicators in the Pacific. The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration estimates there is more than an 80 per cent chance it will become “very strong”, which would make it one of the most powerful events in a record that dates back to 1950.

While some modelling studies have suggested that anthropogenic climate change could increase the frequency of extreme El Niño events, the World Meteorological Organization says there is “no evidence” that this is already happening.

What is clear, however, is that global warming has been increasing the risks from El Niño events by altering the baseline conditions in which they occur. These events commonly raise the annual global average temperature by one- or two-tenths of a degree Celsius — a shift that’s now layered on top of an already dangerous 1.4C of human-driven warming since the pre-industrial era. And because a warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, the destructive downpours that El Niño can fuel in regions such as east Africa look still more threatening.

Another reason for concern is the broader economic context within which this event is happening. Global fertiliser flows have been disrupted this year by the turmoil in the Strait of Hormuz, with serious implications for crop output — notably in developing nations that are expected to suffer some of the worst impacts from El Niño.

Commodities crunch

Worries about all this are already conspicuous in the agricultural commodity market, as the FT’s Susannah Savage reported a few days ago. As west African cocoa producers face an elevated threat of drought, prices of the chocolate ingredient have risen 37 per cent since the start of June. Arabica coffee prices are up 26 per cent, as Brazilian producers anticipate a harvest reduced by excessive heat and volatile rainfall.

Wheat production in Australia and rice output in India face serious threats from El Niño’s negative effects on rainfall, according to UN Food and Agriculture Organization chief economist Máximo Torero. Rainfall in India’s crucial monsoon season has so far been more than a tenth below the average level.

A blow to Indian production may push up global sugar prices, reckon analysts at Morgan Stanley, while copper mining could be disrupted in Zambia by drought and in Chile, in contrast, by flooding.

El Niño could also interfere with trade logistics — notably if drought in Central America reduces the depth of the Panama Canal, as has happened previously. Auction prices for slots to navigate the canal’s busiest lanes have jumped to record highs, the FT has reported, with factors including new restrictions on passage amid concerns about falling water levels.

The bigger picture

Like counterparts at other banks, however, Morgan Stanley’s team reckons the impact on major global stock markets is likely to be limited, noting that El Niño has historically had little effect on indices such as the S&P 500. Recent analysis by Capital Economics, meanwhile, found no clear relationship between El Niño events and global food price inflation.

Yet to focus only on these global statistics is to ignore the serious impacts that El Niño events can bring at the national and regional level. Capital Economics warns that there’s a clear risk of significant food price rises in lower-income countries in south Asia and sub-Saharan Africa resulting from this year’s event. This event threatens to push at least 49mn more people into food insecurity, the World Food Programme warned last week.

And the economic impacts may be more serious and long-lasting than is commonly appreciated. A 2023 study in Science found that major El Niño episodes had a severe effect on growth rates in dozens of countries, with income losses persisting for years after each event.

The heightened financial market interest in the El Niño phenomenon probably won’t be much help to those worst affected by it. It may, however, reflect a growing appreciation of the financial impacts of extreme weather events and other environmental threats. As the global temperature continues to ratchet up, those risks are getting ever harder to ignore.

Smart reads

The need for action on global warming is clear to all except the real climate zealots: the anti-net zero brigade, writes Pilita Clark.

OpenAI’s head of ethics Chloé Bakalar has left the company without any public announcement less than a year after joining.

Chinese company Sea Legend has launched the first regular container shipping service through the Arctic, as climate change-driven ice melt makes the route more viable.

item.title: Whither Trump’s tariffs?
item.author: Aime Williams
item.description: Using a patchwork of obscure laws, US officials have set up a series of new probes that could result in fresh duties
item.content:encoded:
Using a patchwork of obscure laws, US officials have set up a series of new probes that could result in fresh duties

Aime Williams

Hello, I’m the FT’s US trade correspondent Aime Williams, filling in for Alan Beattie while he’s on holiday. In today’s newsletter, I’m aiming to give a bit of a dispatch from the US capital, where President Donald Trump’s trade war is riven with new tensions between his diplomatic, economic and political goals.

Charted Waters, where we use data to analyse world trade, is on China’s export engine, which shows no sign of letting up.

Washington keeps its options open

It’s a funny moment for Trump’s trade war. Gone are the heady days when hastily composed rage-tweets threatening huge tariffs on US allies were splashed across the front pages. Now those threats are made less often and mostly draw resigned shrugs.

Trump’s lost ability to use “emergency” tariff powers is one part of that after the US Supreme Court constrained him back in February. Another is the mood in America right now. The administration is staggering towards the midterms still embroiled in a costly war with Iran that has pushed up oil prices, driving inflation across the US economy and, perhaps most devastatingly, at petrol pumps. The combination of those two factors has changed Washington’s approach. 

In recent months, Trump’s advisers have been warning him against doing anything that could risk the shocks of his early trade war days, when his steep tariffs triggered a global stock market rout and a sharp sell-off in US Treasuries.

Since then, we’ve seen a lot of exemptions, carve-outs and general tinkering. We’ve also seen a few “national security” probes which, despite being expected to lead to duties, have concluded only with recommendations of further talks. The Section 232 investigations into critical minerals and aeroplane parts spring to mind.

Trump is not going to give up on tariffs. And he still hasn’t forgiven the Supreme Court for knocking down his original wall: he posted on his Truth Social platform railing against the justices for costing the US “TRILLIONS AND TRILLIONS OF DOLLARS” just a few weeks ago. (The reality is that one dogged judge in the lower Court of International Trade has hounded customs officials into refunding more than $100bn of those duties to date.)

But it’s fair to say the trade war has passed into the hands of the professionals. Now reliant on a patchwork of obscure laws, US officials have set up a series of new investigations and probes that could all lead to tariffs.

These have started bearing fruit. The US hit 60 trading partners with tariff rates ranging from 10 per cent to 12.5 per cent after a probe into “forced labour”, carried out under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, just as previous global levies of 10 per cent — imposed under Section 122 of the same act — expired.

Moreover, officials launched a separate investigation — also carried out under Section 301 — into excess manufacturing capacity. This probe includes the EU, China, Singapore, Switzerland, Norway, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, South Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Mexico, Japan and India.

But what of the previous trade deals Trump struck with partners that promised them specific tariff rates? Behind the scenes, US trade officials are telling many allies that their deals will stand. But a new wave of tariff probes has left diplomats concerned that the agreements will be overwritten by combinations of new levies.

Take the EU. Including the most-favoured nation rate, the bloc now faces an extra US tariff of 10 per cent as a result of the recent “forced labour” probe. But under the bloc’s 2025 trade deal struck in Turnberry, it was handed a 15 per cent duty on most goods. That means if the forthcoming probe into structural overcapacity concludes with a tariff on EU goods of more than 5 per cent, Turnberry gets broken. Many diplomats fret the rate will come in higher.

One thing the Trump administration could do if it wanted to both wield big threats and keep its word on previous deals is diligently complete its investigations and recommend large duties for US trading partners but suspend their implementation pending further negotiation.

Dan Mullaney, a former US trade negotiator, pointed out that in 2018, the first Trump administration threatened tariffs under Section 301 in retaliation for EU digital services taxes, but suspended applying them to allow international talks to take place at the OECD.

Taking this approach would be one way to increase the urgency of talks with some of the US’s partners that are dragging on. India, for example, is continuing to be slow and hard work for US negotiators trying to push forward on progressing a trade deal.

The US has also been sending nasty letters to the EU reminding Brussels of White House demands and complaints about non-tariff barriers. Trump’s US trade representative, Jamieson Greer, has been vocal about the bloc’s slow pace of implementing both tariff cuts and rollbacks of rules and regulations. 

Most recently, EU fines on US tech companies such as Apple, Amazon and Meta have caught Trump’s eye, triggering the threat of more tariffs. These, too, would need to be imposed following an investigation, which Trump officials have previously threatened to start.

It’s worth making a bit of an aside here about Canada, which seems to be the subject of a new experiment by Washington to test out a novel use of Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, an authority that has never before been used to impose duties on a trading partner. Specifically, US officials are trying to hit their northern neighbour with duties on about $20bn worth of goods to retaliate for unfair treatment on American cars, alcohol and cheese.

As ever, though, these duties are suspended for a while to allow the painful trade talks between Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s team to bear fruit. It’ll be worth watching whether those tariffs actually bite, which they’re set to do in less than a fortnight.

Broadly, the mechanisms for ratcheting up pressure on US trading partners again are certainly there, even as Trump’s advisers fret about the US economy in the run-up to the midterms. For now, Washington is keeping its options open.

Charted waters

Despite Trump’s best attempts, China’s trade engine remains robust, with the country’s exports rising by almost a quarter last month on a year earlier.

Trade links

  • Both Trump and young Americans are warming to China, suggests Ali Wyne, senior research and advocacy adviser for US-China relations at think-tank International Crisis Group.
  • China plans to bypass shipping chokepoints with an “Ice Silk Road”, a route through the Arctic that will skirt the north Russian coast on its journey between Ningbo and Felixstowe, UK.
  • Joshua Kurlantzick of the Council on Foreign Relations think-tank points out that, while leaders at a recent Asean foreign ministers meeting were angry at the US, they did almost nothing about it.

Trade Secrets is edited by Harvey Nriapia

item.title: Could AI create a ‘permanent underclass’?
item.author: Adam Shaw
item.description: San Francisco’s language is hyperbolic — but the technology could bifurcate the labour market
item.content:encoded:
San Francisco’s language is hyperbolic — but the technology could bifurcate the labour market

Adam Shaw

In the San Francisco Bay Area, one often hears the same story about AI. The technology, according to many who work at the labs, will create a “permanent underclass”. Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei referenced the phenomenon in an essay this year, estimating that 50 per cent of entry-level white-collar jobs will be disrupted within five years.

The idea is as follows: as the models approach artificial general intelligence, a small tech elite will own the AI platforms, data centres and energy that power much of the economy. Agentic AI and advanced robotics will replace labour as we know it and most jobs will disappear. The majority of the population, according to the San Francisco view, will have few assets and struggle to earn a decent income selling their labour.

Economists should be sceptical of grand narratives that lack hard evidence. Certainly, the views of tech employees are conjecture. Labour market data provides scant, inconclusive proof of AI disruption. And some of the most eminent economists have predicted that AI will have a more modest impact.

But we are in the early days of AI adoption. And the “underclass” theory, though perhaps hyperbolic, could gesture at some uncomfortable truths. If gains accrue primarily to capital holders and some expert employees, labour market dynamics could deskill other workers and push down the cost of their labour. If human capital investment in low-wage workers declines as a result, society could move towards a scenario that somewhat resembles the San Francisco view.

Research suggests that automation could drive bifurcated labour-market outcomes. A paper by David Autor and Neil Thompson finds it can either boost wages by replacing low-expertise tasks or decrease wages by replacing high-expertise tasks. Workers with knowhow that cannot be substituted by machines could see massive wage gains, while others could be deskilled and lose their livelihoods. A recent Anthropic study similarly demonstrated higher returns from Claude Code to high-expertise users. (Amodei has previously referenced Autor’s other work on skill-biased technological change.)

As AI boosts productivity, gains from innovation could concentrate in the hands of those with capital and expertise (that is, a form of human capital). A study on patents filed in the early 2000s provides some evidence for this, showing that for every dollar of value added by a new invention, 30 cents went to workers and 70 cents became profit. Most of the additional worker pay accrued to employees with already high salaries, who presumably had higher expertise.

We shouldn’t be surprised if economic gains from AI accrue primarily to those building the data centres and frontier models. Though economists tend to assume that the labour and capital shares of production stay constant in the long run, the San Francisco crowd insists that agentic AI will substitute capital for labour and shift this paradigm.

Second-order labour-market effects of AI could amplify the gap between high- and low-wage workers. As deskilled workers lose their jobs, an oversupply of newly deskilled labour could push down wages for all low-skilled workers. And while there will probably be new low-skilled jobs that arise from AI models’ tremendous demand for data, such as roles in data gathering and aggregation, it is hard to know today how they will look and pay. 

Productivity divergence could have long-term effects. Upskilling and reskilling workers is difficult. Moreover, research suggests parental wage shocks can weigh on skills development in children, transmitting wage effects on to the next generation. Evidence suggests that workers with lower incomes invest in human capital at lower rates, blunting social mobility. As productivity between workers diverges, the incentive to invest in education and training for low-income people could fall, amplifying the bifurcation.

Some don’t buy the “underclass” view. Instead, they argue, AI productivity gains will boost production, push down prices and benefit consumers. But this depends on how the technology augments production: AI will create lots of cheap software, but will do less to boost the quantity of less supply-elastic essentials, such as housing. Unevenly distributed productivity gains could make these goods less accessible for deskilled workers.

Though a “permanent underclass” is not an imminent reality, in the near term AI could make some people richer and others worse off. Policymakers could today strengthen the social safety net in anticipation of bifurcated labour-market outcomes. But if AI changes the economy in fundamental ways, democratic societies might need to reimagine how productivity gains can better serve the public good, lest the Bay Area’s pessimistic visions materialise.

Send your thoughts to freelunch@ft.com.

Food for thought

What do high minimum wages have to do with robots and automation? This paper explains.

Free Lunch on Sunday is edited by Harvey Nriapia

item.title: US public pension funds and business groups clash on SEC climate risk disclosure shift
item.author: Alexandra White
item.description: Vanguard and Norway’s sovereign wealth fund strike cautious response to regulator
item.content:encoded:
Vanguard and Norway’s sovereign wealth fund strike cautious response to regulator

Alexandra White

Major public investors, including pension funds Calpers and Calstrs, have clashed with big business lobby groups over the Securities and Exchange Commission’s proposal to rescind a rule requiring companies to disclose certain climate-related information. 

The US securities regulator in May proposed rescinding the Biden-era climate risk disclosure rule that was never enacted after it ran into the threat of lawsuits by various Republican-led states and trade groups.

Under the Trump administration, the SEC said the rule was a “dramatic over-reach” of the commission’s authority, but some big asset managers and pension funds have argued that climate-related information is financially material even as big business groups supported rescinding the rules.

Vanguard, the world’s second-largest asset manager and a target of Trump-era legal threats, tried to strike a balance in its submission in response to the SEC 60-day comment period.

The asset manager, with $12tn of assets under management, said it agreed that policymakers should avoid imposing disclosures that are “costly, confusing and overburdensome”.

But it also noted there was value in “standardised and comparable disclosure of material risks, including material climate-related risks”.

“When a company has identified material climate-related risks, disclosure about these risks should enable more accurate valuations and efficient price discovery,” Vanguard said.

Norway’s $2tn sovereign wealth fund was also careful in its response. It opposed the “outright rescission” of the rule but said it believed there were alternatives “that would address the Commission’s concerns about scope and cost, while preserving a baseline of financially material disclosure”. 

Several public pension funds opposed the SEC’s move, including the California Public Employees’ Retirement System (Calpers), the California State Teachers’ Retirement System (Calstrs), as well as the New York state comptroller Thomas DiNapoli, who oversees the $294.4bn New York State Common Retirement Fund. 

Calpers said in a letter the rescission of the rule would result in uneven reporting, forcing investors to gather data through proprietary questionnaires and third-party estimates, which would be fragmented, less reliable and more costly.

In contrast, business groups, including the Business Roundtable — a coalition of more than 200 chief executives of big US companies — backed axing the rule.

The American Petroleum Institute, whose oil and gas company members would be significantly affected by the rules because of the focus on greenhouse gas emissions, climate-related risks and energy transition planning, said a “full and prompt rescission” would “produce real benefits”.

“It will eliminate substantial and unnecessary compliance burdens . . . It will protect investors from being inundated with information that is not material.”

Notably, individual asset managers were split on the issue along geographic lines, demonstrating a transatlantic divide.

Federated Hermes’ London-based EOS arm, which oversees $2.4tn of assets under stewardship, said it continued to believe that investors would benefit from “consistent, comparable and reliable disclosure of material climate-related risks and opportunities”, while agreeing with the SEC that there were opportunities to eliminate redundancies across disclosure requirements.

But, in a separate submission, the overall business of Federated Hermes, based in Pittsburgh, said it supported the proposal to rescind the rule “and return to a disclosure framework centred on materiality, issuer-specific analysis, and the commission’s longstanding principles-based approach”.

“I’m not surprised that there are investors opposing the recession,” said Allison Herren Lee, former commissioner at the SEC who helped oversee the development of the climate risk disclosure rule. “When the SEC proposed the climate risk disclosure rule, it was after lots of feedback from investors and issuers in support of a rule.”

Although US companies may not be subject to a federal sustainability reporting law, they could still be subject to disclosure rules in other jurisdictions.

A variety of states, including New Jersey, Colorado and Illinois, have proposed state-level reporting rules. New York has advanced a bill to mandate that companies disclose their emissions, while California will require companies doing business in the state that meet a revenue threshold exceeding $1bn to release operating emission disclosures by November.

Brooke Lierman, Maryland comptroller, who also oversees the state’s public retirement assets and wrote a letter to the SEC opposing its shift, said the patchwork of emerging state-level reporting requirements will increase the cost of doing business.

“It behoves all of us to have one standard set of disclosures required by the SEC,” she said.

The SEC did not comment.

Additional reporting by Attracta Mooney in London

item.title: Hooked on diesel: the economy looking to kick the habit
item.author: Attracta Mooney
item.description: Pacific island of Palau is fundraising for a pivot to clean energy
item.content:encoded:
Pacific island of Palau is fundraising for a pivot to clean energy

Attracta Mooney

Hello from London. I’m the FT’s climate correspondent, stepping in for Simon Mundy while he’s on sabbatical.

I’ve spent much of this summer writing about extreme weather in Europe and elsewhere, but today I wanted to come back to an issue I often think about and write about — the challenges of financing the energy transition. 

Small islands: big problem

There is a lot of money going into renewable energy, with $2.2tn expected to be invested this year, according to the International Energy Agency. And for every $1 spent on fossil fuels, $2 is spent on clean energy. But nearly all of the green investment — 90 per cent — is in advanced economies and China.

Now the president of Palau is trying to lure some of that money to the south Pacific island archipelago, which is located roughly 900km east of the Philippines.

“The Pacific as a whole consumes $6bn in fuel every year. And there is a huge opportunity for investment in renewable energy,” Surangel Whipps said on a recent London visit.  

As this year’s energy crisis sparked by the war in the Middle East played out, Pacific island leaders invoked the Biketawa Declaration, the region’s highest-level crisis response mechanism. 

This was because those nations, which are at the forefront of the climate crisis because of rising sea levels, are heavily reliant on imported oil.

Excluding Australia and New Zealand, oil accounts for about 80 per cent of the Pacific region’s total energy supply — and almost all of it is imported.

In Palau, the non-profit research group Zero Carbon Analytics estimates that diesel accounts for 70 per cent of electricity generation.

“For us, diesel pricing more than doubled . . . those basic costs at home just skyrocketed and it’s tough when you have no options,” says Whipps. Consumer power bills were subsidised in Palau in response to the energy crisis, he said, while in the Marshall Islands and Tuvalu, the authorities of the small island states implemented emergency measures aimed at conserving dwindling fuel supplies. 

20% by 2020

For the citizens of Palau, the latest energy crisis highlighted how important a shift to renewable sources of power was for energy independence. Whipps told me: “This is a wake-up call.”  

In 2015, Palau set a target for 20 per cent renewables by 2020 — a target it missed.

Whipps said one of the biggest challenges at the time was around costs and convincing consumers “to pay more for power when diesel is less”. That is less of a problem now, as the cost of solar and wind has come down substantially while the oil price remains volatile. 

Research this year suggests shifting to renewables could lower electricity costs by 55 per cent on average across small island states in the Pacific.

Palau is now aiming to add 60 megawatts of solar and battery storage — which Whipps said would mean 90 per cent of its power needs were provided by green energy. Palau currently has about 22MW of installed renewable energy on its grid, the government says.

The island state wants to lure private-sector investors, multilateral development banks and others. “We’re here to get people to invest, get cheap financing and get this done,” Whipps said. About $120mn is needed, he said.

Luring investment 

But the relatively small investment combined with the logistics of getting to Pacific islands — which comes with additional shipping costs and longer procurement timelines — meant drumming up significant institutional interest could be a challenge, he admitted. 

For many big investors there are questions about the cost-effectiveness of backing such projects. Many would rather put their money into projects in Europe or other rich economies, instead of taking on additional risks — whether real or perceived — elsewhere. And even if private-sector investors can be persuaded to invest outside of western economies, they often seek out bigger projects in bigger countries. 

Still, in 2018 when Palau, with the backing of the Asian Development Bank and a loan from the Australian government, issued a request for a proposal during its initial foray into renewables, it managed to attract seven bidders, says Whipps. 

In the end a Filipino group called Solar Pacific won the contract. The efforts revealed problems with grid stability, which have since been addressed, the government says.

“You need to open tender and you need to bring people in and you can really drive [down] the cost,” Whipps said. 

Across the Pacific Islands, energy security financing peaked in 2019 at $367mn, driven by a one-off surge in renewable energy spending, before falling back to an annual average of about $193mn across 2020-22, according to the Australia-based Lowy Institute. 

Palau will host a special climate event as part of the Pacific Islands Forum Leaders Meeting in August, while the region will also co-host the so-called pre-COP summit in October, ahead of the main annual UN climate talks the following month in Antalya, Turkey.

Whipps is hoping to pitch his project — and the need for the shift to renewable energy across the Pacific Islands. 

“We should double down on [the energy transition] . . . because that makes you more energy secure, but it is also cheaper and more stable and reliable for your people.”

Smart reads

The amount of green bonds issued in Europe is set to rebound to record levels this year, taking global issuance to an all-time high, as revived interest in energy security during the US-Iran war helps to offset falling issuance in the US.

Wildfires and heatwaves sweeping across Europe have already cost more than €3bn so far this year, according to FT analysis, in the latest example of how climate change has mounting economic costs.

item.title: European green bonds rebound to take share from ‘greenhushed’ US
item.author: Ramsay Hodgson
item.description: Issuance in the region will drive global sales to record high this year, despite ‘death of ESG’ in Trump’s America
item.content:encoded:
Issuance in the region will drive global sales to record high this year, despite ‘death of ESG’ in Trump’s America

Ramsay Hodgson

The amount of green bonds issued in Europe is set to rebound to record levels this year, taking global issuance to an all-time high, as revived interest in energy security during the US-Iran war helps to offset falling issuance in the US.

A record $242bn of European green-aligned bonds were issued in the first half of 2026, according to the Climate Bonds Initiative, a UK-based NGO. Total global issuance is on track to exceed the $673bn sold in 2024, the previous record year, when issuance in Europe totalled $385bn.

This year’s European green bond revival strikes a markedly different chord from the US, where issuance is expected to fall for the second year running as companies pull back from burnishing their green credentials out of fear of retaliation from Washington.

“In Europe, we have not really seen this kind of death of ESG that was very much present in the US,” said Larissa de Barros Fritz, senior fixed-income strategist at ABN Amro. “This year, the whole ESG story is back.”

She added: “It’s not that [US companies] don’t care about ESG or the energy transition. It’s much more of a ‘greenhush’. They’re doing it, but they are not putting the label on it . . . there’s a lot of political influence and backlash.”

US President Donald Trump has pursued a so-called Drill Baby Drill agenda to promote the use of fossil fuels and has celebrated terminating “hundreds of Biden-era Green New Scam projects”.

Green bonds are a type of debt sold by corporations and governments to raise capital for spending on environmental projects. Their prominence has grown over the past decade, most significantly in Europe where the market is most mature and where sellers and asset managers have been eager to demonstrate their environmental, social and governance credentials.

Around $374bn of green bonds were sold in Europe last year, according to the Climate Bonds Initiative, about 55 per cent of global issuance. This year, the continent is on track to deliver almost two-thirds of new green debt worldwide.

“Last year was very much marked by a sort of step back in ESG agendas . . . in Europe to a lesser extent. Nevertheless, there could have been some spillover [from the US],” said de Barros Fritz.

Juan Valencia, a European credit strategist at Société Générale, said the volume of green bonds being issued in Europe was rising “very quickly”.

“We suspect volumes will rise well above last year’s numbers and 2024 levels to set a new record,” he said.

Global green debt sales flatlined in 2025 as European and North American issuance dipped amid the Trump administration’s anti-ESG agenda and as issuers waited for regulatory clarity. Despite this, rising issuance in China helped to keep levels close to the previous year’s total.

Sales in Europe last year were hampered by issuers awaiting the rollout of the EU’s voluntary but tougher green bond standards and the International Capital Market Association’s fresh guidance on green bonds.

US green debt sales peaked in 2021 with $94bn sold. Issuance has since declined, with $77bn raised last year and expectations that it will fall again in 2026, after bonds with a value of just $34bn were sold in the first half.

“[Europe’s] increase in market share has helped offset declines in green bond issuance from the US,” said Mitch Reznick, head of fixed income at Federated Hermes.

Utilities companies have been particularly strong issuers in 2026, as Europe has renewed its focus on energy security following the energy shock from the US-Iran war. Valencia at Société Générale predicted that the market would continue to grow on the back of an acceleration in the green transition.

In June, Spain’s Iberdrola raised €1.5bn by issuing two green bonds, while German-based and Chinese-owned EEW Energy from Waste raised €550mn. In February, EDF raised €2.75bn through green bonds.

“The energy transition story did lose a bit of breath last year and now it’s regaining traction,” de Barros Fritz said.

“With the US-Iran conflict there was a lot of demand for utilities debt and the whole idea about the energy transition has regained a lot of attention.”

item.title: Plurilateral deals are last best hope for world trading system
item.author: Peter Foster
item.description: Agreements between ‘coalitions of the willing’ can gain traction over time and be subsumed into WTO frameworks
item.content:encoded:
Agreements between ‘coalitions of the willing’ can gain traction over time and be subsumed into WTO frameworks

Peter Foster

Good afternoon, and welcome to Trade Secrets. I’m Peter Foster, the FT’s world trade editor, standing in again for Alan who is on his hols. This week I wanted to look at how global trade governance is functioning in a time of evident dysfunction. Five months after the failed MC14 ministerial conference in Cameroon, the World Trade Organization remains moribund in several key respects, but in an era when technology is transforming both the nature and process of trade, business craves global rulemaking more than ever.

Andy Burnham has showered the nation in announcements since becoming UK prime minister, often dressing up relatively small amounts of cash as big “retail” offerings to voters struggling with the cost of living. In Charted Waters, with the help of the wonks at the UK Trade Policy Observatory, we unpack why promises to cut tariffs on consumer goods by his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer aren’t going to make an appreciable difference at the checkout.

Flicker of hope

It’s been five months since that long and steamy night in the Cameroonian capital Yaoundé when a political stand-off between the US and Brazil saw the WTO’s ministerial conference end in failure. The talks had been billed as a “last chance to save the WTO”. But, despite the best efforts of politicians, inertia won the day. 

As a result, a multipronged programme to reform the workings of the WTO fell by the wayside, as did efforts to add the Investment Facilitation for Development (IFD) Agreement to the rule book and renew the “ecommerce moratorium” that for 28 years had stopped tariffs being levied on digital transmissions. 

For longtime WTO sceptics such as US trade representative Jamieson Greer, the impasse proved a point. As he put it: “I have always been sceptical of the value of the WTO, and this week’s conference confirmed that this organisation will play only a limited role in future global trade policy efforts.” 

But will it? Senior WTO diplomats in Geneva concede, with mild understatement, that the Yaoundé debacle caused a “dip in confidence” in the organisation, particularly given how much store had been publicly set on it succeeding. And yet, out of the wreckage of MC14, a new reform process has emerged, with talks starting in Geneva this month on how to make the WTO more functional. As another WTO diplomat put it, “we’ve ended up pretty much where we would have if we’d struck a deal in Cameroon”. 

This is not to overstate the progress, given the nugatory fruits of past labours. At the top level, diplomats concede the organisation remains moribund: the US isn’t going to move any time soon to unblock the Appellate Body, the legal mechanism that gives the WTO teeth. Nor are there any signs of India moving on its blocking of so-called “plurilateral” agreements, where “coalitions of the willing” make deals on areas such as ecommerce or investment rules with the option for other nations to join later.

The challenge is that, even though plurilateral agreements have been around since before the WTO’s inception in 1995, as the rules currently stand, India’s stance means new ones cannot be added to the organisation’s legal architecture. This creates a perverse situation where one or two countries can block a deal that has been agreed by 100 others.

So, while no one is suggesting the WTO is rising Phoenix-like from the ashes of Yaoundé, the renewed tilt at a reform process offers a flicker of hope that something can be salvaged. There are perhaps two reasons to be mildly optimistic: first, there still isn’t really a viable alternative to the WTO, and second, the business world is demanding joined-up regulation at a moment of both technological and geopolitical upheaval. 

That is the thrust of a paper produced last month by the International Chamber of Commerce, which advocates for greater use of plurilateral agreements in the absence of a functioning multilateral system. In theory, plurilaterals can create pools of like-minded players prepared to agree rules in areas such as fair investment, the green transition (carbon taxing and measurement), modern trade facilitation (digitised trade documents and other emerging technologies) and other areas of global trade regulation. There is one success story already: after Cameroon, a group of 66 countries, including the EU and China, nonetheless decided to press ahead with the ecommerce agreement on digital trade. 

Clearly, there is something of a paradox here. Creating coalitions of the willing around, say, digital trade, risks exacerbating the very challenge of fragmentation that they seek to address. Which rather brings us back to the WTO. Even if it isn’t working, the report’s authors argue that such deals should ideally feed back into the organisation’s framework over time.

As they write:

“The point is not that these arrangements replace WTO rulemaking. Their value is that they can test approaches, build confidence and create practical models that may later be brought back into the WTO, whether as reference points for discussion, building blocks for future agreements or templates for broader participation.” 

They also suggest practical ways to guard against fragmentation, such as ensuring agreements are open to new joiners, kept up to date with regular review to stop them atrophying, have a meaningful enforcement mechanism and provide technical support to prevent less-developed countries from being excluded. 

Much of this can feel quite abstruse, but ultimately it comes down to greasing the gears of the global trade engine to deliver concrete commercial gains. The ICC cites an OECD study that estimated that a 10 per cent improvement in border procedures via streamlined documentation and stronger co-operation among border agencies could boost global goods exports by up to 18 per cent. Even a fraction of that wouldn’t be half bad. 

The ICC’s head of trade, Valerie Picard, argues that given the state of the world, it’s time to stop seeing plurilateral agreements as second best. “There are coalitions of the willing, as existing plurilaterals like the IFD and ecommerce agreements show,” she told me. “Sure, business would ideally want full, multilateral deals, but in the absence of those, business is saying ‘let’s get on with what we can’.”

A similar attitude appears to be driving emerging diplomatic coalitions. The EU and the transpacific CPTPP group are, for example, exploring a digital trade deal. And there’s the emerging “FIT Partnership” (FIT-P) group of 19 smaller countries (you read it here first) which met in Auckland last month and agreed to work on several areas, including supply chains and subsidies. 

The official line is that the FIT-P is “not a substitute for the multilateral trading system — it is a catalyst for it”. In practice, argue insiders, that means developing norms and behaviours that can gain traction over time and — as and when the big players are ready — be subsumed into the WTO frameworks. 

We’ll see. It’s a noble ambition. The hard truth, as another WTO diplomat concedes, is the cupboard is quite bare. The process that delivered the IFD and ecommerce agreements started in 2017 and concluded in 2024. The fact that there are no further deals in the pipeline, despite the pressing question raised by the digital and climate transitions, arguably tells its own story.

But the alternative is to stand by and do nothing. And continued efforts to resuscitate the WTO and build these coalitions stand as testament to a collective will to resist. By these fragments do we shore against our ruin.

Charted waters

Governments of all stripes love a “big number”, particularly when they’re in trouble. And so it was earlier this year, as Starmer’s government battled for survival after May’s disastrous local elections, that the then chancellor announced a plan to deliver “Great British Summer Savings”. 

These included looking at tariff suspensions on more than 100 types of products, including biscuits and chocolate, that the Treasury said could bring £150mn in benefits to hard-pressed British consumers. The list of proposed suspensions (themselves subject to an industry consultation) followed a previous round of tariff suspensions announced in April, which the government valued at between £100mn and £400mn.

At the time, I quickly crunched those numbers — £150mn amounts to a whopping 0.34 per cent of the £44bn that Britons spent on groceries in 2025. However, the team at the UK Trade Policy Observatory at Sussex university has done a proper analysis and discovered — brace yourself — that the proposed tariff reductions are likely to make very little difference to consumers. 

This is partly because (see chart) most of these goods are already entering the UK tariff-free under preferential trade agreements, and partly because even when tariff suspensions cause prices to fall at the border, the literature suggests those discounts will not feed through to prices on the shelves. 

As co-authors Adriana Brenis and Sahana Suraj put it:

“Most of the products covered already enter the UK tariff-free under existing [free trade agreements], which is why the direct impact of these suspensions is likely to be limited. Furthermore, the goal of easing cost of living pressures on consumers through tariff reductions is further hampered by low pass-through rates.” 

Still, if you didn’t look too closely, the government still got its “big number”.

Trade links

  • The EU and, more slowly, the UK are removing the old customs exemptions for low-value parcels. It’s more complicated than you might think. Customs whizz Anna Jerzewska has done a typically limpid briefing here for UKTPO. 
  • Former EU trade negotiator John Clarke has written a lively piece for Borderlex on how the Trump administration, a master of what Clarke calls “semantic erosion”, has turned the language of trade on its head, with “reciprocal” trade deals meaning the exact opposite. 
  • I am reading a lot about China imbalances at the moment. This acute piece from last year by Daleep Singh, former deputy national security adviser in the Biden administration, is a study in the art of the possible.
  • Last week I noted Chinese pushback against OECD and IMF papers on the systemic use of below-market finance as a subsidy instrument. This piece by FT columnist Gillian Tett is very good on how China deploys subsidies in a far more joined-up way than the west — quantitative arguments aside. 

Trade Secrets is edited by Harvey Nriapia

item.title: What percentage of UK households are net contributors?
item.author: Harvey Nriapia
item.description: Despite attempts, the figure is virtually impossible to calculate
item.content:encoded:
Despite attempts, the figure is virtually impossible to calculate

Harvey Nriapia

Britain is looking for another scapegoat. On the left, it’s the country’s 157 billionaires against everyone else, south versus north, landlord and tenant. On the right, it’s “two-tier” this and that, tradition versus change, citizens against outsiders. These might be valid prisms through which to see the world. And there are countless ways to draw the line. 

One binary that crops up more and more separates those who make a net contribution to the Treasury from those who don’t. As the country buckles under soaring public spending commitments and the tax take approaches a near-record postwar high, that divide has become more salient. The feeling is especially acute in debates about welfare, an issue on which public opinion has flipped after two years of Labour government.

About 53 per cent of Britons live in households that are net recipients of the state, according to the Office for National Statistics. There has been a slow creep upwards: in 1979, this number was about 43 per cent, surpassing 50 per cent around the financial crash, according to a Centre for Policy Studies analysis of ONS data. It then fell during the austerity years and has ticked up since.

But there are important caveats. First, the number shifts with the deficit. When borrowing is up, transfers mechanically exceed tax revenue collected.

Second, although the figure accounts for both direct and indirect taxes, as well as benefits in kind, such as education and the NHS, there are plenty of state services that do not feature on either side of the ledger. Defence, courts, debt interest payments, roads, policing: the government finances lots that UK households benefit from and are liable for — even if it would be virtually impossible to say by how much.

So while 53 per cent is bandied around, the number in reality is much more ambiguous.

The best thing we have to an international comparison is a paper by Michael Christl, associate professor at Universidad Loyola Andalucía and research fellow at Tax Foundation Europe, and Monika Köppl-Turyna, director at research institute EcoAustria, which pulls numbers using a similar methodology for EU countries. Accounting for direct and indirect taxes, education and healthcare, they find that, in most nations in the bloc, net beneficiary households slightly outweigh net contributor ones.

In this context, Britain does not look so dissimilar to the European norm. Italy stands out for its relative paucity of net contributor households, with only 39.4 per cent putting in more than they receive, according to the research. This is in part explained by generous Italian state pensions, which weigh on the top end of the income distribution and push households that might otherwise be net contributors into negative territory.

The figures, however, face similar limitations to the ONS data, in that they omit a range of government-provided services.

So what’s the profile of a “net contributor”? It is not as simple as lining up households with the highest incomes. People across the distribution can qualify. A hard-up graduate who has no need for healthcare services or state education might, on net, contribute more than a well-heeled worker with four kids in a comprehensive school, for instance.

Christl and Köppl-Turyna plot the average fiscal contribution of EU households by disposable income decile. (Note: within-decile contributions still vary widely, in part because of different household-level demands on state services such as education. As a result, a country’s overall share of net contributor households is not simply the population share above the net contribution line.)

The break-even point across EU states ranges from the sixth and seventh decile in Baltic and Nordic states such as Estonia and Sweden, to the eighth decile in Italy and the tenth decile in Greece.

“The targeting of benefits, pension treatment and demographic composition all interact differently across welfare regimes, leading to substantial differences across countries,” says Christl. Countries with lower break-even points tend to feature universal, broad-based taxation models rather than pension-heavy, narrow contributor-base ones. Variation in retirement ages and family composition also makes a difference, Christl adds.

Of course, households change place on the contributor-beneficiary axis across a life cycle, and these positions represent a snapshot in time rather than eternal fiscal destiny. Job losses, births, deaths, health diagnoses and other shocks can shift the balance. We would also expect children to demand more of the state than working-age adults, with experience and education lifting earning potential. And there is some 2015 evidence from the IFS to suggest only a small minority of people across their life wind up being net recipients overall.

The calculus for prudent finance ministers is a simple accounting equation: money in should roughly equal money out. Moreover, households are not the only source of public funds. There are plenty of other revenue streams, from corporation tax, business rates and employer national insurance to stamp duty, environmental levies and duties on capital gains (even if the incidence of these still largely falls on individuals).

Growth in the ratio of pensioners to working-age adults will pile pressure on the biggest tax revenue raisers, which in the UK are currently income tax and national insurance. As workers are squeezed, the contributor-beneficiary binary could become a source of political tension.

Yes, as the welfare bill climbs, UK politicians must grasp the nettle on reform, cutting where they can and trying to eliminate fraudulent claims. But that is a different task from attempting to identify who is not “pulling their weight”, where the statistics used are shaky and there are countless ways to draw the line.

Send your thoughts to freelunch@ft.com.

Food for thought

Most people learn about monetary policy decisions from the news rather than from central banks. New evidence from Turkey suggests heavier coverage of inflation on someone’s preferred news channel raises their inflation expectations.

item.title: How long can big investors ignore climate risk?
item.author: Emiliya Mychasuk
item.description: Shift of funds from a US asset manager to a European one highlights the divergence
item.content:encoded:
Shift of funds from a US asset manager to a European one highlights the divergence

Emiliya Mychasuk

Hello from London, I’m the FT climate editor, stepping in this week for Simon Mundy during his sabbatical.

It has been an intense summer: three heatwaves and another on the way; wildfires in France and Spain, not to mention Canada, and even parts of England and Norway — and it is not yet August. In the space of a few days, I have written both about the rapid drought in Europe and the phenomenon of “fire storms”.

The economic damage of the fires will take a few days to accurately estimate, experts say, though Swiss Re’s head of catastrophe perils Balz Grollimund told the FT’s insurance reporter Lee Harris that he would put a conservative early figure of “at least hundreds of millions of euros” on the losses in France.

The bigger question is how long can major investors and pension funds ignore the financial risks of climate change?

‘Climate risk is investment risk’
