The French asset manager Amundi is due to report its latest quarterly results tomorrow that may show the benefits of a focus on sustainability — in Europe at least.

When it last reported on fund inflows for the first and second quarters, it showed almost €43bn in net new assets had moved into ESG ETFs — or more than three times for the same period the year before.

One of Amundi’s latest wins, albeit modest, is a mandate from the UK endowment Nesta Trust. The endowment today announced the withdrawal from the American asset manager Northern Trust “to ensure investments support climate action”.

It’s not the magnitude of the Amundi win last year when the People’s Pension Fund, one of the largest in the UK, pulled £28bn from State Street, after the US asset manager joined the retreat from ESG. The £20bn developed-market equity mandate went to Amundi, and £8bn of fixed income assets to Invesco.

But it signals an ongoing direction of travel among some long-term asset managers and pension funds. It also follows the Dutch pension funds PFZW and PME and Denmark’s AkademikerPension among those to have pulled funds from US managers for similar reasons.

The Nesta Trust manages and governs the funds behind the UK research and innovation foundation Nesta. It was established in 2012 with £260mn from the National Lottery and now stands at £420mn.

Nesta said it had moved more than one-quarter of those assets to Amundi in June, worth £120mn. This was a direct consequence of Northern Trust’s withdrawal at the start of 2025 from the Net Zero Asset Managers Initiative and the similar Climate Action 100+ group.

Many big name asset managers also pulled out of these industry initiatives after the election of US President Donald Trump coincided with several “red” states taking antitrust action against asset managers.

Northern Trust leaving the industry climate initiatives was “incompatible with its mission to build a sustainable future”, Nesta’s investment committee said.

The handover of Nesta’s passive global equity portfolio (passive management draws lower fees) reflected the “commitment to reducing global greenhouse gas emissions”.

Nesta Trust chief investment officer Jenny Segal said the economic risks of climate change meant it was “the duty of any asset manager to ensure their investments support climate action to protect the portfolio’s growth”.

“Asset managers that step back from climate action initiatives risk compromising their stewardship and so we took the decision that Amundi was a better home for Nesta’s global equity investments.”

“We hope that our disinvestment shows that asset owners do not have to silently accept a rollback of climate commitments, and that this shows others they can hold their fund managers to a high standard.”

Amundi has recently had a reshuffle after the departure of its head of institutional clients and ESG of nearly a decade, Jean-Jacques Barbéris, to another senior role at the asset services arm of Crédit Agricole, which is Amundi’s majority shareholder.

It also attracted scrutiny over its fossil fuel investment policies, which have shifted to exclude oil and gas companies that “significantly exceed operational carbon intensity trajectories without credible corrective action”.

It could vote against board members or downgrade ESG scores at oil and gas companies with high carbon intensity operations or falling investment in low-carbon solutions, however.

Amundi UK chief executive Eric Bramoullé said clients were still looking to ensure assets were invested in a way that reflected the sustainability commitments they had made alongside financial performance.

The independent UK membership group known as Investors for Purpose, which Nesta Trust has joined, noted that in an increasingly polarised world “balancing diverse client expectations on ESG is genuinely challenging, and not every step back from a climate commitment reflects a step back from climate risk management”.

But Charlotte O’Leary, chief executive of Investors for Purpose, summed up the core issue, while issuing a call for a wider conversation across the industry about how managers can navigate the pressure to deliver returns and also keep to the fundamentals of stewardship: “Climate risk is investment risk.”

Smart reads

Investor demand for private capital funds that explicitly seek positive environmental or social outcomes has held steady in recent years despite the political backlash, reports Alexandra Heal.

Scientists are now racing to update their understanding of how wildfires start, spread and intensify in climate feedback loops, writes science commentator Anjana Anhuja.

item.title: Brexit ‘reset’ could constrain UK’s freedom of movement on trade
item.author: Peter Foster
item.description: If Brussels pursues economic defences against Beijing, London might feel pressure to follow suit
item.content:encoded:
If Brussels pursues economic defences against Beijing, London might feel pressure to follow suit

Peter Foster

Good afternoon and welcome to Trade Secrets. I’m Peter Foster, the FT’s world trade editor, covering for Alan who is away for the next three weeks on his grandes vacances. This week I look at the growing drumbeat in Brussels for confronting China over trade imbalances and what that means for the independence (or lack thereof) of UK trade policy. As Prime Minister Andy Burnham takes the reins in Downing Street with a new minister for the EU “reset”, I’ll argue that the two spheres of trade policy are more closely interlinked than is generally understood in Whitehall or Westminster.

In Charted Waters, where we use data to analyse world trade, a startling paper by Jun Du at Aston University demonstrates how “non-tariff barriers” caused small businesses to give up trading with Europe and led to more than half of the individual products previously sold by UK exporters into EU markets disappearing from the trading relationship.

There is an irony here. In 2018, Boris Johnson famously exclaimed “fuck business” when asked to respond to industry concerns about Brexit, which he later defended by suggesting he only meant “big business”. But as Du’s research shows, leaving the bloc firmly entrenched the interests of big companies that were able to keep trading while the smaller ones gave up.

Caught in the middle

Brussels is heading to the beach this week, but already it is clear that a tricky confrontation with China is brewing this autumn.

After Chinese commerce minister Wang Wentao’s visit to Brussels last month, EU trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič set an October deadline to make meaningful progress on longstanding areas of contention, including Chinese export controls, intellectual property rights and industrial subsidies. 

“Dialogue alone will not suffice,” Denis Redonnet, the European Commission’s deputy director-general for trade, told MEPs earlier this month, clearly rolling the pitch for some further EU defensive actions to combat the rising threat of China-driven deindustrialisation.

Based on past experience, you could be forgiven for being sceptical about how far this tough signalling will be matched by reality. But as the requests for anti-dumping duties pile up at the Commission’s door, it’s clear calls are growing for something to be done.

That isn’t likely to mean a President Donald Trump-style trade war, which both sides will want to avoid, but more likely a constellation of trade defence measures which, taken together, will begin to address what French President Emmanuel Macron called the “unbearable imbalances” in the EU-China relationship. 

The trick, as described by Andrew Small in a paper for the European Council on Foreign Relations, will be to avoid a repeat of Trump’s head-on collision that led to Chinese retaliation on rare earths, in favour of a smorgasbord of measures designed to bring about a course correction from Beijing, which he memorably dubs the “art of the swarm”. 

Sitting in London, the direction of travel seems pretty clear — and that has, I think, interesting and underexplored implications for the UK’s relationship with Brussels.

The question is simple: if the UK wants to move closer to the EU, how far and for how long can it remain out of step with Brussels in its increasingly mercantilist efforts to tackle China and boost economic security? 

Just this month we’ve seen the UK reluctantly fall into line with an EU decision to double steel tariffs to 50 per cent and halve its quotas, a move that upset UK trade partners, including India, as well as manufacturers downstream. Even under a Labour government, there is an ideological tension between the UK’s free-trading open-economy instincts and the EU’s increasingly protectionist bent. 

That tension plays out internally in Whitehall, with the Treasury and trade department generally seeking open markets and lower prices, while more strategic voices argue these demands must be weighed against delivering an industrial strategy and addressing security concerns about China.

Then energy secretary Ed Miliband’s decision in March to block the Chinese turbine maker Ming Yang from opening a £1.5bn factory in Scotland was a case in point. The UK’s trade department wanted it to go ahead, but was ultimately over-ruled. 

It is perhaps notable that the new EU relations minister, Hamish Falconer, will, unlike his predecessor, have a double-hatted role in the Cabinet Office and Foreign Office, where Miliband now presides. If that portends a greater accent on economic security in the next phase of the “reset”, it will raise questions about where the UK is prepared to be part of “team Europe” against China and where it wants to go it alone.

There are some interesting choices coming down the tracks. Take the chemical industry, where the EU Commission is inundated with anti-dumping duty requests on many commodity products, such as industrial whitening agent titanium dioxide (TiO₂).

The EU imposed anti-dumping duties on TiO₂ in January 2025. The UK does not have equivalent duties, but earlier this year cleared LB Group, China’s largest producer of TiO₂, to buy a plant in Teesside which, in effect, Chinese excess production had helped to put out of business.

The Teesside plant’s rival in the UK, Tronox, is currently petitioning the UK Trade Remedies Authority to impose anti-dumping duties, arguing that Britain will become a backdoor for Chinese products otherwise, undermining the EU’s own defences.

If the TRA recommends duties, the UK government will have to decide to accept them and upset the Chinese buyers, or over-rule and upset the EU. Brussels will certainly be monitoring the result and UK exports of TiO₂ to the bloc. 

It’s only one small example, but if the EU is about to embark on a concerted effort to defend against Chinese non-market practices, the UK is going to find its freedom of action increasingly constrained if it wants to avoid straining relations with Brussels.

It’s not just chemicals. The UK, unlike the EU, doesn’t have additional tariffs on electric vehicles, an area that is only going to become more politically sensitive as Chinese production and exports grow. 

The EU is also considering widening the application of its carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) tax from primary to downstream products — so not just aluminium, but aluminium wheels, say. If Brussels goes ahead and the UK doesn’t follow suit, the country would quickly become a circumvention risk for the bloc.

As Anton Spisak, a former UK government official now at the Centre for European Reform, observes, the tension is that despite the warm rhetoric around a “reset”, Whitehall sees itself as having a different set of policy interests than other European capitals. 

“While some of that divergence is understandable, it will increasingly ring alarm bells in Brussels and other European capitals (especially in Paris) that the UK could become a back door to the EU single market for cheap Chinese industrial goods,” he said.

Of course, as Small of the ECFR adds, this cuts both ways. Rather than driving a wedge between London and Brussels, it could equally deepen the logic of rapprochement. 

As he puts it: “If the EU does look to enforce defences in critical sectors, as it has done with steel, it begs the question for the UK, ‘do we need to be a bit more joined up?’ Because if the EU loses these sectors, that has implications for UK security too.”

In short, if the UK wants to join forces with the EU on economic security issues, then choices lie ahead. These could be invidious, they could be unifying. But they’re going to be increasingly difficult to avoid.

Charted waters

Today’s chart is taken from a remarkable Brexit impact analysis that takes us beyond the headline numbers of “hit to GDP” to show how leaving the bloc has structurally corroded Britain’s trading relationship with the EU.

Jun Du and her colleagues Oleksandr Shepotylo and Yujie Shi at Birmingham’s Aston University demonstrate how regulatory barriers led to a huge fall in the variety of different products being traded between the EU and UK. They find that more than half (53.8 per cent) of the individual products previously sold by UK exporters into EU markets disappeared after Brexit.

Since the overall value of trade fell by much less, the figure demonstrates the outsized impact on small- and medium-sized enterprises, as well as the concentration effects of trade in larger companies that had the capacity and sunk costs to make doing the paperwork worthwhile. As she writes:

Export varieties fell by more than half, but export values fell by only 16.5 per cent, consistent with embedded relationships maintaining their volume while marginal product lines exited. Where those ties did not exist, in sectors characterised by high consumer-goods orientation, perishability and low product differentiation, product lines exited and have largely not been replaced.

It also contextualises the current low-ambition EU-UK “reset”. As Du tells me: “The UK-EU summit produced what the current debate treats as progress: a deal on food and animal health checks, an emissions trading linkage, a youth mobility scheme. These are welcome, but they are tactical fixes for a structural problem.”

While the UK government has asked for a deal to enable goods to be certified in both markets, I’m old enough to remember EU negotiator Michel Barnier’s warning that the UK could never become a “certification hub” off the coast of Europe. That position shows no sign of changing because, if we’ve learnt anything over the past decade of Brexit negotiations, it’s that economic and political logic often do not coincide. 

Trade links

  • Can an EU trade war be avoided? Thorsten Benner, director of the Global Public Policy Institute in Berlin, argues it can’t in Foreign Affairs.
  • The good people at Global Trade Alert have done God’s work by splitting all 60 of Trump’s new Section 301 tariff directives into separate PDF files.
  • Third time lucky? With 60 separate files, Trump’s Section 301 tariffs are likely to be harder to unpick — but that doesn’t make them legal, according to Alan Wolff at the Peterson Institute.
  • The IMF and OECD have accused China of using “below-market” finance as a form of deep subsidy, but a group of Chinese economists has pushed back in an article on the World Economic Forum website. (The long version is here.)

Trade Secrets is edited by Harvey Nriapia

item.title: Why wages and productivity look set to diverge further
item.author: Joel Suss
item.description: AI and a falling labour share of GDP risk accelerating decoupling trends across the rich world
item.content:encoded:
AI and a falling labour share of GDP risk accelerating decoupling trends across the rich world

Joel Suss

Productivity growth is pretty much all that matters in the long run. Without innovations and new technologies — many of which we now take for granted, such as clothes and flushable toilets — life would be nasty, brutish and short. Indeed, for most humans throughout history, their time on Earth was something resembling that.

According to economic theory, productivity and real wages should grow in tandem, with the benefits of new technology being shared with the workers who produce the stuff. But in the US, Europe and Japan, pay growth has decoupled from productivity growth, with the latter having pulled ahead.

In the US, wage and productivity growth were tightly linked at least since 1947, when official records began, until around 1970, when pay started to fall behind. In recent years, the gap has widened into a chasm. Labour productivity — measured as real GDP per hour worked — is now more than five times greater than in 1947, whereas real hourly compensation is only about three times greater. 

In the UK, which is blessed with data stretching back to the reign of King George III, the same decoupling began earlier. The phenomenon is also evident elsewhere, especially in Japan and most of Europe. 

Economists have put forward myriad explanations for this trend. For example, different deflators are used to strip the effects of inflation from productivity and wage data, with the broad GDP deflator being used for the former and the consumption basket deflator for the latter. Once you adjust for this, the gap shrinks somewhat. (That said, there are arguments for retaining the different deflators. For example, the consumption basket deflator better reflects the price pressures workers face, whereas the GDP deflator better reflects companies’ experience.)

Others suggest decoupling trends can be partially explained by rising economic inequality. Median wage growth has lagged even further behind productivity growth, with inequality pushing the average wage higher than the median. (The figures above show average rather than median wages; plotting median wages would show an even greater divergence.)

But where reality differs from the textbook is perhaps most important. In a perfectly competitive market, productivity improvements raise the marginal product of labour (that is, the output an additional worker could produce). When labour becomes more productive, competition for workers should push up wages. But less competitive market environments, which are evident in rising mark-ups and have come about for reasons such as “superstar” companies, create conditions for wage and productivity growth to diverge.

The flip side of growing company market power is declining worker bargaining power, research suggests. This has weighed on pay growth.

Another way to rationalise the divergence is in terms of labour’s declining share of GDP vis-à-vis capital. For many years, economists believed the labour share was stable over the long run. Indeed, this was enshrined as one of Hungarian-British economist Nicholas Kaldor’s “facts” about the economy. John Maynard Keynes described it similarly. However, in recent decades labour’s share of GDP has declined in many countries. 

As labour’s share falls, pay growth becomes more disconnected from productivity growth. Therefore, insofar as advances in AI constitute capital-biased technological change, the pay-productivity gulf will widen further. Ditto if machines can substitute rather than complement workers (that is, if the elasticity of substitution between labour and capital is greater than one).

This is the subject of active debate, with some arguing that there will be new, hard-to-imagine jobs, or at least a permanent place for human services, in an artificial superintelligence future.

Economist Erik Brynjolfsson tells me that whether AI substitutes or complements workers is a “design question”. He argues that we must resist what he calls the “Turing trap”, whereby the technology is built to imitate workers, which elevates substitution risks.

The productivity miracle that many expect from AI will not by default increase living standards for all. But while AI could predominantly transfer productivity gains to machine and data centre owners, the decoupling of pay and productivity has already been with us for decades. Productivity growth is still all that matters for economic wellbeing in the long run — it just needs to be shared around more.

Food for thought

This working paper finds that the new class of weight-loss drugs has sizeable labour market and fiscal benefits. The authors find that GLP-1 treatment reduces long-term sickness leave by 17.3 per cent and brings total fiscal benefits of approximately 1.3 to 1.5 per cent of annual labour income per employed individual.

Free Lunch on Sunday is edited by Harvey Nriapia

item.title: Will Burnham go big or go home?
item.author: Martin Sandbu
item.description: Reasons to be sceptical about the UK’s new prime minister
item.content:encoded:
Reasons to be sceptical about the UK’s new prime minister

Martin Sandbu

As we enter the UK holiday period, various colleagues will step in to contribute to the Free Lunch column, which will publish on a less frequent schedule in August. We wish all our readers a good northern hemisphere summer!

The UK has a new prime minister. Much ink and many pixels have been devoted to the change of government — in particular the change in chancellor of the exchequer — and what it may portend for economic policy. I recommend in particular Chris Giles’s column on six foolish mistakes the chancellor should avoid, but all the FT’s coverage is good.

Stephen Bush calls the appointment of John Healey as chancellor “a like-for-like substitution”, and has labelled the first few announcements on economic policy “Continuity Reevesonomics”. I think that is right, and I think that makes it very likely this government will soon disappoint much in the same way Sir Keir Starmer’s did. Today’s column is about one deep reason why.

Here are two fundamentally different ways of thinking about how an economy works, which lead to opposite conclusions about what policies the UK needs.

One is to think that economies tend towards a single equilibrium or steady state. This equilibrium determines its size and long-term rate of growth, as well as its sectoral make-up and the rate at which that composition “naturally” changes. Policy measures, in this view, work in one of two ways. Either they push the economy away from its steady state (ideally in a positive direction) temporarily before it gravitates back. A fiscal stimulus can briefly raise the growth rate, for example. Or they tweak the equilibrium itself: regulations, tax rates and interest rates all contribute to determining where exactly the economy comes to rest (where “rest” could mean a steady rate of long-term growth).

This view of the economy leads very naturally to incrementalism and caution. If there is a single equilibrium, you had better make sure that your policies improve it rather than just nudge you above it for a moment — or if you go for temporary improvements, you had better make sure they don’t damage the point of rest you return to. Stability, then, is favoured.

Shifting a steady state is also harder work than simply dancing around it, so it is natural for politicians to focus on the micro policies that can immediately help groups they care about within a slow-to-change context, than on bigger macro policies that will change the context itself. And to the extent there is a conscious macro policy, it will often lean towards fiscal consolidation because this is seen as leaving space for lower interest rates and higher investment.

The other, very different, view of the economy is that it has several equilibria or possible steady states. Each is self-reinforcing. Like in the first paradigm, policy measures can temporarily push you away, or marginally change where the economy comes to rest. But big disruptions can throw you so far out of one steady state that you end up gravitating to another one. So can large “big bang” policy changes.

In this second view, the task of policy is more demanding. If you are lucky, you are in the good equilibrium and must merely avoid falling out of its zone of gravity and getting trapped in the bad one. If you are unlucky, you are in the bad one, and your job is to find a way to escape it and shift the economy to the better steady state. That demands “going big” — administering a shock to the economy that resets expectations and behaviour to a self-reinforcing cycle of faster growth.

A lot depends on whether you think the first or the second economic paradigm is correct. What is sound policy in one may well be outright harmful in the other. If the first is right, radical attempts to “jump” between steady states are likely to lead to tears. If the second is right, what passes for responsibility can lock you into a trap of economic deterioration. Seen this way, hardly anything in economic policymaking is more important than establishing with some confidence which world we are in.

In my view, the second paradigm is the right one but most UK governments act within the first one. The new government shows all the signs of falling into the same trap. This is particularly clear in ditching a cheap but potentially transformative digital ID project. Also, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has immediately adopted the instinct that has made such a complex hash of the UK tax system — playing with a differential VAT rate on domestic power rather than shifting green levies away from electricity to accelerate electrification. Both betray a view of the economy that encourages short-term tweaks rather than big shifts.

You may not agree. But bear with me to think through the implications for policy if the multiple-equilibrium view is correct.

Much of the UK’s poor economic performance since the global financial crisis can be rationalised within the second paradigm. In this perspective, successive shocks have knocked the economy into ever worse self-reinforcing states. Expectations of slow growth lead to retrenchment, unwillingness to invest or raise productivity, which in turn keeps holding growth back and justifies the original pessimistic expectations.

If the task is to jolt the economy from one (worse) steady state to another (better) one, that inescapably requires two things. One is the political boldness to make big changes that inflict losses on vocal special interests, ideally matched with political agility to ride out the storm by mobilising the support of those the changes benefit. The other is a sufficiently confident economic understanding to be able to hammer through the kind of orthodoxy that favours the incrementalism of the unique-equilibrium paradigm. (Let me be clear that I am talking here about justified confidence, not some sort of Dunning-Kruger foolishness.)

I disagree, then, with those (including some of my most esteemed colleagues) who say there are no free lunches. If the economy has several equilibria, and one is better than this in terms of GDP levels, productivity and growth rates, shifting to one would be a free lunch.

I also disagree with those (also including some of my most esteemed colleagues) who say that a deep understanding of the subject matter is not a prerequisite or even necessarily a help for being an effective minister. That is not true in economics, a field shaped by technical arguments apt to bamboozle anyone not trained in them, with paradoxical results and deeply internalised understandings that can only be refuted with sufficient expertise.

This is why chancellors (and finance ministers elsewhere) so often seem captured by their departments. Learning economics on the job virtually guarantees it, for a little economics knowledge is an extremely dangerous thing — it makes you just knowledgeable enough to accept you are more constrained by the economy’s steady state than you thought (and promised your supporters you would be). Doing better requires either enough knowledge of economics to see the holes in conventional arguments, or an obtuseness combined with political instincts that just happen to be exactly right. Both are exceedingly rare.

Of course, even if the second paradigm is true, believing it is not sufficient for good policy. Liz Truss wanted to jolt the UK economy from a worse to a better steady state. So, probably, did Boris Johnson. Instead, the point is that without asking what it would take not just to improve the current equilibrium but to escape it for a better one, nothing much would change. And all the early signs from the Burnham government are that nobody is thinking hard enough about the economy in this sense, nor showing the political determination to follow through on what such an economic analysis would find.

I don’t claim to know what this should amount to. But to make a real difference, the multiple-equilibrium perspective entails that we need to see action at the scale, for example, of abandoning Labour’s red lines on Europe and rejoining the EU’s single market and customs union, if not the EU itself. (Look out for a column from me on this topic in the coming days.) Another example would be the kind of root-and-branch tax reform and simplification I advocated last year.

Could Burnham’s promises on devolution fit the bill? Probably not. First, because it’s not at all clear how much power he will really shift away from a Westminster where he is now in charge. (After all, one of his first acts in power — imposing a £2 bus fare cap — has been to use central government policy to micromanage local transport pricing policy.) Second, because even if a lot of power is devolved, the question remains how the new holders of that power then choose to wield it.

Perhaps the promised 10-year plan will turn out to be both concrete and bold. But so far, the parts of Burnhamonomics that are bold are not concrete, and those that are concrete are not bold.

Other readables

● A tale of two railway systems, both featured in the FT: Japan takes a step closer to its 500km per hour maglev trains, while the US’s only private passenger rail network is teetering on bankruptcy.

● The amount of money bond issuers can save by tokenising their bonds is huge.

● Paul Krugman explains the US government’s bizarrely punitive approach to Brazil’s digital currency.

● The Czech central bank governor takes on both his country’s president and prime minister for their “battle of mistimed ideas” on interest rates and euro membership.

● The European car industry, supposedly in crisis, is racking up profits and reserves like no other regions’ automakers!

item.title: What new EU rules mean for the aviation industry
item.author: Kenza Bryan
item.description: A clever compromise avoids reigniting Brussels-Washington trade tensions
item.content:encoded:
A clever compromise avoids reigniting Brussels-Washington trade tensions

Kenza Bryan

Hello from London, I’m Kenza Bryan, the FT’s climate reporter with news of a plan to bring international aviation into the EU’s emissions trading scheme before the end of the decade.

An incomplete plan to price flight emissions

The first half of the year has brought difficult news about the worsening effects of climate change: a rollercoaster of extreme heat, wildfires, flooding and sea-ice lows. Scientists warned that a core global goal to limit the rise in temperatures was slipping out of reach.

So I hope you will forgive me for a hint of relief as I report on an imperfect proposal that the EU published late last week. After musing on the idea for more than a decade, Brussels said it planned to extend its CO₂ pricing scheme to all flights out of the bloc, including private jets.

One tiny caveat: flights must land within 5,000km of a point in central Europe, which conveniently excludes the US. This appears to be the only way to have avoided reigniting explosive trade tensions with Donald Trump’s America. It was a clever compromise. 

Making polluters pay

The European Commission has proposed bringing international aviation further into its emissions trading scheme starting in 2029.

It has done so as part of a wide-ranging review of its scheme, which places a cost on carbon of about €80 a tonne.

Aviation makes up about 3 per cent of energy-related CO₂ emissions every year, according to the International Energy Agency. Scientists say that its impact on global warming is higher because of the heat-trapping effects of contrails, clouds that planes can leave in their wake at high altitude. 

But making polluters pay in international industries such as aviation and shipping is notoriously difficult. It involves getting countries and companies to agree with each other on the size and shape of a levy or trading scheme.

The EU has previously tied itself in knots trying to work out whether to rely on an international agreement that has so far only priced a fraction of CO₂ emissions from aviation, and done so at a level that may be too cheap to create much of an incentive for change.

Under the EU’s latest proposal, airlines would pay to emit carbon on flights from Paris to Dubai but not from Paris to New York. This is a climbdown from EU efforts in 2012 to price the CO₂ emitted by international flights, which came under immense pressure from the US and China. 

Climate officials earlier this year had initially hoped once again to extend the EU’s carbon trading system to all flights leaving the bloc. But sources of my Brussels-based colleague Ian Johnston told him that the proposal faced pushback from many departments within the Commission, including those in charge of transport and industrial policy. 

These officials were concerned about the impact on the aviation industry and the trade department, where officials were worried about potential blowback from trade partners such as the US and China.

The 5,000km radius proposal that the Commission has landed on falls conveniently short of reaching the US and China. But the Commission hopes it will tackle the challenge of airlines diverting from major European airports in favour of regional hubs that are not subject to carbon costs, such as those in Turkey or the rest of the Middle East.

Tim Johnson, a director at the Aviation Environment Federation, a UK-based non-profit organisation, told me he believed the commission’s earlier ambitions had been tempered by the geopolitical constraints of the Trump era. 

“It’s a measured decision by the Commission that trades what’s the maximum coverage we can get . . . versus the political realities,” he said. “It’s seeking to extend the pricing [as] far as it practically can in the current political environment.”

Missed opportunity

Despite its limitations, the move could go some way towards curbing emissions from the airline industry by creating an added incentive to take routes that are less polluting. But it is worth noting that it still leaves 47 per cent of European aviation exempt from carbon pricing, disappointing some campaigners.

The EU proposal forgoes about €4.2bn in revenues that could have been raised had all departing flights been included, according to modelling by the green transport campaign group T&E.

Its aviation director Diane Vitry said the proposal had been watered down “due to industry pressure” and hoped it would be only a starting point for tougher rules. “Aviation must pay for all its emissions, just like any other sector of the economy.”

One thing to note alongside the proposed change: the Commission also published an assessment of the existing international deal on aviation and climate change, and left the door open to relying on it more heavily in future.

The Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (Corsia), which countries agreed to in 2016, aims to keep the industry’s net emissions at 85 per cent of a 2019 pre-pandemic peak. 

Corsia still only covered about 70 per cent of international aviation emissions and the carbon offsets it relies on may have some methodological “shortcomings”, the report said.

The scheme does not even aim to cut flight numbers, but instead to achieve “carbon-neutral growth” thanks to carbon credits or the use of so-called sustainable aviation fuel. SAF emits the same amount of CO₂ as kerosene at the point of combustion but is not produced from fossil-fuel feedstocks. It is expensive and in short supply. 

Another drawback of Corsia is that participation by states is voluntary, and not all those that have joined have written the rules into law for their national airlines. Future participation by US and Chinese airlines is uncertain.

Given all of this, the Commission said it would once again review Corsia’s performance in addressing international aviation emissions in 2032.

This helped raise hopes among some carbon market developers, traders and insurers. They said the possibility of Corsia’s integration with the EU system would unlock confidence in the market for carbon credits, after a recent shortage that has pushed up prices for airlines. 

Smart reads

Just in case you thought Brussels had stepped up climate action on all fronts, that is not wholly true when it comes to methane emissions.

This profile of the UK’s new energy secretary suggests that Andy Burnham’s new government does not intend to retreat from Keir Starmer’s green agenda.

Letters in response:
EU carbon pricing rules need to cover all aviation emissions / From James Kershaw, Scientific Manager, Opportunity Green, London EC4, UK

Budget airlines already pay for most of their emissions / From Jenny Helle, Aviation and Shipping Expert, Carbon Market Watch, Brussels, Belgium

item.title: Donald Trump orders the ceremonial changing of the tariff guard
item.author: Alan Beattie
item.description: The bogus rationale for duties has rotated from economic emergency to balance of payments to unfair trade
item.content:encoded:
The bogus rationale for duties has rotated from economic emergency to balance of payments to unfair trade

Alan Beattie

President Donald Trump managing to hand the World Cup trophy yesterday to Spain’s captain without dropping it or trying to take it home himself is one of the few things he’s contrived not to screw up in a long time, though his bizarre appearance in the Spanish team’s trophy lift celebrations soon had him back on form. (Incidentally, the destructive arrogance of the ghastly Argentine team is all too symbolic of the governments that have trashed that country for many decades, about which I’ve banged on at length.)

Trump is still throwing out occasional random tariff threats, but my prediction that average import duties would drift down after peaking in 2025 looks solid. Of course part of this is because of the US Supreme Court decision to strike down the supposed emergency IEEPA tariffs, the replacement for which I look at today. Charted Waters, where I look at the data behind world trade, is on crude prices adjusted for the importance of oil in the economy. For the next three weeks, this newsletter will be in the supremely capable hands of my colleagues Peter Foster and Aime Williams, after which I’ll be back.

One bad idea after another

I can’t help but feel that the replacement of one set of Trump tariffs by another warrants some official ceremony, like the Changing of the Guard put on by the British Household Cavalry for tourists in London. In February the administration formally retired the IEEPA tariffs, following the Supreme Court ruling, and instituted the Section 122 balance-of-payments tariffs, which were no more helpful than their predecessors and had an equally absurd justification.

The Court of International Trade (CIT), as it had for IEEPA, emerged from the officers’ mess and barked at the Section 122 tariffs to return to barracks. Given that those duties have a 150-day limit, the US trade representative’s office (USTR) was in any case already preparing another kind, this time under the Section 301 authority based on “unfair” trade, on top of some Section 232 “national security” levies that were already in place.

There will be a messy changeover. The Section 122s expire this week and the administration is racing to get the Section 301s ready. It could otherwise try to set the 150-day clock back to the beginning by creating new Section 122s, creating exciting new opportunities for litigation.

Unless you believe the Supreme Court will keep endlessly striking down tariff authorities, which I do not in the case of the 301s and 232s, you have to assume that a wall of duties will be put in place somehow. The question is how much uncertainty and inefficiency are created by new tariffs being invented all the time.

There’s currently a massive surge in container rates as shippers try to get goods moved before the new duties come in. The port of Los Angeles handled a record amount of cargo in June, for example. Trump’s tariffs are more disruptive to the container industry than is his Iran war, which is quite an achievement.

The US will impose a new tariff on (some) imports from Brazil on Wednesday, while the current Section 122s helpfully expire two days later, meaning that you’d better time your shipments right. This guidance from global freight service Gateway Lines gives a small insight into what a pain such decisions create for the industry. Read it and multiply by dozens for all the new tariffs being devised as the administration goes along.

If you have cargo on the water right now, one thing decides which rules you pay under: the entry date on your customs filing. Not the sail date, not the invoice date, not the day the vessel arrives.

So profits depend on the timing of paperwork. There’s more.

Goods that were loaded on a vessel and in transit on the final mode before 12:01am. ET July 22, and that are entered before 12:01am. ET July 29, stay exempt. If you have Brazilian cargo already sailing, keep the load date documentation clean and make sure your broker files within that window. Missing the July 29 entry cut-off puts otherwise exempt cargo into the 25%.

All clear? Good. Oh hold on, that’s not all.

The surcharge ending is not the same as tariffs ending. In June, USTR issued findings in 60 separate Section 301 investigations tied to forced-labor enforcement and proposed additional duties of 10% to 12.5%. Hearings were held July 7 and the record is closed, so final action could come at any time, and unlike Section 122, a Section 301 action carries no 150-day clock.

The Trump tariffs aren’t economically catastrophic, but they are a massive mess.

The US has legalities, China has leverage

In our regular series of What Did You Expect, You Utter Fools?, Bloomberg reports concern within the US administration that China is reneging on the terms of the deal struck by Trump and President Xi Jinping in their October meeting in Busan, South Korea. Last month the FT reported that China was restricting trade with several US companies involved in rare earth supply chains.

It’s not surprising this is happening. It’s surprising that it’s surprising to anyone. The Busan deal was emphatically not agreed from a position of equals. Trump discovered that his clumsy ordnance of tariffs was inadequate against the precision-guided weaponry of China’s rare-earth controls and backed off.

China’s agreement to suspend rare-earth export restrictions for a year was always going to be fuzzy, given its ability to fine-tune bureaucratic controls on sales. The EU, which also got hit by rare-earth restrictions last autumn, reacted to the potential end of the suspension in October in that most European of ways, by setting up a bureaucratic task force.

We knew what would happen because we have been here before. The first Trump administration signed the Phase One deal with Beijing in 2020, promising a bunch of deregulation plus some soyabean and other purchases. The semi-satirical outcome that China couldn’t even be bothered delivering the latter, let alone the former, shows it knew just how little retribution it would face.

Beijing is extremely good at knowing where the balance of power lies and using leverage accordingly, no matter what the piece of paper it signed says. I’ve never opened Trump’s absurd (and ghostwritten) The Art of the Deal, but I’d certainly read a book by Xi on the same subject.

If I had to guess, I’d say the formal ending of the export control suspension won’t make much difference. China is bound by the agreements it wants to be bound by. One of the reasons it is a pretty enthusiastic member of the World Trade Organization isn’t that Beijing ignores all WTO rules, but that there aren’t many that particularly constrain it.

The way to deal with leverage is leverage. Neither the US nor the EU has enough of it to affect what China is doing. And Washington and Brussels can’t properly work together to develop rare earths or anything else because, correctly, no one trusts Trump to do so. Xi must think it’s hilarious.

Charted waters

Not only have oil prices gone up by a lot less than many feared, but the falling oil intensity of the world economy means that recent cost pressures are well below the levels in the late 2000s and early 2010s in terms of economic impact.

Trade links

  • Speaking of deals with the US, Washington is pushing the EU to produce a firm plan to eliminate import rules the White House doesn’t like.
  • Trump is threatening Canada with tariffs over the unwanted imports of, er, wood smoke from forest fires.
  • A paper for Australia’s Lowy Institute says the proliferation of smaller groupings of countries on trade is causing more confusion than clarity.
  • The EU has only delivered part of the package of economic reforms suggested by former Italian prime minister Mario Draghi.
  • My colleague Soumaya Keynes talks to Adam Hanieh of the School of Oriental and African Studies, whose dire predictions of food and fertiliser crises have not come true, but which he says might yet.
  • Russian drone attacks on the port of Odesa are endangering Ukraine’s ability to export grain via the Black Sea.

Trade Secrets is edited by Harvey Nriapia

item.title: Andy Burnham should pursue a devolution ‘big bang’
item.author: Joel Suss
item.description: If done right, radical decentralisation could boost UK productivity growth and living standards
item.content:encoded:
If done right, radical decentralisation could boost UK productivity growth and living standards

Joel Suss

Saying the UK needs to decentralise is a popular refrain. 

Andy Burnham, who as of tomorrow will be the UK prime minister, is the latest politician to discuss devolving political power and the need to reduce regional inequalities. His grandiose “growth in every postcode” phrase joins a long list that includes former prime minister Boris Johnson’s “levelling up” and former chancellor George Osborne’s “northern powerhouse”. 

But details of Burnham’s devolution strategy are scant and, given the record of the past couple of decades, a new push seems likely to underwhelm. 

The new prime minister could set himself apart by opting for a “big bang” rather than tinkering around the edges. Giving local areas complete control over public services would be a good starting point: decisions about how money is spent on health, transportation, housing and education should be made by local authorities. This is not only good “take back control” politics; it could accelerate productivity and raise living standards. 

The details matter. If combined with a functional system of sticks and carrots — in which poor service provision is punished and outperformance rewarded — public-sector productivity growth could get a shot in the arm, after years of holding back overall economic output.

There are large potential benefits from a devolution “laboratory”, a form of competition between regions that would give them wide latitude and incentives to experiment with provision. Jack Newman, research associate at the University of Manchester, said: “Rather than having one big state that makes a mistake and then pays for it for decades, you have 30 smaller regions that can make mistakes . . . others can learn from that mistake [and] not repeat it.”

According to Gwyn Bevan, emeritus professor at the London School of Economics, for devolution to succeed it is crucial also that there be a “collegial” benchmarking framework set up centrally to transparently and comprehensively measure what does and doesn’t work, so that we have the “capability to learn from these experiments”.

There is much to learn on this front from around the world. Decentralised public health provision in Italy combined with clear reporting standards to enable benchmarking translates into far better health provision and outcomes than in the UK, for example. Italy has better breast and lung cancer survival rates, as well as a higher density of medical specialists and hospital beds, even as it spends substantially less on healthcare than Britain.

Partial fiscal devolution would bring some revenue autonomy, further encouraging experimentation and healthy competition, but also strengthening local accountability. At the moment, though, because most UK regions are net transfer recipients, the scope of this measure is limited and could generate political tensions.

Thus, alongside “big bang” public service devolution, Burnham must renew efforts to “rebalance” the UK economy. A positive-sum approach, which fosters agglomerations outside London without diminishing the capital city, could help.

Building agglomerations is easier said than done. But there are some clear lessons from research.

First, reverse the self-defeating retrenchment in the university sector. Higher-education “anchor institutions” are a known source of economic growth, supplying ideas and talent to local areas. Burnham seems to recognise this, saying recently that he would place universities “at the heart of local economies”.

Second, encourage the conditions under which agglomerations form. Factors such as urban density, transport links, cultural amenities and publicly funded research centres and agencies are key (and helped reshape London’s King’s Cross into a technology cluster, for example). Working to reduce important input costs, chiefly electricity, would also be beneficial.

There are no shortages of possible UK clusters: advanced materials and manufacturing in Sheffield, compound semiconductors in Cardiff, offshore energy and batteries in Newcastle. The devolution of key ingredients — housing, transport, education — would help these industries flourish. Meanwhile, central government could help with research and development funding and ensure long-term, stable finance through vehicles such as the UK Research and Innovation agency.

Now it is time for some caveats. Agglomeration-led growth is not exactly “growth in every postcode”, but it would bring good jobs to the UK’s second-tier cities and set them on a path to greater revenue autonomy. Moreover, it could provide more redistributive capacity to address “left behind” places, a policy challenge in highly centralised and decentralised countries alike.

Indeed, in the short term, it could increase spatial inequality in the UK, with urban centres gaining relative to towns. Neil Lee, professor of economic geography at the LSE, told me: “Are you going to be able to create growth everywhere? Of course you’re not. But we do need growth overall.” 

Radical devolution is not a panacea, although it would make Burnham’s overarching aim, to raise living standards, easier to achieve.

Food for thought

Immigration can boost innovation and growth because migrants tend to settle in urban hubs, according to a study of more than 20mn immigrants to the US between 1880 and 2020.

Free Lunch on Sunday is edited by Harvey Nriapia

item.title: The digital euro gets ready for beta testing
item.author: Martin Sandbu
item.description: A brave new world for EU digital finance
item.content:encoded:
A brave new world for EU digital finance

Martin Sandbu

Over the past month, the EU’s digital finance ecosystem has quietly taken several important steps into the future. In late June, the European parliament’s economics committee voted through a proposal to establish a retail central bank digital currency (CBDC) for the euro area. Last week, the full legislature authorised negotiations over such a digital euro with the Council of the EU (where member state governments are represented).

At the same time, the Council issued a statement on how it wants the bloc to shape its overarching policy on digital finance. (Readers may remember I have complained that the EU lacks a strategic vision in this area. This is a step in the right direction.)

And on Tuesday, the European Central Bank announced the participants in the pilot of the digital euro. They will now start technical preparations for the pilot, which will run next year. In parallel, the ECB is working on “Project Pontes” for a publicly provided digital settlement asset suitable for transactions on decentralised digital ledgers. In time, this should become a full-fledged wholesale CBDC — central bank reserves for tokenised finance, if you like.

These are the — not very widely noticed — counterpoints to news that EU regulation is leading all but 12 per cent of crypto companies operating in the bloc to shut down (including Binance, the exchange). A superficial reading would be that this is again Europeans regulating all innovation out of existence. Superficial and wrong: my overall take is that the EU is more on the ball in digital finance than in many other areas. Today, some thoughts about why.

I have had many conversations with people in the thick of these topics recently. Combining those with the public statements and policy measures, here are some of my takeaways.

The digital euro will happen

It’s not formally quite a done deal — parliamentarians and governments still have to iron out their differences over some detail — but everybody now treats the politics of the digital euro as settled. It is interesting, too, that some of the EU’s biggest banks have signed up to the pilot: it suggests that despite past scepticism, they may be getting on board with the programme.

Next year, we will see digital euros in action. Staff at Eurozone central banks will be able to use digital euros to pay for lunch in their canteen and transfer money between one another. It will be particularly interesting to watch the promised ability to make private payments from one offline device to another, to make the digital currency mimic physical cash as far as possible.

The EU is ever more fintech-friendly . . .

EU policy is often criticised (including by me) for being too protective of the bloc’s legacy banking system and not sufficiently open to new players, non-bank finance and innovative products, such as stablecoins. But I sense there is a change. Certainly the official language is ecumenical — the finance ministers’ statement says:

To accelerate the scaling of tokenisation in Europe, our policies should remain technology-neutral and support the development by the private sector of a range of instruments and use cases . . . 

The focus has, I think very helpfully, moved towards thinking about how public sector initiatives can make it easier for the private sector to innovate productively:

Without shared standards, the multiplication of [distributed ledger technology] networks risks recreating and compounding the fragmentation that we have been trying hard to overcome in the EU financial and payment systems. The EU should therefore seize this historic opportunity and engage in setting common standards and promoting interoperability — both among different DLT networks and between DLTs and traditional systems.

The core policymaking circles now see the digital euro as a tool for facilitating this, for example. But the most important tool will be Pontes, which is also set for a pilot soon. The ministers endorsed central bank work on “a public DLT-based settlement asset and the agenda for expanding eligibility as Eurosystem collateral to further DLT-based assets”. Among the expert officials I have talked to, there is a clear sense that this could be a game-changer for European digital finance in its competition with the US.

. . . but it still likes its legacy banks

As I have written before, I still detect a preference among many EU policymakers that the digital transformation should not be too disruptive for banks. That is not the same as saying they always do what legacy banks want them to (as one person told me, “if this was the case, we would not have gone ahead with the digital euro”).

But there is a strange blend of preference and expectation that Europe’s banking sector will, in the end, make fintech innovations work for it. As I wrote a few weeks ago, for example, many in Europe think tokenised deposits will outcompete stablecoins. Perhaps — but as I wrote, better not count on it. In private conversations, many admit that it is only when threatened — including by a public initiative such as the digital euro — that Europe’s banks get their act together to invest what it takes to improve their products against technologically superior competition.

The ecumenical “technology-neutral” approach set out in the ministers’ statement, and which I also hear endorsed in private conversations, seems to me the right one. But it has to be for real. It is hard to reconcile, for example, with forcing stablecoin issuers to hold a lot of their reserves in banks. It is also hard to reconcile with very low holding limits for digital euros, to prevent them from becoming too attractive an alternative to bank deposits. There is still a risk that being too protective of European banks against European non-bank fintech could cede advantage to non-European fintech against both domestic sectors.

The tokenisation of everything is the future

Still, the embrace of tokenisation is a good policy platform as it does put in place a degree of openness. It suggests — or it should at least entail — that smart contracts and “agentic” payments will be welcomed by policymakers.

(I have it on good authority that the use cases getting excited reactions among top EU policymakers are things such as airline and train tickets that automatically pay the legally required compensation when real-time data shows that the flight or train is late.)

There is also a legitimate hope that tokenisation will help unify and grow capital markets by transcending the fragmentation of the old financial market plumbing along national lines. A fast rate of innovation, in fact, gives the EU a chance to leapfrog the difficulties it has in harmonising national approaches, by opting for common rules by default for the new. It would be a huge wasted opportunity, for example, not to centralise regulation of innovative financial products as much as possible; this will be one of the battlegrounds in the work on the EU’s “Market Integration and Supervision Package”.

So the jury is still out over whether the EU can pull this off. One question is sheer competence — in the private sector the misgivings are less over the direction of travel than doubts about whether the public products will be good enough. Another is philosophical: whether the ostensible technological openness is genuine even if it disrupts the banking-centred model Europe has been run on for centuries. That combines payments, money creation and credit allocation to the same two-tier structure of central banks and licensed private sector banks. Whether Europe is flexible enough to countenance alternatives to that model will in the end determine where these best of intentions lead.

Other readables

● If EU member governments hunker down in their usual trenches over the new seven-year budget, other solutions for financing big common projects will have to be found, I write in my latest FT column. And yesterday, a former Polish finance minister proposed one intriguing option: the EU could borrow to develop its own revenue-generating assets of common benefit, on the model of its satellite systems.

● Could a new plan finally get Europe’s electrification share to come unstuck?

● The Institute for Government takes stock of Sir Keir Starmer’s premiership.

● An impressive list of top economists call for action now to ensure AI benefits people and economies.

item.title: ESG is dead
item.author: Katie Martin
item.description: Long live ESG
item.content:encoded:
Long live ESG

Katie Martin

Good morning. SpaceX’s shares closed yesterday back at their $135 listing price, down about 40 per cent from the June peak of $225 per share. Its bonds are drifting towards junk status. A banker at one of its IPO underwriters told our colleagues on the markets desk: “the people who are buying the stock are actually really smart investors”. Odd, then, that this person didn’t want their name on the record. Has common sense prevailed? Email us: unhedged@ft.com.

ESG

Sustainable investment is so over. A few years ago, banks and asset managers would not shut up about it. Everything came with an ESG label, touting the environmental, social and governance-related virtues of investment vehicles for an investing public keen to put their money to good use.

But since the early 2020s, it has all gone suspiciously quiet. Trump 2.0 gets a lot of the blame for this, but we at the FT made an entire film about the decline and fall of ESG fully two years ago, before he returned to the White House.

So it was not just politics — the ESG craze also collapsed under the weight of its own internal contradictions, its tendency to overpromise and then from the fact it had its butt kicked, first by the outperformance of non-green energy (thanks to Russia, 2022) and then AI. You might even slightly blame it for years of under-investment in defence. Some people will always hate it and hey, it’s a free country (Rob is one of those people, by the way, and never shuts up about it; see here, here, here, here and here).

Demand for dedicated sustainable investment products has undoubtedly wilted. Last year was not good for sustainable fund inflows: $84bn in outflows, according to Morningstar, after $38bn of inflows in 2024. But a big caveat is that outflows from sustainability-focused mutual funds and exchange traded funds are not necessarily outflows from sustainable strategies. As Morningstar stresses, some are just flipping out of off-the-shelf products and into bespoke portfolios.

But something of a revival may be afoot. Data this week from European asset manager Amundi showed record inflows into ESG funds through the course of 2026. It said:

In both Q1 and Q2 of this year, ESG net new assets has come in at more than €21bn, respectively, for a combined first-half total of almost €43bn — a more than three-time increase compared to H1 last year.

The US is probably a lost cause. It has racked up more than three straight years of outflows from sustainable funds, according to Morningstar. Europe, however, has never really given up on it. OK, Amundi is just one shop. But it’s no minnow, and this could end up reflecting the start of a proper revival, especially as the case for investing in green energy in the wake of the Iran crisis is almost too obvious to bother pointing out. Also, even the most dedicated climate change flat-earther struggles to dispute that in Europe right now, it’s quite hot. We should maybe do something about it? Any investor who is not thinking about where this is all heading and how it might affect their strategy in the coming years is doing it wrong.

In a weird way, though, on some level, all investors have some kind of climate focus now. In its latest financial stability report last week, the Bank of England pointed to climate change as one of the key drivers for rising levels of government borrowing globally, right up there with defence and demographics.

Fidelity is one investment house that has done a fair amount of work on this. (You can read its research on the implications of a “disorderly transition” in the climate from July 2024 here.) As you might expect, the impact depends on what we stupid humans do next. They write:

Global GDP losses by 2050 could range from around 7% in an orderly Net Zero pathway to around 14-15% under current policies, relative to a no-climate-risk baseline.

The implications for investors are significant. Our research shows that climate risks can affect expected returns of asset classes, with equities generally more affected than bonds. Specifically, over the next 10 years, we estimate an annual decline in expected global equity returns, ranging from -0.4% in scenarios in which transition is achieved to a steeper -1.1% [per annum] in hothouse and fragmented world scenarios.

And this is all before you consider physical damage from extreme weather events.

Aircon stocks are doing well at the moment. This is nature’s way of telling investors to wake up to the obvious implications of climate change even if they don’t consider themselves to be socks-and-sandals ESG devotees.

One good read

Europe vs the US

item.title: The energy transition’s last mile
item.author: Leyla Boulton
item.description: Lenders and investors are starting to fund households’ adoption of renewable technology
item.content:encoded:
Lenders and investors are starting to fund households’ adoption of renewable technology

Leyla Boulton

Simon Mundy is away for the next four weeks and there will be a roster of reporters covering for him while he is away. Leyla Boulton, FT senior editor, is first and she is writing about households and their access to green technology. The newsletter will be published only once a week while Simon is away.

The last mile to net zero?

Today I want to take you to “the last mile” of the green energy transition — getting sustainable energy into the hands of households. Why does this matter? 

The case for this has never been stronger, as fossil fuel prices have soared in the wake of war in the Middle East. But until most citizens are able to benefit from cheap clean energy, the promise of a decarbonised economy pulsing with the “green” jobs and skills of the future will elude us. 

Meet two British voters whose contrasting experiences sum up both the challenge and the opportunity ahead.

Exhibit A

In south London, architect Natalie Barton paid Emerging Living Technologies* £6,100 to install a heat pump. She now stands to lose close to half that amount after the installer went bust and she was passed around a shocking number of organisations in a rickety regulatory system that is now being overhauled. Insurer IWA last week finally agreed to pay her the full deposit it owed her citing a ‘“clerical error” for the delay. “I’ll feel at peace only once I’ve got an air-source heat pump installed and working,” says Barton, whose MP is Miatta Fahnbulleh, previously the junior minister in charge of domestic energy consumers and now an aide to incoming prime minister Andy Burnham.

The same week, Microgeneration Certification System (MCS), the industry standard-setter, announced the departure of the long-serving chief executive who presided over the old system that failed Barton and many others. A separate government consultation on how to avoid further failures in state-funded retrofit programmes for low-income households promises changes — but only in 2028. 

The missing ingredient in the green transition

A more promising development for the future lies in lenders and investors finally entering the domestic energy fray. Finance is the missing ingredient for the majority of households who can’t afford the upfront investment. And if a majority of voters can’t access the benefits of the transition, they are less likely to defend it at the ballot box.

Exhibit B

Barry Richardson has just installed a storage battery and 12 solar panels on his terraced house in the north-west town of Runcorn. The 44-year-old government employee paid for the £10,105 installation with a zero-interest, five-year loan from Nationwide, his mortgage lender. The installer was recommended by British Gas, his electricity and gas supplier. Richardson told me he wanted to gain “greater self-sufficiency . . . from the grid” with monthly repayments of £166 on top of his 15-year mortgage instalments. But he’s holding off considering a heat pump because there’s still “a lot of conversation about how good they are”.

Some of this hesitation about heat pumps, a technology that works perfectly well when properly installed, stems from botched installations by some officially approved contractors that I reported on last month. That in turn has inhibited the growth of the retrofit sector in a country which owns Europe’s smallest number of heat pumps per 1,000 inhabitants.

The governing Labour Party has embraced renewables as the best way to help households struggling with energy bills. But in a veiled warning against flip-flopping, trade body UK Finance told me it “works with the financial services sector to support clearer policies in areas like clean energy and low-carbon housing, so that firms have the certainty to lend and invest over the long term”.

Speaking at the close of London Climate Action Week, Rhian-Mari Thomas, chief executive of the Green Finance Institute, noted a gap between those driving the transition and the people it is meant to benefit. “I think we could do a better job talking more broadly to the public”, she said. “It’s a bit disappointing that we have 75,000 super-smart people here in London working on this agenda. And yet if you weren’t part of that discussion, you wouldn’t know it was happening.”

One of energy secretary Ed Miliband’s last acts under outgoing prime minister Keir Starmer was to announce a pot of £300mn to encourage banks to lower the interest rate on green home loans in return for a subsidy worth up to 20 per cent of the principal on a long-term loan.

“What we’re seeing now is that it just makes sense — forget about the politics,” says Julian Nutley, managing director for home improvement lending at Tandem Bank, who met this week’s deadline for a first wave of embedded finance providers to join the scheme. “People are saying ‘why wouldn’t I have solar and generate my own electricity, or run my car for free’? But not everybody has £15k lying around to do the work.”

Banks’ involvement can also help clean up the retrofit sector because the consumer code makes a lender responsible for how the installers sell their services and for the quality of the work being financed. 

And if you were wondering about the energy needs of families living in flat blocks or social housing, the private sector has an answer for that too. 

Sero, a start-up part-owned by Legal & General, is preparing to fit solar panels and batteries on to 5,000 social housing units in the north London borough of Camden and another location yet to be announced. Chief executive James Williams tells me the £60mn plus investment will come from a combination of government grants and pension fund money, to be recouped over 30 years.

While customers will enjoy lower energy charges thanks to a building’s solar panels and batteries, Sero will be paid a fixed service fee derived from the sale of discounted electricity back to tenants or at higher rates back to the grid. “This model gives investors value long term and means we haven’t got to rely on government grants that will reach only a minority of social housing residents,” says Williams. “Long-term patient capital is the only way to scale clean energy for households but it needs to earn a return, in this case from sharing the savings that clean energy can generate.”

The first — or the last mile? 

Laura Sandys, the former Conservative MP who chairs Sero, argues I’ve got my metaphor the wrong way around: “My point is about the need for culture change in the energy sector — they talk about the last mile as if the customer was the least important, but the customer is the first place the system needs to focus on.”

Smart reads 

With the help of the humble transformer, my visual journalist colleagues vividly illustrate the supply chain bottlenecks slowing electrification.

And this quote in Nic Fildes’ report on Australia’s Chinese storage battery surge made me laugh out loud: ‘Solar ate coal’s lunch and now batteries are eating gas’s dinner.’

A date for your diary

Are you free on September 5? Join me and my brilliant expert panel at the FT Weekend Festival to answer your questions on Everything you need to know before sticking solar panels to your roof and a battery in your broom cupboard. Subscribers to this newsletter are entitled to a 10 per cent discount on both digital and in-person passes.

This newsletter has been amended to correct the name of the installer used by Natalie Barton.

item.title: A new economic order will be built piece by ad hoc piece
item.author: Alan Beattie
item.description: Traditional trade deals will not address geopolitical concerns
item.content:encoded:
Traditional trade deals will not address geopolitical concerns

Alan Beattie

It’s a speech that still reverberates. Six months ago Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney sketched out a vision of a world order with coalitions of middle powers no longer relying on a US anchor. Every government since — not least Canada itself — has been trying to work out what that actually means.

Even before Donald Trump raised geopolitical tensions, governments frequently oversold routine bits of trade policy as having strategic import, and now they’re really at it. When the EU and India agreed a rather shallow trade deal back in January, it supposedly reflected the coming together of two great strategic powers united by a common geoeconomic purpose, and so on. You know the drill.

Now, as it happens, some security agreements were also concluded between the EU and India. But trade agreements are neither necessary nor sufficient for that. The famous Australia-UK-US (Aukus) submarine and technology pact, announced in 2021 to great fanfare, had nothing to do with trade as such.

The instinct of bureaucrats and public international lawyers, who are drawn to overarching systems of rules like wildebeest to a waterhole, is to try to adapt multilateral arrangements like the World Trade Organization or replace them with others. This is an inadequate response for two reasons.

The obvious one is the lack of consensus to get substantive deals through multilateral institutions. Some governments are striving to put a plurilateral agreement on digital and data trade under the aegis of the WTO, for example, defying India, which always blocks such things. But even if they do succeed, it really doesn’t contain strong enough commitments to control or direct the growing thicket of internet regulation.

The more subtle one is that not much in a traditional preferential trade agreement addresses the salient issues of geopoliticised value networks. Preferential agreements are instruments for commercial peacetime based on tariffs, regulations, intellectual property and the like. They don’t work well in a trade war and they haven’t stopped China using a wide range of tools to establish strategic dominance.

To be clear: the vast bulk of actual goods trade is likely to continue unabated, and what trade deals do get through will facilitate that at the margin. But they will not address bottlenecks and vulnerabilities.

The EU, for example, has long been trying to negotiate some kind of docking mechanism with the Asia-Pacific CPTPP group of countries. So far it has essentially only achieved a milk-and-water statement at the meeting of WTO ministers in March. But the highest ambition that’s even vaguely realistic is some harmonisation of rules of origin to allow supply chains to be built more easily between Asia and Europe that bypass China. Even if they got that, so what? The likelihood that this will significantly undercut low-cost Chinese-dominated production networks is very small. And it will do nothing to threaten the leverage that comes from China’s control of certain critical minerals, notably rare earths, and its dominance of strategically important technologies.

For middle powers or anyone else to challenge these sources of influence will require narrower but much deeper bespoke agreements of production, distribution and exchange. This is the gap Carney’s middle-power alliances are supposed to fill. But in reality, many midsized powers — Pakistan, Indonesia, Malaysia, probably Brazil, and many more — are too close to the Chinese economic orbit or too suspicious of advanced-economy governments to form alliances from which they can’t be extracted by threats or inducements by Beijing.

Earlier this week I mentioned the Clean Technology Partnerships Initiative and its plan for the EU to increase production of strategically significant green tech through agreements with other countries. It’s notable that it proposes a range of public-private tools well beyond a traditional trade deal, including procurement agreements, equity stakes and joint ventures. It’s also striking that most proposed partners — Japan, South Korea, Canada, Australia — are like-minded rich democracies already broadly strategically aligned with Europe.

Sceptics of the multilateral ideal would say that this represents less of a rupture from the previous order than it seems. The WTO’s predecessor was largely a like-minded club of advanced economies held together by cold war politics. As soon as the WTO itself was launched in 1995 and started taking developing country concerns seriously, the negotiating system ground to a halt.

To speak of a new order is itself somewhat misleading. In geopolitically sensitive areas there will be no overarching governance or legal framework, just coalitions or bilaterals of convenience with a bias towards politically friendly countries. This may not sound inspirational. It is, however, much more realistic than imagining that taking the knife of a traditional trade agreement to a critical products gunfight will end up in anything but defeat.

alan.beattie@ft.com

item.content:encoded:
From steroids to ‘supersuits’ — when does performance enhancement go too far?

At the Enhanced Games in Las Vegas earlier this year, athletes used performance-enhancing drugs and banned equipment in an attempt to break world records.
